title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
6. Procedure

6.1 Sample Preparation

Use field-moist soil that has been sieved through a 2 mm sieve per SOP-F02
Samples should be stored at 4 C and processed within 48 hours of collection



6.2 Incubation Setup

Weigh approximately 40 g of field-moist soil into a clean incubation jar
Record the exact mass of soil added
Add the specified volume of deionized water according to the Solvita protocol (the rewetting triggers the microbial CO2 burst)
Insert a fresh CO2-sensitive gel paddle into the jar, ensuring the gel faces the soil surface
Seal the jar immediately and securely
Record the jar number, sample ID, and start time



6.3 Incubation

Place sealed jars in the incubator set to 25 C
Incubate undisturbed for 24 hours
Do not open or move jars during incubation



6.4 Reading Results

After exactly 24 hours, remove the gel paddle from the jar
Immediately read the paddle using the Solvita Digital Color Reader
Record the color number and corresponding CO2-C value
Express results as mg CO2-C kg-1 soil







TipTip



Read paddles promptly after removing them from the jar. Prolonged exposure to ambient air will alter the gel color and compromise the reading.




6.5 Cleanup

Dispose of used soil in the designated waste container
Wash incubation jars thoroughly with soap and water; rinse with deionized water
Dispose of used gel paddles in standard trash
crumbs: Soil Respiration -- Solvita CO2 Burst Test

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
7. Quality Control

Run duplicate samples at a rate of 1 per 10 to assess analytical precision
Include a blank jar (empty, sealed with gel paddle) in each batch to check for background CO2
Verify incubator temperature at the start and end of each 24-hour incubation period
Calibrate the Digital Color Reader according to manufacturer instructions before each batch
crumbs: Soil Respiration -- Solvita CO2 Burst Test

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
8. Data Interpretation
The CO2 burst is proportional to microbial biomass and is directly tied to potential carbon and nitrogen mineralization. Typical values for agricultural soils range from approximately 10 to 200+ mg CO2-C kg-1 soil, with higher values indicating greater microbial activity and labile carbon availability.
crumbs: Soil Respiration -- Solvita CO2 Burst Test

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
9. References

Haney, R.L., Brinton, W.F., & Evans, E. (2008). Soil CO2 respiration: comparison of chemical titration, CO2 IRGA analysis and the Solvita gel system. Renewable Agriculture and Food Systems, 23(2), 171–176.
Solvita. (2019). CO2-Burst soil respiration updated protocol. Woods End Laboratories.
crumbs: Soil Respiration -- Solvita CO2 Burst Test

title: Field Safety
text: This SOP covers field-based research activities and class field trips, addressing transportation, weather-based, and biotic hazards. Although we cannot predict all risks and hazards, it is everyone’s responsibility to identify and mitigate potential risks associated with field work.

title: Field Safety
text: This SOP covers field-based research activities and class field trips, addressing transportation, weather-based, and biotic hazards. Although we cannot predict all risks and hazards, it is everyone’s responsibility to identify and mitigate potential risks associated with field work.

title: Field Safety
text:
2. Scope

Applies to: All field-based research activities, class field trips, and off-campus data collection
Does not apply to: Laboratory-only procedures (see relevant Lab SOPs)
Location: All field sites used by the EA Program

title: Field Safety
text:
3. Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




Instructor / PI
Approve field plans, ensure training compliance


Trained Personnel
Follow this SOP, report deviations and hazards


New Students
Complete training and document review before field work



Anyone conducting research in the field is required to have documented training before commencing field work. Learning about risks and taking the precautions described here is the first step to reducing the risks associated with field work. Anyone working in the field should identify potential risks and attempt to mitigate them.

title: Field Safety
text:
4. Safety and Hazards






WarningGeneral Field Hazards



Reducing risks is one of our main priorities. Like many endeavors in life, field work has certain risks. However, we can reduce these risks dramatically by understanding our physical limits and how these can be tested by uncontrolled environmental factors.
We rely on each individual to be mindful of their own limitations and to advocate for themselves and others to reduce risk exposure.



Required Materials

First Aid Kit (kits are located in EA vehicles; see EA vehicle checklist to document their presence)
Cell phone(s)
Walkie-talkies (optional)
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)



Estimated Time
Preparing to go in the field can take a few minutes to several hours of planning and gathering resources. A good rule of thumb is to double the time you think it will take to get ready.

title: Field Safety
text:
5. Transportation Safety

5.1 Vehicle Requirements

Drivers must have valid driver’s licenses and insurance
Drivers using EA vehicles must be approved by the college; forms can be found in the EA Department



5.2 Planning

Identify meet-up and departure times and locations
Designate a driver
All state and local laws must be obeyed



5.3 Responding to Vehicle Emergencies
Refer to the college’s vehicle emergency procedures. Ensure all occupants are safe, call emergency services if needed, and report the incident to the EA Department.

title: Field Safety
text:
6. Weather-Related Hazards

6.1 Heat Exhaustion and Stroke






WarningRisk Factors




Working outside of shade in desert or arid climates, especially during hot times of day
Lack of shade coverage or proper sun protection
Dehydration



Prevention:

Use and reapply sunscreen
Drink plenty of water
Wear hats and other protective clothing

Response:

Hydrate the affected person
Place ice packs on neck, armpits, etc.
If conditions worsen, leave the field and find air-conditioned conditions



6.2 Cold Conditions
Risk factors: Lack of sun, time of year, wind chill
Prevention: Proper layering and clothing; stay hydrated
Response: Eat, evacuate to warmth, get a professional evaluation


6.3 Lightning
Prevention: Check weather forecast; learn to identify cumulonimbus clouds
Response: Assume lightning position and seek shelter immediately; avoid open areas, tall isolated trees, and bodies of water


6.4 Air Quality and Pollution
Working outside when ozone levels or other pollutants are elevated has a detrimental effect on health, particularly for individuals with asthma or other respiratory conditions. Hot, dry days worsen pollution, and nearby forest fires degrade air quality.
Students with any respiratory disease should be cautious and report the condition to their instructor or laboratory supervisor.
Prevention: Check air quality index (AQI) before field work; postpone if AQI is unhealthy
Response: Leave the field if symptoms develop; seek medical attention if needed

title: Field Safety
text:
7. Geological and Environmental Hazards

7.1 Earthquake
Tectonic movement may occur anywhere in California.
Prevention: Be aware of surroundings at all times
Response: Remain low to the ground; stay away from external building frames; avoid sinkholes, gas lines, and utility wires


7.2 Flooding
Risk factors: Proximity to bodies of water, excessive rainfall
Prevention: Check the forecast for rainfall; be aware of surroundings
Response: Find the highest point in the area; do not attempt to cross rushing water


7.3 Altitude Illness (HAPE/HACE)
Risk factors: High altitudes to which students have not had time to acclimate; reduced oxygen
Symptoms: Headache, nausea, irritability
Response: If mild symptoms, acclimate and take it easy; hydrate. If persistent vomiting and severe headache, evacuate to lower altitude immediately.


7.4 Human Debris and Waste
Illegal dumping of waste and leftover construction materials (sharp metallic objects, etc.) bring risk of injury and exposure to long-term illnesses like tetanus.
Prevention: Avoid and report; be aware of surroundings; think before interacting with unusual objects
Response: Students should be aware of their vaccination history and how to proceed if they require a tetanus shot due to injury


7.5 Toxic Waste Exposure
Exposure may occur via ingestion, inhalation, or dermal contact and can be unpredictable.
Prevention: Wear appropriate PPE; avoid contact with unknown substances
Response: Remove from exposure; decontaminate; seek medical attention

title: Field Safety
text:
8. Biotic Hazards
The field is home to a vast diversity of organisms. Being respectful of their environment is crucial to their safety and our own.

8.1 Allergies






Important



All allergies must be recorded in medical files before the start of field work. Researchers with life-threatening allergies must bring their Epi-pen to the field and keep it accessible at all times.


Mild allergic reaction: Administer 25–50 mg of Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
Severe allergic reaction (swelling of face/throat, respiratory distress): Administer 0.3 mg of Epinephrine; may re-administer after 5 minutes. Follow with 25–50 mg of Diphenhydramine and 20–40 mg of Prednisone. Evacuate from field site immediately.


8.2 Biotic Risk Summary









Organism
Habitats
Risks
Prevention and Response




Mosquitos
Near stagnant water
Vectors for disease (e.g., Malaria)
Use mosquito repellent (e.g., DEET products)


Rodents
Debris, dense underbrush, burrow holes
Disease, infection
Do not touch rodents; if bitten, clean and disinfect


Mountain Lions
Native to North/South America; active early and late in the day
Severe injury
Make yourself look larger; do not run; throw rocks or sticks; avoid being alone


Snakes (Rattlesnakes, Cottonmouth)
Various
Snakebite
Walk in open areas; wear heavy boots; listen for rattle; back away slowly; if bitten, seek immediate medical attention


Spiders (Black Widow, Brown Recluse)
Dark sheltered areas
Spider bite, nausea
Wear gloves while working; shake out clothing and bedding; go to hospital if bitten


Bees and Wasps
Various
Swelling, pain, allergic reaction, anaphylactic shock
Avoid disturbing nests; stay calm when pursued; administer epinephrine for severe reactions; take to hospital


Fleas and Ticks
Underbrush, wooded areas
Lyme disease
Tick check after fieldwork; use insect repellent; wear long clothing; suffocate tick with petroleum jelly before removing with tweezers


Poison Oak
Riparian habitats
Itchy rash; red, swollen skin
Learn to identify; apply Tecnu beforehand; wash affected areas with dish soap


Stinging Nettle
Riparian habitats, meadows
Stinging sensation
Learn to identify and avoid; use anti-itch cream if needed

title: Field Safety
text:
9. Other Illness and Injury

9.1 Fractures and Breaks
Stabilize the injured area and avoid movement. Go to the nearest medical facility for further care.


9.2 Injury from Equipment
Handle all equipment with caution. Carefully read operating procedures. Seek help from fellow students or your instructor if you have questions or doubts. Do not use any equipment if you are unsure of how to handle it.


9.3 Chronic Conditions (Epilepsy, Diabetes, Heart Conditions)
Refer to emergency procedures. Report any chronic conditions to your supervisor. Be aware of your surroundings and be prepared to react in an emergency. Know where the first aid kit is and how to get to the nearest medical facility.

title: Field Safety
text:
10. Field Preparation Checklist

10.1 Before Departure

Check weather report and air quality
Read and understand emergency procedures
Know locations of emergency equipment
Be aware of any special medical conditions of team members
Report to supervisor
Identify hospital closest to the field site
Develop a transportation plan with designated driver
Create a safety plan (itinerary, emergency contacts, risk assessment)



10.2 Supply Checklist

Personal protective equipment
Rain gear (if necessary)
No excessively loose clothing; no sandals or open-toed shoes
Additional clothing/gear for environmental conditions (e.g., poison oak areas)
Sunscreen and sun hat (if necessary)
Full water bottle(s)
Rite in the Rain lab notebook and writing utensil
Watch

Cell phone with the following numbers programmed:

Emergency personnel
Lab supervisor and/or instructor
Lab teammates




10.3 On Site

Identify a time to meet up and depart (if splitting up)
Leave no trace: ensure that the environment remains undisturbed
Supervisor ensures that safety procedures are followed
Report any potential field hazards to supervisor

title: Field Safety
text:
11. Emergency Response Procedure

11.1 Responding to a Medical Emergency

Survey the scene
Identify any potential risks that could affect other team members
Do not move the injured person unless necessary
Summon medical help and share the following information:

Suspected type of injury or illness
Location
Type of assistance required

Identify a location for entry if an emergency vehicle is being summoned



11.2 Documenting the Incident

Identify what happened and how the injury or illness occurred
This information will be used to eliminate hazards and prevent future incidents
Report the injury or illness to the lab supervisor

3. Definitions
Probe (Sonde): The entire Manta2 apparatus that includes the five sensors.

text:
9. Pre-Field Preparation

9.1 Charging
Charge the Amphibian 2 portable PC before going into the field. The charger plugs into the round hole on the bottom edge of the Amphibian. Allow several hours or charge overnight.


9.2 Probe Setup for Calibration

Remove the blue storage plug from the probe and cover the plug with a plastic protector
Insert the underwater cable to connect the Amphibian and the Manta2
Turn on the Amphibian by pressing the power button (bottom right corner)
Press the Windows icon (lower left), then select Amp_2_2_6 (or use shortcut button P1)
Once the interface loads, press “Manta2” on the lower left bar and select “Calibrate”



9.3 pH Calibration (Three-Point)

Select “pH units” from the Manta2 calibration menu
Input the value of your first standard (e.g., 7.00) in the unshaded box
Unscrew the blue cap from the larger cap, leaving the clear plastic cup around the sensors in place
Pour a small amount of the first standard into the cup (probe facing upward), cap it, and shake to rinse the sensors. Repeat twice, pouring used standard into a waste beaker each time
Fill the cup with approximately 1 inch of the standard
Wait for the red line on the Amphibian chart to stabilize (flatten), then press “Ok”
When prompted for the second standard, rinse twice with DI water, then twice with the second standard, fill to 1 inch, and repeat
Select the option for three-point calibration and repeat with the third standard
Accept the calibration when the SRF falls within the acceptable range (consult Prof. Los Huertos if uncertain)



9.4 Conductivity Calibration (One-Point)

Rinse the probe twice with DI water to remove any residual pH standard
Tap “Manta2” > “Calibrate” > “spCond mS/cm”
Input 2.765 in the unshaded box
Rinse twice with conductivity standard, then fill the cup to 1 inch
Wait for the red line to stabilize, then press “Ok”
The SRF should be approximately 110–120. If outside this range, recalibrate. If still outside the range after recalibration, contact Prof. Los Huertos







Note



Conductivity standard can be disposed of down the drain. pH standards must go in a waste container.




9.5 Dissolved Oxygen Calibration
Prepare air-saturated water:

Put approximately half a liter of tap water in a liter jar
Shake the jar vigorously for one minute with the lid on
Remove the lid and let the water stand for about five minutes to allow air bubbles to escape

Calibrate HDO %sat:

Rinse the probe twice with DI water
If the circulator is on (check next to “Manta2”), set it to “CircOff”
Tap “Manta2” > “Calibrate” > “HDO %sat”
Input the barometric pressure for your location in mm Hg (find on an online weather station; convert units if needed; round to 3 significant figures)
When prompted to reset HDO to factory settings, select “No”
Fill the calibration cup with aerated water until it covers the sensors by approximately 1 cm
Wait a few minutes for temperature to equilibrate; the reading must be stable for 3 minutes
Press “Ok” to accept. The SRF should be 100. If it differs, redo the calibration. If still not 100, contact Prof. Los Huertos.

Calibrate HDO mg/L:

Immediately after %sat calibration, note the temperature on the snapshot screen
Tap “Manta2” > “Calibrate” > “HDO mg/L”
Use a DO saturation calculator (e.g., waterontheweb.org) to convert %sat to mg/L using the temperature and pressure values
Input the mg/L value as your calibration standard
Wait 20 seconds for the readout to stabilize. If stable, press “Ok”
If the value changes significantly, exit, re-read %sat, and use the new value to recalibrate mg/L

10.1 Connecting and Powering On

Place the weighted protective cap over the sensors
Lower the probe into the water at the measurement point

Annotate the file using the format: Year.Month.Day.Project (e.g., 2026.05.13.StreampH)







TipTip



In flowing water, always measure downstream sites first, then work upstream to avoid disturbing the water at your measurement locations.




10.4 Disconnecting

Remove the probe from the water
Disconnect the underwater cable from the probe
Insert the blue storage plug
Cover the cable end with the plastic protector

title: Shimadzu TOC-L Analyzer with TNM-L and SSM-5000A
text:
This SOP describes the general operation, calibration, maintenance, and shutdown of the Shimadzu TOC-L total organic carbon analyzer and its companion modules: the TNM-L Total Nitrogen Module and the SSM-5000A Solid Sample Module. The TOC-L uses a 680 C combustion catalytic oxidation method, which is one of two principal approaches to TOC analysis (the other being wet chemical oxidation with persulfate); the high-temperature combustion method is preferred for environmental samples because it more completely oxidizes refractory organic matter such as humic substances (Sharp, 1993; Sugimura & Suzuki, 1988).
All instrument control is performed through the LabSolutions TOC software on the dedicated computer.
This SOP covers the instrument itself. For application-specific sample preparation, measurement modes, and calculations, refer to the relevant analytical SOPs:

SOP-L311 Dissolved Organic Carbon in Water (NPOC)
SOP-L407 Total Carbon (Soils) (SSM)
SOP-L409 Microbial Biomass Carbon (CFE extracts)
SOP-L418 Water-Extractable DOC (soil extracts)

title: Shimadzu TOC-L Analyzer with TNM-L and SSM-5000A
text:
4 Definitions

Catalytic combustion: Oxidation of organic carbon in the sample at 680 °C over a platinum catalyst in the presence of oxygen; the standard method used by the Shimadzu TOC-L for liquid samples.
Dissolved organic carbon (DOC): Organic carbon in a water or soil extract sample that passes through a 0.45 µm filter; the NPOC method is the standard approach for DOC measurement.
IC (inorganic carbon): Carbon present as carbonate, bicarbonate, and dissolved CO2; removed by acidification and sparging before NPOC measurement.
NDIR detector (non-dispersive infrared detector): A detector that measures CO2 concentration by its absorption of infrared light at ~4.3 µm; the detection element in the Shimadzu TOC-L.
NPOC (non-purgeable organic carbon): The organic carbon fraction remaining in a sample after acidification and sparging to remove inorganic carbon and purgeable volatile organic carbon; the operationally defined DOC measured by the Shimadzu TOC-L.
SSM-5000A: The Shimadzu Solid Sample Module that combusts dried, ground solid materials (soils, sediments, plant tissue) directly in ceramic boats at up to 900 °C for total carbon analysis.
TC (total carbon): The sum of all carbon forms (organic and inorganic) in a sample; measured by direct combustion without acidification.
TOC (total organic carbon): TC minus IC; in practice, usually determined as NPOC for environmental samples.
TON (total organic nitrogen): Total nitrogen minus inorganic nitrogen; measured simultaneously by the TNM-L module using chemiluminescence detection of NO produced during combustion.

title: Shimadzu TOC-L Analyzer with TNM-L and SSM-5000A
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Thermal: The combustion furnace operates at 680 C in liquid analysis mode and up to 900 C in SSM mode. Ceramic boats, combustion tubes, and furnace surfaces can cause severe burns.
Chemical: Hydrochloric acid (2 M HCl) is used for acidification and inorganic carbon sparging. Phosphoric acid (25%) is used as the IC reagent. Avoid skin and eye contact with both.
Compressed gas: The instrument requires high-purity carrier gas (air or oxygen) supplied from a pressurized cylinder at approximately 200 kPa. Follow all compressed gas safety procedures (National Research Council, 2011).
Electrical: The instrument operates on high-voltage mains power. Do not open instrument panels or attempt internal repairs.
Ozone: The TNM-L chemiluminescence detector uses an ozone generator. The instrument vents ozone through an internal decomposer, but ensure that the exhaust line is connected and unobstructed. If an ozone odor is detected, shut down the TNM-L and ventilate the area.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves (when handling acid, standards, or samples)
Heat-resistant gloves (when handling ceramic boats from the SSM)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For acid splashes, flush the affected area with water for at least 15 minutes. For burns from hot surfaces, apply cool running water and seek first aid. If ozone is detected, shut down the TNM-L, open windows, and leave the room until the odor dissipates. Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety and SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.

title: Shimadzu TOC-L Analyzer with TNM-L and SSM-5000A
text:
6 Instrument Description

6.1 System Overview
The Shimadzu TOC-L is a combustion catalytic oxidation analyzer that quantifies carbon (and, with the TNM-L, nitrogen) in liquid samples (Shimadzu Corporation, 2019b). The system in the EA Program laboratory consists of four main components:

TOC-L analyzer: Combusts liquid samples at 680 C over a platinum catalyst. The resulting CO2 is measured by a non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) detector. The analyzer supports multiple measurement modes (TC, IC, TOC, NPOC, POC).
TNM-L Total Nitrogen Module: Measures total nitrogen (TN) simultaneously with carbon analysis. Nitrogen compounds in the combustion gas are converted to nitric oxide (NO), which is detected by a chemiluminescence detector after reaction with ozone (Shimadzu Corporation, 2019a). The TNM-L operates in parallel with the NDIR carbon detector, so carbon and nitrogen data are acquired from the same injection.
SSM-5000A Solid Sample Module: Accepts solid samples in ceramic boats for direct combustion at up to 900 C. Connects to the TOC-L for CO2 detection. The TNM-L is not used during SSM operation.
ASI-L Autosampler: Holds up to 93 sample vials (8 mL or 40 mL) for unattended sequential analysis of liquid samples. Includes an automated rinse function between injections.



6.2 Measurement Modes (Liquid Samples)








Mode
Full Name
What It Measures




TC
Total Carbon
All carbon (organic + inorganic) by direct combustion


IC
Inorganic Carbon
Carbonate/bicarbonate carbon by acidification and sparging only


TOC
Total Organic Carbon (by difference)
TOC = TC - IC; requires two sequential measurements


NPOC
Non-Purgeable Organic Carbon
Sample is acidified and sparged to remove IC, then combusted; the most common mode for routine analysis (APHA et al., 2012, Section 5310B)


POC
Purgeable Organic Carbon
Volatile organic carbon recovered during the sparging step; POC = TC - (NPOC + IC)


TN
Total Nitrogen (TNM-L)
All nitrogen species measured simultaneously with any carbon mode





6.3 Detection Principles
The TOC-L and TNM-L rely on two detectors operating in series on the same combustion gas stream:

NDIR detector (carbon): Infrared absorption by CO2 is proportional to the mass of carbon injected. The detector is selective for CO2 and insensitive to other combustion gases.
Chemiluminescence detector (nitrogen, TNM-L only): NO in the combustion gas reacts with ozone (O3) to produce excited NO2*, which emits light as it returns to the ground state. The emitted light intensity is proportional to the mass of nitrogen injected (Walsh, 1989).

text:
8 Procedure






ImportantComputer Control Only



All operations described below are performed through LabSolutions TOC. Do not adjust furnace temperature, gas flow, or other parameters using the instrument front panel unless directed by the instrument manager during troubleshooting.



8.1 Instrument Startup (Cold Start)
A cold start applies when the instrument has been fully powered down (furnace off, gas closed). Allow approximately 60 minutes from power-on to running samples.

Open the carrier gas cylinder valve. Verify the regulator output pressure is set to 200 kPa at the instrument inlet. Check for leaks at all fittings (listen for hissing; apply leak-detection solution if uncertain).
Verify that the exhaust line from the TNM-L ozone decomposer is connected and routed to the fume hood or building exhaust
Check consumable levels:

IC reagent bottle (25% phosphoric acid): refill if below the minimum line
Dehumidifier / moisture trap: drain if water is visible
Rinse water reservoir on the ASI-L: fill with fresh deionized water

Power on the TOC-L main unit using the switch on the right side panel
If the TNM-L is needed, power on the TNM-L using the switch on its rear panel
Power on the ASI-L autosampler
Turn on the dedicated computer and launch LabSolutions TOC
In LabSolutions TOC, verify that communication with all modules is established. The status bar should show “Warming Up”
Wait for the furnace to reach 680 C (approximately 20–30 minutes). The software status changes from “Warming Up” to “Ready”
Wait for the TNM-L ozone generator and chemiluminescence detector to stabilize (approximately 30–45 minutes after power-on; the TNM-L status indicator changes to “Ready”)
Run 3–5 injections of deionized water as system conditioning blanks to flush the injection port, syringe, and combustion tube. Discard these results.
Run 3 additional deionized water blanks and verify baseline stability: TC blank values should be below 0.1 mg/L C; TN blank values should be below 0.1 mg/L N



8.2 Instrument Startup (From Standby/Sleep)
When the instrument is in standby mode (furnace at temperature, gas flowing, software idle), startup is faster:

Launch LabSolutions TOC if not already open
Verify that the status bar shows “Ready” for the TOC-L and (if applicable) the TNM-L
Check the IC reagent level and drain the moisture trap
Fill the ASI-L rinse reservoir with fresh deionized water
Run 3 deionized water conditioning blanks. If blanks are below 0.1 mg/L C and 0.1 mg/L N, proceed to calibration.



8.3 Standby and Sleep Modes
Choose the appropriate idle mode based on how soon the instrument will be used again:










Mode
Furnace
Carrier Gas
TNM-L
When to Use




Active standby
680 C (on)
Flowing
On
Next run within 24 hours


Reduced standby
680 C (on)
Flowing

Off (cooling)

8.3.1 Entering Active Standby

After the final sample, run 3–5 deionized water blanks to flush the system
Leave the furnace at 680 C and the carrier gas flowing
Leave the TNM-L powered on
Empty the autosampler rack and cover with a dust cover
The instrument manager may set the software to a low carrier gas flow rate overnight to conserve gas (consult the manual for the minimum flow that maintains a positive purge of the combustion tube)



8.3.2 Entering Reduced Standby

Flush the system with deionized water blanks as above
Power off the TNM-L (rear panel switch). This extends the ozone decomposer lifetime.
Leave the TOC-L furnace at 680 C and gas flowing
Cover the autosampler



8.3.3 Entering Sleep Mode

Flush the system with deionized water blanks
Power off the TNM-L
In LabSolutions TOC, initiate a furnace cooldown (or simply power off the TOC-L)
Once the furnace temperature drops below 200 C (approximately 90 minutes), close the carrier gas cylinder valve
Power off the ASI-L
Close LabSolutions TOC and shut down the computer



8.3.4 Full Shutdown
Follow the Sleep Mode steps, then:

Allow the furnace to cool to room temperature
Disconnect the carrier gas line if the instrument will be moved or serviced
Empty the IC reagent bottle if the shutdown will exceed 30 days (phosphoric acid can corrode the reagent lines over long idle periods)
Empty the ASI-L rinse reservoir to prevent microbial growth
Cover the instrument with a dust cover




8.4 Software Navigation
LabSolutions TOC organizes work into the following areas:

Instrument Monitor: Real-time display of furnace temperature, carrier gas flow, detector signal (NDIR and chemiluminescence), and system status
Method Editor: Define measurement mode (TC, IC, NPOC, TN, etc.), injection volume, number of replicate injections, sparge time (for NPOC), acidification volume, and calibration curve parameters
Sample Table: Enter sample IDs, vial positions, dilution factors, and measurement method for each sample
Calibration: Build, view, and edit calibration curves. The software fits curves by least-squares regression and reports r2 and residuals.
Data Browser: Review completed runs, view peak integrations, export results to CSV, and reprocess data



8.5 Calibration
Calibrate at the start of each analytical session or whenever the method, measurement mode, or concentration range changes. Carbon and nitrogen calibrations are built independently but can be run simultaneously if both detectors are active.

8.5.1 Carbon Calibration

Prepare a multi-point calibration series from KHP dissolved in deionized water. Choose concentrations that bracket the expected sample range (e.g., 0, 1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 mg/L C). Prepare fresh daily or from a refrigerated stock per SOP-L020 (APHA et al., 2012).
For IC calibration, prepare standards from sodium bicarbonate/sodium carbonate in deionized water
In LabSolutions TOC, open the Method Editor and select the measurement mode (e.g., NPOC, TC, or TC-IC)
Enter calibration standard concentrations in the Calibration window
Load standards into the autosampler in order of increasing concentration
Run the calibration sequence. The software will perform replicate injections (typically 3) of each standard and fit a regression
Verify that r2 \(\geq\) 0.999 and that each standard back- calculates to within 10% of its nominal value (15% at the lowest standard is acceptable)
Save the calibration curve



8.5.2 Nitrogen Calibration (TNM-L)

Prepare a multi-point calibration series from KNO3 dissolved in deionized water (e.g., 0, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 25, 50 mg/L N)
In the Method Editor, confirm that TN measurement is enabled alongside the carbon mode
Enter TN calibration concentrations in the Calibration window
The TN calibration runs simultaneously with the carbon calibration if both are loaded in the same sample table; otherwise, run the TN standards as a separate sequence
Verify that r2 \(\geq\) 0.999 for the nitrogen curve
Save the calibration curve




8.6 Setting Up an Analytical Run (Liquid Samples)

In the Method Editor, confirm the measurement mode, injection volume, number of replicate injections, and (for NPOC mode) sparge time and acid volume
In the Sample Table, enter the run sequence:

Calibration verification standard (mid-range) as the first sample
Instrument blanks (deionized water) at the beginning, every 10–15 samples, and the end of the run
Method blanks appropriate to the application (e.g., 0.5 M K2SO4 for soil extracts; consult the analytical method SOP)
Sample vials in the order they are loaded in the autosampler
A final calibration verification standard

Set the dilution factor for each sample if applicable
Verify that autosampler vial positions in the Sample Table match the physical rack positions
Confirm that the rinse reservoir on the autosampler is filled with deionized water
Click Start to begin the sequence







TipReplicate Injection Settings



The software default is 3 replicate injections per sample. If the coefficient of variation (CV) among replicates exceeds 2%, the software can be configured to add up to 2 additional injections automatically (set in Method Editor under “Maximum Injections”). The outlier replicate is excluded from the reported mean.




8.7 Setting Up a Solid Sample Run (SSM-5000A)

In LabSolutions TOC, switch to SSM mode
Pre-combust ceramic boats at 900 C in a muffle furnace (SOP-L111) to remove residual carbon. Allow boats to cool in a desiccator.
Weigh the solid sample into a clean ceramic boat. Record the mass to 0.01 mg.
In the Sample Table, enter the sample ID, boat number, and sample mass
Place the ceramic boat on the SSM sample port and push it into the furnace when prompted by the software
The SSM combusts the sample; evolved CO2 flows to the TOC-L NDIR detector
The software reports carbon content in mg C or as a percentage of sample mass







NoteTNM-L and SSM



The TNM-L chemiluminescence detector is not used during SSM solid sample analysis. Total nitrogen in solid samples requires a separate instrument (e.g., the Flash EA; see SOP-L208).




8.8 Monitoring a Run in Progress

Use the Instrument Monitor to watch real-time peak shapes and detector baselines
If a peak appears saturated (flat top), the sample exceeds the calibration range. Pause the run, dilute the sample, and re-queue.
If the CV among replicate injections exceeds 2%, investigate (air bubble, particulates, insufficient sample volume) and consider re-running.
If the system blank rises above 0.5 mg/L C or 0.5 mg/L N during a run, the combustion tube or catalyst may need replacement. Complete the current run, note affected samples, and consult Section 9.



8.9 Data Export

After the run, open the Data Browser and review all results
Check that calibration verification standards recovered within 90–110% of their nominal values
Export results to CSV: File > Export, including sample ID, mode, mean concentration, SD, CV, and number of valid injections
Save the LabSolutions TOC run file (.toc) to the instrument computer and back up to the lab network drive
Record the run date, analyst, method, and file name in the instrument logbook

title: Shimadzu TOC-L Analyzer with TNM-L and SSM-5000A
text:
9 Quality Control
QC procedures are tailored to each analytical method and are specified in the relevant method SOP. The following instrument-level QC applies to all runs (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2009):

System blanks (deionized water) at the start of every session must read below 0.1 mg/L C and 0.1 mg/L N
A calibration verification standard (mid-range) must be run at the beginning and end of every sample sequence, with recovery within 90–110%
Replicate injection CV must be below 2% for liquid samples
All QC results are recorded in the instrument logbook and in the exported data file
For additional QC requirements (method blanks, duplicates, matrix spikes, continuing calibration verification frequency), refer to SOP-L802 Quality Control

text:
10 Maintenance

10.1 Routine Maintenance Schedule








Task
Frequency
Notes




System blank check
Before each analytical session



Drain moisture trap / dehumidifier
Weekly (more often in humid conditions)
Prevents water from reaching the NDIR detector


Check IC reagent level
Weekly
Refill with fresh 25% H3PO4 when below the minimum line


Inspect injection syringe needle
Weekly
Replace if bent, corroded, or clogged


Check autosampler rinse reservoir
Before each session
Refill with fresh DI water


Inspect combustion tube
Monthly or every 500 injections
Look for discoloration, cracks, or catalyst settling


Replace TC catalyst
Every 3,000–5,000 injections or when blanks rise
Pt on alumina; record replacement date


Replace halogen scrubber
Every 6–12 months
Prevents halide damage to the NDIR detector


Replace TNM-L ozone decomposer
Annually
Degraded decomposer leaks ozone into the room


Replace SSM combustion tube
As needed
Inspect after each batch of solids


Carrier gas cylinder replacement
As needed
Monitor regulator pressure; order when below 500 psi


Software and firmware updates
As released by Shimadzu
Coordinate with instrument manager





10.2 Catalyst Replacement Procedure

Allow the furnace to cool to room temperature (power off the TOC-L and wait at least 3 hours, or use the forced-air cooling function if available)
Wearing heat-resistant gloves and safety glasses, remove the combustion tube from the furnace per the manufacturer’s procedure
Dispose of the spent catalyst (Pt on alumina) as hazardous waste (precious metal content; collect for EH&S pickup per SOP-L006)
Fill the combustion tube with fresh catalyst to the manufacturer’s specified depth (approximately 12 cm)
Add a thin layer of quartz wool above and below the catalyst bed
Reinstall the combustion tube. Reconnect all tubing and fittings.
Restart the furnace and allow it to reach 680 C
Run 20–30 deionized water conditioning injections to stabilize the new catalyst. Blanks should decrease progressively to below 0.1 mg/L C.
Run a calibration verification standard to confirm sensitivity before resuming sample analysis
Record the replacement date, catalyst lot number, and conditioning results in the instrument logbook



10.3 Combustion Tube Inspection and Replacement

Remove the combustion tube as described in Section 9.2, step 2
Inspect for cracks, discoloration, or accumulation of non-volatile residue on the inner walls
If the tube is damaged, replace with a new quartz combustion tube
Repack with catalyst and condition as in Section 9.2



10.4 Syringe and Needle Maintenance

Remove the syringe from the autosampler or manual injection port
Inspect the needle for bends, burrs, or corrosion
Flush the syringe barrel with deionized water, then with dilute HCl (0.1 M), then with deionized water again
If the syringe plunger binds or the needle is damaged, replace the entire syringe assembly
Reinstall and run 3 deionized water blanks to verify proper function

title: eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation
text: This SOP describes field procedures for collecting, filtering, and preserving environmental DNA (eDNA) samples from surface waters. eDNA consists of DNA shed into the environment by organisms through skin cells, mucus, feces, gametes, and decomposing tissue. Detecting eDNA in water samples allows non-invasive detection of aquatic species (fish, amphibians, invertebrates, pathogens) without direct observation or capture (Goldberg et al., 2016). Because eDNA is present at extremely low concentrations, preventing contamination during field collection is critical. This SOP covers the field side of the workflow; laboratory processing (filtration, extraction, inhibition testing) is covered in SOP-L700 DNA Extraction.

title: eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation
text: This SOP describes field procedures for collecting, filtering, and preserving environmental DNA (eDNA) samples from surface waters. eDNA consists of DNA shed into the environment by organisms through skin cells, mucus, feces, gametes, and decomposing tissue. Detecting eDNA in water samples allows non-invasive detection of aquatic species (fish, amphibians, invertebrates, pathogens) without direct observation or capture (Goldberg et al., 2016). Because eDNA is present at extremely low concentrations, preventing contamination during field collection is critical. This SOP covers the field side of the workflow; laboratory processing (filtration, extraction, inhibition testing) is covered in SOP-L700 DNA Extraction.

title: eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Collection and preservation of water samples for eDNA analysis at all EA Program surface water sites (streams, lakes, ponds, wetlands, stormwater basins)
Does not apply to: Soil eDNA or soil microbial sampling (see SOP-F701); tissue biopsy or organism capture for DNA; airborne eDNA sampling; lab-side filtration, extraction, and molecular analysis
Location: All EA Program surface water field sites

title: eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility

before participating in eDNA sampling

title: eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation
text:
4 Definitions

Contamination (eDNA): The introduction of exogenous DNA from sources other than the target organism into a sample or filter; the single largest source of false positives in eDNA surveys; prevented by sterile technique, glove changes between samples, and decontamination of reusable equipment (Goldberg et al., 2016).
eDNA (environmental DNA): Genetic material shed into the environment by organisms through mucus, feces, gametes, skin cells, and other biological material; collected from water without direct capture of the target organism; detectable at extremely low concentrations using PCR-based methods (Goldberg et al., 2016).
Equipment blank: A control sample consisting of deionized water rinsed through decontaminated reusable equipment (e.g., a pump) and collected as a sample; detects carry-over contamination between sites when dedicated equipment is not used.
Field blank: A sterile bottle of molecular-grade deionized water opened and handled at the field site under identical conditions to real samples; filtered and preserved like a field sample; detects airborne or handling contamination during field work; must yield no target amplification (Goldberg et al., 2016).
Filter pore size: The nominal diameter of pores in the filter membrane; 0.45 µm is the standard for eDNA capture from surface water, retaining bacteria, cells, and particulate-bound DNA.
Longmire’s buffer: A non-freezing preservation solution (containing EDTA, Tris, NaCl, SDS, and sucrose) used to preserve eDNA on filters in the field when immediate freezing is not possible; inactivates nucleases and inhibits microbial degradation (Renshaw et al., 2015).
Open-channel filtration: A filtration method using a funnel and vacuum pump or syringe; the filter membrane is exposed to the environment during collection, increasing contamination risk compared to closed-capsule methods.
PCR inhibitor: A substance co-extracted with eDNA that suppresses PCR amplification efficiency; common in natural water samples (humic acids, tannins, metal ions); detected by running a dilution series of the extract and checking for concentration-dependent amplification; managed by diluting the extract or using commercial inhibitor removal kits.
Sterivex filter: A commercially available enclosed 0.22 µm polysulfone cartridge filter; preferred for eDNA because the sealed design minimizes contamination, allows direct addition of preservation buffer, and is compatible with standard extraction kits (Renshaw et al., 2015).
Target species detection: The determination of presence or absence of a specific taxon in a water sample based on amplification of taxon-specific eDNA; sensitivity depends on eDNA shedding rate, water volume filtered, PCR method, and inhibitor load in the extract (Goldberg et al., 2016).
Volume filtered: The total volume of water passed through a filter during sample collection; a required reporting variable for calculating eDNA concentration; record for every filter regardless of whether filtration was complete or the filter clogged (Goldberg et al., 2016).

title: eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Wading and sampling near water carry slip, fall, and drowning hazards. Work in pairs.
Chemical: DNA preservatives (ethanol, Longmire’s buffer) are flammable (ethanol) or contain EDTA and SDS (Longmire’s). Handle with gloves.
Biological: Water may contain pathogens. Wear gloves and avoid ingestion.




5.1 Required PPE

Nitrile gloves (change between every sample)
Safety glasses
Wading boots or waders (if entering the water)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.

title: eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Field Preparation

Prepare all equipment in the lab using UV-decontaminated surfaces and dedicated pre-PCR equipment.
Pre-label all bottles and filters with project ID, site, replicate number, date.
Pack a cooler with ice packs or dry ice.
Include at least one sterile bottle of molecular-grade DI water per sampling event for field blanks.



7.2 Water Collection

Put on fresh nitrile gloves.
Open the sterile bottle only when ready to collect.
Submerge the bottle to 10–20 cm below the water surface, facing upstream, away from your body (Goldberg et al., 2016).
Fill to 1 L and cap immediately.
For composite samples: collect 250 mL from each of 4 microhabitats and combine in one bottle.
Record the GPS coordinates, collection time, and site conditions.



7.3 Field Filtration (If Filtering On-Site)
Sterivex capsule method:

Attach a sterile 60 mL syringe to the Sterivex filter inlet.
Draw water from the sample bottle and push through the filter. Repeat until the filter clogs or 1 L has been filtered. Record the total volume filtered.
Expel remaining water from the capsule.
Add 1–2 mL of Longmire’s buffer or fill with molecular-grade ethanol using a syringe (Renshaw et al., 2015). Cap both ends of the Sterivex.
Label the capsule and place in a ziplock bag on ice.

Open filter funnel method:

Pour the sample through a sterile 0.45 µm PES filter unit.
Use sterile forceps to fold the filter membrane in half (sample side inward) and place in a labeled cryovial.
Add preservative (ethanol or Longmire’s buffer) to cover the filter. Seal.
Place on ice immediately.



7.4 If Not Filtering On-Site
Keep whole-water samples on ice (4 °C) and filter in the lab within 6 hours of collection. Exceeding 6 hours significantly increases DNA degradation (Goldberg et al., 2016).


7.5 Field Blanks and Controls

Field blank: Open the sterile DI water bottle at one site per event, filter it using the same method as field samples, and preserve. This blank detects contamination during field handling.
Equipment blank: If any reusable equipment contacts the sample, collect a deionized water rinse blank after decontamination.
Process blanks through the entire lab workflow alongside samples.



7.6 Decontamination Between Sites

Spray or soak all reusable equipment with 10% bleach solution for at least 1 minute.
Rinse with clean water.
Change gloves.
Single-use items (bottles, filters, syringes) are discarded after each sample.

See SOP-F007 for general decontamination procedures.

title: eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation
text:
8 Sample Transport and Storage

Keep all samples and preserved filters on ice (4 °C) during transport.
Deliver to the lab the same day. If overnight storage is unavoidable, store at -20 °C.
For long-term storage (> 1 week before extraction), store preserved filters at -20 °C or -80 °C.
Complete the chain of custody form per SOP-F008.

title: eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation
text:
9 Quality Control

Minimum 1 field blank per sampling event; 1 equipment blank if reusable equipment is used.
Collect 3 replicate samples per site unless the study design specifies otherwise.
Record the total volume filtered for each sample.
Any field blank positive for target DNA invalidates samples from that event unless below a pre-established threshold. Consult the PI.
Log all glove changes, bottle openings, and deviations in the field notebook.

title: Camera Trap Deployment and AI-Assisted Image Analysis
text:
This procedure describes the deployment, retrieval, data management, and AI-assisted image analysis of camera traps (motion-triggered wildlife cameras) used in the EA Program. Camera traps provide a non-invasive method for documenting wildlife presence, activity patterns, and species richness at field sites (Thornton et al., 2026). The volume of images produced by even a small number of cameras (thousands to tens of thousands per deployment) makes manual review a major bottleneck. This SOP integrates open-source and cloud-based AI tools to automate blank-image filtering and species identification, reducing processing time by an order of magnitude while maintaining scientific rigor through human-in-the-loop verification (Beery et al., 2019; Wildlife Insights, 2026).
The EA Program currently uses the CamPark T20 trail camera, but the deployment and analysis procedures are applicable to other camera trap models with minor adaptations.

title: Camera Trap Deployment and AI-Assisted Image Analysis
text:
This procedure describes the deployment, retrieval, data management, and AI-assisted image analysis of camera traps (motion-triggered wildlife cameras) used in the EA Program. Camera traps provide a non-invasive method for documenting wildlife presence, activity patterns, and species richness at field sites (Thornton et al., 2026). The volume of images produced by even a small number of cameras (thousands to tens of thousands per deployment) makes manual review a major bottleneck. This SOP integrates open-source and cloud-based AI tools to automate blank-image filtering and species identification, reducing processing time by an order of magnitude while maintaining scientific rigor through human-in-the-loop verification (Beery et al., 2019; Wildlife Insights, 2026).
The EA Program currently uses the CamPark T20 trail camera, but the deployment and analysis procedures are applicable to other camera trap models with minor adaptations.

title: Camera Trap Deployment and AI-Assisted Image Analysis
text:
4 Definitions

AI confidence score: A numerical value (0–1 or 0–100%) output by a classification model indicating the model’s certainty in its predicted species identification; predictions below 90% confidence must be manually verified in the EA Program workflow (Beery et al., 2019).
Blank image: A camera trap image with no animal, person, or vehicle visible, typically triggered by vegetation movement or lighting changes; MegaDetector removes these automatically, eliminating the largest portion of review burden.
CamPark T20: The EA Program’s primary trail camera; a 16 MP passive infrared (PIR) triggered camera with infrared night flash; detection range approximately 20 m; 8 AA batteries per deployment (CamPark, 2023).
Detection rate: The number of independent detections of a species per 100 camera-trap-nights; the standard metric for comparing wildlife activity across sites or seasons; depends on both actual animal abundance and camera placement (O’Brien et al., 2010).
Human-in-the-loop verification: A quality control protocol in which a human reviewer examines AI predictions, particularly low-confidence ones, to correct errors before results are used for analysis; essential because AI models fail on rare species, unusual poses, and taxa underrepresented in training data (Thornton et al., 2026).
Independent detection event: A single occurrence of a species at a camera during a defined time window (typically 30 minutes); used to prevent over-counting multiple images of the same individual; defined a priori and reported with any analysis (O’Brien et al., 2010).
MegaDetector: An open-source object detection model (Microsoft/Google) that classifies each camera trap image as containing an animal, a human, a vehicle, or being blank; runs as a pre-processing step before species classification; the current version is MegaDetector v5 (Beery et al., 2019).
PIR (passive infrared) sensor: The motion and heat detection sensor in a trail camera; triggers image capture when it detects a warm moving object within the detection zone; sensitivity and detection range vary with temperature, wind, and vegetation.
SpeciesNet: A deep-learning species classification model developed by Google; trained on over 65 million labeled camera trap images from more than 2,000 species and blank categories; used in both the Wildlife Insights platform and the local CameraTrapAI pipeline (Google Research, 2026; Wildlife Insights, 2026).
Trap night (camera trap night): One camera deployed at one location for one 24-hour period; the standard unit of sampling effort; total trap nights = number of cameras × number of days deployed (O’Brien et al., 2010).
Wildlife Insights: A free cloud-based platform for camera trap data management and AI classification, developed by Google, WWF, Conservation International, the Wildlife Conservation Society, and the Smithsonian (Wildlife Insights, 2026).

7 Procedure – Field Deployment

7.1 Camera Setup

Install 8 AA batteries and insert a formatted SD card (CamPark, 2023).
Power on and enter the settings menu. Configure:









Setting
Recommended Value
Notes




Photo resolution
16 MP
Highest available


Trigger mode
Photo (burst × 3)
Burst increases detection probability


Trigger interval
5 seconds
Balance captures and battery


Time stamp
ON
Required for activity analysis


Date/time
Current local time
Verify at each deployment




Take a test photo to verify function and timestamp.



7.2 Site Selection and Mounting

Select a location based on study objectives (game trails, water sources, habitat edges, or systematic grid points).
Record GPS coordinates and camera bearing (compass direction camera faces) (O’Brien et al., 2010).
Clear vegetation within the detection zone (approximately 20 m cone in front of the lens) to reduce false triggers.
Mount at 30–50 cm above ground for small-to-medium mammals, or 75–100 cm for larger species; angle slightly downward (5–10°).
Secure with mounting strap. Apply a cable lock if at a public site.
Walk through the detection zone to verify the trigger functions.
Record deployment metadata on the field data sheet (Appendix A).



7.3 Retrieval and Redeployment

Power off before removing the SD card.
Replace with a fresh, formatted card; check battery level; replace batteries if below 50%.
Power on, verify settings, and take a test photo.
Record retrieval date, time, and observations on the field data sheet.

title: Camera Trap Deployment and AI-Assisted Image Analysis
section: 8 Procedure – Data Management and AI Analysis
text:
8 Procedure – Data Management and AI Analysis

8.1 Image Download and Organization

Create a folder: CamTrap_SiteID_CameraID_YYYYMMDD-YYYYMMDD.
Copy all images from the SD card.
Back up immediately to external hard drive or cloud storage.
Do not delete images from the SD card until the backup is verified.



8.2 AI-Assisted Analysis Pipeline
The EA Program uses a two-stage AI pipeline following the approach used by Wildlife Insights and the Google CameraTrapAI project (Google Research, 2026; Wildlife Insights, 2026):
Stage 1: Detection (MegaDetector). Identifies whether each image contains an animal, human, vehicle, or is blank; eliminates 50–90% of false-trigger images (Beery et al., 2019).
Stage 2: Classification (SpeciesNet or similar). Identifies detected animals to the lowest possible taxonomic level, trained on over 65 million labeled camera trap images.
Option A: Wildlife Insights (cloud-based). Upload images to wildlifeinsights.org, which runs both stages automatically (Wildlife Insights, 2026). Review AI predictions and export verified data as CSV.
Option B: Local pipeline (Python). For offline or large-volume processing, use the open-source CameraTrapAI package from github.com/google/cameratrapai (Beery et al., 2019; Google Research, 2026).


8.3 Human Verification

Sort AI output by confidence score (ascending).
Manually verify all predictions below 90% confidence (Thornton et al., 2026).
Spot-check a random 10% of predictions above 90% confidence.
Correct misclassifications and record reviewer name, date, and total corrections.



8.4 Data Analysis in R


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(camtrapR)   # Niedballa et al. 2016

detections <- read_csv("classifications_verified.csv") %>%
  mutate(datetime = ymd_hms(timestamp),
         date = as_date(datetime),
         hour = hour(datetime))

# Independent events (30-min threshold)
independent <- detections %>%
  filter(category == "animal") %>%
  arrange(camera_id, species, datetime) %>%
  group_by(camera_id, species) %>%
  mutate(
    time_diff_min = as.numeric(difftime(datetime, lag(datetime),
                                         units = "mins")),
    independent = is.na(time_diff_min) | time_diff_min >= 30
  ) %>%
  filter(independent) %>%
  ungroup()

# Trap-nights per camera
trap_nights <- detections %>%
  distinct(camera_id, date) %>%
  count(camera_id, name = "trap_nights")

# Detection rate (events per 100 trap-nights)
det_rate <- independent %>%
  count(camera_id, species) %>%
  left_join(trap_nights, by = "camera_id") %>%
  mutate(rate_per_100tn = (n / trap_nights) * 100)

print(det_rate)


(Niedballa et al., 2016)

text: This SOP describes standardized methods for surveying pollinator communities at EA Program field sites using timed visual observations and passive pan traps. Pollinator surveys document the diversity and relative abundance of bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, and other flower-visiting insects, providing data for assessing habitat quality, restoration success, and the effects of land use on pollination services (Lebuhn & Fenter, 2013; Potts et al., 2010).

title: Pollinator Observation Surveys
text:
4 Definitions

Diel activity pattern: The temporal distribution of an organism’s activity across a 24-hour period; most bee species are diurnal with peak activity between 09:00 and 15:00 under sunny, warm conditions; surveys outside peak activity hours systematically underestimate community richness (Lebuhn & Fenter, 2013).
Floral density: The number of open flowers per unit area at a survey location; a key covariate for pollinator abundance because visitation scales with resource availability; estimated visually as flowers per m2 or as qualitative categories (low, medium, high) at each survey event.
Focal flower observation: A survey method in which a single flowering plant or patch is observed for a fixed duration (typically 10 minutes) and all pollinators visiting any flower during that period are recorded; useful for comparing visitation rates between plant species or treatments (Westphal et al., 2008).
Functional group: A coarse taxon category used when species-level identification is not possible in the field; the EA Program uses 10 groups: honey bee (HB), bumble bee (BB), small native bee (SB), large native bee (LB), butterfly (BF), syrphid fly (SF), other fly (OF), beetle (BT), wasp (WA), and other (OT).
Independent detection event: A single detection of a pollinator at a flower, counted only once per survey period regardless of how long the individual remains; used to standardize counts across surveys of different duration.
Pan trap: A colored bowl (white, fluorescent yellow, fluorescent blue) filled with soapy water; passively captures flying insects attracted by color resemblance to flowers; effective for small- to medium-sized bees but under-represents large-bodied bees and butterflies (Lebuhn & Fenter, 2013; Westphal et al., 2008).
Pollinator: Any animal that moves pollen from the anther to the stigma of a flower, facilitating plant reproduction; includes bees, flies, butterflies and moths, beetles, and hummingbirds; bees are the dominant pollinators at most EA Program field sites (Potts et al., 2010).
Pollination service: An ecosystem service provided by flower-visiting animals; essential for reproduction of approximately 75% of flowering plant species and 35% of global food crop production (Potts et al., 2010).
Timed observation transect: A standardized survey in which the observer walks a fixed route (typically 50 m x 2 m) at a standardized pace (approximately 10 m per minute) and records all pollinators observed on flowers within the survey corridor; produces a count-based estimate of relative pollinator activity (Dicks et al., 2016; Lebuhn & Fenter, 2013).
Voucher specimen: A preserved insect specimen deposited in a reference collection to document the occurrence of a species at a site; required for any first records and difficult identifications; pinned through the right mesopleuron following standard entomological practice.

title: Pollinator Observation Surveys
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Biological: Bee and wasp stings are the primary hazard. Personnel with known Hymenoptera allergies must carry a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) and inform the field lead before every outing. Africanized honey bees may be present at some Southern California sites.
Chemical: Soapy water in pan traps (low risk). Ethanol (70%) used for specimen preservation is flammable.
Physical: Heat exposure during mid-day surveys. Uneven terrain. Pan traps may be trampled by people or wildlife.




5.1 Required PPE

Closed-toed shoes or field boots
Light-colored clothing (dark colors attract bees)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
EpiPen (if allergic; inform field lead)
Nitrile gloves (when handling preserved specimens)



5.2 Permits
Insect collection may require a Scientific Collecting Permit from CDFW depending on the site and target taxa. No permit is needed for observation-only surveys.


5.3 Emergency Procedures
For anaphylactic reactions: administer EpiPen, call 911. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety. If encountering an aggressive swarm, walk calmly away; do not swat or run erratically.

title: Pollinator Observation Surveys
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Survey Timing and Conditions
Conduct pollinator surveys during peak pollinator activity:

Time of day: 09:00–15:00 local time (peak flight activity)
Weather: Sunny to partly cloudy; wind speed below Beaufort 4 (< 5.5 m/s); temperature above 15 C. Do not survey during rain, heavy overcast, or high winds, as pollinator activity drops sharply.
Season: During peak bloom at the study site. In Southern California, this is typically March through June for most habitats, with a secondary bloom in fall for some species.
Flowering requirement: Surveys are only meaningful when flowers are present. Record the dominant flowering species and estimate floral density (flowers per m2) at each survey location.



7.2 Method A: Timed Observation Surveys
Timed observations record pollinator visits to flowers along a fixed route or within a fixed plot during a standardized time period (Dicks et al., 2016; Lebuhn & Fenter, 2013).
Transect walk method:

Establish a transect (typically 50 m x 2 m, or a 100 m x 1 m corridor) through the area of interest. Record the transect coordinates per SOP-F006.
Walk the transect slowly at a pace of approximately 10 m per minute.
Record every pollinator observed visiting a flower within the 2 m band on either side of the transect center line (or 1 m on each side for a 2 m wide transect).
For each observation, record:

Pollinator group or species (see Section 6.4)
Flower species being visited
Behavior (nectaring, pollen collecting, resting)
Time of observation

Complete the transect in 10–15 minutes. Do not stop and wait for pollinators; maintain a steady pace.
Repeat the transect 2–3 times per sampling event, spaced at least 30 minutes apart.

Focal flower observation method:

Select a flowering plant or patch and observe for a fixed period (typically 10 minutes).
Record every pollinator that visits any flower on the focal plant during the observation period.
This method is useful for comparing visitation rates among plant species or treatments.



7.3 Method B: Pan Trap Sampling
Pan traps passively capture flying insects attracted to colored bowls (Lebuhn & Fenter, 2013; Westphal et al., 2008).

At each sampling station, set out three bowls: one white, one fluorescent blue, one fluorescent yellow. Space bowls approximately 3 m apart.
Fill each bowl approximately 2/3 full with water. Add 2–3 drops of unscented dish soap (this breaks the surface tension so insects sink).
Place bowls at the height of the surrounding vegetation canopy:

In short grass or bare ground: set directly on the ground
In tall vegetation (> 30 cm): elevate on stakes or wire stands so the bowl rim is at canopy height

Deploy traps in the morning (by 09:00) and retrieve after 24 hours. For shorter deployments (4–6 hours), retrieve in the afternoon.
Pour the contents of each bowl through a fine mesh strainer. Transfer captured insects to a labeled Whirl-Pak bag or vial with 70% ethanol.
Label each vial with: site, station number, bowl color, date deployed, date retrieved, and collector initials.
Return specimens to the lab for sorting, pinning, and identification.







Note



Pan traps are biased toward small- to medium-sized bees and may under-represent large-bodied bees (bumble bees) and butterflies (Westphal et al., 2008). Combine pan traps with timed observations for a more complete picture of the pollinator community.




7.4 Pollinator Identification
Identify pollinators to the finest taxonomic level possible in the field. At a minimum, assign each observation to one of the following functional groups:

7.5 Specimen Processing (Lab)

Sort pan trap specimens by order under a dissecting scope.
Pin bee specimens following standard entomological practice (pin through the right mesopleuron) and label with locality, date, collector, and determination.
Store pinned specimens in a labeled unit tray in the insect collection.
Specimens can be submitted to a taxonomic specialist or DNA barcoded (COI) for species confirmation.

title: Pollinator Observation Surveys
text:
8 Quality Control

Record weather conditions (temperature, wind, cloud cover) at the start and end of every survey. Do not compare data collected under different weather conditions without accounting for detectability.
On 10% of surveys, have two observers independently record pollinators on the same transect to assess inter-observer agreement.
Record floral density and dominant flowering species at every survey; pollinator abundance is strongly influenced by floral resource availability.
For pan traps, inspect bowls mid-deployment if wind or wildlife disturbance is likely. Refill or replace tipped bowls and note the interruption.
Voucher-pin at least 5 representative specimens per functional group per site per season for the reference collection.

title: Plant Tissue Sampling
text:
This SOP describes procedures for collecting, handling, and preserving plant tissue samples in the field for subsequent laboratory analysis. Plant tissue analysis provides data on nutrient concentrations (C, N, P, K, metals), stable isotope ratios (\(\delta^{13}\)C, \(\delta^{15}\)N), and structural traits such as leaf mass per area (LMA) (Kalra, 1998; Mills & Jones, 2004). Proper sampling technique is essential to ensure that results represent the target tissue and are not contaminated or degraded during collection and transport.
Foliar nutrient concentrations and LMA form part of the “leaf economics spectrum” (LES), a global axis of plant strategy that links leaf structure to function across biomes: species with low LMA and high leaf nitrogen tend toward fast resource acquisition and short leaf lifespans, while species with high LMA and low nitrogen invest in durable, long-lived leaves (Reich, 2014; Wright et al., 2004). Extending this framework, the “fast-slow” plant economics spectrum integrates leaf, stem, and root traits into a whole-plant strategy axis (Reich, 2014; Westoby et al., 2002). Standardized sampling protocols allow EA Program data to be compared with global trait databases (e.g., TRY, BIEN) and regional reference values (Cornelissen et al., 2003; P’erez-Harguindeguy et al., 2013).

2 Scope

Applies to: Collection of leaf, stem, root, and reproductive tissue from vascular plants for nutrient and isotope analysis at all EA Program field sites
Does not apply to: Soil organic matter sampling (see SOP-F400); algal tissue sampling; plant tissue culture; DNA extraction from plant tissue (see SOP-L700)
Location: All EA Program field sites; initial processing in SGM 133/134

title: Plant Tissue Sampling
text:
3 Definitions

Tissue type: The specific plant organ sampled (e.g., fully expanded mature leaves, current-year stem growth, fine roots less than 2 mm diameter, seeds).
Composite sample: A sample formed by combining tissue from multiple individuals of the same species within a plot to represent the population average. Compositing reduces analytical cost but eliminates information about individual-level variation.
Voucher specimen: A pressed and identified plant specimen collected alongside tissue samples to verify species identification.
Leaf mass per area (LMA): The ratio of leaf dry mass to one-sided leaf area (g m-2). LMA is a key functional trait that reflects the trade-off between resource capture (photosynthesis per unit area) and leaf durability. High-LMA leaves are thicker or denser, with lower nitrogen per unit mass but greater physical toughness (Poorter et al., 2009; Wright et al., 2004).
Specific leaf area (SLA): The inverse of LMA: SLA = 1/LMA, expressed as m2 kg-1. SLA and LMA contain the same information but are used in different contexts; report whichever is standard for the analysis.
Leaf economics spectrum (LES): A global pattern relating leaf traits (LMA, nitrogen, phosphorus, photosynthetic capacity, and leaf lifespan) along a single axis of variation. High-nitrogen, low-LMA species occupy the “fast return” end; low-nitrogen, high-LMA species occupy the “slow return” end (Wright et al., 2004).
Sun leaf / shade leaf: Leaves developed in high-light (sun) or low-light (shade) conditions. Sun and shade leaves from the same tree can differ by 20–40% in nitrogen concentration and by a factor of two or more in LMA (Cornelissen et al., 2003; P’erez-Harguindeguy et al., 2013). Sampling must standardize canopy position to avoid confounding light environment with species-level traits.
Field blank: An empty labeled sample container opened and exposed at the field site, then sealed and processed identically to real samples. Blanks detect contamination introduced during collection and transport.

title: Plant Tissue Sampling
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Sampling Design

Define the target species, tissue type, and number of replicates in the sampling plan before going to the field
Determine whether individual or composite samples are needed. For nutrient analysis where individual variation is important, collect tissue from individual plants. For site-level averages, composite tissue from 5–10 individuals per species per plot.
Select individuals randomly within the sampling area. Avoid plants at plot edges, obviously damaged or diseased individuals, and plants with heavy herbivory or epiphyte loads (unless these are the target condition).



8.2 Leaf Tissue Collection

Put on clean nitrile gloves. Change gloves between species to avoid cross-contamination.
Select fully expanded, mature leaves from the outer canopy (sun leaves) unless the project specifically targets shade leaves or another position. Standardizing canopy position is critical for comparability: sun and shade leaves from the same individual can differ by 20–40% in nitrogen concentration and by a factor of two in LMA (Cornelissen et al., 2003; P’erez-Harguindeguy et al., 2013). For trees, sample from the sunlit portion of the mid- to upper crown; for herbs and grasses, sample the most recently fully expanded leaf.
Using clean pruning shears, clip the petiole at its base. For grasses, clip the most recent fully expanded blade at the ligule.
Collect enough tissue mass for the planned analyses. As a guideline:




Analysis
Minimum dry mass




C, N, S by EA-IRMS
2–5 mg


\(\delta^{13}\)C, \(\delta^{15}\)N
2–5 mg


Total P, metals (acid digestion)
100–500 mg


LMA (requires leaf area scan)
3–5 leaves per individual


Multiple analyses from one sample
2–5 g fresh weight recommended




For composite samples, collect an approximately equal mass of tissue from each individual and combine in a single bag.
Place tissue immediately into a labeled paper envelope (if air-drying) or a labeled Ziplock bag (if freezing or transporting fresh). For frozen samples, place bags into the cooler with ice packs.



8.3 Measuring Leaf Area (for LMA/SLA)
If LMA or SLA is needed, leaf area must be measured on fresh tissue before drying (P’erez-Harguindeguy et al., 2013):

Transport fresh leaves to the lab within 6 hours of collection, keeping them in sealed bags in the cooler to minimize wilting
Scan leaves on a flatbed scanner (600 dpi) or measure with a leaf area meter. Record total one-sided area (cm2) for each sample.
Dry and weigh as described in Section 9.1
Calculate LMA = dry mass (g) / area (m2), or SLA = area (m2) / dry mass (kg)



8.4 Stem, Root, and Reproductive Tissue

Stems: Clip current-year growth. Record the diameter and length of the stem segment.
Fine roots (less than 2 mm diameter): Excavate carefully around the base of the target plant using a trowel. Separate live roots from dead roots and soil. Rinse briefly with DI water in the field or at the first opportunity in the lab.
Seeds/fruits: Collect from a minimum of 5 individuals. Record the phenological stage (e.g., immature, mature, dehisced).



8.5 Decontamination Between Species

Spray pruning shears with 70% ethanol
Wipe dry with a clean paper towel
Allow to air-dry for 30 seconds before cutting the next species
For metal analysis, use stainless steel tools only (no galvanized or painted tools) and rinse with DI water after ethanol to remove residual salts



8.6 Labeling
Every sample must be labeled with:

Site name and plot/transect ID
Species (use the 6-letter code from SOP-F603 Section 12.2)
Tissue type (leaf, stem, root, seed)
Individual or composite (if composite, record the number of individuals)
Date (YYYY-MM-DD)
Collector initials

Write on both the bag/envelope and a separate tag inside (in case the exterior label smudges).


8.7 Field Data Sheet
Record the following for each sample:

Entry

(if composite)

title: Plant Tissue Sampling
text:
9 Sample Preservation and Lab Processing

9.1 Drying
The default preservation method for nutrient and isotope analysis (Jones, 2001):

Transport paper envelopes to the lab within 24 hours
Dry at 60 C in the drying oven (SOP-L105) for at least 48 hours or until a constant mass is reached
Record the dry mass
Store dried tissue in labeled coin envelopes in a desiccator or sealed container until grinding







ImportantTemperature Matters



Do not exceed 60 C for tissue intended for nitrogen or carbon isotope analysis. Higher temperatures can volatilize nitrogen compounds and alter \(\delta^{15}\)N values (Kalra, 1998). For samples intended only for total C and N by combustion (not isotope analysis), drying at 70 C is acceptable and reduces drying time.




9.2 Freezing
For analyses requiring fresh tissue (enzyme assays, gene expression, volatile compounds):

Transport in cooler with ice packs (or snap-freeze with liquid nitrogen in the field)
Transfer to the -80 C freezer (SOP-L106) within 6 hours of collection
Record in the freezer inventory



9.3 Grinding

Grind dried tissue to a fine powder using a ball mill or mortar and pestle
Clean the grinding equipment between samples (brush, then wipe with ethanol)
Store ground tissue in labeled microcentrifuge tubes or coin envelopes

title: Plant Tissue Sampling
text:
10 Quality Control

Collect at least one field blank per sampling event: open an empty labeled bag at the site, expose it to the same conditions as the samples, then seal and process identically
For metal analysis, verify that tools are stainless steel and DI-rinsed
Record the time between collection and drying/freezing on the data sheet; flag any samples exceeding the 24-hour (drying) or 6-hour (freezing) window
For composite samples, verify that approximately equal mass was contributed by each individual
When interpreting foliar nutrient results, compare against published reference ranges for the target species or functional group (Mills & Jones, 2004; Reuter & Robinson, 1997). Values outside the expected range may indicate contamination, analytical error, or genuine ecological signal (e.g., nutrient deficiency or toxicity).
For LMA, verify that leaf area was measured on fresh, fully turgid tissue; wilted leaves underestimate area and inflate LMA (P’erez-Harguindeguy et al., 2013)

title: Canopy Cover (Densiometer and Hemispherical Photography)
text:
This SOP describes two methods for estimating canopy cover: the convex spherical densiometer and hemispherical (fisheye) photography. Canopy cover is a key variable in stream habitat assessments (SWAMP protocol), forest ecology, microclimate studies, and solar radiation modeling. Separating this SOP from SOP-F304 allows the methods to be applied in any habitat, not just stream reaches (Jennings et al., 1999; Lemmon, 1956).
The distinction between canopy cover and canopy closure is important for data interpretation. Canopy cover is the proportion of the forest floor covered by the vertical projection of tree crowns; canopy closure is the proportion of the sky hemisphere obscured by vegetation as seen from a single point below the canopy. The two metrics are related but not equivalent, and values can differ by 10–20% at the same location depending on canopy heterogeneity and the method used (Jennings et al., 1999; Paletto & Tosi, 2009).
