The distinction between canopy cover and canopy closure is important for data interpretation. Canopy cover is the proportion of the forest floor covered by the vertical projection of tree crowns; canopy closure is the proportion of the sky hemisphere obscured by vegetation as seen from a single point below the canopy. The two metrics are related but not equivalent, and values can differ by 10–20% at the same location depending on canopy heterogeneity and the method used (Jennings et al., 1999; Paletto & Tosi, 2009).

title: Canopy Cover (Densiometer and Hemispherical Photography)
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Measurement of overhead canopy cover in forests, riparian corridors, oak woodlands, restoration sites, and any habitat where tree or tall shrub canopy is present; includes both the spherical densiometer method and hemispherical photography
Does not apply to: Canopy closure measured by line-intercept or vertical projection methods (see SOP-F603); leaf area index (see SOP-F605); remote sensing canopy cover from aerial or satellite imagery
Location: All EA Program field sites with tree or tall shrub cover

title: Canopy Cover (Densiometer and Hemispherical Photography)
text:
3 Definitions

Canopy cover: The proportion of the forest floor covered by the vertical projection of tree crowns, expressed as a percentage. Canopy cover is an areal measurement that integrates across an entire stand or plot (Jennings et al., 1999).
Canopy closure: The proportion of the sky hemisphere obscured by vegetation when viewed from a single point below the canopy. Canopy closure is a point measurement and is what both the densiometer and hemispherical photography directly estimate (Jennings et al., 1999).
Canopy openness: The complement of canopy closure: openness = 100% - closure. Some software and instruments report openness rather than closure.
Convex spherical densiometer: A hand-held instrument with a convex mirror etched with a grid. The observer counts sky-visible grid intersections to estimate canopy openness (Lemmon, 1956).
Gap fraction: The fraction of the sky visible through the canopy at a given zenith angle, measured from hemispherical photographs. Gap fraction is the basis for estimating both canopy closure and effective LAI.
Binary threshold: The image-processing step in hemispherical photography analysis where each pixel is classified as either sky (white) or canopy (black). The threshold value strongly influences the estimated canopy closure.
SWAMP: Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (California). The SWAMP protocol uses densiometer readings to characterize stream canopy cover as part of physical habitat assessment.

title: Canopy Cover (Densiometer and Hemispherical Photography)
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Measurement Point Selection
Canopy cover measurements are typically taken at systematic intervals along a transect or at the center and edges of fixed-area plots.

Stream habitat surveys (SWAMP): Measure at 11 equally spaced points along each cross-section transect (left bank, center, right bank at each of the main transect positions). See SOP-F304.
Forest inventory plots: Measure at the plot center and at 4 points on the plot boundary (N, E, S, W).
Transect-based surveys: Measure at regular intervals (e.g., every 10 m or 25 m along a 50 m transect).

Record the GPS coordinates of each measurement point or its position along the transect.


7.2 Method A: Convex Spherical Densiometer
The densiometer has a convex mirror with an etched grid. The observer counts the number of grid intersections that are open to the sky (not obstructed by vegetation) in each of four cardinal directions (Lemmon, 1956; Strickler, 1959).

Hold the densiometer at elbow height (approximately 30–40 cm in front of your body), level it using the bubble level.
Position your head so that its reflection is just outside the grid area. This ensures a consistent viewing angle.
Face north. Imagine the grid divided into 24 squares (4 rows x 6 columns). At each of the 24 grid intersections, determine whether the sky or vegetation is reflected. Count the number of open (sky) intersections. Record this count.
Rotate 90 degrees and face east. Repeat the count.
Repeat for south and west.
Calculate canopy cover:

\[
\text{Canopy openness (\%)} = \frac{\text{sum of 4 counts}}{96} \times 100
\]
\[
\text{Canopy cover (\%)} = 100 - \text{canopy openness (\%)}
\]
where 96 is the total number of possible open points across 4 directions (24 per direction x 4 directions).






ImportantKnown Densiometer Bias



The convex densiometer systematically overestimates canopy openness (and therefore underestimates canopy cover) compared to hemispherical photography because of the wide-angle optics and the observer’s head position (Cook et al., 1995; Fiala et al., 2006). The magnitude of the bias varies with stand density, observer experience, and lighting conditions but is typically 5–15 percentage points (Korhonen et al., 2006; Paletto & Tosi, 2009). Report the method used alongside all canopy cover values, and do not mix methods within a dataset or monitoring program.




7.3 Method B: Hemispherical Photography
Hemispherical photographs capture a 180-degree view of the canopy and are analyzed digitally to classify sky vs. canopy pixels (Frazer et al., 2001).
In the field:

Mount the camera on the tripod at breast height (1.37 m) or at a height specified by the project protocol.
Level the camera using the bubble level. The lens must point directly upward (zenith).
Orient the top of the camera toward magnetic north. Record the declination if relevant.
Set the camera to manual exposure. Bracket the exposure (take 3 photos: one at the metered exposure, one stop under, one stop over) to ensure at least one well-exposed image.
Shoot in overcast or uniformly cloudy conditions whenever possible. Direct sunlight produces bright spots that confound automatic thresholding.
Include a gray card in one reference photo per site for exposure calibration.
Record the photo number, GPS coordinates, date, time, and sky conditions in the field notebook.

In the lab:

Import images into canopy analysis software (Gap Light Analyzer, hemIMAGE, or ImageJ with the Hemispherical plugin).
Register the image (set lens projection, define the circular boundary, orient to north).
Apply a binary threshold to classify each pixel as sky (white) or canopy (black). Adjust the threshold manually if automated thresholding produces obvious errors.
The software calculates canopy openness, canopy cover, leaf area index (effective), and gap fraction by zenith angle.
Export results as a .csv file. Save to the project repository under data/canopy/.



7.4 Reporting
Report canopy cover values with the following metadata:

Method (densiometer or hemispherical photography)
Instrument model (densiometer type; camera and lens model)
Measurement height above ground
Date, time, and sky conditions
Software and thresholding method (for photography)
Number of measurement points and their spatial arrangement
Whether the reported metric is canopy cover (vertical projection) or canopy closure (hemispherical view); see Section 3 definitions

title: Canopy Cover (Densiometer and Hemispherical Photography)
text:
8 Quality Control

Densiometer: Have two observers independently read the same point. Readings should agree within 5 percentage points. If they disagree by more than 10 points, re-read together to identify the source of discrepancy. Observer bias is the largest error source for densiometer measurements (Korhonen et al., 2006).
Hemispherical photography: Process the same image twice using different threshold values (+/- 10 units). If the resulting canopy cover differs by more than 5 percentage points, the image may be poorly exposed; re-shoot if possible.
At a subset of sites, measure canopy cover with both methods and report the comparison. This allows future users to relate datasets collected with different methods and to quantify the systematic offset between them (Fiala et al., 2006; Paletto & Tosi, 2009).
Record the observer’s name with every densiometer measurement.

title: Tree DBH and Forest Inventory
text:
This SOP describes standardized procedures for measuring tree diameter at breast height (DBH), conducting fixed-area plot-based forest inventories, and estimating basal area using prism or angle-gauge sampling. These measurements are fundamental to characterizing forest structure, estimating stand density and biomass, monitoring tree growth, and providing inputs to allometric equations for carbon accounting (Avery & Burkhart, 2002; Westfall & Westfall, 2020). The measurement conventions follow the USDA Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) national standards (USDA Forest Service, 2023).
Accurate DBH measurement is the single most important field variable in forest ecology because nearly all derived quantities (basal area, volume, biomass, and carbon) depend on it through nonlinear allometric relationships. Small systematic errors in DBH propagate disproportionately into biomass estimates, especially for large-diameter trees, which store a disproportionate fraction of stand-level carbon (Lutz et al., 2018; west2009?).

title: Tree DBH and Forest Inventory
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All EA Program field sites with tree cover, including riparian forests, oak woodlands, mixed conifer stands, and planted trees at restoration and campus sites
Does not apply to: Shrubs with DBH below 2.5 cm (use SOP-F603 for shrub cover); timber cruising for commercial harvest; urban tree risk assessment
Location: All EA Program terrestrial field sites with woody vegetation

title: Tree DBH and Forest Inventory
text:
3 Definitions

Diameter at breast height (DBH): The diameter of a tree trunk measured at 1.37 m (4.5 ft) above ground level on the uphill side of the tree. DBH is the standard dimension for characterizing tree size (Avery & Burkhart, 2002; USDA Forest Service, 2023).
Basal area (BA): The cross-sectional area of a tree trunk at breast height, calculated as \(\text{BA} = \frac{\pi}{4} \times
\text{DBH}^2\). Often expressed per hectare (m2/ha) as a measure of stand density.
Basal area factor (BAF): The conversion factor for a wedge prism or angle gauge that translates the number of “in” trees to stand basal area (m2/ha).
Variable-radius plot (point sampling): A sampling method where the probability of a tree being included is proportional to its basal area, achieved using a BAF prism. Originally described by



Fixed-area plot: A plot of known area (e.g., 0.04 ha circular plot, radius 11.28 m) within which all trees above a minimum DBH threshold are measured (Laar & Ak cca, 2007).
Allometric equation: A mathematical model relating an easily measured tree dimension (usually DBH) to a harder-to-measure quantity (usually biomass or volume) through a power function (Chojnacky et al., 2014; Jenkins et al., 2003).
Crown class: A classification of a tree’s position in the canopy: dominant, co-dominant, intermediate, or suppressed. Crown class reflects competitive status and light availability.
Snag: A standing dead tree. Snags provide habitat for cavity nesters and are recorded separately from live trees in inventories.
Stand density index (SDI): A relative measure of stand density that accounts for tree size, allowing comparison across species and sites (pretzsch2009?).
Size distribution: The frequency distribution of tree diameters in a stand. Reverse-J distributions characterize uneven-aged stands with continuous recruitment; normal or bimodal distributions suggest even-aged cohorts or past disturbance (muller-landau2006?).

title: Tree DBH and Forest Inventory
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Measuring DBH
DBH is measured at 1.37 m (4.5 ft) above ground level on the uphill side of the tree (Avery & Burkhart, 2002; USDA Forest Service, 2023).

Identify the measurement height: 1.37 m above the ground surface on the uphill side of the tree. If the ground is level, measure from any side.
Wrap the diameter tape around the trunk at 1.37 m, perpendicular to the axis of the trunk (not perpendicular to the slope).
Ensure the tape is snug against the bark, not twisted, and level. Read the diameter directly from the DBH tape to the nearest 0.1 cm.
Record the measurement in the field notebook or data sheet.

Special cases:







Situation
Measurement Rule




Tree on a slope
Measure at 1.37 m from the uphill side of the base


Forked below 1.37 m
Measure each fork as a separate tree


Forked at or above 1.37 m
Measure as one tree below the fork


Swelling or abnormality at 1.37 m
Measure above and below the abnormality and average


Leaning tree
Measure 1.37 m along the underside of the trunk


Buttressed tree
Measure above the buttress where the trunk becomes cylindrical









TipTip



For permanent monitoring plots, mark the DBH measurement point on the bark with a paint marker or timber crayon so that subsequent measurements are taken at the exact same height. For long-term studies, tag each tree with a numbered aluminum tag nailed above breast height.




7.2 Fixed-Area Plot Inventory
Fixed-area plots are the standard method for forest inventory (Laar & Ak cca, 2007; west2009?). Plot size depends on tree density.



Tree Density
Recommended Plot Size
Radius (circular)




Dense forest
0.01 ha (100 m2)
5.64 m


Moderate forest
0.04 ha (400 m2)
11.28 m


Open woodland
0.10 ha (1000 m2)
17.84 m



Procedure:

Navigate to the plot center and record GPS coordinates per SOP-F006.
Mark the plot center with a stake or flagging tape.
For circular plots, use the measuring tape as a radius to determine which trees are inside the plot boundary. A tree is “in” if more than half of its trunk at DBH lies within the plot radius.
Measure and record the following for every tree with DBH at or above the minimum threshold (typically 2.5 cm or 10 cm, as specified by the project):

Species (common name and/or scientific name)
DBH (cm)
Condition class: live, standing dead (snag), leaning
Crown class (optional): dominant, co-dominant, intermediate, suppressed
Height (optional; measured with a clinometer or rangefinder)

Record the total number of stems and species per plot.



7.3 Variable-Radius Plot Sampling (Basal Area Prism)
The BAF prism provides a rapid estimate of stand basal area without establishing fixed plot boundaries (Avery & Burkhart, 2002; Grosenbaugh, 1952).

Stand at the sample point and hold the BAF prism at arm’s length, looking through it at each surrounding tree at breast height.
For each tree, the prism refracts the image of the trunk. Compare the offset image to the original:

Tree is “in”: The offset image overlaps the unrefracted trunk. Count the tree.
Tree is “out”: The offset image is completely separated from the unrefracted trunk. Do not count.
Borderline: The offset image just touches the trunk edge. Count every other borderline tree.

Rotate 360 degrees, counting all “in” trees.
Calculate basal area:

\[
\text{Basal area (m}^2\text{/ha)} = n \times \text{BAF}
\]
where \(n\) is the number of “in” trees and BAF is the basal area factor of the prism (typically 1, 2, 4, or 5 m2/ha per tree counted; check the prism label).


7.4 Tree Height Measurement (Optional)
Use a clinometer or laser rangefinder to measure total tree height (Laar & Ak cca, 2007; west2009?):

Stand at a known horizontal distance from the tree base (e.g., 15–30 m; measure with a tape or rangefinder).
Sight the tree top through the clinometer and record the angle to the top (\(\alpha\)).
Sight the tree base and record the angle to the base (\(\beta\)). If the base is below eye level, \(\beta\) is negative.
Calculate height:

\[
H = D \times (\tan\alpha - \tan\beta)
\]
where \(D\) is the horizontal distance (m) and \(H\) is the total height (m). This formula assumes the observer’s line of sight to the top of the tree is unobstructed and that the tree is vertical; for leaning trees, measure height along the leaning axis and record the lean angle.

title: Tree DBH and Forest Inventory
text:
8 Derived Calculations

8.1 Basal Area per Tree
\[
\text{BA (m}^2\text{)} = \frac{\pi}{4} \times \left(\frac{\text{DBH}}{100}\right)^2
\]
where DBH is in cm.


8.2 Stand Density and Basal Area per Hectare
\[
\text{Trees/ha} = \frac{n}{\text{plot area (ha)}}
\]
\[
\text{BA/ha (m}^2\text{/ha)} = \frac{\sum \text{BA}_i}{\text{plot area (ha)}}
\]


8.3 Biomass Estimation
Above-ground biomass can be estimated using published allometric equations of the form:
\[
\text{Biomass (kg)} = a \times \text{DBH}^b
\]
where \(a\) and \(b\) are species-specific coefficients from published sources (Chojnacky et al., 2014; Jenkins et al., 2003). Document the allometric equation, source, and species used in the project README. Because the exponent \(b\) typically ranges from 2 to 3, measurement errors in DBH are amplified in biomass estimates: a 1 cm error at DBH = 50 cm produces a roughly 4–6% error in biomass (west2009?). Large-diameter trees store a disproportionately large fraction of aboveground carbon in most forest types; accurate measurement of the largest individuals in a stand is therefore critical for unbiased biomass and carbon stock estimates (Lutz et al., 2018).


8.4 Interpreting Size Distributions
Plotting the diameter distribution (number of trees per DBH class) provides insight into stand history and dynamics. A reverse-J (negative exponential) distribution suggests continuous recruitment across size classes, typical of uneven-aged or mixed-species stands. A bell-shaped or bimodal distribution suggests one or more distinct cohorts established after disturbance events (muller-landau2006?; pretzsch2009?).

title: Tree DBH and Forest Inventory
text:
9 Quality Control

Measure DBH twice (wrap the tape, read, remove, re-wrap, re-read). The two readings should agree within 0.5 cm. Record the mean.
On 10% of plots, have a second observer independently measure all trees. DBH measurements should agree within 1 cm; tree counts should match exactly.
Verify the diameter tape calibration at the start of each field season by measuring a cylinder of known diameter.
For permanent plots, verify that tags are intact and measurement points are correctly located at each re-measurement.
When comparing DBH across re-measurement intervals, confirm that the measurement point has not shifted due to bark ingrowth over tags or paint marks (Westfall & Westfall, 2020).

title: iNaturalist for Biodiversity Documentation
text:
This SOP describes how to use iNaturalist (https://www.inaturalist.org) as a standardized tool for documenting biodiversity at EA Program field sites. iNaturalist is a community science platform that combines field observation, AI-assisted species identification, and expert community verification into a single workflow (ueda2024?). Observations that receive community agreement on identification reach “Research Grade” status and are automatically shared with the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), making them part of the global scientific record (Global Biodiversity Information Facility, 2024).
Community science platforms like iNaturalist generate large volumes of occurrence data, but the scientific value of those data depends critically on the quality of individual observations, including photographic evidence, spatial accuracy, and taxonomic verification (Dickinson et al., 2010). When data quality is maintained, iNaturalist records can support large-scale biodiversity monitoring and contribute meaningfully to national and international biodiversity assessments (Callaghan et al., 2021; Chandler et al., 2017). This SOP covers making high-quality observations, creating and managing collaborative projects for EA Program research, and exporting data for analysis in R.

This SOP describes how to use iNaturalist (https://www.inaturalist.org) as a standardized tool for documenting biodiversity at EA Program field sites. iNaturalist is a community science platform that combines field observation, AI-assisted species identification, and expert community verification into a single workflow (ueda2024?). Observations that receive community agreement on identification reach “Research Grade” status and are automatically shared with the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), making them part of the global scientific record (Global Biodiversity Information Facility, 2024).
Community science platforms like iNaturalist generate large volumes of occurrence data, but the scientific value of those data depends critically on the quality of individual observations, including photographic evidence, spatial accuracy, and taxonomic verification (Dickinson et al., 2010). When data quality is maintained, iNaturalist records can support large-scale biodiversity monitoring and contribute meaningfully to national and international biodiversity assessments (Callaghan et al., 2021; Chandler et al., 2017). This SOP covers making high-quality observations, creating and managing collaborative projects for EA Program research, and exporting data for analysis in R.

title: iNaturalist for Biodiversity Documentation
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All EA Program biodiversity surveys, species inventories, and community science activities where iNaturalist is used to document plant, animal, fungal, or other organism occurrences
Does not apply to: Quantitative vegetation transect surveys (SOP-F603); camera trap image processing (SOP-F620); formal specimen collection requiring voucher preparation; eDNA sampling
Location: All EA Program field sites and campus

title: iNaturalist for Biodiversity Documentation
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




PI / Field Lead
Create and administer iNaturalist projects; review data quality


Project Admin
Manage project settings, curate observations, invite members


Trained Personnel

New Students

title: iNaturalist for Biodiversity Documentation
text:
4 Definitions

Observation: A record of an encounter with an individual organism at a specific place and time, documented with at least one photo or sound recording.
Research Grade: An observation that has a date, location, photo or sound, and community agreement on the identification (at least two-thirds of identifiers agree at the species level). Research Grade observations are shared with GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility, 2024).
Needs ID: An observation that has not yet received enough community identifications to reach Research Grade. These records are scientifically useful but carry higher taxonomic uncertainty.
Casual: An observation that is missing date, location, or evidence (photo/sound), or that the community has voted as not meeting quality standards. Casual observations are excluded from most research exports.
Collection Project: A project that automatically includes all observations matching defined criteria (taxa, place, users, dates, quality grade). No manual curation needed.
Traditional Project: A project where observations must be added manually by members. Can require custom observation fields. Requires the creator to have at least 50 verifiable observations.
Umbrella Project: A project that aggregates observations from multiple other projects. Useful for coordinating across sites or taxa.
Observation Field: A custom data field that can be attached to observations (e.g., “habitat type,” “number of individuals,” “flowering status”). Only Traditional Projects can require observation fields.
Computer Vision (CV) Model: The machine learning model trained on iNaturalist’s community-verified image database that suggests identifications for new observations. The model is retrained periodically and performs best for taxa and regions with large training datasets; accuracy declines for rare, under-photographed, or morphologically cryptic taxa (loarie2023?).
Taxon Geoprivacy: An automatic system that obscures the coordinates of observations for threatened, endangered, or sensitive species to protect them from collection or disturbance.
Coordinate Uncertainty: The estimated spatial accuracy of the GPS location, expressed as a radius in meters. High uncertainty (greater than 1000 m) reduces the value of occurrence records for fine-scale spatial analyses.

title: iNaturalist for Biodiversity Documentation
text:
5 Safety and Hazards
Standard field safety applies when making observations in the field. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety. Additional considerations specific to iNaturalist use:

Location privacy: iNaturalist observations include GPS coordinates by default. Be aware that your location is visible to other users unless you obscure or hide it. Do not post observations from private residences without obscuring the location.
Sensitive species: iNaturalist automatically obscures the locations of threatened and endangered species (“taxon geoprivacy”). Do not override this obscuring for sensitive taxa.
Disturbance: Do not disturb, handle, or collect organisms solely for an iNaturalist photo. Photograph organisms in situ where possible.

title: iNaturalist for Biodiversity Documentation
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Account Setup

Go to https://www.inaturalist.org or download the iNaturalist app
Create an account using your Claremont email address
In your profile settings:

Set your default photo license to CC-BY or CC-BY-NC (this allows your photos to be used in research with attribution)
Set your default observation license to CC0 or CC-BY (this allows your observation data to be shared with GBIF)
Set your default location to “open” (you can obscure individual observations as needed)

Send your iNaturalist username to the project administrator so you can be added to the EA Program project







ImportantLicense Settings Matter for Research



Observations with “All Rights Reserved” licenses are excluded from GBIF exports and many research datasets. For EA Program work, always use a Creative Commons license. CC-BY is recommended.




7.2 Making High-Quality Observations
A useful iNaturalist observation needs four things: a photo (or sound), a date, a location, and enough visual detail for identification. Follow these guidelines to maximize the chances of reaching Research Grade.

7.2.1 Photography Tips

Take multiple photos of each organism from different angles:

Plants: Whole plant habit, close-up of leaves (both sides), flowers or fruit, stem, bark (for trees)
Insects: Dorsal view (top), lateral view (side), close-up of head and wing venation if possible
Birds: Best angle available; include habitat context if possible
Fungi: Top of cap, underside (gills/pores), stem, habitat context

Include something for scale (a finger, a coin, a ruler) when practical
Photograph the organism in its natural position; do not relocate it
For plants, photograph vegetative and reproductive structures together if both are present
Ensure the photo is in focus and adequately lit



7.2.2 Recording the Observation

Open the iNaturalist app and tap the camera icon to start a new observation
Take photos directly in the app, or select photos from your camera roll
The app will suggest an identification using its computer vision

model (loarie2023?). Accept the suggestion if it looks correct, or refine the identification manually. When in doubt, identify to the broadest level you are confident in (e.g., “Plants” or “Oaks” rather than guessing a specific species). The CV model performs best for common, well-photographed taxa in North America and Europe; for under-represented groups (e.g., lichens, mosses, many invertebrate families), manual identification by the observer or community identifiers is essential.

Verify that the date and location are correct. The app captures these automatically from the photo metadata, but check that the GPS pin is accurate on the map. If coordinate uncertainty exceeds 500 m, manually reposition the pin.
Add any relevant notes in the “Notes” field (habitat, behavior, abundance, associated species)
If the observation is part of a Traditional Project, add it to the project before submitting (see Section 7.4)
Tap Submit







TipSound Observations



For birds, frogs, and insects, a sound recording can be as useful as (or more useful than) a photo. The iNaturalist app can record audio directly. Hold the phone steady and minimize background noise.





7.3 Bulk Uploading Observations via CSV
For observations recorded outside the app (for example, transcribed from a field notebook, exported from another platform, or compiled in a spreadsheet during data entry), iNaturalist accepts a bulk CSV import. This is useful when you have many records to create at once and do not want to enter them one at a time. The importer creates the observation records only; it does not upload photos or sound files, so media must be attached afterward (see below).

7.3.1 Preparing the CSV

Build the spreadsheet with up to eight columns, in this order. Only the taxon column is mandatory.









Column
Format / example
Notes




Taxon name
text (e.g., Quercus agrifolia)
Mandatory. Use the scientific name for reliable matching.


Date observed
YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM
Use day-level precision or finer for research use.


Description
text
Free-text notes (habitat, behavior, abundance).


Place name
text
Optional named locality.


Latitude
decimal degrees (34.1064)
Use a decimal point, not a comma.


Longitude
decimal degrees (-117.7120)
Use a decimal point, not a comma.


Tags
tag,tag
Comma-separated tags.


Geoprivacy
open, obscured, or private
Set to obscured for sensitive taxa.




Keep the file under 10,000 rows. Split larger datasets into multiple files.
Wrap any field that contains a comma in double quotes so it is not misread as a column break.
Confirm that coordinates use decimal points. Spreadsheets configured for some locales export decimal commas, which the importer rejects.



7.3.2 Importing

Go to the import page at https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/import#csv_import (or from the upload page, click More import options and choose CSV).
Choose your file and upload it.
Open Edit Observations to review the created records. Use Batch Edit to select multiple observations, attach photos or sound files, and apply a shared location from the map.
Verify dates, coordinates, and identifications, then save.







WarningCSV Imports Do Not Include Media



The CSV importer creates observation records without photos or sounds. An observation with no media cannot reach Research Grade and is treated as Casual, so it will be excluded from most research exports and from GBIF. Attach media through Batch Edit after import if the records are intended for analysis.








TipLarge or Photo-Linked Datasets: Use the API



For large batches, or when you need to match many photos to the correct records automatically, the spreadsheet importer becomes impractical. In those cases, script the upload against the iNaturalist API (https://api.inaturalist.org). The rinat package is read-only (it retrieves data but does not create observations), so creating observations programmatically requires direct authenticated calls, for example with httr2 in R:


Code
library(httr2)

# Requires an OAuth API token from your iNaturalist account.
# Create the observation, then POST the photo to /observation_photos
# using the returned observation id. See the API reference for the
# full request schema before running against your account.


Test any upload script on a handful of records first, and never use it to create observations for organisms you did not personally encounter (see Responsible Use).





7.4 Contributing Identifications
Identifying other people’s observations is as valuable as making your own. It builds community expertise, helps observations reach Research Grade, and improves the CV model.

Go to the Identify tab on the website (or use the Explore page and filter by “Needs ID”)
Filter by your area of expertise (taxa, location)
Add your identification. Agree with the existing suggestion if correct, or provide a different identification with a brief explanation.
Use the “Compare” tool to check similar species
Mark observations as “No, it’s as good as it can be” only if the evidence is genuinely insufficient for identification



7.5 Creating and Managing Projects
iNaturalist offers three project types. Choose based on your research needs:









Feature
Collection Project
Traditional Project
Umbrella Project




Observations added
Automatically (by filter criteria)
Manually by members
From member projects


Custom observation fields
No
Yes (can be required)
No


Creator requirements
Any user
50+ verifiable observations

Best for
Site-based inventories, class bioblitzes
Projects needing custom data fields
Multi-site or multi-taxon coordination


Obscured coordinate access
Yes (with Trust enabled)
Yes (with member permission)
No (via member projects)




7.5.1 Creating a Collection Project
This is the recommended type for most EA Program site inventories and class projects. Observations matching your criteria are included automatically.

Go to https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/new
Click Get Started under Collection Projects
Fill in the project details:

Title: Use a descriptive name (e.g., “EA Program – Bernard Field Station Biodiversity 2025”)
Icon: Upload the EA Program logo or a representative photo
Banner: Upload a site photo
Description: Explain the project’s purpose, study site, and time frame

Set the project requirements (filters):

Place: Select the iNaturalist Place for your study area. If one does not exist, create a custom Place by drawing a boundary on the map (Community > Places > Add a New Place).
Taxa: Leave blank to include all organisms, or restrict to specific groups (e.g., Plantae, Aves)
Users: Leave blank to include anyone, or list specific usernames for a closed team
Date range: Set start and end dates if the project covers a specific period (e.g., a class semester or field season)
Quality grade: Select “Research Grade” and “Needs ID” for most research projects

Under Trust (optional but recommended for research): enable Trust to allow project admins to access the true coordinates of observations with obscured or private locations. Members must individually opt in to share their coordinates.
Click Save







NoteCreating a Custom Place



If your study area (e.g., the Bernard Field Station, a specific watershed) does not exist as an iNaturalist Place, create one:

Go to https://www.inaturalist.org/places/new
Name the place (e.g., “Bernard Field Station, Claremont, CA”)
Draw the boundary on the map using the polygon tool
Save

The place will be available as a filter in your Collection Project. Note that very small places (e.g., a single backyard) work better with Traditional Projects because GPS accuracy and obscured coordinates can cause observations to fall outside tiny boundaries.




7.5.2 Creating a Traditional Project
Use when you need custom observation fields or when the study area is too small for reliable GPS-based filtering.

You must have at least 50 verifiable observations on your account
Go to https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/new
Look for the small text link at the bottom of the page: “click here to create a traditional project”
Fill in the project details (title, icon, banner, description)
Set the membership model:

Open: Anyone can join
Invite-only: Only users you invite can join (recommended for research teams)

Set the submission model:

Any member: All members can add observations
Project curators: Only curators can add observations (recommended when the PI needs to control data quality)

Add observation fields if needed (e.g., “Habitat type,” “Transect number,” “Number of individuals”).

title: iNaturalist for Biodiversity Documentation
text:
8 Data Quality Considerations
iNaturalist data are heterogeneous in quality because they are generated by observers with widely varying skill levels, equipment, and motivations (Dickinson et al., 2010). For EA Program research, apply the following data quality filters when exporting records for analysis:

Quality grade: Use Research Grade observations only for quantitative analyses. Needs ID observations can supplement species inventories but carry higher misidentification risk.
Coordinate uncertainty: Exclude records with positional accuracy greater than 1000 m unless the analysis does not require fine spatial resolution.
Date precision: Exclude records without day-level date precision for phenological analyses.
Taxonomic verification: For critical analyses, manually verify identifications against the photographic evidence, especially for taxa where the CV model is known to struggle (e.g., grasses, juvenile insects, sterile plants).
Spatial bias: iNaturalist data are spatially biased toward accessible, human-frequented areas (trails, roads, urban parks). This bias must be acknowledged and, where possible, corrected for in species distribution models (Callaghan et al., 2021).

These filters should be documented in the methods section of any publication or report using iNaturalist-derived data.

title: iNaturalist for Biodiversity Documentation
text:
9 Data Export and Analysis

9.1 Exporting from iNaturalist

Go to the Explore page and filter to your project, place, or taxa of interest
Click Filters to narrow results
Click Download (bottom of the page) to download a CSV file



9.2 Exporting from GBIF
For Research Grade observations that have been shared with GBIF:

Go to https://www.gbif.org/occurrence/search
Filter by dataset (search for “iNaturalist”), location, and taxa
Click Download and select the desired format
GBIF assigns a DOI to every download; cite the DOI in your publications



9.3 Using rinat in R
The rinat package provides programmatic access to iNaturalist data (barve2025?):


Code

10 Citing iNaturalist Data

Platform citation: iNaturalist. Available at: https://www.inaturalist.org. Accessed [date].
GBIF download citation: Use the DOI provided with the GBIF download.
Individual observations: Cite by observation URL (e.g., https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/123456) when referencing specific records.

When using iNaturalist data in publications, describe the data quality filters applied (e.g., Research Grade only, coordinate uncertainty threshold) and acknowledge the community identifiers whose expertise validated the records (Chandler et al., 2017; Dickinson et al., 2010).

title: iNaturalist for Biodiversity Documentation
text:
11 Responsible Use

Respect copyright: each user retains ownership of their observations and photos. Your rights to use them are governed by the license the user selected. Most iNaturalist photos use CC-BY-NC.
Do not create observations for specimens you did not personally encounter (no uploading photos from field guides, the internet, or other people’s cameras)
Do not harass, collect, or relocate organisms for the purpose of getting a better photo
For sensitive species (rare plants, nesting sites), manually obscure the location even if iNaturalist does not do so automatically
Follow iNaturalist’s Community Guidelines: https://www.inaturalist.org/pages/community+guidelines







WarningStudent Use



Before assigning students to use iNaturalist, read the iNaturalist Teacher’s Guide (https://www.inaturalist.org/pages/teacher's+guide). The majority of low-quality observations and inappropriate content on iNaturalist comes from poorly managed class assignments. Set clear expectations, demonstrate proper technique, and monitor student contributions. Structured class projects with specific data quality goals produce better scientific outcomes and learning (Aristeidou & Herodotou, 2020).

title: Noise Level Monitoring
text:
This procedure describes field measurement and documentation of environmental noise levels using handheld sound level meters and logging dosimeters. Environmental noise is an increasingly recognized pollutant affecting human health (cardiovascular risk, sleep disturbance, cognitive impairment) and wildlife behavior (altered communication, habitat avoidance) (Barber et al., 2010; World Health Organization, 2018).
Noise monitoring in the EA Program supports community environmental assessments, transportation corridor studies, urban ecology research, and environmental justice analyses where noise disproportionately affects disadvantaged communities.

title: Noise Level Monitoring
text:
This procedure describes field measurement and documentation of environmental noise levels using handheld sound level meters and logging dosimeters. Environmental noise is an increasingly recognized pollutant affecting human health (cardiovascular risk, sleep disturbance, cognitive impairment) and wildlife behavior (altered communication, habitat avoidance) (Barber et al., 2010; World Health Organization, 2018).
Noise monitoring in the EA Program supports community environmental assessments, transportation corridor studies, urban ecology research, and environmental justice analyses where noise disproportionately affects disadvantaged communities.

title: Noise Level Monitoring
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Outdoor environmental noise measurements (community noise, traffic noise, construction noise, natural soundscapes) using Type 1 or Type 2 integrating sound level meters and personal noise dosimeters
Does not apply to: Occupational noise exposure assessment (governed by OSHA standards and conducted by campus EH&S); indoor building acoustics; underwater acoustics
Location: All EA Program field sites

title: Noise Level Monitoring
text:
4 Definitions

A-weighting (dBA): A frequency-weighting filter applied to sound level measurements that approximates the frequency-dependent sensitivity of the human ear; attenuates low and very high frequencies; the standard weighting for environmental and community noise assessments.
Calibrator: A portable acoustic device that produces a reference tone of known sound pressure level (typically 94 dB or 114 dB at 1,000 Hz) used to verify sound level meter accuracy before and after each measurement session.
Day-night average sound level (Ldn): A 24-hour energy-averaged sound level with a 10 dB penalty added to nighttime (10 pm–7 am) levels to account for increased sensitivity to noise during sleep; the primary US EPA regulatory descriptor for community noise exposure.
Equivalent continuous sound level (Leq): The steady-state sound level that would contain the same acoustic energy as the actual time-varying sound over a defined measurement period; the primary descriptor for environmental noise measurements; expressed in dB or dBA.
Lmax / Lmin: The maximum and minimum instantaneous A-weighted sound levels measured during a monitoring period; used to characterize the range of noise events and identify peak exposures.
Percentile level (LN): The sound level exceeded for N% of the measurement period (e.g., L90 is the level exceeded 90% of the time); L90 approximates background noise; L10 approximates peak intrusive noise events.
Sound level meter: An instrument that measures sound pressure level in decibels; classified as Type 1 (precision, laboratory and field) or Type 2 (general purpose); Type 1 meters are required for regulatory compliance measurements; both types are acceptable for research.
Sound pressure level (SPL): A logarithmic measure of the effective pressure of a sound wave relative to a reference pressure of 20 µPa (the threshold of human hearing): \(SPL = 20\log_{10}(p /
p_0)\); expressed in decibels (dB).
Windscreen: A porous foam or fur cover placed over the microphone to reduce turbulent airflow noise caused by wind; required for all outdoor measurements to prevent wind-induced artifacts from contaminating sound level data.

title: Noise Level Monitoring
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Traffic: Noise monitoring often occurs near roadways. Wear a high-visibility vest. Never stand in a travel lane.
Hearing: If monitoring near very loud sources (e.g., active construction, aircraft operations above 85 dBA), wear hearing protection.
Personal safety: Monitoring in urban areas may involve working alone or in unfamiliar neighborhoods. Work in pairs when possible and inform someone of your schedule and locations.




5.1 Required PPE

High-visibility vest (near roadways)
Hearing protection (if sustained levels exceed 85 dBA)
Closed-toed shoes
Sun protection

text:

title: Noise Level Monitoring
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Field Calibration

In a quiet indoor location, attach the acoustic calibrator to the microphone and turn on the calibrator
Adjust the sound level meter reading to match the calibrator reference level (e.g., 94.0 dB) per the meter’s calibration procedure
Record the calibration date, time, calibrator serial number, and meter reading in the field notebook
If the meter reading deviates from the reference by more than 0.5 dB, recalibrate or service the instrument



7.2 Site Setup

Select a measurement location that represents the receptor of interest (e.g., residential facade, park boundary, school playground)
Position the microphone on a tripod at 1.2–1.5 m above the ground, at least 3.5 m from any large reflecting surface (building wall, barrier, parked vehicle) to minimize reflections (Acoustics – Description, Measurement and Assessment of Environmental Noise – Part 2, 2017)
Orient the microphone toward the dominant noise source (or upward if the sound field is diffuse)
Attach the windscreen
Record: site ID, GPS coordinates, date, time, weather conditions (wind speed and direction, temperature), distance and bearing to the dominant source(s), ground cover, and any shielding







Important



Do not measure when wind speed exceeds 5 m/s (approximately 11 mph). Wind noise inflates readings even with a windscreen. Record the wind speed at the start and end of each measurement period.




7.3 Measurement Protocol
The following protocol collects standard community noise metrics. Adjust the duration and intervals to match the study design.

Set the meter to: A-weighting, fast time constant, and Leq (equivalent continuous level) integration mode
Start the measurement and let it run for the designated period:

Short-term survey: 15 minutes per measurement location (the minimum recommended by most community noise standards)
1-hour Leq: Run for 60 minutes if comparing to local noise ordinance limits
Long-term (24-hour): Use a dosimeter or logging meter; deploy and secure the instrument

During the measurement, note all significant noise events in the field notebook: vehicle pass-bys, aircraft overflights, dog barking, construction activity, etc. Record the time and estimated duration of each event.
At the end of the measurement period, record the following metrics from the meter display:

Leq (equivalent continuous level)
Lmax (maximum level)
Lmin (minimum level)
L10, L50, L90 (statistical levels, if the meter computes them)

If the meter logs time-history data, download the file after the session



7.4 Post-Field Calibration Check

After the final measurement at the last site, re-check the calibration with the acoustic calibrator
Record the post-measurement calibration reading. If it differs from the pre-measurement value by more than 1.0 dB, flag all data from that session for review.



7.5 Data Recording
For each measurement, record on the data sheet:

Site ID, GPS coordinates, date, start/end times
Meter make, model, serial number
Calibration readings (pre and post)
Weather: wind speed/direction, temperature, sky conditions
Source description and distance
Measurement duration and metrics (Leq, Lmax, Lmin, L10, L50, L90)
Notable noise events and their times
Observer name

title: Noise Level Monitoring
text:
8 Data Interpretation







Metric
Meaning




Leq
Energy-averaged sound level over the measurement period; the single most important descriptor of community noise exposure


Lmax
Highest instantaneous level recorded


Lmin
Lowest instantaneous level recorded


L10
Level exceeded 10% of the time (approximates “loud” events)


L50
Median level


L90
Level exceeded 90% of the time (approximates background or residual noise)


Ldn
Day-night average; Leq with a 10 dB penalty applied to nighttime (10 PM–7 AM) hours









Note



Community noise standards in California (Title 24, local general plans) typically set limits in terms of Ldn (CNEL) or Leq for specific land use categories. A residential exterior standard of 60–65 dB Ldn is common.

title: Noise Level Monitoring
text:
9 Quality Control

Calibrate before and after every measurement session; flag data if drift exceeds 1.0 dB
Use the windscreen for all outdoor measurements
Do not measure when wind speed exceeds 5 m/s
Record all extraneous noise events so they can be identified in the time-history data
For long-term deployments, perform a calibration check at each data retrieval visit
Maintain a calibration and maintenance log for each meter

title: Noise Level Monitoring
text:
10 Waste Disposal
No waste is generated by noise monitoring. Dispose of used batteries per campus battery recycling procedures.

title: Greenhouse Gas Measurements – Picarro G2508 with Eosense Soil Flux Chambers
text:
This procedure describes how to install Eosense eosAC soil gas flux chambers, connect them to the eosMX-P multiplexer, and operate the Picarro G2508 cavity ring-down spectroscopy (CRDS) analyzer for measuring greenhouse gas fluxes (N2O, CH4, CO2, NH3, and H2O) from soil. The SOP also covers data acquisition using the eosAnalyze-AC software and data export for analysis (Eosense Inc., 2019; Picarro, Inc., 2021).
This SOP was originally developed for greenhouse gas emission measurements from strawberry fields in Northern California and has been modified as new projects have come on line.

title: Greenhouse Gas Measurements – Picarro G2508 with Eosense Soil Flux Chambers
text:
This procedure describes how to install Eosense eosAC soil gas flux chambers, connect them to the eosMX-P multiplexer, and operate the Picarro G2508 cavity ring-down spectroscopy (CRDS) analyzer for measuring greenhouse gas fluxes (N2O, CH4, CO2, NH3, and H2O) from soil. The SOP also covers data acquisition using the eosAnalyze-AC software and data export for analysis (Eosense Inc., 2019; Picarro, Inc., 2021).
This SOP was originally developed for greenhouse gas emission measurements from strawberry fields in Northern California and has been modified as new projects have come on line.

title: Greenhouse Gas Measurements – Picarro G2508 with Eosense Soil Flux Chambers
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Field deployment of the Picarro G2508 CRDS analyzer coupled with Eosense eosAC dynamic soil flux chambers and the eosMX-P multiplexer for automated soil greenhouse gas flux measurements
Does not apply to: Laboratory (bench-top) Picarro configuration (see SOP-L504), atmospheric concentration monitoring without flux chambers, or eddy covariance measurements
Location: All EA Program field sites within 30 m cable reach of a power source

text:

title: Greenhouse Gas Measurements – Picarro G2508 with Eosense Soil Flux Chambers
text:
4 Definitions

Cavity ring-down spectroscopy (CRDS): The laser-based optical detection technique used by the Picarro G2508; a laser pulse is injected into a high-finesse optical cavity and the rate of light decay is measured; the decay rate is proportional to the concentration of absorbing gas molecules, enabling parts-per-billion sensitivity.
Chamber closure period: The time interval during which the eosAC chamber lid is sealed over the soil surface; CO2, N2O, CH4, and NH3 accumulate in the chamber headspace during this period; flux is calculated from the rate of concentration change.
Dead volume: The total volume of gas in the measurement system (chamber headspace, tubing, and instrument internal volume) that dilutes gas emitted from the soil; must be accurately characterized to calculate flux.
Drierite: Anhydrous calcium sulfate desiccant used to remove water vapor from the gas stream before it enters the Picarro analyzer; must be regenerated or replaced when exhausted (color change from blue to pink for indicating Drierite).
eosMX-P multiplexer: The Eosense controller that cycles sequentially through up to 16 chamber ports, directing flow from each chamber to the Picarro analyzer in turn; automates multi-chamber deployments without manual valve switching.
eosAC chamber: An automated, transparent polycarbonate flux chamber manufactured by Eosense; opens and closes on a programmable schedule; connected to the eosMX-P multiplexer and Picarro analyzer via Teflon tubing.
Flux calculation: Derivation of the gas flux (µmol m-2 s-1 or nmol m-2 s-1) from the linear or non-linear rate of concentration increase in the chamber headspace, chamber volume, soil surface area enclosed, and air temperature and pressure.
N2O (nitrous oxide): A potent greenhouse gas (298x CO2 warming potential over 100 years) produced in soil by nitrification and denitrification; the primary target of many EA Program field campaigns; measured simultaneously with CH4, CO2, NH3, and H2O by the Picarro G2508.

5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Compressed gas cylinders (calibration standards) pose crush and high-pressure hazards. The generator (if used) presents fuel spill, carbon monoxide, and noise hazards.
Chemical: Drierite desiccant is a mild irritant. Calibration gas cylinders may contain pressurized gases.
Electrical: Power strip, generator, and instrument connections in outdoor conditions; keep connections dry and off the ground.
Environmental: High ambient temperatures (above 35 C) can cause instrument overheating.




5.1 Required PPE

Closed-toed shoes or field boots
Safety glasses (when handling gas cylinders)
Work gloves (when handling cylinders and generator)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
Hearing protection (if generator is running nearby)



5.2 Required Training

SOP-F001 Field Safety
SOP-F101 Electrical Power in the Field



5.3 Emergency Procedures
In case of gas leak from calibration cylinders, move upwind and ventilate the area. For generator fuel spills, contain with absorbent materials. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety for general field emergency response.

title: Greenhouse Gas Measurements – Picarro G2508 with Eosense Soil Flux Chambers
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sampling Design

Locate the Picarro analyzer, multiplexer, and pump at the base station. Choose a level, shaded location if possible.
Use a random number generator to determine the chamber placement locations within the study area
All chambers must be within 30 m of the multiplexer (the length of the cables and tubing)
If a generator is used, place it at least 100 feet downwind of the chambers to avoid contaminating flux measurements with exhaust



7.2 Hardware Setup

Connect the recirculation pump to the analyzer VACUUM port using the corrugated metal hose. Use new Swagelok washers each time. Hand-tighten, then seal with a wrench.
Connect the multiplexer to the Picarro through USB ports on the Picarro (any port)
Connect the monitor, mouse, and keyboard to the Picarro via the remaining USB ports (two additional ports are available on the front of the Picarro)
Connect the blue monitor cable to the Picarro and the monitor power cable to the outlet
Ensure all machines are in the off position (circle symbol = off) before connecting power
Connect power cables for the CRDS analyzer, multiplexer, and pump
Connect the pump to the multiplexer:

Connect the control and data ports on the back of the pump to the Picarro, ensuring the white triangles face upward
Insert the other ends into any USB port on the Picarro

Connect clear tubing from the pump inlet (left side, clear tube) to the multiplexer inlet (right side, labeled)
Connect the outlet tubing: multiplexer outlet to the Picarro inlet (clear tube); pump outlet (right side, silver tube) to the Picarro outlet
Attach one end of the power/data cable to the COMM port on the pump and the other end to the matching COMM port on the multiplexer







Important



Never turn off the pump while the Picarro is running. Never disconnect the vacuum while the analyzer is operating. Doing so can damage the instrument.




7.3 Installing Chamber Rings
Chamber ring installation varies based on experimental design. Install rings in advance of the measurement day to minimize soil disturbance during data collection. TBD – add project-specific ring installation protocols as needed.


7.4 Picarro Startup

Ensure all instruments are off and turn on the power strip
Turn on the recirculation pump first (no wait time required)
Switch on the Picarro. The boot-up sequence initializes the CRDS software and analyzer.
Switch on the multiplexer. The system requires approximately 30 minutes to warm up; warning alarms are normal until the cavity and other components reach operating temperature.
Keep ambient temperature below 35 C. If the DAS temperature approaches 45 C, shut down or use a fan to cool the air around the Picarro.



7.5 Placing Chambers

While the Picarro is warming up, connect all tubing and cables. Route tubing along the bed surface; do not let tubes fall into furrows.
Place chambers onto the ring bases, pressing down to achieve a good seal. Try to avoid disturbing the chamber after installation.
After all chambers have opened, perform a second check for foliage or debris that might obstruct the chamber seal.



7.6 Data Collection
Once the Picarro alarm indicator is green, the system is ready.

Verify typical atmospheric concentrations on the Picarro display:




Gas
Expected Ambient Concentration




N2O
Approximately 0.3 ppm


CH4
Approximately 2.4 ppm


CO2
300–600 ppm


NH3
Variable


H2O
1–5%




Open the FP-Monitor multiplexer software
Uncheck “Default Cycle”
Load the appropriate cycle from the user folder. Available cycles include:

TBD – list current cycle names (e.g., “Straw 5 Chamber,” “Full 12,” “Full 12 minus #4”)

When the Picarro G2508 is warm, press “Start Cycle”
Check all chambers to ensure good seals
If a generator is in use, check fuel every two hours and top off. Release pressure before inserting the nozzle into the filler throat. Open the valve and press the green button for 3–5 second intervals, checking between fills to see if fuel is at or near the red line.
Aim for at least 3 complete measurement cycles. For irrigation studies, target 2 cycles before irrigation, 2 during, and 2 after.



7.7 Shutdown

After at least two post-irrigation cycles (or at the end of the measurement period), begin retrieving chambers after each one completes its measurement, starting with chamber #1
Cap all tube ends with a glove secured by tape
Carefully coil each set of tubes and cables to limit twisting and scratching of the Teflon. Zip-tie or Velcro together and stack in order on the ground.
Remove chambers from the sampling locations. Separate bases from chambers and repackage into boxes.
When the final chamber measurement is complete, end the sampling cycle in the software
Connect a spare chamber to a channel and select the “Desiccate” method. Run dry air through the Picarro for 10 minutes to prevent condensation damage (Picarro, Inc., 2021).
Initiate the Picarro shutdown sequence; select the option for moving the instrument
After the Picarro has fully shut down, manually switch off in this order:

Multiplexer
Picarro
Vacuum pump
Power strip

title: Greenhouse Gas Measurements – Picarro G2508 with Eosense Soil Flux Chambers
text:
8 Calibration
The Picarro G2508 analyzer calibration is intended to be performed infrequently (Picarro, Inc., 2021). The procedure requires three calibration standards per gas species (two points define the calibration line and a third intermediate point is used for verification).

8.1 Calibration Procedure

Select calibration standards that span the representative range of concentrations the analyzer will typically measure. A concentration of zero is acceptable for the low-end standard.
Introduce the first calibration standard into the analyzer for long enough to yield a stable reading
Record the stated concentration of the standard and the analyzer’s displayed value
Repeat for the remaining two standards
Plot the data with the analyzer’s reported concentration on the horizontal axis and the standards’ stated concentrations on the vertical axis
Calculate a linear best-fit equation. The slope and intercept are used to apply a correction to the analyzer’s factory calibration.







Note



TBD – develop a dedicated calibration SOP including parts to order (permeation tubes, calibration gas cylinders) and a step-by-step calibration workflow. Contact Karrin Alstad at Picarro (408-962-3991) for calibration supplies.

title: Greenhouse Gas Measurements – Picarro G2508 with Eosense Soil Flux Chambers
text:
9 Data Export and Analysis

9.1 Using eosAnalyze-AC

On the Picarro desktop, open the “eosAnalyze-AC” program. If it is not on the desktop, navigate to Start Menu and search “eosAnalyze-AC.” Open the “eosAnalyze-AC-v3.4.2” folder and run the .exe application.
You do not need to wait for the Picarro system to warm up if you are only downloading data.
Click “Collect Data.” Enter the start and end times for the period you want to download. Repeat for each cycle separately; combining multiple non-contiguous periods into one export will produce a single table with large time gaps.
Ensure the time zone is set correctly. Pacific Time Zone is UTC-8:00.
Verify the data under “Measurements.” Check that the correct dates, times, and data graphs look reasonable.
Click “Export Data Table” and save the CSV to the desktop or an accessible location.
To export additional data tables, close and reopen the program before creating each new export.
Transfer the .csv files to a USB drive or external hard drive for analysis on another computer. The files are compatible with Excel or R (R Core Team, 2024).



9.2 Troubleshooting Data Export
If data does not load or you see a “No measurements detected” message:

Go to Data > Analyzer Data Path in eosAnalyze-AC. The data path should be \UserData\DataLog_Forerunner\. You should see subfolders organized by year.
Click OK, then retry collecting data.
If the problem persists, use Windows Explorer to search for .DAT files in \UserData\DataLog_Forerunner\YEAR\MONTH\DATE\. The file naming convention is: JFAADS2048-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS-DataLog_Forerunner.dat where JFAADS2048 is the instrument serial number, followed by the date and time the file was created in 24-hour format.



9.3 Flux Calculation
Soil gas fluxes are calculated from the rate of change of gas concentration within the chamber headspace over the closure period. The eosAnalyze-AC software fits both linear and exponential models to the concentration time series for each closure event (Hutchinson & Mosier, 1981; Livingston & Hutchinson, 1995).
\[
F = \frac{V}{A} \cdot \frac{dC}{dt} \cdot \frac{P}{RT}
\]
where:

\(F\) = flux (mass per area per time)
\(V\) = chamber headspace volume (L)
\(A\) = chamber area (m2)
\(dC/dt\) = rate of concentration change (ppm/s)
\(P\) = atmospheric pressure (atm)
\(R\) = ideal gas constant
\(T\) = temperature (K)

TBD – clarify in eosAnalyze-AC output what (L) and (E) designations mean for flux values (likely Linear and Exponential fits). Confirm whether “dead band range” and “chamber offset” in the data processor options need to be set for each deployment.

Verify atmospheric background concentrations before starting each measurement cycle (see table in Section 6.6)

Check chamber seals visually and by monitoring initial concentration traces
Log any chambers that fail to open or close properly and remove them from the dataset
Do not disconnect chambers from the multiplexer during an active measurement cycle, as this can cause the data processor to miss measurements
Ensure the FRMonitor software recognizes all connected chambers at startup; use the “System Info” button to verify. Chambers not recognized will not record data even if they open and close.
Use FRMonitor software version 1.6.2 or later to schedule measurements


10.1 Biases and Interferences

Ambient temperature extremes can prevent the analyzer from stabilizing properly
High-moisture gas samples can cause condensation damage. Always run dry air through the instrument for several minutes before shutdown (Picarro, Inc., 2021).

14 Appendix A: Troubleshooting


14.1 Days with Unexpected Data
If data appears on unexpected Julian days, check whether the system clock or local time on the analyzer has been changed. Compare the processed measurements against field notes to identify obvious gaps that may correspond to mislabeled days.


14.2 Days That Should Have More Data
Errors in FRMonitor log files can cause the data processor to overlook measurements. If measurements appear to be missing, check the FRMonitor logs for errors. Do not disconnect chambers from the multiplexer while it is actively running a measurement cycle, as this can cause the data processor to miss measurements, especially if the chamber was closed when removed.


14.3 Days Where Some Chambers Are Missing
If certain chambers (e.g., #1 or #2) are not sending data, this indicates either a communication issue between the multiplexer and analyzer or that the chambers were not connected. Verify that the FRMonitor software recognizes all connected chambers at startup using the “System Info” button. Disconnecting and reconnecting chambers during a measurement cycle can also cause communication errors.


14.4 N2O Noise
N2O measurements from the Picarro G2508 can be noisy at ambient concentrations. TBD – document strategies for reducing N2O noise (e.g., longer closure times, post-processing smoothing, data filtering thresholds). Contact Picarro technical support for recommendations.

title: Air Quality Monitoring with Portable PM Sensors
text:
This SOP describes the assembly, deployment, data retrieval, and post-processing of low-cost particulate matter (PM) sensor networks built around Raspberry Pi single-board computers and Plantower PMS5003/PMS5004 laser-scattering sensors. These sensors estimate PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 mass concentrations and report particle counts in six size bins (>0.3, >0.5, >1.0, >2.5, >5.0, >10.0 \(\mu\)m).
Low-cost PM sensors (LCS) provide spatial and temporal resolution that is not achievable with Federal Reference Method (FRM) or Federal Equivalent Method (FEM) monitors alone (Snyder et al., 2013). However, LCS data require quality screening, relative humidity correction, and calibration against reference instruments to produce scientifically defensible results (Ardon-Dryer et al., 2023; Barkjohn et al., 2021). When properly corrected and quality-controlled, LCS networks can complement regulatory monitoring by filling spatial gaps, supporting community exposure studies, and providing near-real-time information during wildfire smoke events (Morawska et al., 2018).

title: Air Quality Monitoring with Portable PM Sensors

This SOP describes the assembly, deployment, data retrieval, and post-processing of low-cost particulate matter (PM) sensor networks built around Raspberry Pi single-board computers and Plantower PMS5003/PMS5004 laser-scattering sensors. However, LCS data require quality screening, relative humidity correction, and calibration against reference instruments to produce scientifically defensible results (Ardon-Dryer et al., 2023; Barkjohn et al., 2021). When properly corrected and quality-controlled, LCS networks can complement regulatory monitoring by filling spatial gaps, supporting community exposure studies, and providing near-real-time information during wildfire smoke events (Morawska et al., 2018).

Does not apply to: Indoor air quality monitoring (different correction factors apply), gas-phase pollutant monitoring (O3, NO2, CO), or regulatory compliance monitoring.
Location: Field deployment sites in the Pomona College area and surrounding Inland Empire communities.

title: Air Quality Monitoring with Portable PM Sensors
text:
4 Definitions

PM2.5: Particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter less than 2.5 \(\mu\)m. PM2.5 is a criteria pollutant regulated by the US EPA because of its association with cardiovascular and respiratory health effects.
PM10: Particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter less than 10 \(\mu\)m. Includes both fine (PM2.5) and coarse (2.5–10 \(\mu\)m) fractions.
Low-cost sensor (LCS): A PM sensor costing less than approximately $250 per unit, as distinct from regulatory-grade FRM or FEM instruments costing $10,000–$50,000 (Snyder et al., 2013).
Federal Reference Method (FRM): The EPA-designated reference method for measuring criteria pollutants. For PM2.5, the FRM is a gravimetric filter-based method (see SOP-F503).
Federal Equivalent Method (FEM): An air quality measurement method approved by the US EPA as equivalent to the FRM (e.g., beta attenuation monitors).
CF=1: “Standard particles” output from the Plantower sensor, factory-calibrated against Chinese ambient aerosol. This is the starting value for the EPA US-wide correction (Barkjohn et al., 2021).
AQI: Air Quality Index. A standardized index for reporting daily air quality developed by the US EPA, with breakpoints tied to health-based PM2.5 standards.
Collocation: Placing LCS units alongside a reference instrument (or alongside each other) to assess accuracy, precision, and drift. Pre-deployment collocation is a minimum QC requirement.
Sensor drift: Gradual degradation of sensor accuracy over months to years of continuous operation, caused by fan wear, laser aging, and contamination of the optical chamber (Malings et al., 2020).
Hygroscopic growth: The increase in particle size (and thus light scattering) that occurs when ambient RH exceeds approximately 70%, causing LCS to overestimate PM mass concentration. The EPA correction includes an RH term to account for this (Barkjohn et al., 2021; Jayaratne et al., 2018).
PMS-O / PMS-U: Original (pre-mid-2021) and updated (post-mid-2021) versions of the Plantower PMS5003, which differ in internal calibration. PMS-U sensors read lower at concentrations below approximately 16 \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) (Ardon-Dryer et al., 2023).

title: Air Quality Monitoring with Portable PM Sensors
text:
7 Background

7.1 How the Sensors Work
The Plantower PMS5003 and PMS5004 are optical particle counters that use a laser (680 \(\pm\) 10 nm) and a photodiode to detect light scattered by individual particles drawn through the sensing chamber by a small fan. The sensor reports particle counts in six size bins and uses a proprietary algorithm to estimate PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 mass concentrations in \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) (Barkjohn et al., 2021).
The sensor outputs data in two formats: CF=1 (“standard particles,” factory-calibrated against Chinese urban aerosol) and CF_atm (“atmospheric environment,” with an additional adjustment at higher concentrations). For ambient monitoring in the US, the CF=1 output is used as the starting point for correction (Barkjohn et al., 2021).


7.2 Known Limitations

Relative humidity sensitivity: At RH >70%, hygroscopic particle growth inflates readings. An RH correction term is essential (Barkjohn et al., 2021; Jayaratne et al., 2018).
Particle size dependence: The sensors underestimate PM2.5 when coarse particles (dust) dominate the size distribution. They perform best for fine-mode aerosol (PM1) (Jaffe et al., 2023; Ouimette et al., 2026).
Batch variability: Plantower changed the PMS5003 calibration in mid-2021, producing sensors that read lower at low concentrations. These can be identified by their particle count ratios and corrected (Ardon-Dryer et al., 2023).
Sensor aging: Fan and laser degradation over months to years of continuous operation can reduce sensitivity. Long-term field evaluations show measurable drift after 6–12 months of continuous outdoor deployment (Malings et al., 2020). Periodic collocation with a reference instrument is needed.

title: Air Quality Monitoring with Portable PM Sensors
text:
9 Procedure

9.1 Sensor Assembly and Software Setup

Flash the microSD card with Raspberry Pi OS Lite.
Install the sensor-reading Python script (maintained in the project repository). The script reads the PMS5003/5004 via serial (UART) and the BME280 via I2C, logging timestamped readings to a CSV file on the SD card.
Configure the Pi for headless operation (enable SSH, set Wi-Fi credentials if applicable, set timezone to America/Los_Angeles).
Connect the PMS sensor ribbon cable and the BME280 module.
Power on the unit and verify that the sensor LED illuminates and the fan spins. Check the log file for valid readings.
Allow at least 30 seconds of warm-up before trusting data (Plantower Technology, 2016).



9.2 Collocation (Pre-Deployment Calibration)
Before field deployment, collocate all sensor units at a single location for a minimum of 48 hours:

Place all units within 1 m of each other, at the same height, with inlets facing the same direction.
Compare readings across units to identify outliers or malfunctioning sensors.
If a reference instrument (FRM, FEM, or BAM) is available, collocate sensors with it to develop a site-specific correction factor (Barkjohn et al., 2021).
Calculate inter-sensor coefficients of variation (CV). Units with CV >15% relative to the group median should be inspected and recalibrated or replaced.



9.3 Site Selection

Mount sensors 2–4 m above ground level, away from direct emission sources (exhaust vents, barbecues, construction).
Orient the inlet away from prevailing wind to reduce rain intrusion.
Ensure access to power (AC outlet, solar panel, or battery).
Record GPS coordinates, mounting height, distance to nearest road, and land use context.



9.4 Deployment

Secure the enclosure at the selected location using zip ties, brackets, or straps.
Connect power.
Verify operation by SSH into the Pi and checking the live log.
Record the deployment date/time, site ID, sensor serial number, and any notes in the field notebook and project metadata file.



9.5 Data Retrieval
Retrieve data at regular intervals (weekly to monthly):

SSH into the Pi and copy the CSV log file to your laptop using scp or rsync.
Alternatively, remove the microSD card and copy files directly.
Archive the raw file immediately; never edit the original.
Check the log for gaps (power outages, sensor freezes).



9.6 Sensor Maintenance

Inspect the inlet for debris, spider webs, or insect nests at each data retrieval visit.
Replace sensors after approximately 2 years of continuous outdoor operation, or sooner if collocation checks show degraded performance (Malings et al., 2020).
Clean the exterior of the enclosure. Do not open the PMS sensor housing.



9.7 Decommissioning

Power off the unit.
Retrieve the final data file.
Remove the enclosure and all mounting hardware.
Leave no trace at the site.

title: Air Quality Monitoring with Portable PM Sensors
text:
10 Data Processing and Correction

10.1 Overview
Raw PM2.5 readings from PMS5003/5004 sensors overestimate FRM/FEM concentrations by approximately 40% under typical US ambient conditions (Barkjohn et al., 2021). The EPA US-wide correction reduces root mean square error from approximately 8 \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) to 3 \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) (Barkjohn et al., 2021).


10.2 Data Cleaning


Code
library(tidyverse)

raw <- read_csv("data/raw/site01_20260101_20260201.csv")

raw <- raw %>%
  filter(
    pm25_cf1 >= 0,
    pm25_cf1 < 1000,
    rh_pct >= 0,
    rh_pct <= 100,
    temp_c > -40,
    temp_c < 60
  )

# Flag and remove sensor freeze periods
raw <- raw %>%
  mutate(frozen = pm25_cf1 == lag(pm25_cf1) &
                  pm25_cf1 == lag(pm25_cf1, 2) &
                  pm25_cf1 == lag(pm25_cf1, 3)) %>%
  filter(!frozen | is.na(frozen)) %>%
  select(-frozen)




10.3 EPA US-Wide Correction (Barkjohn et al., 2021)
\[
\text{PM}_{2.5,\text{corrected}} = 0.524 \times \text{PM}_{2.5,\text{cf1}}
  - 0.0862 \times \text{RH} + 5.75
\]
where PM2.5,cf1 is the CF=1 output (\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\)) and RH is relative humidity (%) (Barkjohn et al., 2021).


Code
raw <- raw %>%
  mutate(
    pm25_corrected = 0.524 * pm25_cf1 - 0.0862 * rh_pct + 5.75,
    pm25_corrected = pmax(pm25_corrected, 0)
  )








Important



This correction was developed for typical ambient and smoke-impacted conditions. It underestimates PM2.5 during dust-dominated events. For dust correction, see Jaffe et al. (2023) and Ouimette et al. (2026).




10.4 Identifying Updated (Post-2021) PMS5003 Sensors
If your sensors are PMS-U (post-mid-2021), apply the additional linear correction from Ardon-Dryer et al. (2023) before the EPA correction. PMS-U sensors can be identified by a count0.3/count0.5 ratio approximately 3 times lower than PMS-O sensors.


10.5 Hourly and Daily Averaging


Code
hourly <- raw %>%
  mutate(hour = floor_date(timestamp, "hour")) %>%
  group_by(hour) %>%
  summarize(
    pm25_mean = mean(pm25_corrected, na.rm = TRUE),
    pm25_sd   = sd(pm25_corrected, na.rm = TRUE),
    rh_mean   = mean(rh_pct, na.rm = TRUE),
    temp_mean = mean(temp_c, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_obs     = n(),
    .groups   = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_obs >= 45)

daily <- hourly %>%
  mutate(date = as_date(hour)) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarize(
    pm25_daily = mean(pm25_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_hours    = n(),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_hours >= 18)




10.6 AQI Calculation


Code
calc_aqi <- function(pm25) {
  breakpoints <- tibble(
    lo_pm  = c(0.0, 9.1, 35.5, 55.5, 125.5, 225.5),
    hi_pm  = c(9.0, 35.4, 55.4, 125.4, 225.4, 325.4),
    lo_aqi = c(0, 51, 101, 151, 201, 301),
    hi_aqi = c(50, 100, 150, 200, 300, 500)
  )
  bp <- breakpoints %>% filter(pm25 >= lo_pm, pm25 <= hi_pm)
  if (nrow(bp) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  with(bp, lo_aqi + (hi_aqi - lo_aqi) / (hi_pm - lo_pm) * (pm25 - lo_pm))
}

daily <- daily %>%
  mutate(aqi = map_dbl(pm25_daily, calc_aqi))

title: Soil Profile Description
text: This SOP describes the systematic description of soil profiles exposed in hand-dug pits or road cuts. A soil profile description documents the vertical sequence of horizons, their physical and morphological properties, and the relationships among them. Profile descriptions are fundamental to soil classification, land use assessment, understanding pedogenic processes, and interpreting laboratory analytical data in a landscape context (Schoeneberger et al., 2012; Soil Survey Staff, 2022). The systematic description of soil horizons is the foundation of pedology and provides the morphological evidence from which pedogenic processes (e.g., eluviation, illuviation, gleization) are inferred (Buol et al., 2011; Schaetzl & Anderson, 2015).
