text:
4 Definitions

Consistence: The resistance of soil to deformation or rupture; described at field moisture conditions (loose, very friable, friable, firm, very firm, extremely firm for moist soil) and separately for dry and wet conditions (sticky, plastic ratings).
Horizon: A layer of soil approximately parallel to the land surface with distinct physical, chemical, or biological properties that differ from adjacent layers; the fundamental unit of soil profile description; designated by master symbols (O, A, E, B, C,

and subordinate suffixes (e.g., Bt, Bhs).

Horizon boundary: The contact between two soil horizons; described by distinctness (very abrupt, abrupt, clear, gradual, diffuse based on transition thickness) and topography (smooth, wavy, irregular, broken).
Master horizon: A primary genetic horizon designation: O (organic surface), A (mineral surface with organic matter accumulation), E (eluviated), B (subsoil with illuvial accumulation or alteration), C (parent material), R (bedrock).
Ped: A natural soil aggregate formed by soil-forming processes; described by type (granular, blocky, subangular blocky, prismatic, columnar, platy) and size class (very fine, fine, medium, coarse, very coarse).
Pedon: The smallest three-dimensional body of soil that fully represents the range of properties of a given soil; typically 1–10 m2 in surface area and extending to the C horizon or bedrock.
Soil profile: A vertical cross-section of soil from the surface to the parent material or bedrock, exposing the sequence of genetic horizons; described in a pit or by augering.
Soil structure: The arrangement and organization of soil particles into aggregates (peds); described by type (shape), class (size), and grade (distinctness of development: structureless, weak, moderate, strong).
Texture (field): The relative proportions of sand, silt, and clay in the fine earth fraction (less than 2 mm); estimated in the field by the feel method (see SOP-F401) and confirmed by hydrometer analysis (see SOP-L401).

title: Soil Profile Description
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Soil pits deeper than 50 cm can collapse, especially in sandy or dry soils. Pits deeper than 1.2 m (4 ft) require shoring or sloping per OSHA regulations (29 CFR 1926, Subpart P). Never enter an unshored pit deeper than 1.2 m.
Biological: Soil-borne pathogens; ticks, snakes, and burrowing insects in riparian or wildland settings.
Environmental: Heat exposure; dehydration during summer fieldwork.




5.1 Required PPE

Closed-toed shoes or field boots
Nitrile gloves
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
Safety glasses (when chopping through indurated horizons)
Hard hat (if working in deep pits or near road cuts)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety. If a pit wall collapses while someone is inside, call 911 immediately. Do not attempt excavation without proper rescue training and equipment.

title: Soil Profile Description
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pit Excavation

Select the pit location based on the project objectives and landscape position. Avoid disturbed areas, utility lines, and locations near structures.
Excavate a pit approximately 50 cm wide and 80–120 cm deep (or to the parent material or restrictive layer, whichever is shallower). One vertical face should be oriented to receive even light (face the sun or open shade).
Pile excavated soil upslope and on a tarp to facilitate backfilling.
Clean the profile face with the flat-edged spade or soil knife to expose a fresh, undisturbed surface. Avoid smearing.



7.2 Identifying Horizon Boundaries

Examine the profile face for changes in color, texture, structure, roots, pores, and cementation. Each distinct zone is a horizon.
Mark horizon boundaries with flagging tape pins or nails.
Measure the depth of each boundary from the soil surface using the metric tape. Record the upper and lower boundary depth for each horizon (e.g., A: 0–18 cm; Bt: 18–45 cm).
Describe the boundary distinctness and topography:




Distinctness
Width of Transition




Abrupt
< 2 cm


Clear
2–5 cm


Gradual
5–15 cm


Diffuse
> 15 cm






Topography
Description




Smooth
Nearly a plane


Wavy
Pockets wider than deep


Irregular
Pockets deeper than wide


Broken
Discontinuous



Boundary distinctness reflects the rate and nature of pedogenic change between horizons; abrupt boundaries often indicate a lithologic discontinuity or a strong process boundary (e.g., plowing), while diffuse boundaries suggest gradual, ongoing translocation (Schaetzl & Anderson, 2015).


7.3 Describing Each Horizon
For each horizon, record the following properties:
Horizon designation: Use standard USDA master horizon symbols (O, A, E, B, C, R) with appropriate suffixes (t, k, w, g, etc.) (Soil Survey Division Staff, 2017). When assigning subordinate suffixes (e.g., t for clay accumulation, k for carbonate, g for gleying), verify the morphological evidence for each suffix against the criteria in Keys to Soil Taxonomy (Soil Survey Staff, 2022) to ensure that the designation supports formal classification.
Color: Determine moist and dry color using Munsell charts per SOP-F405. Record matrix color and any mottles.
Texture: Determine texture by feel per SOP-F401. Record the USDA textural class (e.g., sandy loam, clay loam).
Structure: Describe the type, size, and grade:



Type
Shape Description




Granular
Roughly spherical, porous


Blocky (angular)
Sharp-edged blocks


Blocky (subangular)
Rounded-edge blocks


Platy
Flat, plate-like


Prismatic
Vertical columns, flat tops


Columnar
Vertical columns, rounded tops


Massive
No visible structure (coherent mass)


Single grain
No structure (loose, individual particles)



Size: very fine, fine, medium, coarse, very coarse (ranges depend on structure type; consult the Field Book for Describing and Sampling Soils).
Grade: weak, moderate, strong.
Soil structure type and grade influence water movement, root penetration, and aeration. Strongly developed angular blocky structure in B horizons often correlates with high clay content and shrink-swell behavior, while granular structure in A horizons is associated with biological activity and high organic matter (Schaetzl & Anderson, 2015; Soil Survey Division Staff, 2017).
Consistence: Describe the resistance to rupture at the appropriate moisture state:

Dry: loose, soft, slightly hard, hard, very hard, extremely hard
Moist: loose, very friable, friable, firm, very firm, extremely firm
Wet: nonsticky/nonplastic to very sticky/very plastic

Roots: Record abundance (few, common, many) and size (very fine, fine, medium, coarse).
Pores: Record abundance and size.
Effervescence: Apply 1–2 drops of 10% HCl to the horizon face and record the reaction:



Effervescence
Description




None
No visible bubbles


Slight
Few bubbles, barely audible


Strong
Obvious bubbles, clearly audible


Violent
Vigorous bubbling, foam



Other features: Record any clay films, coatings, concretions, cementation, or biological features (krotovinas, worm casts).


7.4 Site Description
Record the following site-level information:

GPS coordinates per SOP-F006
Slope (percent) and aspect (degrees)
Landscape position (summit, shoulder, backslope, footslope, toeslope)
Parent material (if identifiable: alluvium, colluvium, residuum, loess, etc.). At EA Program sites in the Pomona/Claremont area, parent materials are commonly alluvium derived from the San Gabriel Mountains or residuum from granitic bedrock, and argillic horizons (Bt) are frequently developed in older geomorphic surfaces (Buol et al., 2011).
Vegetation and land use
Drainage class (excessively drained to very poorly drained)
Depth to water table or bedrock (if encountered)
Evidence of erosion or deposition



7.5 Photography

Place a ruler or scale bar vertically against the profile face.
Photograph the entire profile with horizon labels visible.
Take close-up photos of features of interest (mottles, clay films, cementation, root channels).
Record photo numbers in the field notebook.



7.6 Backfilling
Backfill the pit promptly after description and sampling. Replace soil in reverse order (subsoil first, topsoil last). Compact gently to prevent subsidence. Restore surface litter.

8 Quality Control

Use the NRCS Field Book for Describing and Sampling Soils as the authoritative reference for all terminology and classification.
Have a second observer verify at least the horizon designations and colors for profiles used in research publications.
Photograph every profile with a scale bar as a permanent record.
Cross-check field texture estimates with laboratory hydrometer results (SOP-L401) for at least one horizon per profile.

title: Soil Color Determination (Munsell)
text: This SOP describes the field determination of soil color using the Munsell Soil Color Charts. Soil color is one of the most readily observable soil properties and provides information about organic matter content, drainage and aeration status, mineralogy, and degree of weathering (Munsell Color, 2009; Schoeneberger et al., 2012). Lower values (darker soils) generally reflect higher organic matter content, especially in A horizons, while high chroma indicates well-drained, oxidized conditions and low chroma suggests prolonged saturation or reducing environments (Lynn & Pearson, 1993; Shields et al., 1966). Red and yellow hues are controlled primarily by iron oxide mineralogy: hematite produces redder hues (5YR and redder), while goethite produces yellowish-brown hues (7.5YR–10YR) (Schwertmann, 1993; Torrent & Schwertmann, 1983). Consistent color determination is essential for soil profile descriptions (SOP-F407), wetland delineation, and site characterization.

title: Soil Color Determination (Munsell)
text:
4 Definitions

Chroma: The colorimetric purity or saturation of a color; the third component of Munsell notation (e.g., the 4 in 10YR 4/4); low chroma (2 or less) in subsurface horizons indicates gleying and periodic waterlogging.
Gleying: A reduction process in waterlogged soils that depletes iron and produces low-chroma (gray, blue-gray, or green-gray) matrix colors; a diagnostic indicator of hydric soil conditions.
Hue: The dominant spectral color in Munsell notation (e.g., 10YR, 7.5YR, 2.5Y, Gley 1); the first element of a Munsell designation; corresponds to the dominant wavelength of reflected light.
Matrix color: The dominant color occupying more than 50% of the exposed soil face; recorded first in the Munsell notation before mottles or redoximorphic features.
Mottle: A spot or blotch of color contrasting with the matrix color; described by abundance (few, common, many), size (fine, medium, coarse), and contrast (faint, distinct, prominent).
Munsell color system: A standardized three-dimensional color notation (Hue Value/Chroma) used universally in soil science for objective color description; readings must be made in consistent natural or reference lighting conditions.
Redoximorphic features: Color patterns caused by reduction and oxidation of iron and manganese under fluctuating saturation; include masses (concentrations of iron oxides) and depletions (zones of low chroma); diagnostic for hydric soil identification and wetland delineation.
Value: The lightness or darkness of a color in Munsell notation; ranges from 0 (black) to 10 (white); the second component of Munsell notation (e.g., the 4 in 10YR 4/4).

title: Soil Color Determination (Munsell)
text:
7 Background: The Munsell System
Munsell color notation has three components (Munsell Color, 2009; Soil Survey Staff, 2022):

Hue: The dominant spectral color (e.g., 10YR, 2.5Y, 5YR). Pages in the chart book are arranged by hue.
Value: Lightness, from 0 (absolute black) to 10 (absolute white). Vertical axis on each page.
Chroma: Color intensity or saturation, from 0 (neutral gray) outward. Horizontal axis on each page.

A complete Munsell notation is written as: Hue Value/Chroma (e.g., 10YR 4/3). The corresponding color name (e.g., “brown” or “dark yellowish brown”) is listed on each chip.

title: Soil Color Determination (Munsell)
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Sample Preparation

Expose a fresh soil surface by breaking a ped or cutting with a trowel. Do not use smeared or scraped surfaces, as smearing compresses the soil and alters the apparent color.
Determine color on moist soil. If the soil is dry, add a few drops of DI water to a small subsample and allow it to absorb for 30 seconds before reading.
If both moist and dry colors are needed (e.g., for profile descriptions), read the moist color first, then allow a portion to air-dry and read the dry color.



8.2 Reading the Color

Work in natural daylight, ideally under an overcast sky or in open shade. Avoid direct sunlight on the soil or the chart, as glare distorts color perception. Do not read colors under artificial light or at twilight.
Hold the soil sample behind the chart page apertures so that the soil is visible through the holes.
Compare the soil to the color chips (Schoeneberger et al., 2012). Start with the hue page that appears closest, then move to the value row that matches, then slide along the chroma axis.
Select the chip that most closely matches the soil. If the soil falls between two chips, record the notation of the nearest chip and note “between X and Y” in the field notebook.
Record the full Munsell notation and the color name:

Example: 10YR 3/2 (very dark grayish brown)

If the soil contains mottles or redoximorphic features, record the matrix color and then the mottle color(s) separately, noting the abundance (few, common, many), size (fine, medium, coarse), and contrast (faint, distinct, prominent).



8.3 Special Cases
Organic soils (O horizons, peat): Use the Gley pages or the 10YR page with very low value and chroma. Very dark colors (value 2 or less) are common.
Gleyed soils: Use the Gley 1 and Gley 2 pages for soils with chroma of 2 or less and hues bluer than 5Y. Gleyed colors indicate prolonged saturation and reducing conditions.
Mottled soils: Record:

Matrix color (dominant color occupying more than 50% of the surface)
Mottle colors (each distinct color)
For each mottle: abundance, size, and contrast




Abundance
Definition




Few
< 2% of exposed surface


Common
2–20% of exposed surface


Many
> 20% of exposed surface






Size
Definition




Fine
< 5 mm diameter


Medium
5–15 mm diameter


Coarse
> 15 mm diameter










Contrast
Definition




Faint
Hue, value, and chroma differ by 1 unit or less from matrix


Distinct
Differ by 2–3 units in value or chroma


Prominent
Differ by more than 3 units



Redoximorphic features are diagnostic for hydric soil identification and wetland delineation; consistent recording of mottle properties is critical for regulatory applications (Soil Survey Division Staff, 2017).

title: Soil Color Determination (Munsell)
text:
9 Quality Control

At the start of each field season, have two or more observers independently read the same soil samples to assess inter-observer agreement. Readings should agree within one chip (one unit of value or chroma) in at least 80% of comparisons.
Replace Munsell charts when color chips are faded, soiled, or damaged. Faded chips produce systematic errors.
Record lighting conditions (overcast, open shade, sunny) in the field notebook; lighting affects color perception.
Always specify whether the reading was on moist or dry soil.

Digital colorimeters and smartphone-based color apps are increasingly used as supplements to visual Munsell matching; however, instrument readings and visual assessments can disagree, especially at low chroma and low value, so visual Munsell determination remains the standard for USDA soil survey and regulatory work (Viscarra Rossel et al., 2006).

title: Soil Infiltration Rate – Ring Infiltrometer Method
text: This procedure describes the field measurement of soil infiltration rate using single-ring and double-ring infiltrometers. Infiltration rate is the velocity at which water enters the soil surface, typically expressed in cm/h or mm/h. It is a key parameter for evaluating stormwater management, irrigation efficiency, soil compaction, hydrologic modeling, and land use impacts on soil physical properties. The double-ring method follows ASTM D3385 (ASTM International, 2018); the single-ring method follows Bouwer (1986). Infiltration measurements are also essential for calibrating hydrologic models and for evaluating the effects of soil sealing in urban environments (Hillel, 1998; Reynolds et al., 2002).

title: Soil Infiltration Rate – Ring Infiltrometer Method

title: Soil Infiltration Rate – Ring Infiltrometer Method
text:
4 Definitions

Double-ring infiltrometer: A measurement apparatus consisting of two concentric steel rings driven into the soil surface; the inner ring provides the measurement zone; the outer ring creates a buffer that minimizes lateral flow from the inner ring, enforcing predominantly vertical infiltration.
Final infiltration rate (steady-state rate): The constant rate at which water enters the soil after the soil profile is saturated and the infiltration rate has stabilized; approximates the saturated hydraulic conductivity (\(K_{sat}\)) of the surface soil.
Green-Ampt model: A physically based infiltration model that describes the rate of water entry into soil as a function of saturated hydraulic conductivity, matric suction at the wetting front, and soil moisture deficit; used to interpret falling-head infiltration data.
Infiltration rate: The volumetric flux of water entering the soil surface per unit area per unit time, expressed in mm h-1 or cm h-1; decreases from an initially high rate in dry soil to a lower, stable final rate as the soil wets.
Macropore flow: Preferential movement of water through large continuous pores (earthworm burrows, root channels, structural cracks); produces non-uniform wetting and anomalously high initial infiltration rates that do not reflect bulk soil hydraulic conductivity.
Matric potential: The energy status of soil water due to capillary and adsorptive forces; expressed in kPa or cm H2O; drives water movement from wet to dry zones during infiltration.
Saturated hydraulic conductivity (\(K_{sat}\)): The proportionality constant in Darcy’s law relating water flux to hydraulic gradient under saturated conditions; the primary soil hydraulic property controlling drainage, runoff, and deep percolation; approximated by the steady-state infiltration rate.
Single-ring infiltrometer: A simplified apparatus using one ring driven into the soil; easier to deploy than double-ring but subject to lateral flow error; appropriate for screening or comparative measurements when absolute \(K_{sat}\) is not required.

title: Soil Infiltration Rate – Ring Infiltrometer Method
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Site Selection and Preparation

Select test locations based on the project sampling plan. Avoid locations with visible animal burrows, large root channels, cracks, or other macropore features unless the objective is specifically to characterize preferential flow.
Record GPS coordinates and site description
Clear surface litter and loose organic debris from a 1 x 1 m area without disturbing the mineral soil surface
Note antecedent conditions in the field notebook: recent rainfall, soil moisture (qualitative: dry, moist, wet), and surface condition (bare, vegetated, crusted)







TipTip



Collect a companion bulk density core (SOP-F402) and a texture-by-feel assessment (SOP-F401) at each infiltration test location. These measurements help interpret the infiltration results.




7.2 Ring Installation – Double-Ring Method

Center the inner ring at the test location
Place the driving cap or wooden plank on top of the ring
Drive the inner ring vertically into the soil to a depth of approximately 5–10 cm (2–4 in) using even blows from the sledge. Avoid tilting the ring; check periodically with the level.
Measure and record the insertion depth on at least two sides
Center the outer ring around the inner ring. Drive it to approximately 10–15 cm (4–6 in), deeper than the inner ring, to prevent test water from escaping beneath the outer ring.
Check that the inner ring is still centered and level







Important



Do not drive the rings deeper than necessary. Over-driving compresses the soil along the ring walls and creates an artificial seal that reduces measured infiltration rates. If the soil cracks or separates from the ring wall, abandon the test location and start at a new spot.




7.3 Ring Installation – Single-Ring Method

Place the single ring at the test location
Drive to approximately 5 cm depth using the same technique as above
For best accuracy, use the largest diameter ring available (90 cm or larger reduces lateral flow error) (Bouwer, 1986). Single-ring measurements tend to overestimate true vertical infiltration because lateral divergence below the ring cannot be eliminated; the magnitude of overestimation decreases as ring diameter increases (Gregory et al., 2006).



7.4 Initial Filling

Place a sheet of plastic or burlap on the soil surface inside the inner ring (and inside the annular space for the double-ring method) to cushion the water and prevent soil disturbance during filling
Gently pour water into the outer ring (annular space) first, then into the inner ring, to approximately 10–15 cm depth
Carefully remove the plastic or burlap
For the double-ring method, maintain the water level in the outer ring at approximately the same height as the inner ring throughout the test. This eliminates the lateral pressure gradient and forces flow beneath the inner ring to be vertical.



7.5 Measuring Infiltration Rate
Falling-head method (most common for EA Program):

Record the initial water level in the inner ring and the start time
Allow the water to infiltrate. Record the water level at regular time intervals. Suggested intervals:




Elapsed Time
Recording Interval




0–30 minutes
Every 5 minutes


30–60 minutes
Every 10 minutes


60–120 minutes
Every 15 minutes


120+ minutes
Every 30 minutes




When the water level drops to approximately 3 cm above the soil surface, refill to the original level and record the new starting level and time. Record each refill event.
Maintain the water level in the outer ring by refilling as needed.
Continue the test until the infiltration rate reaches a steady state (three or more consecutive readings with less than 10% change). This is the steady-state or “final” infiltration rate.
For most soils, steady state is reached within 1–3 hours. Clayey soils may require 4–6 hours or longer.

Constant-head method (Mariotte bottle):

Set up the Mariotte bottle to maintain a constant water depth (typically 5–10 cm) in the inner ring
Record the volume of water consumed from the bottle at regular time intervals
Calculate the infiltration rate from the volume consumed, the ring area, and the time interval
Continue until steady state is reached



7.6 Ending the Test

Record the final water level, time, and cumulative number of refills
Remove the rings by rocking gently and pulling upward
Backfill the holes and restore the site
Record any observations about the wetting front depth, root channels, or other features visible after ring removal

title: Soil Infiltration Rate – Ring Infiltrometer Method
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Calculations
Infiltration rate for each time interval (falling-head method):
\[
f = \frac{\Delta h}{\Delta t}
\]
where \(f\) = infiltration rate (cm/h), \(\Delta h\) = drop in water level (cm) during the interval, and \(\Delta t\) = duration of the interval (h). If the ring was refilled during the interval, add the refill depth to \(\Delta h\).
Cumulative infiltration:
\[
F = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i \times \Delta t_i
\]
where \(F\) = cumulative infiltration (cm) and \(n\) = number of intervals.
Steady-state infiltration rate (\(f_c\)) is the final, approximately constant rate, typically reported as the mean of the last three or more consistent readings.


8.2 Expected Ranges
Steady-state infiltration rates vary widely with soil texture and structure:



Soil Type / Condition
Expected \(f_c\) (cm/h)




Coarse sand, well-structured
5 – 25+


Sandy loam
2.5 – 7.5


Loam, well-structured
1.0 – 5.0


Silt loam
0.5 – 2.5


Clay loam
0.1 – 1.0


Compacted or crusted soil
less than 0.5



Values outside the range of 0.01–50 cm/h should be investigated for measurement error or unusual soil conditions.
Rates measured at EA Program sites in the Pomona/Claremont area should be interpreted in the context of the local aridic moisture regime, where antecedent moisture is often very low and hydrophobicity may develop under prolonged dry conditions (Hillel, 1998). Urban and peri-urban soils may show infiltration rates well below their textural expectation due to compaction from foot traffic and construction (lai2010?).


8.3 QC Requirements

Conduct a minimum of three replicate tests per plot or treatment to capture spatial variability
Record antecedent soil moisture and recent precipitation for each test; these strongly affect initial rates
Verify that the outer ring water level is maintained throughout the test (double-ring method)
Inspect ring installation for gaps between the ring wall and the soil; if gaps are visible, the test is invalid
Ring insertion depth and ponded water depth both influence measured infiltration rate; standardize these dimensions across replicates and sites to ensure comparability (Gregory et al., 2006).
Plot the infiltration rate versus time curve for each test. A monotonically decreasing curve approaching a constant value is expected. Erratic increases may indicate macropore activation or ring leakage.

section: 13 Appendix B: Example Calculation and Plotting
text:
13 Appendix B: Example Calculation and Plotting



Code
library(tidyverse)

# Example data from a falling-head double-ring test
# Ring inner diameter = 30 cm
ring_diam_cm <- 30
ring_area_cm2 <- pi * (ring_diam_cm / 2)^2

infiltration <- tibble(
  elapsed_min = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180),
  water_level_cm = c(15.0, 13.8, 12.9, 12.1, 11.4, 10.2, 8.8, 7.6,
                     5.8, 4.2, 2.8, 1.5)
)

# Calculate interval infiltration rates
infiltration <- infiltration %>%
  mutate(
    delta_h_cm = -diff(c(NA, water_level_cm)),
    delta_t_h = c(NA, diff(elapsed_min)) / 60,
    rate_cm_h = delta_h_cm / delta_t_h,
    cumulative_cm = cumsum(replace_na(delta_h_cm, 0))
  )

# Steady-state rate (last 3 intervals)
f_c <- mean(tail(infiltration$rate_cm_h[!is.na(infiltration$rate_cm_h)], 3))
cat(sprintf("Steady-state infiltration rate: %.2f cm/h\n", f_c))

# Plot infiltration rate vs time
ggplot(infiltration %>% filter(!is.na(rate_cm_h)),
       aes(x = elapsed_min, y = rate_cm_h)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = f_c, linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = max(infiltration$elapsed_min) * 0.7,
           y = f_c + 0.3,
           label = sprintf("f[c] == %.2f~cm/h", f_c),
           parse = TRUE, color = "blue") +
  labs(
    x = "Elapsed time (min)",
    y = "Infiltration rate (cm/h)",
    title = "Double-Ring Infiltration Test"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

14 Appendix C: Troubleshooting









Symptom
Probable Cause
Corrective Action




Water leaks around the outside of the ring
Insufficient insertion depth; gap between ring wall and soil
Drive ring deeper; pack bentonite or moist soil around the outside base


Infiltration rate increases mid-test

Ring deformed during installation
Rocks or roots; excessive force

Soil disturbed inside the ring

Single-ring rate much higher than expected
Lateral flow beneath the ring

title: Soil Texture Determination by Feel (Ribbon Method)
text: This SOP describes the field determination of soil texture using the texture-by-feel (ribbon) method. This rapid, equipment-free technique classifies soil into one of 12 USDA textural classes based on how a moistened soil sample behaves when formed into a ball, extruded into a ribbon, and rubbed between the fingers (Soil Survey Division Staff, 2017; Thien, 1979). Field texturing provides an immediate estimate of sand, silt, and clay content without laboratory analysis.

title: Soil Texture Determination by Feel (Ribbon Method)
text: This SOP describes the field determination of soil texture using the texture-by-feel (ribbon) method. This rapid, equipment-free technique classifies soil into one of 12 USDA textural classes based on how a moistened soil sample behaves when formed into a ball, extruded into a ribbon, and rubbed between the fingers (Soil Survey Division Staff, 2017; Thien, 1979). Field texturing provides an immediate estimate of sand, silt, and clay content without laboratory analysis.

title: Soil Texture Determination by Feel (Ribbon Method)
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Field characterization of mineral soils at all EA Program sites; preliminary texture assessment for soil sampling campaigns
Does not apply to: Soils with very high organic matter content (>20%, e.g., peat); quantitative particle size analysis (use the hydrometer method, SOP-L401); soils with large gravel or rock fragment content (assess the fine fraction only)
Location: All EA Program field sites; can also be performed on samples brought back to the lab

title: Soil Texture Determination by Feel (Ribbon Method)
text:
4 Definitions

Clay: The finest soil particle size class, with equivalent spherical diameter less than 0.002 mm; imparts stickiness, plasticity, and cohesion to the moist soil; forms a long, flexible ribbon when extruded between thumb and forefinger.
Loam: A textural class with roughly balanced proportions of sand, silt, and clay; exhibits moderate ribbon length (25–50 mm), moderate grittiness, and moderate stickiness; the most common agricultural soil texture.
Plasticity: The ability of moist soil to be molded and deformed without cracking or crumbling; highest in clay-rich soils; assessed by rolling soil into a thread between the palms.
Ribbon: The flat, continuous strip extruded when moist soil is pushed between the thumb and forefinger; ribbon length is the primary diagnostic criterion in the field texture-by-feel method; longer ribbons indicate higher clay content.
Sand: Soil mineral particles with equivalent spherical diameter 0.05–2.0 mm; feels gritty between the fingers; does not form a ribbon; individual grains are visible to the naked eye.
Silt: Soil mineral particles with equivalent spherical diameter 0.002–0.05 mm; feels smooth and floury when dry; slippery and slightly plastic when moist; imparts a silky texture to the soil.
Texture class: A USDA classification category (e.g., sandy loam, silt clay loam, clay) based on the relative percentages of sand, silt, and clay; determined from the USDA textural triangle and confirmed by laboratory hydrometer analysis (see SOP-L401).
Water content (field): The moisture status of the soil at the time of testing; texture-by-feel must be performed on soil adjusted to a defined moist or wet state to produce consistent results across operators.

6.1 Soil Particle Size Fractions

6.2 The USDA Textural Triangle
The 12 USDA textural classes are defined by the percentages of sand, silt, and clay. The texture-by-feel method estimates which class a soil belongs to without measuring exact percentages.





6.3 Why Field Texture Matters

Determines water-holding capacity, drainage, and aeration
Guides sampling strategy (e.g., different sample weights for carbon analysis; see SOP-L406)
Informs the soil texture correction factor for nutrient extractions (see SOP-L403)
Rapid enough to characterize many points across a landscape in a single field day

title: Soil Texture Determination by Feel (Ribbon Method)
text:
9 Procedure

9.1 Collect the Sample

Select a representative location and record GPS coordinates
Clear surface litter and organic debris
Collect approximately a golf-ball-sized amount of mineral soil from the target depth (typically 0–15 cm)
Remove visible roots, gravel, and organic fragments



9.2 Moisten the Sample

Place the soil in your palm
Add water drop by drop from the squeeze bottle while kneading the soil
Continue adding water and kneading until the soil reaches the consistency of modeling clay or putty
The soil should be uniformly moist but not dripping wet
Crush all aggregates between your fingers during kneading







ImportantGetting the Moisture Right



This is the most critical step. If the soil is too dry, it will crumble and you’ll underestimate clay content. If too wet, it will be slippery and you’ll overestimate clay. The target is a smooth, pliable consistency similar to play dough. This may take 2–3 minutes of kneading.






9.3 Test 1: Form a Ball

Try to form the moistened soil into a ball (bolus) by squeezing and rolling in your palm
If the soil will not form a ball, it is Sand. Record and move to the next sample.
If a ball forms, proceed to Test 2





9.4 Test 2: Ribbon Test

Place the ball between your thumb and forefinger
Gently push the soil forward with your thumb, squeezing it into a flat ribbon about 2 mm thick and 1 cm wide
Let the ribbon extend over your forefinger, unsupported, until it breaks from its own weight
Measure the ribbon length with a ruler before it breaks
Repeat 3–5 times and use the longest consistent ribbon

Ribbon length determines clay content:



Ribbon Length
Clay Content
Category




No ribbon forms
< 10%
Low clay


< 2.5 cm (< 1 inch)
10–20%
Low-moderate clay


2.5–5 cm (1–2 inches)
20–35%
Moderate clay


> 5 cm (> 2 inches)
> 35%
High clay







9.5 Test 3: Feel Test (Grittiness and Smoothness)

Take a pea-sized piece of the moistened soil
Place it in your palm and add excess water to make a muddy slurry
Rub the slurry between your thumb and forefinger using a circular motion
Classify the dominant feel:









Feel
Sensation
Dominant Fraction




Gritty
Like rubbing sugar or fine sand between fingers; individual grains felt and possibly heard
Sand-dominated


Smooth
Like rubbing flour or talc; silky, no grains felt
Silt-dominated


Neither
Neither gritty nor silky dominates; sticky
Sand and silt balanced





9.6 Determine Textural Class
Combine the ribbon length and feel test results using the following decision matrix (Thien, 1979):










Gritty Feel
Smooth Feel
Neither Gritty nor Smooth




No ribbon
Sand
Silt
Loam


< 2.5 cm
Sandy loam
Silt loam
Loam


2.5–5 cm
Sandy clay loam
Silty clay loam
Clay loam


> 5 cm
Sandy clay
Silty clay
Clay









TipAdditional Clues




Loamy sand falls between sand and sandy loam: barely forms a ball, very gritty, ribbon <1 cm
Silt (pure): very smooth, almost soapy when wet, forms a weak ball but no ribbon
When in doubt between two classes, record both (e.g., “sandy loam / loam”) and note the uncertainty





9.7 Record Results
Record the textural class, ribbon length, feel, and any notes on the field data sheet (Appendix A). Photograph the ribbon if possible for documentation.

title: Soil Texture Determination by Feel (Ribbon Method)
text:
10 Supplementary Test: Jar Sedimentation
For a semi-quantitative confirmation of field texture, you can perform a jar test on the same soil:

Fill a clear, straight-sided jar (mason jar or pasta sauce jar) one-third full with soil
Fill the jar with water, leaving 2 cm of headspace
Add a pinch of non-foaming dish soap (dispersing agent)
Cap tightly and shake vigorously for 2 minutes
Set the jar on a level surface and do not disturb
After 1 minute, mark the settled layer on the jar (this is sand)
After 2 hours, mark the next layer (this is silt)
After 24–48 hours, the remaining suspended material has settled (this is clay); the water above may still be slightly turbid
Measure the thickness of each layer and calculate approximate percentages









Note



The jar test provides a rough visual estimate only. For precise particle size distribution, use the hydrometer method (SOP-L401).

title: Soil Texture Determination by Feel (Ribbon Method)
text:
11 Quality Control

Calibration: Before independent fieldwork, each observer must practice on at least 5 soils of known texture (confirmed by hydrometer analysis). Results should match the confirmed texture class for at least 4 of 5 samples.
Inter-observer agreement: When multiple observers are surveying, have each observer independently classify at least 10% of the same samples. Agreement should be within one textural class. Inter-observer variability is a well-documented limitation of texture-by-feel; training and calibration reduce but do not eliminate systematic differences among observers (Salley et al., 2018).
Documentation: Record ribbon length to the nearest 0.5 cm, not just the textural class, so results can be reviewed later.
Confirmation: For critical projects, bring duplicate samples back to the lab for hydrometer analysis on at least 10% of field-textured samples.

When texture-by-feel results will inform quantitative analyses (e.g., pedotransfer functions for water-holding capacity), confirm at least 10% of field-textured samples with hydrometer analysis (SOP-L401). The accuracy of the feel method varies by textural class: sandy and clayey soils are identified most reliably, while loams and silt loams are misclassified more often (Salley et al., 2018).

title: eDNA Water Sample Collection
text:
This procedure describes site-specific water collection strategies for environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling across the range of aquatic habitats encountered in EA Program projects: wadeable streams, non-wadeable rivers, lakes and reservoirs, ponds and vernal pools, and constructed wetlands. It supplements SOP-F700 eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation, which covers the core filtration, preservation, and contamination- control protocols that apply to all eDNA water samples regardless of habitat type.
The separation recognizes that contamination prevention, filtration, and preservation (SOP-F700) are universal, while the physical act of collecting water varies with habitat. This SOP addresses the collection step: where to sample within a water body, how many samples to collect, and how to adapt the approach to different hydrological settings (Deiner et al., 2017; Goldberg et al., 2016).

title: eDNA Water Sample Collection
text:
This procedure describes site-specific water collection strategies for environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling across the range of aquatic habitats encountered in EA Program projects: wadeable streams, non-wadeable rivers, lakes and reservoirs, ponds and vernal pools, and constructed wetlands. It supplements SOP-F700 eDNA Field Sampling and Preservation, which covers the core filtration, preservation, and contamination- control protocols that apply to all eDNA water samples regardless of habitat type.
The separation recognizes that contamination prevention, filtration, and preservation (SOP-F700) are universal, while the physical act of collecting water varies with habitat. This SOP addresses the collection step: where to sample within a water body, how many samples to collect, and how to adapt the approach to different hydrological settings (Deiner et al., 2017; Goldberg et al., 2016).

title: eDNA Water Sample Collection
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Water collection for eDNA analysis at all EA Program aquatic field sites. Once water is collected, filtration and preservation follow SOP-F700.
Does not apply to: Soil eDNA or sediment eDNA sampling (see SOP-F701); airborne eDNA; tissue-based DNA sampling; lab-side filtration and extraction (see SOP-L700)
Location: All EA Program surface water field sites

title: eDNA Water Sample Collection
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




PI / Field Lead
Approve sampling design, confirm permits


Trained Personnel
Collect eDNA water samples per this SOP and SOP-F700


New Students

title: eDNA Water Sample Collection
text:
4 Definitions

Capture efficiency: The proportion of target eDNA in the water column that is retained on a filter during collection; influenced by filter pore size, clogging, sample volume, and the physical state (dissolved vs. particulate) of the eDNA.
Closed-system filtration: An eDNA collection method in which water passes through a filter enclosed in a sterile capsule (e.g., Sterivex) without contact with the external environment; minimizes contamination risk compared to open filtration.
Decontamination: The removal or inactivation of exogenous DNA from sampling equipment and surfaces using bleach (10% sodium hypochlorite), UV irradiation, or other validated methods; essential between sites to prevent cross-contamination.
eDNA (environmental DNA): Genetic material shed into the environment by organisms through mucus, feces, gametes, skin cells, and other biological material; collected from water without direct capture of the target organism.
Field blank: A bottle of laboratory-grade water opened and handled at the field site under identical conditions to real samples; processed through the full filtration and extraction workflow to detect field contamination; must yield no target amplification.
Filter pore size: The nominal diameter of pores in the filter membrane; 0.45 µm is the standard for eDNA capture from surface water, retaining bacteria, cells, and particulate-bound DNA while allowing water to pass.
Longmire’s buffer: A non-freezing preservation solution (containing EDTA, Tris, NaCl, SDS, and sucrose) used to preserve eDNA on filters in the field when immediate freezing is not possible; inactivates nucleases and inhibits microbial degradation.
Peristaltic pump: A battery-operated pump used to draw large volumes of water through a filter in the field without the water contacting the pump mechanism; preferred for high-volume eDNA filtration because it reduces contamination risk.
Sterivex filter: A commercially available enclosed 0.22 µm polysulfone cartridge filter; widely used in eDNA studies because the sealed design minimizes contamination, allows direct addition of preservation buffer, and is compatible with standard DNA extraction kits.
Target species detection: The determination of presence or absence of a specific taxon in a water sample based on amplification of taxon-specific eDNA; sensitivity depends on eDNA shedding rate, water volume filtered, detection method (PCR, ddPCR, metabarcoding), and inhibitor load in the extract.

WarningAdditional Hazards by Habitat




Non-wadeable rivers and lakes: Boat access required; drowning risk. PFDs mandatory.
Vernal pools: Often in remote locations with limited access; fragile habitat. Minimize trampling of pool margins.
Constructed wetlands: May contain treated wastewater. Wear doubled gloves and avoid ingestion or skin contact.

title: eDNA Water Sample Collection
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 General Principles (All Habitats)
These principles supplement SOP-F700:

Sample where the target organism is most likely detected. eDNA concentration varies spatially: it is higher near organism activity centers (spawning areas, resting pools, feeding zones) and downstream of occupied habitat in lotic systems (Jane et al., 2015).
Sample volume: Collect at least 1 L per replicate (the volume actually filtered may be less if the filter clogs). Plan for 3 replicates per site unless the study design specifies otherwise.
Sampling order: Within a day, sample sites from least likely to most likely occupied (downstream to upstream in a connected system, or reference sites before impacted sites) to minimize carry-over contamination (Goldberg et al., 2016).



7.2 Wadeable Streams

Approach the sampling point from downstream
Face upstream; submerge the sterile bottle to 10–20 cm below the surface, tilted slightly into the current
Fill to the 1 L mark and cap immediately
For a reach-level composite: collect 250 mL from each of 4 microhabitats (pool tail, riffle margin, run, and backwater) and combine into one bottle
Proceed to filtration per SOP-F700 Section 6.4



7.3 Non-Wadeable Rivers and Bridges

From a bridge or bank, lower a sterile bottle attached to an extension pole or a pre-sterilized Van Dorn sampler to mid-depth
If using an extension pole: open the bottle at depth, fill by current flow, and cap using a pull-string mechanism or retrieve and cap immediately
Record the approximate depth and distance from shore
Decontaminate the extension pole between sites per SOP-F700 Section 6.7



7.4 Lakes and Reservoirs

Collect samples from a boat positioned over the target area (e.g., littoral zone for nearshore species, open water for pelagic species)
For surface eDNA: submerge a sterile bottle to 15–30 cm below the surface from the upwind side of the boat to avoid contamination from the vessel
For depth-specific eDNA (e.g., below the thermocline): deploy a pre-sterilized Van Dorn bottle to the target depth, trip, and retrieve. Transfer to a sterile sample bottle.
If sampling multiple depths, work from deepest to shallowest to minimize disturbance
Record collection depth, water depth, and location (GPS)



7.5 Ponds and Vernal Pools

Approach slowly to minimize sediment disturbance (eDNA can be resuspended from sediment, creating false-positive risk for species no longer present) (Turner et al., 2015)
Collect water from 5–10 cm below the surface near the center or deepest point of the pool
For very shallow pools (less than 15 cm), tip the bottle on its side to fill without disturbing the bottom
If the pool is small (less than 10 m2), a single 1 L grab from the center is acceptable; for larger pools, composite from 3–5 points around the perimeter



7.6 Constructed Wetlands and Treatment Systems

Wear doubled nitrile gloves; these systems may contain treated wastewater, elevated pathogen loads, or chemical residues
Collect from the outflow or from an open water area; avoid collecting from areas with dense emergent vegetation where filtration may be rapid
Collect a field blank at the site using the molecular-grade DI water from the field kit (this is especially important in constructed systems where background DNA loads are high)



7.7 Filtration and Preservation
After collection in any habitat, proceed immediately to filtration and preservation per SOP-F700 Section 6.4. If on-site filtration is not possible, keep samples on ice and filter within 6 hours.

title: eDNA Water Sample Collection
text:
8 Quality Control
All QC requirements from SOP-F700 Section 8 apply. Additional habitat-specific considerations:

For lake depth samples, collect a field blank at the same depth using the same equipment to detect cross-contamination from the Van Dorn or pump
For bridge sampling with an extension pole, collect an equipment blank (DI water poured through the pole apparatus) at least once per event
When sampling connected sites in a watershed, record the order of site visits and the time elapsed between sites

title: Lake and Reservoir Profiling
text: This procedure describes the collection of vertical depth profiles of water quality parameters (temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, conductivity, turbidity, and chlorophyll fluorescence) in lakes, reservoirs, and deep ponds. Depth profiling characterizes thermal stratification, the location and extent of the thermocline and oxycline, and vertical gradients in water chemistry that control nutrient cycling, habitat availability, and water treatment operations (Kalff, 2002; Wetzel, 2001).

title: Lake and Reservoir Profiling
text: This procedure describes the collection of vertical depth profiles of water quality parameters (temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, conductivity, turbidity, and chlorophyll fluorescence) in lakes, reservoirs, and deep ponds. Depth profiling characterizes thermal stratification, the location and extent of the thermocline and oxycline, and vertical gradients in water chemistry that control nutrient cycling, habitat availability, and water treatment operations (Kalff, 2002; Wetzel, 2001).

title: Lake and Reservoir Profiling
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Vertical profiling from boats, docks, or platforms in lentic water bodies (lakes, reservoirs, ponds) and slow-moving deep river pools. Covers both manual sonde profiles and Secchi depth measurements.
Does not apply to: Continuous deployed sonde monitoring (see future SOP); horizontal spatial surveys; stream cross-section water quality (see SOP-F200 for general sonde operation); bathymetric mapping
Location: All EA Program lake and reservoir field sites

title: Lake and Reservoir Profiling
text:
4 Definitions

Epilimnion: The warm, well-mixed, oxygen-rich surface layer of a thermally stratified lake; bounded below by the thermocline; the zone of primary production and gas exchange with the atmosphere.
Hypolimnion: The cold, dense, isolated bottom layer of a thermally stratified lake; oxygen depleted in productive lakes due to decomposition of settling organic matter; often enriched in dissolved nutrients and reduced metals (Fe2+, Mn2+).
Metalimnion: The layer of rapid temperature change between the epilimnion and hypolimnion; also called the thermocline layer; may harbor distinct biological communities (e.g., deep chlorophyll maxima) and chemical gradients.
Oxycline: The depth zone of rapid decline in dissolved oxygen concentration; typically coincides with or lies below the thermocline in stratified lakes; marks the transition from aerobic to anaerobic conditions.
Secchi depth: The depth at which a Secchi disk (a white or black-and-white patterned disk lowered on a calibrated line) becomes invisible; an index of water transparency and light penetration; negatively correlated with phytoplankton biomass and suspended sediment concentration.
Sonde: A multi-sensor instrument lowered through the water column on a cable to measure temperature, dissolved oxygen, conductivity, pH, turbidity, and chlorophyll a at defined depth intervals; the primary instrument for lake profiling.
Stratification: The separation of a water body into distinct horizontal layers of differing density, driven primarily by temperature differences; limits vertical mixing and controls the distribution of oxygen, nutrients, and organisms.
Thermocline: The plane or narrow zone of maximum rate of temperature decrease with depth; defined operationally as a gradient exceeding 1 °C m-1; the boundary between the epilimnion and metalimnion.
Trophic state: A classification of a lake’s biological productivity based on nutrient concentrations, phytoplankton biomass, and water clarity: oligotrophic (low nutrients, clear), mesotrophic (intermediate), eutrophic (high nutrients, low transparency), hypereutrophic (very high nutrients, algal bloom prone).

title: Lake and Reservoir Profiling
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Drowning: All lake work involves drowning risk. Personal flotation devices (PFDs) are mandatory for all personnel on boats, docks, and platforms.
Weather: Lightning, high winds, and sudden storms pose serious hazards on open water. Abort profiling if thunderstorms are within 10 miles or winds exceed safe boating conditions for the vessel.
Sun exposure: Extended time on open water increases UV exposure and heat stress.
Equipment: Heavy sonde and cable assemblies can cause hand and back injuries when deployed over the side of a boat.




5.1 Required PPE

Personal flotation device (PFD) – worn at all times on the water
Closed-toed shoes with non-slip soles
Nitrile gloves (when handling calibration solutions)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen, sunglasses)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety. All boat occupants must know the location of PFDs, throwable flotation devices, and communication equipment (VHF radio or charged cell phone). If a person falls overboard, deploy the throwable device immediately and maneuver the boat to the person.

title: Lake and Reservoir Profiling
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Field Preparation

Calibrate the sonde per SOP-F200 Eureka Manta2 before departing for the field
Verify that the sonde cable is marked at depth intervals (0.5 m or 1 m). If using a direct-read cable, confirm depth readings against a tape measure.
Check weather forecast; postpone if thunderstorms are likely or sustained winds exceed the vessel’s safe operating threshold
Review the profiling station coordinates and planned depth intervals



7.2 Station Setup

Navigate to the profiling station (typically the deepest point of the lake or a fixed monitoring location)
Record GPS coordinates, date, time, weather conditions (sky cover, wind speed and direction, air temperature), and total water depth
Anchor or tie off the boat to minimize drift during the profile
Perform the Secchi disk measurement per SOP-F207



7.3 Sonde Deployment and Profile Collection

Lower the sonde to 0.5 m below the surface. Allow at least 60 seconds for the sensors to equilibrate (longer for optical DO in cold water).
Record all parameters (temperature, DO, pH, conductivity, turbidity, chlorophyll) at that depth. If the sonde is logging internally, note the time and depth; if reading from the handheld display, record values on the data sheet.
Lower the sonde to the next depth increment (typically 0.5 m in the epilimnion and through the thermocline; 1 m increments are acceptable in deep hypolimnetic water where parameters change slowly).
At each depth, allow 30–60 seconds for sensor equilibration before recording.
Continue to within 0.5 m of the bottom. Do not allow the sonde to contact the sediment (stirs up sediment and can foul sensors).
After the deepest reading, raise the sonde steadily to the surface. If time permits, record an ascending profile for comparison.







Tip



In productive lakes, the most rapid changes in temperature and DO occur at the thermocline and oxycline. When you detect these transitions, switch to 0.5 m or even 0.25 m intervals to resolve the gradient.




7.4 Discrete-Depth Water Sampling (Optional)
If the study design requires water samples at specific depths (e.g., epilimnion, metalimnion, hypolimnion):

Use a Van Dorn or Kemmerer bottle lowered to the target depth
Trip the sampler and raise to the surface
Dispense into pre-labeled sample bottles per SOP-F300 preservation requirements
Record the collection depth and time for each sample



7.5 Post-Profiling

Rinse the sonde sensors with deionized water
Replace the sonde in its calibration/storage cup with storage solution (especially the pH sensor)
Download logged data or scan the data sheet for completeness
Confirm that GPS coordinates, Secchi depth, total depth, and all profile readings are recorded

title: Lake and Reservoir Profiling
text:
8 Data Interpretation
A typical stratified lake profile shows three zones:







Zone
Characteristics




Epilimnion
Warm, well-mixed surface layer; high DO, uniform temperature


Metalimnion (thermocline)
Rapid temperature decrease with depth (at least 1 C per meter)


Hypolimnion
Cold, dense bottom layer; may be anoxic in productive lakes









Note



Not all lakes stratify. Shallow, wind-exposed, or polymictic lakes may be fully mixed during some or all seasons. Record whether stratification is present and the depths of the thermocline boundaries.

title: Lake and Reservoir Profiling
text:
9 Quality Control

Calibrate the sonde on the day of profiling; record calibration results on the calibration log
Allow adequate sensor equilibration time at each depth (minimum 30 seconds; 60 seconds at the first depth and near the thermocline)
Record an ascending profile periodically to check for sensor drift during the profile
Verify depth markings on the cable against a tape measure at least once per season
If the sonde includes an internal depth (pressure) sensor, compare cable-marked depth to the sensor depth at several points; discrepancies greater than 0.3 m require investigation
For long-term monitoring, profile at the same station, same time of day (within 2 hours), and same depth intervals for comparability

title: Sediment Sampling – Streams and Lakes
text: This procedure describes the collection, handling, and field documentation of sediment samples from streams, rivers, lakes, and reservoirs. Sediment is a major sink and source of nutrients, metals, organic contaminants, and fine particles in aquatic systems. The procedures in this SOP are designed to produce samples suitable for physical characterization (grain size, organic matter content), chemical analysis (metals, nutrients, organic contaminants), and biological assessment (benthic invertebrate habitat substrate) (Mudroch et al., 1999; US Environmental Protection Agency, 2001).

title: Sediment Sampling – Streams and Lakes
text: This procedure describes the collection, handling, and field documentation of sediment samples from streams, rivers, lakes, and reservoirs. Sediment is a major sink and source of nutrients, metals, organic contaminants, and fine particles in aquatic systems. The procedures in this SOP are designed to produce samples suitable for physical characterization (grain size, organic matter content), chemical analysis (metals, nutrients, organic contaminants), and biological assessment (benthic invertebrate habitat substrate) (Mudroch et al., 1999; US Environmental Protection Agency, 2001).

title: Sediment Sampling – Streams and Lakes
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Surficial sediment sampling (top 0–10 cm) in wadeable streams, non-wadeable rivers (from bridges or boats), and lentic systems (lakes, ponds, reservoirs). Deeper cores for stratigraphic or paleolimnological work follow the same safety and documentation requirements but use specialized coring equipment not covered in detail here.
Does not apply to: Soil sampling on upland or riparian surfaces (see SOP-F400); suspended sediment sampling by filtration (see future SOP-L312); bedload transport measurements; marine sediment sampling
Location: All EA Program surface water field sites

title: Sediment Sampling – Streams and Lakes
text:
4 Definitions

Benthic sediment: Material that has settled and accumulated on the bed of a stream, lake, or estuary; composed of mineral particles, organic matter, and biological material; the primary matrix for sampling of trace metals, nutrients, and benthic organisms.
Core sample: A cylindrical sediment sample extracted with a tube corer or freeze corer that preserves the vertical stratigraphy and depth profile of deposited material; used for porewater analysis, dating, and historical pollutant records.
Disturbed sample: A bulk sediment sample collected without preserving internal structure (e.g., by grab sampler or trowel); used for bulk chemical analysis, particle size, and loss on ignition when stratigraphy is not required.
Ekman grab: A spring-loaded, box-shaped sampler lowered on a cable that closes on impact with the sediment bed; collects an undisturbed surface sample from soft, fine-grained sediments in lakes and slow-moving water.
Fine earth fraction: The portion of sediment passing through a 2 mm sieve (sand, silt, and clay); the standard fraction for chemical analysis; gravel and coarser material are excluded.
Grab sample: A surface sediment sample collected from the top 1–5 cm of the bed using a grab sampler, trowel, or scoop; represents recently deposited material and is appropriate for screening contamination in surface sediments.
Porewater: Water occupying the spaces between sediment particles; often enriched in dissolved nutrients, metals, and gases released by diagenetic processes; collected by in situ peepers or by centrifugation of sediment cores.
Sediment trap: A cylindrical or funnel-shaped container deployed in the water column to intercept settling particles; used to measure particle flux rates and collect settling material for chemical characterization.

title: Sediment Sampling – Streams and Lakes
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Wading in streams and working from boats carry slip, fall, and drowning hazards. Sediment sampling often involves bending, lifting, and handling heavy wet material.
Biological: Sediment may harbor pathogens, parasites (e.g., Schistosoma, Naegleria), and sharp debris (glass, metal).
Chemical: Sediment from urban or industrial sites may contain heavy metals, hydrocarbons, or pesticides. Avoid skin contact and do not ingest.




5.1 Required PPE

Nitrile gloves (doubled for contaminated sites)
Wading boots or hip waders
Personal flotation device (boat sampling)
Safety glasses
Sun protection



5.2 Emergency Procedures
A minimum of two people must be present for any in-water work. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.

title: Sediment Sampling – Streams and Lakes
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Site Selection and Documentation

Identify the sampling location based on the study design (e.g., depositional zones for contaminant assessment, riffles for substrate characterization)
Record GPS coordinates, date, time, water depth, and a visual description of the sediment surface (color, texture, odor, presence of debris or biota) in the field notebook
Photograph the site and the sediment surface before disturbing it



7.2 Stream Sediment (Wadeable)

Approach the sampling location from downstream to avoid disturbing the target area
Using a stainless steel scoop or trowel, carefully skim the top 5–10 cm of sediment. Avoid collecting underlying undisturbed substrate unless the study requires a depth profile.
Transfer the sediment into a stainless steel bowl
If a composite sample is required, collect sediment from 3–5 locations within the reach (e.g., across the channel width at the designated transect) and combine in the bowl
Homogenize using a stainless steel spoon; remove large rocks, sticks, and debris
Transfer the homogenized sample into the appropriate container(s) (see Section 7)



7.3 Lake and Reservoir Sediment (Grab Sampler)

Lower the Ponar or Ekman grab sampler to the bottom on a measured line from a boat or dock. Record the water depth.
Trip the sampler per the manufacturer’s instructions
Raise the sampler slowly to avoid losing material; keep it horizontal as it breaks the water surface
Inspect the sample: a successful grab is at least half full with an undisturbed sediment surface and overlying water. Reject and re- sample if the grab is less than one-third full, tilted, or shows evidence of washout (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2001).
Carefully drain overlying water without disturbing the sediment surface
For surficial samples, subsample the top 2–5 cm using a stainless steel spoon
Homogenize and containerize as in Section 6.2



7.4 Intact Cores (Hand Corer)

Push the acrylic core tube vertically into soft sediment to the desired depth (typically 10–30 cm)
Cap the top of the tube (creating suction) before pulling the core from the sediment
Once extracted, cap the bottom immediately
Label the core tube with sample ID, date, depth, and orientation (top/bottom)
Keep the core vertical during transport and store at 4 C



7.5 Decontamination Between Sites

Scrub all stainless steel equipment with a brush and rinse with site water
Follow with a deionized water rinse
For trace metal work, perform an additional acid rinse (10% HNO3) followed by a triple DI water rinse
See SOP-F007 Field Decontamination

Collect field duplicates at a rate of at least 1 per 10 samples (or 1 per sampling event, whichever is greater)
Collect one equipment blank per sampling event: rinse decontaminated equipment with DI water and submit the rinse as a sample

title: Groundwater Monitoring Well Sampling
text:
This SOP describes procedures for collecting representative groundwater samples from monitoring wells using the low-flow (minimal drawdown) purging and sampling method. Low-flow sampling minimizes disturbance to the well and surrounding formation, reduces turbidity artifacts, and yields samples that are more representative of in-situ groundwater chemistry than traditional high-volume purge methods (Puls & Barcelona, 1996).
The procedures follow EPA low-flow guidance (Puls & Barcelona, 1996), EPA Region 4 groundwater sampling procedures (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, Science and Ecosystem Support Division, 2017), and Cal-EPA DTSC guidance on representative groundwater sampling.

title: Groundwater Monitoring Well Sampling
text:
This SOP describes procedures for collecting representative groundwater samples from monitoring wells using the low-flow (minimal drawdown) purging and sampling method. Low-flow sampling minimizes disturbance to the well and surrounding formation, reduces turbidity artifacts, and yields samples that are more representative of in-situ groundwater chemistry than traditional high-volume purge methods (Puls & Barcelona, 1996).
The procedures follow EPA low-flow guidance (Puls & Barcelona, 1996), EPA Region 4 groundwater sampling procedures (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, Science and Ecosystem Support Division, 2017), and Cal-EPA DTSC guidance on representative groundwater sampling.

title: Groundwater Monitoring Well Sampling
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Sampling of existing groundwater monitoring wells with an inside diameter of 2 inches (5 cm) or greater, screened intervals of 3 m (10 ft) or less, and a water level above the top of the screen
Does not apply to: Well installation or development; direct-push (e.g., Geoprobe) sampling; spring or seep sampling; wells requiring high-volume purging for regulatory compliance; wells with water levels below the top of the screen (consult the PI for alternative procedures)
Location: All EA Program groundwater monitoring sites

title: Groundwater Monitoring Well Sampling
text:
4 Definitions

Dedicated pump: A pump permanently installed in a single well and not removed between sampling events; eliminates inter-well cross-contamination and decontamination burden; preferred for long- term monitoring programs.
Drawdown: The decline in water level within a well caused by pumping; in low-flow sampling, drawdown must remain at or below 10 cm to minimize vertical mixing within the screened interval and preserve the representativeness of the sample (Puls & Barcelona, 1996).
E-tape (electric tape, water level indicator): An electronic device consisting of a two-conductor cable with a sensing probe at the tip; when the probe contacts the water surface, an audible alarm sounds; used to measure depth to water from a reference point (typically the top of casing, TOC).
Flow-through cell: A sealed flow cell into which purge water is routed so that a multiparameter probe can measure field parameters continuously without exposure to the atmosphere; prevents degassing of CO2 and O2 that would bias pH, DO, and ORP readings.
High-volume purge: The traditional well purging approach in which 3–5 well volumes (or more) are removed before sampling; causes high drawdown, turbulence, and resuspension of fine particles; generally produces less representative samples than low-flow methods (Puls & Barcelona, 1996).
Low-flow (minimal-drawdown) sampling: A groundwater sampling technique in which the pump is set at the mid-screen interval and the flow rate is adjusted to maintain drawdown of 10 cm or less; sampling begins only after field parameters have stabilized (Puls & Barcelona, 1996; Standard Practice for Low-Flow Purging and Sampling for Wells and Devices Used for Ground-Water Quality Investigations, 2021).
ORP (oxidation-reduction potential): A measure of the electron-donating or -accepting capacity of a groundwater sample; expressed in millivolts; sensitive to exposure to atmospheric oxygen; must be measured in a flow-through cell without headspace.
Parameter stabilization: The criterion indicating that the water being pumped from the well is representative of the aquifer rather than stagnant casing water; defined as three consecutive readings within specified limits for pH, temperature, specific conductance, DO, ORP, and turbidity (see §7.3 criteria table).
Screen interval (screened interval): The perforated section of the well casing through which groundwater enters the well from the surrounding aquifer; the pump intake should be positioned at the center of this interval during low-flow sampling.
Standing water volume: The volume of water within the well casing above the bottom of the well screen; calculated as \(V = \pi r^2 h\), where \(r\) is the inside casing radius and \(h\) is the height of the water column; used to determine whether enough water exists for low-flow sampling.
TOC (top of casing): The surveyed reference elevation from which all depth-to-water measurements are taken; must be marked on the well casing with a permanent reference point.
Trip blank: A set of 40 mL VOC sample vials filled with laboratory-grade water in the lab, transported to the field in a sealed cooler alongside field samples, and returned to the lab unopened; detects contamination introduced during transport (APHA et al., 2012).
Well volume: The volume of water stored in the well casing above the screen; typically calculated from well construction records; one well volume is the minimum purge volume before parameter monitoring in high-volume purge methods.

title: Groundwater Monitoring Well Sampling
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Sampling Preparation

Review well construction logs for each well: casing material, diameter, total depth, screen interval, and previous water level data.
Calculate the volume of standing water in the well casing above the screen using \(V = \pi r^2 h\).
Calibrate the multiparameter probe per the manufacturer’s instructions. Record calibration data on the purge log.
Assemble pump, tubing, and flow-through cell. For non-dedicated equipment, decontaminate with deionized water before use at each well.



7.2 Water Level Measurement

Remove the well cap. Note the condition of the well (damage, standing water in vault, obstructions).
Wipe the e-tape sensor with a clean paper towel.
Lower the e-tape slowly until the alarm sounds at the water surface.
Record depth to water from the TOC to the nearest 0.3 cm (0.01 ft).
Measure well depth from the same reference point (after sampling, to avoid resuspending settled solids).
Calculate the water column height and standing water volume.







TipTip



Always measure water level before inserting the pump. Lowering the pump displaces water and changes the apparent water level.




7.3 Pump Placement and Low-Flow Purging

Slowly lower the pump intake to the center of the screened interval. Avoid dropping the pump or allowing it to contact the bottom of the well.
Start the pump at the lowest speed setting and slowly increase until discharge begins. Target a flow rate of 0.1–0.5 L/min (Puls & Barcelona, 1996; Standard Practice for Low-Flow Purging and Sampling for Wells and Devices Used for Ground-Water Quality Investigations, 2021).
Check the water level. Drawdown must not exceed 10 cm. If drawdown exceeds 10 cm, reduce the pumping rate.
Route discharge through the flow-through cell for continuous monitoring.
Record field parameters and cumulative purge volume on the purge log at 3–5 minute intervals.
Continue purging until field parameters have stabilized (Puls & Barcelona, 1996):








Parameter
Stabilization Criterion




pH
±0.1 units over three consecutive readings


Temperature
±0.2 °C over three consecutive readings


Specific conductance
±3% over three consecutive readings


Dissolved oxygen
±0.3 mg/L over three consecutive readings


ORP
±10 mV over three consecutive readings


Turbidity
±10% over three readings (or < 10 NTU)




Once all parameters are stable, proceed immediately to sample collection. Do not turn off the pump between purging and sampling.







ImportantIf the Well Purges Dry



If the well dewaters before stabilization, stop pumping and allow the well to recover. Sample as soon as adequate volume has recovered. Record the dewatering event and recovery time on the purge log. Note that samples from wells purged to dryness may not be representative.




7.4 Sample Collection

Disconnect the flow-through cell from the discharge line. Collect samples directly from the pump tubing (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, Science and Ecosystem Support Division, 2017).
Maintain the same low flow rate used during purging.
Collect samples in this order to minimize bias:

VOCs (if applicable) – 40 mL glass vials, zero headspace
Dissolved gases (if applicable)
Total metals and other unfiltered analytes
Filtered (dissolved) analytes – attach a 0.45 µm in-line filter
General chemistry (pH, conductivity, alkalinity, nutrients)
Bacteria (use sterile bottles)

Fill bottles slowly to minimize aeration and turbulence.
Cap immediately, label, and place in ice.



7.5 Post-Sampling Procedures

Measure and record the final depth to water.
Measure the total well depth.
Remove the pump and tubing. Replace the well cap and lock.
Containerize all purge water per the site waste management plan.
Decontaminate non-dedicated equipment and collect an equipment blank.
Complete the chain of custody form.



7.6 Decontamination Between Wells

Flush the pump and tubing with ≥ 1 L of laboratory-grade detergent solution (Alconox or equivalent).
Flush with ≥ 3 L of deionized water.
Change nitrile gloves between wells.
Collect one equipment blank per sampling event (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text: This SOP describes the procedure for measuring stream discharge (volumetric flow rate) in wadable streams using the USGS midsection velocity-area method with Price Pygmy or Price Type AA mechanical current meters. Discharge data are fundamental to characterizing watershed hydrology, calculating pollutant loads, and supporting water quality assessments (Rantz et al., 1982; Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010).

title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text: This SOP describes the procedure for measuring stream discharge (volumetric flow rate) in wadable streams using the USGS midsection velocity-area method with Price Pygmy or Price Type AA mechanical current meters. Discharge data are fundamental to characterizing watershed hydrology, calculating pollutant loads, and supporting water quality assessments (Rantz et al., 1982; Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010).

title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Wadable streams and channels where personnel can safely stand in the flow (generally depths < 3–4 ft and velocities < approximately 4 ft/s)
Does not apply to: Non-wadable rivers requiring bridge, cableway, or boat measurements; acoustic Doppler instruments (see SOP-F202); or flume and weir installations
Location: All EA Program stream monitoring sites

title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




Lab PI
Approve measurement sites and protocols


Field Lead
Select cross-section locations, verify equipment


Trained Personnel
Perform measurements and record data per this SOP


New Students
Complete training before making independent measurements

title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text:
4 Definitions

AquaCalc: A digital flow computer that counts current meter revolutions and computes velocity automatically; eliminates manual timing with a headset and stopwatch and reduces transcription errors.
Cross-section: The plane perpendicular to the direction of flow at which discharge is measured; ideally straight, uniform, and free of eddies or dead zones (Rantz et al., 1982).
Discharge (Q): The volumetric flow rate of a stream, expressed in cubic feet per second (cfs) or liters per second (L/s); computed as the sum of the products of water velocity, depth, and width across all subsections of the cross-section (Rantz et al., 1982).
Midsection method: The standard USGS computational approach in which the discharge of each subsection is calculated as the product of the measured velocity, the depth at that vertical, and the horizontal distance to the midpoints on either side of the station (Rantz et al., 1982; Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010).
Price Pygmy meter: A small-cup mechanical current meter (5 cm diameter) used in shallow water (< 1.5 ft depth) or when velocities are low; 1 revolution = 1 click per second at approximately 0.1 ft/s (Rantz et al., 1982).
Price Type AA meter: The standard USGS mechanical cup-type current meter (12.5 cm diameter) used in deeper flows; more accurate than the Pygmy for velocities above approximately 0.2 ft/s (Rantz et al., 1982).
Six-tenths-depth method: Placement of the current meter at 0.6 of the total depth below the water surface; yields the mean vertical velocity in most natural channels; the standard method for shallow profiles (depth ≤ 2.5 ft) (Rantz et al., 1982).
Spin test: A quality control check in which the current meter bucket wheel is spun by hand and the time for it to stop is measured; the wheel should spin freely for a minimum number of seconds (see SOP-F201); indicates bearing condition and mechanical integrity.
Tag line: A measuring tape stretched taut across the stream perpendicular to the flow; anchored at both banks; used to measure horizontal distances to each measurement station (Rantz et al., 1982).
Thalweg: The line of deepest flow along the channel axis; usually the zone of highest velocity and the target for closely spaced measurement stations.
Two-point method: Placement of the current meter at 0.2 and 0.8 of the total depth; the arithmetic mean of the two velocities gives the mean vertical velocity; preferred when depth > 2.5 ft (Rantz et al., 1982).
Wetted width: The horizontal distance across the stream from water’s edge to water’s edge at the measurement cross-section.

title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Drowning and swift water: Do not wade in flows deeper than approximately waist height or where you feel unstable. Use a wading rod as a support. Always face upstream while wading.
Slippery substrates: Cobble, gravel, and algae-covered rocks are extremely slippery. Wear felt-soled or studded wading boots.
Hypothermia: Prolonged immersion in cold water can cause hypothermia. Wear insulated waders in cold conditions.
Biological: Waterborne pathogens may be present. Avoid swallowing water. Wash hands and equipment after each site visit.




5.1 Required PPE

Chest or hip waders (neoprene or breathable)
Wading boots with felt or studded soles
PFD if flow conditions are marginal
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
Nitrile gloves (optional, for concurrent water quality sampling)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
If a team member loses footing, release the wading rod and equipment and focus on self-rescue by floating feet-first downstream. Never attempt a discharge measurement alone; a minimum of two people must be present. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.
