title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Site Selection
Select a measurement cross-section with as many of the following characteristics as possible (Rantz et al., 1982):

Straight channel reach for at least 3–5 channel widths upstream and downstream
Uniform flow – no eddies, backwater, or dead zones
Stable streambed (no excessive soft sediment or mobile cobbles)
Flow perpendicular to the tag line
Avoid locations immediately downstream of bridges, confluences, debris jams, or sharp bends
Depth sufficient to submerge the current meter cups; shallow enough to wade safely







TipTip



Ideal cross-sections are trapezoidal with gradually varying depth. Avoid abrupt depth changes, undercut banks, and boulders that create turbulence (Rantz et al., 1982).




8.2 Establishing the Tag Line

Stretch the measuring tape across the stream perpendicular to the flow direction.
Anchor each end with a tape stake driven into the bank.
Pull the tape taut so it does not sag into the water.
Record the distance at the left water’s edge (LEW) and the right water’s edge (REW), looking downstream. All station distances are measured from the same reference bank (typically the left bank, looking downstream).



8.3 Determining Station Spacing
Divide the wetted width into subsections. The goal is 20–30 subsections; no single subsection should carry more than 5–10% of total estimated discharge (Rantz et al., 1982).



Wetted Width
Recommended Station Spacing




< 5 ft (1.5 m)
0.5 ft (0.15 m)


5–15 ft (1.5–4.5 m)
1.0 ft (0.3 m)


> 15 ft (4.5 m)
Divide into 20–30 equal intervals



Space stations more closely near the thalweg where depth or velocity changes rapidly.


8.4 Assembling and Testing the Meter

Mount the current meter on the wading rod per SOP-F201, Section 7.1.
Connect the cable to the AquaCalc or headset.
Perform a spin test and record the result on the data sheet.



8.5 Making the Measurement
Work from one bank to the other. At each station:

Position yourself downstream of the wading rod; your body must not disturb the flow at the measurement point.
Record the station distance from the tag line.
Measure and record the water depth to the nearest 0.01 ft.


8.5.1 Setting the Meter Depth








Method
Meter Position
When to Use




Six-tenths
0.6 × depth from the surface
Depth ≤ 2.5 ft or Pygmy


Two-point
0.2 and 0.8 × depth (average the two)
Depth > 2.5 ft


Surface
0.2 × depth; apply coefficient 0.85–0.90
Very shallow or weedy



(Rantz et al., 1982; Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010)

Count revolutions for a minimum of 40 seconds (up to 70 s at low or unsteady velocities). Record revolutions and elapsed time (or velocity if using the AquaCalc).
Move to the next station and repeat.







Important



When counting revolutions manually, look up velocity in the rating table for your meter model (see SOP-F201, Section 9.3).





8.6 Edge Measurements
At the left and right water’s edges, record depth = 0 and velocity = 0. These close the cross-section.


8.7 Post-Measurement Spin Test
Repeat the spin test after completing the measurement. A reduced spin time indicates potential bearing damage; the measurement quality is suspect (Rantz et al., 1982).

title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text:
9 Discharge Calculation – Midsection Method
Total discharge is the sum of discharge through each subsection (Rantz et al., 1982; Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010):
\[
Q = \sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i \cdot d_i \cdot w_i
\]
where for station \(i\):

\(V_i\) = mean vertical velocity (ft/s or m/s)
\(d_i\) = water depth (ft or m)
\(w_i\) = width of the subsection = distance from the midpoint to the adjacent station on each side (ft or m)

Report discharge in cfs or L/s, rounded to three significant figures following USGS conventions (Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010):



Discharge Range
Rounding




< 1 cfs
Nearest 0.01 cfs


1–10 cfs
Nearest 0.1 cfs


10–100 cfs
Nearest 1 cfs

title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text:
10 Data Processing

Enter field data into the lab’s standard discharge spreadsheet template on the same day as the measurement.
Verify the total discharge calculation matches the field computation.
Flag any station carrying more than 10% of total discharge in a single subsection – this indicates station spacing was too wide.
Archive the original field data sheet (scan if paper).

title: Stream Discharge Measurement – Wadable Streams
text:
11 Quality Control

No single subsection should carry more than 5–10% of total discharge (Rantz et al., 1982).
Pre- and post-measurement spin tests must meet minimum thresholds (see SOP-F201).
If two measurements are made at the same cross-section, they should agree within 5%; if they differ by more than 5%, make a third measurement and use the mean of the two closest values (Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010).
Oblique flow: If current is not perpendicular to the tag line, velocity readings underestimate true velocity. Reposition or apply a cosine correction.
Wading disturbance: Stand downstream of the meter; avoid shuffling feet near the measurement point.
Unsteady flow: In flashy streams, stage may change during measurement. Record the time at each station.

text:

Rantz et al. (1982)
Turnipseed & Sauer (2010)

title: Dissolved Oxygen Meter (Field)
text: This SOP describes the calibration, field operation, and maintenance of standalone handheld dissolved oxygen (DO) meters for in situ measurement of dissolved oxygen concentration and percent saturation in surface waters. Dissolved oxygen is a fundamental indicator of water quality and aquatic habitat condition (APHA et al., 2012). This SOP covers both optical (luminescent) and electrochemical (polarographic and galvanic) DO probes operated as standalone instruments, separate from multiparameter sondes.

title: Dissolved Oxygen Meter (Field)
text: This SOP describes the calibration, field operation, and maintenance of standalone handheld dissolved oxygen (DO) meters for in situ measurement of dissolved oxygen concentration and percent saturation in surface waters. Dissolved oxygen is a fundamental indicator of water quality and aquatic habitat condition (APHA et al., 2012). This SOP covers both optical (luminescent) and electrochemical (polarographic and galvanic) DO probes operated as standalone instruments, separate from multiparameter sondes.

title: Dissolved Oxygen Meter (Field)
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Handheld DO meters (e.g., YSI Pro20i, YSI ProSolo, Hach HQ40d with LDO probe, Extech DO600) used for in situ DO measurements at EA Program surface water field sites
Does not apply to: DO measured by the Eureka Manta2 multiprobe (see SOP-F200); Winkler titration (laboratory method); BOD5 analysis (see SOP-L306); continuously deployed sondes
Location: All EA Program surface water field sites

title: Dissolved Oxygen Meter (Field)
text:
4 Definitions

Barometric pressure correction: Adjustment of the 100% saturation calibration point for the ambient atmospheric pressure; oxygen solubility decreases with decreasing pressure (increasing altitude); entered in mmHg or hPa at the time of calibration (APHA et al., 2012).
DO percent saturation (%sat): The measured DO concentration expressed as a percentage of the equilibrium saturation concentration at the same temperature and pressure; 100% indicates equilibrium with the atmosphere; supersaturation (> 100%) indicates net photosynthesis; values well below 100% indicate high oxygen demand or poor reaeration (APHA et al., 2012).
Electrochemical (polarographic/galvanic) probe: A DO sensor in which oxygen diffuses through a gas-permeable membrane and is reduced at the cathode, generating a current proportional to DO concentration; requires periodic membrane and electrolyte replacement and is flow- dependent (needs water movement past the membrane) (APHA et al., 2012).
KCl electrolyte: The potassium chloride solution filling the electrode cavity of polarographic DO probes; must be replaced when the membrane is changed or when readings become erratic.
LDO (luminescent dissolved oxygen) probe: An optical sensor that measures DO by the quenching of luminescence from a ruthenium-dye sensing element by oxygen molecules; requires no electrolyte or membrane, no warm-up time, and no stirring (Hach Company, 2023).
Membrane (DO probe): The gas-permeable Teflon or polyethylene film covering the electrode of an electrochemical DO probe; must be free of bubbles, tears, or debris; replace if damaged or if readings are erratic.
Sensing cap: The replaceable luminescent element on an optical DO probe; replace when the cap expires (typically 1–2 years) or when readings become erratic (YSI Inc., 2022).
Winkler titration: The reference wet-chemical method for DO determination; used to verify DO meter accuracy and required for calibration validation in some regulatory programs (APHA et al., 2012).
Zero-oxygen calibration: A secondary calibration point using an oxygen-free solution (sodium sulfite with cobalt chloride catalyst) to verify the zero response of the DO probe; recommended when expected DO values are below 2 mg/L.

title: Dissolved Oxygen Meter (Field)
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Measuring DO requires placing the probe in or near water. Slip, fall, and drowning hazards apply. Work in pairs at stream sites.
Chemical: Polarographic DO probes use KCl electrolyte solution, a mild irritant. Sodium sulfite (used for zero-oxygen calibration) is a mild irritant and reducing agent.
Biological: Water may contain pathogens. Avoid ingestion; wash hands after field work.




5.1 Required PPE

Closed-toed shoes or wading boots
Nitrile gloves (especially for impaired waters)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.

title: Dissolved Oxygen Meter (Field)
text:
6 Instrument Types

6.1 Optical (Luminescent) DO Probes
Optical probes (e.g., Hach HQ40d with LDO101 probe, YSI ProSolo ODO) measure DO by detecting luminescence quenching. They require no electrolyte, no warm-up time, no stirring, and no membrane replacement (Hach Company, 2023).







Advantage
Limitation




No membrane or electrolyte
Higher initial cost


No stirring required
Sensing cap has finite lifespan (1–2 yr)


Fast stabilization



Lower maintenance






6.2 Electrochemical (Polarographic / Galvanic) DO Probes
Electrochemical probes (e.g., YSI Pro20i) measure DO through an oxygen-permeable membrane (YSI Inc., 2022).







Advantage
Limitation




Lower initial cost
Requires membrane and electrolyte replacement


Well-established method
Needs 5–15 min warm-up


Widely available

title: Dissolved Oxygen Meter (Field)
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Calibration
Calibrate the DO meter before each field day using the water-saturated air method.
Water-saturated air calibration:

Ensure the calibration chamber (probe storage cap with damp sponge) is moist but not dripping; the probe tip must not touch the sponge.
Turn on the meter. Allow electrochemical probes to warm up for 5–15 minutes (see instrument manual) (YSI Inc., 2022).
Enter the current barometric pressure (mmHg or hPa). Verify the displayed value against a Kestrel or weather station.
Place the probe in the calibration chamber; wait for the reading to stabilize (1–3 min for optical; 5–10 min for electrochemical).
Press Cal per the instrument prompts; the meter sets 100% saturation at the current temperature and pressure.
Record in the field notebook: calibration date, time, barometric pressure, temperature, and whether calibration was accepted.

Zero-oxygen calibration (optional – low-DO environments):

Dissolve excess sodium sulfite in DI water with a pinch of cobalt chloride catalyst.
Immerse the probe and wait for the reading to stabilize.
Calibrate the zero point per meter instructions.



8.2 Field Measurement

Immerse the probe to mid-depth at the sampling location. For electrochemical probes, maintain a minimum flow of 0.3 m/s past the membrane (gently move the probe in still water). Optical probes do not require flow (Hach Company, 2023).
Wait for the reading to stabilize.
Record in the field notebook:

DO concentration (mg/L) and percent saturation (%)
Water temperature (°C) as reported by the probe
Date, time, sample ID, and measurement depth
Flow conditions (riffle, pool, still water with manual stirring)

For depth profiles, lower the probe in 0.5 or 1.0 m increments and allow stabilization at each depth.



8.3 Post-Field Care

Rinse the probe with DI water after each use.
For electrochemical probes, check the membrane for tears, bubbles, or deposits; replace membrane and electrolyte if damaged (YSI Inc., 2022).
For optical probes, gently wipe the sensing cap with a soft, damp cloth if biofouling is visible; do not use solvents.
Store the probe in the calibration chamber with a moist sponge (not submerged).
Turn off the meter; remove batteries if storing for more than one month.

title: Dissolved Oxygen Meter (Field)
text:
9 Data Interpretation
DO concentrations are influenced by temperature, atmospheric pressure, salinity, photosynthesis, respiration, and reaeration (APHA et al., 2012).



DO (mg/L)
Condition




> 8
Well-oxygenated; suitable for most aquatic life


5–8
Adequate for many species; marginal for cold-water fish


2–5
Stressful for most fish; hypoxic conditions


< 2
Severe hypoxia; lethal to most aquatic organisms

title: Dissolved Oxygen Meter (Field)
text:
10 Quality Control

Calibrate at the start of each field day.
At the end of the field day, check calibration by returning the probe to the water-saturated air chamber; reading must be within ±2% of 100% saturation. If drift exceeds 5%, note it and recalibrate.
When possible, verify against a second DO meter or the Eureka Manta2; readings should agree within ±0.5 mg/L.
For long field days (> 6 hours), perform a mid-day calibration check.
Record all QC results in the field notebook (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Secchi Disk and Secchi Disk Tube
text: This SOP describes the use of the standard Secchi disk and the Secchi disk tube (transparency tube) for measuring water transparency in lakes, reservoirs, and streams. Secchi depth is one of the oldest and simplest limnological measurements, providing a rapid estimate of the photic zone depth and an index of suspended particle concentration (Carlson, 1977; Wetzel, 2001).

title: Secchi Disk and Secchi Disk Tube
text: This SOP describes the use of the standard Secchi disk and the Secchi disk tube (transparency tube) for measuring water transparency in lakes, reservoirs, and streams. Secchi depth is one of the oldest and simplest limnological measurements, providing a rapid estimate of the photic zone depth and an index of suspended particle concentration (Carlson, 1977; Wetzel, 2001).

title: Secchi Disk and Secchi Disk Tube
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Visual transparency measurements in lakes, ponds, and reservoirs (standard Secchi disk) and in streams, shallow wetlands, and stormwater basins (Secchi tube)
Does not apply to: Quantitative turbidity measurements (see SOP-F205); laboratory transmissometry; PAR light profiles (requires an underwater quantum sensor)
Location: All EA Program surface water field sites

title: Secchi Disk and Secchi Disk Tube
text:
4 Definitions

Euphotic zone depth (\(z_{eu}\)): The depth receiving at least 1% of surface irradiance; approximately 2–3 times the Secchi depth in most lakes; defines the lower boundary of net photosynthesis (Wetzel, 2001).
Photic zone: The surface layer of a water body receiving sufficient light to support photosynthesis; its depth is inversely related to turbidity and Secchi depth.
Secchi depth (\(z_{SD}\)): The depth at which a standard Secchi disk becomes just invisible when lowered, averaged with the depth at which it becomes visible again when raised; \(z_{SD} = (D_1 + D_2) / 2\); an index of water transparency inversely related to suspended particle concentration and dissolved color (Carlson, 1977).
Secchi tube (transparency tube): A clear acrylic tube, typically 60 or 120 cm long, with a Secchi disk pattern printed at the bottom and a drain valve at the base; filled with sample water and drained until the pattern disappears; used in shallow or turbid waters where a standard disk cannot be deployed vertically.
Trophic state index (TSI): A numerical scale relating Secchi depth, chlorophyll a, and total phosphorus to lake trophic status; Carlson’s TSI for Secchi depth: \(\text{TSI}(SD) = 60 - 14.41 \ln(z_{SD})\) (Carlson, 1977).
Viewscope: A tube, box, or bucket with a transparent bottom used to eliminate surface glare when reading Secchi depth; improves consistency between observers but must be noted and applied consistently within a dataset.

title: Secchi Disk and Secchi Disk Tube
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Secchi disk measurements from boats, docks, or bridges require caution to prevent falls. Wear a personal flotation device (PFD) when sampling from boats.
Biological: Surface water may contain pathogens. Avoid ingestion; wear gloves if hands contact water.
Sun glare: Measuring Secchi depth requires looking directly into the water; use polarized sunglasses or a viewscope to reduce glare (note use in the field notebook for consistency).




5.1 Required PPE

Closed-toed shoes or wading boots
Personal flotation device (boat sampling)
Nitrile gloves (recommended for impaired waters)
Sun protection (hat, sunglasses)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety. If sampling from a boat, ensure all occupants know the location of PFDs and throwable flotation devices.

title: Secchi Disk and Secchi Disk Tube
text:
6 Equipment and Materials

6.1 Standard Secchi Disk







Item
Notes

Item
Notes

Item

title: Secchi Disk and Secchi Disk Tube
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Standard Secchi Disk (Lakes, Reservoirs, Deep Pools)
Take measurements on the shaded side of the boat or dock, between 10:00 and 14:00 local time for consistency. Avoid measurements during heavy cloud cover, rain, or high wind (Wetzel, 2001).

Lower the Secchi disk on the shaded side until it just disappears from view. Record this depth as D1 (disappearance depth).
Slowly raise the disk until it just reappears. Record this depth as D2 (reappearance depth).
Calculate Secchi depth: \[\text{Secchi depth} = \frac{D_1 + D_2}{2}\]
Record in the field notebook:

Secchi depth (m) and D1, D2 individually
Date and time
Sky conditions (clear, partly cloudy, overcast)
Wind and water surface conditions
Whether a viewscope was used
Observer name (readings vary between observers)

If the disk is visible on the bottom, record “Secchi depth > [bottom depth]” and note the bottom depth.
Repeat the measurement a second time; the two readings should agree within 0.5 m. Record both and report the mean.



7.2 Secchi Tube (Streams, Shallow Waters)

Collect a water sample from mid-depth using a bucket or wide-mouth bottle; avoid disturbing sediment.
Pour the sample into the Secchi tube until full.
Hold the tube vertically and look down through the water column at the Secchi pattern on the bottom.
Open the drain valve slowly. Watch the Secchi pattern.
When the pattern just disappears, close the valve and read the water level on the graduated scale. Record as Secchi tube depth (cm).
Refill the tube and repeat; the two readings should agree within 2 cm. Record both and report the mean.
Rinse the tube with DI water between sites to prevent cross-contamination.

title: Secchi Disk and Secchi Disk Tube
text:
8 Data Interpretation
Secchi depth is inversely related to turbidity and suspended particle concentration (Carlson, 1977; Wetzel, 2001). Approximate trophic-state guidelines for lakes:



Secchi Depth (m)
Trophic Class




> 5
Oligotrophic


2–5
Mesotrophic


1–2
Eutrophic


< 1
Hypereutrophic









Note



These categories are approximate and vary with dissolved color, algal species, and suspended sediment type. Do not use Secchi depth alone to classify trophic state; combine with nutrient and chlorophyll data (Carlson, 1977).

title: Secchi Disk and Secchi Disk Tube
text:
9 Quality Control

Use the same observer for repeated measurements at a monitoring site whenever possible; inter-observer variability is the largest source of error (Wetzel, 2001).
Always take duplicate measurements and report the mean.
Record consistently whether sunglasses or a viewscope were used.
Verify Secchi tube graduation markings against a ruler at least once per year.
When both a Secchi disk and a turbidity meter are available, pair the measurements to develop a site-specific Secchi-turbidity regression.

title: HOBO Weather Station Deployment
text: This SOP describes the deployment, programming, data retrieval, and maintenance of Onset HOBO pendant and MX-series data loggers used for unattended monitoring of air temperature, relative humidity, and light intensity at EA Program field sites. These compact loggers provide continuous microclimatic data for characterizing site conditions, supporting ecological studies, and supplementing manual weather observations (Onset Computer Corporation, 2023; World Meteorological Organization, 2018).

title: HOBO Weather Station Deployment
text: This SOP describes the deployment, programming, data retrieval, and maintenance of Onset HOBO pendant and MX-series data loggers used for unattended monitoring of air temperature, relative humidity, and light intensity at EA Program field sites. These compact loggers provide continuous microclimatic data for characterizing site conditions, supporting ecological studies, and supplementing manual weather observations (Onset Computer Corporation, 2023; World Meteorological Organization, 2018).

title: HOBO Weather Station Deployment
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: HOBO Pendant MX2201, MX2202 (temperature/light), HOBO MX2301 (temperature/RH), HOBO Pendant UA-002 (temperature/ light, legacy), and similar Onset loggers deployed at EA Program field sites
Does not apply to: HOBO water level loggers (see SOP-F203); fixed, permanently installed weather stations managed by other departments; air quality sensors (see SOP-F502)
Location: All EA Program field sites

title: HOBO Weather Station Deployment
text:
4 Definitions

Bluetooth logging: A wireless communication protocol used by MX-series HOBO loggers; enables programming and data download via the HOBOconnect smartphone app without cables; requires proximity (typically within 15 m of the logger) (Onset Computer Corporation, 2023).
Data gap: A period within a logger deployment during which no data were recorded; caused by battery failure, logger reset, or memory overflow; must be documented in the project data log.
HOBOconnect: The Onset smartphone app (iOS and Android) used to program, launch, and download data from Bluetooth-enabled MX-series HOBO loggers; requires the logger to be within Bluetooth range (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021).
HOBOware: The Onset desktop software used to program and download data from legacy UA-series HOBO loggers via optical USB coupler; also supports barometric compensation for water level loggers (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021).
Logging interval: The time between successive measurements stored to the logger memory; typical intervals for EA Program deployments are 5 minutes (microclimatic studies) or 15 minutes (long-term monitoring); shorter intervals fill memory faster and require more frequent downloads (Onset Computer Corporation, 2023).
MX2301: The Onset HOBO MX temperature and relative humidity logger; Bluetooth-enabled; ±0.2 °C temperature accuracy and ±2.5% RH accuracy; internal memory stores 500,000 readings (Onset Computer Corporation, 2023).
Radiation shield: A ventilated, white polypropylene housing that surrounds a temperature or RH logger and prevents direct solar radiation from inflating the measured air temperature; a radiation shield is mandatory for any logger exposed to sunlight (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
Relative humidity (RH): The ratio of the partial pressure of water vapor in air to the saturation vapor pressure at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage; values above approximately 70% promote sensor drift in some sensor types (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
Sensor drift: A gradual, systematic change in sensor readings over time not attributable to true environmental change; detected by co-deployment with a reference sensor or comparison with a nearby weather station.

title: HOBO Weather Station Deployment
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Deployment may involve climbing, ladder use, or working on uneven terrain. Use a spotter when mounting loggers at height.

Wildlife: Insects (bees, wasps), ticks, and snakes may be present at deployment sites.

title: HOBO Weather Station Deployment
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Pre-Deployment Programming
MX-series (Bluetooth):

Open the HOBOconnect app and connect to the logger via Bluetooth (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021).
Configure:

Logging interval: 5 or 15 minutes
Start mode: delayed start (set to a round time, e.g., top of the next hour)
Logger name: use the convention SiteID_Parameter_LoggerSN (e.g., BFS_TempRH_20456789)

Verify the battery level. Replace if below 20%.

UA-series (legacy):

Connect the logger via the optical USB coupler and open HOBOware.
Select Launch and configure the logging interval and start time (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021).
Click Start to begin logging.



8.2 Deployment

Mount the radiation shield at 1.5 m above ground on a post, tree, or tripod in a location representative of the site. Avoid positions within 3 m of heat-absorbing surfaces (pavement, metal walls) (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
Insert the logger into the shield. Ensure the sensor faces are unobstructed and the shield ventilation holes are unblocked.
Secure the shield to the mounting structure with cable ties.
Record in the field notebook:

Logger serial number
Deployment coordinates per SOP-F006
Date and time of deployment
Logging interval and start time
Sensor height above ground

Photograph the deployed logger with surrounding context visible.



8.3 Downloading Data at Regular Intervals
MX-series (Bluetooth):

Open HOBOconnect app and connect to the logger.
Select Download to transfer all stored data to the smartphone (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021).
Export the data as a CSV file.
Save using the naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_Parameter_LoggerSN.csv
Upload to the project GitHub repository under data/microclimate/ within 48 hours.

UA-series (legacy):
Connect via optical USB coupler and use HOBOware to read out data.


8.4 Logger Retrieval (End of Deployment)

Download all remaining data.
Remove the logger and mounting hardware.
Clean the logger housing with a damp cloth. For waterproof models, rinse with fresh water.
Inspect the radiation shield for damage; replace desiccant packs if applicable.
Store loggers in a dry, room-temperature location.

title: HOBO Weather Station Deployment
text:
9 Quality Control

At each download visit, compare the logger temperature reading against a handheld thermometer. Discrepancies greater than 1 °C should be investigated (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
At least once per year, co-deploy two loggers of the same model at the same location for a minimum of 48 hours to check inter-unit agreement. Temperature should agree within 0.5 °C; RH within 5%.
Inspect data for signs of sensor failure: constant readings, sudden offsets, or readings pegged at the sensor limit.
Check battery level at every download. Replace batteries proactively if below 20%.
For light loggers, verify that the sensor face has not shifted orientation by comparing the deployment photograph to current position.

title: SonTek Acoustic Velocity Meters
text: This SOP describes the operation, calibration verification, and maintenance of SonTek acoustic Doppler velocity meters used for point velocity and discharge measurements in wadeable streams. Acoustic Doppler instruments measure water velocity by transmitting ultrasonic pulses and detecting the frequency shift of sound reflected by suspended particles in the water column (Rehmel, 2007). Unlike mechanical current meters (SOP-F201), acoustic meters have no moving parts, respond faster to turbulent fluctuations, and can measure very low velocities.

Acoustic Doppler instruments measure water velocity by transmitting ultrasonic pulses and detecting the frequency shift of sound reflected by suspended particles in the water column (Rehmel, 2007). Unlike mechanical current meters (SOP-F201), acoustic meters have no moving parts, respond faster to turbulent fluctuations, and can measure very low velocities.

title: SonTek Acoustic Velocity Meters
text:
4 Definitions

ADV (acoustic Doppler velocimeter): An instrument that measures water velocity at a single point by transmitting ultrasonic pulses and measuring the Doppler frequency shift of sound scattered back from suspended particles in a small sampling volume located at a fixed distance from the transducer head (Rehmel, 2007).
Averaging time: The duration over which velocity samples are collected and averaged at each measurement vertical; the FlowTracker default is 40 seconds; increase to 60 seconds in low-velocity or highly turbulent flows to improve measurement stability (SonTek/Xylem, 2019).
Beam check: A pre-measurement quality check in which the FlowTracker2 tests all three acoustic beams and reports signal-to- noise ratio (SNR) for each; all beams must return SNR > 4 dB before a measurement can proceed (SonTek/Xylem, 2019).
Boundary flag: An automated QC flag set by the FlowTracker when the probe is too close to the streambed or water surface for the sampling volume to be fully within the water column; corrected by adjusting the depth setting.
Doppler effect: The change in frequency of a wave (sound or light) observed when the source or the reflector is in motion relative to the observer; the physical basis of acoustic Doppler velocity measurement – the frequency shift of reflected ultrasound is proportional to the component of particle velocity along the acoustic beam axis (Rehmel, 2007).
FlowTracker2: The current production SonTek handheld ADV for wading discharge measurements; uses three acoustic beams and integrated pressure depth sensor; stores data internally and transfers via USB; includes automated QA/QC flagging (SonTek/Xylem, 2019).
Mid-section method: The standard USGS discharge calculation method in which each vertical’s discharge is the product of measured velocity, depth, and the horizontal width extending halfway to the adjacent verticals on each side; computed automatically by the FlowTracker (Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010).
MMT file: The proprietary binary data file format produced by the SonTek FlowTracker; stores raw velocity data, QC flags, site information, and the computed discharge summary; must be archived before exporting to CSV.
Sampling volume: The small water volume approximately 10 cm from the FlowTracker transducer head from which velocity data are collected; must be free of boundary interference (streambed, water surface, or large obstacles) for valid measurements (SonTek/Xylem, 2019).
SNR (signal-to-noise ratio): The ratio of acoustic signal strength returned from suspended particles to background noise; expressed in dB; the FlowTracker requires SNR > 4 dB on all three beams for a valid measurement; low SNR typically indicates insufficient suspended particles in very clear water (SonTek/Xylem, 2019).
Spike flag: An automated QC flag set by the FlowTracker when a single velocity sample deviates significantly from the running mean, indicating a transient disturbance (bubble, debris, wading disturbance); the affected sample is excluded from the average.

title: SonTek Acoustic Velocity Meters
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Pre-Field Setup

Charge the FlowTracker2 battery fully before each field day (SonTek/Xylem, 2019). For the original model, install fresh batteries.
Power on the instrument and verify that the firmware version is current. Update if prompted.
Set the site information: site name, station ID, date, and operator initials.
Select the measurement method:

Mid-section (default, consistent with USGS practice (Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010))
Mean-section (if required by the project)

Set the measurement parameters:

Averaging time: 40 seconds (default; increase to 60 seconds for low or turbulent flows) (SonTek/Xylem, 2019)
Number of measurements per vertical: 1 (six-tenths method) or 2 (two-point method at 0.2 and 0.8 depth) (Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010)




8.2 Beam Check
Perform a beam check before each measurement (SonTek/Xylem, 2019).

Submerge the probe head at least 15 cm below the water surface in a location with minimal turbulence.
On the FlowTracker2, select QC > Beam Check from the menu.
The instrument tests all three acoustic beams and reports SNR for each beam.
All beams must report SNR > 4 dB. If any beam fails, clean the transducer faces and retest. If the beam check still fails, do not proceed with the measurement.
Record the beam check result in the field notebook.



8.3 Site Selection and Tag Line
Follow the site selection and tag line procedures described in SOP-F301 Stream Discharge Measurement, Sections 7.1–7.3 (Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010). The same cross-section criteria apply to acoustic and mechanical meters.


8.4 Making the Measurement

Mount the FlowTracker probe on the wading rod at the correct depth setting:

Six-tenths method: Set the probe at 0.6 of the total depth below the water surface (same as for mechanical meters)
Two-point method: Measure at 0.2 and 0.8 of the depth

At each vertical, the instrument automatically records velocity (Vx, Vy components) and runs QC checks (SNR, spike detection, boundary check, flow angle).
If a measurement is flagged, the instrument displays the reason. Common flags and responses:









Flag
Meaning
Response




Low SNR
Insufficient suspended particles
Increase averaging time; stir bed gently upstream


Boundary
Probe too close to bed or surface
Adjust depth setting


High flow angle
Flow not perpendicular to tag line
Reposition tag line or note angle


Spike
Velocity spike detected
Repeat measurement



(SonTek/Xylem, 2019)

After completing all verticals, the instrument computes total discharge automatically using the mid-section method (Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010).
Review the on-screen discharge summary before leaving the site.



8.5 Post-Measurement

Save the measurement file on the instrument.
Record a backup note in the field notebook: site, date, total discharge, number of verticals, and any flagged stations.
Rinse the probe with clean water. Do not use solvents or abrasives on the transducer faces.
Decontaminate per SOP-F007 before moving to the next site.



8.6 Data Download

Connect the FlowTracker2 to a laptop via USB.
Open the SonTek desktop software and download all measurement files (SonTek/Xylem, 2019).
Export each measurement as a .csv and a .dis (discharge summary) file.
Save files using the naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_discharge_FT2.csv
Upload to the project GitHub repository under data/discharge/ within 48 hours.
Archive the raw .mmt file to the lab shared drive.

title: SonTek Acoustic Velocity Meters

9 Maintenance

9.1 After Each Field Day

Rinse the entire probe head and cable with clean fresh water.
Dry with a lint-free cloth.
Inspect the transducer faces for scratches, algae buildup, or debris. Clean gently with a soft brush if needed.
Charge the battery (FlowTracker2) or remove batteries (original model) if storing for more than one week.



9.2 Periodic Maintenance

Monthly (active use): Inspect the wading rod mounting bracket for wear. Verify firmware version.
Annually: Contact SonTek for factory calibration verification if the instrument is used for regulatory or compliance monitoring (Rehmel, 2007).

title: SonTek Acoustic Velocity Meters
text:
10 Quality Control

Beam check before every measurement (§7.2) (SonTek/Xylem, 2019).
If two measurements are made at the same cross-section, they should agree within 5%; if they differ by more than 5%, make a third measurement and use the mean of the two closest values (Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010).
Compare FlowTracker results with mechanical meter results at least once per year; results should agree within 5–8% (Rehmel, 2007).
Review all automated QC flags during data processing. Do not discard flagged data without documentation.

text: This SOP describes the procedures for calibrating, operating, and maintaining the Eureka Manta2 Sub2 Multiprobe for water quality measurements including temperature, pH, depth, conductivity, and dissolved oxygen (mg/L and % saturation) (APHA et al., 2012; Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).

text: This SOP describes the procedures for calibrating, operating, and maintaining the Eureka Manta2 Sub2 Multiprobe for water quality measurements including temperature, pH, depth, conductivity, and dissolved oxygen (mg/L and % saturation) (APHA et al., 2012; Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).

title: Eureka Manta2 Multiprobe for Water Quality Testing
text:
2 Scope

Does not apply to: Groundwater monitoring wells (requires different deployment procedures); laboratory bench-top water analysis
Location: All EA Program field water sampling sites

title: Eureka Manta2 Multiprobe for Water Quality Testing
text:
4 Definitions

Amphibian 2: The ruggedized handheld field computer (portable PC) manufactured by Eureka that controls the Manta2 probe, displays real-time readings, stores data snapshots, and connects to the probe via the underwater cable (Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).
Barometric pressure: Atmospheric pressure at the measurement location, expressed in mm Hg; required as an input for dissolved oxygen calibration because oxygen solubility decreases with decreasing pressure (increasing altitude) (APHA et al., 2012).
Calibration: The process of adjusting sensor readings to match known reference standards before field use; required before every field outing to ensure data accuracy (Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).
Conductivity (specific conductance, spCond): A measure of a water sample’s ability to conduct electrical current, expressed in µS/cm or mS/cm; proportional to the concentration of dissolved ions; temperature-corrected to 25 °C for comparability across sites and seasons (APHA et al., 2012).
Dissolved oxygen (DO): The concentration of oxygen dissolved in water, expressed as mg/L or percent saturation (%sat); measured by the HDO sensor using luminescent optical technology; decreases with increasing temperature, salinity, and altitude (APHA et al., 2012).
HDO (Handheld Dissolved Oxygen): The luminescent optical dissolved oxygen sensor on the Manta2; measures both %sat and mg/L; calibrated in water-saturated air or with an air-saturated water standard (Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).
PDOP (Position Dilution of Precision): A dimensionless measure of GPS accuracy based on satellite geometry; lower values indicate better positional accuracy; values below 3 are acceptable for most field applications.
Reference electrode: The electrochemical half-cell that provides a stable reference potential for pH measurement; requires periodic refilling with reference electrolyte to maintain accurate pH readings (Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).
Sensor Response Factor (SRF): A calibration diagnostic value indicating how the sensor responded to the reference standard; acceptable ranges are sensor-specific and indicate whether calibration was successful (Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).
Snapshot: A single instantaneous record of all sensor readings captured and stored by the Amphibian at a specific date, time, and GPS location.
Sonde (probe): The cylindrical instrument body of the Manta2 that houses all sensors (temperature, pH, conductivity, dissolved oxygen, and reference electrode) and is submerged during measurements (Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).

title: Eureka Manta2 Multiprobe for Water Quality Testing

Biological/Chemical: Water bodies may be contaminated; avoid ingestion and direct skin contact.

Chemical: pH standards (pH 4, 7, 10) and conductivity standard are mild irritants.




5.1 Required PPE

Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety for general field safety, transportation, and emergency response.

title: Eureka Manta2 Multiprobe for Water Quality Testing
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Startup

Connect the underwater cable to both the sonde and the Amphibian.
Power on the Amphibian.
Open the Amp_2_2_6 app (or press P1 shortcut).
Allow sensors to stabilize for 5–10 minutes before calibration.



7.2 Calibration
Calibrate before every field outing (APHA et al., 2012; Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018). Record all calibration data (SRF values, standard concentrations, date, operator) in the field notebook.

7.2.1 pH

Remove the storage cup. Rinse sensors with DI water.
Submerge the sonde in pH 7 standard. Select Calibrate > pH and follow the on-screen prompts.
Rinse with DI water. Submerge in pH 4 standard. Accept the second calibration point.
(Optional) Verify with pH 10 standard. Record the SRF (acceptable range: 95–105).



7.2.2 Conductivity

Rinse sensors with DI water.
Submerge in the appropriate conductivity standard.
Select Calibrate > Conductivity. Enter the standard value and accept (Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).
Record the SRF (acceptable range: 110–120).



7.2.3 Dissolved Oxygen (HDO)

Remove the sonde from the calibration cup. Allow the HDO sensor to equilibrate in water-saturated air for 2 minutes (sensor face moist but not submerged).
Enter the current barometric pressure in mm Hg.
Select Calibrate > DO and accept the 100% saturation calibration (Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).
Record the SRF (should equal 100%).




7.3 Field Measurement

Lower the sonde to the desired depth. Allow 1–2 minutes for readings to stabilize before recording.
Press Snapshot on the Amphibian to save readings. Record the snapshot ID, location, and notes in the field notebook.
For depth profiles, lower the sonde in 0.5 or 1 m increments, pausing 30–60 s at each depth (Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).



7.4 Disconnecting

Remove the probe from the water.
Disconnect the underwater cable from the probe.
Insert the blue storage plug.
Cover the cable end with the plastic protector.

title: Eureka Manta2 Multiprobe for Water Quality Testing
text:
8 Post-Field Procedures

8.1 Cleaning the Probe

Clean the probe with warm soapy water (liquid dish soap or mild household cleaner).
Clean sensor stems with a soft brush.
Rinse thoroughly with tap water.
Store sensors with tap water inside the cup.



8.2 Downloading Data

Connect the Amphibian to your PC using a USB cable.
A green window will appear with four options; select File Management.
In the next window, navigate to the hard drive, then select My Documents.
Locate the Excel document with your data.
Copy the file to your project data folder.



8.3 Charging
Return the Amphibian to its charging station after each field outing.

title: Eureka Manta2 Multiprobe for Water Quality Testing
text:
9 Quality Control

Calibrate all sensors before every field outing (APHA et al., 2012; Eureka Environmental Engineering, 2018).
Verify SRF values are within acceptable ranges; do not proceed if any sensor fails calibration.
Record a post-deployment calibration check on return to the lab; if any sensor has drifted beyond acceptable limits, flag the data.
Compare spot readings against an independent DO meter or multiprobe where possible; readings should agree within ±0.3 mg/L for DO and ±0.1 units for pH (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Eureka Manta2 Multiprobe for Water Quality Testing
text:
10 Troubleshooting







Problem
Solution




No power
Check the green LED on the Manta2; if off, the voltage is insufficient. Try another cable.


pH SRF out of range
Recalibrate with fresh standards. If still out of range, refill the reference electrolyte and contact the PI.


Conductivity SRF outside 110–120
Recalibrate. If still out of range, contact the PI.


HDO %sat SRF ≠ 100
Redo the calibration with freshly aerated water.


GPS not acquiring satellites
Ensure the top cap (antenna) is uncovered; move to an open area.

title: EA Program Vehicle Use
text:
4 Definitions

Authorized driver: A person who holds a valid driver’s license and has a completed, approved Pomona College driver insurance form on file with the EA Coordinator; the only persons permitted to operate EA Program vehicles.
Drowsy driving: Operating a motor vehicle while significantly impaired by fatigue; a leading cause of serious crashes on long drives to remote field sites; if any crew member feels impaired by fatigue, pull over safely and rest before continuing.
Fuel card: A fleet credit card stored in the center console of each EA vehicle; used to purchase regular unleaded gasoline (87 octane) at participating stations; if declined, pay out of pocket and submit the receipt to the EA Coordinator for reimbursement.
Pre-trip inspection: A walk-around check of the vehicle before departure to identify safety issues (warning lights, tire damage, fluid leaks) that would make the vehicle unsafe to drive; required before every trip.
Post-trip return standard: The condition in which the vehicle must be returned after every use – clean interior, at least 3/4 tank of fuel, fuel card in the center console, no warning lights, parked in the designated garage spot.
Pomona College driver authorization: The college insurance form required before driving any Pomona College-owned or -leased vehicle; submitted to the EA Coordinator with a copy of a valid driver’s license; must be approved before the first trip.

title: EA Program Vehicle Use
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Motor vehicle operation on public roads and unpaved field-site access roads; loading and unloading heavy field equipment.
Environmental: Driving in adverse weather, reduced visibility, or on unfamiliar roads near field sites.
Fatigue: Long drives to remote field sites increase the risk of drowsy driving.




5.1 Requirements

Valid driver’s license (must be carried while driving)
Completed and approved Pomona College driver insurance form on file with the EA Coordinator
Familiarity with this SOP and SOP-F001 Field Safety



5.2 Emergency Procedures
In the event of an accident or breakdown:

Ensure all occupants are safe; move to a safe location if possible
Call 911 if anyone is injured
Contact Pomona College Campus Safety: (909) 621-8170
Notify the EA Coordinator and PI
Document the incident (photos, written description, other party information if applicable)
Do not admit fault at the scene; exchange insurance and contact information only
Complete a college incident report within 24 hours

Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety for general emergency response procedures.

7 Procedure

7.1 Before You Drive: Insurance Authorization
Before driving any EA vehicle for the first time, you must:

Obtain the Pomona College driver authorization and insurance form from the EA Coordinator.
Complete and submit the form with a copy of your valid driver’s license.
Wait for written approval before operating any EA vehicle.







ImportantNo Exceptions



You may not drive an EA vehicle until your insurance form has been approved and is on file with the EA Coordinator. This is a college requirement, not a suggestion. Driving without approval puts you and the program at serious liability risk.




7.2 Reserving a Vehicle

Contact the EA Coordinator to check availability.
Provide: date(s) and times needed, destination, number of passengers, and the name of the PI or instructor authorizing the trip.
Confirm the reservation before your trip; cancellations should be communicated as early as possible so others can use the vehicle.



7.3 Pre-Trip Inspection
Before departing, walk around the vehicle and verify:

Fuel gauge reads at least 3/4 full (refuel before departing if below 3/4; see §6.5)
Fuel card is present in the center console
Tires appear properly inflated with no visible damage
All lights (headlights, brake lights, turn signals) are functional
Mirrors are adjusted for the driver
Windshield is clean and wipers are functional
First aid kit is present and stocked (see SOP-F001)
No warning lights are illuminated on the dashboard
Any pre-existing damage is noted and reported to the EA Coordinator before departing

If any safety issue is found (warning lights, tire damage, brake problems), do not drive the vehicle. Contact the EA Coordinator immediately.


7.4 During the Trip

Obey all state and local traffic laws at all times.
All occupants must wear seatbelts (California law).
The driver must not use a handheld cell phone while driving (California Vehicle Code §23123).
Do not exceed the vehicle’s passenger capacity.
Secure all field equipment so it cannot shift during transport.
On unpaved roads, reduce speed and increase following distance.
If conditions become unsafe (severe weather, road hazards, driver fatigue), pull over and reassess before continuing.



7.5 Refueling

Use the fuel card located in the center console.
Select regular unleaded gasoline (87 octane).
If the fuel card is declined or missing, pay out of pocket and submit the receipt to the EA Coordinator for reimbursement.
Replace the fuel card in the center console after refueling.



7.6 Returning the Vehicle
After every trip, complete the following before leaving the vehicle:

Refuel: Return with at least a 3/4 tank of gas. If you used the vehicle, you are responsible for refueling.
Clean: Remove all personal items, trash, and field equipment. Brush or vacuum out dirt and mud. Wipe down surfaces if visibly soiled.
Fuel card: Confirm the fuel card is back in the center console.
Park: Return the vehicle to its designated spot in the campus garage.
Report problems: If anything is wrong with the vehicle (warning lights, unusual noises, damage, low tire pressure), notify the EA Coordinator immediately. Do not assume someone else will report it.







WarningReturn It Ready



The next person to use the vehicle should find it clean, fueled to at least 3/4 tank, with the fuel card in the center console, parked in the garage, and free of warning lights.

title: Field Decontamination Protocols
text: This SOP describes standardized procedures for decontaminating field equipment between sampling sites and between field outings. Proper decontamination serves two purposes: (1) preventing cross-contamination of samples that would compromise analytical results, and (2) preventing the transfer of invasive species, pathogens, and nuisance organisms between water bodies and field sites (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2016; Hosea & Finlayson, 2005). These procedures apply to all equipment that contacts environmental media (water, soil, sediment, biological tissue) or that is transported between sites.

title: Field Decontamination Protocols
text: This SOP describes standardized procedures for decontaminating field equipment between sampling sites and between field outings. Proper decontamination serves two purposes: (1) preventing cross-contamination of samples that would compromise analytical results, and (2) preventing the transfer of invasive species, pathogens, and nuisance organisms between water bodies and field sites (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2016; Hosea & Finlayson, 2005). These procedures apply to all equipment that contacts environmental media (water, soil, sediment, biological tissue) or that is transported between sites.

title: Field Decontamination Protocols
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All reusable field sampling equipment, wading gear (boots, waders, nets), sampling instruments (sondes, meters), containers, and hand tools used at EA Program field sites
Does not apply to: Disposable, single-use items (e.g., individually packaged sterile Colilert bottles, disposable filter cartridges); laboratory glassware cleaning (see SOP-L101); drone or camera equipment (wipe with dry cloth only unless visibly contaminated)
Location: Performed at field sites (between-site decontamination) and in the lab (post-field cleaning in SGM 131–134)

title: Field Decontamination Protocols
text:
4 Definitions

2% bleach solution: A dilute sodium hypochlorite solution prepared by adding 200 mL of household bleach (5–8% NaOCl) to 10 L of tap water; the standard decontamination solution for wading gear, nets, and hand tools in the EA Program; must be prepared fresh each field day as bleach degrades within hours (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2016).
Aquatic invasive species (AIS): Non-native organisms introduced to a water body where they cause ecological or economic harm; common AIS of concern in Southern California include New Zealand mudsnail, quagga mussel, didymo, and chytrid fungus; transferred between water bodies on wet gear (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2016).
Chytrid fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, Bd): A waterborne pathogenic fungus lethal to many amphibian species; transmitted via contaminated water, soil, and equipment; killed by 2% bleach or thermal decontamination at 60 °C (Hosea & Finlayson, 2005).
Cross-contamination: Transfer of analytes, biological material, or organisms from one sample or site to another via inadequately cleaned equipment; can invalidate analytical results and introduce invasive species.
Didymo (Didymosphenia geminata): A freshwater diatom that forms dense mats on stream substrates; tolerates damp conditions for many hours; felt-soled wading boots are a primary vector; killed by 2% bleach or drying for at least 48 hours (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2016).
Equipment blank: A sample of deionized water rinsed through decontaminated sampling equipment and collected as a QC sample; analyzed alongside field samples to verify that decontamination removes analytes below detection limits.
New Zealand mudsnail (Potamopyrgus antipodarum): An invasive snail less than 5 mm long that survives transit on damp wading gear for up to 28 hours; a significant concern in Southern California streams; killed by 2% bleach immersion for at least 10 minutes or thermal decontamination at 60 °C (Hosea & Finlayson, 2005).
Thermal decontamination: Application of water at ≥ 60 °C to kill aquatic invasive species and pathogens; preferred over bleach for equipment sensitive to sodium hypochlorite (rubber gaskets, sensor membranes) (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2016; Hosea & Finlayson, 2005).

title: Field Decontamination Protocols
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Dilute bleach (sodium hypochlorite) is a skin and eye irritant and can damage clothing. Handle with gloves and avoid splashing.
Physical: Hot water (60 °C or above) used for thermal decontamination poses a scald risk. Use insulated containers and pour carefully.
Biological: Equipment that has contacted contaminated water or soil may carry pathogens. Wear gloves during decontamination.




5.1 Required PPE

Nitrile gloves
Safety glasses (when using bleach solution)
Lab coat or field clothing you are willing to bleach-stain



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For bleach splashes to skin or eyes, flush with clean water for at least 15 minutes. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety and SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.

text:
6 Equipment and Materials

6.1 Decontamination Supplies







Item
Notes

6.2 Solution Preparation
Prepare a 2% bleach solution by adding 200 mL of household bleach (5–8% sodium hypochlorite) to 10 L of tap water. Prepare fresh solution each field day; bleach degrades within hours (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2016).
For thermal decontamination (alternative to bleach), heat water to at least 60 °C. Preferred for equipment that may be damaged by bleach (e.g., rubber gaskets, certain sensor membranes) (Hosea & Finlayson, 2005).

title: Field Decontamination Protocols
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Between-Site Decontamination (Field)
Perform the following steps before moving to the next sampling site.
Wading gear (boots, waders, chest packs):

Remove from the water body and inspect for visible organisms (snails, plant fragments, mud).
Use the scrub brush and tap water to remove all visible debris, paying special attention to boot soles, lace eyelets, and wader seams.
Spray all surfaces with 2% bleach solution or immerse boot soles in the bleach bucket for at least one minute (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2016).
Rinse with tap water to remove bleach residue before entering the next water body.

Nets, sieves, and kick screens:

Remove all visible organisms and debris by hand and with the scrub brush.
Soak in 2% bleach solution for at least one minute, or pour hot water (≥ 60 °C) over all mesh surfaces (Hosea & Finlayson, 2005).
Rinse with tap water.

Sampling instruments (sondes, meters, tubing):

Rinse the sensor housing and cable with tap water.
Wipe external surfaces with a cloth dampened with DI water.
Do not immerse sensitive electronics in bleach. If the manufacturer recommends a specific decontamination procedure, follow it instead.

Hand tools (trowels, augers, calipers, measuring tapes):

Scrub off visible soil or sediment with tap water and the brush.
Spray with 2% bleach solution or rinse with DI water.
Dry with paper towels before packing.



7.2 Post-Field Decontamination (Laboratory)
Upon return to the lab, before storing equipment:

Unpack all field equipment in the designated cleaning area (SGM 134 sink or outdoor wash area).
Repeat the cleaning steps from §6.1, using DI water for the final rinse of any equipment that contacts samples.
Allow all equipment to air-dry completely before storing. Incompletely dried equipment promotes mold and bacterial growth.
Inspect nets and mesh for tears; report damage to the lab manager.
Return all equipment to designated storage locations per SOP-L007.



7.3 Invasive Species of Concern
The following organisms are of particular concern in Southern California watersheds (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2016; Hosea & Finlayson, 2005):







Organism
Concern




New Zealand mudsnail (Potamopyrgus antipodarum)
< 5 mm; survives on wet gear up to 28 hours


Quagga/zebra mussel (Dreissena spp.)
Veligers invisible to the naked eye


Didymo (Didymosphenia geminata)
Algal cells survive on damp felt soles


Chytrid fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis)
Lethal to amphibians; transmitted via water and mud


Invasive aquatic plants (e.g., Arundo donax fragments)
Fragments root easily at new sites









Important



If sampling in a watershed known to harbor New Zealand mudsnails or quagga mussels, use thermal decontamination (≥ 60 °C) rather than bleach, as hot water is more reliably lethal to these organisms (Hosea & Finlayson, 2005). Allow gear to dry completely (at least 48 hours) before using it at another site.

The field lead verifies that decontamination supplies are packed before departure (include on the SOP-F002 Field Equipment Checklist).

For chemical sampling, submit one equipment blank per sampling event: rinse decontaminated equipment with DI water and collect the rinse as a sample. Analyze alongside field samples to verify that decontamination removes analytes below detection limits.

title: Random Sampling Design
text: This SOP provides standardized procedures for designing and executing random sampling in field and laboratory settings. Random sampling ensures that every unit in the target population has an equal and independent probability of selection, eliminating researcher bias and supporting valid statistical inference (Elzinga et al., 1998; Krebs, 1999).

title: Random Sampling Design
text: This SOP provides standardized procedures for designing and executing random sampling in field and laboratory settings. Random sampling ensures that every unit in the target population has an equal and independent probability of selection, eliminating researcher bias and supporting valid statistical inference (Elzinga et al., 1998; Krebs, 1999).

title: Random Sampling Design
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Any EA Program study where population estimates are the goal, including vegetation surveys, soil sampling, water quality monitoring, and laboratory subsampling
Does not apply to: Targeted or judgmental sampling designs (e.g., hot-spot investigations); mark-release-recapture studies for mobile organisms (see separate SOP)
Sampling types covered: Simple random sampling, grid-based random sampling, and stratified random sampling

title: Random Sampling Design
text:
4 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards



Field sampling involves site-specific hazards including uneven terrain, heat exposure, wildlife encounters, and sharp equipment (stakes, pins). Review site conditions before each sampling event.



4.1 Required PPE

Closed-toe shoes or boots
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
Gloves (when handling equipment or samples)



4.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety. Carry a first aid kit and charged cell phone to all field sites.

title: Random Sampling Design
text:
5 Definitions

Border rule: A convention for counting organisms that overlap a quadrat edge; the standard rule is to count organisms touching the top and right edges and exclude those touching the bottom and left edges; must be applied consistently within a study to avoid double-counting (Elzinga et al., 1998).
Grid-based random sampling: A method in which a coordinate grid is laid over the study area and quadrat locations are selected using randomly generated X and Y coordinates; the standard approach for quadrat-based ecological surveys (Elzinga et al., 1998).
Power analysis: A calculation to determine the minimum sample size (\(n\)) needed to detect a biologically meaningful effect with acceptable Type I error (\(\alpha\)) and Type II error (\(\beta\)) probability; should be completed before fieldwork begins (Krebs, 1999).
Quadrat: A square frame of known area (typically 0.25, 0.5, or 1.0 m2) used to delineate sampling units in the field (Elzinga et al., 1998).
Sampling frame: A numbered list or spatial grid that enumerates every unit in the population; units missing from the frame have zero probability of selection and introduce bias (Krebs, 1999).
Sampling universe (population): The complete set of units from which a sample will be drawn; must be explicitly defined before generating a sampling frame (Krebs, 1999).
Simple random sampling: A design in which \(n\) units are selected at random from a numbered list (sampling frame) such that every possible combination of \(n\) units has an equal probability of selection; appropriate when the population is homogeneous (Krebs, 1999).
Stratified random sampling: A design in which the population is divided into internally homogeneous subgroups (strata) and random samples are drawn independently from each stratum; reduces variance compared to simple random sampling when strata differ from each other (Elzinga et al., 1998; Krebs, 1999).
Stratum: A subdivision of the sampling universe into zones that are internally homogeneous (e.g., by elevation band, vegetation type, or soil moisture class); the basis for stratified random sampling.

Item

title: Random Sampling Design
text:
7 Biases and Interferences
Representative sampling requires strict adherence to randomized procedures. Common sources of bias include:

Incomplete sampling frames. Any unit missing from the frame has zero probability of selection (Krebs, 1999).
Haphazard placement. Never “throw” a quadrat to choose a location; human throws cluster toward the center of the area, violating equal probability assumptions (Elzinga et al., 1998).
Environmental heterogeneity. If the study area contains distinct gradients, simple random sampling may under-represent one end. Use stratified random sampling instead (§8.4).
Edge effects. Establish and apply a consistent border rule when counting organisms in quadrats (§8.3).

title: Random Sampling Design
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Generating Random Numbers
Use a software-based random number generator to produce unbiased selections. Never rely on manual or mental number selection (Krebs, 1999).
In R, generate a set of random integers within a defined range:


Code
# Generate 15 random integers between 1 and 100
set.seed(NULL)  # ensure a fresh seed each session
random_vals <- sample(1:100, size = 15, replace = FALSE)
sort(random_vals)

8.2 Simple Random Sampling
Use this approach when the population can be enumerated as a list (e.g., lab samples, batch numbers, individual organisms in a database) (Krebs, 1999).

Define the target population and compile a complete, numbered sampling frame.
Determine the required sample size (\(n\)) using a power analysis.
Use sample() in R to draw \(n\) unit numbers without replacement.
Document the random seed (if reproducibility is desired), the selected unit IDs, and the date of selection.
Collect the data or specimens from the selected units.



8.3 Grid-Based Random Sampling (Field)
Use this approach when the sampling universe is a spatially defined area (Elzinga et al., 1998).

8.3.1 Establishing the Baseline Grid

Locate the boundaries of the study site.
Drive a stake at the origin point and lay two tape measures at 90 degrees to create X and Y axes.
Secure the tapes with ground pins to define a coordinate grid (e.g., 20 m × 20 m).



8.3.2 Generating Coordinates and Placing Quadrats

Generate pairs of random integers within the range of each axis:



Code
x_max <- 20; y_max <- 20; n_quadrats <- 15
coords <- data.frame(
  X = sample(0:x_max, size = n_quadrats, replace = TRUE),
  Y = sample(0:y_max, size = n_quadrats, replace = TRUE)
)
coords <- coords[order(coords$X), ]
coords$QuadratID <- seq_len(nrow(coords))
knitr::kable(coords, row.names = FALSE)

Walk along the axes to each coordinate intersection and place the bottom-left corner of the quadrat at that point.
Never reposition a quadrat after placement; if a coordinate falls on an obstruction, record the obstruction and sample as-is (Elzinga et al., 1998).



8.3.3 Recording Data Within Quadrats

Quantify the target variable using one of three standardized metrics:

Density: Count every individual within the frame
Percent cover: Estimate the fraction of ground area covered
Frequency: Score presence (1) or absence (0)

Apply the border rule consistently (§4).
Aim to sample at least 5–10% of total grid area, or a minimum of 30 quadrat placements, for adequate statistical power (Krebs, 1999).
Calculate the mean count (or cover) per quadrat and extrapolate:

\[
\text{Estimated population} =
\bar{x}_{\text{quadrat}} \times
\frac{\text{Total site area}}{\text{Area of one quadrat}}
\]



8.4 Stratified Random Sampling
Use this approach when the study area contains distinct environmental gradients that would increase variance under simple random sampling (Elzinga et al., 1998; Krebs, 1999).

Divide the study area into homogeneous strata based on a relevant environmental variable.
Within each stratum, establish an independent coordinate grid following §8.3.
Generate random coordinates separately for each stratum.
Sample each stratum independently; do not pool random selections across strata.
Weight stratum means by the proportion of total area each stratum represents when calculating site-level estimates.



8.5 Map-Based Sampling with Exclusion Zones

Obtain or create a georeferenced map of the study area.
Delineate exclusion zones and calculate the remaining accessible area.
Generate random coordinates across the full extent, then discard any that fall within exclusion zones.
Continue generating coordinates until the target sample size is met within the accessible area.
Record discarded coordinates in the sampling log.







TipR Implementation



An R script for map-based random sampling with exclusion polygons can be built using the sf package. Generate random points with sf::st_sample(), then filter against exclusion polygons with sf::st_difference().

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
This SOP establishes the minimum standards for field documentation in the EA Program. Complete, legible, and contemporaneous field notes are the foundation of defensible environmental data (Kanare, 1985). Notes recorded in the field cannot be reconstructed later from memory; what is not written down at the time is effectively lost. This SOP ensures that every field visit produces a record sufficient for another trained researcher to understand what was done, where, when, by whom, and under what conditions.
For laboratory notebook requirements, see SOP-L010 Laboratory Notebook Recording.

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
This SOP establishes the minimum standards for field documentation in the EA Program. Complete, legible, and contemporaneous field notes are the foundation of defensible environmental data (Kanare, 1985). Notes recorded in the field cannot be reconstructed later from memory; what is not written down at the time is effectively lost. This SOP ensures that every field visit produces a record sufficient for another trained researcher to understand what was done, where, when, by whom, and under what conditions.
For laboratory notebook requirements, see SOP-L010 Laboratory Notebook Recording.

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All EA Program field activities, including sampling, sensor deployment and retrieval, site reconnaissance, equipment installation, and monitoring visits.
Does not apply to: Laboratory work or purely digital data collection on tablets and phones (though digital entries should follow the same content standards described here).
Location: All EA Program field sites.

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




Lab PI
Set documentation standards; review notebooks periodically


Field Lead
Ensure all team members record required entries


All Field Personnel
Maintain a field notebook per this SOP


New Students
Read this SOP before their first field outing

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
4 Definitions

Chain of custody (COC): A documented record of sample possession at every transfer point from collection to laboratory analysis; the COC form number must be cross-referenced in the field notebook entry for the corresponding samples.
Contemporaneous record: An entry made at the time the observation or action occurs, not reconstructed from memory afterward; the defining characteristic of a legally defensible field or laboratory record (Kanare, 1985).
Deviation: Any departure from a written SOP during field activities; must be recorded in the notebook with the reason for the deviation and an assessment of its potential effect on data quality.
Field notebook: A bound, weather-resistant notebook with numbered pages used to record all field observations, measurements, and activities; the primary raw-data record for a field project (Kanare, 1985).
Good Documentation Practice (GDP): A set of principles for creating accurate, legible, contemporaneous, original, and attributable records; the foundation of data integrity in regulated and research laboratories (Broman & Woo, 2018).
Header block: A standardized set of fields (date, time, site, personnel, weather, purpose, SOPs in use) recorded at the top of each field visit entry before any observations or data are logged.
Rite in the Rain: A brand of field notebook and paper products printed on water-resistant stock that can be written on with ballpoint or mechanical pencil even in rain; the preferred notebook format for EA Program field work.
Sample ID: A unique alphanumeric code assigned to each sample at the moment of collection, cross-referencing the field notebook, sample label, COC form, and laboratory data file.
Tare mass: Not applicable in field notebooks – see SOP-L400 Soil Moisture.
Time stamp: The date and time of a discrete field action, recorded in the notebook at the moment of the action; use ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM) or a consistent AM/PM scheme throughout the notebook.

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
5 Notebook Selection and Preparation

5.1 Acceptable Notebooks
Use a bound, weather-resistant field notebook with numbered pages. Acceptable options include:

Rite in the Rain (top-spiral or side-spiral, any size)
Any hardbound notebook with numbered pages (if weather protection is not required for the site)

Do not use loose-leaf paper, spiral notebooks with perforated pages, or sticky notes for primary field records (Kanare, 1985).


5.2 Front Matter
On the inside front cover or first page of a new notebook, record:

Your name, phone number, and email
“If found, please return to: EA Program, Pomona College, SGM 133”
Project name(s)
Date the notebook was put into service



5.3 Page Numbering
If pages are not pre-numbered, number them in ink before going to the field. Never remove pages from a field notebook.

title: Field Notebook Protocols
section: 6 Required Entries for Every Field Visit
text:
6 Required Entries for Every Field Visit
Every field visit entry must begin with the following header information. Write it before you do anything else on site.

6.1 Header Block
Record at the top of a new page or clearly separated section:







Field
Example




Date
2026-05-18 (ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD)


Time of arrival
08:15 PST


Site name / ID
Bernard Field Station, Plot BFS-03


GPS coordinates
34.0975 N, 117.7125 W (WGS84)


Personnel present
M. Los Huertos, J. Smith


Weather conditions
Clear, ~25 °C, light wind from W, no recent rain


Purpose of visit
Soil sampling for CN analysis; sensor download


SOPs in use
F400, F401, F510





6.2 Time Stamps
Record the time of every discrete action: sample collection, instrument reading, equipment start/stop, calibration check, photo taken. Use 24-hour format or AM/PM consistently throughout the notebook (Broman & Woo, 2018).


6.3 Site Observations
Before beginning work, note anything relevant:

Visible changes since the last visit (new construction, vegetation removal, standing water, animal activity, vandalism, equipment condition)
Odors or visual indicators of contamination
Land use activities in progress nearby (mowing, irrigation, construction)



6.4 Sample and Measurement Records
For each sample collected or measurement taken, record at minimum:

Sample ID (use the project’s established naming convention)
Time of collection or measurement
Location (plot, transect position, depth, or other descriptor)
Value or description (e.g., “pH = 7.2,” “soil moist, dark brown, loamy texture”)
Preservation method applied (e.g., “filtered, acidified with HNO3 to pH < 2”)
Container type and label verification







TipWrite More Than You Think You Need



Include observations that seem obvious at the time. “Soil was saturated and smelled of sulfide” or “sensor housing had a spider web across the inlet” may be critical for interpreting data months later (Kanare, 1985).




6.5 Equipment and Instrument Notes
Record for every instrument used:

Instrument ID (serial number or lab asset tag)
Calibration status (date of last calibration; field check performed?)
Settings (logging interval, flow rate, method name)
Any malfunctions, error messages, or anomalies



6.6 Deviations from SOPs
If you deviate from the standard procedure for any reason, record:

What you did differently and why
Whether the deviation may affect data quality
Who authorized the deviation (if applicable)



6.7 Departure
Before leaving the site, record:

Time of departure
Summary of work completed and any work left undone
Disposition of samples (e.g., “cooler with ice, to lab by 12:00”)
Any follow-up actions needed

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
7 Sketches and Diagrams
A simple sketch is often more informative than a paragraph of text (Kanare, 1985). Include sketches of:

Site layout showing sampling locations, landmarks, and compass orientation
Equipment placement (sensor positions, transect layout, plot boundaries)
Anything unusual (erosion features, spill boundaries, wildlife sightings relevant to the study)

Label all sketches with a north arrow, approximate scale, date, and your initials.

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
8 Photographs

8.1 When to Photograph

At the start of every visit: a general site photo showing conditions
Each sampling location before and after sampling
Equipment installations and sensor positions
Anything unusual or noteworthy (damage, contamination indicators, unexpected conditions)
Calibration setups



8.2 Photo Naming and Logging
Record in the notebook the photo number or filename and a brief description for every photo taken:

“Photo IMG_4231: Plot BFS-03 looking NE, pre-sampling, 08:22”

Transfer photos to the project folder within 48 hours and rename using the convention:
YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_Description_PhotoNumber.jpg
Back up photos to the project GitHub repository or shared drive (Broman & Woo, 2018).

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
9 Corrections and Errors

Never erase, white-out, or obliterate an entry.
To correct an error, draw a single line through the incorrect text so it remains legible. Write the correction nearby and initial and date the change.
If you skip a page or leave blank space, draw a diagonal line through the unused area and initial it to prevent later additions (Kanare, 1985).

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
10 Chain of Custody
When samples will be submitted to an analytical laboratory (internal or external), complete a Chain of Custody (COC) form. The COC must accompany the samples and include:

Project name and PI
Sample IDs matching the field notebook entries
Date and time of collection
Number and type of containers
Analyses requested
Preservatives applied
Signatures at each transfer (field to transport, transport to lab)

Record the COC form number in the field notebook entry for cross-reference. See SOP-F008 Sample Labeling, COC, and Transport for the full chain-of-custody procedure.

title: Field Notebook Protocols
text:
11 Notebook Archiving

At the end of a field season or project, submit completed notebooks to the PI for archiving.
Notebooks are stored in labeled binders in SGM 133 and must be retained for a minimum of 5 years after project completion.
Transcribe key data from notebooks to digital spreadsheets within 48 hours of each field visit, following the tidy data principles in

Flag any discrepancies between the notebook and the digital record and resolve them with the field lead.
