title: Field Safety
text: This SOP covers field-based research activities and class field trips, addressing transportation, weather-based, and biotic hazards. Although we cannot predict all risks and hazards, it is everyone’s responsibility to identify and mitigate potential risks associated with field work (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).

title: Field Safety
text: This SOP covers field-based research activities and class field trips, addressing transportation, weather-based, and biotic hazards. Although we cannot predict all risks and hazards, it is everyone’s responsibility to identify and mitigate potential risks associated with field work (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).

title: Field Safety
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All field-based research activities, class field trips, and off-campus data collection
Does not apply to: Laboratory-only procedures (see relevant Lab SOPs)
Location: All field sites used by the EA Program

title: Field Safety
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




Instructor / PI
Approve field plans, ensure training compliance


Trained Personnel
Follow this SOP, report deviations and hazards


New Students
Complete training and document review before field work



Anyone conducting research in the field is required to have documented training before commencing field work. Learning about risks and taking the precautions described here is the first step to reducing the risks associated with field work. Anyone working in the field should identify potential risks and attempt to mitigate them.

title: Field Safety
text:
4 Definitions

Field lead: The trained, designated person responsible for safety decisions during a field outing; authorizes resumption of work after a stop-work condition, maintains communication with the PI, and is the first point of contact in an emergency.
Heat illness: A spectrum of conditions caused by overheating, ranging from heat cramps and heat exhaustion to heat stroke; heat stroke (core temperature above 40 °C, altered mental status) is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate 911 activation (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Incident report: A written record of any injury, illness, near-miss, or property damage occurring during field work; submitted to the PI and the college risk management office within 24 hours of the event (Pomona College, 2024).
Minimum crew size: Two persons at all times during field work; one person must be capable of summoning help if the other is incapacitated. Solo field work is prohibited unless explicitly waived in writing by the PI for low-hazard, high-visibility situations.
PPE (personal protective equipment): Equipment worn to minimize exposure to field hazards, including closed-toed shoes, long pants, safety glasses, sun protection, and task-specific items such as hard hats and cut-resistant gloves (National Research Council, 2011).
Risk assessment: A structured evaluation of the hazards at a field site and the probability and severity of resulting harm; used to select appropriate control measures and documented on the Field Work Planning Form (Appendix A).
Stop-work authority: The right – and duty – of any crew member to stop field operations without prior approval when they observe an imminent safety hazard. No crew member may be penalized for exercising stop-work authority in good faith (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Two-person rule: See “Minimum crew size” above.
Widow-maker: A dead branch, dead tree, or tree with structural defects that may fall without warning; a leading cause of fatalities in forest work; avoid working beneath or near hazard trees, especially in high wind.

title: Field Safety
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningGeneral Field Hazards



Reducing risks is one of our main priorities. Like many endeavors in life, field work has certain risks. We can reduce these risks dramatically by understanding our physical limits and how these can be tested by uncontrolled environmental factors.
We rely on each individual to be mindful of their own limitations and to advocate for themselves and others to reduce risk exposure.



5.1 Required Materials

First Aid Kit (kits are located in EA vehicles; see EA vehicle checklist to document their presence)
Cell phone(s) with emergency contacts programmed
Walkie-talkies (optional but recommended for sites with poor cell service)
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) appropriate for the site and task

title: Field Safety
text:
6 Estimated Time
Preparing to go in the field can take a few minutes to several hours of planning and gathering resources. A good rule of thumb is to double the time you think it will take to get ready.

title: Field Safety
text:
7 Field Preparation Checklist

7.1 Before Departure

Check weather report and air quality index
Read and understand emergency procedures for the specific site
Know locations of emergency equipment (first aid kit, fire extinguisher if applicable)
Be aware of any special medical conditions of team members
Report departure time and expected return to supervisor
Identify the hospital or urgent care facility closest to the field site
Develop a transportation plan with a designated driver
Complete a risk assessment and safety plan (Appendix A)



7.2 Supply Checklist

PPE appropriate for the task (see §8 for task-specific items)
Rain gear (if precipitation is forecast)
Closed-toed shoes or field boots (no sandals or open-toed shoes)
Additional clothing/gear for site conditions (e.g., long sleeves and gaiters for poison oak areas)
Sunscreen and sun hat
Adequate water (minimum 1 L per person per 2 hours in warm conditions)
Rite in the Rain field notebook and waterproof pen
Watch or phone for time-stamping field records
First aid kit
Cell phone with the following numbers programmed:

911 (emergency)
Campus safety: (909) 621-8170 (Pomona College)
Lab supervisor and/or instructor
Field team members




7.3 On Site

Identify a meeting time and departure plan if the team splits up
Leave no trace: ensure the environment remains undisturbed
Field lead ensures that safety procedures are followed
Report any potential field hazards to the field lead immediately

title: Field Safety
text:
8 Hazard-Specific Procedures

8.1 Transportation

All passengers must wear seatbelts at all times
Designated driver is identified before departure; no impaired driving
Allow extra time on unpaved or unfamiliar access roads
Do not drive into flooded washes or roads



8.2 Weather Hazards

8.2.1 Lightning
Follow the 30-30 rule: if the time between a lightning flash and thunder is 30 seconds or less, the storm is within 10 miles – seek shelter immediately. Remain sheltered for 30 minutes after the last flash or thunder (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
When lightning threatens:

Move away from tall isolated objects (trees, towers, open hilltops)
Avoid open fields and water bodies
Seek a low-lying area away from individual trees
Do not hold metal equipment
If no shelter is available, spread the team out (at least 30 m apart) to reduce the risk of multiple casualties



8.2.2 Heat
Southern California field sites can exceed 40 °C. Carry adequate water, take shade breaks, and monitor for heat-related illness. Symptoms of heat exhaustion include heavy sweating, weakness, cold or clammy skin, weak pulse, nausea, and fainting. Heat stroke (hot/dry/red skin, rapid strong pulse, unconsciousness) is a medical emergency: call 911 immediately and cool the person rapidly (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).


8.2.3 High Wind
Sustained winds above 25 mph (above 20 mph when working near trees or overhead hazards) require stopping work. High winds increase the risk of widow-makers and can topple equipment.



8.3 Overhead Hazards (Widow-Makers)
Before working under or near any tree:

Look up and assess the crown for dead branches, leaning limbs, or structural failure
Do not work beneath or near hazard trees in high wind
Wear a hard hat when working in forested areas with overhead hazard potential
If a hazard tree is identified, flag it and report it to the field lead; do not attempt to remove it



8.4 Sharp Tools
When using hand saws, loppers, pruners, or other cutting tools:

Keep blades sheathed while walking
Pass tools handle-first; never toss tools
Never carry open blades through brush
Wear cut-resistant gloves when operating cutting tools



8.5 Biotic Hazards

8.5.1 Poison Oak
Wear long sleeves, long pants, and gloves when working in potential poison oak habitat. Learn to identify the plant. Wash exposed skin with soap and water as soon as possible after potential contact. Do not burn plant material that may contain poison oak.


8.5.2 Ticks
Wear long pants tucked into socks and long sleeves. Use permethrin- treated clothing or DEET-based repellent in tick habitat. Perform a full-body tick check at the end of every field day. Remove attached ticks promptly with fine-tipped tweezers.


8.5.3 Stinging Insects
Know whether any team member has a history of anaphylaxis. Ensure that at least one team member knows the location of any prescribed epinephrine auto-injectors (EpiPens) in the group. Call 911 immediately if anaphylaxis is suspected.


8.5.4 Wildlife
Do not approach, feed, or attempt to handle wildlife. Report unusual wildlife behavior (particularly in mammals that could indicate rabies) to the field lead.

title: Field Safety
text:
9 Emergency Response Procedure

9.1 Responding to a Medical Emergency

Survey the scene; identify any risks to other team members
Do not move the injured person unless they are in immediate danger
Call 911; provide the following information:

Suspected type of injury or illness
Location (GPS coordinates if known; nearest landmark otherwise)
Type of assistance required
Number of persons injured

Identify a location for emergency vehicle access and send someone to meet the vehicle
Notify the PI or instructor as soon as possible (Pomona College, 2024)



9.2 Chronic Conditions
Personnel with chronic conditions (epilepsy, diabetes, heart conditions, severe allergies) must inform the field lead before each field outing. The field lead will ensure the team knows relevant first aid steps and the location of any required medications.


9.3 Injury from Equipment
Handle all equipment with caution. Read operating procedures before use. Do not use any equipment you are unsure of how to handle – ask a trained team member first.


9.4 Documenting the Incident

Record what happened and how the injury or illness occurred in the field notebook
Complete a formal incident report and submit it to the PI and the college risk management office within 24 hours
This information is used to eliminate hazards and prevent future incidents (Pomona College, 2024)

title: Field Safety
text:
10 Stop-Work Conditions
Stop all field operations immediately if any of the following occur:

Lightning is detected within about 10 miles, or thunder is audible
Wind is sustained above 25 mph (above 20 mph when working near trees or other overhead hazards)
A crew member shows signs of heat illness, injury, or allergic reaction
An unexpected utility or buried line is found within the work zone
Crew size drops below the two-person minimum

Resume only when the field lead confirms conditions are safe (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).

It establishes reproducible workflows for exploratory data analysis, hypothesis testing, regression modeling, and reporting, ensuring that all analyses are transparent, well-documented, and consistent across projects (Wickham et al., 2023; Zuur et al., 2010).

text: This SOP provides standardized R analysis templates for common statistical procedures used in EA Program research. It establishes reproducible workflows for exploratory data analysis, hypothesis testing, regression modeling, and reporting, ensuring that all analyses are transparent, well-documented, and consistent across projects (Wickham et al., 2023; Zuur et al., 2010).

title: Statistical Analysis Templates (R)
text:
2 Scope

Does not apply to: Bioinformatics sequence analysis (see SOP-L705); GIS-specific spatial statistics (see SOP-L804); instrument calibration curve fitting (see method-specific SOPs)

text:

title: Statistical Analysis Templates (R)
text:
4 Definitions

ANOVA (Analysis of Variance): A statistical test that partitions total variance in a response variable into components attributable to one or more categorical factors; tests whether group means differ significantly; assumes normality and homogeneity of variance.
Confidence interval: A range of values computed from sample data that, under repeated sampling, contains the true population parameter with a stated probability (e.g., 95%); wider intervals reflect greater uncertainty.
Effect size: A standardized measure of the magnitude of a difference or relationship, independent of sample size; examples include Cohen’s d (mean differences), \(r^2\) (explained variance), and Hedge’s g; should always accompany p-values.
Mixed model: A statistical model containing both fixed effects (factors whose levels are deliberately chosen) and random effects (factors whose levels represent a random sample from a larger population); appropriate when data have hierarchical or repeated-measures structure.
p-value: The probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as the one obtained (or more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true; does not measure the probability that the null hypothesis is true; must be interpreted with effect size.
Power: The probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false; increases with sample size, effect size, and significance level; should be considered in study design to ensure adequate sample sizes.
Residual: The difference between an observed value and the value predicted by a statistical model; examination of residuals is the primary diagnostic for checking model assumptions.

title: Statistical Analysis Templates (R)
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Analysis Workflow Overview
Every statistical analysis should follow this sequence:

State the research question and hypotheses
Import and validate data (see SOP-L803)
Conduct exploratory data analysis (EDA)
Check assumptions for the intended statistical test
Fit the model
Evaluate model diagnostics
Interpret results and generate figures/tables
Write up methods and results in a Quarto document
Commit the complete analysis to Git



7.2 Quarto Document Header
Begin every analysis with a standard Quarto header:
---
title: "Analysis: [Project Name]"
author: "[Your Name]"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true
    embed-resources: true
bibliography: references.bib
---


7.3 Exploratory Data Analysis Template


Code
library(tidyverse)

# --- 1. Load and inspect data ---
dat <- read_csv("data/processed/project_data.csv")
glimpse(dat)

# --- 2. Summary statistics ---
dat %>%
  group_by(treatment) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(response, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(response, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(response, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(response, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(response, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# --- 3. Distributional plots ---
ggplot(dat, aes(x = response)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment) +
  labs(x = "Response Variable (units)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(dat, aes(x = treatment, y = response)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Response Variable (units)") +
  theme_minimal()

# --- 4. Missing data assessment ---
dat %>%
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "n_missing") %>%
  filter(n_missing > 0)




7.4 Two-Sample Comparisons


Code
# --- Check normality within groups ---
dat %>%
  group_by(treatment) %>%
  summarize(
    shapiro_p = shapiro.test(response)$p.value
  )

# --- Check equal variances ---
car::leveneTest(response ~ treatment, data = dat)

# --- Parametric: two-sample t-test ---
t_result <- t.test(response ~ treatment, data = dat, var.equal = FALSE)
t_result

# --- Nonparametric alternative: Wilcoxon rank-sum ---
wilcox.test(response ~ treatment, data = dat)

# --- Effect size ---
library(effectsize)
cohens_d(response ~ treatment, data = dat)




7.5 One-Way ANOVA Template


Code
# --- Fit ANOVA ---
aov_model <- aov(response ~ treatment, data = dat)

# --- Check assumptions ---
# Normality of residuals
shapiro.test(residuals(aov_model))
qqnorm(residuals(aov_model)); qqline(residuals(aov_model))

# Homogeneity of variance
car::leveneTest(response ~ treatment, data = dat)

# Residual vs. fitted plot
plot(aov_model, which = 1)

# --- ANOVA table ---
summary(aov_model)

# --- Post-hoc pairwise comparisons ---
library(emmeans)
emm <- emmeans(aov_model, ~ treatment)
pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")

# --- Nonparametric alternative: Kruskal-Wallis ---
kruskal.test(response ~ treatment, data = dat)








TipTip



Always check assumptions before interpreting p-values. If residuals are non-normal or variances are unequal, consider a transformation (log, square root) or switch to a nonparametric test. Document the reasoning in your analysis script (Zuur et al., 2010).




7.6 Linear Regression Template


Code
# --- Fit linear model ---
lm_model <- lm(response ~ predictor1 + predictor2, data = dat)

# --- Model summary ---
summary(lm_model)

# --- Tidy output ---
library(broom)
tidy(lm_model, conf.int = TRUE)
glance(lm_model)

# --- Diagnostics ---
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(lm_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Check multicollinearity
car::vif(lm_model)

# --- Model performance ---
library(performance)
check_model(lm_model)

# --- Visualization ---
ggplot(dat, aes(x = predictor1, y = response)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Predictor (units)", y = "Response (units)",
       caption = sprintf("R-squared = %.3f, p = %.4f",
                         summary(lm_model)$r.squared,
                         glance(lm_model)$p.value)) +
  theme_minimal()




7.7 Mixed-Effects Model Template
For data with nested or repeated-measures structure:


Code
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)  # For p-values via Satterthwaite

# --- Fit mixed model ---
# Fixed effect: treatment
# Random effect: site (multiple samples per site)
mixed_model <- lmer(response ~ treatment + (1 | site_id), data = dat)

# --- Summary with p-values ---
summary(mixed_model)

# --- Marginal and conditional R-squared ---
MuMIn::r.squaredGLMM(mixed_model)

# --- Post-hoc comparisons ---
library(emmeans)
emm <- emmeans(mixed_model, ~ treatment)
pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")

# --- Residual diagnostics ---
plot(mixed_model)
qqnorm(resid(mixed_model)); qqline(resid(mixed_model))




7.8 Multivariate / Community Analysis Template


Code
library(vegan)

# --- Prepare community matrix ---
# Rows = sites, columns = species/variables
comm_matrix <- dat %>%
  select(site_id, species, abundance) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = species, values_from = abundance,
              values_fill = 0) %>%
  column_to_rownames("site_id")

# --- Diversity indices ---
diversity_h <- diversity(comm_matrix, index = "shannon")
richness <- specnumber(comm_matrix)

# --- Ordination (NMDS) ---
nmds <- metaMDS(comm_matrix, distance = "bray", k = 2,
                trymax = 100)
stressplot(nmds)

# Plot
ordiplot(nmds, type = "n")
points(nmds, col = as.factor(env_data$treatment), pch = 16)
legend("topright", legend = levels(as.factor(env_data$treatment)),
       col = 1:nlevels(as.factor(env_data$treatment)), pch = 16)

# --- PERMANOVA ---
adonis2(comm_matrix ~ treatment, data = env_data,
        method = "bray", permutations = 999)




7.9 Figure Formatting Standards
All figures for reports and publications must follow these conventions:

Use theme_minimal() or a consistent custom theme
Label axes with variable names and units
Use colorblind-friendly palettes (e.g., viridis, RColorBrewer “Set2”)
Include figure captions using the #| fig-cap: chunk option
Save publication figures at 300 DPI as both PDF and PNG:



Code
ggsave("analysis/output/fig_treatment_response.pdf",
       width = 6, height = 4, units = "in")
ggsave("analysis/output/fig_treatment_response.png",
       width = 6, height = 4, units = "in", dpi = 300)




7.10 Reporting Statistical Results
When writing results in a Quarto document, follow APA conventions:

Report test statistics, degrees of freedom, and p-values: “Treatment had a significant effect on soil pH (F(2, 27) = 4.53, p = 0.020)”
Report effect sizes alongside p-values
Include confidence intervals for parameter estimates
Round to a consistent number of decimal places (typically 2 for test statistics, 3 for p-values)
Use broom::tidy() and knitr::kable() for formatted tables



Code
library(broom)
library(knitr)

tidy(aov_model) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "ANOVA results for soil pH by treatment")

Analyses must be committed to Git with clear commit messages

title: GIS and Spatial Data Management
text:
4 Definitions

Coordinate reference system (CRS): A framework that associates coordinates with locations on Earth; consists of a datum (reference ellipsoid), a projection (for 2D maps), and a coordinate system (e.g., latitude/longitude or meters); data layers must share the same CRS for spatial operations.
Geodatabase: A structured container for storing multiple spatial datasets, attribute tables, and topological rules in a single file; the preferred format for complex GIS projects with many related layers.
GeoTIFF: A TIFF image file with embedded geospatial metadata (CRS, extent, resolution); the standard raster format for spatial data exchange in remote sensing and GIS.
Raster: A spatial data model representing continuous surfaces as a grid of equally sized cells (pixels), each with one or more attribute values; used for elevation, imagery, and interpolated surfaces.
Shapefile (.shp): A common vector spatial data format introduced by Esri; stores geometry (points, lines, polygons) and attribute data in multiple associated files (.shp, .dbf, .shx, .prj minimum); widely supported but limited by 2 GB file size and 10-character field name constraints.
Vector: A spatial data model representing discrete features as points, lines, or polygons defined by coordinate pairs; used for sample locations, stream networks, and land parcel boundaries.
WGS84 (World Geodetic System 1984): The global geodetic datum used by GPS; EPSG code 4326; the required CRS for all EA Program GPS-collected point data before projection into a local coordinate system.

7 Procedure

7.1 Coordinate Reference Systems
All EA Program spatial data must use one of the following coordinate reference systems (CRS). Document the CRS in every file, script, and metadata record.








CRS Name
EPSG Code
Use Case




WGS 84 (geographic)
4326
GPS data, web maps, data exchange


NAD83 / UTM Zone 11N
26911
Local analysis in Southern California


NAD83 / California Zone 5
2229
County and municipal data









TipTip



When in doubt, store data in EPSG:4326 (latitude/longitude, WGS 84). Transform to a projected CRS for distance and area calculations.


When loading spatial data in R, always verify and set the CRS explicitly:


Code
library(sf)

# Read a shapefile
sites <- st_read("data/spatial/sampling_sites.shp")

# Check CRS
st_crs(sites)

# Transform to UTM Zone 11N for area calculations
sites_utm <- st_transform(sites, crs = 26911)




7.2 File Formats









Format
Extension
Use Case
Notes




GeoPackage
.gpkg
Preferred for all vector data
Single file, open standard


Shapefile
.shp + .dbf + .shx + .prj

Keep all component files together

.tif
Raster data
Include CRS in header


CSV with XY
.csv
Simple point data
Requires separate CRS documentation


GeoJSON
.geojson
Web applications
Always WGS 84



GeoPackage (.gpkg) is the preferred format for new projects because it stores geometry, attributes, and CRS in a single file without the limitations of shapefiles (10-character field names, 2 GB size limit) (Pebesma & Bivand, 2023).


7.3 File Naming and Directory Structure
Follow the conventions in SOP-L803 with the addition of a data/spatial/ subdirectory:
project_name/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   ├── processed/
│   ├── spatial/
│   │   ├── raw/          # Downloaded or collected spatial data
│   │   ├── processed/    # Clipped, projected, joined layers
│   │   └── metadata/     # FGDC or ISO metadata files
│   └── metadata/
├── analysis/
│   ├── scripts/
│   └── maps/             # Exported map figures
└── README.md


7.4 Spatial Data Acquisition

Source

When downloading external data, record the source URL, download date, and any subsetting parameters in the metadata file.


7.5 Spatial Data Processing in R
A standard workflow for processing spatial data:


Code
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(tidyverse)

# --- 1. Load vector data ---
sites <- st_read("data/spatial/raw/sampling_sites.gpkg")
watershed <- st_read("data/spatial/raw/claremont_watershed.gpkg")

# --- 2. Verify and harmonize CRS ---
st_crs(sites) == st_crs(watershed)
sites <- st_transform(sites, crs = st_crs(watershed))

# --- 3. Spatial operations ---
# Clip sites to watershed boundary
sites_in_watershed <- st_intersection(sites, watershed)

# Buffer sites by 100 m
site_buffers <- st_buffer(sites_in_watershed, dist = 100)

# --- 4. Load and extract raster data ---
dem <- rast("data/spatial/raw/dem_10m.tif")
sites_in_watershed$elevation_m <- extract(dem, sites_in_watershed)$value

# --- 5. Save processed outputs ---
st_write(sites_in_watershed,
         "data/spatial/processed/sites_with_elevation.gpkg",
         delete_dsn = TRUE)




7.6 Map Production
All maps for reports and publications must include:

North arrow
Legend with clear labels and units

library(tmap)

tm_shape(watershed) +
  tm_polygons(col = "lightblue", alpha = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(sites_in_watershed) +
  tm_dots(col = "elevation_m", size = 0.5,
          palette = "viridis",
          title = "Elevation (m)") +
  tm_scale_bar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_compass(position = c("right", "top")) +
  tm_layout(
    title = "Sampling Sites: Claremont Watershed",
    title.size = 1.2,
    legend.outside = TRUE
  )

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
This SOP establishes the overarching quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC) framework for all analytical work in the EA Program laboratory. It defines the minimum QC requirements that apply across methods, describes how to calculate and interpret QC metrics, specifies detection limit procedures, and establishes the data documentation and reproducibility practices required for every analysis. Individual analytical SOPs reference this document for general QC principles and add method-specific requirements (APHA et al., 2012; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
Quality assurance is the system of management actions that ensures the analytical process produces results of known and documented quality. Quality control is the set of technical activities (blanks, standards, duplicates, spikes) embedded in each analytical batch to measure and control that quality in real time (Taylor, 1987).

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
This SOP establishes the overarching quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC) framework for all analytical work in the EA Program laboratory. It defines the minimum QC requirements that apply across methods, describes how to calculate and interpret QC metrics, specifies detection limit procedures, and establishes the data documentation and reproducibility practices required for every analysis. Individual analytical SOPs reference this document for general QC principles and add method-specific requirements (APHA et al., 2012; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
Quality assurance is the system of management actions that ensures the analytical process produces results of known and documented quality. Quality control is the set of technical activities (blanks, standards, duplicates, spikes) embedded in each analytical batch to measure and control that quality in real time (Taylor, 1987).

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All quantitative chemical, physical, and biological analyses performed in the EA Program laboratory, including those described in SOPs L002 through L999 and analyses of field-collected samples (SOPs F001 through F999)
Does not apply to: Qualitative screening tests (e.g., visual soil texture by feel, SOP-F401) unless those tests include a quantitative component
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




Lab PI (QA Manager)
Approve this SOP; review QC data quarterly; authorize corrective actions


Lab Manager
Maintain instrument logs, reagent inventory, and QC records; train new analysts


Analyst
Implement all QC requirements for each batch; flag QC failures; document corrective actions


Data Reviewer
Verify QC compliance before data are reported or published

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
4 Definitions

Accuracy: The closeness of a measured value to the true or accepted reference value; assessed using certified reference materials (CRMs) and laboratory-fortified blanks (LFBs) (Taylor, 1987).
Calibration blank: A solution containing only the analytical solvent or reagent matrix (no analyte); used to establish the instrument baseline (zero) for each calibration sequence.
Certified reference material (CRM): A material with certified analyte concentrations traceable to a national or international metrology institute (NIST, USGS, IRMM); used to verify analytical accuracy across instruments and over time (APHA et al., 2012).
Control chart (Shewhart chart): A time-series plot of QC sample results with control limits (typically ±2σ warning limits and ±3σ action limits); used to distinguish random analytical variation from systematic drift or instrument malfunction.
Continuing calibration verification (CVS): A mid-range calibration standard analyzed at regular intervals (typically every 10 samples) during an analytical run; must recover within ±10% of the stated value; failure requires re-calibration and re-analysis of affected samples (APHA et al., 2012).
Detection limit – Method Detection Limit (MDL): The minimum concentration of an analyte that can be detected with 99% confidence under stated method conditions; determined from at least 7 replicate analyses of a low-level spike following 40 CFR Part 136 Appendix B (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2016).
Detection limit – Limit of Blank (LOB): The highest signal expected from a blank sample; LOB = meanblank + 1.645 × SDblank (Armbruster & Pry, 2008).
Detection limit – Limit of Detection (LOD): The lowest analyte concentration that can be reliably distinguished from the LOB; LOD = LOB + 1.645 × SDlow-concentration; represents 95% detection probability (Armbruster & Pry, 2008).
Detection limit – Limit of Quantitation (LOQ): The lowest concentration at which the analyte can be measured with acceptable precision and accuracy, typically defined as 10 × SD at the LOD spike concentration; also known as the practical quantitation limit (PQL) (Armbruster & Pry, 2008).
Field blank: A sample of reagent-grade water processed through the entire field collection and preservation procedure; detects contamination introduced during sampling and transport.
Laboratory-fortified blank (LFB): A reagent water blank spiked with a known concentration of target analytes and processed through the full analytical procedure; monitors ongoing accuracy and extraction efficiency.
Laboratory-fortified matrix (LFM): A field sample spiked with a known concentration of target analytes; detects matrix-specific suppression or enhancement of the analytical signal.
Method blank: A reagent water sample carried through the full analytical procedure alongside field samples; detects contamination introduced by reagents, equipment, or laboratory environment (APHA et al., 2012).
Precision: The reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same sample; expressed as relative percent difference (RPD) for duplicates or relative standard deviation (RSD) for replicate analyses (Taylor, 1987).
Relative percent difference (RPD): |A - B| / ((A + B) / 2) × 100; the standard measure of duplicate precision; typical acceptance criteria are RPD ≤ 10–20% depending on method and matrix.
Spike recovery (%): (Measured spiked concentration – Unspiked concentration) / Added concentration × 100; typical acceptance range is 80–120% for most environmental matrices (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
5 Safety and Hazards
QC samples contain the same analytes as field samples and are subject to the same hazard considerations as the parent analytical method. Consult the relevant analytical SOP for safety information.

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
6 General QC Requirements

6.1 Every Analytical Batch
Every analytical batch must include at minimum (APHA et al., 2012; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2007):








QC Element
Minimum Frequency
Purpose




Method blank
1 per batch
Detect laboratory contamination


Calibration blank
Start of each calibration
Instrument baseline


CVS (check standard)
Every 10 samples
Detect calibration drift


Duplicate
10% of samples
Assess precision


LFB
1 per batch
Assess accuracy





6.2 Additional Elements (as applicable)







QC Element
When Required




Field blank
Each sampling event


Matrix spike (LFM)
5% of samples or 1 per batch


CRM
1 per batch (where certified material is available)


Equipment blank
When non-dedicated sampling equipment is used

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
7 Acceptance Criteria








QC Element
Typical Acceptance Criteria
Action if Failed




Method blank
< MDL (analyte absent)
Investigate contamination; do not report affected samples


CVS
±10% of stated value
Re-calibrate; re-analyze affected samples


Duplicate RPD
≤ 10–20% (method-specific)
Flag results; investigate and re-analyze if warranted


LFB recovery
80–120%
Flag results; check reagents and instrument


LFM recovery
70–130%
Suspect matrix interference; consult PI


CRM recovery
Within certified uncertainty interval
Recalibrate; re-analyze



Acceptance criteria in individual analytical SOPs take precedence over these general values when they are stricter or when regulatory requirements apply.

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
8 Detection Limit Determination

8.1 Method Detection Limit (MDL)
The MDL is determined following 40 CFR Part 136 Appendix B (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2016):

Select a spike concentration at 1–5× the estimated MDL.
Prepare and analyze at least 7 replicates of the spiked solution through the full analytical method.
Calculate the standard deviation (\(s\)) of the replicates.
Multiply by the one-tailed \(t\)-value at 99% confidence (\(t_{n-1, 0.99}\); for \(n=7\): \(t = 3.143\)):

\[\text{MDL} = t_{(n-1,\, 0.99)} \times s\]

If the spike concentration is outside the range of 0.5–20× the computed MDL, repeat with an adjusted spike concentration (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2016).



8.2 Limit of Detection and Limit of Quantitation
The LOB, LOD, and LOQ hierarchy follows Armbruster & Pry (2008):
\[\text{LOB} = \mu_{\text{blank}} + 1.645\,\sigma_{\text{blank}}\]
\[\text{LOD} = \text{LOB} + 1.645\,\sigma_{\text{low}}\]
\[\text{LOQ} = 10\,\sigma_{\text{low}}\]
where \(\sigma_{\text{low}}\) is the standard deviation of replicate analyses at the low-level spike concentration. For right-censored environmental data, apply the non-parametric methods described in Helsel (2012).

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
9 Control Charts
Maintain control charts for each analyte/method combination to track long-term analytical performance:

Plot CRM, LFB, or CVS recovery for each batch on a time-series chart.
Calculate and draw lines for:

Center line: Mean recovery over the last 20+ batches
Warning limits: ±2 standard deviations from the mean
Action limits: ±3 standard deviations from the mean

A result between warning and action limits is a warning; investigate but do not necessarily re-analyze.
A result beyond the action limits requires corrective action and re-analysis.
Systematic trends (7+ consecutive results on one side of the center line, or a steady drift) require investigation even if individual points are within limits (Taylor, 1987).

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
10 Corrective Actions
When a QC failure occurs:

Stop the analytical run; do not report affected samples.
Identify the probable cause (contaminated blank, degraded standard, instrument malfunction, matrix interference).
Correct the problem (replace reagents, recalibrate, perform maintenance).
Re-run the affected samples with fresh QC elements.
Verify that the repeated run passes all QC criteria.
Document the failure, root cause, corrective action, and re-analysis results in the QC log and lab notebook.

title: Quality Control and Quality Assurance
text:
11 Metadata Documentation and Reproducibility

11.1 Laboratory Notebook Requirements
Every analytical session must be documented with at minimum:

Date, analyst name, SOP number and revision
Instrument ID and calibration status
Reagent lot numbers and preparation dates
Sample IDs, matrix type, and collection dates
Calibration data (standards, equation, \(r^2\))
QC results (blanks, duplicates, LFBs, spikes, CRMs) with pass/fail
Raw data file names and storage location
Any deviations from the SOP, with justification
Corrective actions taken for QC failures



11.2 Electronic Data Management

Store all raw instrument data files on the lab shared drive in a folder structure organized by project, year, and instrument.
Never modify raw data files. All processing must be done programmatically in R with version-controlled scripts.
Commit all analysis scripts to the lab GitHub repository per SOP-L801 (Gandrud, 2015; Xie, 2015).



11.3 R-Based QC Tracking System
The following R framework is the EA Program standard for QC documentation and reproducibility (Gandrud, 2015; Xie, 2015):


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(knitr)

session_meta <- list(
  analyst    = "Your Name",
  date       = Sys.Date(),
  sop        = "SOP-L802 v1.1",
  method_sop = "SOP-LXX vX.X",
  instrument = "Instrument ID",
  project    = "Project Name"
)

cat(sprintf("QC session: %s | Analyst: %s | Instrument: %s\n",
            session_meta$date, session_meta$analyst,
            session_meta$instrument))




Code
calc_mdl <- function(reps, alpha = 0.01) {
  n <- length(reps); s <- sd(reps)
  t_val <- qt(1 - alpha, df = n - 1)
  list(n = n, sd = s, t_value = round(t_val, 3),
       MDL = round(t_val * s, 4), LOQ = round(10 * s, 4))
}

calc_rpd <- function(a, b) abs(a - b) / ((a + b) / 2) * 100

calc_recovery <- function(measured, expected) (measured / expected) * 100


Each analytical R script should:

Read the raw data file
Run all QC checks programmatically
Produce a formatted QC summary table
Generate calibration plots and control charts
Export a clean, QC-verified dataset as CSV
Render to HTML or PDF for archiving

Store templates in the project GitHub repository under analysis/templates/ (Gandrud, 2015; Xie, 2015).

title: eDNA Metabarcoding Lab Workflow
text:
This SOP describes the end-to-end laboratory workflow for environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding, from receipt of field-collected water filter samples through DNA extraction, PCR amplification, library preparation, sequencing, and bioinformatics analysis. eDNA metabarcoding combines universal or group-specific primers with high-throughput sequencing to detect and characterize aquatic biodiversity from water samples without capturing organisms (Deiner et al., 2017; Taberlet et al., 2012).
This SOP serves as the integrating document that ties together the field collection procedures in SOP-F700 with the molecular and computational SOPs in the L700 series. It does not repeat detailed procedures described in other SOPs but provides the eDNA-specific modifications, QC requirements, and decision points that distinguish eDNA metabarcoding from standard amplicon sequencing of soil or tissue samples.

2 Scope

title: eDNA Metabarcoding Lab Workflow
text:
4 Definitions

Amplification blank (no-template control, NTC): A PCR reaction containing all reagents except sample DNA; run with every PCR plate; any amplification in the NTC indicates contamination and invalidates the entire plate.
Blocking primer: A modified oligonucleotide added to a PCR reaction to selectively suppress amplification of abundant non-target DNA (e.g., host DNA in gut or tissue eDNA samples); allows rare target sequences to be amplified competitively.
eDNA metabarcoding: A method that uses universal or group-specific primers to amplify and sequence a short, taxonomically informative DNA region (barcode) from environmental DNA, yielding a community- level inventory of taxa present in a sample.
Environmental DNA (eDNA): Genetic material shed into the environment by organisms through mucus, feces, skin cells, eggs, and other biological material; collected non-invasively from water, sediment, or air.
Extraction blank: A tube containing only extraction reagents and no biological material, processed through the full extraction procedure; detects reagent or handling contamination; must yield no target amplification.
Field blank: A filter or collection vessel processed through all field collection steps but with no environmental sample; detects airborne or handling contamination during field work.
Metabarcode locus: The specific genomic region amplified for community identification; common loci include 12S rRNA (fish), 16S rRNA (bacteria, invertebrates), 18S rRNA (eukaryotes), COI (invertebrates, fish), and ITS2 (fungi, plants).
Occupancy model: A statistical model that accounts for imperfect detection in eDNA surveys by estimating the probability that a species is truly present given detection/non-detection across replicate samples or PCR replicates.
PCR replicate: One of multiple independent PCR reactions run from the same DNA extract; increases detection sensitivity for rare targets and allows estimation of false-negative rates; standard eDNA practice is 3–8 replicates per sample.
Sequence read depth (coverage): The total number of sequencing reads assigned to a sample; directly affects the number of rare taxa detected; EA Program target is a minimum of 10,000 reads per sample after quality filtering.

title: eDNA Metabarcoding Lab Workflow
text:
7 Procedure: eDNA-Specific Modifications

7.1 Sample Receipt and Logging

Upon receipt from the field, verify that all samples match the chain of custody form per SOP-F008.
Inspect Sterivex capsules or filter bags for integrity (no leaks, caps intact, preservative present).
Log each sample in the lab notebook and Freezer Inventory Google Sheet.
Store preserved filters at -20 C (short-term) or -80 C (long-term) until extraction.



7.2 DNA Extraction from Filters
Follow SOP-L700 with the following eDNA-specific modifications:

Sterivex capsules: Open the capsule aseptically using a sterile razor blade or the Sterivex extraction adapter. Transfer the membrane into the PowerBead Pro tube using sterile forceps. If Longmire’s buffer was used as preservative, add the buffer to the bead tube as well.
Open membrane filters: Transfer the folded filter directly into the bead tube using sterile forceps.
Extraction blanks: Process one extraction blank per batch. For eDNA, this means running an empty bead tube through the full protocol.
Field blanks: The field blank filter (from SOP-F700) is extracted alongside samples and serves as the primary contamination control for the entire field-to-lab chain.



7.3 Inhibition Testing
eDNA extracts from natural waters frequently contain PCR inhibitors (humic acids, tannins, metal ions) (McKee et al., 2015). Test for inhibition before committing to full library preparation:

Run an internal positive control (IPC) qPCR assay on a subset of extracts (or all extracts, if the batch is small). The IPC uses a synthetic DNA target spiked into the PCR reaction at a known concentration.
If the IPC Ct value shifts by more than 2 cycles compared to the uninhibited control, the extract is inhibited.
For inhibited samples, dilute the extract 1:5 or 1:10 with nuclease-free water and retest. Alternatively, clean the extract using a OneStep PCR Inhibitor Removal Kit (Zymo Research).

Note



Primer choice determines which taxa can be detected. Discuss target taxa and primer selection with the PI before beginning library preparation. Multi-marker approaches (e.g., 12S + COI) provide broader taxonomic coverage but require separate library preparations and sequencing runs (Deiner et al., 2017).




7.5 PCR and Library Preparation
Follow SOP-L703 for initial PCR screening and SOP-L704 for library preparation, with these eDNA-specific considerations:

Replicates: Run 3 independent PCR replicates per sample to improve detection probability for rare species (Ficetola et al., 2015). Pool the replicates after PCR1 before cleanup and indexing.
Cycle number: Use 35 cycles for PCR1 (higher than standard 16S amplicon work) because eDNA concentrations are typically very low. Be aware that additional cycles increase the risk of chimera formation and tag-jumping (Schnell et al., 2015).
Blocking primers (optional): If non-target taxa (e.g., human DNA) dominate the PCR product, consider using blocking primers or PNA (peptide nucleic acid) clamps to suppress amplification of non-target sequences.
Controls: In addition to the standard NTC and extraction blank, include the field blank and (if available) a positive control consisting of a mock community of known species at known concentrations.



7.6 Bioinformatics and Taxonomic Assignment
Follow SOP-L705 for denoising and taxonomic classification, with these modifications:

Reference database: Use a curated database matched to the marker and target taxa:

12S fish: MitoFish or MIDORI2
COI: BOLD / MIDORI2
16S/18S: SILVA or GenBank nt

Species-level assignment: For eDNA, species-level identification is the primary goal (unlike microbiome studies where genus-level is often sufficient). Use BLAST-based classification (classify-consensus- blast in QIIME 2) in addition to or instead of the Naive Bayes classifier for improved species-level resolution (Goldberg et al., 2016).
Decontamination: Use the decontam R package to identify and remove contaminant ASVs using the field blank and extraction blank data (Davis et al., 2018).
Detection criteria: An ASV is considered a positive detection for a species only if:

It matches a reference sequence at greater than or equal to 97–99% identity (marker-dependent)
It is absent from all negative controls (field blank, extraction blank, NTC), or its abundance in the sample exceeds 10x the abundance in the highest-read control
It is detected in at least 2 of 3 PCR replicates (if replicates were sequenced independently) (Ficetola et al., 2015)




7.7 Reporting
eDNA metabarcoding results are reported as a species detection list per site with the following metadata:

ASV sequence and percent identity to reference
Number of reads per ASV per sample
Detection across replicates (e.g., detected in 2/3 replicates)
Negative control results
Any taxa flagged as potential contaminants







Important



eDNA metabarcoding provides presence/detection data. Quantitative interpretation of read counts as species abundance is not recommended without careful validation, because PCR amplification bias, primer affinity, and DNA shedding rates vary among taxa (Kelly et al., 2019).

title: eDNA Metabarcoding Lab Workflow
text:
8 Quality Control

Field blanks: Must be negative for all target taxa. Any target taxon detected in a field blank compromises the detection claim for that taxon across all samples in the same sampling event.
Extraction blanks: Must be negative. Positive extraction blanks indicate lab contamination; the entire extraction batch is suspect.
NTC: Must be negative. Positive NTCs indicate PCR contamination.
Positive control (mock community): Must recover all expected species. Failure to detect a known species in the mock community indicates primer bias or PCR failure.
Replication: A minimum of 3 PCR replicates per sample is recommended for occupancy-based detection analyses.
Document all control results in the project data file and report alongside species detections.

title: Amplicon Library Preparation for Sequencing
text: This SOP describes the preparation of amplicon sequencing libraries for Illumina platforms, following a two-step PCR approach. The first PCR amplifies the target marker gene (e.g., 16S rRNA for bacteria, ITS for fungi) with gene-specific primers tailed with Illumina adapter overhangs. The second PCR attaches unique dual-index barcodes and the full Illumina adapter sequences, enabling multiplexed sequencing of many samples per run. This protocol is based on the Illumina 16S Metagenomic Sequencing Library Preparation guide and the Earth Microbiome Project (EMP) standards (Caporaso et al., 2012; Illumina, Inc., 2013; Thompson et al., 2017).

title: Amplicon Library Preparation for Sequencing
text: This SOP describes the preparation of amplicon sequencing libraries for Illumina platforms, following a two-step PCR approach. The first PCR amplifies the target marker gene (e.g., 16S rRNA for bacteria, ITS for fungi) with gene-specific primers tailed with Illumina adapter overhangs. The second PCR attaches unique dual-index barcodes and the full Illumina adapter sequences, enabling multiplexed sequencing of many samples per run. This protocol is based on the Illumina 16S Metagenomic Sequencing Library Preparation guide and the Earth Microbiome Project (EMP) standards (Caporaso et al., 2012; Illumina, Inc., 2013; Thompson et al., 2017).

Does not apply to: Shotgun metagenomic library preparation; long- read amplicon sequencing (PacBio, Nanopore); ddPCR (see SOP-L701); eDNA metabarcoding using non-Illumina workflows

title: Amplicon Library Preparation for Sequencing
text:
4 Definitions

Adapter: A short double-stranded DNA sequence ligated to both ends of a library fragment; contains the sequencing primer binding site, an index sequence, and the flow cell binding sequence required for Illumina cluster generation.
Amplicon library: A sequencing library prepared by PCR amplification of a target region (e.g., 16S rRNA gene V4 region or ITS2) using primers that incorporate Illumina adapter sequences; represents the diversity of that locus in a community sample.
Index (barcode): A unique 6–12 bp sequence incorporated into the adapter of each sample’s library; allows multiple samples to be pooled and sequenced together (multiplexed) and computationally separated (demultiplexed) after sequencing.
Library normalization: Adjustment of each sample’s library to the same molar concentration before pooling; ensures approximately equal sequencing depth across samples; performed by quantification (Qubit or qPCR) followed by dilution.
Library pooling: Combining equimolar amounts of individually indexed libraries from multiple samples into a single tube for multiplexed sequencing; the total library pool is loaded onto the sequencer.
Paired-end sequencing: A sequencing strategy in which both ends of a DNA insert are sequenced, producing two reads (R1 and R2) per cluster; paired reads overlap for amplicons shorter than twice the read length, enabling error correction by merging.
PCR inhibitor: A substance carried over from DNA extraction that suppresses amplification efficiency (e.g., humic acids, tannins, residual ethanol); detected by inhibition testing and remedied by further purification or dilution of the template.
Size selection: A step in library preparation that removes off-target fragments (primer dimers, non-specific products) using bead-based cleanup (e.g., AMPure XP beads) or gel excision; improves sequencing quality and reduces wasted reads.

title: Amplicon Library Preparation for Sequencing
text:

Every library prep run must include: positive control (mock community, if available), NTC, and extraction blank carried through both PCR1 and PCR2
NTC and extraction blanks must show no visible band on the verification gel and no detectable concentration on the Qubit. If blanks are positive, the entire batch is suspect (Salter et al., 2014).
Verify amplicon size on gel after PCR1; verify library size (amplicon

adapters) on gel after PCR2

Record the number of PCR1 cycles and the index assignments for every sample; these are required for data analysis and troubleshooting

title: ddPCR Data Export and Analysis – Nitrogen Cycle Gene Abundance
text:
4 Definitions

Amplitude threshold: The fluorescence intensity boundary set in DropletQuant (or equivalent software) that separates positive droplets (containing amplified target) from negative droplets; correct threshold placement is the single most critical step in ddPCR data analysis.
Copies per microliter (copies/µL): The absolute concentration of target DNA in the final ddPCR reaction volume as calculated by Poisson statistics from the fraction of positive droplets; must be back-calculated through all dilution steps to report concentration in the original sample.
DropletQuant / QuantaSoft: Bio-Rad software used to read the QX200 droplet reader output, set amplitude thresholds, and calculate target concentrations; raw .qlp files must be archived unmodified.
Duplex assay: A ddPCR assay in which two targets (e.g., a gene of interest and a reference gene) are quantified simultaneously using two spectrally distinct fluorescent probes (FAM and HEX/VIC) in the same reaction; requires careful threshold setting for each channel.
Fractional abundance: The proportion of positive droplets relative to total accepted droplets: \(\lambda = -\ln(1 - p)\) where \(p\) is the positive fraction; used by Poisson correction to calculate copies/µL.
No-template control (NTC): A reaction containing all ddPCR components except sample DNA; must yield zero or near-zero positive droplets; persistent positive droplets in NTCs indicate reagent contamination.
Poisson correction: The statistical adjustment applied by DropletQuant to account for the probability that some droplets contain more than one target molecule; assumes random partitioning and is essential for accurate absolute quantification.
Rain: Droplets with intermediate fluorescence amplitude between the positive and negative clusters; caused by partial amplification, degraded DNA, or probe competition; must be assigned to positive or negative by threshold adjustment and noted in data records.
Rejected droplets: Droplets excluded from analysis by the instrument because they fall outside acceptable size or fluorescence quality criteria; runs with fewer than 10,000 accepted droplets per well should be flagged and potentially repeated.

title: ddPCR Data Export and Analysis – Nitrogen Cycle Gene Abundance
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Data Export from QuantaSoft

Open the completed experiment file (.qlp) in QuantaSoft
Review the droplet plots for each well. Confirm that the positive/negative threshold was set appropriately during the run (see SOP-L701, Section 6.6)
If threshold adjustment is needed, use QuantaSoft Analysis Pro to re-apply thresholds manually. Document any threshold changes in the lab notebook.
Export data using Options > Export CSV to generate a comma-separated file containing well-level results
The exported CSV includes the following key columns:

Well: plate position (e.g., A01)
Sample: sample name as entered during plate setup
Target: gene target name
Concentration: copies per uL of the final ddPCR reaction (Poisson-corrected) (Hindson et al., 2011)
Positives: number of positive droplets
Negatives: number of negative droplets
AcceptedDroplets: total accepted droplets
MeanAmplitudeOfPositives: mean fluorescence of positive cluster
MeanAmplitudeOfNegatives: mean fluorescence of negative cluster

Save the CSV with the naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_gene_project_plate.csv (e.g., 2025-05-14_amoA_wetland_plate1.csv)
Copy the .qlp file and the exported .csv to the lab shared drive under ddPCR_raw_data/



7.2 Quality Control Checks
Perform the following checks on the exported data before proceeding to analysis. These can be scripted in R for reproducibility.

Droplet count filter: Exclude any well with fewer than 10,000 accepted droplets. Wells below this threshold have unreliable Poisson statistics (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).
No-template controls (NTC): NTC wells must show 0 or fewer than 3 positive droplets. If NTC wells show more than 3 positives, the entire plate or the affected target should be considered contaminated and rerun.
Extraction blanks: Extraction blanks (from SOP-L80) must show fewer positive droplets than the NTC acceptance threshold. Elevated counts in extraction blanks indicate contamination in the DNA extraction workflow.
Positive controls: Positive control gBlock wells should fall within 20% of the expected concentration based on the dilution prepared.
Technical replicate agreement: If technical replicates were run, calculate the coefficient of variation (CV) across replicates. A CV greater than 25% suggests pipetting error or sample heterogeneity.







TipTip



Create a QC report template in R Markdown or Quarto that automatically flags wells failing any of the criteria above. This makes batch QC efficient and ensures nothing is missed.




7.3 Calculating Gene Copy Numbers
The QuantaSoft Concentration output is in copies per uL of the ddPCR reaction mixture. To express results per gram of dry soil (or per unit of extracted DNA), apply the following conversions:
\[
\text{Copies per g dry soil} =
\frac{C_{\text{ddPCR}} \times V_{\text{reaction}} \times DF \times V_{\text{elution}}}{V_{\text{template}} \times m_{\text{soil}} \times (1 - \theta_g)}
\]
where:

\(C_{\text{ddPCR}}\) = concentration from QuantaSoft (copies/uL)
\(V_{\text{reaction}}\) = total ddPCR reaction volume (typically 20 uL)
\(DF\) = dilution factor of the DNA template (e.g., 10 if diluted 1:10)
\(V_{\text{elution}}\) = total DNA elution volume from extraction (uL; see SOP-L80)
\(V_{\text{template}}\) = volume of DNA template added to the ddPCR reaction (uL)
\(m_{\text{soil}}\) = mass of soil extracted (g)
\(\theta_g\) = gravimetric soil moisture (as a decimal; see SOP-L400)

To express results per ng of extracted DNA instead:
\[
\text{Copies per ng DNA} =
\frac{C_{\text{ddPCR}} \times V_{\text{reaction}}}{V_{\text{template}} \times C_{\text{DNA}}}
\]
where \(C_{\text{DNA}}\) is the Qubit DNA concentration (ng/uL) from SOP-L80.


Code
# Example calculation: copies per g dry soil
c_ddpcr <- 52.3         # copies/uL (from QuantaSoft)
v_reaction <- 20         # uL
dilution_factor <- 10    # 1:10 dilution of template
v_elution <- 100         # uL (from SOP-L80)
v_template <- 2          # uL added to ddPCR reaction
soil_mass_g <- 0.25      # g soil extracted
moisture_decimal <- 0.35 # gravimetric moisture as decimal

copies_per_g <- (c_ddpcr * v_reaction * dilution_factor * v_elution) /
                (v_template * soil_mass_g * (1 - moisture_decimal))

cat(sprintf("Gene copies per g dry soil: %.0f\n", copies_per_g))


Gene copies per g dry soil: 3218462


Code
cat(sprintf("Gene copies per g dry soil (log10): %.2f\n", log10(copies_per_g)))


Gene copies per g dry soil (log10): 6.51




7.4 Data Organization and Merging

Merge the QC-filtered ddPCR results with the sample metadata (site, treatment, depth, date, soil moisture, DNA concentration) using a shared sample ID column
Organize the merged data in a tidy (long) format with one row per sample-by-gene combination (Wickham, 2014)
Save the merged analysis-ready dataset as a .csv in the project GitHub repository under data/processed/
TBD – define the standard column naming convention for the lab’s ddPCR datasets (e.g., sample_id, gene, copies_per_g_dry, copies_per_ng_dna, site, treatment, depth_cm, date)



7.5 Statistical Analysis






Note



The choice of statistical approach depends on the experimental design (e.g., paired vs. independent sites, factorial treatments, time series). The guidance below covers common analyses for nitrogen cycle gene abundance. Consult the PI before selecting a final analytical approach.



7.5.1 Data Exploration and Visualization

Plot gene copy numbers (log10-transformed) by treatment, site, or depth using boxplots or dot plots
Assess normality of log-transformed data using Shapiro-Wilk tests and Q-Q plots
Check for outliers and investigate whether they represent true biological variation or analytical artifacts



7.5.2 Comparing Gene Abundance Across Treatments

For two-group comparisons (e.g., amended vs. control): use Welch’s t-test on log10-transformed copies per g dry soil, or the non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test if normality assumptions are not met (Frosteg aard et al., 1999)
For multi-group comparisons: use one-way ANOVA on log10-transformed data with Tukey HSD post hoc tests, or Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn’s test for non-parametric data
For factorial designs (e.g., treatment x depth): use two-way ANOVA or linear mixed-effects models with site as a random effect (Pinheiro & Bates, 2000)



7.5.3 Gene Ratios
Ratios of functional gene abundances can provide insight into the balance of nitrogen cycling processes (Hallin et al., 2009):

nirK/nirS: relative contribution of the two nitrite reductase pathways to denitrification
nosZ/(nirK + nirS): completeness of denitrification (higher values suggest greater N2O reduction capacity)
amoA AOA/amoA AOB: relative dominance of archaeal vs. bacterial ammonia oxidation
nrfA/(nirK + nirS): relative importance of DNRA vs. denitrification

TBD – determine which gene ratios are most relevant for the lab’s current research questions and establish standard visualization formats.


7.5.4 Correlations with Environmental Variables

Correlate gene abundances with soil physicochemical data (pH, moisture, total C, total N, nitrate, ammonium) using Pearson or Spearman correlations
TBD – evaluate whether multivariate approaches (e.g., PCA, redundancy analysis) are appropriate given the number of samples and variables
TBD – determine whether gene abundance data should be related to process rate measurements (e.g., N2O flux, nitrification potential) and define the analytical framework for doing so



7.5.5 Reporting

Report gene abundance as copies per g dry soil (mean +/- standard error) and/or copies per ng DNA
Present data on a log10 scale in figures; report back-transformed means and confidence intervals in tables where appropriate (Bolker et al., 2009)
Include all QC metrics (droplet counts, NTC results, positive control recovery) as supplementary tables
TBD – create a standardized R Markdown/Quarto reporting template for ddPCR results that the lab can reuse across projects

section: 12 Appendix A: Example QC Filtering Script
text:
12 Appendix A: Example QC Filtering Script



Code
library(tidyverse)

# Read exported QuantaSoft CSV
raw <- read_csv("data/raw/2025-05-14_amoA_wetland_plate1.csv")

# QC filtering
qc_filtered <- raw %>%
  filter(
    AcceptedDroplets >= 10000        # Minimum droplet threshold
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    qc_flag = case_when(
      Sample == "NTC" & Positives > 3 ~ "NTC_contamination",
      Sample == "Extraction_Blank" & Positives > 3 ~ "Extraction_contamination",
      TRUE ~ "Pass"
    )
  )

# Flag and report QC failures
qc_failures <- qc_filtered %>%
  filter(qc_flag != "Pass")

if (nrow(qc_failures) > 0) {
  warning("QC failures detected:")
  print(qc_failures %>% select(Well, Sample, Target, Positives, qc_flag))
}

# Retain only passing sample wells
analysis_ready <- qc_filtered %>%
  filter(qc_flag == "Pass",
         !Sample %in% c("NTC", "Extraction_Blank", "Positive_Control"))

title: Primer Selection and Design for Nitrogen Cycle Genes – ddPCR
text: This procedure describes the selection, design, and validation of primers and probes targeting functional genes of the nitrogen cycle for use with droplet digital PCR (ddPCR). The nitrogen cycle genes covered include those encoding nitrification (amoA for both ammonia-oxidizing bacteria and archaea), denitrification (nirK, nirS, nosZ), nitrogen fixation (nifH), and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (nrfA). The SOP covers literature-based primer selection, in silico evaluation, and bench validation on the Bio-Rad QX200 ddPCR system (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024; Hindson et al., 2011).

title: Primer Selection and Design for Nitrogen Cycle Genes – ddPCR
text:
4 Definitions

Amplicon length: The size in base pairs (bp) of the PCR product generated by a primer pair; for ddPCR, optimal amplicon length is 60–200 bp; shorter amplicons partition more efficiently into droplets and produce cleaner positive/negative separation (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024; Hindson et al., 2011).
amoA (ammonia monooxygenase alpha subunit): The gene encoding the alpha subunit of ammonia monooxygenase; used as a functional marker for ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB; Nitrosomonas-like) and ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA; Thaumarchaeota); quantified separately because AOB and AOA primers differ (Francis et al., 2005; Rotthauwe et al., 1997).
Annealing temperature (\(T_a\)): The temperature at which primers bind to their complementary template sequences during PCR cycling; determined by gradient PCR optimization; typically 55–65 °C for nitrogen cycle gene assays; primer pairs should be within 2 °C of each other (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).
ddPCR (droplet digital PCR): A third-generation PCR technology that partitions a reaction into approximately 20,000 nanoliter droplets and amplifies target DNA to endpoint within each droplet; the fraction of positive droplets is fit to a Poisson distribution to calculate absolute target concentration without a standard curve (Hindson et al., 2011).
DNRA (dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium): A microbial process that reduces NO3- to NH4+, retaining nitrogen in the ecosystem rather than losing it as gas; marker gene: nrfA (Levy-Booth et al., 2014).
EvaGreen: A fluorescent intercalating dye used as a non-specific reporter in ddPCR and qPCR; binds double-stranded DNA; less specific than hydrolysis probes but useful for assay development and for targets without validated probe sequences (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).
FunGene: A curated functional gene database (http://fungene.cme.msu.edu/) that provides reference sequences, primer coverage analysis, and taxonomy for nitrogen cycle genes including amoA, nirK, nirS, nosZ, and nifH (Fish et al., 2013).
gBlock (synthetic DNA fragment): A double-stranded DNA fragment (IDT) with a sequence matching the target amplicon; used as a positive control for ddPCR assay validation and as a template for limit-of-detection determination (Hindson et al., 2011).
Hydrolysis probe (TaqMan probe): A short oligonucleotide labelled with a 5’ fluorophore (e.g., FAM) and a 3’ quencher (e.g., Iowa Black FQ); cleaved by Taq polymerase during extension, releasing the fluorophore and generating a signal; provides higher specificity than intercalating dyes and is required for multiplexed ddPCR (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).
In silico primer evaluation: Computational assessment of primer specificity, coverage, and secondary structure using tools such as NCBI Primer-BLAST, IDT OligoAnalyzer, and FunGene; a required step before ordering primers for bench validation (Fish et al., 2013; Ye et al., 2012).
nifH (nitrogenase reductase): The gene encoding nitrogenase iron protein; the universal marker for biological nitrogen fixation (diazotrophy); highly conserved across diverse diazotrophic bacteria and archaea (Levy-Booth et al., 2014; Poly et al., 2001).
nirK / nirS: Genes encoding the two structurally distinct nitrite reductases in denitrifiers: nirK encodes a copper-containing (Cu) enzyme; nirS encodes a cytochrome cd1 enzyme; the two forms serve the same function and are often both targeted to capture the full denitrifying community (Braker et al., 2000; Henry et al., 2006).
nosZ: The gene encoding nitrous oxide reductase, which reduces N2O to N2 in the final step of denitrification; divided into Clade I (classical denitrifiers; Henry et al. (2006)) and Clade II (diverse non-denitrifiers; Jones et al. (2013)); the sum of both clades estimates the community capacity to consume the greenhouse gas N2O.
nrfA: The gene encoding cytochrome c nitrite reductase, the enzyme catalyzing DNRA; a functional marker for organisms that retain nitrogen in the ecosystem as NH4+ rather than releasing it as N2O or N2 (Welsh et al., 2014).
Rain (ddPCR): Droplets with intermediate fluorescence amplitude that fall between the positive and negative clusters in a ddPCR amplitude plot; indicates suboptimal primer binding, non-specific amplification, or partial inhibition; reduced by increasing annealing temperature or decreasing primer concentration (Lievens et al., 2016).

7 Procedure

7.1 Literature-Based Primer Selection

Search the published literature for validated primer sets targeting each gene of interest. Prioritized references include Rotthauwe et al. (1997), Francis et al. (2005), Braker et al. (2000), Henry et al. (2006), Poly et al. (2001), Jones et al. (2013), and Welsh et al. (2014).
For each candidate primer pair, record: primer names, sequences (5’ to 3’), amplicon length, annealing temperature, and the original publication.
Evaluate published primer sets against the following criteria:

Amplicon length between 60 and 200 bp (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024; Hindson et al., 2011)
Demonstrated use in environmental samples similar to your matrix
Broad coverage of the target gene clade verified by in silico analysis (see §6.3)
Minimal off-target amplification in non-target organisms








Note



Many classic nitrogen cycle primers (e.g., nosZ primers from Henry et al. (2006)) were designed for conventional qPCR with amplicons of 250–400 bp. These may need to be redesigned or replaced with shorter alternatives optimized for ddPCR (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).




7.2 Recommended Primer Sets

7.3 In Silico Primer Evaluation

Check primer specificity using NCBI Primer-BLAST against the nr/nt database, restricting the search to bacteria and/or archaea as appropriate (Ye et al., 2012).
Verify primer coverage against curated functional gene databases:

FunGene (http://fungene.cme.msu.edu/) for amoA, nirK, nirS, nosZ, nifH (Fish et al., 2013)
TBD – identify additional databases for nrfA coverage analysis

Check for primer dimers and secondary structures using IDT OligoAnalyzer (https://www.idtdna.com/calc/analyzer) or Primer3 (https://primer3.ut.ee/).
Confirm that the melting temperature (\(T_m\)) of each primer falls between 55 and 65 °C, with no more than 2 °C difference between forward and reverse primers.
For hydrolysis probe (TaqMan) assays, design the probe to have a \(T_m\) 5–10 °C higher than the primers, with no G at the 5’ end (quenches FAM fluorescence), and a length of 15–30 bases (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).



7.4 Primer and Probe Ordering

Order desalted primers at 25 nmol scale from IDT (Integrated DNA Technologies) or equivalent supplier.
Order hydrolysis probes HPLC-purified with 5’-FAM (or HEX for multiplexing) and 3’-Iowa Black FQ quencher.
For positive controls, order synthetic double-stranded DNA fragments (gBlocks) matching the target amplicon sequence. Include at least 50 bp of flanking sequence on each side of the primer binding sites.
Resuspend lyophilized primers in nuclease-free water to a stock concentration of 100 µM. Store at –20 °C.
Prepare 10 µM working stocks by diluting 1:10 in nuclease-free water. Store at –20 °C.



7.5 ddPCR Thermal Cycling Optimization

Set up a temperature gradient experiment on the Bio-Rad C1000 Touch to determine the optimal annealing temperature for each primer set.
Use a thermal gradient spanning \(T_m\) ± 5 °C (typically 55–65 °C).
Use positive control gBlock DNA diluted to approximately 1,000 copies per µL as template.
Recommended cycling protocol (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024):

Enzyme activation: 95 °C for 10 min
40 cycles: 94 °C for 30 s, then annealing/extension at gradient temperature for 60 s
Signal stabilization: 98 °C for 10 min
Hold at 4 °C (indefinite)
Ramp rate: 2 °C/s for all steps

Read droplets on the QX200 Droplet Reader.
Select the annealing temperature that produces the clearest separation between positive and negative droplet clusters in the QuantaSoft amplitude plot.







Tip



If positive and negative droplet populations overlap (rain), try increasing the annealing temperature by 1–2 °C or reducing the primer concentration from 900 nM to 450 nM (Lievens et al., 2016).




7.6 Assay Validation

Specificity: Run no-template controls (NTC) and extraction blanks from SOP-L700 to confirm the absence of false positives.
Dynamic range: Prepare a serial dilution of gBlock positive control (10 to 100,000 copies per reaction) and verify linearity of the ddPCR response across the range (Huggett et al., 2013).
Limit of detection (LOD): Determine the lowest copy number that produces a statistically significant positive call above NTC background; typically 1–10 copies per 20 µL reaction (Hindson et al., 2011).
Matrix effects: Run environmental DNA extracts at multiple dilutions (undiluted, 1:5, 1:10) to check for PCR inhibition. If the 1:10 dilution value (back-calculated) disagrees by more than 20% from the 1:5 value, inhibition is likely present (Ra vcki et al., 2014).
Document all validation results in the primer/probe registry (Appendix A) before approving the assay for routine use.

8 Primer and Probe Registry
Maintain a lab registry of all validated and candidate assays. The registry must include at minimum: gene target, primer names and sequences, probe sequence (if applicable), amplicon length, validated annealing temperature, LOD, matrix tested, validation date, and analyst initials. Store the registry as a version-controlled file in the lab GitHub repository.

title: Soil Enzyme Assays (Fluorometric Microplate Method)
text: This SOP describes the fluorometric microplate method for measuring the potential activity of extracellular enzymes in soils. Extracellular enzymes mediate the decomposition of organic matter and the cycling of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur in soils. Assays use fluorogenic substrates based on 4-methylumbelliferone (MUB) and 7-amino-4-methylcoumarin (AMC), which release a fluorescent product upon enzymatic hydrolysis (Bell et al., 2013; German et al., 2011; Sinsabaugh & Moorhead, 1994). The method is high-throughput (96-well microplate format), sensitive, and widely used in soil biogeochemistry and ecosystem ecology.

The method is high-throughput (96-well microplate format), sensitive, and widely used in soil biogeochemistry and ecosystem ecology.

text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Measurement of potential hydrolytic enzyme activities in field-moist, sieved (less than 2 mm) mineral and organic soils from EA Program sites, using MUB- and AMC-linked fluorogenic substrates in a 96-well microplate format
Does not apply to: Oxidative enzyme assays (e.g., phenol oxidase, peroxidase), which use colorimetric substrates (L-DOPA); enzyme assays in aquatic samples (requires modified dilution); commercially available enzyme activity kits with different substrates
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Soil Enzyme Assays (Fluorometric Microplate Method)
text:
4 Definitions

Fluorometric enzyme assay: An enzyme activity assay in which substrate hydrolysis releases a fluorescent product (typically methylumbelliferone, MUB, or methylcoumarin, MCA) measurable at low concentrations by a fluorometer; more sensitive than colorimetric assays.
Maximum velocity (\(V_{max}\)): The maximum rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction when substrate is saturating; expressed in units of nmol product g-1 dry soil h-1; reflects the potential activity of the enzyme in soil.
Methylumbelliferone (MUB): A fluorescent product released by many hydrolytic enzymes when they cleave a methylumbelliferyl-linked substrate; detected at excitation ~365 nm and emission ~450 nm; the basis of most fluorometric soil enzyme assays.
Potential enzyme activity: The enzyme activity measured under optimized laboratory conditions (excess substrate, controlled pH, temperature 25 °C); an index of the extant enzyme pool rather than actual in situ activity.
Quench correction: A correction applied to fluorometric assays to account for reduction in fluorescence signal caused by soil colloids and dissolved organic matter; calculated from samples spiked with a known amount of MUB standard.
Substrate: The molecule acted upon by an enzyme; in fluorometric assays, a synthetic substrate linked to MUB or MCA is cleaved by the target enzyme to release the fluorescent product.
Turnover rate: The number of substrate molecules converted per enzyme molecule per unit time; an intrinsic property of the enzyme that depends on temperature, pH, and substrate concentration.
