title: Soil Enzyme Assays (Fluorometric Microplate Method)
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Soil Slurry Preparation

Weigh 1.0 g of field-moist, sieved (less than 2 mm) soil into a clean container.
Add 125 mL of 50 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH adjusted to match the soil pH, typically 5.0 for acidic soils or 7.8 for alkaline soils) (German et al., 2011).
Homogenize with a magnetic stir bar or by vortexing for 1 minute.
Keep the slurry stirring continuously during pipetting to maintain a uniform suspension.



8.2 Substrate Stock Preparation

Dissolve each MUB or AMC substrate in DMSO to prepare a 10 mM stock solution. Store at –20 °C in amber vials; stable for at least 6 months.
Prepare working solutions by diluting the DMSO stock in buffer to the target concentration (typically 200 \(\mu\)M final concentration in the well).
Prepare MUB and AMC calibration standards in buffer at concentrations of 0, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, and 25 \(\mu\)M.



8.3 Microplate Layout
For each soil sample, set up the following wells (8 analytical replicates per enzyme) (Bell et al., 2013):








Well Type
Contents
Purpose




Sample assay (n = 8)
200 \(\mu\)L slurry + 50 \(\mu\)L substrate
Enzyme activity


Sample control (n = 8)
200 \(\mu\)L slurry + 50 \(\mu\)L buffer
Soil background fluorescence


Substrate control (n = 8)
200 \(\mu\)L buffer + 50 \(\mu\)L substrate
Substrate autofluorescence


MUB/AMC standard curve
200 \(\mu\)L buffer + 50 \(\mu\)L standard
Calibration


Blank
200 \(\mu\)L buffer + 50 \(\mu\)L buffer
Instrument blank





8.4 Incubation

Seal the plate with an adhesive seal.
Incubate at 20 °C (or field-relevant temperature) in the dark on a plate shaker at low speed for 2–4 hours. The incubation time depends on expected activity; 3 hours is a standard starting point (Sinsabaugh & Moorhead, 1994).







TipTip



For soils with unknown activity, run a pilot plate at 1, 2, and 4 hours to identify the linear range. Activity calculations assume linearity over the incubation period; if the reaction plateaus, shorten the incubation.




8.5 Stopping and Reading

After incubation, add 10 \(\mu\)L of 1 N NaOH to each well to stop the reaction and maximize fluorescence of the MUB/AMC product (the fluorophore is brightest above pH 10).
Read fluorescence on the microplate reader at excitation 365 nm / emission 450 nm within 5 minutes of adding NaOH.
Export the raw fluorescence data for analysis.

title: Soil Enzyme Assays (Fluorometric Microplate Method)
text:
9 Data Analysis and Calculations

9.1 Activity Calculation
For each enzyme, calculate the net fluorescence:
\[
F_{\text{net}} = F_{\text{sample}} - F_{\text{soil control}} - F_{\text{substrate control}} + F_{\text{blank}}
\]
Convert net fluorescence to nmol of product released using the MUB or AMC standard curve (linear regression of fluorescence vs. concentration).
Calculate enzyme activity:
\[
\text{Activity} \; (\text{nmol g}^{-1} \text{h}^{-1}) =
\frac{F_{\text{net}} / m \times V_{\text{well}}}{M_{\text{soil}} \times t}
\]
where \(m\) = slope of the standard curve (fluorescence per nmol), \(V_{\text{well}}\) = total well volume (L), \(M_{\text{soil}}\) = dry mass equivalent of soil in the well (g, corrected for moisture content per SOP-L400), and \(t\) = incubation time (h).


Code
# Example enzyme activity calculation
library(tidyverse)

# Standard curve data
standards <- tibble(
  conc_uM = c(0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.5, 5.0, 10.0, 25.0),
  fluorescence = c(120, 850, 1580, 3750, 7200, 14100, 34500)
)

# Fit linear model
cal_model <- lm(fluorescence ~ conc_uM, data = standards)
slope <- coef(cal_model)[2]  # fluorescence units per uM

# Sample data (means of 8 replicates)
F_sample <- 5200
F_soil_ctrl <- 350
F_sub_ctrl <- 180
F_blank <- 125

F_net <- F_sample - F_soil_ctrl - F_sub_ctrl + F_blank

# Convert to concentration (uM in well)
conc_well <- F_net / slope

# Calculate activity
V_well_L <- 250e-6          # 250 uL total well volume in liters
soil_fresh_g <- 1.0         # g fresh soil in 125 mL slurry
frac_in_well <- 200 / (125 * 1000)  # fraction of slurry in well
soil_in_well_g <- soil_fresh_g * frac_in_well
moisture <- 0.25            # gravimetric moisture content
soil_dry_g <- soil_in_well_g * (1 - moisture)
incubation_h <- 3

activity <- (conc_well * V_well_L * 1e6) / (soil_dry_g * incubation_h)
# Result in nmol / g dry soil / h

cat(sprintf("Net fluorescence: %.0f\n", F_net))
cat(sprintf("Activity: %.1f nmol g-1 h-1\n", activity))

title: Soil Enzyme Assays (Fluorometric Microplate Method)
text:
10 Quality Control

Run 8 analytical replicates per enzyme per sample. Report the mean and coefficient of variation; CV should be less than 20%.
Include substrate and soil quench controls on every plate.
Run the MUB/AMC standard curve on each plate (do not carry over calibrations between plates, as reader sensitivity may drift).
Include a laboratory reference soil in each batch to track inter-batch variability.
Verify that activity is linear over the incubation period by running a time-course pilot for new soil types.

2 Scope

Does not apply to: Fresh tissue assays that require unfixed material (e.g., chlorophyll extraction from fresh leaves, enzyme activity assays); seed or fruit tissue with high oil content (requires freeze-drying); soil organic matter (see SOP-L406)

title: Plant Tissue Drying, Grinding, and Preparation for Analysis
text:
4 Definitions

Acid washing (plant tissue): Cleaning tissue with dilute HCl to remove surface contamination (dust, soil particles, fertilizer residues) before analysis for trace metals or nutrients; may be inappropriate for samples requiring analysis of acid-labile compounds.
Air drying: Drying plant tissue at ambient temperature (typically 20–40 °C) to a stable moisture content; used as a preliminary step before oven drying; preserves enzyme activity and RNA better than direct oven drying.
Ball milling: Size reduction by grinding samples between hardened steel or ceramic balls inside a rotating vessel; the preferred method for producing a homogeneous powder from fibrous plant tissue for EA-IRMS and elemental analysis.
Critical tissue concentration: The minimum concentration of a nutrient required for maximum growth; below this level the plant is deficient; above it, growth is normal or the nutrient may be toxic at very high levels.
Lyophilization (freeze drying): Removal of water from tissue under vacuum after rapid freezing; preserves cell structure, volatile compounds, and biological activity better than oven drying; required for enzyme, RNA, and some metabolite analyses.
Subsampling: Drawing a representative small portion from a bulk dried, ground sample for analysis; requires thorough mixing and homogenization of the bulk powder before subsampling to ensure the subsample is representative.

title: Plant Tissue Drying, Grinding, and Preparation for Analysis
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Drying ovens operate at 60–105 °C; burn risk from hot trays and glassware. The Wiley mill and ball mill contain rapidly moving parts; keep hands, hair, and loose clothing away from the grinding chamber.
Noise: The Wiley mill generates noise above 85 dBA. Wear hearing protection during operation.
Dust: Grinding produces fine particulate matter. Work in a well-ventilated area or use a dust mask, especially when processing large batches.
Biological: Field-collected plant tissue may harbor ticks, spiders, or allergenic compounds (e.g., poison oak resin). Inspect samples before handling; wear gloves.

title: Plant Tissue Drying, Grinding, and Preparation for Analysis
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Receiving and Cleaning

Log incoming samples in the laboratory tracking spreadsheet. Verify site ID, date, species or tissue type, and collector.
If tissue was not rinsed in the field, briefly rinse leaf or stem material with deionized water to remove surface soil, dust, and epiphytes. Do not soak, as leaching of soluble compounds will occur (Kalra, 1998).
Blot excess water with paper towels.
For root samples, remove adhering soil by gentle agitation in DI water; multiple rinses may be required.



7.2 Drying

Place cleaned tissue in labeled paper bags or foil trays. Do not overload bags; tissue should be loosely arranged to allow air circulation.
Dry at 60 °C in the forced-air oven for a minimum of 48 hours, or until constant mass is achieved (two consecutive weighings 4 hours apart differ by less than 0.1% of sample mass) (Jones, 2001).
For samples intended only for total C and N by combustion (not volatile compound analysis), drying at 70 °C is acceptable and reduces drying time.







Important



Do not exceed 70 °C for samples intended for nitrogen analysis, as volatile nitrogen compounds may be lost at higher temperatures. Do not exceed 60 °C for samples intended for analysis of volatile organic compounds, essential oils, or lipids (Kalra, 1998).



Remove dried samples from the oven and cool in a desiccator for at least 30 minutes before weighing or grinding.
Record the dry mass if gravimetric moisture content is needed.



7.3 Coarse Grinding (Wiley Mill)

Inspect the mill: confirm the 1 mm (20-mesh) screen is installed and the cutting blades are sharp and properly seated.
Turn on the mill and allow it to reach full speed before feeding material.
Feed dried tissue into the hopper in small amounts, pushing material gently with the wooden plunger. Do not force tissue into the blades.
Collect the ground material passing through the screen in a clean, labeled container or bag.
Between samples, disassemble the grinding chamber and clean thoroughly:

Brush all surfaces with a stiff brush to remove residual material
Wipe with 70% ethanol
Run a small amount of acid-washed quartz sand through the mill as a blank grind if cross-contamination of trace metals is a concern
Allow to dry before the next sample




7.4 Fine Grinding (for IRMS or Homogeneity-Critical Analyses)
For EA-IRMS analysis, the Wiley-milled material (less than 1 mm) must be further ground to a fine, homogeneous powder (less than 250 \(\mu\)m):

Transfer approximately 1–2 g of coarsely ground tissue to a clean ball mill vial with grinding balls.
Grind for 2–3 minutes until the material is a uniform fine powder.
Alternatively, use an agate mortar and pestle, grinding until no gritty texture remains.
Transfer the powder to a labeled vial or sample bag.
Clean the ball mill vial and balls between samples with 70% ethanol and Kimwipes.



7.5 Weighing into Tin Capsules (for EA-IRMS)

Using the analytical balance, tare a tin capsule on the balance pan.
Weigh 3–5 mg of finely ground tissue into the capsule (Brodie et al., 2011). Record the mass to 0.001 mg.
Fold the capsule into a tight pellet using forceps, ensuring no material escapes.
Place the pellet in a labeled well of a microplate or sample tray.
Include blanks (empty tin capsules) and reference materials (e.g., acetanilide, USGS-40) in the run sequence per SOP-L414.

title: Plant Tissue Drying, Grinding, and Preparation for Analysis
text:
8 Quality Control

Grind and analyze duplicate subsamples at a rate of at least 1 per 10 samples to assess preparation variability. Analytical duplicates should agree within 5% RPD for C and N concentrations.
Include a laboratory reference material (e.g., NIST SRM 1515 Apple Leaves or NIST SRM 1547 Peach Leaves) in each analytical batch to verify accuracy (Kalra, 1998).
Document all cleaning steps in the laboratory notebook, especially the blank grind between samples when trace metal analysis is planned.
Confirm drying completeness by re-weighing a subset of samples after an additional 4 hours of drying.

title: Preparing a Wet Mount for Microscopy
text: This procedure describes how to prepare a wet mount slide for light microscopy. A wet mount suspends a specimen in a thin layer of water (or other mounting medium) beneath a cover slip, preserving the natural shape and motility of living cells and small organisms. It is the standard preparation method for examining fresh biological samples under bright field or phase contrast illumination (Murphy & Davidson, 2012).

title: Preparing a Wet Mount for Microscopy
text: This procedure describes how to prepare a wet mount slide for light microscopy. A wet mount suspends a specimen in a thin layer of water (or other mounting medium) beneath a cover slip, preserving the natural shape and motility of living cells and small organisms. It is the standard preparation method for examining fresh biological samples under bright field or phase contrast illumination (Murphy & Davidson, 2012).

2 Scope

Does not apply to: Permanent slide preparation (fixed, stained, and sealed mounts); dry mounts; hanging-drop preparations for motility studies; fluorescence specimen preparation (see SOP-L211)

title: Preparing a Wet Mount for Microscopy
text:
4 Definitions

Cover slip (coverslip): A thin (0.13–0.17 mm) square or circular piece of optical glass placed over the specimen on a microscope slide; standardizes the optical path length and protects the objective from liquid samples; the EA Program standard is No. 1.5 (0.17 mm), matched to the objectives on the Echo Revolve microscope (Murphy & Davidson, 2012).
Immersion medium: Liquid placed between the specimen and the coverslip to improve optical contact, reduce refraction artifacts, and support live organisms during observation; options include water, glycerol, or immersion oil depending on the application.
Live mount: A wet mount prepared without fixation or staining; allows observation of living organisms and motile behavior; must be examined quickly before evaporation or oxygen depletion affects the specimen.
Mounting medium: The liquid in which the specimen is suspended; distilled or deionized water is standard; saline, glycerol, or specific staining solutions may be used depending on the application (Murphy & Davidson, 2012).
Refraction artifact: Optical distortion caused by differences in refractive index between the sample, mounting medium, coverslip, and objective; minimized by matching refractive indices and maintaining thin, uniform wet mounts.
Wet mount: A temporary microscopy preparation method in which a specimen is suspended in a drop of liquid (usually water) on a glass slide and covered with a coverslip; the standard preparation for aquatic microorganisms, algae, macroinvertebrates, and other specimens examined under transmitted light (Murphy & Davidson, 2012).

title: Preparing a Wet Mount for Microscopy

title: Preparing a Wet Mount for Microscopy
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Placing the Specimen

Clean a microscope slide with a lint-free wipe to remove dust and fingerprints.
Using forceps, place the specimen in the center of the slide. For liquid samples (pond water, culture broth), skip to Step 3 and pipette the sample directly.



8.2 Adding the Mounting Liquid

Using a transfer pipette or eyedropper, place one to two drops of water onto the specimen. Adjust the volume based on specimen size: larger or thicker specimens may need slightly more water, while very small specimens need less.



8.3 Applying the Cover Slip

Pick up a cover slip by its edges with forceps or clean, dry fingers. Never touch the flat surfaces.
Place one edge of the cover slip on the slide adjacent to the specimen, holding it at approximately a 45-degree angle.
Slowly lower the cover slip using the tip of a toothpick or forceps, allowing the water to spread gradually beneath the glass. Lowering at an angle lets air escape and minimizes bubble formation (Murphy & Davidson, 2012).







TipAvoiding Air Bubbles



Air bubbles distort the image and can be mistaken for cellular structures. If bubbles are present after placing the cover slip, gently tap the cover slip with the eraser end of a pencil or press lightly with a toothpick to work bubbles toward the edge. If large bubbles persist, remove the cover slip, add a fresh drop of water, and try again.




8.4 Adjusting Water Volume

Too much water: If the cover slip floats or slides freely, the water layer is too thick. Hold the edge of a lint-free wipe against the edge of the cover slip and let capillary action draw off excess water until the cover slip sits flat.
Too little water: If dry areas are visible beneath the cover slip, place a small drop of water at the edge and let capillary action draw it underneath. Do not lift the cover slip.



8.5 Examining the Slide

Place the prepared slide on the microscope stage and examine following SOP-L211 Echo Labs Revolve Microscope. Start at low magnification (4× or 10×) and increase as needed.
For unstained, transparent specimens, phase contrast mode typically provides better visibility than bright field (see SOP-L211, Section 6.5).

title: Preparing a Wet Mount for Microscopy
text:
9 Quality Control

Verify that the cover slip lies flat and is not tilted by air bubbles or excess sample material.
Confirm that the water layer is thin enough for the specimen to remain in a single focal plane at high magnification.
If examining motile organisms, note that excessive pressure from the cover slip can restrict movement; use slightly more water to provide adequate space.

title: Soil Labile Amino-Nitrogen – Solvita SLAN Test
text:
This procedure describes the determination of soil labile amino-nitrogen (amino-N) using the Solvita SLAN test (Woods End Laboratories) (Brinton, 2016b). The SLAN test measures a chemically labile fraction of organic nitrogen present in soil humus as amino-sugars and related amino compounds. These forms represent a “potentially available” nitrogen pool that lies between the immediately available mineral nitrogen (NH4+ and NO3-) measured by conventional extraction and the total nitrogen pool measured by combustion or Kjeldahl digestion.
The test uses alkali hydrolysis with 2 mol L-1 NaOH to release NH3 from amino-N compounds in soil (Mulvaney & Khan, 2001). The liberated NH3 diffuses into a Solvita gel probe during a 24-hour room-temperature incubation. The color change of the gel is proportional to the quantity of labile amino-N and is quantified using the Solvita Digital Color Reader (DCR) in NH3 mode, yielding results in mg kg-1 amino-N.
The SLAN procedure is chemically analogous to the Illinois Soil Nitrogen Test (ISNT), which uses the same 2 mol L-1 NaOH reagent but requires heating. The SLAN test offers two practical advantages over the ISNT: heating is not needed, and fewer reagents are required (Moore et al., 2019a). In combination with the Solvita CO2 Burst test (SOP-L408), SLAN provides a complementary assessment of biological soil fertility by pairing a measure of microbial activity (CO2 respiration) with a measure of organic nitrogen reserves (Brinton, 2016a).
This SOP is distinct from SOP-L408, which measures microbial CO2 respiration from rewetted soil, and from SOP-L403, which measures immediately available mineral nitrogen by KCl extraction.

title: Soil Labile Amino-Nitrogen – Solvita SLAN Test
text:
This procedure describes the determination of soil labile amino-nitrogen (amino-N) using the Solvita SLAN test (Woods End Laboratories) (Brinton, 2016b). text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Air-dried, sieved mineral soils from all EA Program sites; assessment of organic nitrogen reserves and humus quality; screening for management effects on labile nitrogen pools
Does not apply to: Measurement of immediately available mineral nitrogen (NH4+ or NO3-; see SOP-L403 or SOP-L404); total soil nitrogen determination (see SOP-L407 and elemental analysis); compost maturity testing (see SOP-L413); field-moist soils (samples must be air-dried before testing)

title: Soil Labile Amino-Nitrogen – Solvita SLAN Test
text:
4 Definitions

Alkali-hydrolyzable nitrogen (AHN): The fraction of organic nitrogen released by hydrolysis in sodium hydroxide solution; operationally defined by the extraction conditions; highly correlated with amino acid nitrogen and microbially available N (Mulvaney & Khan, 2001).
Amino acid nitrogen: Organic nitrogen in the form of free amino acids and simple peptides; the most labile fraction of soil organic nitrogen; the primary substrate measured by the Solvita SLAN test.
Diffusion cell: The sealed incubation jar used in the Solvita SLAN test in which NaOH releases NH3 from hydrolyzed soil nitrogen into the headspace, where it is captured and measured by a gel probe.
Digital Color Reader (DCR): The Solvita handheld device that reads gel probe color and converts it to a numerical amino-N concentration (mg kg-1); set to NH3 mode for SLAN measurements.
Gel probe (SLAN): The colorimetric sensor in the Solvita SLAN test that changes color in proportion to accumulated NH3; read with the DCR after exactly 24 hours of incubation.
Labile amino nitrogen (LAN): The nitrogen fraction estimated by the Solvita SLAN test; a proxy for readily mineralizable organic nitrogen; expressed as mg N kg-1 dry soil (Moore et al., 2019b).
Nitrogen mineralization: The biological conversion of organic nitrogen to inorganic forms (NH4+ and eventually NO3-) by soil microorganisms; the primary process by which plant-available N is replenished from organic matter; positively correlated with LAN (Moore et al., 2019a).

title: Soil Labile Amino-Nitrogen – Solvita SLAN Test
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) at 2 mol L-1 is strongly corrosive and can cause severe burns to skin, eyes, and mucous membranes. Handle with care; refer to the NaOH Safety Data Sheet (SDS) posted in the lab. The SLAN test requires use of a strong reagent and is not intended for casual or unsupervised use.
Biological: Soil samples may contain soil-borne pathogens. Wash hands thoroughly after handling soil.
Physical: Minor risk of glass breakage from incubation jars. Handle jars carefully.




5.1 Required PPE

Nitrile gloves (chemical-resistant)
Safety glasses or splash goggles
Lab coat



5.2 Emergency Procedures

For NaOH contact with skin, immediately flush the affected area with copious water for at least 15 minutes. Remove contaminated clothing.
For NaOH contact with eyes, flush with water at the eyewash station for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention.
For spills, neutralize with dilute acid (e.g., 0.1 M HCl or vinegar) or contain with absorbent material, then clean up and dispose per institutional guidelines.
Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety for general emergency procedures.

6.3 Reagent Preparation
2 mol L-1 NaOH solution:

Weigh 80.0 g of ACS-grade NaOH pellets.
Dissolve in approximately 800 mL of deionized water in a 1 L volumetric flask or heat-resistant beaker. The dissolution is exothermic; add pellets slowly and stir.







Warning



Always add NaOH to water, never water to NaOH. Use a heat-resistant container and allow the solution to cool to room temperature before bringing to final volume.



Bring to a final volume of 1000 mL with deionized water.
Transfer to a labeled, tightly sealed polyethylene bottle. NaOH solutions absorb CO2 from the atmosphere; keep sealed when not in use.

title: Soil Labile Amino-Nitrogen – Solvita SLAN Test
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Preparation

Use soil that has been air-dried and sieved through a 2 mm sieve per SOP-F400. Do not grind the soil.
If samples were stored at 4 °C after sieving, allow them to equilibrate to room temperature (20–25 °C) for at least 30 minutes before beginning the assay.
Gently mix each sample to ensure homogeneity before weighing.







Note



The SLAN test is designed for air-dried soil. Results from field-moist soil are not comparable to published SLAN norms or the manufacturer’s interpretation guidelines (Brinton, 2016b).




7.2 Incubation Setup

Weigh 4.0 g of air-dried, sieved soil into a clean 50 mL plastic beaker. Record the exact mass to 0.01 g.
Place the beaker containing soil inside a clean, dry 250 mL incubation jar.
Using the graduated cylinder, add 20 mL of 2 mol L-1 NaOH directly to the soil in the beaker.
Remove a fresh NH3-sensitive gel probe from its sealed foil packet. Inspect the gel: it should be uniform in color with no cracks, discoloration, or signs of prior exposure. Discard any compromised probes.
Place the gel probe in the air space surrounding the plastic beaker. The gel face must be exposed to the headspace and must not contact the NaOH solution or the soil.
Seal the jar immediately and securely with the silicone-gasketed lid.
Record the jar number, sample ID, soil mass, and start time.







Important



Work efficiently once the NaOH is added. NH3 begins volatilizing immediately upon contact with the soil; seal the jar as quickly as possible to capture the full emission.




7.3 Incubation

Place sealed jars at room temperature (20–25 °C), shielded from direct sunlight and drafts.
Incubate undisturbed for 24 hours.
Do not open, move, or disturb jars during incubation.



7.4 Reading Results

After exactly 24 hours (±30 minutes), open the jar and immediately remove the gel probe.
Read the probe promptly; prolonged exposure to ambient air will alter the gel color.

Using the Solvita Digital Color Reader (DCR – recommended):

Set the DCR to NH3 mode.
Insert the gel probe into the DCR and record the numerical reading.
The DCR reading corresponds to amino-N concentration in mg kg-1 per the manufacturer’s calibration (Brinton, 2016b).

Using the Solvita Color Chart (visual – semi-quantitative only):

Compare the gel probe to the Solvita NH3 color chart.
Record the color number.







TipTip



Read probes within 2 minutes of opening the jar. The DCR is strongly recommended for all quantitative work; the color chart provides semi-quantitative screening only.




7.5 Recording Results
Record the following for each test:

Date and time (start and end of incubation)
Sample ID, site, and depth
Soil mass (g)
NaOH volume added (mL)
DCR reading (NH3 mode) or color chart number
Amino-N concentration (mg kg-1)
Any anomalies (unusual soil color or odor, probe defects)



7.6 Cleanup

Carefully pour the NaOH-soil slurry into the designated waste container. Do not pour corrosive solutions down the drain without neutralization (see Section 8).
Rinse plastic beakers and incubation jars with deionized water. Dry completely before reuse.
Dispose of used gel probes in standard trash.

title: Soil Labile Amino-Nitrogen – Solvita SLAN Test
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 QC Requirements







QC Element
Requirement




Duplicates
At least 1 per 10 samples; RPD within 15%


Blank
One jar with 20 mL NaOH, no soil, and a gel probe per batch; probe should show no or minimal color change


DCR calibration
Calibrate per manufacturer instructions before each batch; set to NH3 mode


Gel probe storage
Store sealed in foil at room temperature, away from light; check expiration dates; never use expired probes


NaOH solution
Verify 2 mol L-1; check expiration; keep tightly sealed





8.2 Corrective Actions

If the blank reading exceeds baseline by more than one color increment, check for NH3 contamination sources (nearby ammonium reagents, compost, inadequate ventilation) and repeat the batch.
If duplicate RPD exceeds 15%, re-run the sample pair. Persistent poor precision may indicate sample heterogeneity; increase homogenization effort before weighing.
If NaOH solution appears cloudy or shows precipitate, prepare a fresh solution.



8.3 Limitations
The SLAN test does not detect nitrate or urea, and normal ammonium fertilizer rates do not interfere with the measurement. Known limitations include:

The test may not be sensitive in very low-organic-matter soils (e.g., sandy soils with less than 1% SOM), where results may fall below the detection limit.
Color matching by visual chart is subjective; the DCR is required for quantitative reporting.
SLAN measures a chemically defined labile N pool, not the biologically available fraction directly; interpret alongside other soil health indicators.



8.4 Interpretation Guide








SLAN Amino-N (mg kg-1)
Interpretation
Implication




Less than 30
Very low
Severely depleted organic N reserves; management intervention warranted


30–60
Low
Limited labile N pool; consider cover crops or organic amendments


60–120
Moderate
Adequate organic N reserves for many soils


120–200
High
Good labile N pool; indicative of healthy humus


Greater than 200
Very high
Abundant organic N reserves; common in high-SOM, no-till, or prairie soils



Thresholds are approximate guidelines adapted from Woods End Laboratories and published field studies (Moore et al., 2019c, 2019b). Interpret SLAN values in the context of soil organic matter content, soil texture, and management history.

title: Water-Extractable Dissolved Organic Carbon (Soil)
text:
This procedure describes the extraction and quantification of water-extractable dissolved organic carbon (WEOC) from soil. WEOC represents the fraction of soil organic matter that is readily soluble in water and includes simple sugars, organic acids, amino acids, and other low-molecular-weight compounds. It is a sensitive indicator of labile carbon availability, microbial substrate supply, and changes in soil management or land use (Ghani et al., 2003; Jones et al., 2006).
WEOC is distinct from the K2SO4-extractable DOC measured in the chloroform fumigation-extraction method (SOP-L409) and from total soil organic carbon (SOP-L407). The water extraction uses no salt, making it a closer analogue to the dissolved organic carbon that would leach from soil under natural rainfall or irrigation.

title: Water-Extractable Dissolved Organic Carbon (Soil)
text:
4 Definitions

Dissolved organic carbon (DOC): Organic carbon that passes through a 0.45 µm filter; in soil extracts, includes low-molecular-weight organic acids, fulvic acids, amino acids, and other water-soluble organic compounds.
Hot-water extractable carbon (HWEC): A more aggressive extraction using hot water (80 °C); releases more labile organic carbon than cold-water extraction; a closer proxy for microbially available carbon and total labile carbon.
KHP (potassium hydrogen phthalate): The primary standard for TOC calibration; a pure, stable organic acid weighed accurately to prepare standards of known carbon concentration.
Labile organic carbon: Readily decomposable organic carbon fractions that turn over on timescales of days to months; includes microbial biomass, water-extractable organic carbon, and dissolved organic carbon; sensitive to management and land use.
NPOC (non-purgeable organic carbon): The organic carbon remaining in a sample after acidification and sparging to remove inorganic carbon; the quantity measured by the Shimadzu TOC-L and the operational definition of DOC.
Soil-to-water ratio: The ratio of soil mass to extraction water volume (typically 1:5 or 1:10 w/v) in the water extraction step; must be reported alongside results and held constant within a study.

title: Water-Extractable Dissolved Organic Carbon (Soil)
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Preparation

If using field-moist soil, determine gravimetric moisture content on a separate subsample per SOP-L400
If using air-dried soil, pass through a 2 mm sieve and determine residual moisture content



7.2 Extraction

Weigh 5.0 g (oven-dry equivalent) of soil into a 50 mL centrifuge tube. Record the exact mass.
Add 25 mL of deionized water (1:5 soil-to-water ratio) (Ghani et al., 2003; Jones et al., 2006)
Cap the tube and shake on an end-over-end or orbital shaker at approximately 150 rpm for 1 hour at room temperature
Centrifuge at 4,000 x g for 10 minutes to separate the supernatant







Tip



Some protocols use a hot water extraction (80 C for 16 hours) to capture a larger fraction of labile carbon (Ghani et al., 2003). If hot water extraction is desired, specify the temperature and duration explicitly in the lab notebook and report, as the two methods are not directly comparable.




7.3 Filtration

Filter the supernatant through a 0.45 um filter into a pre-combusted glass vial
If using syringe filters, discard the first 2–3 mL of filtrate to flush any carbon leached from the filter
Collect at least 15 mL of filtrate for TOC analysis (enough for multiple injections plus rinse volume)



7.4 Storage

If extracts cannot be analyzed within 24 hours, acidify to pH less than 2 with 2 M HCl (approximately 1 drop per 10 mL) and store at 4 C
Analyze within 7 days of extraction; prolonged storage may alter DOC concentrations even when acidified



7.5 DOC Analysis

Analyze filtered extracts on the Shimadzu TOC-L in NPOC mode per SOP-L204
Prepare a deionized water blank and extraction blanks (DI water processed through the full extraction procedure) alongside samples
Run calibration standards (potassium hydrogen phthalate, KHP) as described in SOP-L204



7.6 Calculations
\[
\text{WEOC (mg C kg}^{-1}\text{ dry soil)} =
\frac{(C_{\text{sample}} - C_{\text{blank}}) \times V_{\text{extract}}}{m_{\text{soil}}}
\]
where:

\(C_{\text{sample}}\) = DOC concentration in the filtered extract (mg C/L)
\(C_{\text{blank}}\) = DOC concentration in the extraction blank (mg C/L)
\(V_{\text{extract}}\) = total volume of extractant added (L; e.g., 0.025 L)
\(m_{\text{soil}}\) = oven-dry mass of soil extracted (kg)

title: Water-Extractable Dissolved Organic Carbon (Soil)
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Include extraction blanks (DI water only, no soil) in each batch to quantify background carbon from filters, tubes, and water
Run sample duplicates for at least 10% of samples; CV between duplicates should be less than 10%
Include a laboratory reference soil in each batch
Verify that extraction blank DOC is less than 1 mg/L; if higher, troubleshoot water quality and filter blanks
Instrument QC follows SOP-L204 requirements (calibration verification, instrument blanks, replicate injection CV less than 2%)

title: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)
text: This SOP describes the determination of cation exchange capacity (CEC) and exchangeable base cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+) in soils using the ammonium acetate (NH4OAc) saturation and displacement method at pH 7.0 (Chapman, 1965; Sumner & Miller, 1996). CEC quantifies the total capacity of a soil to hold exchangeable cations and is a fundamental indicator of soil fertility, buffering capacity, and nutrient retention (Sparks, 2003).

title: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)
text: This SOP describes the determination of cation exchange capacity (CEC) and exchangeable base cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+) in soils using the ammonium acetate (NH4OAc) saturation and displacement method at pH 7.0 (Chapman, 1965; Sumner & Miller, 1996). CEC quantifies the total capacity of a soil to hold exchangeable cations and is a fundamental indicator of soil fertility, buffering capacity, and nutrient retention (Sparks, 2003).

title: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Air-dried, sieved (< 2 mm) mineral soils from all EA Program sites. The method is also applicable to compost and organic amendments, although CEC values for highly organic materials should be interpreted with caution due to pH-dependent charge (Sumner & Miller, 1996).
Does not apply to: Soils dominated by variable-charge minerals (e.g., highly weathered Oxisols, Andisols) where CEC measured at pH 7.0 may overestimate field-effective CEC. For such soils, a compulsive exchange method at field pH may be more appropriate (Gillman & Sumpter, 1979). Does not apply to water samples.
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)
text:
4 Definitions

Buffered salt solution: A reagent at a defined pH used to saturate exchange sites with a known index cation (e.g., NH4+ at pH 7.0 in the ammonium acetate method); the buffer pH controls which exchange sites are measured.
Base saturation: The percentage of CEC occupied by base cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+); calculated as the sum of base cations divided by CEC, expressed as %; important for liming and fertility management.
Cation exchange capacity (CEC): The total capacity of a soil to hold exchangeable cations, expressed in cmol\(_c\) kg-1 (or meq 100 g-1); governed by clay mineralogy and organic matter content; the higher the CEC, the greater the soil’s buffering capacity against acidification and nutrient leaching.
Effective CEC (ECEC): CEC measured at the soil’s natural pH (using an unbuffered salt such as 1 M KCl or BaCl2); represents the actual exchange capacity at field conditions; lower than pH 7-buffered CEC in acid soils.
Exchange sites: Negatively charged surfaces on clay minerals and organic matter that hold cations electrostatically; released by displacing the sorbed cations with a high-concentration competing ion.
Index cation: The cation used to saturate exchange sites before measurement (e.g., NH4+ in the ammonium acetate method, Ba2+ in the compulsive exchange method); subsequently displaced and quantified to calculate CEC.

title: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: 1 M ammonium acetate (NH4OAc) is a mild irritant. Concentrated acetic acid used in reagent preparation is corrosive and produces irritating vapors. Concentrated ammonium hydroxide (NH4OH) used for pH adjustment is caustic and produces strong vapors. Ethanol (95%) is flammable.
Physical: Reciprocating shaker can pinch fingers if containers are not secured properly.









ImportantEngineering Controls



Prepare 1 M NH4OAc from concentrated reagents inside a chemical fume hood. Once diluted to working concentration, the solution can be used on the open bench.

Safety glasses or chemical splash goggles (goggles when preparing reagents)
Laboratory coat
Nitrile gloves
Closed-toed shoes



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For chemical spill or splash, refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety or call campus safety. For acetic acid or ammonium hydroxide contact with eyes, flush immediately with water for at least 15 minutes.

title: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Reagent Preparation

7.1.1 M Ammonium Acetate (pH 7.0)

In a fume hood, dissolve 77.08 g of ammonium acetate (NH4C2H3O2, MW 77.08) in approximately 800 mL of DI water in a 1 L volumetric flask.
Adjust to pH 7.0 using dilute acetic acid (to lower pH) or dilute ammonium hydroxide (to raise pH).
Bring to 1 L with DI water and mix thoroughly.







TipTip



Prepare this solution the day before extraction. It is stable indefinitely at room temperature in a capped container. Verify pH before each use, as CO2 absorption can lower the pH over time.




7.1.2 M Potassium Chloride
Prepare per SOP-L403, Section 7.1.



7.2 Moisture Subsample
A companion gravimetric moisture determination is required to express results on an oven-dry soil basis.

Set aside approximately 10 g of soil from each sample for moisture determination
Dry at 105 °C for 24 hours and record the dry weight
Calculate gravimetric moisture content per SOP-L400 Soil Moisture



7.3 Ammonium Acetate Saturation (Exchangeable Cations)

Weigh 5.00 g of air-dried, sieved (< 2 mm) soil into a labeled 50 mL centrifuge tube. Record the exact mass to 0.01 g.
Add 30 mL of 1 M NH4OAc (pH 7.0) to the tube. Cap securely.
Place on the reciprocating shaker for 30 minutes.
Centrifuge at 2,000–3,000 x g for 5 minutes. Decant the clear supernatant into a 250 mL volumetric flask. Retain the soil pellet.
Repeat steps 2–4 two additional times (three extractions total), combining all supernatants in the same 250 mL volumetric flask.
Bring the combined extract to 250 mL with 1 M NH4OAc and mix. This extract is used for exchangeable cation analysis (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, Na+) by ICP-OES, AAS, or flame photometry (Helmke & Sparks, 1996).



7.4 Ethanol Wash
The ethanol wash removes excess (non-exchanged) NH4+ from the soil without displacing adsorbed NH4+ (Sumner & Miller, 1996).

Add 30 mL of 95% ethanol to the soil pellet remaining in the centrifuge tube. Cap and shake for 5 minutes.
Centrifuge at 2,000–3,000 x g for 5 minutes. Discard the supernatant ethanol wash.
Repeat the ethanol wash two additional times (three washes total).







ImportantCritical Step



Incomplete removal of excess NH4OAc will cause CEC to be overestimated. Ensure three full ethanol washes with clear supernatant before proceeding.




7.5 Displacement of Adsorbed NH4+ (CEC Determination)

Add 30 mL of 2 M KCl to the washed soil pellet. Cap and shake for 30 minutes.
Centrifuge at 2,000–3,000 x g for 5 minutes. Decant the supernatant into a clean 250 mL volumetric flask.
Repeat steps 1–2 two additional times (three displacements total), combining all supernatants in the same flask.
Bring the combined KCl extract to 250 mL with 2 M KCl and mix.
Determine the NH4+-N concentration in this extract by colorimetric analysis (indophenol blue method), flow injection, or steam distillation (Mulvaney, 1996). This value represents the CEC.



7.6 Cleanup

Discard spent soil in standard solid waste.
Rinse all glassware and centrifuge tubes with DI water.
Return reagents to labeled storage areas.

title: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)
text:
8 Calculations

8.1 Cation Exchange Capacity
\[
\text{CEC (cmol}_c\text{/kg)} = \frac{C_{\text{NH}_4} \times V_{\text{KCl}} \times 10^{-3}}{m_{\text{dry}} \times 14.01} \times 100
\]
where:

\(C_{\text{NH}_4}\) = NH4+-N concentration in the KCl displacement extract (mg N/L)
\(V_{\text{KCl}}\) = total volume of combined KCl extract (mL; typically 250 mL)
\(m_{\text{dry}}\) = oven-dry equivalent mass of soil (g), calculated as \(m_{\text{air\text{-}dry}} / (1 + \theta_g)\)
14.01 = atomic mass of nitrogen (g/mol)
The factor of 100 converts from molc/g to cmolc/kg



8.2 Exchangeable Cations
Report exchangeable Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, and Na+ from the NH4OAc extract (§6.3) in cmolc/kg:
\[
\text{Exchangeable cation (cmol}_c\text{/kg)} =
\frac{C_{\text{cation}} \times V_{\text{extract}} \times \text{valence}}{M_{\text{cation}} \times m_{\text{dry}}} \times \frac{1}{10}
\]
where \(C_{\text{cation}}\) is in mg/L, \(V_{\text{extract}}\) in mL, \(M_{\text{cation}}\) is the atomic mass (Ca = 40.08, Mg = 24.31, K = 39.10, Na = 22.99), and valence is 2 for Ca and Mg and 1 for K and Na.


8.3 Base Saturation
\[
\text{Base Saturation (\%)} =
\frac{\text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{Mg}^{2+} + \text{K}^{+} + \text{Na}^{+}}{\text{CEC}} \times 100
\]
where all values are in cmolc/kg.


8.4 Interpretation








CEC (cmolc/kg)
Classification
Typical Soil Textures




< 5
Very low
Sands, degraded tropicals


5–15
Low
Sandy loams, kaolinitic clays


15–25
Medium
Loams, silt loams


25–40
High
Clay loams, smectitic soils


> 40
Very high
Heavy clays, organic soils



Source: adapted from Sparks (2003) and Brady & Weil (2008).

title: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)
text:
9 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Include a reagent blank (NH4OAc and KCl through the full procedure without soil) in each batch. NH4+-N in the blank must be below the method detection limit.
Run extraction duplicates on at least 10% of samples. Duplicate results should agree within 10% RPD.
Include a laboratory reference soil with known CEC when available.
Sum of exchangeable base cations should not exceed CEC. If the sum substantially exceeds CEC, suspect incomplete ethanol washing or analytical error.
Verify NH4OAc pH is 7.0 ± 0.05 before each extraction batch.

text:
13 Appendix A: Example Calculation



Code
# --- CEC Calculation Example ---

# Input values
nh4_mg_L    <- 42.5    # NH4-N in KCl displacement extract (mg/L)
vol_KCl_mL  <- 250     # Total volume of combined KCl extract (mL)
mass_air_g  <- 5.00    # Air-dried soil mass (g)
moisture    <- 0.032   # Gravimetric moisture content (decimal)

# Oven-dry mass
mass_dry_g <- mass_air_g / (1 + moisture)

# CEC in cmol_c/kg
cec <- (nh4_mg_L * vol_KCl_mL * 1e-3) / (mass_dry_g * 14.01) * 100

cat(sprintf("Oven-dry soil mass: %.3f g\n", mass_dry_g))
cat(sprintf("CEC: %.1f cmol_c/kg\n", cec))

# --- Exchangeable Cation Example (Ca from NH4OAc extract) ---
ca_mg_L      <- 85.2   # Ca concentration in NH4OAc extract (mg/L)
vol_ext_mL   <- 250    # Total volume of NH4OAc extract (mL)
ca_mw        <- 40.08  # Atomic mass of Ca
ca_valence   <- 2

exch_ca <- (ca_mg_L * vol_ext_mL * ca_valence) / (ca_mw * mass_dry_g) / 10

cat(sprintf("Exchangeable Ca: %.1f cmol_c/kg\n", exch_ca))

text:
This SOP describes the complete workflow for determining \(\delta^{13}\)C, \(\delta^{15}\)N, and elemental concentrations (%C, %N) in soil and sediment samples by combustion on the Thermo Scientific Flash IRMS Elemental Analyzer (EA) coupled to the Delta V IRMS through the ConFlo IV interface (Werner & Brand, 2001). It covers sample preparation, sequence design, the analytical run, and post-analysis data correction including blank correction, linearity correction, scale normalization, and drift correction (Coplen, 2011; Paul et al., 2007).
For general instrument operation, startup/shutdown, gas checks, tuning, and pre-analysis tests, see SOP-L208.

2 Scope

Does not apply to: Sulfur isotope analysis (NCS mode; requires dedicated reactor and Sulfinert column), GasBench applications (see SOP-L415), TC/EA applications (\(\delta^{2}\)H, \(\delta^{18}\)O), or liquid samples.

title: Soil Carbon and Nitrogen Analysis by Flash EA-IRMS
text:
4 Definitions

Blank correction: Subtraction of the isotopic and elemental contribution of an empty tin capsule from each sample signal; necessary because capsule tin contributes a small amount of C and N (Paul et al., 2007).
\(\delta^{13}\)C: Stable carbon isotope ratio expressed in per mil (‰) relative to Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB): \(\delta^{13}C =
\left(\tfrac{R_\text{sample}}{R_\text{standard}} - 1\right)\times
1000\) where \(R = {}^{13}C/{}^{12}C\) (Coplen, 2011).
\(\delta^{15}\)N: Stable nitrogen isotope ratio expressed in per mil (‰) relative to atmospheric N2 (AIR): \(\delta^{15}N =
\left(\tfrac{R_\text{sample}}{R_\text{standard}} - 1\right)\times
1000\) where \(R = {}^{15}N/{}^{14}N\) (Coplen, 2011).
Drift correction: Adjustment for systematic temporal change in measured \(\delta\) values during a sequence, estimated from bracketing reference materials (Paul et al., 2007).
Flash EA: The Thermo Scientific Flash IRMS Elemental Analyzer peripheral; combusts samples at 1020 °C in an O2 pulse and separates N2 and CO2 chromatographically before delivery to the IRMS via the ConFlo IV.
Isodat: ThermoFisher software used to design analytical sequences, control the instrument, and export raw isotope data.
Linearity correction: Adjustment applied to account for the dependence of measured \(\delta\) values on peak signal amplitude.
Reference material (RM): A substance with a certified or consensus \(\delta\) value used to anchor measured values to the VPDB or AIR scale (Werner & Brand, 2001).
Scale normalization: Two-point (or multi-point) correction that maps measured \(\delta\) values to the international isotope-ratio scale using certified RMs spanning the expected sample range (Paul et al., 2007).
Tin capsule: 5 x 9 mm pressed-tin container used to encapsulate solid samples; tin ignites in the O2 pulse, raising combustion temperature briefly to ensure complete combustion.

title: Soil Carbon and Nitrogen Analysis by Flash EA-IRMS
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Sample Preparation

Dry samples at 60 °C to constant mass per SOP-L105.
Grind and homogenize to <150 µm per SOP-L116.
For carbonate removal (inorganic C), acidify with 1 M HCl, re-dry, and record the treatment in the lab notebook before proceeding.
Clean the micro-balance pan and zero the balance.
Using clean tweezers, place a tin capsule on the balance. Tare.
Weigh 10–30 mg of ground sample into the capsule (adjust to keep the N2 and CO2 peaks within the instrument’s linear range).
Fold and crimp the capsule tightly, removing all air.
Record the capsule mass in the lab notebook and in the sequence spreadsheet.



8.2 Sequence Design

Open Isodat Sequence Editor and load the NC dual-reactor method.
Build the sequence in this order:

3–5 conditioning samples (similar matrix to unknowns)
1 blank capsule
Bracketing RMs (at least 2 certified materials, e.g., USGS40 + USGS41a for \(\delta^{13}\)C; IAEA-N1 + IAEA-N2 for \(\delta^{15}\)N)
Unknowns, with 1 RM per 10 samples
Check standard at end
1 blank capsule at end

Save the sequence file as YYYYMMDD_Project_SeqID_User.seq.



8.3 Analytical Run

Complete the pre-analysis checklist in SOP-L208.
Load the capsule plate into the Flash EA autosampler carousel.
Press Start in Isodat.
Monitor the first 5 injections for expected peak shape and amplitude.



8.4 Post-Analysis Data Correction
Apply corrections in this order using the R script in the project repository:


Code
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Import raw Isodat export (.csv)
raw <- read_csv("data/raw/YYYYMMDD_Project_SeqID_User_raw.csv")

# 2. Blank correction
#    Subtract mean blank d13C and blank area from each sample

# 3. Linearity correction
#    Regress RM d-values on peak amplitude; apply slope correction

# 4. Scale normalization (two-point)
#    Use two certified RMs to anchor measured values to VPDB / AIR

# 5. Drift correction
#    Regress RM residuals on run order; apply time-based correction

# 6. QC evaluation
#    Check RM recoveries; flag samples outside ±0.3 permil

text:
9 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Reference material \(\delta^{13}\)C and \(\delta^{15}\)N must recover within ±0.2‰ of certified values after all corrections.
Blank capsules must produce peak areas below 0.5 Vs (N2) and 1 Vs (CO2).
Replicate analyses of a check standard (n >= 3) must show SD <= 0.15‰.
Flag and investigate any sequence where >20% of RMs fall outside acceptance criteria before reporting results.

title: Nitrification Potential – Shaken Soil Slurry Method
text:
This procedure describes a rapid method for measuring the potential rate of ammonium oxidation in soils using a shaken soil slurry. The method provides an estimate of the activity of the existing ammonium-oxidizing microbial population at the time of sampling. It is based on ISO 15685 (Soil quality – Determination of potential nitrification and inhibition of nitrification – Rapid test by ammonium oxidation) (International Organization for Standardization, 2012).
Ammonium oxidation is the first step in autotrophic nitrification. Soil is incubated in a buffered (pH 7.2) ammonium sulfate solution with sodium chlorate added to inhibit nitrite oxidation. The accumulation of nitrite (NO2-) over a 6-hour incubation period serves as the measure of potential nitrification activity. Because the generation time of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria exceeds 10 hours, the assay measures the activity of the population present at sampling, not population growth.
This method can be used to compare soils (e.g., polluted vs. reference), to screen the effects of management practices or chemical substances on nitrifying communities, and to evaluate the impact of biosolids or waste materials on soil nitrification.

title: Nitrification Potential – Shaken Soil Slurry Method
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Field-moist soils containing a population of nitrifying microorganisms; assessment of nitrification inhibition by chemical substances (except volatiles with Henry’s constant H > 1), biosolid extracts, and polluted soil mixtures
Does not apply to: Soils with no detectable nitrifying population; measurement of in situ nitrification rates (this is a potential activity assay under optimized conditions); volatile inhibitors
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Nitrification Potential – Shaken Soil Slurry Method
text:

title: Nitrification Potential – Shaken Soil Slurry Method
text:
4 Definitions

Ammonia oxidation: The first step of nitrification; conversion of NH4+ to NO2- by ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and archaea (AOA); the rate-limiting step of nitrification in most soils.
Autotrophic nitrification: Nitrification carried out by chemolithoautotrophic microorganisms (AOB, AOA, and nitrite oxidizers) that use the energy from ammonia oxidation to fix CO2; distinguished from heterotrophic nitrification.
Chlorate inhibition: Addition of sodium chlorate (ClO3-) to suppress nitrite oxidation, allowing NO2- to accumulate and be measured as the product of ammonia oxidation; used in some nitrification potential assays.
Nitrite oxidation: The second step of nitrification; conversion of NO2- to NO3- by nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB); not rate-limiting under normal conditions.
Nitrification potential (NP): The short-term rate of NO3- (or NO2- + NO3-) production in a soil slurry amended with excess NH4+ and incubated aerobically; reflects the size and activity of the extant nitrifier community; expressed as µg NO3--N g-1 soil h-1.
Slurry method: The standard technique for measuring nitrification potential; soil is suspended in a buffered ammonium sulfate solution at a defined soil-to-solution ratio and shaken aerobically at 25 °C; sequential subsamples are taken and analyzed for NO2- + NO3-.

title: Nitrification Potential – Shaken Soil Slurry Method
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Sodium chlorate (NaClO3) is an oxidizer; avoid contact with organic materials and combustible substances. Potassium chloride (4 M KCl) is a mild irritant. Ammonium sulfate is a mild irritant.
Physical: The orbital shaking incubator has moving parts; keep hair and loose clothing clear. Centrifuge operation poses standard mechanical hazards.

Safety glasses
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For chemical spills, refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling. For sodium chlorate spills, do not use organic absorbents (sawdust, paper towels); use vermiculite or sand.

title: Nitrification Potential – Shaken Soil Slurry Method
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Stock Solution A (Phosphate Buffer)
Combine the following in a volumetric flask and bring to 200 mL with distilled water:

28 mL of 0.2 mol/L KH2PO4
72 mL of 0.2 mol/L K2HPO4

This yields a phosphate buffer at approximately pH 7.2.


7.2 Test Medium
Prepare 1 L of test medium as follows:

Transfer 10 mL of Stock Solution A to a 1 L volumetric flask
Add 10–30 mL of 0.5 mol/L NaClO3 (see note below on concentration selection)
Add 0.198 g of (NH4)2SO4
If a carbon source is needed (e.g., when testing biosolids with high nitrate), add 10 mL of 5 mmol/L NaHCO3
Dilute to 1 L with distilled water
Verify that the pH is approximately 7.2; adjust if necessary

The final test medium contains approximately 1 mmol/L potassium phosphate buffer, 5–15 mmol/L sodium chlorate, and 1.5 mmol/L ammonium sulfate.






Note



The sodium chlorate concentration should be sufficient to inhibit biological nitrite oxidation without negatively affecting ammonium oxidation. If the appropriate concentration for your soil type is unknown, run a preliminary trial at 5, 10, and 15 mmol/L NaClO3 to identify the optimal level.




7.3 Preparing the 4 M KCl Stop Solution
Dissolve 298.2 g KCl in distilled water and bring to 1 L in a volumetric flask. This solution is used to halt ammonium oxidation at each sampling time.


7.4 Soil Moisture Determination
Determine the gravimetric moisture content of the soil per SOP-L400 (dry at 105 C, 24 h). This value is needed to calculate the volume of water in the initial soil sample and to express results on a dry-mass basis.


7.5 Setting Up the Incubation

Weigh approximately 25 g of field-moist soil into each of at least three replicate 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks
Calculate the volume of water already present in the soil:

\[
V_{\text{water}} = M_{\text{soil}} \times \theta_g
\]
where \(M_{\text{soil}}\) = mass of moist soil (g) and \(\theta_g\) = gravimetric moisture content (g water / g dry soil).

Calculate the volume of test medium to add:

\[
V_{\text{medium}} = V_{\text{total}} - V_{\text{water}}
\]
where \(V_{\text{total}}\) = desired total liquid volume (typically 100 mL).

Add the calculated volume of test medium to each flask
Place the flasks upright on the orbital shaking incubator set to 25 +/- 2 C and 175 rpm (sufficient to keep solids suspended)







Important



If testing chemical substances, dissolve them in the phosphate buffer and add to the test medium before diluting to 1 L. For substances with low water solubility, use mechanical dispersion or a low-toxicity vehicle (organic solvent, emulsifier). If a vehicle is used, include an additional control to assess its effect on ammonium oxidation.




7.6 Sampling the Slurry

At 2 h and 6 h after the start of incubation, shake each flask well to resuspend solids and withdraw a 2 mL aliquot of the slurry. Ensure the ratio of solution to soil is consistent across all samples.
Dispense the 2 mL aliquot into a test tube
Immediately add 2 mL of 4 M KCl to stop ammonium oxidation
Centrifuge at 3,000 x g for 2 minutes, or filter through high-speed filter paper
Transfer the clear supernatant or filtrate to a clean, labeled tube



7.7 Nitrite Analysis
Analyze the extracts for NO2--N using a suitable colorimetric method (e.g., ISO 14256-2; diazotization with sulfanilamide and N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine). Extracts may be stored at 4–8 C but must be analyzed within 24 hours.

title: Nitrification Potential – Shaken Soil Slurry Method
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Calculations
Potential ammonium oxidation rate:
\[
\text{Rate} = \frac{[\text{NO}_2^{-}\text{-N}]_{6h} - [\text{NO}_2^{-}\text{-N}]_{2h}}{\Delta t \times M_{\text{dry}}} \times V_{\text{total}}
\]
where the NO2--N concentrations are in ug/mL (= mg/L), \(\Delta t\) = time interval (4 h), \(M_{\text{dry}}\) = dry mass of soil (g), and \(V_{\text{total}}\) = total liquid volume in the flask (mL). Report results as ng NO2--N per g dry soil per hour.
Inhibition (%) by a test chemical:
\[
\text{Inhibition} \; (\%) = \frac{R_{\text{control}} - R_{\text{treatment}}}{R_{\text{control}}} \times 100
\]
where \(R\) = ammonium oxidation rate.
Toxicity assessment for polluted soil mixtures:
When mixing polluted and unpolluted (reference) soils, the polluted soil is considered toxic if:
\[
A_m + s_m < 0.9 \times \frac{A_c + A_p}{2}
\]
where \(A_m\) = mean activity in the mixture, \(s_m\) = standard deviation in the mixture, \(A_c\) = mean activity in the control soil, and \(A_p\) = mean activity in the polluted soil (each tested separately). This threshold applies with a minimum of four replicates.


8.2 QC Requirements

Use a minimum of three replicates per treatment
Four replicates are required when applying the toxicity assessment equation above
Include a negative control (soil with no ammonium addition) and a positive control (reference soil with known nitrification activity) in each batch
Verify that ammonium oxidation is linear between the 2 h and 6 h sampling points. If non-linearity is suspected, add sampling at 0 h and 4 h to characterize the time course.
Blank controls (test medium without soil) should show no significant nitrite accumulation
Report the coefficient of variation among replicates. A CV greater than 15% suggests sampling inconsistency or soil heterogeneity; consider additional replicates.

# Nitrification potential calculation per ISO 15685

# Input data
no2_2h_mg_L <- 0.15       # NO2-N at 2 h (mg/L in the extract)
no2_6h_mg_L <- 0.95       # NO2-N at 6 h (mg/L in the extract)
delta_t_h <- 4             # Time interval (h)
soil_moist_g <- 25.0       # Mass of field-moist soil (g)
theta_g <- 0.22            # Gravimetric moisture (g water / g dry soil)
V_total_mL <- 100          # Total liquid volume in the flask (mL)

# Dry mass of soil
M_dry_g <- soil_moist_g / (1 + theta_g)

# Potential ammonium oxidation rate (ng NO2-N / g dry soil / h)
# Convert mg/L to ug/mL (same units), then multiply by V_total to get
# total ug in the flask, divide by dry mass and time, convert to ng.
rate_ng_per_g_per_h <- ((no2_6h_mg_L - no2_2h_mg_L) *
                          V_total_mL / (delta_t_h * M_dry_g)) * 1000

cat(sprintf("Dry soil mass:            %.2f g\n", M_dry_g))
cat(sprintf("Delta NO2-N:              %.2f mg/L\n",
            no2_6h_mg_L - no2_2h_mg_L))
cat(sprintf("Nitrification potential:  %.1f ng NO2-N / g dry soil / h\n",
            rate_ng_per_g_per_h))

title: Hot-Plate Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
This procedure describes the open-vessel, hot-plate acid digestion of soil, sediment, and sludge samples for near-total extraction of lead (Pb) and other trace metals, following US EPA Method 3050B (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 1996). The digested extract can be analyzed by ICP-OES, ICP-MS, or flame/ graphite furnace AAS. This is a near-total-dissolution method; silicates and some refractory oxides are not fully dissolved, but environmentally available metals are recovered.
For microwave-assisted digestion using the MARS 5 system, see SOP-L411. The microwave method is faster but processes fewer samples per batch; the hot-plate method described here is slower but requires only standard fume-hood equipment.

Does not apply to: Water samples (direct acidification or separate digestion); samples requiring total silicate dissolution (HF-based methods); microwave digestion (see SOP-L411)

title: Hot-Plate Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
4 Definitions

Aqua regia: A 3:1 (v/v) mixture of HCl and HNO3; dissolves noble metals (gold, platinum) and many sulfide minerals not attacked by HNO3 alone; more aggressive than single-acid digestion but rarely necessary for soil and sediment.
Certified reference material (CRM): A soil or sediment with certified elemental concentrations from an accredited producer (NIST, USGS); run alongside every digestion batch to verify accuracy.
Digestion blank (method blank): A vessel containing only acid reagents and no soil, processed through the entire digestion procedure; detects contamination from acids, vessels, or the hot plate environment.
EPA Method 3050B: The US EPA hot-plate acid digestion procedure for soils, sediments, and sludges; uses repeated refluxes with HNO3 and H2O2 to dissolve environmentally available trace metals; the reference method for this SOP.
Matrix spike: A sample to which a known concentration of analyte has been added before digestion; used to assess matrix-specific recovery and method accuracy.
Partial digestion: Dissolution of the environmentally available or acid-soluble metal fraction of a sample (EPA 3050B); does not dissolve silicate minerals; appropriate for assessing bioavailability and regulatory compliance; distinguished from total digestion (which requires HF).
Reflux: Heating an acid-sample mixture such that acid vapors condense and return to the vessel; increases digestion efficiency for resistant matrices.

title: Hot-Plate Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
5 Safety and Hazards

5.1 Critical Safety Warning
This procedure uses concentrated mineral acids (HNO3, HCl) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) at elevated temperatures in open vessels. All acid handling and digestion must be performed in a certified chemical fume hood.


5.2 Hazards

Chemical: Concentrated HNO3 (15.8 M) is a severe oxidizer and corrosive. Concentrated HCl (12 M) is severely corrosive. 30% H2O2 is a reactive oxidizer that can cause exothermic reactions with organic matter.
Physical: Hot plate operates at approximately 95 C; digestion vessels and watch glasses are hot. Burns from contact with heated glassware or splashing acid.
Inhalation: HNO3 digestion produces toxic NOx fumes. HCl produces irritating HCl vapor. All heating must occur in the fume hood.



5.3 Required PPE

Chemical splash goggles or face shield
Lab coat
Acid-resistant gloves (neoprene or heavy-duty nitrile, long-cuffed)
Closed-toed shoes



5.4 Emergency Procedures
For acid splashes to skin or eyes, flush immediately at the eyewash station or safety shower for at least 15 minutes. For inhalation of fumes, move to fresh air. For acid spills, neutralize small spills with sodium bicarbonate; for large spills, evacuate and use the spill kit. Refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.






Important



Never add water to concentrated acid. Add acid slowly to samples. Never allow digestion vessels to go to dryness; this can volatilize analytes and damage vessels.

title: Hot-Plate Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Preparation

Air-dry the soil at room temperature or at 60 C until constant mass
Pass through a No. 10 sieve (2 mm) per SOP-F400 Soil Sampling
Homogenize thoroughly using a mortar and pestle
Determine gravimetric moisture on a companion subsample per SOP-L400



7.2 Glassware Cleaning
Acid-wash all vessels, volumetric flasks, and watch glasses per SOP-L101 Glassware Cleaning, Section 6.3 (10% HNO3 acid bath). Rinse with reagent water and dry in a clean environment.


7.3 Weighing

Weigh 0.50–1.00 g of prepared soil into a clean digestion vessel
Record the exact mass to the nearest 0.001 g in the lab notebook



7.4 Initial Nitric Acid Digestion

Working in the fume hood, add approximately 10 mL of concentrated HNO3 to the vessel
Cover with a watch glass
Place on the hot plate set to approximately 95 C. Do not allow the solution to boil.
Reflux gently until the initial vigorous reaction subsides and the volume begins to reduce. Do not allow the sample to go to dryness.
Continue heating for approximately 30–60 minutes, periodically lifting the watch glass to rinse the underside with DI water back into the vessel



7.5 Oxidation with H2O2

Remove the vessel from the hot plate and allow to cool slightly
Add 1–2 mL of 30% H2O2 dropwise. Wait for effervescence to subside between drops.
Return to the hot plate and resume heating at 95 C
Repeat the H2O2 additions until the reaction is minimal (typically 2–4 additions) and the digest appears light-colored







Warning



Add H2O2 very slowly. The reaction with organic matter is exothermic and can cause violent spattering if added too quickly, especially to hot solutions. Always cool the vessel first.




7.6 HCl Treatment

Add approximately 5 mL of concentrated HCl to the digest
Cover and heat at approximately 95 C for 15–30 minutes
This step dissolves residual metal precipitates and improves recovery of metals such as Fe, Al, and Pb



7.7 Volume Reduction

Remove the watch glass and continue heating at approximately 95 C
Reduce the volume to approximately 5 mL
Monitor closely and do not allow the sample to go to dryness







Important



Evaporation to dryness will cause loss of volatile analytes (As, Se, Hg) and can bake residues onto the vessel walls, making quantitative recovery impossible.




7.8 Dilution and Filtration

Remove from the hot plate and allow to cool to room temperature
Rinse the vessel walls and watch glass with small portions of DI water
If undissolved material is present, filter through Whatman No. 41 filter paper into a clean 50 mL volumetric flask, rinsing the filter and vessel quantitatively
If the solution is clear, transfer directly to the volumetric flask
Bring to 50.0 mL with DI water
Mix thoroughly
Transfer to a clean, labeled polyethylene or polypropylene storage bottle. Store at 4 C until analysis.

title: Hot-Plate Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 QC Requirements

Method blank: Include one vessel containing reagents only (no soil) in each digestion batch. The blank must read below the MDL for all target analytes.
Certified reference material (CRM): Digest a CRM with known metal concentrations in each batch. Recovery: 80–120%.
Matrix spike: Spike a duplicate sample with a known concentration of the target analyte(s). Recovery: 75–125%.
Duplicate digestions: At least 10% of samples. Relative percent difference (RPD) less than 20%.
Calibration verification: Verify with a mid-range check standard every 10 samples during instrumental analysis.



8.2 Calculations
Metal concentration in soil (mg/kg dry weight):
\[
C_{\text{soil}} = \frac{C_{\text{digest}} \times V_{\text{final}}}{M_{\text{soil}}}
\]
where \(C_{\text{digest}}\) = concentration in the digest (mg/L), \(V_{\text{final}}\) = final volume (mL, typically 50), and \(M_{\text{soil}}\) = mass of dried soil (g).
For soil dried at 60 C, apply a moisture correction to report on a 105 C oven-dry basis (see SOP-L400):
\[
C_{\text{soil, OD}} = C_{\text{soil}} \times \frac{100 + \theta_{60}}{100 + \theta_{105}}
\]

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
This SOP describes the measurement of soil microbial respiration using the Solvita CO2 burst test. The method quantifies CO2 evolution from rewetted, air-dried soil as an index of microbial activity and labile carbon availability (Haney et al., 2008a; Haney et al., 2008b).
The CO2 burst exploits the “Birch effect,” the well-documented pulse of microbial respiration that occurs when dry soil is rapidly rewetted (Birch, 1958; Fierer & Schimel, 2003). Drying and rewetting disrupts soil aggregates, lyses a fraction of the microbial biomass, and releases intracellular osmolytes, all of which provide readily mineralizable substrate that surviving microbes respire as CO2 (Fierer & Schimel, 2002; Xiang et al., 2008). The magnitude of the burst integrates microbial biomass size, community physiological status, and the pool of labile organic carbon, making it a useful single-number indicator of biological soil fertility (Haney et al., 2008b).

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
This SOP describes the measurement of soil microbial respiration using the Solvita CO2 burst test. The method quantifies CO2 evolution from rewetted, air-dried soil as an index of microbial activity and labile carbon availability (Haney et al., 2008a; Haney et al., 2008b).
The CO2 burst exploits the “Birch effect,” the well-documented pulse of microbial respiration that occurs when dry soil is rapidly rewetted (Birch, 1958; Fierer & Schimel, 2003). Drying and rewetting disrupts soil aggregates, lyses a fraction of the microbial biomass, and releases intracellular osmolytes, all of which provide readily mineralizable substrate that surviving microbes respire as CO2 (Fierer & Schimel, 2002; Xiang et al., 2008). The magnitude of the burst integrates microbial biomass size, community physiological status, and the pool of labile organic carbon, making it a useful single-number indicator of biological soil fertility (Haney et al., 2008b).

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Air-dried, sieved soil samples collected per SOP-F400 for microbial activity assessment
Does not apply to: Compost maturity testing (see SOP-L413); field-moist basal respiration; long-term (7–28 day) incubation-based respirometry; or chamber-based field CO2 flux measurements (see SOP-F406)
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

text:

Role

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
4 Definitions

Basal respiration: The rate of CO2 production from soil under controlled, standardized conditions (specific moisture, temperature, incubation time) without additional substrate; reflects the size and activity of the soil microbial community.
CO2 burst: The pulse of CO2 released from dry soil immediately upon rewetting; caused by osmotic stress on microorganisms, physical disruption of aggregates, and rapid oxidation of previously protected organic matter; the basis of the Solvita CO2 Burst test.
Colorimetric gel pad: The CO2-sensitive indicator element in the Solvita kit; changes color in proportion to the CO2 concentration in the jar headspace; read with a Solvita paddle reader or digitally.
Digital Color Reader (DCR): The Solvita handheld device that reads the color of the gel pad and converts it to a numerical Solvita Index value.
Solvita Index: A unitless scale (1–8) reported by the Solvita CO2 Burst test; higher values indicate greater biological activity and organic matter availability; values correlate with potentially mineralizable nitrogen.
Soil microbial biomass: The mass of living microbial cells (bacteria, fungi, protozoa) in soil; the primary driver of organic matter decomposition and nutrient cycling; estimated indirectly by CO2 respiration or directly by fumigation-extraction (see SOP-L409).
Water-holding capacity (WHC): The maximum amount of water a soil can hold after free drainage; expressed as a percentage of dry soil mass; the Solvita protocol adjusts sample moisture to a defined fraction of WHC for standardization.

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Preparation

Use soil that has been collected per SOP-F400.
If samples were stored at 4 C after sieving, allow them to equilibrate to room temperature (20–25 C) for at least 30 minutes before beginning the assay.
Sieve soils through a 2mm sieve. Use a mortar and pestle to break up soil clumps that did not pass through the sieve initially and resieve it. Discard any rocks or other materials that do not pass through the sieve.







Note



The CO2 burst test is designed for air-dried soil. Drying standardizes the starting moisture across samples and maximizes the rewetting response. Results from field-moist soil are not comparable to published Solvita norms (Woods End Laboratories, 2019).




7.2 Incubation Setup

Measure 30ccs of the dried and sieved soils using a 30cc volume scoop and add it to a small beaker. Weight the soil (do not include weight of beaker) and record the exact mass to 0.1 g. Shake it gently to level the surface.
Gently sprinkle 9ccs of deionized water onto the surface of the soil using a pipette. The rewetting triggers the microbial CO2 burst (Fierer & Schimel, 2003).
Remove a fresh CO2-sensitive gel probe from its sealed foil packet. Inspect the gel: it should be attached to the probe, uniform in color with no cracks, discoloration, or signs of prior exposure. Discard compromised probes. Make sure not to touch the gel while handling the probe.
Insert the probe into the jar so that the gel face is exposed to the headspace above the soil surface. Do not bury the probe in soil.
Seal the jar immediately and securely.
Record the jar number, sample ID, soil mass, water volume added, and start time.



7.3 Incubation

Place sealed jars in the incubator set to 25 +/- 1 C
Incubate undisturbed for 24 hours
Do not open or move jars during incubation



7.4 Reading Results

After exactly 24 hours (+/- 15 minutes), remove the gel probe from the jar
Immediately insert the probe into the Solvita Digital Color Reader (DCR) and record the numerical reading
Record the color number and the corresponding CO2-C concentration (mg CO2-C kg-1 soil) from the DCR or the Solvita conversion table







TipTip



Read probes promptly after removing them from the jar. Prolonged exposure to ambient air will alter the gel color and compromise the reading. The manufacturer recommends reading within 2 minutes of opening the jar.




7.5 Calculating Results
Express results on a dry-soil basis:
\[\text{CO}_2\text{-C (mg kg}^{-1}\text{)} = \frac{\text{DCR reading (mg CO}_2\text{-C)}}{\text{oven-dry soil mass (kg)}}\]
If the oven-dry mass is not known, calculate it from the air-dried mass and the gravimetric moisture content of a companion subsample determined by SOP-L400.


7.6 Cleanup

Dispose of used soil in the designated waste container (return to field site if uncontaminated, or standard trash)
Wash incubation jars thoroughly with soap and water; rinse with deionized water; dry completely before reuse
Dispose of used gel probes in standard trash

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
8 Quality Control

8.1 Routine QC







QC Element
Requirement




Duplicates
At least 1 per 10 samples; duplicates should agree within 15% relative percent difference (RPD)


Control
One empty, sealed jar with gel probe per batch; probe should read at or near baseline


Incubator temperature
Verify and record at start and end of each 24 h period; must be 25 +/- 1 C


DCR calibration
Calibrate per manufacturer instructions before each batch


Gel probe storage
Store sealed in foil packets at room temperature, away from light; check expiration dates before use





8.2 Corrective Actions

If the blank reading exceeds the baseline by more than one color increment, check for CO2 contamination sources (e.g., proximity to gas burners, poor jar seals) and repeat the batch
If duplicate RPD exceeds 15%, re-run the sample pair. Persistent poor precision may indicate sample heterogeneity; increase the number of subsamples

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
9 Data Interpretation
The CO2 burst is proportional to microbial biomass and labile carbon and is correlated with potential carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus mineralization (Haney et al., 2008b). Typical ranges for the Solvita CO2 burst test on agricultural and wildland soils are given below, adapted from Haney et al. (2008a) and the Solvita technical literature (Woods End Laboratories, 2019):








CO2-C (mg kg-1)
Interpretation
Implication




< 20
Very low
Severely depleted microbial activity; very low labile C


20–50
Low
Limited biological activity; management intervention may be needed


50–100
Moderate
Adequate microbial activity for many soils


100–150
High
Active microbial community; good labile C supply


> 150
Very high
Highly active soil; common in recently amended or high-organic soils









Important



These thresholds are general guidelines. Interpret results in the context of soil type, land use, climate, and management history. Comparisons are most meaningful when made across treatments within a single study using the same sampling and analytical protocol.
