title: Soil Organic Matter – Loss on Ignition
text: This SOP describes the estimation of soil organic matter (SOM) content using the loss-on-ignition (LOI) method. SOM is quantified by measuring the mass lost when oven-dried soil is combusted at 550 °C in a muffle furnace (Heiri et al., 2001; Nelson & Sommers, 1996).

title: Soil Organic Matter – Loss on Ignition
text: This SOP describes the estimation of soil organic matter (SOM) content using the loss-on-ignition (LOI) method. SOM is quantified by measuring the mass lost when oven-dried soil is combusted at 550 °C in a muffle furnace (Heiri et al., 2001; Nelson & Sommers, 1996).

title: Soil Organic Matter – Loss on Ignition
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Air-dried, sieved soil samples collected per SOP-F400 Soil Sampling and Processing.
Does not apply to: Soils with high calcium carbonate content (CaCO3 decomposes above ~450 °C and may inflate LOI values; consider an alternative method such as elemental analysis for calcareous soils (Heiri et al., 2001)).
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133.

title: Soil Organic Matter – Loss on Ignition
text:
3 Definitions

Ash-free dry mass (AFDM): The mass remaining after removing water (drying at 105 °C) and organic matter (igniting at 550 °C); equivalent to the inorganic mineral mass of the sample.
Crucible: A heat-resistant porcelain or ceramic container used to hold soil samples during furnace ignition; must be pre-ignited and weighed to constant mass before use.
Inorganic carbon (IC): Carbon associated with carbonates (CaCO3, MgCO3); released as CO2 during ignition above ~550 °C; can inflate LOI values in calcareous soils if ignition temperature is not controlled or if acid pre-treatment is omitted (Heiri et al., 2001).
Loss on ignition (LOI): The percentage mass loss when an oven-dried soil is ignited at 550 °C for 4 hours: \(LOI = (M_{105} - M_{550}) / M_{105} \times 100\); used as a proxy for SOM content (Heiri et al., 2001).
Soil organic matter (SOM): The organic fraction of soil, including plant and animal residues at various stages of decomposition, microbial biomass, and stabilized humus; estimated by LOI as approximately \(\text{SOM} \approx 1.72 \times \text{LOI}\) (the Van Bemmelen factor) when organic carbon is the target (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).
Tare mass: The pre-weighed mass of the empty, pre-ignited crucible; subtracted from all subsequent measurements to obtain sample mass.
Van Bemmelen factor: The empirical conversion factor (1.724) relating organic carbon content to SOM by assuming that SOM contains 58% carbon by mass; use with caution for soils with unusual organic matter composition (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).

5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Thermal: Muffle furnace operates at 550 °C; severe burn risk. Drying oven operates at 105 °C. Ceramic crucibles remain extremely hot for many minutes after removal from the furnace.
Physical: Crucible tongs can slip; always use two hands when moving hot crucibles.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses
Laboratory coat
Heat-resistant gloves (mandatory when handling furnace-hot crucibles)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety and SOP-L111 Muffle Furnace. For burns, cool with running water for at least 10 minutes and seek medical attention.

title: Soil Organic Matter – Loss on Ignition
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Crucible Preparation

Pre-ignite crucibles in the muffle furnace at 550 °C for at least 1 hour to remove any residual organic matter.
Transfer to a desiccator and cool to room temperature.
Weigh each crucible to the nearest 0.0001 g and record as the tare mass (\(W_{\text{crucible}}\)).



7.2 Oven Drying at 105 °C

Using a spatula, transfer 5–10 g of air-dried, sieved soil into a pre-weighed crucible.
Record the mass of crucible plus moist or air-dry soil.
Place uncovered crucibles in the drying oven at 105 °C for at least 24 hours.
Transfer crucibles to a desiccator and cool to room temperature (approximately 20–30 minutes).
Weigh to the nearest 0.0001 g and record as \(W_{\text{105}}\) (mass of oven-dried soil only, i.e., crucible + dry soil mass minus crucible tare).



7.3 Combustion at 550 °C

Transfer the crucibles containing oven-dried soil directly into the muffle furnace (Heiri et al., 2001).
Ramp the furnace to 550 °C (if programmable, use a ramp rate of approximately 10 °C per minute to prevent crucible cracking and reduce convective loss of fine particles).
Hold at 550 °C for 4 hours (Heiri et al., 2001).
Turn off the furnace and allow crucibles to cool inside the furnace until they can be safely transferred (below approximately 200 °C).
Transfer crucibles to a desiccator and cool to room temperature.
Weigh to the nearest 0.0001 g and record as \(W_{\text{550}}\) (mass of combusted soil, excluding crucible).



7.4 Calculation
Soil organic matter content is calculated as (Heiri et al., 2001):
\[
\text{SOM (\%)} = \left( \frac{W_{105} - W_{550}}{W_{105}} \right) \times 100
\]
where:

\(W_{105}\) = mass of oven-dried soil (g)
\(W_{550}\) = mass of soil after combustion at 550 °C (g)

To convert LOI (%) to approximate organic carbon (%OC), divide by 1.724 (the Van Bemmelen factor); note that this conversion assumes constant elemental composition and is less accurate for samples with unusual organic matter (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).

title: Soil Organic Matter – Loss on Ignition
text:
8 Quality Control

Run analytical duplicates for at least 10% of samples; coefficient of variation between duplicates should be less than 5% (Heiri et al., 2001).
Include an empty crucible blank in each furnace run to verify no mass gain from ambient contamination.
Include a laboratory reference soil with known SOM content in each batch.
Verify oven (105 °C) and furnace (550 °C) temperatures using a calibrated thermocouple at regular intervals.

title: Soil Nitrate Quick Test – Test Strip Method
text: This procedure describes a rapid, semi-quantitative field or laboratory method for estimating soil nitrate (NO3-) concentration using colorimetric test strips in a calcium chloride (CaCl2) extracting solution (Bronikowski & Thomason, 2022; Hartz, 2010). The method is useful as a screening tool for assessing soil nitrogen status, guiding fertilizer decisions, and identifying spatial patterns in nitrate availability across a site (Magdoff et al., 1984). It is not a substitute for the quantitative KCl extraction and colorimetric analysis described in SOP-L403 (Mulvaney, 1996), but provides rapid, low-cost results that can be obtained in the field or with minimal laboratory equipment.

title: Soil Nitrate Quick Test – Test Strip Method
text: This procedure describes a rapid, semi-quantitative field or laboratory method for estimating soil nitrate (NO3-) concentration using colorimetric test strips in a calcium chloride (CaCl2) extracting solution (Bronikowski & Thomason, 2022; Hartz, 2010). The method is useful as a screening tool for assessing soil nitrogen status, guiding fertilizer decisions, and identifying spatial patterns in nitrate availability across a site (Magdoff et al., 1984). It is not a substitute for the quantitative KCl extraction and colorimetric analysis described in SOP-L403 (Mulvaney, 1996), but provides rapid, low-cost results that can be obtained in the field or with minimal laboratory equipment.

2 Scope

Does not apply to: Quantitative reporting of soil nitrate for publication (use SOP-L403); ammonium determination (test strips do not measure NH4+); water sample nitrate (use SOP-L303 Hach Colorimetric)

title: Soil Nitrate Quick Test – Test Strip Method
text:
4 Definitions

Calcium chloride (CaCl2) extractant: A dilute salt solution (approximately 0.01 M) used in the quick test to displace some exchangeable NO3- from soil without requiring the high-ionic-strength KCl used in quantitative extractions; minimizes matrix effects on the test strip reaction.
Colorimetric test strip: A plastic strip impregnated with reagents that react with nitrate (or another target) to produce a visible color change; read visually against a printed color chart or with a reflectometer; semi-quantitative.
Detection range: The span of concentrations over which a test strip or method produces a distinguishable response; for most nitrate strips, approximately 0–500 mg NO3--N L-1 in the extract; values outside this range require dilution or a quantitative method.
Matrix effect: Interference from sample components (chloride, organic matter, pH) that alter the test strip reaction; minimized by using CaCl2 extractant and diluting dark or strongly colored samples.
Semi-quantitative: A measurement that provides an approximate concentration within broad categories (e.g., 0, 10, 25, 50, 100 mg/L) rather than a precise numerical value; appropriate for screening but not for publication or regulatory reporting.

title: Soil Nitrate Quick Test – Test Strip Method
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Preparing the Extracting Solution

Add 6 g (approximately 1 teaspoon) of anhydrous CaCl2 to 1 gallon (3.78 L) of distilled water
Cap and shake until dissolved
This produces approximately 0.014 M CaCl2, sufficient for approximately 125 tests
Label the container with the reagent name, concentration, and preparation date
Store at room temperature. The solution is stable indefinitely.







Note



CaCl2 is used instead of plain water because the calcium ions displace nitrate from soil exchange sites, giving a more complete extraction (Gelderman & Beegle, 2015; Houba et al., 1986). The low concentration avoids interference with the test strip chemistry.




7.2 Collecting the Soil Sample

Collect soil from the target depth (typically 0–15 cm or 0–30 cm) using a probe or auger per SOP-F400 Soil Sampling
Composite multiple subsamples if a plot-level estimate is desired
Homogenize the soil in a bucket by hand-mixing
Remove visible roots and stones



7.3 Performing the Quick Test

Fill a graduated centrifuge tube with 30 mL of the CaCl2 extracting solution
Add soil to the tube until the total volume reaches the 40 mL mark (approximately 10 mL of soil displaced)
Cap the tube securely
Shake vigorously until all soil is well mixed (approximately 30 seconds)
Allow the tube to stand upright for the soil particles to settle. Wait at least 10 minutes but no more than 1 hour.
Dip a nitrate test strip into the clearer supernatant near the top of the tube for 1 second. Do not stir up settled soil.
Remove the strip and hold horizontally
Compare the strip to the manufacturer’s color chart at both 30 seconds and 60 seconds after dipping
Record the nitrate reading (ppm NO3--N or ppm NO3-, depending on the strip brand) and the reading time used







Important



Read the strip at the times specified by the manufacturer. Reading too early or too late gives inaccurate results. If the strip brand reports in ppm NO3-, divide by 4.43 to convert to ppm NO3--N.




7.4 Applying the Soil Texture Correction Factor
The test strip reads the nitrate concentration in the extract solution, not in the soil. To estimate the nitrate concentration in the soil itself, apply a correction factor based on soil texture and moisture status (Gelderman & Beegle, 2015):



Texture
Moist Soil Factor
Dry Soil Factor




Sand
2.3
2.6


Loam
2.0
2.5


Clay
1.7
2.2



\[
\text{Soil NO}_3^{-}\text{-N (ppm)} = \text{Strip reading (ppm)} \times \text{Correction factor}
\]
Determine the soil texture using SOP-F401 Texture by Feel or SOP-L401 Hydrometer.


7.5 Recording Results
Record the following in the field notebook or data sheet for each test:

Date, time, site, plot ID
Sampling depth (cm)
Soil condition (moist or dry)
Estimated texture (sand, loam, or clay)
Strip reading (ppm) and reading time (30 s or 60 s)
Correction factor applied
Corrected soil NO3--N (ppm)

title: Soil Nitrate Quick Test – Test Strip Method
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Limitations
The test strip method is semi-quantitative. Results should be interpreted as approximate categories (low, moderate, high) rather than precise concentrations (Hartz, 2010; Schmidhalter, 2005). Key limitations include:

Strip resolution is typically 10–25 ppm increments; fine differences are not detectable
Color matching is subjective (ambient lighting affects perception)
The method does not measure ammonium (NH4+); total inorganic N requires SOP-L403
Soil moisture, organic matter, and temperature all influence extraction efficiency



8.2 Interpretation Guide








Corrected Soil NO3--N (ppm)
Interpretation
Agronomic Implication




Less than 10
Low
N likely limiting; fertilization may be warranted


10 – 25
Moderate
Adequate for many crops


25 – 50
High
Sufficient N; reduce or defer applications


Greater than 50
Very high
Excess N; potential leaching risk



These thresholds are general guidelines adapted from Magdoff et al. (1984) and Hartz (2010). Consult crop-specific guidelines and local extension recommendations.


8.3 QC Requirements

Run a blank (CaCl2 solution only, no soil) at the start of each testing session. The strip should read 0 ppm or below the lowest detection increment.
Run a duplicate test on at least 1 in 10 samples. Duplicates should agree within one color-chart increment.
Verify test strip expiration date before use. Expired strips may give unreliable color development.
For critical decisions, confirm quick-test results with the quantitative KCl extraction method (SOP-L403)

title: Soil Nitrate Quick Test – Test Strip Method
text:
12 Appendix A: Example Calculation



Code
# Nitrate quick test correction example

strip_reading_ppm <- 15       # ppm NO3-N from test strip
soil_texture <- "loam"
soil_condition <- "moist"     # "moist" or "dry"

# Correction factors
factors <- data.frame(
  texture = c("sand", "loam", "clay"),
  moist = c(2.3, 2.0, 1.7),
  dry = c(2.6, 2.5, 2.2)
)

cf <- factors[factors$texture == soil_texture, soil_condition]

corrected_ppm <- strip_reading_ppm * cf

cat(sprintf("Strip reading:     %d ppm NO3-N\n", strip_reading_ppm))
cat(sprintf("Texture:           %s\n", soil_texture))
cat(sprintf("Condition:         %s\n", soil_condition))
cat(sprintf("Correction factor: %.1f\n", cf))
cat(sprintf("Corrected value:   %.0f ppm NO3-N\n", corrected_ppm))

title: Soil pH and Salinity
text:
This procedure describes the measurement of soil pH and electrical conductivity (EC, as a proxy for salinity) on soil-water and soil-CaCl2 extracts. Soil pH controls nutrient availability, metal solubility, microbial activity, and the fate of contaminants. Soil salinity (estimated from EC) affects plant growth, soil structure, and is a primary criterion for classifying saline, sodic, and saline-sodic soils. The methods follow Thomas (1996) for pH and Rhoades (1996) for EC, as described in the SSSA Methods of Soil Analysis, Part 3 (Rhoades, 1996; Thomas, 1996).
For meter operation, calibration, and electrode maintenance, see SOP-L300 pH and Conductivity – Bench-Top Measurements.

title: Soil pH and Salinity
text:
This procedure describes the measurement of soil pH and electrical conductivity (EC, as a proxy for salinity) on soil-water and soil-CaCl2 extracts. Soil pH controls nutrient availability, metal solubility, microbial activity, and the fate of contaminants. Soil salinity (estimated from EC) affects plant growth, soil structure, and is a primary criterion for classifying saline, sodic, and saline-sodic soils. The methods follow Thomas (1996) for pH and Rhoades (1996) for EC, as described in the SSSA Methods of Soil Analysis, Part 3 (Rhoades, 1996; Thomas, 1996).
For meter operation, calibration, and electrode maintenance, see SOP-L300 pH and Conductivity – Bench-Top Measurements.

title: Soil pH and Salinity
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Air-dried, sieved (less than 2 mm) mineral soils from all EA Program sites; compost and potting media (with appropriate extraction ratios noted in Section 6)
Does not apply to: In situ field pH measurements with portable probes (see SOP-F200); water sample pH and conductivity (see SOP-L300); saturated paste extraction for formal salinity classification of irrigation water
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Soil pH and Salinity
text:
3 Definitions

Cation exchange capacity (CEC): The total capacity of a soil to hold exchangeable cations; closely related to soil pH buffering capacity (see SOP-L416).
Electrical conductivity (EC): A measure of a soil extract’s ability to conduct electricity, proportional to total dissolved ion concentration; expressed in dS m-1 or mS cm-1; used as a surrogate for soluble salt content.
Paste extract (saturated paste): A soil-water mixture prepared at the saturation moisture content; the USDA standard extract for measuring soil salinity.
pH: The negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity; soil pH is measured in a defined soil-to-water or soil-to-CaCl2 suspension and controls nutrient availability and microbial activity.
Salinity: The total concentration of dissolved salts in soil solution; high salinity reduces plant-available water and can be toxic to salt-sensitive crops; typically characterized by EC of the saturation extract (ECe).
Soil-to-water ratio: The ratio of soil mass to water volume used in pH and EC measurements (e.g., 1:1, 1:2, 1:5); must be reported alongside the result because pH and EC values differ between ratios.

title: Soil pH and Salinity
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Preparation

Air-dry the soil at room temperature until constant mass (typically 24–48 hours)
Pass the dried soil through a 2 mm sieve. See SOP-F400 Soil Sampling for details on sieving and homogenization.
Store the sieved soil in a labeled bag or container at room temperature



7.2 Selecting the Extraction Ratio
Two standard soil-to-solution ratios are used. The choice depends on the project objectives and the need for comparability with published data:








Ratio
Method
When to Use




1:1
10 g soil : 10 mL water (or CaCl2)
Most common in agronomic soil testing; closest to field conditions


1:5
10 g soil : 50 mL water (or CaCl2)
Useful for saline soils, compost, or when more extract volume is needed for subsequent analyses









Note



Soil pH measured in 0.01 M CaCl2 is typically 0.3–0.5 units lower than pH measured in DI water because the salt displaces H+ and Al3+ from exchange sites. CaCl2 pH is less sensitive to seasonal variation in soil salt content and is preferred for monitoring studies where consistency over time matters (Thomas, 1996). Record the extraction medium (water or CaCl2) and ratio with every result.




7.3 Preparing the Soil Slurry (1:1 Method)

Weigh 10.0 g of air-dried, sieved soil into a clean beaker
Add 10 mL of DI water (for pHwater and EC) or 10 mL of 0.01 M CaCl2 (for pHCaCl2)
Stir vigorously with a glass rod for 30 seconds
Allow to stand for 10 minutes
Stir briefly again before measurement



7.4 Preparing the Soil Extract (1:5 Method)

Weigh 10.0 g of air-dried, sieved soil into a clean beaker
Add 50 mL of DI water (or 50 mL of 0.01 M CaCl2)
Stir vigorously for 30 seconds
Allow to stand for 30 minutes, stirring occasionally
For EC measurement on the 1:5 extract, allow the soil to settle and insert the conductivity cell into the clear supernatant. For pH, insert the electrode into the slurry while still partially suspended.



7.5 Measuring Electrical Conductivity






Important



Always measure EC before pH on the same aliquot. The pH electrode’s KCl reference junction leaks electrolyte into the sample and will artificially elevate the EC reading (APHA et al., 2012).



Calibrate the conductivity meter per SOP-L300, Section 6.3
Rinse the conductivity cell with DI water and blot dry
Insert the cell into the supernatant (1:5 method) or into the settled portion of the slurry (1:1 method). Tap gently to dislodge air bubbles.
Allow the reading to stabilize with automatic temperature compensation active
Record the specific conductance (uS/cm at 25 C), sample ID, and extraction ratio
Rinse the cell with DI water between samples



7.6 Measuring Soil pH

Calibrate the pH meter with a three-point calibration per SOP-L300, Section 6.2
Rinse the pH electrode with DI water and blot gently
Insert the electrode into the slurry so that the glass bulb and reference junction are fully immersed. For the 1:1 method, the electrode should contact the settled soil.
Allow the reading to stabilize (typically 30–60 seconds; may take 2–3 minutes for poorly buffered soils)
Record the pH value, extraction medium (water or CaCl2), ratio, and sample ID
Rinse the electrode with DI water between samples



7.7 Converting 1:5 EC to Estimated Saturated Paste EC (ECe)
The saturated paste extract (ECe) is the standard for soil salinity classification, but the 1:5 extract is quicker to prepare. An approximate conversion can be made using the following relationship, though the factor varies with texture (Rhoades, 1996):
\[
EC_e \approx EC_{1:5} \times f
\]
where \(f\) is an empirical factor:



Soil Texture
\(f\) (approximate)




Sand
6 – 8


Loam
8 – 10


Clay
10 – 13









Warning



These conversion factors are approximate and site-specific. For formal salinity classification (e.g., land-use planning, irrigation suitability), prepare an actual saturated paste extract per USDA Handbook 60.

Record extraction medium, ratio, calibration data, and QC results in the lab notebook

12 Appendix A: Example Calculation and Reporting



Code
library(tidyverse)

# Example data entry
soil_data <- tibble(
  sample_id = c("PV-01", "PV-02", "PV-03", "PV-04", "PV-05"),
  pH_water_1_1 = c(6.82, 7.45, 5.91, 8.12, 7.03),
  pH_CaCl2_1_1 = c(6.48, 7.10, 5.55, 7.78, 6.68),
  EC_1_5_uS_cm = c(245, 1820, 85, 3450, 310),
  texture = c("loam", "clay", "sand", "clay", "loam")
)

# Estimate EC_e from 1:5 EC using texture-based conversion factors
conversion <- c(sand = 7, loam = 9, clay = 11.5)

soil_data <- soil_data %>%
  mutate(
    EC_e_dS_m = (EC_1_5_uS_cm / 1000) * conversion[texture],
    salinity_class = case_when(
      EC_e_dS_m < 2 ~ "Non-saline",
      EC_e_dS_m < 4 ~ "Slightly saline",
      EC_e_dS_m < 8 ~ "Moderately saline",
      EC_e_dS_m < 16 ~ "Strongly saline",
      TRUE ~ "Very strongly saline"
    ),
    pH_class = case_when(
      pH_water_1_1 < 4.5 ~ "Extremely acidic",
      pH_water_1_1 < 5.5 ~ "Strongly acidic",
      pH_water_1_1 < 6.5 ~ "Moderately acidic",
      pH_water_1_1 < 7.5 ~ "Neutral",
      pH_water_1_1 < 8.5 ~ "Moderately alkaline",
      TRUE ~ "Strongly alkaline"
    )
  )

print(soil_data %>% select(sample_id, pH_water_1_1, pH_CaCl2_1_1,
                           EC_e_dS_m, salinity_class, pH_class))

title: Soil Moisture – Gravimetric Method
text: This SOP describes the gravimetric determination of soil moisture content. Gravimetric moisture is a fundamental soil property required for expressing analytical results on a dry-weight basis (e.g., microbial biomass carbon, nutrient concentrations) and for characterizing site conditions (Gardner, 1986).

title: Soil Moisture – Gravimetric Method
text: This SOP describes the gravimetric determination of soil moisture content. Gravimetric moisture is a fundamental soil property required for expressing analytical results on a dry-weight basis (e.g., microbial biomass carbon, nutrient concentrations) and for characterizing site conditions (Gardner, 1986).

title: Soil Moisture – Gravimetric Method
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All soil samples collected per SOP-F400 Soil Sampling and Processing that require moisture correction or moisture characterization.
Does not apply to: Volumetric soil moisture measured with in-situ probes (TDR, capacitance sensors); soil water potential measurements.
Location: EA Program laboratory.

title: Soil Moisture – Gravimetric Method
text:
3 Definitions

Air-dry moisture content: The moisture content of soil equilibrated with ambient laboratory air (typically 20–40 °C, 30–60% relative humidity); generally a few percent and varies with humidity (Gardner, 1986).
Constant mass: The criterion for complete drying: successive weighings separated by at least 2 hours of additional oven time agree within 0.01 g.
Dry-weight correction factor (\(f\)): The ratio of moist soil mass to oven-dry soil mass for the same sample; used to convert results expressed per gram of moist soil to per gram of oven-dry soil: \(f = (W_{\text{moist}} - W_{\text{container}}) /
(W_{\text{dry}} - W_{\text{container}})\).
Field-moist soil: Soil at the moisture content it had when collected from the field; the reference state for biological and enzyme activity measurements (Robertson et al., 1999).
Gravimetric moisture content (\(\theta_g\)): Mass of water per mass of oven-dry soil: \(\theta_g = (M_{\text{wet}} - M_{\text{dry}}) /
M_{\text{dry}}\); expressed as g g-1 or as a percentage (Gardner, 1986).
Oven-dry soil: Soil dried at 105 °C to constant mass; the standard reference state for expressing soil chemical and physical properties (Gardner, 1986).
Soil moisture: The amount of water contained in the pore spaces of soil; may be expressed as gravimetric content (\(\theta_g\), g g-1), volumetric content (\(\theta_v\), m3 m-3), or as a percentage (Gardner, 1986).
Volumetric moisture content (\(\theta_v\)): Volume of water per volume of soil: \(\theta_v = \theta_g \times \rho_b / \rho_w\) where \(\rho_b\) is bulk density and \(\rho_w\) is the density of water (1.0 g cm-3).

title: Soil Moisture – Gravimetric Method
text:
4 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Thermal: Drying ovens operate at 105 °C. Use heat-resistant gloves and tongs when removing samples.
Physical: Hot aluminum tins retain heat for several minutes after removal from the oven. Do not handle bare-handed.




4.1 Required PPE

Laboratory coat
Heat-resistant gloves (when handling hot tins)

title: Soil Moisture – Gravimetric Method
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Preparation

Print copies of the Soil Moisture Datasheet (Appendix A) for recording measurements.
Label aluminum tins or ceramic crucibles with a permanent marker or engraving tool.
Pre-dry the empty containers at 105 °C for at least 1 hour to remove any residual moisture (Gardner, 1986).
Cool the containers in a desiccator to room temperature.
Weigh each empty container to the nearest 0.01 g and record as Tin Weight on the datasheet.



7.2 Sample Weighing

Using a spatula, transfer approximately 10–20 g of field-moist soil into a pre-weighed container.
Record the mass of the container plus moist soil to the nearest 0.01 g as Wet Weight on the datasheet.
Avoid compacting the soil; a loose arrangement promotes even drying.







TipTip



Process moisture subsamples at the same time as other subsamples (e.g., for microbial biomass or respiration) to ensure the moisture value accurately reflects the condition of the soil used in those analyses (Robertson et al., 1999).




7.3 Drying

Place the uncovered containers in the drying oven set to 105 °C (Gardner, 1986).
Dry for a minimum of 24 hours.
After 24 hours, remove one or two containers, cool in the desiccator, and re-weigh. If the mass has decreased by more than 0.01 g compared to a check 2 hours earlier, return all samples to the oven for an additional 4 hours and re-check.
Drying is complete when the mass is constant (change of less than 0.01 g between successive weighings).



7.4 Cooling and Final Weighing

Transfer all containers from the oven to a desiccator.
Allow to cool to room temperature (approximately 20–30 minutes).
Weigh each container plus dry soil to the nearest 0.01 g and record as Dry Weight on the datasheet.



7.5 Calculations
Gravimetric soil moisture content (%):
\[
\theta_g (\%) = \left( \frac{W_{\text{moist}} - W_{\text{dry}}}{W_{\text{dry}} - W_{\text{container}}} \right) \times 100
\]
where:

\(W_{\text{moist}}\) = mass of container + moist soil (g)
\(W_{\text{dry}}\) = mass of container + oven-dried soil (g)
\(W_{\text{container}}\) = mass of empty container (g)

Dry-weight correction factor (for converting field-moist analytical results to a dry-weight basis):
\[
f = \frac{W_{\text{moist}} - W_{\text{container}}}{W_{\text{dry}} - W_{\text{container}}}
\]
To convert a result expressed per gram of moist soil to per gram of dry soil, multiply by \(f\) (Gardner, 1986).

title: Soil Moisture – Gravimetric Method
text:
8 Quality Control

Run analytical duplicates for at least 10% of samples; the coefficient of variation between duplicates should be less than 5% (Robertson et al., 1999).
Verify oven temperature with a calibrated thermometer at the start of each drying cycle.
Ensure the desiccator contains active (indicating) desiccant; replace or regenerate when the indicator changes color.
Re-weigh a subset of samples after an additional 2 hours of drying to confirm mass constancy (Gardner, 1986).

Disposal Method

Standard trash or return to field site


Aluminum tins
Clean and reuse, or recycle

title: Metals in Water (ICP-MS Prep and Acidification)
text: This SOP describes the acidification, trace metal preservation, and digestion protocols for aqueous environmental samples prior to Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) analysis. It covers dissolved metals (filtration + acidification) and total recoverable metals (acid digestion) (Creed et al., 1994).

title: Metals in Water (ICP-MS Prep and Acidification)
text: This SOP describes the acidification, trace metal preservation, and digestion protocols for aqueous environmental samples prior to Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) analysis. It covers dissolved metals (filtration + acidification) and total recoverable metals (acid digestion) (Creed et al., 1994).

title: Metals in Water (ICP-MS Prep and Acidification)
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Environmental water samples (surface water, groundwater, runoff, wastewater) requiring dissolved or total recoverable metals analysis by ICP-MS.
Does not apply to: Solid matrices (soils, sediments, tissues), total metals by XRF, or organic analyte preparation.
Location: Environmental analysis laboratories.

title: Metals in Water (ICP-MS Prep and Acidification)
text:
3 Responsibilities



Role
Responsibility




Lab PI
Approve SOP, ensure training compliance


Trained Personnel
Follow this SOP, report deviations


New Students
Complete training before independent use

title: Metals in Water (ICP-MS Prep and Acidification)
text:
4 Definitions

Acid digestion (water samples): The addition of concentrated HNO3 (typically 0.5–2% v/v final) to preserved water samples to dissolve any particulate metal and stabilize dissolved metals; a prerequisite for ICP-MS analysis (Creed et al., 1994).
Blank (method blank): A reagent water sample carried through the entire preparation procedure; used to assess and correct for metal contamination introduced during sample processing (APHA et al., 2012).
Certified reference material (CRM): A water sample with certified metal concentrations from an accredited producer (e.g., NIST, USGS); used to verify ICP-MS accuracy (Beauchemin, 2017).
Digestion blank: A solution containing only the acid reagents (no sample) processed through the digestion procedure; detects contamination from reagents and vessels.
ICP-MS (Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry): An analytical technique that vaporizes and ionizes a sample in an argon plasma and separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio to identify and quantify elements at parts-per-trillion concentrations (Beauchemin, 2017).
Method detection limit (MDL): The minimum concentration of an analyte that can be detected with 99% confidence that the true concentration is greater than zero; determined from replicate blank analyses per 40 CFR Part 136 (Creed et al., 1994).
Preservation (acidification): Addition of HNO3 to a water sample at the time of collection to prevent metal adsorption to container walls and to maintain dissolved metals in solution; required for regulatory compliance samples (Creed et al., 1994).
Relative percent difference (RPD): |A - B| / ((A + B) / 2) × 100; used to assess duplicate precision; acceptance criterion is RPD ≤ 20% for environmental matrices (Creed et al., 1994).
Spike recovery: The percentage of a known added concentration of a metal that is measured by the instrument; acceptable range is typically 85–115%; used to check for matrix interferences (Creed et al., 1994).
Total recoverable metals: Metals determined in an unfiltered sample after acid digestion; includes both dissolved and particulate-bound fractions (Creed et al., 1994).

title: Metals in Water (ICP-MS Prep and Acidification)
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical burns and corrosive vapors: Concentrated nitric acid (HNO3, 67–70%) is an extremely corrosive oxidizing agent. Contact causes severe chemical burns. Vapors are highly damaging to respiratory tissue.
Hydrochloric acid: Concentrated HCl produces corrosive fumes and can cause burns on contact.









ImportantEngineering Controls



All acid dispensing, sample acidification, and hot block heating must be performed inside an active chemical fume hood.



5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses or face shield
Laboratory coat
Acid-resistant nitrile gloves (double-gloving recommended)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
In case of acid spill or chemical burn, refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety or call campus safety. For acid contact with skin or eyes, flush immediately with water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention.

6 Equipment and Materials

6.1 Equipment







Item

title: Metals in Water (ICP-MS Prep and Acidification)
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Preservation and Dissolved Metals Fraction

Filtration: Filter the raw, unacidified sample immediately upon collection or arrival through a certified 0.45 µm metal-free membrane filter. Discard the first 5 mL of filtrate to rinse the filter matrix. Collect remaining filtrate into a clean polypropylene tube.
Acidification: Add high-purity trace metal grade HNO3 dropwise to the sample container to achieve a final matrix concentration of 2% (v/v). For example, add 1.0 mL concentrated HNO3 per 50 mL sample matrix (Creed et al., 1994).
Verify pH is < 2 using a narrow-range pH strip. Store acidified samples for at least 16 hours prior to analysis to ensure proper metal desorption from container walls (Creed et al., 1994).



7.2 Total Recoverable Metals Digestion (Hot Block)

Transfer a well-mixed 50.0 mL portion of unfiltered sample into a clean digestion tube.
Working inside a fume hood, add 1.0 mL of trace metal grade HNO3 and 0.5 mL of trace metal grade HCl (Creed et al., 1994).
Place the digestion tube into the hot block. Fit with a ribbed watch glass or vapor reflux cap to prevent evaporation loss.
Program the block heater to 85–95 °C. Heat the sample for 2 hours without allowing the solution to boil (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
Remove from heat, allow to cool to room temperature, and adjust back to the original 50.0 mL volume mark using high-purity DI water. If visible particulates remain, filter the digestate to prevent ICP-MS nebulizer clogging.







TipAvoiding Boil-Over



Monitor samples during the first 15–20 minutes of heating. If the solution begins to bump or boil, reduce the block temperature by 5 °C. Loss of sample volume through boiling invalidates the digestion (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).




7.3 Shutdown and Cleanup

Allow the hot block to cool before removing tubes.
Rinse all non-disposable glassware and equipment with 10% (v/v) HNO3 followed by three rinses of DI water.
Dispose of acid waste per §8 below.

title: Metals in Water (ICP-MS Prep and Acidification)
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria







QC Element
Requirement




Method blank
Process 50 mL DI water through full procedure; analyte concentrations must be below the MDL (Creed et al., 1994)


Laboratory fortified blank (LFB)
Spike multi-element stock into DI water and carry through digestion; recovery must be 85–115% (Creed et al., 1994)


Laboratory fortified matrix (LFM)
Spike a field sample; recovery 70–130% (APHA et al., 2012)


Duplicate samples
RPD ≤ 20% (Creed et al., 1994)


Calibration verification
Initial and continuing calibration per instrument SOP



See Creed et al. (1994) and APHA et al. (2012) for additional QC guidance.

Each use: Wipe down the hot block surface and fume hood sill after acid work.
Monthly: Inspect digestion tubes for etching or discoloration; replace as needed.
As needed: Replace pH strips and membrane filters before expiration dates.

title: Dissolved Organic Carbon in Water – Shimadzu TOC-L (NPOC Mode)
text:
This procedure describes the determination of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in natural water samples (surface water, groundwater, stormwater, treated effluent) by the non-purgeable organic carbon (NPOC) method on the Shimadzu TOC-L analyzer. DOC is a fundamental water quality parameter that influences aquatic ecosystem productivity, light penetration, metal complexation, disinfection byproduct formation, and nutrient cycling (Thurman, 1985; Wetzel, 2001).
The NPOC method acidifies the sample and sparges with carrier gas to remove inorganic carbon (CO2, HCO3-, CO32-) before combustion. The remaining carbon is measured as NPOC, which for most natural waters is operationally equivalent to DOC when the sample has been filtered through 0.45 µm (APHA et al., 2012, Section 5310B).
For instrument operation, startup, and shutdown, see SOP-L204 Shimadzu TOC-L. For water-extractable DOC from soils, see SOP-L418.

title: Dissolved Organic Carbon in Water – Shimadzu TOC-L (NPOC Mode)
text:
4 Definitions

Calibration blank: Deionized water (18.2 MΩ·cm) of verified DOC less than 0.05 mg C/L; used as the zero point for calibration and as the system blank to verify background carbon from the instrument and reagents.
CCV (continuing calibration verification): A mid-range KHP standard analyzed at regular intervals during an analytical run to confirm calibration stability; acceptance criterion is 90–110% recovery; if outside this range, re-calibrate and re-run affected samples (APHA et al., 2012).
Chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM): The fraction of DOC that absorbs UV/visible light; derived primarily from aromatic humic and fulvic acids; a surrogate indicator of DOC concentration in optically characterized waters (Thurman, 1985).
Dissolved organic carbon (DOC): Organic carbon that passes through a 0.45 µm filter; in natural waters, DOC includes humic substances, fulvic acids, amino acids, carbohydrates, and other soluble organic compounds; the operationally defined quantity measured as NPOC by the Shimadzu TOC-L (APHA et al., 2012; Thurman, 1985).
Field blank: A sample of deionized water processed through the field collection equipment (bottles, filters, cooler) and returned to the laboratory for analysis; used to detect contamination introduced during sample collection and transport (Sharp, 1993).
Humic substances: High-molecular-weight, polydisperse aromatic compounds derived from the decomposition of plant and microbial material; typically comprise 40–80% of DOC in natural fresh waters (Thurman, 1985).
IC (inorganic carbon): Carbon present as dissolved CO2, bicarbonate (HCO3-), and carbonate (CO32-); removed from water samples by acidification and sparging before NPOC measurement.
KHP (potassium hydrogen phthalate, KC8H5O4): The primary calibration standard for TOC analysis; a pure, non-hygroscopic organic acid weighed accurately to prepare standards of known carbon concentration; 1.0000 g KHP = 0.4711 g C.
Method blank: Deionized water acidified and processed identically to field samples, including any filtration and preservation steps; used to detect contamination from reagents and equipment; must read less than 0.2 mg C/L (APHA et al., 2012).
NPOC (non-purgeable organic carbon): The organic carbon remaining in a sample after acidification (typically with HCl or H3PO4) and sparging with carrier gas to remove IC and volatile organic carbon (VOC); the quantity reported as DOC by the Shimadzu TOC-L (APHA et al., 2012, Section 5310B).
Particulate organic carbon (POC): Organic carbon retained on a 0.45 µm filter; not measured by this SOP; requires separate filter collection and combustion analysis.
Pre-combusted glass vial: A TOC autosampler vial heated to 450 °C for at least 4 hours to destroy residual organic carbon from the glass or manufacturing process; used to prevent contamination of samples from the container.
PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride) filter: A 0.45 µm syringe filter with low organic carbon leaching; preferred for DOC sample filtration; cellulose acetate filters must not be used because they leach DOC (Kaplan, 1994).
TOC (total organic carbon): The sum of DOC and POC; in this SOP, only DOC (the filtered, NPOC fraction) is measured.

title: Dissolved Organic Carbon in Water – Shimadzu TOC-L (NPOC Mode)
text:
7 Sample Collection and Preservation
Proper sample handling is critical; contamination from fingers, plastic containers, and atmospheric CO2 can bias results (Sharp, 1993).

Collect samples in pre-combusted glass bottles. Do not use plastic bottles for DOC samples.
Filter through 0.45 µm PVDF syringe filters within 4 hours of collection; discard the first 2–3 mL of filtrate.
Acidify filtered samples to pH ≤ 2 with 2 M HCl (approximately 100 µL per 40 mL sample) to suppress microbial activity.
Store acidified samples at 4 °C in the dark; analyze within 28 days (APHA et al., 2012).
Cap vials immediately after filling to minimize atmospheric CO2 contamination.

Adjust the range to match expected sample concentrations. Load standards into pre-combusted autosampler vials and enter into the Sample Table in LabSolutions TOC.


8.2 Setting Up the Sample Table

Open LabSolutions TOC and start a new analysis.
Enter calibration standards (type = Standard), blanks (type = Blank), CCV standards, and samples.
Set the measurement mode to NPOC for all samples and blanks.
Set the number of injections per sample to 3; the software reports the mean and coefficient of variation (CV).
Enter dilution factors for any samples that have been diluted before the run.



8.3 Running the Analysis

Load all vials into the autosampler; verify rack positions match the Sample Table.
Confirm the ASI-L rinse reservoir is full.
Click Start and monitor the first few injections for normal peak shape and baseline stability.
The run proceeds unattended; the autosampler advances automatically.



8.4 Data Review and Export

After the run, open the Data Browser.
Check each result:

Replicate injection CV must be less than 2%.
Blank values must be less than 0.1 mg C/L.
CCV recovery must be 90–110%; re-calibrate and re-run affected samples if outside this range.

Dilute and re-run any sample exceeding the calibration range.
Export results to CSV per SOP-L204 Section 7.9.
Record the run in the instrument logbook.

title: Dissolved Organic Carbon in Water – Shimadzu TOC-L (NPOC Mode)
text:
9 Calculations
The TOC-L software reports NPOC concentration directly in mg C/L, corrected for dilution factor if entered in the Sample Table. Report as DOC:
\[
\text{DOC (mg C/L)} = \text{NPOC}_{\text{reported}} - \text{NPOC}_{\text{method blank}}
\]
If samples were diluted before analysis, apply the dilution factor:
\[
\text{DOC (mg C/L)} = (\text{NPOC}_{\text{reported}} - \text{NPOC}_{\text{blank}}) \times D
\]
where \(D\) is the dilution factor.

9.1 R Code for Batch Processing


Code
# SOP-L311: DOC (NPOC) -- batch calculation from TOC-L CSV export
raw <- read.csv("TOC-L_export.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

blanks <- raw[grepl("^Blank|^DI|^MQ", raw$SampleID, ignore.case = TRUE), ]
ccv    <- raw[grepl("^CCV|^CVS|^Check", raw$SampleID, ignore.case = TRUE), ]

mean_blank <- mean(blanks$NPOC_mg_L, na.rm = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Mean method blank: %.3f mg C/L\n", mean_blank))

samples <- raw[!grepl("^Blank|^DI|^MQ|^CCV|^CVS|^Check|^Std",
                       raw$SampleID, ignore.case = TRUE), ]
samples$DOC_mg_L <- (samples$NPOC_mg_L - mean_blank) * samples$Dilution
samples$DOC_mg_L[samples$DOC_mg_L < 0] <- 0
samples$QC_flag <- ifelse(samples$CV_pct > 2, "CV>2%", "")

print(samples[, c("SampleID", "NPOC_mg_L", "Dilution", "DOC_mg_L", "QC_flag")],
      row.names = FALSE)

title: Pesticide Analysis via Gas Chromatography
text: This SOP defines the protocols for extraction verification, instrument parameters, operation, and safety requirements for analyzing trace pesticide residues using Gas Chromatography (GC) coupled with specialized detectors (ECD or MS) (McNair et al., 2019; United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).

title: Pesticide Analysis via Gas Chromatography
text:
2 Scope

Does not apply to: LC-amenable pesticides, non-targeted screening, or preparative-scale separations
Location: Environmental analysis laboratories

title: Pesticide Analysis via Gas Chromatography
text:
4 Definitions

Autosampler: A robotic device that withdraws a precise volume from each GC vial and injects it into the inlet without manual intervention; reduces injection variability and allows unattended overnight sequences.
Capillary column: A fused-silica column (typically 15–60 m × 0.18–0.32 mm ID) coated on its interior with a thin film of stationary phase; separates pesticides by their differential affinity for the stationary phase relative to the carrier gas (McNair et al., 2019).
Carrier gas: An inert gas (helium, nitrogen, or hydrogen) that moves sample vapor through the column; flow rate and mode (constant pressure or constant flow) affect retention times and peak shape (McNair et al., 2019).
CCV (continuing calibration verification) standard: A mid-range calibration standard analyzed every 10 injections to confirm that instrument response has not drifted; must recover within ±15% of the true value (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
Column bleed: Gradual decomposition and volatilization of the GC stationary phase at high temperature; produces a rising baseline at the end of a temperature program; distinguished from analyte peaks by reproducible retention and broad peak shape.
ECD (electron capture detector): A selective detector that measures current suppression caused by electron-capturing compounds (organochlorine pesticides, polychlorinated biphenyls); extremely sensitive (pg range) for halogenated compounds (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
GC-MS (gas chromatography-mass spectrometry): Coupling of a GC with a mass spectrometer; provides compound identification by mass spectrum matching in addition to retention time; the confirmatory technique for pesticide analysis (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2018).
Inlet liner: A deactivated glass tube inside the split/splitless inlet; protects the column from non-volatile matrix residues; replaced daily or after every 50–100 injections to prevent sample carry-over and peak degradation.
MDL (method detection limit): The minimum analyte concentration that can be detected with 99% confidence under the stated method conditions; determined from replicate analyses of low-level standards; listed per analyte in the method SOP.
RPD (relative percent difference): |A - B| / ((A + B) / 2) × 100; used to assess duplicate precision; acceptance criterion is RPD ≤ 20% for environmental matrices (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
Septum: A silicone or PTFE-faced silicone disc that seals the inlet and is penetrated by the autosampler needle; replaced daily or after 50–100 injections to prevent coring fragments from entering the liner.
Splitless injection mode: An inlet mode in which the split vent is closed during injection to transfer nearly all of the sample onto the column; standard for trace pesticide analysis to maximize sensitivity (McNair et al., 2019).
Standby method: A GC method programmed after sequence completion that drops oven, inlet, and detector temperatures while maintaining a reduced carrier gas flow; prevents column oxidation and extends stationary phase lifetime.

title: Pesticide Analysis via Gas Chromatography
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical toxicity: Pesticide standards, target analytes, and extraction solvents (hexane, dichloromethane, acetone) are highly toxic, carcinogenic, or neurotoxic. Inhalation of vapors or skin absorption poses a severe chronic health risk.
Thermal: The GC injection port (200–250 °C) and column oven (50–320 °C) operate at extreme temperatures causing instant severe burns. Ensure the inlet is below 50 °C before opening it.
High-pressure gas cylinders: Carrier gas cylinders (helium, nitrogen, hydrogen) pose crush and high-pressure hazards if dropped or if regulators fail. Hydrogen carrier gas presents an explosion risk if allowed to accumulate in the oven.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses or chemical splash goggles
Laboratory coat (fully fastened)
Nitrile or solvent-resistant gloves (Viton or Silver Shield for bulk chlorinated solvents)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
In case of chemical spill, gas leak, or equipment failure, refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety or call campus safety. For compressed gas emergencies, evacuate the area and contact EH&S.

title: Pesticide Analysis via Gas Chromatography
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Gas Cylinder and Inlet Verification

Verify carrier gas cylinders have sufficient pressure (> 500 psi).
Confirm secondary regulator delivery pressure meets manufacturer specifications (typically 60–80 psi).
Check moisture, oxygen, and hydrocarbon traps; replace if indicator dyes signal saturation.



7.2 Injection Port Maintenance (Pre-Run Check)






ImportantHot Inlet



Ensure the inlet temperature has dropped below 50 °C before opening the inlet assembly.



Replace the injection port septum daily or every 50–100 injections (McNair et al., 2019).
Inspect the glass liner; replace if charring, particulate matter, or matrix deposits are visible.



7.3 Sequence Setup and Sample Loading

Prepare calibration curves from certified pesticide reference materials spanning expected concentration intervals (e.g., 10–1000 µg/L) (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
Aliquot extracts into clean 2 mL amber GC vials; cap with PTFE-faced septa.
Program the injection sequence including:

Solvent blanks (hexane/acetone matrix check)
Multi-point calibration curve
CCV standards every 10 injections
Duplicate sample matrices




7.4 Initiating the GC Run

Load the analytical method and verify parameters (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007):

Inlet: Splitless mode; 250 °C
Oven program: 50 °C (1 min hold) → ramp 10 °C/min → 300 °C (5 min hold)
Carrier gas: Constant flow, 1.2 mL/min helium

Allow all zones to reach setpoint; confirm Ready status in software.
Initiate the sequence; monitor the first injection cycle to confirm the autosampler syringe articulates without bending the needle.



7.5 Post-Analysis and Standby Shutdown

Review chromatogram baselines for peak symmetry, column bleed spikes, or retention time shifts.







TipRetention Time Drift



If retention times shift, trimming 10–20 cm from the front of the analytical column can restore performance. Document the trim in the instrument logbook (McNair et al., 2019).



Upon sequence completion, load the Standby method to drop oven and detector temperatures while maintaining a reduced carrier gas purge to prevent column phase oxidation.

title: Pesticide Analysis via Gas Chromatography
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Initial calibration: \(r^2 \geq 0.995\) (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
CCV standards every 10 injections: recovery within ±15%; halt and re-calibrate if outside this window (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
Method blanks: no target analyte peaks above the MDL.
Duplicate RPD: ≤ 20% (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).

title: ELISA: Bisphenol A, Bisphenol B, and Pesticides in Water
text: This SOP describes the use of competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits to screen water samples for bisphenol A (BPA), bisphenol B (BPB), and selected pesticides (atrazine, glyphosate, and 2,4-D). ELISA provides a rapid, cost-effective immunochemical screening method for detecting trace-level organic contaminants in environmental water samples without the need for extensive sample preparation or chromatographic instrumentation (Aga, 2013; Goda et al., 2000; Voller et al., 1978). Results exceeding the kit detection threshold should be considered presumptive and confirmed by an instrumental method (e.g., LC-MS/MS or GC-MS) when data will be used for regulatory reporting (US Environmental Protection Agency, 1996).

title: ELISA: Bisphenol A, Bisphenol B, and Pesticides in Water
text:
4 Definitions

Absorbance: The logarithm of the ratio of incident to transmitted light through a colored solution, measured at the wavelength of maximum absorption; the raw output of spectrophotometric ELISA readers.
Bisphenol A (BPA): An industrial chemical used in polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins; an endocrine-disrupting compound detected in environmental water samples.
Competitive ELISA: An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay format in which analyte in the sample and a fixed amount of enzyme-labeled analyte compete for binding to a limited number of antibody sites; signal decreases as analyte concentration increases (inverse response).
Cross-reactivity: The degree to which an antibody recognizes structurally similar compounds other than the target analyte; expressed as a percentage and listed in the kit insert; high cross-reactivity with related compounds (e.g., BPB with a BPA kit) can produce false positives.
ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay): A plate-based immunoassay that uses antibody-antigen binding and an enzyme-substrate color reaction to detect and quantify target analytes.
Matrix effect: Interference from sample components (suspended solids, humic acids, pH, salinity) that alter antibody-antigen binding or enzyme activity; minimized by sample dilution, solid-phase extraction, or pH adjustment.
Standard curve: A set of calibration solutions of known analyte concentration used to convert absorbance readings to concentrations; ELISA curves are typically sigmoidal (4-PL fit).

text:
8 Procedure

8.1 General Competitive ELISA Workflow
All competitive ELISA kits in this SOP share the same principle: the analyte in the sample competes with an enzyme-labeled analyte conjugate for a limited number of antibody binding sites coated on the microplate well. Higher analyte concentrations in the sample result in less conjugate binding and therefore lower color development after substrate addition. The relationship between absorbance and concentration is inversely proportional (Goda et al., 2000; Voller et al., 1978).


8.2 Preparation

Remove the ELISA kit from the refrigerator and allow all reagents to equilibrate to room temperature (20–25 °C) for at least 30 minutes before opening.
Prepare wash buffer by diluting the concentrate per kit instructions (typically 1:10 with deionized water). Mix thoroughly.
If samples require dilution (e.g., wastewater with expected high concentrations), prepare dilutions in deionized water or the sample diluent provided with the kit. Record all dilution factors.
Label a plate map in the lab notebook showing the position of standards, controls, blanks, and samples. Each standard and sample should be run in duplicate.



8.3 Assay Procedure
Follow the specific kit insert for exact volumes and incubation times. The general sequence is:

Add standards and samples. Pipette the specified volume (typically 50 \(\mu\)L) of each calibration standard, positive control, negative control (zero standard), and sample into the appropriate wells. Change tips between every addition.
Add enzyme conjugate. Pipette the conjugate solution into each well. The conjugate competes with any analyte present in the sample for antibody binding sites.
Incubate. Cover the plate with foil and incubate on the plate shaker at the specified temperature and duration (typically 60 minutes at room temperature for BPA; consult kit insert for other analytes).
Wash. Aspirate or decant the well contents. Wash each well 3–5 times with wash buffer (approximately 250 \(\mu\)L per wash). After the final wash, invert the plate and tap firmly on absorbent paper to remove residual liquid. Incomplete washing is the most common source of high background and poor precision.
Add substrate. Pipette the TMB substrate solution into each well. Incubate for the specified time (typically 20–30 minutes at room temperature) in the dark. A blue color develops in wells with bound conjugate.
Add stop solution. Pipette the stop solution (acid) into each well. The blue color turns yellow. Read the plate within 15 minutes of adding stop solution.
Read absorbance. Measure absorbance at 450 nm using the microplate reader.







TipTip



Dispense reagents quickly and consistently across the plate. Use a multichannel pipette when possible to minimize time differences between the first and last wells. Stagger plates if running more than one analyte simultaneously.




8.4 Plate Washing Details
Inadequate washing is the most frequent source of assay failure in ELISA. Follow these guidelines:

Aspirate well contents completely (manual flicking or vacuum aspiration)
Fill each well with approximately 250 \(\mu\)L wash buffer
Allow wash buffer to soak for 5–10 seconds
Aspirate again
Repeat for the total number of wash cycles specified by the kit (typically 3–5)
After the final aspirate, invert the plate and tap firmly on a pad of clean paper towels 3–4 times to remove residual buffer

title: ELISA: Bisphenol A, Bisphenol B, and Pesticides in Water
text:
9 Data Analysis and Calculations

9.1 Standard Curve Construction

Calculate the mean absorbance of the duplicate wells for each standard concentration.
Express each standard as a percentage of the zero standard (maximum binding, B0):

\[
\%B/B_0 = \frac{\bar{A}_{\text{standard or sample}}}{\bar{A}_{B_0}} \times 100
\]

Plot %B/B0 (y-axis) against the log of the standard concentration (x-axis). Fit a four-parameter logistic (4PL) curve, which is the standard model for competitive immunoassay calibration (Findlay et al., 2000):

\[
y = D + \frac{A - D}{1 + \left(\frac{x}{C}\right)^B}
\]
where \(A\) = maximum asymptote (zero dose), \(D\) = minimum asymptote, \(C\) = IC50 (inflection point), and \(B\) = slope factor.

Interpolate sample concentrations from the 4PL curve. Most microplate reader software includes 4PL curve fitting. Alternatively, use R:



Code
# Four-parameter logistic (4PL) curve fitting for ELISA data
library(drc)

# Example data: concentration (ug/L) and %B/B0
standards <- data.frame(
  conc = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0, 10.0),
  pct_b_b0 = c(92.3, 84.1, 55.7, 38.2, 12.4, 6.8)
)

# Fit 4PL model
model_4pl <- drm(pct_b_b0 ~ conc, data = standards,
                 fct = LL.4(names = c("Slope", "Lower", "Upper", "IC50")))
summary(model_4pl)

# Predict concentration for a sample with %B/B0 = 45.0
sample_pct <- 45.0
pred_conc <- ED(model_4pl, sample_pct, type = "absolute", display = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("Sample concentration: %.3f ug/L\n", pred_conc[1]))




9.2 Dilution Correction
If samples were diluted before analysis, multiply the interpolated concentration by the dilution factor:
\[
C_{\text{original}} = C_{\text{interpolated}} \times DF
\]


9.3 Reporting
Report results as \(\mu\)g/L (ppb) for water samples. Indicate whether the result is a screening (ELISA) value and whether it exceeds any applicable regulatory threshold. Flag any result that falls outside the linear range of the standard curve (below the lowest standard or above the highest standard) and re-run with appropriate dilution if above range.

title: ELISA: Bisphenol A, Bisphenol B, and Pesticides in Water
text:
10 Quality Control

10.1 Within-Assay QC

Run all standards and samples in duplicate. The coefficient of variation (CV) between duplicates should be less than 15%. If a duplicate pair exceeds 15% CV, re-run those samples.
Include the kit-supplied positive control on every plate. The control must fall within the range stated on the certificate of analysis.
Include at least one reagent blank (deionized water) per plate.
The zero standard (B0) absorbance should typically be greater than 0.8 (consult kit insert for acceptable range). Low B0 values indicate degraded antibody or conjugate.



10.2 Between-Assay QC

Run a laboratory-prepared quality control sample (spiked DI water at a known concentration within the linear range) with each batch. Recovery should be 80–120%.
Track control chart performance (mean and +/- 2 SD limits) over time.
Record kit lot numbers and expiration dates. Do not mix reagents from different kit lots.



10.3 Method Detection Limits
The method detection limit (MDL) for each analyte is kit-specific and is defined as the concentration producing a %B/B0 response statistically distinguishable from the zero standard at the 95% confidence level. MDLs are typically provided in the kit insert. Report results below the MDL as “less than MDL.”


10.4 Cross-Reactivity
Competitive ELISA antibodies may cross-react with structurally related compounds. For example, BPA antibodies may exhibit partial cross-reactivity with BPB, BPS, or BPF. Atrazine antibodies may cross-react with simazine, propazine, or other triazine herbicides. Consult the cross-reactivity table in the kit insert and report results accordingly (e.g., “total triazines” rather than “atrazine” if significant cross-reactivity is known) (Aga, 2013).

title: IDEXX Quanti-Tray 2000 for E. coli/Total Coliform Enumeration
text:
4 Definitions

Colilert: A proprietary IDEXX defined-substrate technology that detects total coliforms and E. coli simultaneously by enzymatic hydrolysis of ONPG (for coliforms) and MUG (for E. coli).
Coliform bacteria (total coliforms): A group of facultatively anaerobic, gram-negative, rod-shaped bacteria that ferment lactose; includes E. coli and many non-fecal genera; used as an indicator of sanitary water quality.
Defined substrate technology (DST): A quantitative detection method based on the enzymatic hydrolysis of a chromogenic or fluorogenic substrate specific to the target organism.
E. coli: Escherichia coli; a fecal indicator bacterium detected by Colilert via MUG hydrolysis, which produces a fluorescent product visible under UV light at 365 nm.
MPN (Most Probable Number): A statistical estimate of the number of organisms per 100 mL, derived from the pattern of positive and negative wells in the Quanti-Tray/2000 using the IDEXX MPN table.
Quanti-Tray/2000: A sealed 97-well tray into which the sample- reagent mixture is sealed and incubated; provides positive/negative results for 49 large wells and 48 small wells, allowing MPN calculation up to 2,419 per 100 mL.
Total holding time: The maximum time from sample collection to the start of incubation; for Colilert, the sample must be incubated within 6 hours of collection or 30 hours if held at 4 °C.

text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Definitions
The following definitions apply throughout this SOP:

Analytical batch: The set of samples processed at the same time.
Control cultures: Known positive and negative cultures used to verify each lot of medium. E. coli serves as the positive control; Staphylococcus aureus serves as the negative control.
Field duplicate (FD): Two samples taken at the same time and place under identical circumstances, treated identically through field and laboratory procedures. Analysis of FDs indicates the precision associated with sample collection, preservation, storage, and laboratory procedures.
Laboratory reagent blank (LRB): An aliquot of sterilized water treated as a sample in all aspects, except that it is not taken to the sampling site. The purpose is to determine if analytes or interferences are present in the laboratory environment, reagents, or apparatus.
Laboratory duplicate (LD): Two aliquots of the same environmental sample treated identically throughout a laboratory analytical procedure. Analysis of LDs indicates precision associated with laboratory procedures but not with sample collection, preservation, or storage.



7.2 Biases and Interferences

Water samples containing humic material or other colored substances may interfere with visual readings. If there is background color, compare inoculated trays to a control tray containing only water (SM, 9223 A) (APHA et al., 2012).
Chlorinated water may inhibit the growth of coliform bacteria. If the water has been chlorinated, use the sodium thiosulfate bottles to neutralize the chlorine.



7.3 Sample Collection

Arrive at the site and record site number, date, and time
Label the bottle with: location (geographic area and stream or lake name), date, time, water temperature, and sampler’s initials. Label the bottle before immersion using a black permanent marker or pre-printed labels.
Put on latex or nitrile gloves before handling bottles. Fingers contain contaminants such as nitrates; bug repellent and sunscreen are particularly troublesome. Once gloves are on, do not touch your face, the ground, or anything other than the bottles.
Collect the sample from flowing (not stagnant) water, facing upstream
Immerse the bottle completely, approximately 10 cm (4 inches) deep, with the mouth pointing upstream so no water flows over your hand into the bottle. Do not allow the bottle to contact the stream bottom where sediments can be disturbed. Collect water 6–12 inches below the surface.
Fill the bottle to the 100 mL line on the first immersion. Pour off any excess and cap immediately. Do not underfill, overfill, or re-dunk. If too much water is poured off, use a new 100 mL container.
Do not touch the bottle mouth or inside of the cap. Be careful not to contaminate the sample with surface film, contact with human skin, or breathing into the bottle or cap. If the stream is too shallow to fully immerse the bottle, collect as much as possible while avoiding the bottom, and note the depth in field notes.







TipTip



Collect one field duplicate (FD) sample every two weeks of sampling. Duplicate sites are selected at random. The duplicate is the second sample when two samples are collected at the same location. Duplicates document repeatability of sample collection and reproducibility of laboratory results.




7.4 Sample Preservation and Storage

Keep samples cool during transport using a cooler with ice
Store at 4 C until analysis; do not freeze
Analyze within 6 hours of collection
Record the location number, bottle numbers, and collection time in the field sample log
Samples must remain in the possession of the researcher who both collects and analyzes them



7.5 Sample Processing

Turn on the Quanti-Tray sealer
Set the incubator to 35 C
Allow samples to reach room temperature before analysis
Aseptically add one packet of Colilert-18 reagent to the 100 mL water sample
Replace the lid and shake well until the reagent has fully dissolved
Label the Quanti-Tray with a permanent marker, recording information that identifies the sample
Open the Quanti-Tray by holding it at the top with the well side facing your palm. Push the top edge inward with your free hand while squeezing the tray into a circle. Gently pull the foil tab away from the plastic side. Be careful not to tear the tab. Do not touch the inside of the tray.
Pour the sample mixture into the Quanti-Tray, avoiding contact with the foil tab
Tap the small wells 2–3 times to release air bubbles. Allow foam to settle.
Place the filled Quanti-Tray on the rubber insert, making sure each well fits its corresponding hole
Push the insert with the tray into the sealer, non-foil-tab end first, until the sealer grabs the tray and pulls it through. If you need to reverse the motor, press and hold the reverse button. However, do not reverse the motor if the rubber insert is completely inside the sealer.
The sealer distributes the sample mixture into the wells, seals them, and partially ejects the sealed tray
Remove the rubber insert and tray from the sealer







Important



If the sealer jams or malfunctions, do not force the tray. Contact the lab manager for assistance.




7.6 Incubation

Incubate the sealed tray at 35 +/- 0.5 C for 18 hours
Do not stack trays or block airflow around them in the incubator



7.7 Reading Results – Total Coliforms

After 18 hours of incubation, remove the tray from the incubator
Count the number of large wells and small wells that are yellow and equal to or greater than the comparator, including the large overflow well at the top
Mark positive wells with a permanent marker as you count
Record the number of positive small wells and positive large wells in the lab notebook



7.8 Reading Results – E. coli

In a darkened area, view the Quanti-Tray under the UV lamp (365 nm)







WarningUV Safety



Be careful to avoid eye damage when using the UV lamp. Do not look directly at the UV light source. Wear UV-protective safety glasses if available.



Count the number of fluorescent wells that are equal to or greater than the comparator
Record the number of fluorescent small wells and fluorescent large wells in the lab notebook



7.9 Determining MPN

Use the IDEXX MPN table (see Appendix) to look up the MPN based on the number of positive large wells and positive small wells
Cross-check results using the IDEXX MPN Generator software: https://www.idexx.com/en/water/resources/mpn-generator/ (Windows only)
Record results on the bench sheet for both total coliforms and E. coli



7.10 Interpreting Results



MPN/100 mL
Risk Level

Medium risk


Greater than 100
High risk





7.11 Review and Sign-Off

The completed bench sheet should be reviewed by the researcher, the laboratory director, and the QA manager
The Lab Director or QA Manager must sign the lab notebook to verify that the results are accurate



7.12 Expected Results for Control Organisms



Organism
Expected Result




Escherichia coli
Yellow wells, fluorescence


Klebsiella pneumoniae
Yellow wells, no fluorescence


Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Clear wells, no fluorescence


Method blank

title: IDEXX Quanti-Tray 2000 for E. coli/Total Coliform Enumeration
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 QA/QC for Each New Lot
For initial analyst demonstration of capability and for each new lot of Quanti-Tray 2000, perform the following checks:

Reagent lot check: Shine the UV lamp on the Colilert media snap packs. If the unopened lot is fluorescent, discard it.
Blank control: Dissolve one packet of Colilert media in 100 mL of distilled water. Check for fluorescence. The blank must show no fluorescence.
Positive control: Dissolve one packet of Colilert media and 1–2 Control Culture vials (stored in freezer) in 100 mL of distilled water. Incubate for 18 hours. Confirm fluorescence.
Reagent water blank: Analyze a sterile reagent water blank with each batch of samples to verify a negative result after 18–22 hours.
Sterile bottle check: Gravimetrically check each new lot of sterile bottles to confirm they are transparent and non-fluorescing.



8.2 Precision
Calculate precision for duplicate analyses using relative percent difference (RPD):
\[
\text{RPD} = \frac{(A - B) \times 100}{(A + B) / 2}
\]
where \(A\) = MPN from aliquot A and \(B\) = MPN from aliquot B.


8.3 Acceptance Criteria

Desired precision: +/- 20% RPD
Desired detection limit: 1 MPN/100 mL
If a precision value exceeds 20%, record in the comments section of the bench sheet: “These data are associated with an out-of-control duplicate analysis. The UCL = 20%.”
If a blank value exceeds 1 MPN/100 mL, record in the comments section: “These data are associated with a blank value that exceeds the detection limit of 1 MPN/100 mL.”
Samples cannot be reanalyzed because the sample volume is depleted after the initial analysis
If data are unacceptable for any reason, the analyst should review their technique before conducting this analysis again

title: Alkalinity – Titration Method
text:
4 Definitions

Acid-neutralizing capacity (ANC): The capacity of a water to neutralize strong acid; for most natural waters, ANC is approximately equal to total alkalinity.
Alkalinity: The capacity of water to resist acidification, expressed in mg/L as CaCO3; in natural waters, primarily contributed by bicarbonate (HCO3-), carbonate (CO32-), and hydroxide (OH-).
Bicarbonate alkalinity: Alkalinity attributable to HCO3-; the dominant form in most fresh waters at pH 6.3–10.3.
Endpoint pH: The pH at which the titration is stopped to correspond to the equivalence point of the reaction between the alkalinity species and the standard acid; 4.5 for routine total alkalinity, 8.3 for phenolphthalein (P) alkalinity.
Normality (N): The number of gram-equivalents of a substance per liter of solution; for H2SO4 used in alkalinity titrations, 1 N = 0.5 M because each H2SO4 donates 2 protons.
Phenolphthalein alkalinity (P alkalinity): Alkalinity measured to the pH 8.3 endpoint; represents OH- and half of CO32- content; zero if the sample pH is initially below 8.3.
Potentiometric titration: Titration in which the endpoint is determined by monitoring electrode potential (pH) rather than by a color indicator.
Standardization: The process of determining the exact concentration of a titrant by titrating a primary standard of known purity and mass (e.g., anhydrous Na2CO3).
Total alkalinity (T alkalinity): Alkalinity measured to the pH 4.3–4.5 endpoint; represents the sum of all alkalinity species.

title: Alkalinity – Titration Method
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Standardizing the 0.1 N H2SO4

Dry 3–5 g of primary standard Na2CO3 at 250 C for 4 hours and cool in a desiccator
Weigh 2.500 +/- 0.200 g (to the nearest 0.001 g) into a 1 L volumetric flask. Dissolve in DI water and bring to volume. This produces an approximately 0.05 N Na2CO3 solution.
Pipette 40.00 mL of the Na2CO3 solution into a 250 mL beaker. Add approximately 60 mL of DI water.
Titrate potentiometrically with the approximately 0.1 N H2SO4 to a pH of about 5
Remove the electrodes, rinse into the beaker, and gently boil the solution for 3–5 minutes under a watch glass to expel CO2
Cool to room temperature, rinse the watch glass into the beaker, and continue titrating to the pH inflection point
Calculate the normality of the acid:

\[N_{\text{acid}} = \frac{A \times B}{53.00 \times C}\]
where \(A\) = g Na2CO3 weighed into the 1 L flask, \(B\) = mL Na2CO3 solution taken for titration, and \(C\) = mL acid used.

Adjust to 0.1000 N or use the measured normality in all subsequent calculations. At 0.1000 N, 1.00 mL = 5.00 mg CaCO3.



7.2 Preparing the 0.02 N H2SO4 Working Titrant

Dilute 200.00 mL of standardized 0.1000 N H2SO4 to 1000 mL with DI water in a volumetric flask
Mix thoroughly
Verify the normality by titrating 15.00 mL of 0.05 N Na2CO3 as described in Section 6.1
At 0.02 N, 1.00 mL = 1.00 mg CaCO3
Store in a tightly capped borosilicate glass or polyethylene bottle. Do not keep for longer than 1 week without re-standardization.



7.3 Sample Collection and Handling

Collect samples in polyethylene or borosilicate glass bottles per SOP-F300
Fill sample bottles completely with no headspace; CO2 exchange with air will alter the alkalinity
Analyze samples as soon as possible after collection, ideally within 24 hours. Refrigerate at 4 C if analysis must be delayed.
Do not filter, dilute, concentrate, or otherwise alter the sample before titration



7.4 Selecting Sample Size and Titrant
Choose the sample volume and titrant normality to use a reasonable volume of titrant (ideally 20 mL or more from a 50 mL buret) for good volumetric precision:








Expected Alkalinity (mg/L as CaCO3)
Sample Volume
Titrant Normality

If the expected alkalinity is unknown, perform a preliminary titration with indicator to estimate the range before running the potentiometric titration.


7.5 pH Meter Calibration
Calibrate the pH meter with a three-point calibration (pH 4.01, 7.00, 10.01) per SOP-L300 before each titration session. Verify that the calibration slope is between 90% and 102% of theoretical.


7.6 Potentiometric Titration

Measure the selected sample volume (e.g., 100 mL) into a clean beaker using a graduated cylinder
Place the beaker on the magnetic stir plate and add a clean stir bar. Set the stirrer to a speed that produces a gentle vortex without splashing or entraining air.
Immerse the pH electrode in the sample. Record the initial pH.
Fill the buret with standardized H2SO4 (0.02 N or 0.1 N as selected in Section 6.4). Record the initial buret reading.
Phenolphthalein alkalinity (P): If the initial pH is above 8.3, titrate to pH 8.3, recording the volume of acid used. This is the P alkalinity endpoint.
Total alkalinity (T): Continue titrating to the total alkalinity endpoint. Select the endpoint pH from the table below based on the expected alkalinity concentration:




Total Alkalinity (mg/L as CaCO3)
Endpoint pH




Approximately 30

4.6

4.5




As the endpoint is approached, add acid in smaller increments (0.1–0.2 mL) and allow pH equilibrium to be reached before adding more titrant
Record the final buret reading







TipTip



For best results, record the pH after each addition of acid and construct a full titration curve. The inflection point (steepest slope) on the curve confirms the endpoint pH. This is especially important for samples with unusual chemistry (e.g., high phosphate or silicate content) where the standard endpoint pH may not correspond to the true equivalence point.




7.7 Low-Alkalinity Method (Below 20 mg/L as CaCO3)
For samples with alkalinity below 20 mg/L, use a 200 mL sample volume and titrate with 0.02 N H2SO4 from a 10 mL microburet. Record intermediate pH values to construct a titration curve and determine the endpoint from the inflection point. Report only low-alkalinity values determined by this method.

8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Calculations
Total alkalinity (mg/L as CaCO3):
\[\text{Alkalinity} = \frac{A \times N \times 50{,}000}{V}\]
where \(A\) = mL of standard acid used, \(N\) = normality of the acid, and \(V\) = mL of sample.
Phenolphthalein alkalinity uses the same formula but substitutes the volume of acid titrated to pH 8.3.


8.2 Alkalinity Species

8.3 QC Requirements

Standardize titrant before each batch and at least weekly
Run a DI water blank at the start of each session; the blank should consume less than 0.2 mL of 0.02 N acid
Prepare and titrate a laboratory fortified blank (LFB) using a known concentration of Na2CO3 at least once per batch of 20 samples. Recovery should be 90–110%.
Run duplicate titrations on at least 10% of samples. Acceptable precision: +/- 5% relative percent difference for samples above 20 mg/L as CaCO3.
Record all QC results in the laboratory notebook

title: Dissecting and Compound Microscope
text:
This procedure describes the operation, image capture, and routine care of the dissecting (stereo) microscopes and compound light microscopes used in the EA Program laboratory. Dissecting microscopes provide low-to-moderate magnification (typically 7–45x) with a wide working distance and are used for sorting biological specimens, gross morphology, and sample preparation. Compound microscopes provide higher magnification (40–1000x) with transmitted illumination and are used for slide-mounted specimens requiring cellular or subcellular resolution (Murphy & Davidson, 2012).
For the Echo Labs Revolve hybrid microscope (which combines upright compound and inverted configurations with an iPad display), see SOP-L211 Revolve Microscope. The Revolve has specialized procedures that differ from the conventional microscopes described here.
