title: Dissecting and Compound Microscope
text:
4 Definitions

Brightfield microscopy: Transmitted-light microscopy in which the specimen is illuminated from below and appears against a bright background; the standard mode for stained biological specimens.
Compound microscope: A microscope with two or more lens systems (objective and eyepiece) that produce a magnified image; used for cells, microorganisms, and fine structural detail at total magnifications of 40x–1,000x.
Condenser: A lens assembly below the stage that focuses and concentrates the illumination light onto the specimen; its numerical aperture and position strongly affect image contrast and resolution.
Dissecting microscope (stereo microscope): A low-magnification (typically 7x–45x) binocular microscope that provides a three-dimensional image of intact specimens; used for macroinvertebrate sorting, plant tissue examination, and dissection.
Immersion oil: A synthetic or natural oil with a refractive index matching glass (~1.515); applied between the 100x objective and the coverslip to eliminate the air-glass interface and maximize numerical aperture.
Iris diaphragm (condenser diaphragm): An adjustable aperture in the condenser that controls the cone of illumination; reducing the diaphragm increases contrast but reduces resolution.
Parfocal: The property of a set of objectives that allows switching between magnifications with only minor focus adjustment; standard on modern compound microscopes.
Working distance: The distance between the front lens of the objective and the specimen surface when in focus; decreases with increasing magnification; limits the thickness of specimens that can be accommodated.

title: Dissecting and Compound Microscope
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Optical: Prolonged viewing through the eyepieces can cause eye strain. Take breaks during extended sorting or identification sessions. Adjust the diopter rings to match your vision before starting work.
Electrical: Keep liquids away from the illumination base and power supply. If liquid enters the base, disconnect power immediately and notify the lab manager.
Physical: Compound microscope objectives (especially 40x and 100x) can contact and crack the slide or cover slip if the stage is raised too quickly. Always use the coarse focus knob with caution when changing objectives.
Chemical/Biological: Specimens may be preserved in ethanol, formalin, or other fixatives. Wear appropriate PPE and handle preserved material in a well-ventilated area.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses (when not viewing through eyepieces)
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves (when handling preserved specimens, stains, or immersion oil)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For chemical spills (e.g., ethanol, formalin) on or near a microscope, clean the spill per SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety and SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling. If liquid enters the microscope body, unplug power and contact the lab manager before attempting further use.

7.2 Dissecting Microscope: Setup and Use

Plug in the microscope and turn on the illumination using the switch on the base. Most units have both incident (top) and transmitted (bottom) light sources. Select the mode appropriate for the specimen:

Incident light: opaque specimens (insects, soil, rocks)
Transmitted light: translucent specimens (small organisms in water, thin sections)
Both: general sorting when mixed materials are present

Adjust the zoom to the lowest magnification (widest field of view) to locate the area of interest
Place the specimen on the stage plate. Use a white plate for dark specimens and a black plate for light or translucent specimens to improve contrast.
Adjust the interpupillary distance by sliding the eyepiece tubes until you see a single merged circle of light
Focus using the focus knob (single knob on most stereo scopes). With both eyes open, adjust the diopter ring on one eyepiece until the image is sharp in both eyes simultaneously.
Increase magnification by turning the zoom dial. Refine focus as needed.
When finished, return the zoom to the lowest setting, remove the specimen, turn off the illumination, and unplug the unit if lab policy requires it



7.3 Compound Microscope: Setup and Use

Plug in the microscope and turn on the light source using the power switch. Adjust the intensity to a comfortable level.
Rotate the nosepiece to the lowest-magnification objective (4x)
Place the prepared slide on the stage, securing it with the stage clips. Center the specimen over the condenser aperture.
Using the coarse focus knob, raise the stage until the specimen comes into approximate focus. Watch from the side to avoid driving the slide into the objective.
Sharpen the image with the fine focus knob
Adjust the condenser height and the iris diaphragm to optimize contrast and resolution. For most work, the condenser should be nearly fully raised (close to the slide) and the diaphragm partially closed to improve contrast without sacrificing too much resolution (Murphy & Davidson, 2012).
Increase magnification by rotating the nosepiece to the next objective (10x, then 40x). Refocus with the fine focus knob only.







ImportantAvoid Slide Damage



When switching from the 10x to the 40x objective, watch from the side to confirm that the longer 40x lens does not contact the cover slip. If the working distance is too short, lower the stage slightly before rotating the objective into position.




7.4 Using Oil Immersion (100x Objective)

Focus the specimen at 40x first
Rotate the nosepiece to an empty position (no objective in the light path)
Place a single small drop of immersion oil directly on the cover slip at the point of illumination. Do not use excess oil.
Rotate the 100x objective into position. The front element of the lens should contact the oil without trapping an air bubble.
Focus carefully using the fine focus knob only
After use, immediately clean the 100x objective with lens cleaning solution and lint-free tissue. Wipe gently from center to edge. Never allow oil to dry on the lens.
Clean the slide or dispose of it as appropriate



7.5 Capturing Images (Camera-Equipped Units)

Focus the specimen and center the region of interest in the field of view
Open the camera software on the connected computer (software varies by camera model; consult the lab manager for the current setup)
Adjust exposure and white balance in the software to match the illumination
Capture the image. Record the magnification, scale bar, and sample ID in the file name or metadata.
Use a consistent file-naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_SampleID_Magnification_Mode.jpg
Export images to the project data folder



7.6 Shutdown and Daily Maintenance

Remove the specimen from the stage
Rotate the nosepiece to the lowest-magnification objective (4x on compound; lowest zoom on dissecting)
If oil immersion was used, clean the 100x objective immediately (see Section 6.4, step 6)
Wipe any residue from the stage with a lint-free tissue
Turn off the light source and unplug if required by lab policy
Cover the microscope with a dust cover

title: Dissecting and Compound Microscope
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Optics Cleaning
If specks or smudges appear in the field of view that do not move when the specimen is translated, the optics need cleaning:

Start with a few short bursts of compressed gas duster to remove loose dust from the objectives and oculars. Do not invert the can.
For objective lens surfaces, apply a small amount of lens cleaning solution to a piece of lint-free optical tissue and gently wipe in a circular motion from center to edge. Do not use dry tissue on coated optics.
Clean the oculars (eyepieces) the same way. Fingerprints on the eye lens are the most common source of image degradation.
For persistent contamination on internal optics, contact the lab manager. Do not disassemble the microscope.



8.2 Illumination Check

Replace burned-out bulbs promptly. LED-equipped units should not require bulb replacement during normal use.
If transmitted light appears uneven, check that the condenser is properly centered and the iris diaphragm is functioning.



8.3 Image Quality Checklist
Before accepting a micrograph for publication or analysis, verify:

Focus is sharp across the region of interest
Illumination is even (no hot spots or vignetting)
A scale bar or magnification is recorded
The specimen is oriented consistently with project conventions

title: QX200 Droplet Digital PCR System: Instrument Familiarization and Standard Operation
text:
This procedure orients new personnel to the Bio-Rad QX200 Droplet Digital PCR (ddPCR) system and describes its safe, standard operation: the components of the system, the consumables and reagents, the four-stage workflow (droplet generation, plate sealing, thermal cycling, and droplet reading), basic use of QuantaSoft software, routine maintenance, and common troubleshooting.
It is a familiarization and operation SOP. It does not cover the science of assay or primer design (see SOP-L701) or the analysis and interpretation of results (see SOP-L702 Applications Guide). The workflow described here follows Bio-Rad’s published guidance for the platform (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2018, 2024), which itself implements the droplet-counting principle of absolute quantification (Hindson et al., 2011).

2 Scope

Applies to: Operation of the QX200 ddPCR system in the lab, comprising the QX200 Droplet Generator, the PX1 PCR Plate Sealer, the C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler with 96-deep-well reaction module, and the QX200 Droplet Reader, together with QuantaSoft software.
Does not apply to: Assay/primer design (SOP-L701), data analysis and interpretation (SOP-L702), or DNA extraction (SOP-L700).
Prerequisite: A prepared, validated reaction mix and plate plan from SOP-L701.







NoteSOP numbering



This instrument SOP is numbered L214, placing it ahead of the L700-series analysis SOPs in the lab scheme. Conceptually it precedes analysis: complete this familiarization before running samples for SOP-L702.

title: QX200 Droplet Digital PCR System: Instrument Familiarization and Standard Operation
text:
4 Definitions

Amplitude: The fluorescence signal intensity of a droplet; positive droplets (containing target DNA) have high amplitude; negative droplets have low amplitude; a clear separation between positive and negative populations is required for accurate quantification.
Droplet digital PCR (ddPCR): A method of absolute quantification of nucleic acids in which the sample is partitioned into ~20,000 nanoliter-sized water-in-oil droplets, each containing zero or one target molecule; after PCR amplification, the fraction of fluorescent positive droplets is used to calculate target concentration using Poisson statistics.
FAM: A green fluorescent dye (fluorescein amidite) used to label one probe or primer in a duplex ddPCR assay; detected in the FAM channel (channel 1) by the QX200.
HEX: A yellow-orange fluorescent dye used to label a second probe in a duplex ddPCR assay, or as an alternative to VIC; detected in channel 2 by the QX200.
Poisson correction: A statistical adjustment applied by the DropletQuant software to account for the probability that some droplets contain more than one target molecule; necessary when target concentrations are high.
Copies per microliter (copies/µL): The absolute concentration of the target DNA in the final ddPCR reaction, as reported by DropletQuant; must be back-calculated to the original sample concentration using the appropriate dilution factor.
Threshold: The fluorescence amplitude boundary separating positive from negative droplets; set manually or automatically in the analysis software; incorrect threshold setting is the most common source of ddPCR quantification error.

title: QX200 Droplet Digital PCR System: Instrument Familiarization and Standard Operation
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards and precautions




Droplet generation oil and reader oil. Use the oil specified for the chemistry (probe vs. EvaGreen). Avoid skin and eye contact; wear gloves and eye protection; consult the SDS for each oil. Clean spills promptly.
Reagents. ddPCR supermixes and any sample DNA are handled with gloves. Environmental soil DNA is low biohazard risk, but treat all extracts with standard lab precautions.
Moving parts. The droplet reader autosampler moves during a run. Keep hands clear and the lid closed while running.
Electrical and thermal. Standard bench-instrument electrical safety. The thermal cycler block reaches high temperatures; do not touch the block during or immediately after a run.
Sharps / glass. None in normal operation; cartridges and plates are single-use plastics.









ImportantConsumables are not interchangeable



ddPCR requires Bio-Rad’s proprietary droplet-generation reagents, cartridges, and gaskets. Substituting non-specified consumables will produce unusable droplets (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2018). Match the oil to the supermix chemistry.

title: QX200 Droplet Digital PCR System: Instrument Familiarization and Standard Operation
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 System Overview
The QX200 system performs absolute quantification by partitioning, amplifying, and counting (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2018; Hindson et al., 2011). A single 20 uL reaction is split into roughly 20,000 uniform water-in-oil droplets. Each droplet is a tiny independent PCR. After endpoint amplification, the reader passes droplets one at a time through a two-color optical detector (channel 1 for FAM, channel 2 for HEX or VIC), scoring each droplet as positive or negative. QuantaSoft fits the positive fraction to a Poisson model to return target concentration in copies per microliter.
The work proceeds through four instruments in sequence:

Droplet Generator (Section 6.4) makes the droplets.
PX1 Plate Sealer (Section 6.5) seals them into a plate.
C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler (Section 6.6) amplifies.
Droplet Reader (Section 6.7) counts.



7.2 Daily Startup

Power on the instrument computer and the instruments to be used.
Launch QuantaSoft and confirm it connects to the droplet generator and/or reader.
Check oil levels in the droplet generator and the reader; top up or replace bottles per the manual (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).
Empty the reader’s waste bottle if near full.
Confirm consumable stock for the planned run (cartridges, gaskets, oil, plate, foil).



7.3 Consumables Orientation
Before the first run, identify each consumable and where it loads:

DG8 cartridge seats in the cartridge holder. The middle row of wells receives sample; the bottom row receives generation oil; the top row collects the generated droplets.
Gasket snaps over the loaded cartridge to seal it for generation.
Generation oil is chemistry-specific. Using probe oil with EvaGreen supermix (or vice versa) will fail.
Pierceable foil is the only seal type compatible with the reader’s autosampler; do not use hard-seal films.



7.4 Droplet Generation

Prepare reactions per SOP-L701 and load into the cartridge holder with a DG8 cartridge.
Pipette each sample into the sample wells (avoid bubbles; pipette to the first stop).
Pipette the matched generation oil into the oil wells.
Place the gasket over the cartridge.
Load the holder into the QX200 Droplet Generator and close the lid; the run takes about two minutes per cartridge.
After generation, slowly transfer the droplets from the top row of the cartridge to the corresponding wells of a ddPCR 96-well plate using a multichannel pipette. Pipette gently and at an angle; droplets are fragile and shearing them lowers the usable count.







Warning



Damaged or sheared droplets reduce accepted-droplet counts and can fail the QC threshold (see SOP-L702, Section 6.2). Pipette droplets slowly and avoid introducing air.




7.5 Plate Sealing (PX1)

Place the plate and a sheet of pierceable foil in the PX1 Plate Sealer.
Seal at the manufacturer-specified temperature and time (commonly 180 C for 5 s; confirm against the current manual (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024)).
Inspect the seal: the foil should be uniformly bonded with no lifted edges.



7.6 PCR Amplification

Transfer the sealed plate to the C1000 Touch with the 96-deep-well module.
Run the validated cycling program for the assay (from SOP-L701).
Set the ramp rate to about 2 C/s. This slower ramp is important for even amplification across the droplet population on this platform (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2018).
Include a final hold and store at 4 C if not reading immediately; read within the window specified for the chemistry.

A generic template program is given in Appendix B; the assay-specific anneal temperature and cycle number come from SOP-L701.


7.7 Droplet Reading

Place the amplified, sealed plate in the QX200 Droplet Reader plate holder with the retaining clamp.
In QuantaSoft, set up the plate layout: sample names, assay/target names, fluorophores (FAM, HEX/VIC), experiment type (e.g., absolute quantification), and supermix/chemistry.
Start the run. The autosampler aspirates droplets well by well and the detector reads two channels per droplet.
Do not open the reader or disturb the plate while running.



7.8 QuantaSoft Orientation (Reading the Output)
This is orientation only; thresholding decisions and full analysis are covered in SOP-L702.

1-D plot: fluorescence amplitude vs. droplet (event) number for one channel. Positive droplets sit above the threshold line; negatives below.
2-D plot: channel 1 (FAM) vs. channel 2 (HEX/VIC) amplitude. In a duplex assay, droplets fall into four clusters: double-negative, FAM-only, HEX-only, and double-positive (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2018).
Thresholding: the boundary between positive and negative clusters. Review it for every well; adjust manually in QuantaSoft Analysis Pro where the automatic call is poor.
Well merging: replicate wells of the same sample/target may be merged to increase the effective partition count before concentration is calculated.
Concentration: QuantaSoft reports copies per microliter from the Poisson fit. Export as described in SOP-L702, Section 6.1.



7.9 Shutdown

Close the experiment and export/back up data (SOP-L702).
Remove and discard the plate and used cartridges/gaskets (Section 8).
Check and, if needed, empty the reader waste bottle.
Power down per the manual; leave the system in the state your lab specifies for the reader oil lines.



7.10 Maintenance and Care

Each session: check oil levels and the waste bottle; inspect for leaks.
Routine: keep the reader’s fluidics maintained per the manual; do not let oil bottles run dry mid-run.
Do not: force cartridges or gaskets, reuse single-use consumables, mix oil chemistries, or use non-pierceable seals.
Records: log each run (date, operator, assay, plate, instrument notes) and any maintenance or service in the instrument logbook.



7.11 Troubleshooting








Symptom
Likely cause
Action




Low accepted-droplet count
Sheared droplets; pipetting too fast; bubbles
Pipette droplets slowly at an angle; avoid air; re-generate


Few or no droplets generated
Wrong/insufficient oil; cartridge/gasket seated poorly
Use matched oil; reseat cartridge and gasket


“Rain” (droplets between clusters)
Suboptimal anneal temperature; degraded sample
Optimize anneal (SOP-L701); check DNA quality (SOP-L700)


Reader error / clog
Low oil; debris; fluidics issue
Check oil and waste; run reader maintenance; see manual


High NTC positives
Contamination
Rerun with fresh reagents; review setup (SOP-L702, Section 6.2)

title: QX200 Droplet Digital PCR System: Instrument Familiarization and Standard Operation
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Each well should yield at least 10,000 accepted droplets (target ~12,000 to 20,000); wells below 10,000 are excluded in analysis (SOP-L702).
Run the controls defined in SOP-L702 (NTC, extraction blank, positive control) on every plate.
Confirm uniform plate sealing and correct plate orientation before reading.
Log instrument run metadata to support digital-PCR reporting standards (The dMIQE Group & Huggett, 2020).

title: QX200 Droplet Digital PCR System: Instrument Familiarization and Standard Operation
text:
9 Waste Disposal

Used DG8 cartridges, gaskets, plates, foil, and tips: dispose as standard laboratory plastic/biohazard waste per the lab’s waste plan.
Generation and reader oil and oily waste: collect and dispose per the SDS and the lab’s chemical-waste procedures; do not pour oil down the drain.
Reagent containers: rinse and dispose per local guidance.

text: This procedure describes the operation, calibration, and maintenance of the Invitrogen Qubit 4 Fluorometer. title: Qubit 4 Fluorometer
text:
4 Definitions

Broad Range (BR) assay: A Qubit assay kit designed for DNA concentrations of 2–1,000 ng/µL; less sensitive than the HS assay but covers a wider dynamic range; used when high DNA yield is expected.
dsDNA: Double-stranded DNA; the form quantified by most Qubit DNA assay kits; the fluorescent dye binds specifically to dsDNA, not to ssDNA, RNA, or protein contaminants.
Fluorophore: A fluorescent chemical compound that absorbs light at a specific excitation wavelength and emits light at a longer emission wavelength; the Qubit dye is a fluorophore that binds selectively to dsDNA, ssDNA, or RNA depending on the kit.
High Sensitivity (HS) assay: A Qubit assay kit designed for DNA concentrations of 0.2–100 ng/µL; more sensitive than BR; preferred for low-yield environmental DNA extractions from soil or water.
Qubit assay tube: A thin-walled 0.5 mL PCR tube in which the working solution and sample are mixed for measurement; must be free of fluorescent contaminants; do not substitute with other tube types.
Working solution: A freshly prepared mixture of Qubit reagent diluted in buffer at a ratio specified by the kit (usually 1:200); prepared fresh for each session; stable for up to 3 hours at room temperature.

text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Selecting the Assay
Choose the assay based on expected concentration (Invitrogen, 2019):








Assay
Detection Range
When to Use




dsDNA BR
2–1,000 ng
Most soil/sediment extractions


dsDNA HS
0.2–100 ng
Low-yield samples (e.g., water filters, dilute extracts)


RNA BR / HS
See kit documentation
RNA quantification


Protein
See kit documentation
Protein quantification





7.2 Preparing the Working Solution

Calculate the volume of working solution needed: 200 uL per assay tube (all samples plus 2 standards)
Dilute the Qubit reagent concentrate 1:200 in Qubit buffer. For example, for 10 tubes: 10 uL reagent + 1,990 uL buffer = 2,000 uL total.
Vortex briefly to mix







Important



Prepare the working solution fresh for each session. Do not store diluted working solution.




7.3 Preparing Standards

Label two Qubit assay tubes: Std 1 and Std 2
Add 190 uL of working solution to each tube
Add 10 uL of Standard 1 to the first tube and 10 uL of Standard 2 to the second tube
Vortex each tube briefly (2–3 seconds)



7.4 Preparing Samples

Label one Qubit assay tube per sample
Add 198 uL of working solution to each tube
Add 2 uL of sample (DNA extract, RNA, or protein solution) to the corresponding tube
Vortex each tube briefly (2–3 seconds)







Tip



The sample volume can range from 1–20 uL as long as the total volume in each tube equals 200 uL (adjust the working solution volume accordingly). Using 2 uL of sample minimizes consumption of precious extracts.




7.5 Incubation

Incubate all tubes (standards and samples) at room temperature for 2 minutes (Invitrogen, 2019)
Do not incubate for longer than 30 minutes; fluorescence signal decays over time



7.6 Calibration

On the Qubit home screen, select the appropriate assay (e.g., dsDNA Broad Range)
Tap Read Standards
Insert the Std 1 tube, close the lid, and tap Read
When prompted, insert the Std 2 tube, close the lid, and tap Read
Verify that the calibration is accepted (green checkmark). If it fails, prepare fresh standards and repeat.



7.7 Reading Samples

Tap Run Samples
Set the sample volume to match the volume of sample added (e.g., 2 uL)
Set the output units (ng/uL is standard for DNA extracts)
Insert the sample tube, close the lid, and tap Read
Record the concentration (ng/uL, corrected for dilution by the instrument)
Repeat for all samples



7.8 Data Export

Export results via USB or Wi-Fi to the designated project folder
Use a consistent file-naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_Qubit_ProjectName.csv
Record results in the lab notebook and/or project data sheet



7.9 Shutdown and Daily Maintenance

Remove all tubes from the instrument
Wipe the sample chamber with a lint-free tissue if any liquid was spilled
Close the lid
Dispose of used assay tubes (see Section 8)

title: Qubit 4 Fluorometer
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Run fresh standards at the beginning of each session; do not rely on a previous calibration
Standards must be within the acceptable range indicated by the instrument (green checkmark)
If a sample reads “Out of Range,” re-prepare it using the other assay sensitivity (e.g., switch from BR to HS for low-concentration samples)
Acceptable DNA yield from 0.25 g of soil: typically 1–20 ng/uL in a 100 uL elution, depending on soil type
If the NanoDrop and Qubit concentrations disagree by more than a factor of two, the NanoDrop reading is likely inflated by contaminants; trust the Qubit value for downstream planning

TBD – establish a periodic performance check using Qubit DNA standards of known concentration.

title: Echo Labs Revolve Microscope
text: This procedure describes the operation, image capture, and maintenance of the Echo Labs Revolve microscope. The Revolve is a hybrid instrument that combines an upright microscope (for prepared glass slides) and an inverted microscope (for live samples in dishes) in a single rotating platform, with an iPad retina display replacing the traditional eyepiece (Echo Labs, 2016; Murphy & Davidson, 2012). The microscope supports bright field, phase contrast, fluorescence, and dark field imaging modes. It represents a substantial investment by the EA Program and requires careful handling.

title: Echo Labs Revolve Microscope
text:
4 Definitions

Brightfield illumination: Standard transmitted-light microscopy in which the sample is illuminated from below and absorbing or scattering structures appear dark against a bright background; the most common mode for stained biological specimens.
Darkfield illumination: A transmitted-light mode in which the direct beam is blocked; only obliquely scattered light reaches the objective, making unstained transparent structures appear bright against a dark background.
Epifluorescence: A fluorescence microscopy mode in which excitation light is directed through the objective onto the sample, and the emitted fluorescence is collected back through the same objective; enables fluorescent stain visualization.
Eyepiece (ocular): The lens assembly through which the observer views the magnified image; typically 10x; total magnification equals eyepiece magnification times objective magnification.
Fluorescence filter cube: An interchangeable optical block containing an excitation filter, dichroic mirror, and emission filter matched to a specific fluorophore (e.g., DAPI, FITC, TRITC).
Numerical aperture (NA): A dimensionless number characterizing the angular range of light an objective can accept; higher NA provides better resolution and light-gathering; the resolving power is approximately \(d = 0.61\lambda / NA\).
Objective: The primary lens closest to the specimen; available in magnifications of 4x, 10x, 20x, 40x, and 100x (oil immersion); higher magnification objectives have shorter working distances.
Working distance: The distance between the front lens of the objective and the coverslip when the specimen is in focus; decreases with increasing magnification; critical for thick samples.

title: Echo Labs Revolve Microscope
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Optical: The fluorescence LED produces intense illumination. Avoid looking directly into the excitation light source. The iPad display eliminates the need to view through an eyepiece, reducing direct optical exposure, but reflected excitation light can still cause eye strain.
Electrical: Keep liquids away from the iPad and the microscope base. If immersion oil or sample fluid contacts the electronics, disconnect power immediately and notify the lab manager.
Physical: The microscope is heavy. Use both hands when rotating the platform between upright and inverted modes. Objective lenses and condensers are precision optics; handle with care.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses (especially during fluorescence mode)
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves (when handling biological specimens or immersion oil)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
If a biological spill occurs on or near the microscope, clean and disinfect per SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety. If immersion oil contacts the iPad or electronics, power off immediately and contact the lab manager before attempting cleanup.

title: Echo Labs Revolve Microscope
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Microscopy Modes Overview
The Revolve supports four imaging modes. Select the mode appropriate for the specimen and analysis:








Mode
Best For
Staining Required?




Bright field
Stained specimens, gross morphology
Recommended


Phase contrast
Unstained transparent specimens, live cells
No


Fluorescence
Specimens with fluorescent labels or autofluorescent pigments (e.g., cyanobacteria)
Fluorophore-dependent


Dark field
Fine structures, edges, unstained specimens
No





7.2 Starting the Microscope

Press the power button on the top left corner of the iPad (Echo Labs, 2016).
Swipe to unlock. The overhead microscope light should turn on and a live image should appear on the screen.
If the light does not turn on or no image appears, open the Echo Labs app from the home screen
If the screen reads “Light Off,” tap BF at the top of the screen to enable bright field illumination
Load the prepared slide into the stage clips (upright mode) or place the culture dish on the stage (inverted mode)



7.3 Rotating Between Upright and Inverted Mode






Important



This is the most mechanically delicate operation on the Revolve. Follow each step carefully to avoid damaging the objectives or condenser.



Rotate the nosepiece to move all objective lenses out of the optical path
Unscrew the stage and carefully lift it away from the microscope body without contacting the condenser
Push the iPad flat so it is out of the rotation path
Press the release button on the upper back of the microscope body
Rotate the microscope body 180 degrees counterclockwise until it clicks into place
Reinstall the stage and tighten the mounting knob until secure
Rotate the desired objective lens back into position and realign the iPad



7.4 Using Bright Field Mode

Confirm that BF is selected on the screen
Place the slide or specimen on the stage
Start with the lowest magnification objective (4x) to locate the region of interest
Use the outer coarse focus knob (to the right of the iPad) to bring the specimen into approximate focus, then use the inner fine focus knob to sharpen the image
Use the stage translation knobs to move the slide: the lower knob moves the stage left/right, the upper knob moves it toward/away from you
Increase magnification by rotating the nosepiece to the next objective (10x, 40x)
Adjust brightness, contrast, and color balance using the sliding controls on the bottom right of the screen. Adjust the physical light intensity using the flat knob on the bottom right of the microscope body.



7.5 Using Phase Contrast Mode
Phase contrast converts differences in refractive index into differences in brightness, allowing transparent, unstained specimens to be visualized.

Set up the specimen in bright field mode first and bring it into focus
Select the phase contrast ring that matches the current objective:




Objective
Phase Ring




4x
PhL


10x
Ph1


40x
Ph2


100x
Ph3




Tap the PH mode selector on the screen (if available) or manually rotate the condenser turret to the matching phase ring
Fine-tune focus and centering as needed







Note



Phase contrast images may exhibit a bright “halo” around large objects (positive phase contrast) or a dark edge (negative phase contrast). This is a normal optical artifact caused by diffracted light passing through the phase ring. A “shade-off” effect, in which homogeneous regions appear at the same intensity as the background, is also expected.




7.6 Using Fluorescence Mode

Tap FL at the top of the screen to switch to fluorescence mode
The fluorescence LED will illuminate automatically
Place the specimen on the stage and focus using the same procedure as bright field
Minimize illumination time to reduce photobleaching. Locate the region of interest in bright field first, then switch to fluorescence only for image capture.







Warning



Fluorophores lose their ability to fluoresce over time when illuminated (photobleaching). Work quickly, minimize unnecessary excitation, and consider using photoprotective mounting media when possible.




7.7 Using Dark Field Mode
Section TBD. Consult the lab manager for dark field setup procedures until this section is completed.


7.8 Capturing and Exporting Images

To capture an image, tap the white camera shutter button on the left side of the screen
Enable the anti-shake feature (hand icon below the shutter button; it should turn orange when active) to reduce vibration blur
To review captured images, tap the gallery icon (square) at the top left of the screen. Tap Done to return to the live view.
Export images via a flash drive connected to the iPad, AirDrop, or the cloud sharing option in the Echo Labs app
Use a consistent file-naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_SampleID_Objective_Mode.jpg



7.9 Using Oil Immersion (100x Objective)

Focus the specimen at 40x first
Rotate the nosepiece to an empty position (no objective in the light path)
Place a single small drop of immersion oil directly on the cover slip at the point of illumination
Rotate the 100x objective into position. The lens front element should contact the oil without trapping an air bubble.
Focus carefully using the fine focus knob only
After use, immediately clean the 100x objective with lens cleaning solution and lint-free tissue. Never allow oil to dry on the lens.
Clean the slide or dispose of it as appropriate



7.10 Replacing the Condenser
The Revolve has two condensers: one for low magnification (4x through 60x) and one for 100x oil immersion. Condenser swaps require care to avoid contaminating or scratching the optics. Consult the lab manager before performing this procedure for the first time.
Detailed replacement steps TBD; to be documented with the lab manager.


7.11 Shutdown and Daily Maintenance

Remove the specimen from the stage
Rotate the nosepiece to the lowest-magnification objective (4x) or to an empty position
If oil immersion was used, clean the 100x objective immediately
Wipe any sample residue or oil from the stage with a Kimwipe dampened with lens cleaning solution
Close the Echo Labs app on the iPad
Press and hold the power button to turn off the iPad
Cover the microscope with the dust cover

title: Echo Labs Revolve Microscope
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Optics Cleaning
If specks or smudges appear in captured images that do not move when the specimen is translated, the optical path may need cleaning:

Do not attempt to clean internal optics without the lab manager present
For objective lens surfaces, apply a small amount of lens cleaning solution to lint-free tissue and gently wipe in a circular motion from center to edge
For dust on internal surfaces, remove the arm and use short bursts of compressed gas duster. Do not allow the compressed air canister to become cold, as it will deposit a film on the optics.
For persistent contamination, contact Echo Labs support or the lab manager



8.2 Image Quality Checklist
Before accepting an image for publication or analysis, verify:

Focus is sharp across the region of interest
Illumination is even (no hot spots or vignetting)
Scale bar or magnification metadata is recorded
Anti-shake was enabled during capture
In fluorescence mode, confirm that photobleaching has not significantly degraded the signal

title: X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) Sample Preparation and Analysis
text: This SOP describes the complete workflow for preparing geological rock samples and analyzing their major-element oxide composition by wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence (WD-XRF). The procedure covers sample powdering, flux fusion bead preparation, bead polishing, and instrument operation on the PANalytical XRF spectrometer using the SuperQ software with the “Geology Beads” application (Claisse, 2003; Norrish & Hutton, 1969; PANalytical, 2012).

title: X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) Sample Preparation and Analysis
text: This SOP describes the complete workflow for preparing geological rock samples and analyzing their major-element oxide composition by wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence (WD-XRF). The procedure covers sample powdering, flux fusion bead preparation, bead polishing, and instrument operation on the PANalytical XRF spectrometer using the SuperQ software with the “Geology Beads” application (Claisse, 2003; Norrish & Hutton, 1969; PANalytical, 2012).

title: X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) Sample Preparation and Analysis
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Rock, mineral, and geological samples analyzed as lithium tetraborate fusion beads for major-element oxide determination (e.g., SiO2, Al2O3, Fe2O3, CaO, MgO, Na2O, K2O, TiO2, P2O5, MnO)
Does not apply to: Pressed-pellet trace-element analysis, handheld (portable) XRF measurements, or non-geological materials
Locations: Rock preparation lab (powdering and polishing); analytical lab / wet lab (weighing, fusion); XRF lab (instrument operation)

title: X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) Sample Preparation and Analysis
text:
4 Definitions

Certified reference material (CRM): A geological standard with certified major-element oxide concentrations from an accredited producer (e.g., NIST, USGS, BCR); used to verify XRF accuracy during each analytical session (Norrish & Hutton, 1969).
Detection limit (MDL): The lowest concentration of an element reliably detected above background; varies by element, matrix, and instrument settings; typically 1–50 mg/kg for common elements by WD-XRF.
Flux (dilithium tetraborate, Li2B4O7): A reagent mixed with the rock powder in a 2:1 (flux:sample) ratio; lowers the melting point and produces a homogeneous glass bead that eliminates mineralogical matrix effects during analysis (Claisse, 2003).
Fluorescence (X-ray): The emission of characteristic X-rays from a sample excited by primary X-rays; each element emits at unique energies that identify and quantify it (Norrish & Hutton, 1969).
Fundamental parameters (FP) method: An XRF calibration approach that uses known physical constants to calculate element concentrations from measured fluorescence intensities without matrix-matched standards for every sample type.
Fusion bead: A glass disc produced by melting the powdered rock sample with lithium tetraborate flux at 1000 °C; the homogeneous glass eliminates mineralogical matrix effects (Claisse, 2003).
Geology Beads: The SuperQ application/archive configured for major-element oxide analysis of fusion beads on the PANalytical XRF spectrometer (PANalytical, 2012).
K-alpha and K-beta lines: The most commonly measured characteristic X-ray emission lines for elements; produced when an electron is ejected from the K shell and replaced from the L or M shell, respectively.
Loss on ignition (LOI): The mass percentage lost when a pre-weighed rock powder is heated to 1000 °C; reflects H2O, CO2, and organic matter content; used as a correction in major-element summation (Norrish & Hutton, 1969).
Matrix effects: Absorption and enhancement of X-ray signals by other elements in the sample; minimized by the flux fusion method (Claisse, 2003).
Shatterbox: A vibratory ring-and-puck mill used to grind rock chips to a fine powder suitable for fusion.
SuperQ: The PANalytical software used to control the XRF spectrometer, define measurement sequences, and retrieve results (PANalytical, 2012).
WD-XRF (wavelength-dispersive XRF): An XRF configuration in which characteristic X-rays are separated by a crystal monochromator before detection; provides higher spectral resolution and lower detection limits than energy-dispersive (ED-XRF) systems.
X-ray fluorescence (XRF): A non-destructive elemental analysis technique in which a sample excited by a primary X-ray beam emits characteristic fluorescent X-rays that are measured to determine elemental composition (Norrish & Hutton, 1969).

title: X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) Sample Preparation and Analysis
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




High-temperature furnace: The muffle furnace operates at 1000 °C. Crucibles and tiles removed from the furnace are extremely hot. Do not touch them, even with gloves, until fully cooled.
Compressed air: Loud; wear ear protection when blowing out equipment.
Rock chipper: Flying rock fragments are common. Always wear safety glasses. Never look into the chipper while it is running.
Shatterbox: The unit vibrates intensely and can travel across the floor. Get help repositioning it if needed.
Chemical reagents: Dilithium tetraborate flux is a fine powder; avoid inhalation. Ethanol is flammable.
X-ray radiation: The XRF instrument contains an X-ray source. Follow all posted radiation safety procedures. Do not open the instrument lid while the arm is moving or the flap is up.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses (required in the rock prep lab at all times)
Laboratory coat
Nitrile gloves (powder handling and polishing)
Ear protection (when using the shatterbox or compressed air)
Heat-resistant gloves (when handling crucibles or the tile from the furnace)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Do not work in the lab without letting someone know your plans and estimated return time. Phones and safety showers are in all labs. Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety for all emergency procedures.

title: X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) Sample Preparation and Analysis
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Step 1: Powdering the Sample
A complete fusion batch is 9 samples. If you plan fusions, turn on the furnace first (see §6.3) since it takes about 1 hour to reach 1000 °C.

8.1.1 Chipping

Use the rock chipper to reduce each sample to pieces smaller than approximately 1 cm. Wear safety glasses. Clean the chipper jaws thoroughly between samples with compressed air and an ethanol wipe.
Weigh out approximately 20–30 g of chipped material into a labeled sample bag.



8.1.2 Shatterbox Milling

Place a piece of brown butcher paper under the shatterbox head assembly to catch any spillage.
Wipe all shatterbox bowl components (ring, puck, and bowl) with an ethanol-dampened Kimwipe. Allow to dry completely.
Load the chipped sample into the tungsten carbide bowl. Do not overfill (maximum ~two-thirds full).
Lock the lid and run the shatterbox for 60–90 seconds. Longer milling times reduce particle size further.
Unlock the lid and carefully transfer the powder onto white printer paper, keeping all components on the paper edge so exterior metal surfaces do not contact the sample. Funnel the powder into the labeled container. Use a fresh sheet of paper for every sample.



8.1.3 Cleaning the Shatterbox

If powder is stuck, scrub with a green Brillo pad. If that is insufficient, run a scoop of sand for 15 seconds and discard.
Detail all pieces with compressed air (hold pieces in the airflow; scrub with the Brillo pad). Do not let the metal hose tip touch any bowl surface. Use ear protection.
Finish with an ethanol wipe on a Kimwipe. After the last sample, clean up, recycle paper, replace the bowl, and turn off the shatterbox.




8.2 Step 2: Weighing and Mixing

Bring your powdered samples to the analytical lab. Get an XRF sample sheet from the drawer left of the weigh station, fill out the top portion, and keep it on a wooden tray next to the balance.
Retrieve a small cup of flux from the desiccator.
For each sample:

Label a plastic cup lid with the sample number.
Place the cup (no lid) in the cardboard holder on the balance, close the sliding door, and zero.
Weigh 3.5000 g (±0.0004 g) of sample powder. Record the exact mass. Zero the balance.
Add 7.0000 g (±0.0004 g) of flux (2:1 flux-to-sample ratio) (Claisse, 2003). Record the mass. If you add too much flux, remove the excess but do not return it to the reagent container.
Seal the lid tightly.

Mix each cup on the Vortex mixer for about one minute. If powder clings to the sides, pass the deionizing bar over the cup.



8.3 Step 3: First Fusion

8.3.1 Furnace Startup

Flip the black switch on the front of the furnace.
Press the T1 temperature button and confirm T = 1000 °C.
Set a duration (e.g., 24, 48, or 72 hours). Press Enter and Start. It takes roughly 1 hour to reach 1000 °C.







Caution



Do not spill glass in the furnace or introduce liquids. Do not use this furnace for temperatures below 500 °C – use a regular drying oven instead. Do not shut off the furnace mid-cycle with the power button; let it run out its programmed time and shut off automatically.




8.3.2 Loading Crucibles

Select 9 graphite crucibles from the drawer under the furnace. Clean each inside by gently wiping with a Kimwipe and blowing out with compressed air.
Back at the analytical lab, carefully empty each cup into the corresponding crucible. Maintaining the correct order is critical – once the powder is in the crucible, there is no way to tell samples apart.
Place the empty cups (lids on) in the box labeled “Dirty Cups for Blowing Out.”



8.3.3 Fusing

In the wet lab, place a tile on the brick stand (small hole facing toward you) and crank the stand up until the tile is about halfway up the side of the furnace.
Put on both long heat-resistant gloves. Using the tongs, slide the tile into the furnace. Close the door as quickly as possible.
Wait 20–30 minutes for the furnace to recover to 1000 °C, then leave the samples for 10–15 minutes. Longer fusion times help carbon-rich samples degas fully.


The tile and crucibles are extremely hot when removed from the furnace. Do not touch them, even with gloves, until fully cooled.


Wearing gloves, open the furnace and carefully pull the tile out using the tongs and the tile hole. Move the tile to the hot plate and close the furnace.




8.4 Step 4: Regrinding and Second Fusion

Once the crucibles are cool enough to handle, pour the first-fusion glass back into the shatterbox bowl. Re-grind for 60 seconds.
Return the powder to the crucible and re-fuse at 1000 °C for 15–20 minutes to remove any remaining bubbles and produce a homogeneous bead.
Once cooled, inspect each bead visually. Beads should be clear, bubble-free glass covering the full crucible bottom. If a bead has a dark carbon pellet at the bottom, fuse for an additional 15 minutes.



8.5 Step 5: Polishing the Bead
Polish the flat (analytical) surface of each bead on the 4-stage grinding/polishing laps to remove surface scratches and contamination that would scatter X-rays.

Use the coarsest lap first (e.g., 600 grit SiC), working through progressively finer stages.
After each stage, clean the bead in the ultrasonic cleaner with distilled water (3 minutes).
After the final lap, inspect the flat surface under the lab light; it must be mirror-smooth with no visible scratches.
Label each bead on the curved (non-analytical) side using a diamond-tipped pen or rotary tool.



8.6 Step 6: XRF Analysis

Open a “Measure and Analyze” window from the SuperQ Manager. Wear gloves and avoid touching the flat (analytical) surface of the bead (PANalytical, 2012).
Click the multi-cup icon to open the Sample Changer. Double-click position A1. Enter the sample name; set type to “Routine,” application to “Geology Beads,” priority to “Normal,” and verify weights are correct. Click Add. Available positions are A1–A8 and B5–B8.
Once all samples are entered, click Measure.







Note



If the XRF has not been running recently, the instrument needs to warm up until the front-panel readouts display 60 and 50. Run the first bead until those values are reached, then click Abort. Wait for the arm to return the sample, then restart. Running samples before warm-up can compromise the analysis (PANalytical, 2012).




8.7 Step 7: Retrieving Results

Open a “Results Evaluation” window. Set the archive to “Geology Beads” and adjust the date range. Use the “Name Mask” field to filter results. Click on a sample and then click “View.”
To export data: open a “Results Quantitative” window. Adjust date and name mask. Click the Print icon, then “Delimited Values Report” to clipboard. Paste into a spreadsheet.

Verify the 2:1 flux-to-sample ratio for every sample; record exact masses on the XRF sample sheet (Claisse, 2003).
Visually inspect beads before loading; reject cracked, broken, or bubble-compromised beads.
Run at least one CRM alongside unknowns to monitor instrument drift and accuracy (Norrish & Hutton, 1969).
If a bead required a third fusion, note this on the sample sheet.

title: Analytical Balance Calibration and Operation – Mettler Toledo
text: This procedure describes the routine calibration, verification, and proper operation of Mettler Toledo analytical balances used in the EA Program laboratory. Accurate mass measurements are fundamental to nearly every quantitative laboratory procedure, including soil moisture determination (SOP-L400), loss on ignition (SOP-L406), DNA extraction (SOP-L700), and chemical reagent preparation. Regular calibration ensures that balance readings are traceable to national standards and within acceptable tolerance for analytical work (Harris & Lucy, 2020; Mettler Toledo, 2023).

title: Analytical Balance Calibration and Operation – Mettler Toledo
text: This procedure describes the routine calibration, verification, and proper operation of Mettler Toledo analytical balances used in the EA Program laboratory. Accurate mass measurements are fundamental to nearly every quantitative laboratory procedure, including soil moisture determination (SOP-L400), loss on ignition (SOP-L406), DNA extraction (SOP-L700), and chemical reagent preparation. Regular calibration ensures that balance readings are traceable to national standards and within acceptable tolerance for analytical work (Harris & Lucy, 2020; Mettler Toledo, 2023).

title: Analytical Balance Calibration and Operation – Mettler Toledo
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All Mettler Toledo analytical balances (0.1 mg readability) and precision balances (0.01 g or 0.001 g readability) in the EA Program laboratory
Does not apply to: Portable field balances, top-loading balances used only for rough weighing (greater than 1 g tolerance), or microbalances (0.001 mg readability) requiring specialized calibration procedures
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Analytical Balance Calibration and Operation – Mettler Toledo
text:
3 Definitions

Accuracy: The closeness of a measurement to the true (reference) value; assessed by weighing a certified reference weight and comparing the result to the certified mass.
Calibration: Comparison of a balance’s readings against reference weights of known mass to establish a correction curve or verify performance within tolerance.
Certified reference weight: A weight whose mass is traceable to national or international measurement standards (NIST or equivalent); classified by tolerance class (OIML E1 through M3 or ASTM 0 through 7).
Drift: Slow, systematic change in balance readings over time, caused by temperature fluctuation, vibration, or electronic aging.
External calibration: Calibration using calibrated weights placed manually on the pan; required on balances without internal weights.
Internal calibration (AutoCal): Automatic calibration using a built-in reference weight that is mechanically engaged by the balance; the Mettler Toledo XPE205 performs internal calibration automatically in response to temperature changes.
Linearity: The degree to which balance readings are proportional to applied mass across the full weighing range; assessed by weighing multiple reference weights spanning the range.
Repeatability: The standard deviation of repeated measurements of the same weight under identical conditions; a key indicator of short-term balance precision.
Tare: The function that zeroes the displayed mass with a container on the pan, so that subsequent readings show only the mass of material added.

text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Calibration weights are dense metal objects; dropping them can cause injury to feet or damage to the balance pan. Handle with forceps only.
Chemical: Some samples weighed on the balance may be hazardous. Refer to the relevant SOP for the material being weighed.




5.1 Required PPE

Lab coat
Nitrile gloves (when handling calibration weights or chemical samples)
Safety glasses (when weighing chemical reagents)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
If a chemical spill occurs on or near the balance, clean the spill per SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling before resuming use. If the balance pan or draft shield is damaged, remove the balance from service and contact the lab manager.

title: Analytical Balance Calibration and Operation – Mettler Toledo
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Balance Placement and Environment
Proper placement is essential for accurate weighing. The balance should remain in the same location and should not be moved unless absolutely necessary (Mettler Toledo, 2023).

Place the balance on a dedicated anti-vibration table or stone slab, away from doors, windows, air vents, and foot traffic
Keep the balance away from direct sunlight and heat sources (ovens, hot plates), which cause thermal drift
Verify the balance is level using the built-in spirit level. Adjust the leveling feet until the bubble is centered.
Allow the balance to warm up for at least 30 minutes after being powered on before performing any measurements or calibration (Harris & Lucy, 2020)



7.2 Internal Calibration (FACT/iSOCAL)
Most Mettler Toledo analytical balances are equipped with an internal calibration function (Fully Automatic Calibration Technology, FACT, or iSOCAL) that uses a built-in reference weight (Mettler Toledo, 2023).

Ensure the balance is unloaded and the draft shield doors are closed
Press the internal calibration button or navigate to Menu > Calibration > Internal Calibration (exact path varies by model)
The balance will automatically perform the calibration sequence. Do not touch the balance, lean on the bench, or create air currents during this process.
When the display reads “Calibration Done” or returns to the weighing screen, record the date and result in the calibration log
If the internal calibration fails, repeat the process. If it fails again, remove the balance from service and contact the lab manager.







Note



If the balance is set to automatic FACT mode, it will self-calibrate whenever it detects a temperature change of 1.5 C or more. However, manual internal calibration should still be performed monthly as part of the verification schedule.




7.3 External Calibration Verification (Monthly)
External verification uses traceable reference weights to confirm that the balance is reading accurately across its range. This check does not replace the annual professional calibration but provides ongoing confidence in measurement quality (aac_guide2019?).

Perform an internal calibration first (Section 6.2)
Allow the balance to stabilize with an empty pan and closed draft shield. Tare to read 0.0000 g (for a 0.1 mg balance).
Using forceps, place the reference weights on the center of the pan one at a time, starting with the smallest. Record the displayed mass for each weight.
Test at a minimum of three points spanning the expected working range of the balance (e.g., low, mid, and high):









Check Point
Reference Weight
Acceptance Criterion (analytical, 0.1 mg)




Low
1 g
Displayed value within +/- 0.5 mg of nominal


Mid
50 g
Displayed value within +/- 0.5 mg of nominal


High
200 g
Displayed value within +/- 1.0 mg of nominal




If any reading falls outside the acceptance criterion, re-zero, repeat the measurement, and clean the pan and weight with a lint-free wipe. If the reading is still out of tolerance, perform an external calibration (Section 6.4) or remove the balance from service.
Record all results, the date, and the operator initials in the calibration log.







TipTip



Always place weights in the center of the pan. Off-center loading (corner loading) can introduce errors, especially on high-resolution balances. Periodically test corner loading by placing a single weight at each corner and comparing readings.




7.4 External Calibration (As Needed)
If the internal calibration or monthly verification indicates the balance is out of tolerance, perform a full external calibration using a traceable reference weight.

Navigate to Menu > Calibration > External Calibration
When prompted, place the specified calibration weight (the balance will display the required mass, typically its full capacity or a specific test weight)
Place the weight on the center of the pan using forceps
Wait for the calibration to complete and record the result
Repeat the verification checks in Section 6.3 to confirm the balance is now within tolerance
TBD – confirm external calibration weight value for the specific Mettler model in the lab



7.5 Annual Professional Calibration

Schedule an annual on-site calibration by a Mettler Toledo service technician or an ISO 17025-accredited calibration laboratory
The technician will perform a comprehensive calibration including linearity, eccentricity (corner loading), repeatability, and hysteresis tests
Retain the calibration certificate in the lab’s quality records binder
TBD – record the current service contract details and contact information for scheduling



7.6 Daily Use and Best Practices
Follow these practices every time you use the balance to ensure accurate and reproducible results (Harris & Lucy, 2020; Mettler Toledo, 2023):

Check that the balance is level before use
Close all draft shield doors before taring or reading a mass
Allow the reading to stabilize fully (stability indicator appears) before recording a value
Use appropriate weighing vessels (aluminum tins, ceramic crucibles, weighing paper, or glass vials depending on the application)
Tare the vessel before adding sample material
Handle objects with forceps, spatulas, or gloves; fingerprints add mass and oils that cause drift
Never place chemicals directly on the pan
Clean up any spills immediately with a lint-free wipe or brush
Leave the draft shield closed and the balance powered on between uses to maintain thermal equilibrium
Record the balance ID, date, and any anomalies in the lab notebook



7.7 Cleaning and Maintenance

Wipe the pan and interior of the draft shield with a lint-free wipe after each use
Use filtered compressed air to remove dust from hard-to-reach areas inside the weighing chamber
If the pan becomes stained or corroded, remove it and clean with mild soap and water; dry thoroughly before replacing
Do not use solvents to clean the draft shield (they may damage acrylic or glass)
Inspect the draft shield gaskets periodically for wear; replace if they no longer seal properly

title: Sonicator – Ultrasonic Bath and Probe
text: This procedure describes the operation and maintenance of the ultrasonic bath and probe sonicator used in the EA Program laboratory. Sonication uses high-frequency sound waves (typically 20–40 kHz) to generate cavitation bubbles in a liquid medium. The collapse of these bubbles produces localized shear forces that disaggregate particles, disperse samples, degas solutions, enhance extraction, and clean labware. In the EA Program, sonication is used for soil particle dispersion, glassware cleaning, sample homogenization, and cell lysis in DNA extraction workflows.

title: Sonicator – Ultrasonic Bath and Probe
text: This procedure describes the operation and maintenance of the ultrasonic bath and probe sonicator used in the EA Program laboratory. Sonication uses high-frequency sound waves (typically 20–40 kHz) to generate cavitation bubbles in a liquid medium. The collapse of these bubbles produces localized shear forces that disaggregate particles, disperse samples, degas solutions, enhance extraction, and clean labware. In the EA Program, sonication is used for soil particle dispersion, glassware cleaning, sample homogenization, and cell lysis in DNA extraction workflows.

title: Sonicator – Ultrasonic Bath and Probe
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: The Fisher Scientific ultrasonic bath (SGM 134) and any probe-tip sonicators available in EA Program laboratories
Does not apply to: Vortex mixing (see future SOP-L104); bead beating for DNA extraction (integral to the extraction protocol in SOP-L700); industrial-scale ultrasonics
Location: SGM 134

title: Sonicator – Ultrasonic Bath and Probe
text:
3 Definitions

Amplitude: The peak displacement of the sonicator probe tip, expressed as a percentage of maximum; higher amplitude delivers more energy per unit time to the sample.
Cavitation: The formation and violent collapse of microscopic bubbles in liquid exposed to ultrasound; the primary mechanism by which ultrasound disrupts cells and disperses particles.
Duty cycle: For pulsed sonication, the fraction of each cycle during which the probe is active (e.g., 0.5 s on / 0.5 s off = 50% duty cycle); used to limit heat input to sensitive samples.
Probe sonicator (ultrasonic processor): A device that converts electrical energy to ultrasonic vibrations (typically 20 kHz) via a piezoelectric transducer; the probe tip vibrates in direct contact with the sample.
Sonication bath: An ultrasonic cleaning bath in which the sample container is immersed in water through which ultrasound is transmitted; less intense than probe sonication; used for dispersing particles or aiding extraction.
Specific energy (J mL-1): Total ultrasonic energy delivered per unit volume; the parameter most predictive of cell disruption yield for a given sample type; increases with amplitude, time, and volume.

title: Sonicator – Ultrasonic Bath and Probe
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Hearing: Ultrasonic baths produce audible noise (buzzing/ humming) during operation. Probe sonicators at high power can produce high-intensity noise. Wear hearing protection if exposure exceeds a few minutes at high power settings.
Aerosol generation: Probe sonication of open samples generates aerosols. If the sample contains hazardous biological or chemical material, sonicate inside a fume hood or biological safety cabinet.
Heat: Extended sonication heats the bath water and the sample. Monitor temperature if heat-sensitive analytes are involved.
Skin contact: Do not immerse hands in the bath while it is operating. Cavitation can damage skin tissue.
Glassware: Thin-walled or cracked glassware may fail under sonication. Use containers rated for ultrasonic use.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses
Nitrile gloves
Lab coat
Hearing protection (for probe sonication at high power or extended bath sonication)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For chemical spills from broken containers, follow SOP-L004 Chemical Spill Response. If the sonicator sparks, smokes, or produces unusual odors, unplug immediately and report to the lab manager.

title: Sonicator – Ultrasonic Bath and Probe
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Ultrasonic Bath

7.1.1 Setup

Fill the bath with deionized water to the manufacturer’s recommended level (typically 2–3 cm above the transducer surface or to the fill line). Do not operate the bath without water; this damages the transducer.
If using the bath for cleaning, add the appropriate detergent concentration per SOP-L101
Degas the bath water by running the sonicator for 5 minutes without a load (degassed water transmits ultrasonic energy more effectively)



7.1.2 Operation

Place sample containers (tubes, beakers, flasks) in the bath using a rack or holder. Containers should be partially submerged but not resting on the bath floor (direct contact with the floor can cause hot spots and uneven sonication).
Set the timer for the duration specified in the analytical SOP (typical ranges: 1–15 minutes for sample dispersion, 15–30 minutes for glassware cleaning)
If the bath has a heater, set the temperature as required (common: room temperature for samples, 40–50 C for cleaning)
Start the sonicator. Verify cavitation by observing fine bubbles rising from the bath surface.
Do not open the lid or reach into the bath during operation
When the timer stops, remove containers using tongs or gloves



7.1.3 Post-Use

Turn off the sonicator
If the bath water is visibly contaminated, drain, rinse, and refill with fresh DI water
Replace the bath water at least weekly even if it appears clean
Wipe the exterior with a damp cloth




7.2 Probe Sonicator

7.2.1 Setup

Select the appropriate tip (microtip for volumes less than 10 mL; standard tip for 10–50 mL)
Attach the tip securely; a loose tip reduces energy transfer and can damage the probe
Clamp the probe in a ring stand so the tip is immersed in the sample to approximately one-third of the liquid depth. Do not touch the container walls or bottom with the tip.



7.2.2 Operation

Set the power level and pulse settings per the analytical SOP (common: 20–40% amplitude, 5 seconds on / 5 seconds off pulsing to minimize heating)
If the sample is hazardous, work inside a fume hood or biological safety cabinet with the sash lowered
Start sonication. A faint hissing and visible agitation confirm cavitation.
Monitor sample temperature; if overheating is a concern, place the sample container in an ice bath during sonication
After the prescribed duration, stop the sonicator



7.2.3 Post-Use

Immediately wipe the probe tip with a lint-free tissue dampened with 70% ethanol or DI water
For molecular biology work (eDNA, PCR), decontaminate the tip with 10% bleach, rinse with DI water, then wipe with 70% ethanol
Inspect the tip for pitting or erosion; a heavily pitted tip reduces performance and should be replaced

title: Laminar Flow Cabinet Operation
text:
This procedure describes the operation, decontamination, and maintenance of the ESCO laminar flow cabinet (clean bench) used in the EA Program laboratory. The cabinet provides an ISO Class 5 (Class 100) particle-free work environment by passing HEPA-filtered air across the work surface in a unidirectional (laminar) flow pattern. It is used for aseptic work that requires protection of the sample or product from airborne contamination, including eDNA extraction setup, PCR master mix preparation, sterile media preparation, and filter handling for microplastics analysis.






Important



A laminar flow cabinet (clean bench) protects the work from contamination. It does not protect the operator from hazardous aerosols, pathogens, or chemical vapors. For work involving biohazardous materials (BSL-2 organisms, human pathogens), a biological safety cabinet (BSC, Class II) is required. The EA Program does not currently work with BSL-2 materials, but if the scope changes, consult the PI and campus biosafety officer.

title: Laminar Flow Cabinet Operation
text:

The cabinet provides an ISO Class 5 (Class 100) particle-free work environment by passing HEPA-filtered air across the work surface in a unidirectional (laminar) flow pattern. It is used for aseptic work that requires protection of the sample or product from airborne contamination, including eDNA extraction setup, PCR master mix preparation, sterile media preparation, and filter handling for microplastics analysis.






Important



A laminar flow cabinet (clean bench) protects the work from contamination. It does not protect the operator from hazardous aerosols, pathogens, or chemical vapors. For work involving biohazardous materials (BSL-2 organisms, human pathogens), a biological safety cabinet (BSC, Class II) is required. The EA Program does not currently work with BSL-2 materials, but if the scope changes, consult the PI and campus biosafety officer.

title: Laminar Flow Cabinet Operation
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All use of the ESCO laminar flow cabinet in SGM 134, including eDNA and PCR work, sterile reagent preparation, and microplastics filter handling
Does not apply to: Fume hoods (for chemical vapor protection); biological safety cabinets (BSC, Class II); field work
Location: SGM 134

title: Laminar Flow Cabinet Operation
text:
3 Definitions

Biosafety cabinet (BSC): A ventilated enclosure that protects both the user and the environment from aerosols; classified as Class I, II, or III depending on the level of protection. Not the same as a laminar flow cabinet.
HEPA filter (High-Efficiency Particulate Air): A filter rated to remove at least 99.97% of particles 0.3 µm or larger; used in laminar flow cabinets to produce particle-free air over the work surface.
Horizontal laminar flow cabinet: A clean bench in which HEPA- filtered air flows horizontally from the back of the cabinet toward the user; protects samples from particles but does not protect the user from aerosols (not suitable for hazardous biological agents).
Laminar flow: Smooth, parallel flow of air in one direction at uniform velocity; prevents turbulence that would re-introduce particles to the work surface.
UV germicidal lamp: A short-wave ultraviolet lamp installed in some cabinets to reduce surface contamination between work sessions; effective only on exposed surfaces; never operate with personnel present.
Vertical laminar flow cabinet: A clean bench in which HEPA- filtered air flows downward from the top onto the work surface; the standard configuration in the EA Program lab.

title: Laminar Flow Cabinet Operation
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Startup

Ensure the UV lamp is off
Raise or open the sash to the working position
Turn on the blower fan and allow it to run for at least 15 minutes before beginning work. This purges the cabinet interior and establishes stable laminar flow.
While the cabinet purges, wipe down the entire work surface, side walls, and interior of the sash with 70% ethanol using lint-free wipes. For eDNA work, follow the ethanol wipe with a 10% bleach wipe, then a final ethanol wipe to remove bleach residue.
Place only the materials needed for the immediate task inside the cabinet. Minimize clutter; objects block airflow and create turbulence.







Tip



Arrange items so that clean (sterile) materials are upstream (closer to the HEPA filter) and used/contaminated items are downstream (closer to the operator). This prevents contaminated air from passing over clean surfaces.




7.2 Working in the Cabinet

Wear clean nitrile gloves; spray gloves with 70% ethanol before reaching into the cabinet
Work at least 10 cm from the front edge to stay within the laminar flow zone
Move slowly and deliberately; rapid arm movements disrupt laminar flow and pull room air into the work zone
Do not block the air intake grilles (front and/or rear) with equipment, paper, or notebooks
Do not use open flames (Bunsen burners) inside a laminar flow cabinet; they disrupt airflow and can damage the HEPA filter
Keep the cabinet running continuously while working; do not turn the blower off between tasks during a session



7.3 Shutdown

Remove all materials from the cabinet
Wipe the work surface with 70% ethanol (and bleach for eDNA work)
Lower the sash if applicable
Optionally, turn on the UV lamp for 15–30 minutes for surface decontamination. Ensure no personnel are exposed to UV light during this period. Post a “UV Lamp Active” sign.
After UV exposure, turn off the UV lamp
Turn off the blower (or leave it running on low if lab policy requires continuous operation to maintain cabinet cleanliness)



7.4 UV Lamp Use

The UV lamp is a supplemental decontamination tool, not a substitute for chemical wipe-down
Run the UV lamp for 15–30 minutes after each use session
Record UV lamp use in the UV lamp log (posted on the cabinet). UV lamps lose efficacy over time; replace after the manufacturer’s recommended hours (typically 5,000–8,000 hours).
Do not rely solely on UV decontamination for eDNA work; chemical wipe-down with bleach is more effective at destroying DNA.

title: Muffle Furnace Operation
text: This procedure describes the safe operation, temperature programming, and maintenance of the muffle furnace used in the EA Program laboratory. The muffle furnace provides controlled high-temperature combustion (up to 1,100 C) for loss-on-ignition analysis (SOP-L406), pre-combustion of crucibles and glass fiber filters, ashing of organic materials, and flux fusion preparations.

title: Muffle Furnace Operation
text: This procedure describes the safe operation, temperature programming, and maintenance of the muffle furnace used in the EA Program laboratory. The muffle furnace provides controlled high-temperature combustion (up to 1,100 C) for loss-on-ignition analysis (SOP-L406), pre-combustion of crucibles and glass fiber filters, ashing of organic materials, and flux fusion preparations.

title: Muffle Furnace Operation
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All use of muffle furnaces in EA Program laboratories, including routine ignition (550 C for SOM), high- temperature ashing (up to 1,000 C), and pre-combustion of labware
Does not apply to: Drying ovens operating below 300 C (see SOP-L105); tube furnaces for elemental analysis (integral to analytical instruments); kilns
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 134

title: Muffle Furnace Operation
text:
3 Definitions

Ashing: High-temperature combustion of organic matter in an open crucible in the muffle furnace, leaving only the inorganic (mineral) residue; the basis of loss-on-ignition analysis.
Crucible: A heat-resistant container (ceramic, porcelain, or platinum) used to hold samples during furnace ignition; must be pre-ignited to constant mass before use.
Loss on ignition (LOI): The mass loss when a dried sample is ignited at 550 °C for 4 hours, expressed as a percentage of dry mass; used as a proxy for soil organic matter content.
Muffle: The interior chamber of the furnace, thermally isolated from the heating elements; provides a controlled oxidizing atmosphere for combustion.
Pre-combustion: Heating glassware, crucibles, or glass fiber filters to 450–550 °C to destroy any organic contamination before use in carbon or organic matter analyses.
Ramping: Programming the furnace to increase temperature at a controlled rate (e.g., 5 °C min-1) to prevent thermal shock to crucibles and to avoid rapid oxidation that can cause sample loss.
Set point temperature: The target temperature programmed into the furnace controller; verify with a calibrated thermocouple if precise temperature is critical.

title: Muffle Furnace Operation
text:

Role

title: Muffle Furnace Operation
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Thermal: The furnace exterior, door, and chamber reach extremely high temperatures. Crucibles removed from the furnace at 550 C or above can cause severe burns on contact. The furnace remains hot for hours after shutdown.
Fire: Combustible materials (paper, wood, plastic) placed on or near the furnace can ignite. Keep a 30 cm clear zone around the furnace on all sides.
Fumes: Combustion of organic matter produces CO2, water vapor, and potentially odorous or irritating fumes. Ensure adequate room ventilation or connect the furnace exhaust to a fume hood or duct if available.
Electrical: The furnace draws high current. Do not use extension cords. Inspect the power cord for damage before each use.




5.1 Required PPE

Heat-resistant gloves (rated to at least 500 C)
Safety glasses or face shield
Lab coat (cotton preferred; synthetic fabrics melt)
Closed-toed shoes



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For burns, apply cool running water immediately and seek first aid. If the furnace produces unusual smoke, odors, or sparks, shut it off at the circuit breaker and evacuate the room. Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety.

title: Muffle Furnace Operation
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Use Inspection

Inspect the furnace chamber for debris, cracked insulation, or damage to the heating elements. Do not operate if damage is visible; report to the lab manager.
Verify that the area around the furnace is clear of combustible materials (minimum 30 cm clearance on all sides and top)
Confirm that the furnace is plugged directly into a dedicated wall outlet (no extension cords or power strips)



7.2 Loading

Arrange crucibles or boats inside the chamber so they do not touch each other or the heating elements. Leave space for air circulation.
Close the furnace door gently; do not slam (the refractory lining is fragile)



7.3 Temperature Programming

Set the target temperature and ramp rate per the analytical SOP:

Loss on ignition (SOP-L406): ramp to 550 C, hold 4 hours
Pre-combustion of glass fiber filters: ramp to 450 C, hold 4 hours
Pre-combustion of crucibles: ramp to 550 C, hold 1 hour
Ceramic boat preparation (SSM, SOP-L407): ramp to 900 C, hold 30 minutes

If the furnace is programmable, set the ramp rate to approximately 10 C per minute unless the analytical SOP specifies otherwise
Start the program and verify that the displayed temperature begins to rise







Tip



Avoid placing samples into a furnace that is already at full temperature unless the analytical SOP explicitly requires it. Rapid thermal shock can crack crucibles and cause spattering.




7.4 During Operation

Do not leave the furnace unattended during the initial ramp-up (first 30 minutes). Check that the temperature is tracking the set point.
Post a “Furnace in Use” sign on the furnace and the lab door, noting the expected completion time
Do not open the furnace door during the hold period unless troubleshooting



7.5 Unloading

After the hold period, turn off the furnace or allow the programmed cooldown to proceed
Allow the furnace to cool to below 200 C before opening the door. Opening at higher temperatures causes rapid thermal shock to samples and exposes the operator to radiant heat.
Using crucible tongs and heat-resistant gloves, transfer crucibles to a heat-resistant pad, then immediately to the desiccator
Allow crucibles to cool to room temperature in the desiccator (approximately 30–45 minutes) before weighing



7.6 Shutdown

Verify that the furnace is off and the temperature is decreasing
Remove the “Furnace in Use” sign
Leave the furnace door slightly ajar (1–2 cm) after it has cooled below 100 C to prevent moisture buildup inside the chamber

Record the verification date and result in the instrument logbook.
If temperature uniformity is critical (e.g., for large batches), place thermocouples at the front, center, and back of the chamber and record any gradient.
