text: This SOP describes the safe operation, maintenance, and hazard mitigation for laboratory hot plates, stirring hot plates, and digital dry bath heaters used within the environmental analysis laboratories.

title: Hot Plates and Dry Bath
text: This SOP describes the safe operation, maintenance, and hazard mitigation for laboratory hot plates, stirring hot plates, and digital dry bath heaters used within the environmental analysis laboratories.

title: Hot Plates and Dry Bath
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Hot plates, stirring hot plates, and digital dry bath (heat block) heaters used for sample heating, digestion, reagent preparation, and enzymatic or thermal incubations
Does not apply to: Muffle furnaces (see SOP-L111), water baths, autoclaves, or microwave digestion systems
Location: Environmental analysis laboratories

title: Hot Plates and Dry Bath
text:
3 Definitions

Dry bath (heating block): An aluminum block with drilled wells that fits standard tubes (1.5 mL, 15 mL, 50 mL); heated by a resistive element to provide uniform, conductive temperature control without the hazard of a liquid bath.
Flash point: The lowest temperature at which a liquid’s vapor can ignite in air; flammable solvents must never be heated above their flash point on an open hot plate.
Hot plate: An electrically heated flat surface used to heat beakers, flasks, or evaporating dishes; may or may not include an integrated magnetic stirrer.
Hot plate / stirrer: A combination unit providing both heating and magnetic stirring; the most common configuration in the EA Program laboratory.
Magnetic stir bar: A PTFE-coated magnetic rod placed in a vessel; rotated by the stirrer magnet beneath the hot plate surface to provide mixing.
Set temperature vs. actual temperature: The temperature displayed on the hot plate controller may differ substantially from the actual liquid temperature; always verify with a calibrated thermometer.
Surface temperature limit: The maximum safe surface temperature of the hot plate; organic solvents should never be heated on an open hot plate above their boiling point or flash point.

5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Thermal: Heating surfaces and metal blocks can exceed 300 °C and remain dangerously hot long after power is disconnected. Contact causes severe thermal burns.
Fire and Explosion: Heating volatile, flammable solvents on an open-bench hot plate can ignite vapors. Standard hot plates are not explosion-proof and may generate sparks from mechanical switches or internal cycling.
Electrical: High current draw can overload circuits. Liquid boil-overs or spills create immediate electrical short risks.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses or chemical splash goggles
Laboratory coat (fully buttoned)
Heat-resistant thermal gloves (when handling active or cooling vessels, blocks, or glassware)
Nitrile gloves (underneath thermal gloves if chemical handling is simultaneous)



5.2 Emergency Procedures

title: Hot Plates and Dry Bath
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Operational Inspection

Inspect the power cord and plug for fraying, exposed wires, or chemical degradation. Do not use if damaged.
Ensure the cord does not drape across or contact the heating surface.
Verify that the heating surface and aluminum blocks are free of residual chemical films, crusts, or signs of pitting. Clean with a damp cloth if necessary (unit must be unplugged and cool).



7.2 Sample and Vessel Preparation

Glassware inspection: For hot plates, use only borosilicate glassware (e.g., Pyrex, Kimax) certified for high thermal stress. Inspect for star cracks, hairline fractures, or deep scratches. Discard compromised glassware.
Dry bath alignment: Ensure the interchangeable aluminum block profile matches your specific sample tubes (e.g., 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes vs. 15 mL conical tubes). Incorrect sizing limits thermal contact and degrades temperature control accuracy.







ImportantSealed Containers



Never heat completely sealed containers on a hot plate. Pressure buildup can cause catastrophic vessel failure.




7.3 Operation and Parameter Adjustment

Plug the unit directly into a grounded wall outlet. Avoid extension cords or daisy-chained power strips due to high wattage requirements.
Toggle the main power switch to the ON position.
Temperature control: Set the target temperature via the digital interface or analog dial.







TipExternal Temperature Probes



If using an external temperature probe (thermocouple), ensure it is securely immersed in the solution and not resting directly against the bottom or side walls of the glassware.



Stirring control (if applicable): Place the stir bar flat inside the container. Turn the RPM dial slowly from zero to the target velocity. Sudden adjustments can cause the stir bar to decouple (spin erratically), requiring the dial to be reset to zero to re-engage.



7.4 Shutdown and Post-Run Monitoring

Turn off the heating and stirring functions by switching controls to 0 or pressing Stop.
Turn the main power switch to OFF.
Hot Top warning: If the unit features a “Hot Top” indicator light, leave the unit plugged in until the surface drops below 50 °C and the warning light turns off.
Once completely cool, wipe down any condensed moisture or accidental spills.

8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Verify the set temperature against an independent calibrated thermometer or thermocouple before use with critical samples.
If the measured temperature deviates by more than ±5 °C from the set point, remove the unit from service and arrange calibration or repair.

title: Using Drying Ovens
text: This procedure describes the safe operation of gravity convection and forced-air drying ovens used in the EA Program laboratory. Drying ovens are used to determine gravimetric moisture content of soil, sediment, and plant tissue samples (see SOP-L400 Soil Moisture), to pre-dry samples before loss on ignition (see SOP-L406 Loss on Ignition), to dry glassware, and to regenerate desiccants. Consistent oven operation ensures accurate and reproducible mass-loss measurements across the laboratory (Gardner, 1986; Robertson et al., 1999).

title: Using Drying Ovens
text: This procedure describes the safe operation of gravity convection and forced-air drying ovens used in the EA Program laboratory. Drying ovens are used to determine gravimetric moisture content of soil, sediment, and plant tissue samples (see SOP-L400 Soil Moisture), to pre-dry samples before loss on ignition (see SOP-L406 Loss on Ignition), to dry glassware, and to regenerate desiccants. Consistent oven operation ensures accurate and reproducible mass-loss measurements across the laboratory (Gardner, 1986; Robertson et al., 1999).

title: Using Drying Ovens
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All gravity convection and forced-air drying ovens in the EA Program laboratory, operated at temperatures up to 250 C
Does not apply to: Muffle furnaces (550+ C; see SOP-L50), vacuum ovens, microwave drying, or autoclaves
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Using Drying Ovens
text:
3 Definitions

Desiccator: An airtight container holding a hygroscopic drying agent (typically silica gel or Drierite) used to cool crucibles or dried samples to room temperature without re-absorbing atmospheric moisture.
Forced-air oven (mechanical convection): A drying oven with a fan that circulates hot air to produce uniform temperature and faster drying; preferred when rapid or even drying is required.
Gravity convection oven: A drying oven without a fan; relies on natural convection. Slightly less temperature-uniform than forced-air but adequate for most soil and sediment drying.
Gravimetric moisture content: The mass of water lost on drying expressed as a proportion of the dry mass: \(\theta_g = (M_{wet} -
M_{dry}) / M_{dry}\); expressed as g g-1 or as a percentage.
Oven-dry basis: The convention of expressing soil or sediment concentrations relative to the mass of material dried at 105 °C to constant mass; the standard reference state for soil analysis.
Set point: The target temperature programmed into the oven controller; the actual chamber temperature should be verified with a calibrated thermometer and may differ from the set point by a few degrees.
Tare mass: The mass of an empty, pre-dried container (crucible, tin, or pan) recorded before adding sample; subtracted from the gross mass to obtain sample mass.

text:

text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Oven surfaces and contents reach temperatures up to 250 C. Severe burns can result from touching hot surfaces, shelves, or sample containers without proper PPE. Steam may escape when opening the door if drying wet samples.
Chemical: Do not dry samples containing volatile organic solvents, flammable materials, or corrosive chemicals in these ovens. Drying ovens are not explosion-proof. Volatile fumes can accumulate inside the oven chamber and pose fire or explosion risks.
Electrical: Do not operate ovens with damaged power cords or plugs. Ensure the oven is properly grounded.




5.1 Required PPE

Heat-resistant gloves or oven mitts (required when loading/unloading)
Safety glasses
Lab coat
Closed-toed shoes



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For burns, cool the affected area under cool running water for at least 10 minutes. Seek medical attention for burns with blistering. If smoke or unusual odors are detected, turn off the oven, unplug it, and ventilate the area. Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety.

title: Using Drying Ovens
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Use Checks

Verify the oven is clean and free of residue from previous use
Check that the oven vent is unobstructed (gravity convection ovens rely on passive airflow; blocked vents cause uneven heating)
Confirm the temperature setpoint using the oven’s built-in display or controller
Verify the temperature against an independent thermometer or thermocouple placed inside the oven. The reading should agree within +/- 2 C of the setpoint. If it does not, contact the lab manager.



7.2 Setting the Temperature
Common drying temperatures used in the EA Program laboratory:









Application
Temperature
Duration
Reference SOP




Gravimetric soil moisture
105 C
24+ hours
SOP-L41


Pre-drying soil for LOI
105 C
24+ hours
SOP-L50


Drying glassware

65–70 C

210 C

105 C
Until dry
SOP-L51




Set the temperature using the oven controller dial or digital display
Allow the oven to reach the target temperature and stabilize before loading samples (typically 30–60 minutes)
Record the setpoint and actual temperature in your lab notebook



7.3 Loading Samples

Arrange samples on oven shelves with adequate spacing to allow air circulation. Do not stack containers or block vents.
Place containers with the lids removed or loosely resting to allow moisture to escape
For large batches, distribute samples evenly across shelves to minimize temperature gradients
Close the oven door promptly after loading







TipTip



Place a small label or sign on the oven door indicating: your name, the setpoint temperature, the date and time samples were loaded, and the expected removal time. This prevents others from accidentally changing the temperature or disturbing your samples.




7.4 Monitoring

Check the oven temperature at the start and end of each drying cycle using the independent thermometer
Do not open the oven door unnecessarily during drying, as this introduces cool air and extends drying time
For multi-day drying, check the oven temperature at least once daily



7.5 Removing Samples

Wear heat-resistant gloves or oven mitts
Use metal tongs for small containers (aluminum tins, crucibles)
Transfer hot containers directly into a desiccator to cool to room temperature. Do not weigh hot samples; thermal convection currents around hot objects cause unstable balance readings (Harris & Lucy, 2020).
Allow samples to cool in the desiccator for 20–30 minutes before weighing
Close the oven door after removing samples



7.6 Verifying Dryness (Constant Mass)
For analytical applications (soil moisture, LOI), drying is complete only when the sample reaches constant mass:

After the initial drying period, remove the sample, cool in the desiccator, and weigh
Return the sample to the oven for an additional 2–4 hours
Cool and re-weigh
If the mass has changed by less than 0.01 g between successive weighings, constant mass has been achieved
If the mass has decreased by more than 0.01 g, return to the oven and repeat until constant mass is reached



7.7 Shutdown

If the oven will not be used for several days, turn it off using the power switch or controller
Leave the door slightly ajar to prevent moisture buildup and odors inside the chamber
Ensure no samples remain in the oven before shutting down

title: Using Drying Ovens
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Verify oven temperature against an independent thermometer at least monthly; record in the oven calibration log
Acceptable temperature accuracy: +/- 2 C of setpoint at 105 C
If the oven temperature drifts beyond +/- 5 C, remove the oven from service and contact the lab manager
Ensure the desiccator contains active (indicating) desiccant; regenerate or replace when the indicator changes color
For analytical drying, always confirm constant mass (Section 6.6) rather than relying on a fixed drying time alone


8.1 Interferences

Overcrowding the oven can create temperature gradients and uneven drying, leading to inconsistent results
Opening the oven door frequently extends drying time and introduces moisture
Drying samples containing volatile compounds at 105 C will cause mass loss beyond water content, biasing moisture determinations

title: Using Micropipettes
text: This procedure describes the proper use, volume setting, tip loading, sample aspiration and dispensing, and care of Gilson Pipetman micropipettes. Micropipettes are precision instruments used to transfer small volumes of liquid (less than 1 mL) with high accuracy. Correct technique is essential for reproducible results in chemical, biological, and environmental analyses.

title: Using Micropipettes
text: This procedure describes the proper use, volume setting, tip loading, sample aspiration and dispensing, and care of Gilson Pipetman micropipettes. Micropipettes are precision instruments used to transfer small volumes of liquid (less than 1 mL) with high accuracy. Correct technique is essential for reproducible results in chemical, biological, and environmental analyses.

title: Using Micropipettes
text:
2 Scope

Does not apply to: Serological pipettes, Pasteur pipettes, bottle- top dispensers, or Repipet-type dispensers
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

text:

title: Using Micropipettes
text:
4 Definitions

Aerosol-resistant (filter) tip: A pipette tip containing a hydrophobic filter that prevents aerosols and liquid from entering the pipette barrel; required when pipetting volatile, radioactive, infectious, or PCR-sensitive samples.
Air-displacement pipette: The standard laboratory micropipette in which a piston displaces air in the tip, which in turn displaces liquid; the most common type; accuracy depends on tip seal quality and pipetting technique.
Dead volume: The small volume of liquid remaining in the tip after dispensing; varies by tip type and affects accuracy at low volumes.
Forward pipetting: The standard technique in which the plunger is depressed to the first stop before immersing the tip, then liquid is aspirated by releasing the plunger; used for aqueous solutions.
Reverse pipetting: A technique in which the plunger is depressed past the second stop before aspirating; liquid is dispensed only to the first stop, leaving excess in the tip; used for viscous or volatile liquids to improve accuracy.
Systematic error: A consistent, directional bias in pipette delivery; detected by gravimetric calibration; caused by worn seals, incorrect technique, or using tips not matched to the pipette model.
Volume range: The minimum and maximum volume a given pipette model is designed to deliver accurately; pipetting below 10% of the maximum volume significantly increases relative error.

title: Using Micropipettes
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Liquids being pipetted may be hazardous. Consult the relevant SOP and Safety Data Sheet for the material being transferred.
Physical: Repetitive pipetting can cause repetitive strain injuries. Take breaks during extended pipetting sessions.
Biological: When pipetting biological samples, use filter tips to prevent aerosol contamination of the pipette barrel.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves



5.2 Emergency Procedures
If hazardous liquid enters the pipette barrel, stop immediately. Decontaminate the pipette per the manufacturer’s instructions and refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.

title: Using Micropipettes
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Selecting the Correct Pipette
Always select the smallest pipette that covers the target volume. using an unnecessarily large pipette for a small volume reduces accuracy. The volume ranges are:



Pipette
Range
Smallest Graduation




P10
1.0 – 10.0 \(\mu\)L
0.02 \(\mu\)L


P20
2.0 – 20.0 \(\mu\)L
0.02 \(\mu\)L


P200
20 – 200 \(\mu\)L
0.2 \(\mu\)L


P1000
200 – 1000 \(\mu\)L
2 \(\mu\)L









Important



Never set the pipette below the minimum or above the maximum of its range. Exceeding these limits will damage the piston seal and put the pipette out of calibration.




7.2 Setting the Volume

Identify the volume display window on the front face of the pipette. The three-digit display reads differently for each pipette size:

P10: digits represent ones, tenths, and hundredths of uL
P20: digits represent tens, ones, and tenths of uL
P200: digits represent hundreds, tens, and ones of uL
P1000: digits represent thousands, hundreds, and tens of uL

Turn the volume adjustment ring clockwise to increase volume or counterclockwise to decrease volume
If you overshoot the target while dialing down, dial below the desired setting and then dial back up to the correct value. This avoids mechanical backlash in the piston mechanism.



7.3 Loading a Tip

Select the correct tip size for the pipette being used. Tip boxes are labeled with the compatible pipette sizes. When in doubt, confirm with the lab manager.
Press the pipette shaft firmly into a tip in the tip box. A slight twist while pressing helps ensure a secure, airtight seal.
Do not touch the tip with your hands.
Always use a fresh tip for each different reagent or sample to prevent cross-contamination.



7.4 Aspirating (Loading) a Sample

Depress the plunger slowly to the first stop (the point of initial resistance). This is the calibrated load volume.
While holding the plunger at the first stop, immerse the tip into the liquid just enough to cover the opening (3–4 mm). Do not plunge the tip to the bottom of the vessel.
Slowly and steadily release the plunger to draw liquid into the tip. Do not let the plunger snap back.
Wait one to two seconds before removing the tip from the liquid, especially with viscous solutions. This allows the full volume to enter the tip and prevents air bubbles.
Visually inspect the tip: there should be no air gap or bubble at the distal end. If there is, dispense the liquid back and repeat.







TipTip



For viscous liquids (glycerol, concentrated DNA solutions), use the “reverse pipetting” technique: depress the plunger to the second stop before immersing the tip, draw up the liquid by releasing to the rest position, and then dispense by pressing only to the first stop. The small amount of liquid remaining in the tip is discarded.




7.5 Dispensing a Sample

Touch the tip to the inner wall of the receiving vessel at a slight angle
Depress the plunger slowly to the first stop to dispense most of the liquid
Continue pressing to the second stop to expel the final drop
Hold the plunger at the second stop while withdrawing the tip from the vessel
Release the plunger only after the tip is clear of the liquid



7.6 Ejecting the Tip

Hold the pipette over the tip waste container
Press the tip ejector button on the back of the pipette
Never reuse a tip between different solutions



7.7 Important Precautions

Never point a pipette upward with liquid in the tip. Liquid can flow back into the barrel and damage the piston and seals.
Never lay a pipette down with a loaded tip.
When not in use, set the pipette to its maximum volume and hang it vertically on the pipette stand. This relaxes the piston spring and extends the instrument’s life.
Do not use a pipette as a stirring rod.
If the plunger action feels rough, sticky, or inconsistent, stop using the pipette and report the issue to the lab manager.

title: Glassware Cleaning and Preparation
text: This procedure describes the inspection, routine cleaning, acid washing, drying, and storage of laboratory glassware used in the EA Program laboratory. Properly cleaned glassware is essential for reliable analytical results; residual detergent, organic films, or trace metals can introduce systematic bias into water quality, soil extraction, and instrumental analyses. The cleaning tier required depends on the downstream analysis, ranging from routine detergent washing for general use to trace-metal-grade acid washing for ICP-MS and other sensitive techniques.

title: Glassware Cleaning and Preparation
text: This procedure describes the inspection, routine cleaning, acid washing, drying, and storage of laboratory glassware used in the EA Program laboratory. Properly cleaned glassware is essential for reliable analytical results; residual detergent, organic films, or trace metals can introduce systematic bias into water quality, soil extraction, and instrumental analyses. The cleaning tier required depends on the downstream analysis, ranging from routine detergent washing for general use to trace-metal-grade acid washing for ICP-MS and other sensitive techniques.

title: Glassware Cleaning and Preparation
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All reusable borosilicate glass labware (beakers, Erlenmeyer flasks, graduated cylinders, volumetric flasks, watch glasses, funnels, and media bottles) used in the EA Program laboratory
Does not apply to: Disposable glassware (e.g., serological pipettes), plastic labware, quartz cuvettes, or specialty items requiring manufacturer-specific cleaning (e.g., NMR tubes, electrochemistry cells)
Location: Glassware washing station, EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Glassware Cleaning and Preparation
text:
3 Definitions

Acid bath: A polyethylene tub containing 10% (v/v) HCl or HNO3 in deionized water, used to remove trace-metal contamination from glassware; kept in the fume hood at all times.
Acid washing: A multi-step cleaning procedure in which glassware is soaked in dilute acid after routine detergent washing to remove adsorbed trace metals; required for ICP-MS, ICP-OES, and nutrient analyses.
Borosilicate glass: A glass formulation with low thermal expansion, high chemical resistance, and suitability for laboratory use; the standard material for EA Program glassware.
Deionized (DI) water: Water from which ions have been removed by ion-exchange resin; used for all rinsing steps. Type I (18.2 MOhm) water from the Milli-Q system is required for final rinses of trace-metal-grade glassware.
Routine cleaning tier: Washing with Alconox detergent and tap water, followed by DI water rinses; appropriate for general-use glassware not destined for trace-metal or nutrient analysis.
Trace-metal grade: A cleaning standard requiring acid washing with HNO3 (Trace Metal grade) and Type I water rinses; used for glassware that contacts samples destined for ICP-MS or similar sensitive analyses.
Volumetric glassware: Glassware calibrated to contain or deliver a precise volume (volumetric flasks, graduated cylinders, pipettes); must not be oven-dried because thermal expansion permanently alters calibration.
Water-break test: A visual check for cleanliness in which DI water is rinsed through glassware; a continuous, uniform film (no beading) indicates adequate cleaning.

5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Broken or chipped glassware can cause lacerations. Hot glassware from the drying oven (105 C) causes burns on contact.
Chemical: Concentrated acids (HCl, HNO3) used in acid baths are corrosive and emit irritating fumes. Alconox detergent is a mild irritant.

5.2 Emergency Procedures

Broken glass injury: Apply pressure with a clean cloth. If the cut is deep or contaminated with chemicals, seek medical attention.
Acid spill: Neutralize small spills with sodium bicarbonate; for large spills, use the spill kit and evacuate the area. See SOP-L003.

title: Glassware Cleaning and Preparation
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Inspection Before Use

Inspect every piece of glassware before use. Check for chips, cracks, stars, or deep scratches, especially around rims, spouts, and the base
Discard any piece that is broken, chipped, starred, or badly scratched. Place it in the designated broken-glass box (rigid cardboard container labeled “BROKEN GLASS”), not in the regular trash
Check volumetric glassware (flasks, graduated cylinders) for legible graduation marks. Do not use glassware with faded or unreadable scales.







TipTip



Run your fingernail gently around the rim of a beaker or flask. If you feel a nick or irregularity, the piece should be discarded. Chipped rims create stress points that can propagate into cracks during heating.




7.2 Routine Cleaning (General Laboratory Use)
Use this procedure for glassware that will be used for general chemistry, soil extractions (KCl, K2SO4), gravimetric analyses, and other procedures that do not require trace-metal cleanliness.

Rinse the glassware with tap water immediately after use to prevent residues from drying
Prepare a warm solution of Alconox detergent (approximately 10 g per liter of warm tap water) in the wash basin
Submerge the glassware and scrub all interior and exterior surfaces with an appropriately sized brush. Use brushes with wooden or plastic handles only; metal-handled brushes and worn brushes where the spine contacts the glass will scratch the surface
Pay special attention to the interior bottom of beakers and flasks, where residues accumulate
Rinse thoroughly under running tap water, inverting and filling each piece at least three times to remove all detergent
Perform a final rinse with three changes of deionized (DI) water
Invert the glassware on a peg-style drying rack or place upright in the drying oven at 105 C for 2–4 hours (see SOP-L105)







ImportantCritical



Do not allow acid to contact glassware before detergent is thoroughly removed. Acid reacting with residual soap creates a hydrophobic film that is difficult to remove and will interfere with subsequent analyses.




7.3 Acid Washing (Trace-Metal and Nutrient Analysis)
Use this procedure for glassware destined for trace-metal analysis (ICP-MS, ICP-OES, XRF digestions), nutrient analysis, or any procedure where the SOP specifies “acid-washed glassware.” All acid bath work must be performed in the fume hood.

Complete the routine cleaning procedure (Section 6.2) first. Glassware must be detergent-free before entering the acid bath.
Prepare the acid bath in a dedicated polyethylene tub inside the fume hood:

General acid bath: 10% (v/v) HCl in DI water
Trace-metal acid bath: 10% (v/v) HNO3 (Trace Metal grade) in DI water

Submerge the clean glassware completely in the acid bath, ensuring no air bubbles are trapped inside
Cover the tub with its lid and soak for a minimum of 4 hours; overnight soaking (12–24 hours) is preferred
Using acid-resistant gloves and splash goggles, remove the glassware from the acid bath
Rinse each piece with at least five changes of DI water. For trace-metal work, use Type I (18.2 M-ohm) water from the Milli-Q system for the final three rinses.
Place the rinsed glassware on a clean drying rack or in the drying oven. Do not use paper towels or Kimwipes to dry the interior of acid-washed glassware, as fibers introduce contamination.
Once dry, cover the opening of each piece with a clean watch glass, aluminum foil, or parafilm and label it “ACID WASHED” with the date







Note



The acid bath should be replaced when it becomes visibly discolored or after approximately 20 uses, whichever comes first. Record replacement dates in the acid bath log on the fume hood.




7.4 New Glassware
New borosilicate glassware is slightly alkaline from the manufacturing process. Before first use in quantitative analyses:

Soak the new glassware in a 1% HCl or 1% HNO3 solution for several hours
Proceed with the routine cleaning procedure (Section 6.2)
For trace-metal applications, also complete the acid-washing procedure (Section 6.3)



7.5 Stubborn Residues and Special Cases



Residue Type
Cleaning Method




Dried organic matter
Soak overnight in Alconox; scrub with brush


Mineral scale or precipitates
Soak in 10% HCl for 4+ hours


Grease or stopcock lubricant
Rinse with acetone in the fume hood, then routine wash


Biological residues (agar, culture media)
Autoclave before washing; see SOP-L002


Unknown or heavily stained
Soak in 10% HNO3 overnight; if persistent, contact the lab manager









WarningDo Not Use Chromic Acid



Chromic acid (potassium dichromate in sulfuric acid) was historically used as a glassware cleaner but is a potent human carcinogen and is prohibited in this laboratory. Use the acid-wash procedures described above instead.




7.6 Drying and Storage

Air-dry inverted on a peg rack, or oven-dry at 105 C for 2–4 hours (see SOP-L105)
Do not oven-dry volumetric glassware (volumetric flasks, graduated cylinders). Thermal expansion can permanently alter the calibration. Air-dry volumetric glassware only.
Store clean, dry glassware in designated cabinets with shelf liner
Store glassware inverted or covered to prevent dust accumulation
Keep acid-washed glassware in a separate, labeled section of the cabinet or on a dedicated shelf to prevent accidental use for non-critical applications

title: Glassware Cleaning and Preparation
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Water-Break Test
The water-break test is a simple visual check for cleanliness:

Rinse the interior of the glassware with DI water
Observe the drainage pattern as water sheets off the surface
Pass: Water forms a uniform, unbroken film across the entire interior surface
Fail: Water beads up, forms droplets, or breaks into rivulets, indicating residual organic contamination or grease

If the water-break test fails, repeat the cleaning procedure. If it fails again after acid washing, discard the piece, as surface damage may be preventing adequate cleaning.


8.2 Routine Verification

Perform the water-break test on a representative sample (1 in 10 pieces) from each cleaning batch
For acid-washed glassware, run a DI water blank through the glassware and analyze it on the target instrument (e.g., ICP-MS) to confirm background levels are below method detection limits
Record cleaning batch dates and water-break test results in the glassware cleaning log

text:
13 Appendix B: Acid Bath Preparation


13.1 10% HCl Acid Bath

Place the clean polyethylene tub in the fume hood
Fill the tub approximately 90% full with DI water
Slowly add concentrated HCl (approximately 37%) to reach a final concentration of 10% (v/v). For a 20 L bath, add approximately 2 L of concentrated HCl to approximately 18 L of DI water.
Always add acid to water, never water to acid
Label the tub with: acid type, concentration, preparation date, and a hazard warning
Cover with the fitted lid when not in use



13.2 10% HNO3 Acid Bath (Trace Metal Grade)

Follow the same steps as above, substituting Trace Metal grade HNO3 (Fisher A509P500) for HCl
Use Type I DI water from the Milli-Q system
This bath is reserved for trace-metal glassware only; do not cross-contaminate with the general HCl bath

title: Foreign Soil Handling and Import Permits
text:
This SOP outlines the mandatory practices for securely and safely handling, analyzing, and disposing of soils and sediments collected from outside the United States. The importation and movement of untreated foreign soil is classified by the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) as an extremely high-risk activity (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024b). Several levels of review and approval are required before a permit can be issued. This SOP has been written to fulfill the conditions of the EA Program’s APHIS foreign soil permit.
These practices are mandatory for all personnel working with foreign soils in the EA Teaching and Research Laboratory at Pomona College. Additionally, all persons working in the laboratory, even those not directly handling foreign soils, must read this SOP and be aware of standard operations involving quarantine materials so that a safe and secure laboratory environment is maintained.

title: Foreign Soil Handling and Import Permits
text:
This SOP outlines the mandatory practices for securely and safely handling, analyzing, and disposing of soils and sediments collected from outside the United States. The importation and movement of untreated foreign soil is classified by the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) as an extremely high-risk activity (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024b). Several levels of review and approval are required before a permit can be issued. This SOP has been written to fulfill the conditions of the EA Program’s APHIS foreign soil permit.
These practices are mandatory for all personnel working with foreign soils in the EA Teaching and Research Laboratory at Pomona College. Additionally, all persons working in the laboratory, even those not directly handling foreign soils, must read this SOP and be aware of standard operations involving quarantine materials so that a safe and secure laboratory environment is maintained.

title: Foreign Soil Handling and Import Permits
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All soils and sediments collected outside the United States and its territories that are imported to or processed in the EA Program laboratory
Does not apply to: Domestic soils (including soils from Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, which are not foreign countries under APHIS regulations); fully sterilized or commercially prepared soil reference materials
Analyses covered: ICP-MS, EA-IRMS (total C, N, S and stable isotope ratios), texture, organic matter content, and other parameters where soils can be disposed of properly after analysis
Location: Foreign soil storage in SGM 133 (designated cabinet); processing in SGM 134 (dedicated area)

text:
3 Responsibilities

title: Foreign Soil Handling and Import Permits
text:
4 Definitions

APHIS (Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service): The USDA agency responsible for protecting US agriculture from pests and diseases; regulates genetically engineered organisms and administers quarantine regulations; issues permits for importing soil and biological materials that could harbor plant pests or pathogens (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024b).
Autoclave sterilization: Treatment of soil at 121 °C and 15 psi for at least 30–60 minutes to inactivate plant pathogens, weed seeds, nematodes, and other regulated organisms; required by USDA APHIS before foreign soil may be used in experiments outside a permitted facility.
CBP (U.S. Customs and Border Protection): The federal agency that clears imported soils and plant material for entry into the United States, working alongside APHIS inspectors at Plant Inspection Stations.
Controlled import permit (PPQ Form 588): A USDA APHIS document authorizing the importation of specified soil or biological material under defined containment and handling conditions; the PI must obtain this before any foreign soil enters the United States (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024b).
Decontamination: A procedure that eliminates or reduces microbial contamination to a safe level with respect to transmission of infection; for foreign soils, typically achieved by autoclave or dry-heat sterilization.
Foreign soil: Soil or sediment originating outside the United States and its territories; regulated by USDA APHIS under 7 CFR Part 330 because of the risk of introducing exotic plant pests, pathogens, and invasive species (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024b).
Permitted facility: A laboratory or greenhouse that has been inspected and approved by USDA APHIS for work with imported soil or regulated biological materials; must meet physical containment requirements specified in the permit.
Plant Inspection Station (PIS): A USDA/CBP facility at a port of entry where imported shipments are inspected and cleared by APHIS and CBP inspectors before release.
PPQ Form 508: The green and yellow APHIS shipping label required for shipments of 3 lb or less that will be treated at the Plant Inspection Station.
PPQ Form 550: The black and white APHIS shipping label required for shipments routed directly to a USDA-approved permitted facility.
Regulated article: Any soil, plant material, or organism whose importation is controlled by USDA APHIS because of its potential to harbor or transmit plant pests or diseases.
ePermits: The USDA APHIS online system for applying for and managing import permits and requesting shipping labels (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024a).

title: Foreign Soil Handling and Import Permits
text:
5 Safety and Hazards

5.1 APHIS Quarantine Requirement
Soil is strictly controlled under APHIS quarantine regulations 7 CFR Part 330 because it can readily provide a pathway for introducing dangerous organisms into the United States. Importation of soil from foreign sources is prohibited unless authorized by APHIS under specific conditions, safeguards, and controlled circumstances described in a valid permit and/or compliance agreement. Noncompliance can result in permit revocation, fines, and legal action (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024b).


5.2 Required PPE

Standard laboratory coat
Nitrile gloves
Lab safety goggles
Closed-toe shoes



5.3 Storage Restrictions

Foreign soils must be stored only in the designated quarantine cabinet in SGM 133
Foreign soils must be processed only in the dedicated area in SGM 134
Soils must never be opened or processed outside these designated areas



5.4 Chemical Hazards
If chemicals are used during analysis (e.g., acids for digestion), review the Safety Data Sheets before beginning. For isopropyl alcohol used in decontamination, work in a well-ventilated area and keep away from ignition sources.


5.5 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety and SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling. For spills of foreign soil, see §11 (Spill Cleanup).

title: Foreign Soil Handling and Import Permits
text:
6 Personnel and Training Requirements
All personnel working with foreign soils must complete the following before handling any quarantine material:

Complete SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety training, including the annual Pomona College lab safety course
Read the USDA/APHIS Compliance Agreement (current agreement number on file with the PI)
Read the current Foreign Soil Permit (permit number on file with the PI) (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024b)
Read this SOP in full
Complete SOP-L105 Drying Ovens training (required for sterilization procedures)
Be signed off by the PI or lab manager







ImportantAll Lab Users



Even personnel who do not work directly with foreign soils must read this SOP so they understand the quarantine protocols in effect in SGM 133 and SGM 134. This is a condition of the APHIS permit.








NoteAPHIS Contact



For questions about the permit, shipping, or compliance, contact the local APHIS Plant Protection and Quarantine office. Verify current contact information with the PI before each import event, as personnel assignments may change.

title: Foreign Soil Handling and Import Permits
text:
8 Sample Collection and Import

8.1 Equipment Decontamination at the Collection Site
All field equipment must be thoroughly cleaned and disinfected of all soil residues at the collection site before packing for transport. Acceptable methods:

Soak in isopropyl alcohol for one hour, or
Soak and wash in hot water with detergent for 30 minutes



8.2 Shipping Foreign Soils

Pack soil and sediment samples in sturdy, leak-proof containers. Declare contents as “Soil samples.”
The primary container must be securely closed and watertight.
Enclose the primary container in a second, durable, watertight secondary container. Each container must be capable of containing the soil independently.
Attach the appropriate APHIS shipping label to the exterior of each shipping package (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024b):

PPQ Form 508 (green and yellow): For shipments of 3 lbs or less that will be treated at the PIS
PPQ Form 550 (black and white): For shipments routed directly to the USDA-approved facility (Pomona College)








WarningLabel Placement



Packages without APHIS shipping labels on the exterior may be refused entry even if labels are enclosed inside the package.



Each label is individually numbered with a distinctive barcode. The permit holder must request the appropriate labels at the time of permit issuance.
Additional labels can be obtained through the “My Shipments/Labels” feature in ePermits (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024a) or by emailing BlackWhiteGreenYellowlabelrequest@aphis.usda.gov.



8.3 Waybills

PPQ Form 508 shipments require two waybills: one international waybill to direct the shipment to the PIS, and one domestic waybill (placed inside the package) to direct the shipment from the PIS to the permit holder.
PPQ Form 550 shipments require one waybill to direct the shipment to the permit holder.

The waybill must include: carrier account number or postage, permit holder name, permit number, label number, delivery address, and telephone number. If the waybill address does not match the permit address, the package may be refused entry by CBP.


8.4 Hand-Carrying Soils into the United States
Permitted articles may be hand-carried into the U.S. only if (USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, 2024b):

Hand carrying was requested in the permit application and authorized in the permit conditions
The permit conditions list the specific steps that must be followed
If someone other than the permit holder will hand-carry, that person must be identified on the permit
The authorized hand-carrier must follow all permit conditions pertaining to hand-carried shipments

title: Foreign Soil Handling and Import Permits
text:
9 Receiving, Storage, and Logging

9.1 Receiving

Transport soils directly to the Biogeochemistry Lab quarantine cabinet in SGM 133. Under no circumstances may soils be opened or processed until they reach the quarantine cabinet.
Open containers only inside the designated closed room area in SGM 133 or SGM 134. Take all precautions to prevent the escape of any potential pest that may be in the soil.



9.2 Logging
Upon arrival at Pomona College, log every sample in the Foreign Soils Log Book. Each entry must include:







Field
Description

Year and consecutive number (e.g., 18-01)


Date of arrival
YYYY-MM-DD

Who collected the sample in the field

Unsterilized (red tag) on arrival





9.3 Labeling and Storage

Samples remain sealed in original Whirl-Pak bags within Ziplock bags until processed.
Store bags on shelf trays within the closed quarantine cabinet. Samples must not be left on tables or elsewhere when not in use.
All stored, unsterilized soils must be labeled with red tags stating “Quarantine Soil – Unsterilized.”
Sterilized samples must be labeled with green tags stating “Quarantine Soil – Sterilized.”
Any individual sample being processed outside its storage cabinet must also be clearly labeled to indicate sterilization status.

title: Foreign Soil Handling and Import Permits
text:
10 Treatment, Sterilization, and Disposal

10.1 Sterilization Method
Soil samples must be sterilized by dry heat treatment at 250 °C for 24 hours, or by one of the other approved methods documented in the Foreign Soils Log Book.






ImportantAll Residues Must Be Sterilized



All residues from processing (including ash, rinse water filter residues, and equipment rinse material) must be sterilized using the same methods as the soil itself.




10.2 Disposal
After sterilization, soils may be disposed of in standard solid waste. Document disposal date, mass, and method in the Foreign Soils Log Book.

text:

title: Chemical Inventory Management
text: This SOP establishes the procedures for managing the chemical inventory in EA Program laboratories. A current, accurate inventory is essential for safety (knowing what is on hand in an emergency), regulatory compliance (fire code limits on flammable storage, Pomona College Chemical Hygiene Plan), waste minimization (avoiding duplicate purchases and expired stockpiles), and research efficiency (knowing what is available before ordering) (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012; Standard on Fire Protection for Laboratories Using Chemicals, 2019).

title: Chemical Inventory Management
text: This SOP establishes the procedures for managing the chemical inventory in EA Program laboratories. A current, accurate inventory is essential for safety (knowing what is on hand in an emergency), regulatory compliance (fire code limits on flammable storage, Pomona College Chemical Hygiene Plan), waste minimization (avoiding duplicate purchases and expired stockpiles), and research efficiency (knowing what is available before ordering) (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012; Standard on Fire Protection for Laboratories Using Chemicals, 2019).

title: Chemical Inventory Management
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All chemicals stored in EA Program laboratories (SGM 133, 134, 135), including reagents, standards, solvents, acids, bases, compressed gases, and prepared solutions
Does not apply to: Common consumables that are not hazardous (Kimwipes, gloves, filter paper, etc.), or chemicals stored exclusively in other departments’ spaces
Location: All EA Program laboratory spaces

title: Chemical Inventory Management
text:
3 Definitions

CAS number (Chemical Abstracts Service Registry Number): A unique numerical identifier assigned to every chemical substance by CAS; the most reliable identifier for chemicals because, unlike common names, it is unambiguous; required on every inventory spreadsheet row.
Chemical Hygiene Plan (CHP): A written program required by OSHA’s Laboratory Standard (29 CFR 1910.1450) describing the safety procedures, equipment, and work practices in place to protect laboratory workers from hazardous chemicals; Pomona College’s CHP is maintained by EH&S (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Expiration date: The manufacturer-recommended date after which a chemical’s stated purity, concentration, or safety characteristics may no longer be guaranteed; after this date, the chemical must be tested or disposed of.
GHS (Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals): The United Nations system for standardizing chemical hazard communication; governs the content and format of Safety Data Sheets and container labels in the United States under the OSHA Hazard Communication Standard (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Hazard class: A classification of a chemical’s primary physical or health hazard (flammable, corrosive, oxidizer, toxic, carcinogen, etc.) per OSHA/GHS criteria; used to assign compatible storage locations and set fire code quantity limits (Standard on Fire Protection for Laboratories Using Chemicals, 2019).
NFPA 45: The National Fire Protection Association standard governing fire protection for laboratories using chemicals; sets maximum allowable quantities (MAQs) of flammable and combustible liquids that may be stored in different lab occupancy types (Standard on Fire Protection for Laboratories Using Chemicals, 2019).
Peroxide-forming solvent: A solvent that can spontaneously form explosive organic peroxides during storage (e.g., diethyl ether, THF, isopropanol); must be tested periodically with peroxide test strips and disposed of before the safe shelf life is exceeded; open-date label required on every container (National Research Council, 2011).
Safety Data Sheet (SDS): A standardized 16-section document (GHS format) describing a chemical’s identity, hazards, safe handling, storage, disposal, and emergency response; legally required to be accessible in the workplace for all hazardous chemicals; Section 7 (Handling and Storage) and Section 13 (Disposal) are most relevant to inventory management (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Small Quantity Generator (SQG): A US EPA RCRA designation for facilities generating 100–1,000 kg of hazardous waste per month; Pomona College’s classification, which sets specific accumulation time and storage requirements.
Surrogate chemical: A non-hazardous chemical used for training and demonstration purposes in place of a hazardous substance.

title: Chemical Inventory Management
text:
5 Safety Considerations
Accurate inventory management is a safety measure (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012; Standard on Fire Protection for Laboratories Using Chemicals, 2019):

First responders and the fire department use the chemical inventory to assess hazards during emergencies.
NFPA 45 fire code limits the total quantity of flammable liquids that may be stored outside of approved flammable-storage cabinets (Standard on Fire Protection for Laboratories Using Chemicals, 2019).
Knowing what is stored and where prevents accidental mixing of incompatible chemicals.
Expired chemicals (especially peroxide-forming solvents) can become hazardous over time (National Research Council, 2011).

See SOP-L003 for chemical storage, compatibility, and labeling requirements.

title: Chemical Inventory Management
text:
6 The Inventory System

6.1 Electronic Inventory
The EA Program maintains a shared Google Sheet (or equivalent spreadsheet) as the master chemical inventory. The spreadsheet is stored on the lab shared drive and accessible to all lab personnel.
Required columns:







Column
Description




Chemical name
Full name (no abbreviations or formulas only)


CAS number
Chemical Abstracts Service registry number


Manufacturer
Supplier name


Catalog number
Supplier catalog/part number


Lot number
Manufacturer lot number


Date received
YYYY-MM-DD

Amount and units (e.g., 500 mL, 100 g)


Current quantity
Updated when significantly depleted


Concentration/purity
If applicable (e.g., “ACS reagent grade, 37%”)


Expiration date
From manufacturer label, or calculated shelf life


Hazard class
Flammable, corrosive, oxidizer, toxic, etc.


Storage location
Room, cabinet/shelf code (e.g., SGM 133, Flam-1)


SDS on file
Yes/No


Owner/project
Who ordered it and for what project


Status
In use / Sealed / Expired / Disposed





6.2 Physical Labels
Every chemical container in the lab must have a label that includes:

Chemical name (spelled out)
Concentration (if a prepared solution)
Hazard warning(s) per GHS
Date received or date prepared
Researcher name
Expiration date (if applicable)

See SOP-L003, Section 6.4 for detailed labeling requirements.

title: Chemical Inventory Management
text:
7 Procedures

7.1 Receiving New Chemicals

Inspect the container for damage, leaks, or missing labels when the shipment arrives.
If the container is damaged or leaking, do not accept it into the lab. Notify the lab manager. Follow spill procedures in SOP-L004 if needed.
Add the chemical to the inventory spreadsheet immediately, completing all required columns.
Verify that the SDS is on file. If not, download it from the manufacturer’s website and add it to the SDS binder and the electronic SDS folder.
Label the container with the date received and the researcher’s name if not already present.
Store the chemical in the correct location based on its hazard class (see §5.3).



7.2 Ordering Chemicals
Before ordering a new chemical:

Check the inventory spreadsheet to see if the chemical is already in stock.
Check with other lab users to see if someone has an open container that can be shared.
Order only the quantity needed for the project. Purchasing excess chemicals generates waste and occupies storage space.
For highly hazardous chemicals, consult the PI and review the SDS before ordering (National Research Council, 2011).



7.3 Storage Assignment
Assign storage based on hazard class. Chemicals must be segregated by compatibility (Standard on Fire Protection for Laboratories Using Chemicals, 2019):







Hazard Class
Storage Location




Flammable liquids
Flammable-storage cabinet (yellow, self-closing)


Corrosive acids
Acid cabinet (under fume hood) – separate from bases


Corrosive bases
Base cabinet (under fume hood) – separate from acids


Oxidizers
Separate from flammables and organics


Toxics / reagents
General chemical shelves, secured


Compressed gases
Chained to wall or bench; away from corrosives


Refrigerated/frozen
Lab refrigerator or freezer (no food)









Important



Never store chemicals on the floor. Use low shelves or cabinets with front lips. Ensure shelves are fastened to the wall. See SOP-L003, Section 6.3 for detailed storage rules.




7.4 Using and Depleting Chemicals

When you open a sealed container for the first time, write the date opened on the label.
When a container is nearly empty or fully consumed, update the “Current quantity” and “Status” columns in the inventory spreadsheet.
Return every chemical to its designated storage location after use.



7.5 Disposing of Chemicals
When a chemical is expired, no longer needed, or in poor condition:

Update the inventory spreadsheet: change Status to “Disposed” and record the disposal date.
Follow the waste disposal procedures in SOP-L003, Section 8: fill out a waste tag, complete the packing manifest, and schedule pickup.
Do not pour chemicals down the drain unless explicitly permitted by the SDS and local regulations for that specific chemical.



7.6 Periodic Audits
Conduct a full physical audit of the chemical inventory at least once per year (typically at the start of the fall semester) (National Research Council, 2011):

Print the current inventory spreadsheet.
Walk through every storage location and physically verify each item.
Note discrepancies between the spreadsheet and actual stock.
Remove expired chemicals for disposal.
Update the spreadsheet to reflect the audit results.
File the annotated printout as the audit record.

title: Chemical Inventory Management
text:
8 Waste Minimization

Order the smallest quantity that will meet your needs.
Share chemicals across projects when possible.
Prepare only the volume of working solutions needed for an analytical session.
Substitute less hazardous chemicals when feasible (e.g., replace a halogenated solvent with a non-halogenated alternative).
Dispose of expired chemicals promptly rather than letting them accumulate.

See SOP-L003, Section 8.3 for additional waste minimization guidance.

Role

title: Hazardous Materials Handling
text:
4 Definitions

Caustic chemicals: Chemicals such as ammonium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, and sodium hydroxide that are able to burn or corrode organic tissue by chemical action.
Combustible liquid: A liquid with a flashpoint at or above 60 °C (140 °F); can burn at temperatures usually above normal working temperatures.
Corrosive chemicals: Strong acids and bases, dehydrating agents, nonmetal chlorides, and halogens that are health hazards and can damage skin, eyes, and respiratory tissue on contact. Store corrosives under the fume hood on low shelving or in approved storage cabinets. Gas cylinders should not be stored in the same cabinet with corrosive liquids. Segregate acids from bases and oxidizing acids from organic acids; separate nitric acid from all other acids.
Flammable liquid: A liquid with a flashpoint below 60 °C (140 °F) that can ignite easily at normal working temperatures.
Hazardous material: Any substance posing a physical or health hazard as defined by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200, including flammables, corrosives, oxidizers, toxins, and carcinogens (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 1990).
Safety Data Sheet (SDS): A standardized document describing a chemical’s hazards, safe handling, storage, disposal, and emergency response procedures; located on the counter near the east entrance and at the PPE shelves in SGM 133.

title: Hazardous Materials Handling
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Acids, bases, flammables, oxidizers, and toxic reagents are used routinely in EA Program labs.
Physical: Glassware breakage, heat from hot plates and ovens, compressed gas cylinders.
Biological: Soil and water samples may contain pathogens.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses / goggles
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves
Face shield (concentrated acids and bases)



5.2 Required Training

SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety before handling any hazardous chemical

title: Hazardous Materials Handling
text:
6 General Safe Handling Procedures

6.1 Working with Hazardous Materials

Read the SDS for every chemical before first use.
Never work alone when handling concentrated acids, bases, or flammables.
Use the fume hood when working with volatile, toxic, or corrosive chemicals.
Cap unused containers immediately; return chemicals to designated storage after use.
Purchase the smallest quantity needed; order corrosives in plastic-coated containers where available.



6.2 Physical Hazards
Glassware: Inspect glassware for cracks before use. Use extreme care when inserting glass tubing into stoppers. Use heat-resistant gloves near hot glassware.
Burns: Use hot plates or water baths instead of open flames. Tie up loose hair and wear snug-fitting, non-synthetic clothing when possible. Always use a fume hood with volatile organic compounds.
Chemical spills: Read the SDS before working with any hazardous chemical. Always wear PPE, cap unused chemical containers, and use fume hoods. Never work alone.
Mercury spills: Follow the college’s emergency instructions for mercury spill response.
Explosions: Develop written protocols for explosive chemicals. Use fume hoods; avoid experiments in closed containers; always wear PPE.
Chemical inhalation: Never breathe deeply from a chemical mixture. Use a fume hood; consider gas monitoring equipment for experiments that generate toxic gases.

title: Hazardous Materials Handling
text:
7 Chemical Storage

7.1 General Rules

Store chemicals by hazard class, not alphabetically.
Never store chemicals on the floor; use low shelves or cabinets with front lips.
Secure shelves to the wall. Ensure shelves have lips to prevent containers from falling.



7.2 Storage by Hazard Class







Hazard Class
Storage Location




Flammable liquids
Flammable-storage cabinet (yellow, self-closing)


Corrosive acids
Acid cabinet under fume hood (separate from bases)


Corrosive bases
Base cabinet under fume hood (separate from acids)


Oxidizers
Separate from flammables and organics


Toxics / reagents
General chemical shelves, secured


Compressed gases
Chained to wall; away from corrosives


Refrigerated
Lab refrigerator (no food); door labeled

title: Hazardous Materials Handling
text:
8 Waste Disposal
See SOP-L006 Waste Disposal for the complete waste classification and disposal procedures. Key rules:

Segregate waste by chemical compatibility (acids, bases, halogenated solvents, non-halogenated solvents, heavy metals).
Label every waste container with the chemical name, hazard class, and accumulation start date.
Never pour hazardous chemicals down the drain without verifying local discharge limits.
Schedule EH&S pickup when a container reaches 75% capacity or after 270 days of accumulation, whichever comes first.

title: General Laboratory Safety Plan
text:
5 Definitions
Laboratory Manager: A student, staff, or faculty member who has been trained and identified as the laboratory manager. The laboratory manager oversees all training and monitors all activities in the laboratory. The current laboratory manager is Assoc. Professor Marc Los Huertos.
Chemical Safety Officer: Assigned annually; responsible for maintaining SOPs, training researchers, and ensuring safe laboratory conditions (see SOP-L003).
PPE (Personal Protective Equipment): Protective clothing, goggles, gloves, or other garments designed to protect the wearer from injury or infection.
SDS (Safety Data Sheet): A document describing the hazards, safe handling, storage, disposal, and first aid for each chemical used in the lab. The SDS binder is located on the counter next to the east entrance to SGM 133. - Carcinogen: A substance capable of causing cancer in living tissue; classified by IARC (Group 1, 2A, 2B) or NTP; requires special handling, documentation, and medical surveillance in many jurisdictions. - Emergency eyewash station: A plumbed fixture that delivers a continuous low-pressure flow of water to both eyes simultaneously; located within 10 seconds of any area where corrosive chemicals are used; activate immediately after any eye contact with a hazardous substance and flush for a minimum of 15 minutes. - Fume hood: A ventilated enclosure that captures and exhausts chemical vapors, dusts, and fumes away from the work area; the sash must be kept at or below the safe working height marked on the hood. - Personal protective equipment (PPE): Wearable protection including safety glasses, splash goggles, face shields, lab coats, nitrile or other chemically appropriate gloves, and closed-toe shoes; selected based on the specific hazards of each procedure. - Safety Data Sheet (SDS): A standardized 16-section document (GHS format) describing a chemical’s identity, physical and health hazards, safe handling, storage, disposal, and emergency response; must be accessible for every hazardous chemical in the lab. - Secondary containment: A tray, cabinet, or outer container that holds spilled liquid if the primary container fails; required under all liquid chemicals stored above bench height and all corrosives.

title: General Laboratory Safety Plan
text:
6 Health and Safety

6.1 General Safety Rules

Developing a safe and productive environment is key to sustaining a strong scientific ethic; reflect on how you and your colleagues can promote safe conditions
All personnel must always employ a buddy system, whether working within or outside traditional work hours (8 AM – 5 PM), and on weekends
You must obtain written permission to work in the lab outside traditional hours
No work is allowed in the laboratory without expressed permission from the Laboratory Manager
No food, drink, or cosmetics in the laboratory
No headphones or earbuds that block auditory hazard warnings
Long hair must be tied back; loose clothing and dangling jewelry must be secured
Wash hands thoroughly before leaving the laboratory
Report all accidents, injuries, and near-misses to the lab manager immediately



6.2 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
When entering the lab:

Your legs should be covered
Wear closed-toed shoes (no sandals)
Put on a lab coat as you enter
Safety glasses or goggles (when working with chemicals)
Nitrile gloves (when handling chemicals or biological materials)
Wear a mask when working in the lab with another person (to protect against infectious diseases)

Additional PPE may be required depending on the procedure. Consult the specific SOP and the SDS for each chemical.


6.3 Emergency Equipment Locations
Know the location of the following before beginning any work:

Fire extinguisher (near the front entrance)
Safety shower (right and left sides of the lab)
Eyewash station (right and left sides of the lab)
First aid kit
Spill kit (mounted on the wall near the PPE shelves, entrance to SGM 133)
SDS binder (counter next to the east entrance)
Emergency exits
Lab contact list (posted in SGM 133; notify the lab manager if it seems out of date)

title: General Laboratory Safety Plan
text:
7 Emergency Procedures






ImportantEmergency Numbers




Campus Safety: (909) 607-2000 (from a campus phone, dial x72000) – open 24/7
Emergency: 911
Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222
CUC Student Health Services: 909-621-8222
CUC Environmental Health and Safety: 909-621-8538

When calling Campus Safety, be ready to provide your name, the location of the emergency, and your contact phone number. Campus Safety will assess the situation and call any necessary services (ambulance, fire department, etc.).
Pomona College On-Call Deans and the Monsour On-Call Counselor are reachable via Campus Safety’s emergency number.



7.1 Earthquakes
Earthquakes are common in southern California. Developing an effective strategy before an earthquake strikes is key to laboratory safety.
Indoor response:

Move away from windows, filing cabinets, shelves, chemicals, and other heavy objects that may fall
“Duck, Cover, and Hold” until shaking stops
If not near a table or sturdy desk, crouch against an interior wall and cover your neck and head
Once shaking stops, take any necessary items (phone, wallet, medication) and leave the building
Go to the nearest Pomona College evacuation site and wait for further instructions
Put on shoes as there could be broken debris
DO NOT USE ELEVATORS

Outdoor response:

Move away from buildings, trees, signs, electrical poles, and wires
Protect your head and neck
After shaking stops, go to the nearest evacuation site

Aftershocks may occur. Be prepared and follow appropriate evacuation plans if they do.


7.2 Fires and Evacuation
In the case of a small fire, you may attempt to use a fire extinguisher. Remember:

Remove people from the area
Activate the closest fire alarm
Call Campus Safety
Extinguish the fire only if safe to do so:

Place yourself between the fire and the exit
Pull the pin
Aim the nozzle toward the base of the fire
Squeeze the handle to release the extinguishing agent
Sweep the base of the fire from side to side

Use only one fire extinguisher; if the fire is not controlled after one, leave the room, close the door, and evacuate

If trapped in a building:

Call Campus Safety
Close all windows and doors
Wet and place cloth material around and under the door to prevent smoke from entering



7.3 Medical Emergencies

Call Campus Safety; let them know the victim’s condition
Provide necessary first aid until Campus Safety and/or emergency services arrive (only if trained)
Do not move the injured person unless necessary
See the campus evacuation map for AED locations



7.4 Chemical Spills
If there is a hazardous chemical spill in the laboratory, do not attempt to clean it up unless trained and equipped to do so. Refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling for spill response procedures.

If chemicals get in your eye, flush for 15 minutes at the eyewash station
If toxic materials are spilled on your body, remove all clothing and stand beneath the lab shower for 15 minutes
In the event of inhalation, move to fresh air
If someone is at risk, protect yourself first; only provide assistance if you can do so safely



7.5 Crime on Campus
Active shooter: Exit the building if safe to do so. If not, close and lock the laboratory door, turn off lights, pull down window shades, keep quiet, silence phones, and call Campus Safety.
Bomb threat and utilities failure: Review the Emergency Brochure posted near laboratory exits for detailed procedures.

title: General Laboratory Safety Plan
text:
9 Housekeeping

When you arrive, look around to identify any safety concerns and report them immediately to the Lab Manager
Keep work areas clean and organized
Return all chemicals and equipment to their designated storage locations after use
Clean up spills immediately using appropriate procedures
Dispose of waste in the correct containers (chemical waste, sharps, biohazard, general trash)
Do not block emergency exits, safety showers, or eyewash stations
Report broken or malfunctioning equipment to the lab manager

title: General Laboratory Safety Plan
text:
10 Ethical Efforts and Contributions
Working in the lab requires thinking carefully about what you are contributing and how others using the lab will find it. Each researcher is expected to leave the lab in better condition than they found it and to contribute to the ongoing improvement of safety documentation.

title: Chemical Spill Response
text:
5 Definitions

Carcinogen: A substance capable of causing cancer with repeated or prolonged exposure; minor spills of carcinogens (e.g., acrylamide, formaldehyde, chloroform, benzene) require extra precautions including respiratory protection and disposal as hazardous waste regardless of volume (National Research Council, 2011).
Corrosive: A chemical that causes visible destruction or irreversible alteration of skin, eye, or mucous membrane tissue on contact, or that corrodes steel or aluminum; includes strong acids (pH < 2) and strong bases (pH > 12); neutralized before disposal with appropriate Spill-X material (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Emergency eyewash station: A plumbed or pressurized portable fixture that delivers a continuous flow of clean water to both eyes simultaneously; required to be within 10 seconds of unobstructed travel from any hazardous chemical work area; must be activated for at least 15 minutes for any eye chemical contact (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Flammable liquid: A liquid with a flash point below 60 °C (140 °F); includes common laboratory solvents such as ethanol, methanol, acetone, hexane, and isopropanol; minor spills of flammables must be cleaned up with absorbent pads, not paper towels, and all ignition sources must be extinguished immediately (National Research Council, 2011).
Flash point: The minimum temperature at which a liquid produces sufficient vapor to ignite momentarily in the presence of a flame or spark; the key property for classifying a spilled liquid as a flammable hazard.
Major spill: A spill that cannot be safely managed by lab personnel; any spill meeting the criteria in §5.2 – including spills involving injury, unknown chemicals, large volumes, or highly toxic/reactive materials – requires evacuation and a call to Campus Safety; do not attempt to clean up a major spill.
Minor spill: A small spill of a known chemical with known hazards that trained lab personnel can safely clean up using available PPE and spill control materials; all criteria in §5.1 must be met before treating a spill as minor.
Safety Data Sheet (SDS): A standardized 16-section document describing a chemical’s identity, hazards, safe handling, first aid, spill response, and disposal; Section 6 (Accidental Release Measures) is the primary reference for spill response; must be accessible in the laboratory at all times (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Secondary containment: A tray, cabinet, or other physical barrier that holds spilled or leaked chemical if the primary container fails; required under all liquid chemical containers in storage; prevents spills from spreading and simplifies cleanup.
Spill-X-A / Spill-X-C / Spill-X-S: Commercial spill control kits manufactured by Ansul (Johnson Controls): A = acid neutralizer (for strong acids), C = caustic/base neutralizer (for strong bases), S = solvent absorbent (for flammable organic solvents); each kit changes color when neutralization is complete.
Universal absorbent: An inert granular or pad material (e.g., diatomaceous earth, Zorb-All pads) that absorbs chemical spills without reacting; suitable for a wide range of chemicals but does not neutralize acids or bases.

title: Chemical Spill Response
text:
6 Spill Classification
Before responding, classify the spill. Your response depends on the classification (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).

6.1 Minor Spill
A spill is minor if ALL of the following are true:

The chemical and its hazards are known (you have read the SDS)
The volume is small (less than approximately 500 mL of liquid or 100 g of solid)
No one is injured or exposed
The spill is confined to a small area (benchtop or floor, not spreading)
You have the proper PPE and spill control materials on hand
The chemical is not highly toxic, volatile, flammable, or reactive at the spilled quantity

Action: Clean it up yourself using the procedures in Section 7.


6.2 Major Spill
A spill is major if ANY of the following are true:

Someone is injured, contaminated, or experiencing symptoms
The chemical is unknown
The volume is large (more than approximately 500 mL or 100 g)
The spill involves a highly toxic, volatile, flammable, or reactive material at any quantity
The spill is spreading and cannot be easily contained
You do not have proper PPE or cleanup materials
You are unsure whether you can handle it safely

Action: Evacuate and call for help (Section 6).

title: Chemical Spill Response
text:
7 Major Spill Response

7.1 If in Doubt, Get Out
If you are unsure whether a spill is minor or major, treat it as major. Your safety is more important than preventing property damage.


Protect yourself and others.

Alert everyone in the lab. Help anyone who is injured or contaminated only if you can do so without endangering yourself.
If chemicals are on someone’s skin or in their eyes, begin flushing with water immediately (safety shower for body, eyewash for eyes). Continue flushing for at least 15 minutes (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Remove contaminated clothing while flushing.

Evacuate.

Clear all personnel from the room and close (do not lock) doors.
Activate the building fire alarm if there is a fire risk or if toxic vapors require building evacuation.

Call for help.

Call Campus Safety: x72000 or 909-621-8170.
For life-threatening emergencies: 911.
Notify the lab manager and PI.

Stay available.

Wait near the lab entrance (not inside) to brief first responders.
Bring the SDS for the spilled chemical to the responders.

title: Chemical Spill Response
text:
8 Minor Spill Response

8.1 General Procedure

Put on appropriate PPE before approaching the spill: gloves, safety glasses, lab coat at minimum; add face shield for large acid/base spills (National Research Council, 2011).
Inform others in the lab that you are cleaning up a spill.
Select the correct cleanup material (Section 7.2–7.4).
Apply cleanup material from the outside edge of the spill toward the center to prevent spreading.
Allow sufficient time for neutralization (Spill-X-A and Spill-X-C change color when complete).
Scoop up the spent absorbent and place in a labeled waste container (hazardous waste).
Wipe the area with a damp paper towel; dispose of used paper towels as hazardous waste.
Remove PPE carefully; wash hands.
Document the spill (Section 9).



8.2 Acid Spills
Use Spill-X-A (acid neutralizer). Apply the powder to the spill and mix gently with a spatula. When the color indicator shows neutralization is complete, sweep or scoop into a waste container. For spills involving HF (hydrofluoric acid): treat as a major spill regardless of volume; HF causes deep, potentially lethal burns with delayed onset.


8.3 Base Spills
Use Spill-X-C (caustic neutralizer). Apply and mix as for acid spills. Monitor for heat generation; some base reactions with neutralizer can be exothermic.


8.4 Flammable Organic Solvent Spills

Extinguish all ignition sources immediately (no open flames, turn off hot plates, do not use electrical switches).
Increase ventilation (open sash of fume hood, turn on exhaust fan).
Use Spill-X-S absorbent pads or granular universal absorbent. Do not use paper towels (can generate static or wick the solvent).
Collect all absorbent material in a waste container.
If vapors persist, evacuate and call Campus Safety (National Research Council, 2011).



8.5 Toxic or Unknown Chemicals
If the chemical is toxic (acutely hazardous, carcinogenic, or unknown): treat as a major spill and call Campus Safety. Do not attempt to clean up acutely toxic or carcinogenic spills without specific training and proper respiratory protection.

title: Chemical Spill Response
text:
10 Body and Eye Exposure Response

10.1 Skin Contact

Remove contaminated clothing immediately.
Flush the affected area with large volumes of water for at least 15 minutes (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2012).
Do not apply neutralizing agents directly to skin.
Seek medical attention.



10.2 Eye Contact

Immediately go to the eyewash station.
Hold eyelids open and flush both eyes continuously for at least 15 minutes.
Call Campus Safety or 911; all chemical eye exposures require medical evaluation.

title: Chemical Spill Response
text:
11 Documentation and Reporting
After every spill, including minor ones that were cleaned up successfully:

Complete the EA Program Spill/Incident Report Form (posted on the lab shared drive).
Record: date, time, location, chemical name and CAS number, volume spilled, who was involved, any exposures or injuries, actions taken, waste disposal method.
Submit the form to the PI within 24 hours.
The PI submits a report to Pomona College EH&S for any spill that resulted in an exposure or injury, required evacuation, or involved a reportable quantity of a regulated chemical (Pomona College, 2024).
Review the incident with the lab group within one week to identify how to prevent recurrence.
