title: Waste Disposal and Hazardous Waste Pickup
text:
4 Definitions

Characteristic hazardous waste: Waste that exhibits ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, or toxicity as defined by 40 CFR Part 261; must be managed as RCRA hazardous waste regardless of quantity.
EH&S (Environmental Health and Safety): The Pomona College department responsible for regulatory compliance, hazardous waste pickup scheduling, safety training, and chemical spill response coordination.
Hazardous waste manifest: A shipping document that tracks hazardous waste from the point of generation to the final disposal facility; prepared by EH&S and signed by the PI as generator.
Listed hazardous waste: Waste from specific industrial processes or containing specific chemicals appearing on EPA lists (F, K, P, U lists under 40 CFR Part 261); managed as RCRA hazardous waste.
Satellite accumulation area (SAA): A designated location at or near the point of waste generation where up to 55 gallons of hazardous waste (or 1 quart of acutely hazardous waste) may be accumulated without a time limit; must be under the control of the operator who generates the waste.
Small Quantity Generator (SQG): A US EPA RCRA classification for facilities generating 100–1,000 kg of hazardous waste per month; Pomona College’s status, which sets 270-day accumulation limits and specific storage, training, and emergency planning requirements.
Waste stream: A category of hazardous waste defined by chemical composition and hazard class (e.g., halogenated solvents, non-halogenated solvents, corrosive acids, heavy metal solutions); wastes must be segregated by compatible stream to prevent dangerous reactions during storage and transport.

title: Waste Disposal and Hazardous Waste Pickup
text:
5 Regulatory Context
Pomona College is classified as a Small Quantity Generator (SQG) of hazardous waste under RCRA (40 CFR Part 262) and California DTSC regulations. Key requirements:

Hazardous waste may be accumulated in satellite accumulation areas (SAAs) near the point of generation in containers of 55 gallons or less (1 quart for acutely hazardous waste)
Once full, containers must be moved to the central accumulation area and picked up by EH&S within 3 days
All containers must be labeled with the words “Hazardous Waste,” the contents, the hazard(s), and the accumulation start date
The generator (Lab PI) must sign the packing manifest

6.2 Hazardous Chemical Waste
Any waste that is ignitable, corrosive, reactive, or toxic (per RCRA D-list), or that is a listed waste (F, K, P, or U list), must be collected and disposed as hazardous waste. Common EA Program hazardous waste streams:

6.5 Drain-Disposable Waste

title: Waste Disposal and Hazardous Waste Pickup
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Labeling Waste Containers

Every waste container in the SAA must have a hazardous waste label (available from EH&S or the lab manager) before any waste is added
Fill in: waste description (chemical names and approximate percentages), hazard(s) (corrosive, flammable, toxic, etc.), accumulation start date, and laboratory location
Update the label if new constituents are added to the container



7.2 Accumulating Waste

Add waste to the appropriate labeled container in the SAA
Keep containers closed when not actively adding waste
Do not fill containers beyond 80% capacity (leave headspace for thermal expansion and safe handling)
Inspect containers weekly for leaks, corrosion, or label degradation



7.3 Requesting EH&S Pickup

When a container is full (or the study is complete), notify the lab manager
The lab manager contacts campus EH&S to schedule a pickup
Prepare a packing manifest listing: container number, contents (chemical names and approximate percentages), volume, hazard class, and generator (PI) name
The PI reviews and signs the manifest
Move the container to the central pickup area designated by EH&S
EH&S collects the waste, provides a manifest copy, and arranges off-site treatment or disposal



7.4 Empty Container Management

Triple-rinse empty reagent bottles with the appropriate solvent (water for aqueous chemicals, the same solvent for organic chemicals)
Remove or deface the original label
Collect rinse liquid as waste (add to the corresponding waste stream)
Clean, delabeled glass bottles may be reused for non-critical purposes or recycled
Do not reuse containers that held acutely hazardous (P-listed) chemicals; dispose as hazardous waste

title: Waste Disposal and Hazardous Waste Pickup
text:
8 Satellite Accumulation Area (SAA) Management

Each SAA is located at or near the point of waste generation (e.g., the fume hood where digestions are performed, the bench where extractions occur)
Maximum volume in an SAA: 55 gallons of hazardous waste (or 1 quart of acutely hazardous waste)
Containers in the SAA must be in good condition, compatible with the waste, and kept closed except when adding waste
Spill containment (secondary tray) is required under all liquid waste containers
The lab manager inspects SAAs monthly and logs the inspection on the SAA checklist posted in each area

title: Waste Disposal and Hazardous Waste Pickup
text:
9 Emergency Spill Response
For waste container spills, follow SOP-L004 Chemical Spill Response. Key points:

Contain the spill using absorbent materials appropriate to the waste type (do not use paper towels for solvent spills; use chemical absorbent pads)
Contaminated absorbent becomes hazardous waste; bag, label, and include in the next EH&S pickup
Report all spills to the lab manager and PI; document in the incident log

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
This SOP establishes the physical documentation standards for laboratory notebooks in the EA Program. A properly maintained notebook is a legal record that establishes what was done, when, by whom, and what was observed. These standards follow Good Documentation Practice (GDP) principles used in regulated laboratories and ensure that EA Program data are traceable, contemporaneous, and defensible (Kanare, 1985; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2002).
This SOP covers how to record. For what to record during an analytical session, see SOP-L802 Quality Control, Section 7.1. For field notebook protocols, see SOP-F003 Field Notebook Protocols.

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
This SOP establishes the physical documentation standards for laboratory notebooks in the EA Program. A properly maintained notebook is a legal record that establishes what was done, when, by whom, and what was observed. These standards follow Good Documentation Practice (GDP) principles used in regulated laboratories and ensure that EA Program data are traceable, contemporaneous, and defensible (Kanare, 1985; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2002).
This SOP covers how to record. For what to record during an analytical session, see SOP-L802 Quality Control, Section 7.1. For field notebook protocols, see SOP-F003 Field Notebook Protocols.

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All laboratory work performed under EA Program SOPs, including sample preparation, instrument operation, calibration, data reduction, and reagent/standard preparation
Does not apply to: Field notebooks (see SOP-F003) or purely electronic records in R scripts and Git (see SOP-L801), though electronic records should meet the same traceability standards (US Food and Drug Administration, 2004)
Location: All EA Program laboratories (SGM 133, 134, 135)

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




Lab PI
Set documentation standards; review notebooks


Lab Manager
Issue notebooks; maintain archive; verify compliance


All Lab Personnel
Maintain a notebook per this SOP


New Students
Read this SOP before beginning any lab work

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
4 Definitions

Archival ink: Ink formulated to resist fading, water, and chemical degradation over decades; required for all permanent laboratory notebook entries; ballpoint or pigment-based pens are preferred over roller-ball gel inks (Kanare, 1985).
Carbon-copy notebook: A notebook with interleaved carbonless copy pages that produce a duplicate of each entry; the copy is torn out and stored separately as a backup, while the original remains bound in the notebook.
Contemporaneous record: An entry made at the time the observation or action occurs, not reconstructed from memory afterward; the defining characteristic of a legally defensible laboratory record (Kanare, 1985).
GDP (Good Documentation Practice): A set of principles for creating accurate, legible, contemporaneous, original, and attributable records; the foundation of data integrity in regulated and research laboratories (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2002).
Single-strikethrough correction: The required method for correcting an error in a laboratory notebook: draw a single line through the incorrect entry so it remains legible, write the correct entry nearby, and sign and date the correction; erasing or using white-out is prohibited (Kanare, 1985).
Table of Contents (TOC): A running index of entries, maintained on the first 2 pages of every notebook, linking dates and topics to page numbers; enables rapid retrieval of specific entries.
Witness signature: A second person’s signature and date on a notebook entry confirming that they observed or reviewed the work; required for patent-related records and recommended for any significant observation.

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
5 Required Notebook Type
Use a bound, carbon-copy laboratory notebook with numbered pages (e.g., a 200-page carbonless copy notebook). Do not use spiral-bound notebooks, loose-leaf paper, or stapled pages as primary records. The carbon-copy notebook provides a built-in backup: the copy page is removed and stored separately, and the original remains permanently bound (Kanare, 1985).
Acceptable notebooks are available from the lab manager. Notify the lab manager when you are on the last 20 pages so a replacement can be ordered.

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
6 Setting Up a New Notebook

Write your name, contact information, the notebook serial number (if present), and the start date on the outside spine.
On the inside front cover, record: your name, contact information, project name, and the date the notebook was put into service.
Reserve the first two pages for a Table of Contents. Update the TOC as you fill the notebook.

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
7 Writing Instruments

7.1 Required
Write all entries in permanent, non-erasable ink (Kanare, 1985). Use a ballpoint pen that produces a clear impression on both the original and the carbon-copy page. Black or dark blue ink is preferred.


7.2 Not Permitted

Pencil (can be erased)
Gel ink or felt-tip pens that do not transfer reliably to the carbon copy
Erasable ink pens







Tip



Test your pen on a spare carbon-copy page before starting a new notebook. Press firmly enough to produce a legible duplicate, but not so hard that you tear the paper.

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
8 Entry Formatting

8.1 Every Entry Begins With
At the top of each new entry (or new day), record:

Date in ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD (e.g., 2026-05-18)
Your name (or initials, if your full name is on the inside cover and you are the sole user)
Purpose of the work session in one sentence (e.g., “TOC-L calibration and K2SO4 extract analysis, Project: BFS Soils”)
SOP(s) in use with revision numbers



8.2 Contemporaneous Recording
Write entries at the time the work is performed, not from memory afterward (Kanare, 1985). If you record a result on a printout, sticky note, or scrap paper during an urgent moment, tape or staple the original into the notebook and initial and date it at the earliest opportunity. Never discard the original note.


8.3 Level of Detail
Write enough detail so that another trained researcher could reproduce your work using only the notebook and the referenced SOP. At minimum, include all items listed in SOP-L802, Section 7.1 (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2002).


8.4 Printouts, Graphs, and Attachments
Tape or staple instrument printouts, chromatograms, calibration reports, or other documents directly into the notebook. Write across the border of the attachment and the notebook page so that it is clear the attachment was placed at that time. Initial and date each attachment.


8.5 Tables and Calculations

Draw tables with a ruler if practical.
Show all calculations, including units and intermediate steps, so that results can be verified.
Circle or box final results for easy identification.



8.6 Blank Space and Unused Pages

Do not leave large blank areas within an entry. If you finish an entry partway down a page, draw a diagonal line through the remaining blank space and initial and date it. This prevents later additions.
Never skip pages. If you accidentally skip a page, draw a diagonal line through it, write “INTENTIONALLY LEFT BLANK,” and initial and date it (Kanare, 1985).

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
9 Error Correction
If you make a mistake in the notebook (Kanare, 1985):

Draw a single horizontal line through the incorrect text so it remains legible.
Write the correct information directly above, below, or beside the crossed-out entry.
Write your initials and the date next to the correction.
If the error is extensive (e.g., an entire wrong entry), strike through the full section, write “Error – see page XX,” and rewrite the correct entry on the next available page.







ImportantProhibited Correction Methods




White-out, correction tape, or liquid paper
Erasing or scratching out (even when using pencil)
Tearing out or cutting out pages
Writing over an existing entry

Any of these actions raises data integrity concerns and may invalidate the record (Kanare, 1985).

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
10 Electronic Data References
When analysis is performed electronically (R scripts, instrument software, spreadsheets), record in the notebook:

The name and location of the electronic file (e.g., full file path or GitHub repository URL)
The date and time the file was created or the analysis was run
The software version or R version used

Cross-referencing electronic records ensures that the notebook and the digital record are linked and neither stands alone (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2002; US Food and Drug Administration, 2004).

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
11 Carbon-Copy Management

After completing each session, remove the carbon-copy page.
Review the copy for legibility. If the copy is not readable, note this on the original and on the copy.
Place the copy in the project’s designated folder on the lab shared drive or in the physical project file.
The original stays bound in the notebook permanently.

title: Laboratory Notebook Recording
text:
12 Signature and Witness

Sign and date each entry when you complete it.
If your work produces a significant new observation or result (a new datum, a method validation, a reproducibility test), have a witness (a labmate or the PI) sign and date the entry as well.
For IP-sensitive work, all entries should be witnessed at the time of writing, not retroactively.

13 Carbon Copy Storage and Notebook Archiving

13.2 Full Notebooks

Update the Table of Contents on the first two pages.

text: This procedure describes general best practices for preparing, labeling, storing, and documenting laboratory reagents and calibration standards used across EA Program analytical methods. Individual analytical SOPs specify the exact reagents and concentrations required for each method; this SOP provides the overarching framework for solution preparation that ensures traceability, accuracy, and safety.

title: Reagent and Standard Preparation
text: This procedure describes general best practices for preparing, labeling, storing, and documenting laboratory reagents and calibration standards used across EA Program analytical methods. Individual analytical SOPs specify the exact reagents and concentrations required for each method; this SOP provides the overarching framework for solution preparation that ensures traceability, accuracy, and safety.

title: Reagent and Standard Preparation
text:
2 Scope

Does not apply to: Preparation of biological growth media (covered in microbiology SOPs); preparation of molecular biology reagents (master mixes, primers, probes; see SOP-L701 and related SOPs); field reagent preparation (covered in field SOPs)

Role

title: Reagent and Standard Preparation
text:
4 Definitions

Blank solution: A solution prepared identically to calibration standards and samples but containing no analyte; used to correct for background signal and verify the absence of contamination in reagents and glassware.
Calibration standard: A solution of known analyte concentration prepared from a primary or secondary standard; used to establish the relationship between instrument signal and concentration.
Matrix-matched standard: A calibration standard prepared in the same solvent or extract matrix as the samples (e.g., 2 M KCl for soil extracts); minimizes matrix effects on instrument response.
Primary standard: A highly pure, chemically stable substance whose mass can be accurately weighed to prepare a solution of precisely known concentration without prior standardization; examples include potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP) and anhydrous sodium carbonate.
Reagent grade: A chemical purity classification (also called ACS grade) meeting minimum purity specifications set by the American Chemical Society; appropriate for most analytical work; trace-metal-grade or ultrapure-grade reagents are required for trace analysis.
Secondary standard (working standard): A solution prepared from a primary standard or a certified reference material (CRM) and used as the working calibration solution; must be verified against the primary standard periodically.
Stock solution: A concentrated solution of a reagent or standard prepared in bulk and used to prepare working solutions by dilution; labeled with concentration, preparation date, expiration date, preparer’s name, and any hazard information.
Volumetric dilution: Dilution performed using Class A volumetric glassware (volumetric flasks, pipettes) to achieve accurate, traceable concentrations; pipette to volume, mix thoroughly, then bring to final volume.

title: Reagent and Standard Preparation
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Concentrated acids, bases, and organic solvents used in reagent preparation are corrosive, toxic, and/or flammable. Review the SDS for every chemical before use.
Thermal: Dissolving some solutes (e.g., NaOH, H2SO4 dilution) is exothermic. Add solute to solvent slowly, never the reverse for acid dilutions.
Glassware: Volumetric flasks and graduated cylinders can break during mixing. Inspect for cracks before use.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses or splash goggles (for concentrated acids/bases)
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves
Fume hood (for volatile or fuming reagents)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For chemical splashes, flush with water for at least 15 minutes. For spills, follow SOP-L004 Chemical Spill Response.

title: Reagent and Standard Preparation
text:
6 Water Quality
All reagent and standard preparation must use water of appropriate purity:








Water Grade
Source
Use

title: Reagent and Standard Preparation
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Planning

Consult the relevant analytical SOP for the exact reagent name, concentration, and grade required
Calculate the mass or volume of solute needed using the target concentration and final volume. Document the calculation in the lab notebook.
Verify that the chemical in inventory matches the required grade (ACS reagent grade, trace metal grade, molecular biology grade, etc.)



7.2 Weighing Solids

Calibrate or verify the analytical balance per SOP-L200
Use a clean, dry weighing vessel (weigh boat or beaker)
Tare the vessel on the balance
Transfer the required mass of solid reagent using a clean spatula. Record the actual mass to the precision of the balance.
Return the reagent bottle cap immediately to prevent contamination and moisture uptake



7.3 Dissolving and Diluting

Transfer the weighed solid to a clean beaker and add approximately 75% of the final volume of water. Stir with a magnetic stir bar or glass rod until dissolved.
For acid dilutions: always add acid to water (“Do as you oughta, add acid to water”). Stir continuously and allow the solution to cool before adjusting to final volume.
Transfer the solution quantitatively to a volumetric flask of the target volume
Rinse the beaker and stir bar with small portions of water and add the rinses to the flask
Bring to the mark on the volumetric flask at room temperature. Read the meniscus at eye level.
Stopper the flask and invert 10 times to mix



7.4 Preparing Calibration Standards by Serial Dilution

Prepare or obtain a stock standard of known concentration (certified reference material or gravimetrically prepared stock)
Using calibrated volumetric pipettes or micropipettes (SOP-L103), transfer the calculated aliquot of stock solution into a volumetric flask
Dilute to the mark with the appropriate matrix (water, extractant solution, or acid matrix matching the samples)
Prepare the full calibration curve (typically 5–7 points plus a blank) in order from lowest to highest concentration to minimize carryover contamination
Record all dilution steps, pipette volumes, and flask sizes in the lab notebook







Tip



For trace-level calibration standards (ppb range), prepare fresh daily or per the stability guidance in the analytical SOP. Dilute standards degrade faster than concentrated stocks due to adsorption to container walls.




7.5 pH Adjustment (When Required)

After dissolving, measure the pH with a calibrated pH meter per SOP-L300
Adjust to the target pH using the appropriate acid or base (as specified in the analytical SOP), added dropwise with stirring
Record the final pH and the volume of acid/base added



7.6 Labeling
Every prepared solution must be labeled with the following information before it leaves the preparation bench:

Solution name and concentration (e.g., “0.5 M K2SO4”)
Solvent or matrix (e.g., “in DI water”)
Date prepared
Expiration date or shelf life (per the analytical SOP or manufacturer recommendation)
Preparer’s initials
Hazard warnings if applicable (e.g., “Corrosive,” “Flammable”)







Important



Never use an unlabeled solution. If you find an unlabeled container, do not use it. Dispose per SOP-L006 Waste Disposal.




7.7 Storage







Solution Type
Storage Conditions




Aqueous inorganic standards
Room temperature, dark; amber bottles for light-sensitive analytes


Organic solvent solutions
Flammable cabinet; fume hood if volatile


Buffer solutions
Room temperature or 4 C per the analytical SOP


Concentrated acids and bases
Acid cabinet (acids) or base shelf (bases); never store together


Molecular biology reagents
-20 C (primers, probes, enzymes) or 4 C (buffers) per manufacturer





7.8 Documentation
Record the following in the lab notebook for every prepared solution:

Reagent name, lot number, manufacturer, and grade
Calculation showing target concentration and volumes/masses
Actual mass weighed (to balance precision)
Final volume and flask size
Date prepared, preparer’s initials
Expiration date
Any deviations from the standard procedure

title: Reagent and Standard Preparation
text:
8 Quality Control

Verify the concentration of each new stock standard by analyzing it against the previous batch or against a certified reference material (CRM). Agreement should be within 5%.
For critical calibration standards, prepare from a second independent source (different manufacturer or lot) and compare
Discard solutions past their expiration date; do not extend shelf life without re-verification
Check volumetric glassware calibration (Class A tolerance) annually by gravimetric verification
Verify micropipette accuracy quarterly per SOP-L103

title: Using Balances
text: This procedure describes the proper use, zeroing, taring, and routine quality checks for the laboratory balances in the EA Program. Correct weighing technique is fundamental to virtually every quantitative laboratory procedure. For calibration and verification protocols, see SOP-L200 Analytical Balance Calibration.

title: Using Balances
text: This procedure describes the proper use, zeroing, taring, and routine quality checks for the laboratory balances in the EA Program. Correct weighing technique is fundamental to virtually every quantitative laboratory procedure. For calibration and verification protocols, see SOP-L200 Analytical Balance Calibration.

title: Using Balances
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All Mettler Toledo balances in the EA Program laboratory, including the basic balances (MS1602TS/00) and the precision balance (XPE205 DeltaRange) (Mettler Toledo, 2015a, 2015b)
Does not apply to: Portable field balances or calibration procedures (see SOP-L200)
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Using Balances
text:
3 Responsibilities



Role
Responsibility

Trained Personnel

New Students

title: Using Balances
text:
4 Definitions

Capacity (maximum load): The maximum mass that can be placed on the weighing pan without risking damage to the weighing cell; exceeding the rated capacity will damage the load cell and require expensive repair; the MS1602TS capacity is 1620 g and the XPE205 capacity is 220 g / 81 g (DeltaRange) (Mettler Toledo, 2015a, 2015b).
Draft shield: The glass or acrylic enclosure surrounding the weighing pan on the XPE205 precision balance; reduces air current disturbances that cause reading instability; always keep closed except when placing or removing items.
Drift: Gradual, directional change in the balance reading under constant load; caused by temperature changes, vibration, or electronic instability; the balance should be allowed to warm up for at least 30 minutes before critical weighing.
Linearity: The degree to which balance readings are proportional to applied mass across the full weighing range; verified during calibration per SOP-L200.
Net weight: The mass of sample only, after the tare weight of the container has been subtracted; what is displayed after pressing the Tare key with the container on the pan.
Readability (resolution): The smallest increment the balance can display; the MS1602TS reads to 0.01 g and the XPE205 reads to 0.1 mg (0.0001 g) (Mettler Toledo, 2015a, 2015b).
Repeatability: The standard deviation of repeated measurements of the same weight under identical conditions; a key short-term precision indicator; affected by vibration, draft, and sample placement position.
Spirit level (bubble level): A small bubble vial mounted on the balance base; the bubble must be centered in the target circle before weighing; off-level readings can introduce systematic errors.
Tare: The function that zeroes the displayed mass when a container is on the pan, so subsequent readings show only the mass of material added (Mettler Toledo, 2023).
Weighing cell: The internal transducer (typically an electromagnetic force compensation cell) that converts the mechanical load on the pan to an electrical signal; the most sensitive and expensive component of the balance; protect it from impact, overloading, and corrosive chemicals.
Zeroing: Setting the balance display to exactly zero with an empty pan and no load; performed at the start of each session and whenever the balance is moved; distinct from taring, which zeroes the balance with a container already on the pan.

title: Using Balances
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Dropping heavy items onto the balance pan can damage the weighing cell. Handle objects carefully and never exceed the rated capacity.
Chemical: Some materials weighed on the balance may be hazardous. Refer to the relevant SOP for the material being weighed. Never place chemicals directly on the weighing pan; always use a sample vessel.




5.1 Required PPE

Lab coat
Nitrile gloves (when handling chemical samples)
Safety glasses (when weighing chemical reagents)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
If a chemical spill occurs on or near the balance, clean the spill per SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling before resuming use.

title: Using Balances
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Startup and Warm-Up
Allow the balance to warm up for at least 30 minutes before making critical weighings (< 0.001 g significance) (Mettler Toledo, 2015b). This allows the internal components to reach thermal equilibrium.


7.2 Leveling the Balance

Check the spirit level before each use session.
If the bubble is not centered, adjust the leveling feet at the base of the balance.
For the XPE205, use the built-in leveling aid: Balance menu > Leveling aid (Mettler Toledo, 2015b).



7.3 Zeroing

Verify the balance is empty and the draft shield is closed.
Press Zero (or On/Zero). The display should read 0.000 g (for the MS1602TS) or 0.0000 g (for the XPE205).
If the display does not settle, check that the balance is level, no air currents are present, and the pan is clean and dry.



7.4 Taring

Zero the balance (§[sec-zeroing]).
Open the draft shield.
Place the sample vessel on the center of the weighing pan.
Close the draft shield.
Press the Tare key. The display reads zero and the Net indicator appears.



7.5 Performing a Weighing

Open the draft shield (if applicable).
Place the weighing object into the tared sample vessel.
Close the draft shield and wait for the stability indicator.
Record the displayed mass in the lab notebook.
If using the XPE205 electronic results feature, tap Add result to append the value to the results list.



7.6 Completing and Saving Results (XPE205)

Tap Complete to open the task completion dialog.
Select an option to save or print the results list.
Follow the on-screen instructions.
Tap Complete to finalize; the results list is saved or printed and then cleared.



7.7 Shutdown

Remove all samples and vessels from the weighing pan.
Clean the pan and draft shield interior with a lint-free wipe.
Close the draft shield.
To enter standby mode, hold the power/standby key. The display goes dark but the balance remains powered on and thermally stable.
To switch the balance off completely, disconnect from the power supply. Note that the balance will require a full warm-up before its next use.

title: Using Balances
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Leveling the Balance
Exact horizontal positioning is essential for repeatable and accurate results (Mettler Toledo, 2015b):

Check the spirit level before each use session.
If the message “Balance is out of level” appears, tap Level the balance to open the leveling aid.
Adjust the leveling feet following the on-screen instructions until the bubble is centered.



8.2 Internal Adjustment (XPE205)

Navigate to Methods > Adjustments.
Verify that the adjustment strategy is set to Internal adjustment.
Select the adjustment and tap Start.
Do not touch the balance during the adjustment.
When complete, review the adjustment results.
Tap Print if a record is needed, then tap Finish adjustment (Mettler Toledo, 2015b).

For external calibration verification using traceable reference weights, see SOP-L200.

text:
9 Waste Disposal
No waste is generated by this procedure. Cleaning materials (Kimwipes) can be disposed of in standard trash unless they contacted hazardous chemicals, in which case follow SOP-L003.

title: Using a Vortex Mixer
text: This procedure describes the operation and care of vortex mixers used in the EA Program laboratory. Vortex mixers produce a rapid orbital or oscillating motion that creates a vortex inside a tube or small container, providing fast and thorough mixing of liquids, suspensions, and reagents. They are used routinely in DNA extraction (SOP-L700), Qubit sample preparation (SOP-L213), chemical extractions, and general reagent mixing.

title: Using a Vortex Mixer
text: This procedure describes the operation and care of vortex mixers used in the EA Program laboratory. Vortex mixers produce a rapid orbital or oscillating motion that creates a vortex inside a tube or small container, providing fast and thorough mixing of liquids, suspensions, and reagents. They are used routinely in DNA extraction (SOP-L700), Qubit sample preparation (SOP-L213), chemical extractions, and general reagent mixing.

title: Using a Vortex Mixer
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All vortex mixers in the EA Program laboratory, including the Fisher Scientific vortex mixers (SGM 134, qty 3) and the Vortex-Genie 2 (SGM 133)
Does not apply to: Orbital shakers (for extended, gentle agitation of multiple samples); magnetic stir plates; sonicators (see SOP-L115)
Location: SGM 133 and SGM 134

text:

title: Using a Vortex Mixer
text:
4 Definitions

Continuous mode: A vortex mixer operating mode in which the platform spins continuously when the power switch is on; used when mixing many tubes in sequence without holding each one.
Touch mode: A vortex mixer operating mode in which the platform spins only when downward pressure is applied to the platform; allows the user to control mixing duration for each tube individually.
Vortex: A spiral or whirling motion of liquid produced when a tube’s closed end is pressed off-center against a spinning platform; efficient for resuspending pellets, dissolving solids, and homogenizing small volumes.
Vortex mixer (Vortex-Genie): A benchtop mixer with an eccentric rotating cup or platform that creates a vortex in tubes pressed against it; operated at variable speeds (typically 0–3,200 rpm).

title: Using a Vortex Mixer
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Aerosol generation: Vortexing uncapped or loosely capped tubes can spray liquid and generate aerosols. Always cap tubes securely before vortexing. If the sample contains hazardous biological or chemical material, vortex inside a fume hood or biological safety cabinet.
Tube ejection: At high speed, improperly held tubes can slip from the cup head and be thrown from the mixer. Hold tubes firmly against the cup or use the hands-free cup attachment.
Breakage: Thin-walled glass tubes may shatter under vigorous vortexing. Use polypropylene or thick-walled borosilicate tubes whenever possible.
Entanglement: Keep hands, hair, jewelry, and loose clothing away from the spinning cup head.
Electrical: Do not operate the mixer with a damaged power cord or loose components. Inspect the cord before use; report damage to the lab manager.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses
Nitrile gloves (standard lab PPE)
Lab coat

title: Using a Vortex Mixer
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Use Inspection

Verify the vortex mixer is clean and free from visible damage
Ensure the power cord is intact and properly connected
Check that the rubber cup head or attachment is securely installed and not cracked or deformed



7.2 Setup

Verify that the vortex mixer is on a stable, flat bench surface and that the rubber feet are intact (prevents the unit from walking during operation)
Confirm that the appropriate head is installed:

Cup head: for individual tubes (microcentrifuge tubes, 15 mL and 50 mL centrifuge tubes, glass test tubes)
Platform head: for microplates or tube racks (if available)

Set the speed dial to the desired setting. For most routine mixing, a medium speed (setting 5–7 on the Vortex-Genie 2 dial) is sufficient. Use lower speeds for gentle mixing and higher speeds for vigorous vortexing (e.g., bead disruption steps in DNA extraction).



7.3 Operation – Touch Mode
Touch mode is the default for most applications. The mixer runs only while the tube is pressed against the cup head.

Cap the tube securely
Hold the tube at a slight angle (approximately 15–30 degrees from vertical) and press the bottom of the tube firmly into the center of the cup head
The motor engages automatically. A visible vortex should form in the liquid.
Vortex for the duration specified in the analytical SOP (typically 2–5 seconds for brief mixing, 10–30 seconds for thorough resuspension)
Release the tube from the cup to stop



7.4 Operation – Continuous Mode
Use continuous mode for hands-free operation or when extended vortexing is required.

Switch the mode selector to Continuous (or On)
Adjust the speed dial to the desired setting
Place the capped tube in the cup head or in a tube holder secured to the platform head
The motor runs continuously at the set speed
After the prescribed duration, switch back to Touch mode or turn off the unit
Remove the tube



7.5 Vortexing Multiple Tubes
For rapid sequential vortexing of many tubes (e.g., a rack of Qubit assay tubes):

Set the mixer to touch mode at the desired speed
Work through the rack systematically, pressing each tube against the cup for 2–3 seconds
Return each tube to the rack before picking up the next

For simultaneous vortexing of a plate or rack, attach the platform head and secure the plate or rack with the provided clamp or tape. Run in continuous mode for the prescribed duration.

text: This procedure describes the proper use, sample storage protocols, and inventory management for the laboratory refrigerator (4 C), freezer (approximately –30 C), and ultra-low freezer (approximately –80 C). Proper cold storage is essential for preserving sample integrity for chemical, biological, and molecular analyses (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Refrigerators and Freezers
text: This procedure describes the proper use, sample storage protocols, and inventory management for the laboratory refrigerator (4 C), freezer (approximately –30 C), and ultra-low freezer (approximately –80 C). Proper cold storage is essential for preserving sample integrity for chemical, biological, and molecular analyses (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Refrigerators and Freezers
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All use of the laboratory refrigerator (4 C), freezer (–30 C), and ultra-low freezer (–80 C) for sample preservation and reagent storage
Does not apply to: Food storage (prohibited), field coolers, or cryogenic storage (liquid nitrogen)
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Refrigerators and Freezers
text:
3 Definitions

Cold chain: The unbroken sequence of refrigerated storage and transport that maintains samples at the required temperature from collection through analysis; a break in the cold chain may compromise sample integrity.
Cryogenic storage: Storage at temperatures below -80 °C, achieved with ultra-low freezers or liquid nitrogen dewars; required for DNA, RNA, enzymes, and some biological samples.
Freezer burn: Dehydration and oxidation of samples stored improperly in a freezer, caused by sublimation of ice crystals; prevented by airtight sealing of containers.
Holding temperature: The target storage temperature specified by the analytical method or regulatory protocol for a given sample type (e.g., 4 °C for water samples, -20 °C for soil extracts, -80 °C for nucleic acids).
Temperature excursion: An event in which the storage temperature falls outside the acceptable range; must be documented and the potential impact on sample integrity evaluated.
Ultra-low freezer (-80 °C): A mechanical freezer capable of maintaining temperatures between -70 °C and -86 °C; used for long- term storage of DNA, RNA, microbial cultures, and enzyme preparations.

5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: The –80 C freezer poses a risk of cold burns (frostbite) upon contact with surfaces or samples. Heavy drawers and racks can cause crush injuries if dropped.
Chemical: No flammable materials may be stored in the laboratory refrigerator or freezers. These units are not explosion-proof and can generate significant static electricity, which can cause an explosion in the presence of flammable fumes.
Electrical: Power outages can compromise stored samples (see Section 7).









Important



No food or beverages shall be stored in the laboratory refrigerator or freezers under any circumstances.

5.2 Emergency Procedures
For cold burns, warm the affected area gradually with lukewarm water; do not rub. Seek medical attention if blistering occurs. Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety.

7 Procedure

7.1 Refrigerator (4 C)

7.2 Freezer (–30 C)

Label all containers with: sample ID, date, researcher name, and project
Organize samples by project; do not mix projects within the same shelf area
TBD – define shelf assignment and inventory system for the –30 C freezer



7.3 Ultra-Low Freezer (–80 C)
The –80 C freezer is organized using a hierarchical location system. Every sample must be documented in the Freezer Inventory Google Sheet and in your laboratory notebook.

7.3.1 Loading Protocol

When loading the freezer for the first time or after defrosting, install a few drawers at a time from top to bottom, allowing the freezer to stabilize between additions
Only open the freezer when you are ready to place or remove samples. Minimize the time the door is open.
Wear insulated cryogenic mittens and a lab coat when accessing the freezer



7.3.2 Location Hierarchy
The freezer inventory uses the following hierarchy:

Shelf: Each shelf is contained behind an inner door, numbered from top to bottom. (Note: Shelf 1 is currently empty.)
Divider: Each divider is a column of drawers within the shelf, labeled A through E from left to right
Drawer: Drawers are numbered sequentially from top to bottom within each divider
Box: Each drawer contains five boxes, labeled 1 through 5 from front to back
Box position: Each box is divided into 100 positions. Numbering runs from front-left (position 1) to back-right (position 100), counting along rows from left to right



7.3.3 Required Inventory Fields
Record the following in the Google Sheet and in your lab notebook each time you store or remove a sample:

Date sample was collected in the field

Unique sample identifier

Description including any relevant analytical results (e.g., NanoDrop concentration)









TipTip



Before opening the freezer, identify the exact shelf, divider, drawer, box, and position you need. Have all your samples labeled and ready to go. This minimizes the time the door is open and protects the integrity of all stored samples.

title: Refrigerators and Freezers
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Temperature Monitoring

Check and record the temperature of each unit daily (or use a continuous temperature logger)
Acceptable ranges: refrigerator 2–6 C; freezer –25 to –35 C; ultra-low freezer –75 to –85 C
If temperature is outside the acceptable range, investigate immediately (door left ajar, power outage, compressor failure)
TBD – establish an alarm system or temperature logging protocol with automatic notifications



8.2 Power Outage Protocol






ImportantPower Outage Response



If the power goes out, it is imperative that valuable samples in either freezer be moved to a location where power is currently available to maintain freezing conditions. The laboratory generators do not provide sufficient power to keep any of the refrigerators or freezers at their appropriate temperatures.

Contact the lab manager and PI immediately
Do not open freezer doors unless moving samples to a backup location
A closed –80 C freezer can maintain temperature for approximately 24 hours if the door remains shut
If power is not expected to be restored within 4 hours, arrange to transfer critical samples to a backup freezer on campus
TBD – identify backup freezer locations on campus and establish agreements for emergency sample transfer





8.3 Inventory Maintenance

Conduct a full inventory audit of the –80 C freezer at least once per semester
Remove samples from completed or abandoned projects promptly
Ensure the Google Sheet is current; discrepancies between the sheet and actual contents must be resolved immediately

title: Thermo Scientific Sorvall ST8R Centrifuge
text: This procedure describes the safe setup, operation, and maintenance of the Thermo Scientific Sorvall ST8R centrifuge. The centrifuge is used to separate substance mixtures of different densities and is integral to sample preparation workflows across multiple laboratory SOPs (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).

title: Thermo Scientific Sorvall ST8R Centrifuge
text: This procedure describes the safe setup, operation, and maintenance of the Thermo Scientific Sorvall ST8R centrifuge. The centrifuge is used to separate substance mixtures of different densities and is integral to sample preparation workflows across multiple laboratory SOPs (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).

title: Thermo Scientific Sorvall ST8R Centrifuge
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Thermo Scientific Sorvall ST8/8R centrifuge in the EA Program laboratory
Does not apply to: Clinical centrifuges (see SOP-L108), microcentrifuges (see SOP-L26), or field-portable centrifuges
Location: EA Program laboratory, Pomona College

title: Thermo Scientific Sorvall ST8R Centrifuge
text:
3 Definitions

Balancing: The process of pairing tubes of equal mass (within 0.1 g) in opposite rotor positions; required to prevent rotor imbalance, vibration, and bearing damage; failure to balance is the leading cause of centrifuge damage and injury (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).
Fixed-angle rotor: A rotor that holds tubes at a fixed angle (typically 20–45° from vertical); particles pellet against the side and bottom of the tube.
g-force (relative centrifugal force, RCF): The centrifugal acceleration expressed as a multiple of gravitational acceleration (9.81 m s-2); calculated as \(\text{RCF} = 1.118 \times 10^{-5} \times r \times N^2\) where \(r\) is the rotor radius in cm and \(N\) is speed in rpm (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).
Pellet: The solid material sedimented to the bottom (or side-bottom) of a centrifuge tube after centrifugation.
Supernatant: The liquid layer remaining above the pellet after centrifugation; the fraction of interest in many extraction procedures.
Swinging-bucket rotor: A rotor whose buckets pivot to a horizontal position during spinning; particles pellet at the base of the tube, producing a well-defined pellet and cleaner supernatant.

title: Thermo Scientific Sorvall ST8R Centrifuge
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Rotating rotor stores significant kinetic energy; rotor or bucket failure can eject debris. Maintain a 30 cm clear zone around the centrifuge during operation. Never open the door until the rotor has completely stopped and the display confirms it (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).
Chemical: Corrosive samples can damage rotors and accessories if not cleaned promptly after use.
Biological: Pathogenic or biohazardous samples require sealed tubes or biosafety rotor lids. The centrifuge is not aerosol-tight in the event of mechanical failure (World Health Organization, 2020).




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves (when handling samples)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
In the event of a hazardous spill or rotor failure:

Turn off the power supply immediately; pull the power plug if necessary.
Leave the area and do not attempt to open the centrifuge.
Contact the lab manager and refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.
The emergency door release may be used only to recover samples during a power failure, not during mechanical failure (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).

title: Thermo Scientific Sorvall ST8R Centrifuge
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Site Selection and Setup

Operate the centrifuge indoors only.
Place on a horizontally leveled, rigid surface with adequate load-bearing capacity.
Maintain a safety zone of at least 30 cm around the centrifuge; do not place any hazardous substances within this zone (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).
Ensure the setup location is well-ventilated and not exposed to heat or direct sunlight.
Plug only into properly grounded sockets.
Keep the main plug freely accessible at all times.



7.2 Preparation

Inspect the rotor, buckets, and accessories for signs of corrosion, cracks, or removed protective coating; do not use damaged components (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).
Do not modify the mechanical components of the rotor or alter any electronic components of the centrifuge.
Load the rotor properly: always balance samples symmetrically.
Never overload the rotor beyond its rated capacity.
Verify that the rotor is locked securely into place before closing the door.
When working with corrosive samples, ensure tubes are fully sealed.







ImportantHazardous Substances




Do not centrifuge explosive or flammable materials.
Do not centrifuge toxic, radioactive, or pathogenic materials without appropriate safety precautions and sealed rotor lids (World Health Organization, 2020).
The centrifuge is neither inert nor explosion-protected; never operate in an explosion-prone environment.
Use fully sealed tubes for highly corrosive substances that could impair rotor mechanical stability.





7.3 Operation

Close the centrifuge door before starting a run.
Set the desired speed, temperature (8R model), and time using the control panel.
Press START to begin the run.
Do not move, lean on, or place anything on top of the centrifuge while it is running.
Minimize time spent near the centrifuge during operation (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).
Wait until the rotor has come to a complete stop and the display confirms it before opening the door.
Never open the centrifuge while the rotor is spinning.







TipEmergency Stop



Press the STOP key to shut down the centrifuge at any time. In an emergency, pull the power supply plug to disconnect power immediately (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).




7.4 Shutdown and Cleanup

Remove samples promptly after the run is complete.
Inspect the rotor and chamber for spills or condensation.
If corrosive samples were centrifuged, clean the rotor, buckets, and chamber thoroughly with deionized water and dry before storage (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).
If toxins or pathogenic substances have contaminated the centrifuge, carry out appropriate disinfection before further use (World Health Organization, 2020).
Wipe down the exterior of the centrifuge.
Leave the door slightly ajar to allow the chamber to dry (if no hazardous residues are present).



7.5 Cover Panel and Door Safety

Never operate the centrifuge if cover panels are damaged or missing.
Do not attempt to bypass the door interlock mechanism.
If mechanical failure occurs (rotor or bucket crash), the centrifuge is not aerosol-tight; leave the room and contact the lab manager (World Health Organization, 2020).

8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Visually inspect the rotor and accessories before each use for cracks, corrosion, or wear (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).
Verify that samples are properly balanced before every run.
Confirm the door closes and latches securely.
Report any unusual vibrations, noises, or error messages to the lab manager immediately.
Follow the manufacturer’s maintenance schedule in the instruction manual (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2016).

title: Autoclave and Steam Sterilization
text: This procedure describes the safe operation and maintenance of the laboratory autoclave for steam sterilization of glassware, media, reagent water, and biohazardous waste. Autoclaving uses saturated steam under pressure (typically 121 C at 15 psi for 15–30 minutes) to achieve sterilization by denaturing proteins and nucleic acids in microorganisms. In the EA Program, the autoclave is used to sterilize equipment for microbiological analyses (e.g., SOP-L305 Colilert), to decontaminate foreign soil samples (SOP-L015), and to sterilize waste before disposal.

title: Autoclave and Steam Sterilization
text: This procedure describes the safe operation and maintenance of the laboratory autoclave for steam sterilization of glassware, media, reagent water, and biohazardous waste. Autoclaving uses saturated steam under pressure (typically 121 C at 15 psi for 15–30 minutes) to achieve sterilization by denaturing proteins and nucleic acids in microorganisms. In the EA Program, the autoclave is used to sterilize equipment for microbiological analyses (e.g., SOP-L305 Colilert), to decontaminate foreign soil samples (SOP-L015), and to sterilize waste before disposal.

title: Autoclave and Steam Sterilization
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All use of the laboratory autoclave in EA Program laboratories for sterilization of liquids, solids, glassware, and biohazardous waste
Does not apply to: Dry heat sterilization (use muffle furnace or drying oven); chemical sterilization (e.g., bleach, ethylene oxide); filter sterilization (see SOP-L114)
Location: TBD (confirm autoclave location; shared facility or SGM)

title: Autoclave and Steam Sterilization
text:
3 Definitions

Autoclave: A pressurized vessel that uses saturated steam to achieve sterilization by heating materials to 121 °C at 15 psi (103 kPa) for a defined exposure time.
Biological indicator: A standardized preparation of resistant bacterial spores (typically Geobacillus stearothermophilus) used to verify that the autoclave cycle achieved sterilization; must be run periodically to validate cycle effectiveness.
Chemical indicator (autoclave tape): Tape printed with a dye that changes color when exposed to steam and heat; indicates that the item was exposed to the cycle but does not confirm sterilization.
Gravity displacement cycle: A standard autoclave cycle in which steam enters from the top, displaces cooler air downward and out through a drain; used for wrapped instruments, glassware, and liquid media.
Liquid cycle: An autoclave cycle with a slow exhaust phase to prevent superheated liquids from boiling violently when pressure is released; required for all liquid loads.
Sterilization: The complete elimination of all viable microorganisms, including bacterial endospores; achieved by saturated steam at 121 °C for at least 15 minutes at 15 psi.
Wrapped load: Items wrapped in autoclave paper or placed in autoclave pouches before sterilization; wrapping maintains sterility after the cycle.

title: Autoclave and Steam Sterilization
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Thermal/Pressure: The autoclave operates at 121 C and 15 psi. Pressurized steam causes severe burns. Never attempt to open the door while the chamber is pressurized.
Scalding liquids: Autoclaved liquids are superheated and can boil violently (bumping) when disturbed. Allow liquids to cool inside the chamber for at least 10 minutes after the cycle completes, and open the door slowly.
Glassware failure: Cracked or starred glassware may shatter under pressure. Inspect all glassware before loading.
Biological: Biohazardous waste must be contained in autoclave bags. Assume the exterior of bags is contaminated until the cycle is verified.




5.1 Required PPE

Heat-resistant gloves (autoclave gloves, rated for steam)
Safety glasses or face shield
Lab coat
Closed-toed shoes



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For steam burns, flush with cool running water for at least 20 minutes and seek medical attention. If the autoclave fails to depressurize, do not force the door; shut off power and contact the lab manager. Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety.

text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Use Inspection

Check the water level in the autoclave reservoir; refill with distilled or deionized water if below the minimum mark
Inspect the door gasket for cracks, brittleness, or debris; clean if needed
Verify that the drain screen/strainer is clear of debris
Ensure the pressure gauge reads zero and the chamber is at ambient temperature



7.2 Loading

Select the appropriate cycle for the load type:

Cycle

Place items in autoclave-safe trays. Do not overload; leave space for steam circulation.
For liquids: loosen caps or cover with foil. Place containers in a secondary tray to catch boil-over.
For waste bags: leave bags slightly open or use bags with steam-permeable patches. Place bags upright in a tray.
Place a chemical integrator strip inside the center of the load (the coldest point)
Apply autoclave indicator tape to the outside of each package or bag



7.3 Running the Cycle

Close and latch the autoclave door securely
Select the appropriate cycle (see table above)
Start the cycle and record the start time in the autoclave logbook
Monitor the temperature and pressure gauges during the initial pressurization to confirm normal operation
Do not leave the area until the autoclave has reached operating temperature and pressure



7.4 Unloading

When the cycle is complete, verify that the chamber pressure has returned to zero before opening the door
Crack the door open 1–2 cm and wait 2–5 minutes to allow residual steam to vent (prevents steam flash and liquid bumping)
Wearing autoclave gloves and face shield, open the door fully
Allow liquids to sit in the chamber for an additional 10 minutes after opening the door before removing
Remove trays using autoclave gloves; place on a heat-resistant surface away from foot traffic
Check the chemical integrator strip: it should show a complete color change indicating adequate steam exposure. If incomplete, the load must be re-processed.
Record the cycle completion time, temperature, pressure, and integrator result in the autoclave logbook



7.5 Waste Handling After Sterilization

After a successful waste cycle, seal the autoclave bags
Sterilized biohazardous waste can be disposed in the regular trash only if the institution’s waste policy permits this and the biological indicator program confirms efficacy
Label the sealed bag with “Autoclaved” and the date
If the chemical integrator did not pass, do not dispose; re-run the cycle or contact the lab manager



7.6 Shutdown

After the final cycle of the day, drain the chamber if the manufacturer recommends it
Leave the door slightly ajar to allow the chamber to dry and prevent odor buildup
Wipe the door gasket with a damp cloth to remove debris

title: Autoclave and Steam Sterilization
text:
8 Verification and Quality Control

Chemical indicators: Include a Class 5 integrator strip in every load. This confirms that the load reached the target temperature for the required duration.
Biological indicators: Run a Geobacillus stearothermophilus spore test at least monthly (or per campus EH&S policy). Incubate the exposed ampoule per the manufacturer’s instructions. A positive (growth) result means the autoclave failed; quarantine all loads processed since the last successful test and contact the lab manager.
Autoclave logbook: Record every cycle: date, operator, load description, cycle type, temperature, pressure, duration, and indicator results.
Annual maintenance: Schedule a professional inspection and calibration of the pressure gauge, safety valve, and temperature sensor at least annually.

title: Vacuum Filtration Apparatus
text: This procedure describes the assembly, operation, and maintenance of vacuum filtration systems used in the EA Program laboratory. Vacuum filtration separates suspended solids from liquids by drawing the liquid through a filter membrane or glass fiber filter under reduced pressure. It is used across many analytical methods, including soil and water extract filtration (SOPs L403, L409, L418), microplastics analysis (SOP-L308), chlorophyll extraction (SOP-L310), and eDNA concentration (SOP-L700).

title: Vacuum Filtration Apparatus

2 Scope

Applies to: All vacuum filtration in EA Program laboratories using filter flasks, filter funnels (Buchner, glass frit, analytical, or Nalgene disposable units), and Fisher Scientific Maxidry vacuum pumps or building vacuum lines
Does not apply to: Syringe filtration (push-through, no vacuum); centrifugal ultrafiltration; field filtration of eDNA samples (covered in SOP-F700)
Location: SGM 133 and SGM 134

title: Vacuum Filtration Apparatus
text:
3 Definitions

Filter funnel: The upper component of a vacuum filtration assembly that holds the filter membrane and directs liquid onto it; typically borosilicate glass or polysulfone.
Filtrate: The liquid that passes through the filter membrane and collects in the side-arm flask; the fraction of interest in most dissolved-analyte analyses.
Glass fiber filter (GFF): A depth filter composed of borosilicate glass microfibers; commonly 0.7 µm nominal pore size (GF/F); used for chlorophyll, particulate carbon, and TSS analyses.
Membrane filter: A thin polymeric film with a defined pore size (typically 0.45 µm); used to separate dissolved from particulate fractions in water samples.
Nominal pore size: The manufacturer-stated pore size of a filter; actual retention varies by manufacturer and depends on the particle size distribution of the material being filtered.
Retentate: The material retained on the filter membrane; the fraction of interest for TSS, chlorophyll, and particulate analyses.
Side-arm (vacuum) flask: A thick-walled borosilicate flask with a side arm for connection to the vacuum line; designed to withstand the pressure differential during filtration.
Vacuum trap: A secondary flask or bottle interposed between the filtration funnel and the vacuum pump to catch filtrate overflow and protect the pump.

5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Glassware under vacuum: Filter flasks (Erlenmeyer with sidearm) are under reduced pressure during operation. Cracked or starred flasks can implode. Inspect all glassware before each use; reject any with visible damage.
Chemical: Filtrates may contain hazardous chemicals (acids, solvents). Handle filtrate according to the analytical SOP.
Biological: Samples may contain pathogens. Wear gloves.

If a filter flask implodes, do not touch the broken glass. Sweep up fragments with a brush and dustpan (not hands) and dispose in a sharps container or labeled “Broken Glass” box. If contaminated with hazardous chemicals, follow SOP-L004 Chemical Spill Response.

title: Vacuum Filtration Apparatus
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Assembly

Inspect the filter flask for cracks or stars. Do not use damaged flasks.
Connect vacuum tubing from the flask sidearm to the vacuum trap inlet, and from the vacuum trap outlet to the pump
Place the rubber stopper into the neck of the flask
Seat the appropriate funnel into the stopper
If using a 47 mm filter holder: assemble the base, place the filter on the fritted support using forceps (avoid touching the filter with fingers), and clamp the funnel top in place



7.2 Pre-Wetting or Pre-Combustion (If Required)

For gravimetric analyses (TSS): pre-dry and pre-weigh the filter per the analytical SOP
For DOC filtration: pre-rinse the filter with 50–100 mL of sample or DI water and discard the first rinse (removes filter-leached carbon)
For pre-combusted GF/F filters (chlorophyll, DOC): filters should have been fired at 450 C for 4 hours per SOP-L111 and stored in a clean container



7.3 Filtration

Turn on the vacuum pump. Verify suction by briefly covering the funnel opening with a gloved hand (you should feel resistance).
Pour the sample into the funnel slowly and steadily. For particulate-laden samples, add in small aliquots to avoid overloading the filter.
Allow the liquid to pass through completely
Rinse the funnel walls with a small volume of DI water (or the matrix specified in the analytical SOP) to transfer any adhering particles to the filter
Continue vacuum for 10–30 seconds after the last visible liquid has passed through to remove residual moisture (do not over-dry if the filter will be extracted for chlorophyll or DOC)
Turn off the vacuum pump
Carefully disconnect the funnel from the stopper



7.4 Filter Handling

Remove the filter from the funnel using clean forceps
Transfer the filter to the appropriate container per the analytical SOP:

Aluminum tin (for drying/weighing: TSS)
Amber vial with extraction solvent (chlorophyll)
Extraction tube (eDNA, microplastics)
Petri dish (if storing before analysis)

Label the container immediately



7.5 Filtrate Handling

If the filtrate is the analyte of interest (e.g., dissolved nutrients, DOC), transfer it from the filter flask to a labeled sample vial using a clean graduated cylinder or by pouring
Acidify or preserve the filtrate per the analytical SOP
If the filtrate is waste, dispose per SOP-L006



7.6 Cleanup

Discard used disposable funnels and filters per the analytical SOP
Rinse reusable funnels, stoppers, and filter flasks with DI water immediately after use
For glass frit funnels: back-flush with DI water, then soak in an appropriate cleaning solution (acid bath for inorganic work, detergent for general use) per SOP-L101
Coil vacuum tubing loosely (do not kink) and store

title: Sample Grinding and Homogenization – Ball Mill, Mortar and Pestle
text: This procedure describes the grinding and homogenization of dried soil, sediment, plant tissue, and other solid environmental samples to produce a fine, uniform powder suitable for chemical, elemental, and isotopic analysis. Many analytical methods require a homogeneous subsample of 0.5–20 mg (e.g., EA-IRMS capsules, SOP-L414) or 0.5–1.0 g (e.g., acid digestion, SOP-L410, SOP-L411). Without thorough grinding and homogenization, small subsamples drawn from an incompletely mixed bulk sample may not represent the true composition of that sample, introducing analytical error unrelated to the instrument or method (Bremner, 1996; Nelson & Sommers, 1996). Particle-size reduction to \(\leq\) 150 \(\mu\)m also improves combustion completeness in high-temperature elemental analyzers and reduces between-capsule mass variance in EA-IRMS work (Sollins et al., 1996; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2010).

title: Sample Grinding and Homogenization – Ball Mill, Mortar and Pestle
text: This procedure describes the grinding and homogenization of dried soil, sediment, plant tissue, and other solid environmental samples to produce a fine, uniform powder suitable for chemical, elemental, and isotopic analysis. Many analytical methods require a homogeneous subsample of 0.5–20 mg (e.g., EA-IRMS capsules, SOP-L414) or 0.5–1.0 g (e.g., acid digestion, SOP-L410, SOP-L411). Without thorough grinding and homogenization, small subsamples drawn from an incompletely mixed bulk sample may not represent the true composition of that sample, introducing analytical error unrelated to the instrument or method (Bremner, 1996; Nelson & Sommers, 1996). title: Sample Grinding and Homogenization – Ball Mill, Mortar and Pestle
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Dry grinding and homogenization of air-dried or oven-dried (60–105 °C) solid samples, including mineral soils, organic soils, sediments, dried plant tissue, compost, and biochar, using agate or steel mortar and pestle, ball mill, or mechanical grinder.
Does not apply to: Wet grinding or homogenization of fresh tissue (cryogenic grinding for molecular biology applications); sieving-only sample preparation (see SOP-F400 for 2 mm sieving); bead beating for DNA extraction (integral to SOP-L700); ball milling specifically for TC and EA-IRMS (see SOP-L117).
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 134, Edmunds 017 - Rock Grinding

title: Sample Grinding and Homogenization – Ball Mill, Mortar and Pestle
text:
4 Definitions







Term
Definition




Grinding
Mechanical size reduction of solid particles by impact, compression, or abrasion (Bernhardt, 1994).


Homogenization
Mixing and size reduction to produce a sample in which any subsample of a given mass has the same composition as any other subsample of that mass (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).


Particle size (\(d_{50}\))
Median particle diameter by mass; the most common target for soil analysis is 150 \(\mu\)m (U.S. No. 100 mesh sieve) (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).


Cross-contamination
Transfer of material from a previously processed sample to a subsequent one via residue retained on grinding equipment surfaces (Boutton, 1991).


Sacrificial subsample
A small amount of the upcoming sample ground and discarded before collecting the analytical aliquot, to purge residual material from equipment surfaces (Boutton, 1991).


Respirable crystalline silica (RCS)
Quartz and cristobalite particles \(\leq\) 10 \(\mu\)m aerodynamic diameter released during grinding of mineral soils; an IARC Group 1 carcinogen (International Agency for Research on Cancer, 1997).


Air-dried
Dried at ambient temperature (\(\leq\) 40 °C) until mass is constant; the standard pre-treatment for 2 mm sieving (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).

title: Sample Grinding and Homogenization – Ball Mill, Mortar and Pestle
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Respirable dust and silica: Grinding dry soil and plant tissue generates fine respirable dust including crystalline silica (quartz), which is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen at particle sizes \(\leq\) 10 \(\mu\)m (International Agency for Research on Cancer, 1997). Always perform grinding inside a fume hood or wear a NIOSH-approved N95 respirator.
Contaminated soils: Soils from legacy-contaminated sites (Pb, As, Hg, pesticides, PAHs) pose additional inhalation and dermal hazards during grinding. Consult the Lab PI before processing (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
Noise: Ball mills and mechanical grinders can exceed 85 dB. Wear hearing protection for runs \(>\) 1 min (National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, 1998).
Pinch/crush hazards: Milling cups and clamps are heavy. Secure milling cups before starting the mill and keep hands clear during operation.
Heat: Milling cups may get hot if samples are run for extended periods of time. Use protective gloves to handle hot items, or wait until they have cooled down enough to avoid burns.
Cross-contamination: Residual sample in grinding equipment is the primary quality risk in sequential grinding. Thorough cleaning between samples is essential (Section 6.5).




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves
N95 dust mask or work in fume hood
Hearing protection (ball mill or mechanical grinder)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For dust inhalation, move to fresh air immediately. For cuts from broken equipment, apply first aid per SOP-L002. Report all incidents to the Lab Manager.

title: Sample Grinding and Homogenization – Ball Mill, Mortar and Pestle
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Selection and Drying
Samples must be thoroughly dry before grinding. Residual moisture causes particles to clump, impedes size reduction, and can promote microbial activity that alters sample chemistry during storage (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).

Use air-dried samples sieved to 2 mm (SOP-F400), or oven-dry per the drying requirements in the table below:








Analytical Pathway
Drying Temperature
Rationale




TC, LOI, metals, or general chemistry
105 °C to constant mass
Standard gravimetric drying; isotope fractionation not a concern (Nelson & Sommers, 1996)


\(\delta^{15}\)N, \(\delta^{13}\)C (EA-IRMS)
40–60 °C to constant mass
Temperatures \(>\) 60 °C volatilize \(^{14}\)N-enriched NH\(_4^+\), artificially elevating \(\delta^{15}\)N (Kool et al., 2011; Guntiñas2012?)


Plant tissue (any analysis)
60 °C to constant mass
Higher temperatures degrade labile N compounds and alter tissue \(\delta^{15}\)N (Kalra, 1998)



Cool samples to room temperature in a desiccator before grinding.
Record drying temperature, start and end times, and initial and final mass in the lab notebook.



7.2 Mortar and Pestle (Manual Grinding)
Manual grinding with mortar and pestle is appropriate for small batches (\(<\) 50 g), hard materials requiring careful size control, and laboratories where a ball mill is unavailable (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).

Place a clean, dry mortar on a stable bench surface. If working with contaminated soil or generating visible dust, work inside a fume hood.
Add a small amount of dried sample (5–20 g) to the mortar.
Grind with a circular and pressing motion, periodically scraping material from the sides back to the center.
Continue grinding until the sample passes through the target sieve (No. 60 [250 \(\mu\)m] for general chemistry; No. 100 [150 \(\mu\)m] for EA-IRMS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2010)). For plant tissue, grind to a uniform fine powder.
Transfer the ground sample to a labeled vial or coin envelope with a clean spatula.
Record the sample ID and particle size achieved.







Tip



For hard or fibrous samples (e.g., woody roots, calcium carbonate nodules), pre-crush coarsely with a hammer inside a thick plastic bag before transferring to the mortar. This reduces grinding time and wear on the mortar.




7.3 Ball Mill (Mechanical Grinding)
Ball milling provides more reproducible particle size reduction and higher throughput than manual grinding, and is preferred for batches \(>\) 20 samples or where particle size uniformity is critical (Bernhardt, 1994).

Select the appropriate milling cup and ball material (confirm which materials we have for balls/jars):








Material
Best Use Case
Notes




Stainless steel
General chemistry (non-metal)
Faster; may contribute Fe, Cr, Ni, Mn


Ceramic
TBD
TBD



Load the sample and milling balls into the milling cup. The milling cup’s volume should be occupied roughly by 1/3 sample, 1/3 grinding ball(s) and 1/3 air.







TipSafe Running




Filling: Sample quantity should not be below 25% of the milling cup’s holding capacity.
Material Milling ball and milling cup material must always be the same.
Single Running Do not run machine with only one milling cup loaded. If you only need to use one milling cup, still load the second one completely empty (no sample nor milling balls)




Tightly seal milling cup and load it into the milling cup holder. Make sure to insert cups in the correct orientation, as shown below:




Orientation of milling cup for left hand side holder. Cup should be mirrored for the right hand side holder.



Turn locking pin into the locked position as shown in the image below and turn the handwheel until maximum clamping range is reached. Close hood.




Locked and unlocked pin positions



Set speed and duration per the table below or per the analytical SOP:



Sample Type
Frequency (Hz)
Duration
Target Size




Organic soil
30
2 min
\(\leq\) 75 \(\mu\)m


Quartz Sand
30
1 min
N/A



Run the mill. If the milling cup becomes warm to the touch, alternate 2-minute grinding intervals with 1-minute rest periods to prevent thermal alteration of labile organic matter and N compounds (Kool et al., 2011).
After run ends, open the hood and unlock the locking pin before removing milling cups. Wait 30 seconds after stopping before opening the milling cup (dust settles). Open inside the fume hood or with N95 protection.
Transfer the ground sample to a labeled container.
If required, verify particle size by passing a subsample through the target sieve.
Perform cleaning run with quartz sand in between sample runs. Add the same volume of quartz sand as the samples you are running, and the milling balls you are using. The quartz run will help clean the cups and remove any sample that might have gotten stuck to the cup. After the quartz run, clean cup thoroughly according to the “Cleaning Between Samples” section.



7.4 Mechanical Grinder (Plant Tissue)
A Wiley-type or Thomas-type cutting mill provides rapid coarse grinding of dried plant tissue and is generally faster than mortar and pestle for batch processing (Kalra, 1998).

Set the screen mesh to the target particle size (1 mm [No. 18] or 0.5 mm [No. 35]).
Feed dried tissue into the hopper slowly; do not overload.
Collect ground material from the output chamber.
For analyses requiring finer particle size (e.g., EA-IRMS), follow with mortar and pestle or ball mill to reduce further (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2010).



7.5 Cleaning Between Samples
Cross-contamination is the primary quality risk in sequential grinding. For isotope work, residues as small as 0.05 mg C from a high-carbon sample can produce measurable \(\delta^{13}\)C bias in a subsequent low-carbon sample (Boutton, 1991). Clean thoroughly between every sample:

Disassemble the mortar/pestle or milling cup and balls.
Brush out all visible residue with a soft-bristle brush.
Wipe all surfaces with a lint-free tissue dampened with 70% ethanol.
Trace metal work: rinse with 10% HNO\(_3\) (trace-metal grade), then triple-rinse with Type I deionized water (18.2 M\(\Omega\)), and air-dry (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2007).
Isotope work: rinse with Type I deionized water, wipe with ethanol, and blow dry with clean compressed air.
Wiley mill: run a small amount of clean quartz sand through the mill between samples to abrade residues from the cutting chamber, then brush and wipe.
Allow all equipment to dry completely before grinding the next sample.







Important



When transitioning between samples with very different compositions (e.g., high-carbon compost followed by low-carbon mineral soil), grind a sacrificial subsample of the next sample and discard it before collecting the analytical aliquot. This purges micro-residues that ethanol-wiping alone may not remove (Boutton, 1991). This step is mandatory for EA-IRMS work.




7.6 Storage

Transfer ground powder to a labeled vial (glass or polypropylene with a polyethylene-lined cap). Avoid foam-gasketed caps, which can off-gas organic vapors.
Label with: sample ID, date ground, equipment and milling cup material, and target particle size.
Store in a desiccator at room temperature. Ground samples have large surface area and are hygroscopic; even brief exposure to humid air can add 0.5–2% mass as adsorbed water (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).
For long-term storage (\(>\) 2 weeks), seal with Parafilm and store at $-$20 °C.
Record grinding date, equipment, milling cup material, speed, and duration in the lab notebook and sample tracking spreadsheet.

title: Trilogy Laboratory Fluorometer
text:
4 Definitions

Blank correction: Subtraction of the fluorescence signal from a blank (solvent only, no sample) from sample readings to remove background fluorescence from the solvent and optical components.
Chlorophyll a: The primary photosynthetic pigment in phytoplankton and algae; quantified by the Trilogy using a chlorophyll a module (excitation ~430 nm, emission ~685 nm); expressed in µg L-1 (water) or µg g-1 (sediment) (Arar & Collins, 1997).
Emission wavelength: The wavelength at which the fluorophore emits light after excitation; detected by the fluorometer’s photodetector.
Excitation wavelength: The wavelength of light used to illuminate the sample; chosen to match the absorption maximum of the target fluorophore.
Fluorometer: An instrument that measures fluorescence intensity emitted by a sample after excitation; more sensitive than spectrophotometry for low-concentration analytes such as chlorophyll a and CDOM (Turner Designs, 2014).
Linear dynamic range (LDR): The concentration range over which instrument response is linear; for the Trilogy chlorophyll module, approximately 0–1000 µg/L (Turner Designs, 2014).
Module (Trilogy): An interchangeable optical block that sets the excitation and emission wavelengths for a specific analyte; available modules include chlorophyll a (acidification and non-acidification), CDOM, rhodamine WT, and turbidity.
Pheophytin a: A degradation product of chlorophyll a formed by loss of the central magnesium ion; contributes to total fluorescence and is distinguished from chlorophyll a by the acidification step of EPA Method 445.0 (Arar & Collins, 1997).
Quinine sulfate unit (QSU): A fluorescence unit based on the fluorescence of a standard quinine sulfate solution; used for CDOM and some other modules.
