title: Trilogy Laboratory Fluorometer
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Startup

Turn on the Trilogy using the power switch on the back of the instrument.
Allow the instrument to warm up for approximately 10 minutes before taking measurements (Turner Designs, 2014).
Connect the Trilogy to a printer or PC if data export is needed.



7.2 Installing an Optical Module

Select the appropriate optical module for the analysis:

Fluorescence module for chlorophyll a, rhodamine WT, or other fluorescent analytes
Absorbance module for colorimetric assays
Turbidity module for nephelometric turbidity measurements

Open the sample compartment lid.
Align the module with the slot and press firmly until it clicks into place.
The Trilogy will automatically detect the installed module and display the corresponding menu on the touch screen.
If using the absorbance module, install the appropriate filter paddle for the target wavelength.



7.3 Selecting the Measurement Mode







Mode
When to Use




Raw mode
Qualitative measurements; no calibration required; results in RFU, raw absorbance, or NTU


Direct Concentration mode
Quantitative measurements in concentration units; calibration required





7.4 Fluorescence Module: Chlorophyll a (EPA Method 445.0)
EPA Method 445.0 is the standard fluorometric method for measuring extracted chlorophyll a and pheophytin a in marine and freshwater algae (Arar & Collins, 1997).

Calibrate the fluorescence module in Direct Concentration mode using a known concentration of pure chlorophyll a in 90% acetone (see §7.3).
Insert the glass test tube containing the extracted sample.
Touch Measure Fluorescence to obtain the pre-acidification reading.
Add the prescribed volume of 0.1 N HCl, mix gently, and wait 90 seconds.
Measure again to obtain the post-acidification reading.
Calculate chlorophyll a and pheophytin a per EPA 445.0 (Arar & Collins, 1997).







TipStandard Stability



Recalibrate with a fresh chlorophyll a standard every few months. The standard degrades over time, especially if exposed to light or warmth (Turner Designs, 2014).




7.5 Single-Sample Measurements

Open the lid and insert the appropriate cuvette or test tube.
Close the lid.
Optionally, touch Sample ID to name the sample; touch Save.
Touch the Measure button corresponding to the installed module.
The Trilogy measures the sample for 6 seconds and reports the average reading.
Results for the most recent 20 measurements are displayed on the home screen.







Important



The Trilogy stores a maximum of 20 measurements at a time. Older readings are overwritten. Measurements are not retained between power cycles. Always export data to a printer or PC before turning off the instrument or exceeding 20 readings.




7.6 Shutdown

Export all data to a printer or PC.
Remove the cuvette or test tube from the sample compartment.
Clean the cuvette holder if any liquid was spilled (wipe with 70% ethanol and a lint-free tissue).
Close the sample compartment lid.
Turn off the instrument using the rear power switch.

title: Trilogy Laboratory Fluorometer
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 When to Calibrate

Before running a new batch of samples
After a temperature change of ±5 °C in the lab
After changing to a different optical module or analyte
When verification readings deviate unacceptably from the expected value



8.2 Calibration Overview
Calibration converts the raw instrument signal to concentration units. The Trilogy supports single-point and multi-point calibrations (up to five standards plus a blank). Multi-point calibrations provide superior accuracy across a wide concentration range (Turner Designs, 2014).


8.3 Direct Concentration Calibration Procedure

Turn on the Trilogy and confirm the correct module is installed.
Touch Calibrate on the home screen.
Select Run New Calibration.
Select the desired unit of measurement.
Insert the blank (ultrapure water or 90% acetone, as appropriate) and touch OK.
Enter the concentration of the first standard. For multi-point calibrations, begin with the lowest concentration.
Insert the standard and touch OK.
After the reading, either select Proceed with Current Calibration or Enter More Standards.
Optionally, save the calibration for future use.
Verify calibration by measuring the same standard used in step 6; the displayed concentration should match the known value within the acceptable tolerance (Turner Designs, 2014).



8.4 Verification

After calibration, re-read a mid-range standard to confirm accuracy.
Re-read the standard every few hours during extended sessions to detect drift.
Optionally, read the solid secondary standard and record its value for instrument stability tracking.
If verification readings drift beyond acceptable limits, recalibrate before continuing.



8.5 QC Acceptance Criteria

Laboratory reagent blank (LRB) every 10–15 samples; must read below the lower detection limit.
QC standards must recover within ±20% of the known value (Arar & Collins, 1997).
Relative standard deviation (RSD) of replicate measurements must be within ±20%.
Field duplicates must agree within ±20% RPD.
Samples, standards, LRBs, and QCs must all be at ambient room temperature; fluorescence is temperature-dependent (APHA et al., 2012).

title: ThermoFisher Delta V IRMS – General Instrument Use
text:
4 Definitions

ConFlo IV: Interface hub connecting peripherals, reference gases, and the IRMS; handles reference-gas dilution and peak-center switching.
Delta V IRMS: The ThermoFisher Delta V Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometer housed in the Oxtoby Isotope Lab, SGM Rm 135.
Flash IRMS EA: Elemental analyzer peripheral that combusts samples at 1020 °C to produce N2, CO2, and (optionally) SO2 for simultaneous \(\delta^{15}\)N and \(\delta^{13}\)C analysis.
GasBench II: Low-flow peripheral for headspace gas sampling from sealed vials; used for carbonate CO2, DIC, and water \(\delta^{18}\)O.
H3\(^{+}\) Factor: Correction applied to \(\delta^{2}\)H data for H3\(^{+}\) ions formed in the source that interfere with HD\(^{+}\) at m/z 3.
Isodat: ThermoFisher software used to design analytical sequences, control the instrument, and export raw isotope data.
Linearity: The dependence of measured \(\delta\) on signal amplitude; a well-tuned instrument shows minimal linearity offset across the working signal range (Werner & Brand, 2001).
Super-User: Staff or faculty member certified for IRMS operation and minor maintenance (gas replacement, reactor exchange).
TC/EA: Thermal Conversion/Elemental Analyzer peripheral; pyrolyzes samples at ~1450 °C to produce H2 and CO for \(\delta^{2}\)H and \(\delta^{18}\)O analysis.
User: Student, staff, or faculty member certified to prepare samples and operate the IRMS without direct supervision.
Zero-Enrichment Test: Series of reference-gas on/off pulses run before analysis to verify the IRMS produces consistent \(\delta\) values independent of signal amplitude (Coplen, 2011).

title: ThermoFisher Delta V IRMS – General Instrument Use
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 User Certification
Before operating the IRMS independently, personnel must complete the Training Record (Section 13). Contact the lab manager to schedule certification.


7.2 Pre-Analysis Checklist

Sign in to the lab logbook.
Verify He carrier gas pressure (minimum 1500 psi on the regulator).
Check reference gas pressures (CO2, N2 as applicable).
Confirm Isodat is running and the instrument status screen shows no error flags.
Verify the correct peripheral is selected in Isodat.
Run a Zero-Enrichment Test (3 on/off pulses) and confirm \(\delta\) values are stable within ±0.1‰.
Run an on/off linearity check if not done within the past 48 h.



7.3 Analytical Sequence Design

Open the Isodat Sequence Editor.
Load the appropriate method file for the peripheral and analyte.
Build the sequence: blank(s), conditioning samples, reference materials, unknowns, check standards, blanks.
Reference material placement: minimum 1 RM per 10 unknowns; two-point normalization requires at least 2 different RMs.
Save the sequence file using the naming convention: YYYYMMDD_Project_SeqID_User.seq



7.4 Starting and Monitoring a Run

Load samples into the autosampler or carousel per the application SOP.
Press Start in the Isodat Sequence Editor.
Monitor the first 3–5 injections on-screen to confirm peaks are present, within expected amplitude, and baseline-resolved.
Do not leave the instrument unattended during the first 30 min.



7.5 Shutdown

After the sequence completes, export raw data per the application SOP.
Remove all samples and consumables from the autosampler.
Log gas usage and any issues in the lab logbook.
Leave the instrument in standby per the lab manager’s current instructions (the Delta V and ConFlo IV are typically left powered on continuously).

title: NanoDrop One Spectrophotometer
text:
4 Definitions

A260: Absorbance at 260 nm; the wavelength at which double-stranded DNA and RNA absorb most strongly; used to quantify nucleic acid concentration.
A280: Absorbance at 280 nm; absorbed primarily by aromatic amino acids (tyrosine, tryptophan) and by phenolic contaminants; used to assess protein contamination in nucleic acid preparations.
A260/A280 ratio: The ratio of absorbance at 260 nm to 280 nm; pure dsDNA gives ~1.8; pure RNA gives ~2.0; values below 1.7 indicate protein or phenol contamination.
A260/A230 ratio: The ratio of absorbance at 260 nm to 230 nm; values of 2.0–2.2 are expected for pure nucleic acids; low values indicate contamination with chaotropic salts (guanidinium), carbohydrates, or humic acids.
Micro-volume spectrophotometry: Absorbance measurement using 1–2 µL of sample held by surface tension between a pedestal and an optical fiber arm; eliminates the need for cuvettes and allows measurement of very small volumes.
Pedestal: The fixed lower optic of the NanoDrop on which the sample droplet is placed; must be cleaned with a lint-free wipe between measurements to prevent carryover.
Pathlength normalization: Automatic adjustment of the measured absorbance to a standardized 10 mm pathlength equivalent; allows direct comparison with traditional cuvette measurements.

title: NanoDrop One Spectrophotometer
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Startup

Open the NanoDrop One software (or wake the integrated touchscreen)
Select the appropriate application (e.g., Nucleic Acid, Protein A280, or UV-Vis)
Clean the upper and lower pedestals with 2 uL of nuclease-free water; wipe with a lint-free tissue
Perform a blank measurement (see Section 6.2)



7.2 Blanking

Pipette 2 uL of the blank solution onto the lower pedestal. The blank must match the sample matrix – use the same elution buffer or solvent that the samples are dissolved in.
Lower the sampling arm and tap Blank
Verify that the blank spectrum is flat and the baseline absorbance at 260 nm is near zero
Wipe both pedestals with a lint-free tissue







Tip



Re-blank whenever you switch sample types, change buffers, or if the instrument has been idle for more than 30 minutes.




7.3 Measuring Samples

Pipette 2 uL of sample onto the lower pedestal
Lower the sampling arm and tap Measure
Record the following for each sample:

Concentration (ng/uL)
A260/A280 ratio
A260/A230 ratio

Wipe both pedestals with a lint-free tissue between every sample
Repeat for all samples



7.4 Interpreting Results








Parameter
Expected Range
Interpretation




A260/A280
1.8–2.0
Values below 1.8 suggest protein or phenol contamination


A260/A230
2.0–2.2
Values below 2.0 suggest humic acid, carbohydrate, salt, or guanidine contamination









Note



For environmental DNA extracts, A260/A230 ratios are frequently below 2.0. If the NanoDrop concentration is more than twice the Qubit reading, the UV absorbance is likely inflated by co-extracted contaminants; use the Qubit value for planning downstream reactions.




7.5 Data Export

Save the session file (.tsv or .csv) to the designated project folder on the connected laptop
Use a consistent file-naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_NanoDrop_ProjectName.tsv
Record results in the lab notebook and/or project data sheet



7.6 Shutdown and Daily Maintenance

Wipe both pedestals with 2 uL of nuclease-free water, then dry with a lint-free tissue
If protein or concentrated DNA residue is visible, clean with 2 uL of 0.5 M HCl, wait 10 seconds, then rinse with nuclease-free water
Close the software and lower the sampling arm
Cover the instrument with the dust cover if available

title: Bio-Rad QX200 Droplet Digital PCR System
text:
4 Definitions

Amplitude: The fluorescence signal intensity of a droplet; positive droplets (containing target DNA) have high amplitude; negative droplets have low amplitude; a clear separation between positive and negative populations is required for accurate quantification.
Droplet digital PCR (ddPCR): A method of absolute quantification of nucleic acids in which the sample is partitioned into ~20,000 nanoliter-sized water-in-oil droplets, each containing zero or one target molecule; after PCR amplification, the fraction of fluorescent positive droplets is used to calculate target concentration using Poisson statistics.
FAM: A green fluorescent dye (fluorescein amidite) used to label one probe or primer in a duplex ddPCR assay; detected in the FAM channel (channel 1) by the QX200.
HEX: A yellow-orange fluorescent dye used to label a second probe in a duplex ddPCR assay, or as an alternative to VIC; detected in channel 2 by the QX200.
Poisson correction: A statistical adjustment applied by the DropletQuant software to account for the probability that some droplets contain more than one target molecule; necessary when target concentrations are high.
Copies per microliter (copies/µL): The absolute concentration of the target DNA in the final ddPCR reaction, as reported by DropletQuant; must be back-calculated to the original sample concentration using the appropriate dilution factor.
Threshold: The fluorescence amplitude boundary separating positive from negative droplets; set manually or automatically in the analysis software; incorrect threshold setting is the most common source of ddPCR quantification error.

title: Bio-Rad QX200 Droplet Digital PCR System
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-PCR Setup (Clean Area)






Important



All pre-PCR work (reaction assembly, droplet generation) must be performed in the designated pre-PCR area to prevent amplicon contamination. Use dedicated pipettes and wear clean gloves.



Thaw the ddPCR Supermix and DNA templates on ice
Prepare the reaction master mix according to the assay protocol (see SOP-L701 for primer/probe concentrations and cycling conditions)
Dispense 20 uL of each assembled reaction into the sample wells (middle row) of a DG8 cartridge
Add 70 uL of Droplet Generation Oil to the oil wells (bottom row)
Attach a DG8 gasket to the cartridge



7.2 Droplet Generation

Place the loaded cartridge into the QX200 Droplet Generator
Close the lid and press Start. Generation takes approximately 2 minutes per cartridge.
When complete, carefully open the lid. Do not tilt or shake the cartridge – the droplets are fragile.
Using a multichannel pipette set to 40 uL, gently aspirate the droplets from the top row of the cartridge and dispense into the 96-well plate. Pipette slowly (approximately 3 seconds to aspirate, 3 seconds to dispense) to avoid shearing droplets.
Repeat for each cartridge



7.3 Plate Sealing

Place the pierceable foil heat seal over the loaded 96-well plate
Seal using the PX1 PCR Plate Sealer at 180 C for 5 seconds
Visually confirm a uniform seal across all wells



7.4 Thermal Cycling

Place the sealed plate into the C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler with the 96-Deep Well Reaction Module
Program the thermal cycling protocol per SOP-L701 (typical: 95 C activation, 40 cycles of denaturation/annealing, 98 C droplet stabilization, 4 C hold)
Set the ramp rate to 2 C/s (critical for ddPCR; do not use the default maximum ramp rate)
Start the run. Cycling typically takes 2–2.5 hours.
After cycling, plates can be held at 4 C for up to 24 hours before reading, but immediate reading is preferred



7.5 Droplet Reading

Open QuantaSoft software on the connected computer
Set up the plate layout: assign sample names, target names, experiment type (ABS for absolute quantification), and supermix type
Place the sealed plate into the QX200 Droplet Reader
Confirm that the reader waste and buffer bottles are at appropriate levels (refill or empty as needed before starting a full plate)
Tap Start to begin reading. The reader processes each well individually (approximately 1–2 minutes per well).
Monitor the first few wells to confirm that droplet counts exceed 10,000 accepted events per well



7.6 Data Review

After reading, review the 1-D amplitude plots in QuantaSoft to verify clear separation between positive and negative droplet clusters
Set the fluorescence amplitude threshold manually using the NTC and positive control wells as guides
Check that all wells have at least 10,000 accepted droplets; flag any wells below this threshold
Export results as .csv for downstream analysis (see SOP-L702)



7.7 Shutdown and Daily Maintenance

Remove the plate from the Droplet Reader
Check the reader waste bottle; empty if more than 75% full
Check the reader buffer bottle; refill if less than 25% full
Wipe down the Droplet Generator cartridge holder with a lint-free tissue
Dispose of used cartridges and gaskets (see Section 8)
Close QuantaSoft and shut down instruments if no further runs are scheduled

text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Every run must include: no-template controls (NTC, minimum 2 wells), extraction blanks (from SOP-L700), and positive controls (gBlock or plasmid at known concentration)
Droplet count per well must exceed 10,000 accepted droplets (out of approximately 20,000 generated); wells below this threshold should be excluded
NTC wells must show 0 or fewer than 3 positive droplets; more than 3 indicates contamination and the plate or affected target should be rerun
Positive/negative droplet cluster separation must be unambiguous on the 1-D amplitude plot
TBD – define acceptable coefficients of variation for technical replicates (typically less than 15–25% for ddPCR)

title: Hach DR3900 Benchtop Spectrophotometer
text:
This procedure describes the setup, operation, routine maintenance, and troubleshooting of the Hach DR3900 benchtop spectrophotometer as a laboratory instrument. The DR3900 uses a tungsten lamp (visible range) and a deuterium lamp (UV range) to measure absorbance and transmittance across 320–1100 nm, supporting both factory-stored programs for Hach reagent kits and user-defined wavelength methods (Hach Company, 2024a, 2024b).
For method-specific chemistry, reagent handling, and the analyte Method Registry (nutrients, metals, and general water quality parameters), see SOP-L303 Hach Colorimetric Analysis. For field use of the portable Hach DR900 colorimeter, see SOP-F208 Portable Spectrophotometer / Colorimeter (Field).

title: Hach DR3900 Benchtop Spectrophotometer
text:
4 Definitions

Absorbance (A): The negative base-10 logarithm of transmittance: \(A = -\log_{10}(T)\); directly proportional to analyte concentration (Beer-Lambert law) within the linear range of the instrument.
Beer-Lambert law: The relationship between absorbance, path length, and concentration: \(A = \varepsilon \cdot c \cdot l\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the molar absorptivity, \(c\) is concentration, and \(l\) is the optical path length (cell width); the basis for all colorimetric quantification.
Blank (reagent blank): A sample containing all reagents except the analyte; used to zero the instrument and correct for absorbance contributed by the reagent matrix.
Colorimetric method: An analytical technique in which a chemical reagent reacts with the analyte to produce a colored complex whose absorbance is proportional to analyte concentration.
TNT plus vial: A Hach proprietary pre-dosed reagent vial for the DR3900; contains all required reagents sealed in a glass vial; provides consistent results without manual reagent preparation.
Transmittance (T): The fraction of incident light that passes through the sample: \(T = I/I_0\); related to absorbance by \(A = -\log_{10}(T)\).
Wavelength scan: A measurement mode in which the instrument records absorbance across a range of wavelengths to identify the absorption maximum of an unknown compound.

title: Hach DR3900 Benchtop Spectrophotometer
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Startup and Self-Check

Verify that the sample compartment is empty and the lid is closed
Turn on the DR3900 using the power switch on the rear panel
The instrument performs an automatic self-check, including lamp tests and wavelength verification. This takes approximately 30 seconds. Do not open the lid or insert samples until the home screen appears.
Allow the lamps to warm up for at least 15 minutes before making measurements that require high photometric accuracy (e.g., user-defined methods at low absorbance). For routine stored-program analyses, measurements may begin after the self-check completes.



7.2 Selecting an Operating Mode
From the home screen, select one of the following modes:



Mode
When to Use




Stored Programs
Pre-programmed Hach reagent kit methods; see SOP-L303 for the Method Registry


Single Wavelength
User-defined absorbance or %T at a specific wavelength


Multi Wavelength
Simultaneous measurement at 2–4 wavelengths


Wavelength Scan
Absorbance spectrum over a defined range


Time Course
Kinetic measurement at a fixed wavelength over time





7.3 Preparing and Inserting Sample Cells

Select the correct cell type for the method (see Section 5). Square cells must be oriented so the clear optical faces align with the light path (arrow on the cell pointing toward the detector).
Fill the cell to the level required by the method. Do not overfill; liquid on the outside of the cell causes erroneous readings.
Clean the exterior of the cell with a lint-free wipe. For 1-inch round cells, apply a thin film of silicone oil and wipe with the oiling cloth to eliminate fingerprints and water droplets (Hach Company, 2024a).
Insert the cell into the cell holder. Close the sample compartment lid fully before reading.







TipCuvette Selection for UV Work



Standard glass and plastic cells absorb UV light below approximately 340 nm. For measurements below 340 nm in user-defined or wavelength scan modes, use quartz cells (Skoog et al., 2018).




7.4 Zeroing (Blanking) the Instrument

Fill a clean cell with the blank solution. The blank must match the sample matrix: DI water for simple aqueous samples, or the reagent blank specified by the Hach method.
Insert the blank cell and close the lid
Press Zero (stored-program mode) or Zero/Blank (single wavelength mode)
Verify that the display reads 0.000 Abs (or 100.0 %T)
Remove the blank cell







Note



Re-zero whenever you change wavelengths, switch cell types, or if the instrument has been idle for more than 30 minutes.




7.5 Measuring Samples

Insert the sample cell and close the lid
Press Read (or Measure in scan/time-course modes)
Record the result (absorbance, concentration, or %T depending on mode)
Remove the cell. Rinse and refill for the next sample, or use a fresh cell.



7.6 Wavelength Scan Mode

From the home screen, select Wavelength Scan
Set the start and end wavelengths and the scan increment (typically 1 nm)
Zero the instrument with a blank across the full scan range
Insert the sample and press Start Scan
The spectrum is displayed on screen. Use the cursor to read peak wavelengths and absorbance values.
Export the scan data via USB (see Section 6.8)



7.7 User-Defined Programs
The DR3900 allows creation of custom calibration curves for analytes not covered by the factory-stored programs:

Select User Programs from the home screen, then New
Set the measurement wavelength, units, and cell type
Prepare a series of standards spanning the expected concentration range (minimum 5 points plus a blank)
Read each standard and enter the known concentration when prompted
The instrument fits a calibration curve (linear, polynomial, or segmented). Review the correlation coefficient (\(r^2\)); accept only if \(r^2 \geq 0.995\) for linear methods (Harris & Lucy, 2020).
Save the program with a descriptive name and program number



7.8 Data Export

Connect a USB flash drive to the USB-A port on the front panel
From the home screen, select Data Log
Select the readings to export and press Send to USB
Data are saved as .csv files that can be opened in R or Excel
Alternatively, connect the DR3900 to a PC via USB cable and use Hach’s LINK2SC or Claros software for direct data transfer



7.9 Shutdown

Remove all cells from the sample compartment
Wipe the cell holder with a dry lint-free tissue to remove any spilled liquid
Close the sample compartment lid
Turn off the instrument using the rear power switch
Cover the instrument with the dust cover if one is available

title: Hach DR3900 Benchtop Spectrophotometer
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Daily Verification
Before each analytical session:

Run a DI water blank; the reading should be 0.000 \(\pm\) 0.005 Abs at the working wavelength
Run a Hach-supplied verification standard (e.g., StablCal formazin standard or NIST-traceable absorbance filter) at the working wavelength. Acceptance: within \(\pm\) 0.01 Abs of the certified value, or \(\pm\) 5%, whichever is larger.



8.2 Lamp Monitoring
The DR3900 tracks lamp hours internally. When a lamp approaches its rated lifetime (typically 2000 hours for deuterium, longer for tungsten), the instrument displays a warning.

Record lamp hours monthly in the instrument log
Replace lamps per the Hach service manual or contact Hach technical support
After lamp replacement, run the full wavelength verification procedure



8.3 Annual Verification
At least once per year (or after any service event):

Run a multi-wavelength check using a NIST-traceable holmium oxide filter to verify wavelength accuracy (\(\pm\) 1 nm)
Run a multi-point photometric accuracy check using neutral density filters or potassium dichromate standards across the range 0.1–1.5 Abs (Skoog et al., 2018)
Record results in the instrument log and retain the verification report

text: This procedure describes bench-top measurement of pH and specific conductance (conductivity) in water samples, soil extracts, and other aqueous solutions using a laboratory pH/conductivity meter. title: pH and Conductivity – Bench-Top Measurements
text:
4 Definitions

Buffer solution: A solution that resists changes in pH upon addition of small amounts of acid or base; used to calibrate pH electrodes; standard buffers are pH 4.00, 7.00, and 10.01 at 25 °C.
Calibration slope: The millivolt change per pH unit measured during two-point calibration; theoretical value is -59.16 mV/pH at 25 °C (Nernst equation); acceptable range is 90–102% of theoretical.
Conductivity: A measure of a solution’s ability to conduct electrical current, expressed in µS/cm or mS/cm; proportional to the concentration of dissolved ions; temperature-dependent.
Junction potential: A small voltage that develops at the reference electrode junction where two solutions of different composition meet; a source of measurement error that is minimized by proper electrode storage and frequent replacement of the reference filling solution.
pH: The negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity: \(pH = -\log_{10}[H^+]\); measured potentiometrically using a glass electrode and a reference electrode.
Specific conductance: Conductivity corrected to a reference temperature of 25 °C; allows comparison of measurements made at different temperatures.
Temperature compensation: Automatic adjustment of conductivity readings to 25 °C using a built-in thermistor; essential for accurate comparisons because conductivity changes approximately 2% per °C.

title: pH and Conductivity – Bench-Top Measurements
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Electrode Preparation

Remove the pH electrode from its storage solution. Inspect the glass bulb for cracks, chips, or deposits. If the bulb is damaged, replace the electrode.
If the electrode has a refillable reference junction, check the KCl fill level. Refill to the indicated line with 3 M KCl or saturated KCl solution if low. Open the fill hole during measurements to allow proper electrolyte flow (Rundle, 2011).
Rinse the pH electrode thoroughly with DI water and blot gently with a Kimwipe. Do not rub the glass bulb.
Rinse the conductivity cell with DI water and blot dry.



7.2 pH Calibration (Three-Point)
Calibrate before each measurement session and whenever the meter has been turned off (APHA et al., 2012).

Pour approximately 30–50 mL of each buffer solution into clean, labeled beakers. Do not pour used buffer back into the stock bottle.
Rinse the pH electrode with DI water and blot gently.
Place the electrode into pH 7.00 buffer first. Allow the reading to stabilize (stability indicator on the meter display).
Accept or set the first calibration point to 7.00.
Rinse with DI water, blot, and place into pH 4.01 buffer. Allow to stabilize and accept.
Rinse with DI water, blot, and place into pH 10.01 buffer. Allow to stabilize and accept.
The meter should display the slope (ideally 95–102% of theoretical Nernstian slope, i.e., approximately 56–60 mV/pH unit at 25 C). If the slope falls below 90%, the electrode may need cleaning or replacement (Illingworth, 1981).
Record the calibration date, buffer lot numbers, slope, and any offset in the meter calibration log.







TipTip



Always calibrate starting with pH 7.00, then move to pH 4.01, and finish with pH 10.01. The 7.00 buffer sets the zero point (offset), while the acidic and basic buffers define the slope. If you only have two buffers, bracket the expected sample range (e.g., pH 4 and 7 for acidic samples, pH 7 and 10 for alkaline samples).




7.3 Conductivity Calibration (One-Point)

Rinse the conductivity cell with DI water and blot dry
Pour approximately 30–50 mL of the 1413 uS/cm standard into a clean beaker
Immerse the conductivity cell fully in the standard. Tap gently to release air bubbles from the cell opening.
Allow the reading to stabilize with temperature compensation active
Calibrate (adjust the cell constant) so that the display reads 1413 uS/cm (at 25 C)
Record the calibration date and standard lot number in the log
TBD – if your lab uses a different primary conductivity standard (e.g., 84 uS/cm for low-conductivity water or 12,880 uS/cm for brackish water), adjust accordingly







Important



Never measure conductivity on a water sample that has already been used for pH measurement. The KCl from the pH electrode reference junction leaks into the sample and alters conductivity. Always measure conductivity first, or use a separate aliquot (APHA et al., 2012).




7.4 Measuring pH

Rinse the pH electrode with DI water and blot gently
Pour approximately 30–50 mL of the sample into a clean beaker. Use a separate aliquot from the one used for conductivity.
Immerse the electrode so that the glass bulb and reference junction are fully submerged
Allow the reading to stabilize (typically 30–60 seconds for well-buffered samples; may take 2–3 minutes for low-ionic-strength water)
Record the pH value, sample temperature, and sample ID in the lab notebook
Rinse the electrode with DI water between samples



7.5 Measuring Conductivity

Rinse the conductivity cell with DI water and blot dry
Pour approximately 30–50 mL of the sample into a clean beaker
Immerse the cell fully. Tap gently to dislodge air bubbles.
Allow the reading to stabilize
Record the specific conductance (uS/cm at 25 C), sample temperature, and sample ID in the lab notebook
Rinse the cell with DI water between samples



7.6 Measuring Soil pH and Conductivity (Soil Slurry Method)
For soil pH and electrical conductivity, prepare a soil-water slurry (Rhoades, 1996; Thomas, 1996):

Weigh 10 g of air-dried, sieved (2 mm) soil into a clean beaker
Add 10 mL of DI water for a 1:1 soil-water ratio (or 50 mL for a 1:5 ratio, depending on the protocol). Record the ratio used.
Stir the slurry vigorously for 30 seconds, then allow to stand for 10 minutes
Stir again briefly, then insert the pH electrode into the slurry while it is still suspended. Allow to stabilize and record.
For conductivity, use a separate slurry aliquot or prepare a fresh slurry. Insert the conductivity cell into the supernatant after the soil has settled. Record.
See also SOP-L57 Soil pH and Salinity for additional detail.



7.7 Electrode Storage and Maintenance

After use, rinse the pH electrode with DI water and return it to its storage solution (pH 4 buffer or KCl storage solution as recommended by the manufacturer). Never store the pH electrode dry or in DI water, as this damages the glass membrane (Illingworth, 1981).
Store the conductivity cell dry or in DI water (per manufacturer recommendation).
If the pH electrode response becomes sluggish (stabilization takes more than 3 minutes) or the calibration slope drops below 90%, soak the electrode in electrode cleaning solution or dilute HCl (0.1 M) for 15–30 minutes, rinse with DI water, and recalibrate.
Replace the pH electrode if the slope remains below 90% after cleaning or if the glass bulb is cracked.

title: pH and Conductivity – Bench-Top Measurements
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Calibrate the pH meter before each measurement session using a three-point calibration
Calibrate the conductivity meter before each session using a traceable standard
Acceptable pH calibration slope: 90–102% of theoretical Nernstian slope (approximately 54–60 mV/pH at 25 C)
Check calibration by re-reading pH 7.00 buffer after every 10 samples. If the reading has drifted by more than +/- 0.05 pH units, recalibrate.
Check conductivity by re-reading the 1413 uS/cm standard after every 10 samples. If the reading has drifted by more than +/- 5%, recalibrate.
Run duplicate measurements on at least 10% of samples. Acceptable precision: +/- 0.1 pH units and +/- 5% for conductivity.
Record all calibration data, standard lot numbers, electrode condition, and QC check results in the meter log.

title: Hach Colorimetric Analysis Spectrophotometer / Colorimeter
text: This procedure describes the general operation, calibration, and quality control framework for colorimetric water analysis using the Hach DR3900 benchtop spectrophotometer and the Hach DR900 portable colorimeter. The SOP is designed as a modular framework: Section 6 covers instrument operation common to all analyses, while the Method Registry (Section 7) provides chemistry-specific parameters for each analyte (reagent kit, Hach method number, wavelength, range, reaction time, and interferences). New chemistries can be added to the registry as the lab’s needs evolve, without rewriting the core SOP (APHA et al., 2012; Hach Company, 2024a, 2024b).

title: Hach Colorimetric Analysis Spectrophotometer / Colorimeter
text:
4 Definitions

Absorbance (A): The negative base-10 logarithm of transmittance: \(A = -\log_{10}(T)\); directly proportional to analyte concentration within the linear range of the instrument (Beer-Lambert law) (Hach Company, 2024a).
Beer-Lambert law: The relationship between absorbance, path length, and concentration: \(A = \varepsilon c l\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the molar absorptivity, \(c\) is concentration, and \(l\) is the optical path length; the physical basis for all colorimetric quantification (APHA et al., 2012).
Blank (reagent blank): A sample containing all reagents except the analyte; used to zero the instrument and correct for background absorbance contributed by the reagent matrix (APHA et al., 2012).
Continuing calibration verification (CCV): A known-concentration mid-range standard analyzed at regular intervals during a run to confirm that factory-programmed calibration curves remain accurate; acceptance criterion is ±10% of the stated value (Hach Company, 2024a).
Detection limit (MDL): The minimum analyte concentration reliably distinguished from a blank; method-specific and listed in the Method Registry (§7); the blank must read within the MDL of zero at the start of each session (APHA et al., 2012).
DR3900: The Hach benchtop spectrophotometer; wavelength range 320–1100 nm; uses stored Hach programs or user-defined methods; supports 10 mm square, 1-inch round, and 16 mm round cells (Hach Company, 2024a).
DR900: The Hach portable colorimeter; battery-operated; uses the same stored-program approach as the DR3900; limited to a subset of Hach methods compatible with the 1-inch round cell format (Hach Company, 2024b).
Hach method number: A unique numeric identifier for each Hach reagent-kit and instrument-program combination; used to select the correct stored program on the DR3900 or DR900 and to ensure that the correct reagent is paired with the correct calibration curve (Hach Company, 2024c).
Method Registry: The table in §7 of this SOP listing all validated Hach methods in use in the EA Program laboratory, with analyte, chemistry, program number, reagent catalog number, instrument compatibility, range, sample volume, reaction time, key interferences, and validation status.
Powder pillow: A heat-sealed foil packet containing a pre-weighed, factory-prepared reagent mixture; added directly to the sample to initiate the color-forming reaction; eliminates manual reagent preparation and reduces sources of error (Hach Company, 2024c).
RPD (relative percent difference): |A - B| / ((A + B) / 2) × 100; used to assess duplicate precision; acceptable RPD is less than 20% for concentrations above 5 × the detection limit (APHA et al., 2012).
TNT plus vial: A Hach proprietary pre-dosed reagent vial containing all required reagents sealed in glass; used with the DR3900 for total-nutrient digestion methods (e.g., total phosphorus, total nitrogen) (Hach Company, 2024c).
Zeroing: The process of inserting a reagent blank into the sample cell and pressing Zero to set the baseline absorbance to zero for the selected program; required before each analytical batch (Hach Company, 2024a).

text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Startup and Instrument Check

Turn on the DR3900 and allow it to complete its self-check (approximately 30 seconds).
Verify the lamp status indicator shows “Ready.”
Select the stored program for your analyte by program number (see §7, Method Registry) (Hach Company, 2024a).



7.2 Zeroing

Fill a clean sample cell with DI water to the fill line.
Wipe the cell exterior with a lint-free cloth. Apply silicone oil for 1-inch round cells.
Insert the cell, close the lid, and press Zero. The display must read 0.00 (within the method detection limit). If it does not, clean the cell and re-zero.



7.3 Sample Analysis

Fill a clean cell to the fill line with the water sample.
Add the reagent (powder pillow or TNT vial) per the method instructions.
Cap, invert, and mix as directed. Start the timer for the required reaction time.
When the reaction time is complete, wipe the cell exterior (apply silicone oil for 1-inch round cells).
Insert the cell, close the lid, and press Read.
Record the result, analyte, program number, sample ID, units, date, and time in the lab notebook.
Rinse the cell three times with DI water before the next sample.



7.4 Shutdown

Remove all samples and reagents from the instrument compartment.
Wipe the cell compartment with a lint-free tissue if any liquid is present.
Log the run in the instrument logbook (date, analyst, analytes run, and any instrument issues).
Turn off the DR3900 if the session is complete.

text:
9 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

9.1 Every Analytical Session

Blank: Run a DI water blank at the start of each session; must read within the method MDL of zero (APHA et al., 2012).
Standard check: Run one mid-range Hach standard at the start and end of each session; acceptance: ±10% of the stated value (Hach Company, 2024a).
Duplicates: Analyze at least 10% of samples in duplicate; acceptable RPD less than 20% above 5 × the detection limit.



9.2 Calibration Verification
The DR3900 and DR900 use factory-programmed calibration curves that do not require user calibration under normal conditions (Hach Company, 2024a, 2024b). However:

Run a multi-point verification using Hach-supplied standards at least annually or when the instrument is serviced.
If a standard check deviates by more than 10%, clean the cell, re-zero, and re-read. If the problem persists, contact Hach technical support.

title: Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD5)
text: This SOP describes the determination of five-day biochemical oxygen demand (BOD5) in water and wastewater samples using the manometric method (WTW OxiTop system). BOD5 is a measure of the dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms during the aerobic decomposition of organic matter over a five-day incubation period at 20 °C and is the standard regulatory indicator of organic pollution load in water (APHA et al., 2012; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 1978).

text: This SOP describes the determination of five-day biochemical oxygen demand (BOD5) in water and wastewater samples using the manometric method (WTW OxiTop system). BOD5 is a measure of the dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms during the aerobic decomposition of organic matter over a five-day incubation period at 20 °C and is the standard regulatory indicator of organic pollution load in water (APHA et al., 2012; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 1978).

title: Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD5)
text:
4 Definitions

Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD): The mass of dissolved oxygen consumed per unit volume of sample by microbial oxidation of organic matter under aerobic conditions at 20 °C; expressed in mg/L (APHA et al., 2012).
BOD5: BOD measured over a 5-day incubation period at 20 °C; the standard regulatory measure of organic pollution load in surface water and effluent (APHA et al., 2012; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 1978).
Carbonaceous BOD (CBOD): BOD attributable to carbon-containing organic compounds; measured in the presence of a nitrification inhibitor (allylthiourea) to prevent oxygen consumption by nitrifying bacteria from contributing to the result.
Dilution water: Aerated, buffered, nutrient-supplemented deionized water used to dilute concentrated samples to bring the expected BOD5 into the measurable range of the OxiTop system (APHA et al., 2012).
Glucose-glutamic acid (GGA) check standard: A standard seed-check solution prepared at 150 mg/L glucose + 150 mg/L glutamic acid; expected BOD5 of 198 ±30.5 mg/L; used to verify seed quality and method performance (APHA et al., 2012, Method 5210 B).
Manometric method (OxiTop): A closed-system BOD measurement technique in which O2 consumption is tracked by measuring the resulting decrease in headspace pressure; CO2 produced during microbial respiration is absorbed by NaOH pellets, ensuring that pressure changes reflect only oxygen consumption (WTW (Xylem Analytics), 2019).
Nitrification: Microbial oxidation of ammonia to nitrate by nitrifying bacteria; consumes dissolved oxygen and can inflate BOD values if not inhibited in carbonaceous BOD analyses.
Seeding: Addition of a microbial inoculum (e.g., diluted wastewater or settled sewage) to dilution water to ensure adequate microbial activity when samples lack native microorganisms (APHA et al., 2012).

5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Nutrient buffer solutions contain phosphate and ammonium salts; NaOH pellets (CO2 absorbent) are corrosive. Handle with gloves and avoid skin or eye contact.
Biological: Wastewater samples may contain pathogens. Treat all samples as potentially infectious.
Physical: Glass BOD bottles are fragile. Handle with care to avoid breakage.

Safety glasses or goggles
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves



5.2 Emergency Procedures
In case of chemical spill or exposure, refer to SOP-L004 Chemical Spill Response or call Campus Safety. For NaOH contact with skin or eyes, flush immediately with copious water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention.

7 Reagents and Dilution Water

7.1 Nutrient Stock Solutions
Prepare the following four stock solutions; add 1 mL of each per liter of dilution water (APHA et al., 2012):

Phosphate buffer: Dissolve 8.5 g KH2PO4, 21.75 g K2HPO4, 33.4 g Na2HPO4·7H2O, and 1.7 g NH4Cl in ~500 mL deionized water and dilute to 1 L (pH 7.2).
Magnesium sulfate: Dissolve 22.5 g MgSO4·7H2O in deionized water; dilute to 1 L.
Calcium chloride: Dissolve 27.5 g CaCl2 in deionized water; dilute to 1 L.
Ferric chloride: Dissolve 0.25 g FeCl3·6H2O in deionized water; dilute to 1 L.



7.2 Dilution Water Preparation

Fill a clean 1 L vessel with deionized water.
Add 1 mL of each stock solution.
Aerate with an air pump for at least 1 hour to bring DO near saturation.
Verify pH is 6.8–7.2; adjust with dilute HCl or NaOH if necessary.
Allow to equilibrate to 20 °C before use.

title: Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD5)
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Preparation (Day 0)

Calibrate the pH meter per SOP-L300.
Prepare dilution water as described above; make enough for all blanks and samples.
Allow refrigerated samples to equilibrate to 20 °C. Add seed inoculum to both sample and blank bottles if seeding is required.
Verify that all OxiTop manometers are functional (battery check, reset previous readings) (WTW (Xylem Analytics), 2019).



8.2 Bottle Setup

Place a clean magnetic stir bar in each BOD5 bottle.
Measure the appropriate sample volume into each sample bottle (see Table 1).
Add the corresponding volume of dilution water.
For the blank bottle, add dilution water only (same total volume as sample bottles).
Place 2 NaOH pellets in each rubber quiver. Insert the quiver into the bottle neck above the liquid surface.
Screw the OxiTop manometer head onto each bottle; ensure a gas-tight seal.







TipLabeling



Label each bottle (Blank, Sample A-1, Sample A-2, etc.) on both the bottle and the manometer before starting incubation. Record bottle assignments in the lab notebook.




8.3 Incubation

Place all bottles on the magnetic stirrer platform inside the incubator at 20.0 ±1.0 °C.
Activate the OxiTop manometers to begin recording pressure.
Incubate for five days (120 ±2 hours) in the dark; keep the incubator door closed except for daily temperature checks (APHA et al., 2012).
Verify incubator temperature at least once daily; record in the instrument logbook.



8.4 Reading Results (Day 5)

Read the BOD5 value from each OxiTop manometer; the instrument converts pressure decrease to mg/L automatically based on the selected measuring range (WTW (Xylem Analytics), 2019).
Record all readings in the lab notebook: setup and reading dates/ times, incubator temperature log, measuring range, sample IDs, and replicate values.
Remove bottles from the incubator. Discard sample water per §9. Clean bottles and stir bars thoroughly with hot water and detergent; rinse with deionized water.

title: Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD5)
text:
9 Data Analysis and Calculations

9.1 OxiTop Direct Reading
The OxiTop system calculates BOD5 internally from the headspace pressure decrease (WTW (Xylem Analytics), 2019). Record the displayed mg/L value directly.


9.2 Blank Correction
\[
\text{BOD}_{5,\text{corrected}} = \text{BOD}_{5,\text{sample}} - \text{BOD}_{5,\text{blank}}
\]
The blank must be less than 0.2 mg/L for unseeded dilution water (APHA et al., 2012). If the blank exceeds 0.2 mg/L, investigate dilution water quality and consider re-running the analysis.


9.3 Dilution Factor
For highly concentrated samples diluted beyond the standard OxiTop protocol:
\[
\text{BOD}_{5,\text{final}} = \text{BOD}_{5,\text{corrected}} \times \frac{V_{\text{total}}}{V_{\text{sample}}}
\]
For standard OxiTop runs, the dilution factor is already incorporated into the displayed result.

title: Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD5)
text:
10 Quality Control

Run at least one blank per analytical batch (APHA et al., 2012).
Run duplicate sample bottles for each sample; RPD must be less than 20%.
If available, include a GGA check standard at 300 mg/L combined (150 mg/L each); expected BOD5 = 198 ±30.5 mg/L (APHA et al., 2012, Method 5210 B).
Blank BOD5 must be less than 0.2 mg/L (unseeded) or less than 0.6 mg/L (seeded) (APHA et al., 2012).
Verify incubator temperature is 20.0 ±1.0 °C throughout incubation.
Log all QC results; flag and consult the PI if criteria are not met.

title: Microplastics in Water – Extraction and Enumeration
text:
This SOP provides methods for extracting, staining, and enumerating microplastics (particles less than 5 mm) from water samples. Microplastics are stained with Nile Red dye, vacuum-filtered onto glass-fiber filters, and counted under fluorescence using either a Crime-Lite forensic light source with goggles or the Echo Revolve microscope (Erni-Cassola et al., 2017; Maes et al., 2017).
This SOP is intended as an internal teaching and research protocol. Where EA Program data will be submitted to external programs or compared with regulatory monitoring datasets, researchers should consult the emerging standardized methods described in Appendix B and adapt procedures accordingly (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2022; Thornton Hampton et al., 2025).

title: Microplastics in Water – Extraction and Enumeration
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Extraction and enumeration of microplastics from drinking water, surface water, stormwater, and other aqueous samples
Does not apply to: Microplastics in soil, sediment, or biological tissue (see SCCWRP Technical Report #1410.A (Thornton Hampton et al., 2025)); chemical identification of polymer type (requires FTIR or Raman spectroscopy)
Regulatory alignment: This SOP provides a Nile Red fluorescence screening method suitable for research and teaching. It does not replace the FTIR- or Raman-based methods required for California regulatory drinking water monitoring (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2022). Consult Appendix B and the PI before submitting data to SWAMP, CEDEN, or other regulatory programs.

title: Microplastics in Water – Extraction and Enumeration
text:
5 Definitions

FTIR (Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy): An analytical technique that identifies polymer type by comparing a sample’s infrared absorption spectrum to reference spectra; the gold standard for confirmatory microplastic characterization (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2022).
Microplastic (MP): A synthetic polymer particle or fiber with at least one dimension between 1 µm and 5 mm; includes fragments, fibers, films, beads, and foam; classified as primary (manufactured at micro-scale) or secondary (degradation products of larger plastic items) (Maes et al., 2017).
Nanoplastic: A plastic particle smaller than 1 µm; not quantifiable by standard visual methods; an emerging concern for ecological and human health research.
Nile Red: A fluorescent dye that selectively stains hydrophobic plastic surfaces, enabling detection under blue-light excitation; used as a screening tool to distinguish plastic particles from organic debris (Erni-Cassola et al., 2017; Maes et al., 2017).
Procedural blank: A sample of laboratory-grade water carried through the complete analytical procedure alongside field samples; used to quantify airborne and procedural contamination; required for every analytical batch.
Raman spectroscopy: A spectroscopic technique that identifies molecular composition from inelastic light scattering; complementary to FTIR; particularly useful for particles smaller than 10 µm (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2022).
Visual sorting: The initial enumeration step in which particles on a filter are examined under a stereomicroscope or the Revolve fluorescence microscope and candidate plastic particles are identified by color, shape, and texture before any confirmatory chemical analysis.

WarningHazards




Chemical: Acetone is flammable (flash point -20 °C) and potentially toxic by inhalation. All Nile Red solution preparation and sample staining must be performed in a fume hood. Review the SDS for acetone before use.

6.2 Emergency Procedures
For acetone spills, extinguish all ignition sources, ventilate the area, and clean up per SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling. For skin or eye contact, flush with water for at least 15 minutes.

title: Microplastics in Water – Extraction and Enumeration
text:
8 Reagent Preparation

8.1 Nile Red Stock Solution

Working in a fume hood, dissolve Nile Red in acetone to 1 mg/mL.
Store in a dark amber glass bottle at room temperature.
Label with concentration, date, and analyst.



8.2 Working Concentration
The working concentration is 10 µg/mL, achieved by a 100:1 dilution of the stock. For a 500 mL water sample, add 0.5 mL of the 1 mg/mL stock solution (Maes et al., 2017).

title: Microplastics in Water – Extraction and Enumeration
text:
10 Procedure

10.1 Sample Preparation and Staining

Minimize synthetic fiber contamination: wear a cotton lab coat, keep samples covered, and work in a clean area.
Prepare samples in 500 mL volumes in glass bottles.
Working in a fume hood, inject the appropriate volume of Nile Red stock solution (e.g., 0.5 mL for a 500 mL sample) to achieve 10 µg/mL. Cap immediately (Maes et al., 2017).
Incubate with the injected dye for at least 30 minutes at room temperature.



10.2 Vacuum Filtration

Place a Whatman 934-AH glass-fiber filter (42.5 mm, 1.5 µm pore) on the fritted base of the vacuum filtration apparatus.
Vacuum-filter each sample through the filter.
Dry the filter on a watch glass in the oven at 60 °C for 10 minutes.



10.3 Enumeration Option A: Crime-Lite with Goggles






WarningLaser Safety



Do not shine the Crime-Lite into anyone’s eyes. Never observe illuminated samples without the orange filter goggles.



Place the dried filter on a dark, non-reflective surface.
Put on the orange filter goggles.
Illuminate the filter with the Crime-Lite (450–510 nm).
Count fluorescing particles through the goggles, or mount the filter under the dissecting scope with a 550 nm emission filter.
Record particle counts and morphology (fiber, fragment, bead, film).



10.4 Enumeration Option B: Echo Revolve Microscope (Fluorescence)

Mount the dried filter on a glass slide per SOP-L211.
Use the fluorescence channel (excitation ~470 nm, emission ~550 nm long-pass).
Photograph and count fluorescent particles in at least 3 randomly selected fields of view.
Import images into the Revolve app; use the annotation tools to mark and count particles.

title: Microplastics in Water – Extraction and Enumeration
text:
11 Quality Control

Include at least one procedural blank per analytical batch; blank particle counts inform the detection threshold for field samples (Erni-Cassola et al., 2017; Maes et al., 2017).
Analyze at least 3 (preferably 10) randomly selected fields of view per filter; report mean, standard deviation, and coefficient of variation.
Include at least one spiked filter (known number of plastic particles added before staining) per batch to verify Nile Red staining performance.







ImportantContamination Controls Are Essential



Every batch must include procedural blanks processed identically to samples. Without blanks, microplastic counts cannot be meaningfully interpreted (Maes et al., 2017).

18 Appendix B: Regulatory and Standards Context

In 2022, the California State Water Resources Control Board approved a policy requiring drinking water agencies to monitor microplastics, specifying FTIR and Raman spectroscopy as the two approved analytical methods (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2022). Standardized collection procedures for aquatic biota and sediment are described in SCCWRP Technical Report #1410.A (Thornton Hampton et al., 2025).
The Nile Red fluorescence screening method in this SOP is appropriate for teaching and exploratory research but does not meet California regulatory requirements (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2022). For data intended for submission to SWAMP or CEDEN:

Use microplastics-analysis-grade water for all blanks and rinses
Adopt SCCWRP contamination control procedures
Confirm polymer identity on a subset of particles by FTIR or Raman
Consult the PI before beginning any study intended for regulatory submission

title: Chlorophyll a Extraction and Fluorometric Analysis
text: This procedure describes the in vitro determination of chlorophyll a and pheophytin a concentrations in marine and freshwater phytoplankton by fluorescence. Chlorophyll-containing cells are concentrated on a glass fiber filter, extracted in 90% acetone, and measured on the Turner Designs Trilogy Fluorometer before and after acidification with 0.1 N HCl. The method is modified from US EPA Method 445.0 and APHA Standard Methods 10200 H (APHA et al., 2012; Arar & Collins, 1997).

title: Chlorophyll a Extraction and Fluorometric Analysis
text:
4 Definitions

Chlorophyll a: The primary photosynthetic pigment in phytoplankton, algae, and higher plants; absorbs red light (~665 nm) and blue light (~430 nm); the standard proxy for phytoplankton biomass in aquatic systems.
Chlorophyll b: An accessory pigment found in green algae and higher plants; absorbs at ~647 nm; distinguishable from chlorophyll a by spectrophotometry or fluorometry.
Fluorometric method: Measurement of chlorophyll a by fluorescence emission (~685 nm) after excitation (~430 nm); more sensitive than spectrophotometry; requires acidification to distinguish chlorophyll a from pheophytin a.
Pheophytin a: The magnesium-free degradation product of chlorophyll a; retains similar absorption properties; distinguished from chlorophyll a by the acidification step, which converts chlorophyll a to pheophytin a and causes a characteristic decrease in fluorescence.
Trichromatic equation: Spectrophotometric calculation of chlorophyll a, b, and c concentrations in an extract from absorbance readings at three wavelengths (665, 647, 630 nm); corrects for spectral overlap among pigments.
Turbid extract correction: Subtraction of non-specific absorbance (measured at 750 nm, where chlorophyll does not absorb) from all pigment wavelength readings to correct for turbidity and colored dissolved compounds in the extract.

title: Chlorophyll a Extraction and Fluorometric Analysis
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Reagent Preparation
0.1 N HCl: Add 0.85 mL of concentrated HCl to approximately 50 mL of Milli-Q water in a 100 mL volumetric flask. Bring to volume with Milli-Q water. Mix thoroughly.
90% Aqueous Acetone: Measure 100 mL of Milli-Q water into a 100 mL volumetric flask, then transfer to a 1 L volumetric flask. Fill to the 1 L mark with HPLC-grade acetone. Mix and transfer to a dark amber bottle. Label and store in the flammables cabinet.
Chlorophyll a Stock Standard Solution (SSS): Working in subdued light, transfer the contents of the chlorophyll a ampoule into a 50 mL volumetric flask and dilute to volume with 90% acetone. Determine the concentration spectrophotometrically. Wrap in foil and label with the lot number. Stable for at least six months in an airtight container at room temperature.
Primary Dilution Standard (PDS): Add 1 mL of SSS to a 100 mL volumetric flask and dilute to volume with 90% acetone. If the SSS was prepared from exactly 1 mg of pure chlorophyll a, the PDS concentration is 200 ug/L. Prepare fresh before use. Wrap in foil.
Quality Control Standards (QCs): Prepare from the PDS at the following concentrations: 5, 20, 50, and 200 ug/L. Wrap in foil.






Important



All photosynthetic pigments are light- and temperature-sensitive. Perform all work in subdued light. Store all standards, QC materials, and filter samples in the dark at –20 C when not in use.




7.2 Filtration

Invert the sample bottle gently several times to suspend particles
Assemble the glass filtration unit: place the fritted glass base on the Erlenmeyer flask, position a GF/F filter on the frit using forceps, seat the glass funnel on top, and secure with the spring clamp
Connect the vacuum hose and turn on the vacuum
Working in subdued light, filter the sample in 20 mL increments using a graduated cylinder. The volume required depends on algal density:




Sample Type
Typical Volume




Benthic samples
approximately 5 mL


Freshwater
20–300 mL


Seawater
100–1000+ mL




Stop filtering when a brown or green tint is visible on the filter. Record the exact filtered volume. If the filter becomes too darkly colored, the sample may exceed the linear dynamic range and require dilution during analysis.
Using forceps and a micro spatula, fold the filter in half with the retained material on the inside
Gently blot excess water from the outside of the filter with a Kimwipe
Place the folded filter in a clean 15 mL centrifuge tube or a plastic petri dish
Include a laboratory reagent blank (100 mL Milli-Q water through a GF/F filter) and a field duplicate every 10–15 samples
Wrap the tubes or dishes in aluminum foil and store at –20 C. Filters may be stored frozen for up to 28 days before extraction.



7.3 Extraction – Sonication Method

Remove samples and QCs from the freezer and allow to reach room temperature
Add 25 mL of 90% aqueous acetone to each tube, ensuring the filter is fully submerged. Cap the tubes and invert several times.
Secure the sonicator probe in its clamp stand
Put on hearing protection
Set the sonicator to 70% amplitude
Submerge the tip halfway into the acetone solution and sonicate, moving the tip around the sample to break up the filter completely
After sonication, shake the tube vigorously, wrap in foil, and steep in the refrigerator (4 C) for a minimum of 2 hours







Important



Never operate the sonicator outside of solution. The tip will overheat and be damaged.




7.4 Extraction – Tissue Grinder Method (Alternative)

Using forceps, transfer the filter into a 30 mL glass grinding tube and push it to the bottom with the pestle or a glass rod
Add 4 mL of 90% acetone and grind with the pestle until the filter is converted to a slurry. Avoid overheating.
Pour the slurry into a 15 mL screw-cap centrifuge tube
Rinse the pestle and grinding tube with 6 mL of 90% acetone and add the rinse to the centrifuge tube
Cap, shake vigorously, wrap in foil, and steep at 4 C for 2 hours
Clean the grinder and pestle with water followed by acetone between samples; wipe dry with a Kimwipe



7.5 Post-Extraction Processing

Remove samples from the refrigerator and allow to reach room temperature (approximately 30 minutes)
Shake each tube vigorously
Centrifuge at 1,000 x g for 5 minutes using the fixed-angle rotor until all filter material is pelleted
Handle tubes carefully after centrifugation; do not resuspend the pellet



7.6 Fluorometric Analysis

Transfer 2.5 mL of clear supernatant from each tube into a clean glass cuvette, taking care not to disturb the pellet
Turn on the Trilogy Fluorometer and allow the 10-minute warm-up to complete (see SOP-L203)
Select the Chlor-A (Chlorophyll Acidification) module on the touch screen
Calibrate using the QCs prepared from the PDS, or load a saved calibration. For a new calibration, follow the Direct Multipoint Calibration procedure in SOP-L203, Section 7.3.
Run a 90% acetone blank
Wipe the outside of each cuvette with a Kimwipe before inserting into the fluorometer
Measure and record the pre-acidification fluorescence (\(F_b\))







Note



If the chlorophyll a reading exceeds 90% of the upper limit of the linear dynamic range (LDR = 1,000 ug/L), dilute the sample before proceeding. For a 1:2 dilution, add 1 mL of sample to 1 mL of 90% acetone. For a 1:100 dilution, add 50 uL of sample to 4.95 mL of 90% acetone.



Add 75 uL of 0.1 N HCl to the cuvette. Seal with parafilm and invert several times to mix. Wait 90 seconds.
Measure and record the post-acidification fluorescence (\(F_a\))
Repeat for all samples, QCs, and blanks

title: Chlorophyll a Extraction and Fluorometric Analysis
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Calculations
Variables:

\([Std]\) = concentration of the calibration standard used (ug/L)
\(S_b\) = standard fluorescence reading before acidification
\(S_a\) = standard fluorescence reading after acidification
\(F_b\) = sample fluorescence before acidification
\(F_a\) = sample fluorescence after acidification
\(V_e\) = volume of extract (mL)
\(V_s\) = volume of sample filtered (mL)

Equations:
\[
AR = \frac{S_b - \text{Blank}}{S_a - \text{Blank}}
\]
\[
\text{InterpB} = [Std] \times \frac{F_b - \text{Blank}}{S_b - \text{Blank}}
\]
\[
\text{InterpA} = [Std] \times \frac{F_a - \text{Blank}}{S_b - \text{Blank}}
\]
\[
\text{Chlorophyll } a \; (\mu\text{g/L}) =
\frac{AR}{AR - 1} \times (\text{InterpB} - \text{InterpA}) \times \frac{V_e}{V_s}
\]
\[
\text{Pheophytin } a \; (\mu\text{g/L}) =
\left(AR \times \text{InterpA} - \text{InterpB}\right) \times \frac{V_e}{V_s}
\]


8.2 QC Requirements

Run a laboratory reagent blank (LRB) every 10–15 samples. The LRB should read below the calculated lower detection limit.
QC standards should recover within +/- 20% of the known value
Relative standard deviation (RSD) of replicate measurements should be within +/- 20%
Field duplicates should agree within +/- 20% relative percent difference
Samples, standards, LRBs, and QCs must all be at ambient room temperature during analysis. Fluorescence is temperature-dependent; cooler samples produce artificially high readings.

title: Chlorophyll a Extraction and Fluorometric Analysis
text:
12 Appendix A: Example Calculation



Code
# Corrected chlorophyll a and pheophytin a calculation
# Per EPA Method 445.0

# Calibration standard
Std_conc <- 50       # ug/L (QC standard concentration)
S_b <- 485           # Standard fluorescence before acid
S_a <- 210           # Standard fluorescence after acid
blank <- 5           # Blank fluorescence

# Sample readings
F_b <- 320           # Sample fluorescence before acid
F_a <- 140           # Sample fluorescence after acid

# Volumes
V_e <- 25            # mL of extract (acetone)
V_s <- 100           # mL of sample filtered

# Calculations
AR <- (S_b - blank) / (S_a - blank)
InterpB <- Std_conc * (F_b - blank) / (S_b - blank)
InterpA <- Std_conc * (F_a - blank) / (S_b - blank)

chl_a <- (AR / (AR - 1)) * (InterpB - InterpA) * (V_e / V_s)
pheo_a <- (AR * InterpA - InterpB) * (V_e / V_s)

cat(sprintf("Acid ratio (AR):        %.3f\n", AR))
cat(sprintf("Chlorophyll a:          %.2f ug/L\n", chl_a))
cat(sprintf("Pheophytin a:           %.2f ug/L\n", pheo_a))

Effect
Mitigation

title: Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS)
text: This SOP describes the gravimetric determination of Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) in environmental water samples (e.g., surface water, groundwater, runoff). TSS represents the portion of solids retained by a glass fiber filter, while TDS represents the portion that passes through the filter and is dried to constant weight in a vessel (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS)
text: This SOP describes the gravimetric determination of Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) in environmental water samples (e.g., surface water, groundwater, runoff). TSS represents the portion of solids retained by a glass fiber filter, while TDS represents the portion that passes through the filter and is dried to constant weight in a vessel (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS)

2 Scope

Applies to: Environmental water samples analyzed for TSS and TDS by gravimetric methods.
Does not apply to: Settleable solids, volatile suspended solids, or non-aqueous matrices.
Location: Environmental analysis laboratories.

title: Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS)
text:
4 Definitions

Constant mass: Successive weighings (after additional drying cycles of at least 1 hour) agree within ±0.5 mg; the criterion confirming complete desiccation.
Detection limit (MDL): The minimum concentration that can be reliably distinguished from a blank; for gravimetric TSS/TDS, the practical lower limit is approximately 5 mg/L, set by the precision of the analytical balance and filter tare variability (APHA et al., 2012).
Fixed residue: The fraction of total solids remaining after ignition at 550 °C; equivalent to inorganic (mineral) solids.
Relative percent difference (RPD): A measure of duplicate precision: RPD (%) = |A - B| / ((A + B) / 2) × 100; acceptance criterion for TSS/TDS duplicates is ≤ 10%.
Total dissolved solids (TDS): The mass of material passing through a 0.45 µm filter per unit volume of sample, determined gravimetrically after evaporation at 180 °C; expressed in mg/L (APHA et al., 2012, Method 2540 C).
Total solids (TS): The residue remaining after evaporation of a sample at 103–105 °C; TS = TSS + TDS.
Total suspended solids (TSS): The mass of material retained on a pre-weighed glass fiber filter per unit volume of sample; expressed in mg/L (APHA et al., 2012, Method 2540 D).
Volatile suspended solids (VSS): The fraction of TSS lost on ignition at 550 °C; approximates the organic content of suspended solids (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS)
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Filter and Dish Preparation

TSS filter prep: Place a glass fiber filter on the filtration apparatus. Apply vacuum and wash with three successive 20 mL volumes of DI water. Continue vacuum until all trace water is removed. Transfer the filter to an aluminum weigh pan and dry in an oven at 103–105 °C for 1 hour. Cool in a desiccator to room temperature and weigh to determine the tare mass (\(B_{\text{TSS}}\)) (APHA et al., 2012).
TDS dish prep: Clean an evaporating dish and heat in an oven at 180 ±2 °C for 1 hour. Cool completely in a desiccator and record the stable tare mass (\(B_{\text{TDS}}\)).



7.2 Filtration and Sample Analysis

Assemble the pre-weighed filter pad into the filtration funnel and wet with a small volume of DI water to seal it against the porous plate. Turn on the vacuum.
Shake the sample bottle vigorously to achieve homogeneous particle distribution. Measure a known sample volume (\(V\), typically 100 mL to 500 mL depending on turbidity) using a graduated cylinder.
Pour the measured sample into the filter funnel. Wash the cylinder and funnel walls with three successive 10 mL aliquots of DI water, allowing total drainage between washings.
For TSS: Carefully remove the filter pad from the funnel using blunt forceps. Place it back in its aluminum pan and dry in the oven at 103–105 °C for at least 1 hour. Cool in the desiccator and weigh to constant mass (\(A_{\text{TSS}}\)).
For TDS: Transfer the entire filtrate volume from the filter flask quantitatively into the pre-weighed evaporating dish. Place the dish into the drying oven at 180 ±2 °C until all liquid evaporates completely. Dry for at least an additional hour, cool inside the desiccator, and weigh to find the final mass (\(A_{\text{TDS}}\)).







TipConstant Mass



“Constant mass” means that successive weighings (after additional drying cycles of at least 1 hour) agree within ±0.5 mg (APHA et al., 2012).




7.3 Shutdown and Cleanup

Discard used filters in solid waste.
Rinse filtration apparatus thoroughly with DI water.
Return evaporating dishes and tongs to storage after cooling.
Turn off the vacuum pump and drying oven if no other users need them.

title: Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS)
text:
8 Calculations
\[
\text{TSS (mg/L)} = \frac{(A_{\text{TSS}} - B_{\text{TSS}}) \times 1{,}000{,}000}{V \text{ (mL)}}
\]
\[
\text{TDS (mg/L)} = \frac{(A_{\text{TDS}} - B_{\text{TDS}}) \times 1{,}000{,}000}{V \text{ (mL)}}
\]
Where:

\(A\) = weight of dry filter or dish plus residue (g)
\(B\) = tare weight of clean filter or dish (g)
\(V\) = sample volume (mL)

If the calculated TSS residue mass is less than 2.5 mg, increase the sample volume and repeat (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS)
text:
9 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Run a method blank (DI water through the full procedure) with each batch. The blank result must be less than the method detection limit (APHA et al., 2012).
Duplicate samples should agree within ±10% RPD.
If the measured residue mass is less than 2.5 mg, use a larger sample volume.

title: eDNA Laboratory Processing
text: This SOP describes contamination-controlled processing protocols for environmental DNA (eDNA) from aquatic collection matrices. It outlines vacuum membrane filtration, total genomic extraction, and subsequent PCR inhibition testing steps (Goldberg et al., 2016).

title: eDNA Laboratory Processing
text: This SOP describes contamination-controlled processing protocols for environmental DNA (eDNA) from aquatic collection matrices. It outlines vacuum membrane filtration, total genomic extraction, and subsequent PCR inhibition testing steps (Goldberg et al., 2016).

title: eDNA Laboratory Processing
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Laboratory processing of aquatic eDNA samples, including filtration, DNA extraction, and inhibition screening prior to PCR amplification.
Does not apply to: Field collection of eDNA water samples, PCR amplification and sequencing workflows, or bioinformatic analysis of sequence data.
Location: Dedicated Pre-PCR clean room, physically separated from post-amplification facilities.

title: eDNA Laboratory Processing
text:

title: eDNA Laboratory Processing
text:
4 Definitions

Amplification inhibition: Suppression of PCR or ddPCR amplification efficiency by co-extracted substances such as humic acids, tannins, heavy metals, or residual ethanol; detected by comparing amplification of a known-concentration internal positive control (Jane et al., 2015; McKee et al., 2015).
Contamination control: Practices that prevent introduction of exogenous DNA into eDNA samples, including use of UV-decontaminated surfaces, negative-pressure rooms, dedicated pre-PCR equipment, and frequent glove changes (Goldberg et al., 2016).
eDNA (environmental DNA): Genetic material shed into the environment by organisms through mucus, feces, skin cells, gametes, and other biological material; collected from water, sediment, or air samples without direct organism capture (Ficetola et al., 2008).
Environmental DNA extraction: The process of lysing filter-captured cells or particles and purifying nucleic acids from co-extracted inhibitors; produces a DNA extract suitable for PCR-based detection (Qiagen, 2024).
Extraction blank (negative control): A reagent-only sample carried through the full extraction procedure without biological material; detects reagent or cross-contamination; must yield no amplification of target sequences (Goldberg et al., 2016).
Field blank: A filter processed through the collection and preservation steps at the site but with no water sample passed through it; detects airborne or handling contamination in the field (Goldberg et al., 2016).
Inhibition testing: A diagnostic assay in which a known-positive control is co-amplified with the sample to detect PCR inhibition; common approaches include an internal amplification control (IAC) or serial dilution (McKee et al., 2015).
Sterivex filter: A polysulfone capsule filter (0.22 or 0.45 µm) used to concentrate eDNA from large water volumes by inline pumping; sealed and stored at -20 °C or -80 °C for later extraction.
Vacuum filtration pressure: Vacuum applied to the filter manifold during eDNA filtration; should be kept below 150 mmHg to minimize cell lysis and DNA shearing on the filter membrane.

text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: 10% bleach solution (0.5% sodium hypochlorite) is corrosive to skin and eyes. Lysis buffers contain chaotropic salts (e.g., guanidinium thiocyanate) that are harmful if ingested or inhaled. Ethanol-based wash buffers are flammable.
Biological: Environmental water samples may harbor unknown pathogens. Treat all samples as potentially infectious.
Physical: Vacuum filtration apparatus operates under reduced pressure; ensure flasks are borosilicate and crack-free.

Clean nitrile gloves (change frequently between sample groups)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
