title: eDNA Laboratory Processing
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Contamination Control and Spatial Separation






ImportantContamination Prevention



Environmental DNA exists at extremely low fragment densities and is exceptionally vulnerable to cross-contamination. Strict spatial separation and decontamination protocols are mandatory (Goldberg et al., 2016; Turner et al., 2015).



All eDNA filtration and extraction work must occur in the dedicated Pre-PCR room, structurally separated from post-amplification thermocycling facilities.
Decontamination regimen: Before and after each protocol sequence, wipe all benchtops, pipettes, and manifold bodies with 10% bleach solution. Allow a 10-minute contact window, then rinse with 70% ethanol and molecular-grade water.
Wear a lab coat dedicated to the Pre-PCR room. Put on clean nitrile gloves and replace them frequently (e.g., between processing separate filtration manifolds or extraction groups).



7.2 Phase A: Membrane Vacuum Filtration

Sanitize the filter manifold station completely using 10% bleach solution and rinse as described in §6.1.
Using sterile, single-use plastic forceps, center a sterile 0.45 µm cellulose nitrate or glass fiber filter disc onto the clean manifold support pad. Mount the upper funnel collar tightly.
Agitate the water sample bottle and pour a precise volume (typically 500 mL to 2 L) into the funnel. Apply low vacuum pressure (< 150 mmHg) to avoid cell lysis on the filter.







NoteVacuum Pressure



Keeping vacuum pressure below 150 mmHg minimizes mechanical disruption of captured cells and reduces DNA loss through the filter membrane. If the filter clogs before the target volume is processed, record the actual volume filtered and proceed to step 4.



Once filtration completes, use sterile forceps to roll or fold the filter disc inward (preventing target loss on exterior surfaces) and insert it into a sterile 2.0 mL microcentrifuge tube containing lysis buffer or silica gel desiccant. Freeze at –20 °C if extraction is deferred.



7.3 Phase B: Genomic eDNA Extraction
This phase uses standard commercial spin-column kits (e.g., DNeasy Blood & Tissue or PowerWater kits (Qiagen, 2024)).

Add 50 µL Proteinase K and the target volume of lysis buffer directly to the microcentrifuge tube containing the folded filter disc. Incubate on a digital dry bath shaker at 56 °C for at least 2–3 hours (or overnight) to thoroughly digest captured cellular structures.
Centrifuge to pellet filter debris. Pass the clear supernatant lysate through a silica spin column. Wash sequentially with ethanol-based buffers to remove protein impurities. Elute clean genomic fragments using a low-ionic-strength buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl or molecular-grade water).







TipElution Volume



A smaller elution volume (e.g., 50–100 µL) increases DNA concentration but may reduce total yield. Choose based on downstream assay sensitivity requirements.




7.4 Phase C: Internal Control Inhibition Testing
Environmental matrices contain co-extracted PCR inhibitors (humic acids, fulvic acids, tannic compounds) that can produce false negative results (Jane et al., 2015; McKee et al., 2015).

Run a dual-plex qPCR assay using an artificial Internal Positive Control (IPC) DNA target sequence and matched primer/probe set alongside your environmental samples.
Analysis threshold: If the IPC amplification curve shifts to the right (\(\Delta C_t > 3.0\) cycles) relative to the control baseline water standard, inhibition is present (McKee et al., 2015).
Remediation: For inhibited extracts, either pass the genomic sample through a secondary commercial inhibitor-removal column (e.g., Zymo OneStep PCR Inhibitor Removal) or perform a 1:10 dilution with molecular-grade water before final target gene amplification. Re-test IPC performance after remediation (McKee et al., 2015).



7.5 Cleanup and Storage

Dispose of used lysis buffer, wash buffer, and flow-through in the appropriate chemical waste stream (§8).
Wipe down all work surfaces with 10% bleach, followed by 70% ethanol and molecular-grade water.
Store extracted DNA at –20 °C (short-term) or –80 °C (long-term archival).

title: Soil Texture Analysis – Hydrometer Method
text:
This procedure describes the determination of soil particle size distribution using the hydrometer method (ASTM D422). Soil texture (the relative proportions of sand, silt, and clay) is a fundamental physical property that controls water-holding capacity, drainage, nutrient retention, and soil structure. The hydrometer method measures the density of a soil-water suspension at timed intervals as progressively finer particles settle, allowing calculation of the percent sand, silt, and clay and assignment of a USDA textural class.
For a rapid field estimate of texture without laboratory equipment, see SOP-F401 Texture by Feel.

2 Scope

Applies to: Mineral soils with less than approximately 20% coarse fragments (greater than 2 mm). Soils with high organic matter or carbonates require pre-treatment (see Section 6.4).
Does not apply to: Pure gravel, organic soils (histosols), or soils where only a textural class estimate is needed (use SOP-F401 instead)
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Soil Texture Analysis – Hydrometer Method
text:
4 Definitions

Clay: Soil mineral particles with an equivalent spherical diameter less than 0.002 mm (2 µm); slow-settling; comprises the finest soil texture fraction.
Dispersion: The process of separating soil aggregates into individual particles by chemical treatment (sodium hexametaphosphate) and mechanical agitation; essential for accurate hydrometer analysis.
ASTM 151H hydrometer: A standardized glass hydrometer calibrated in g L-1 for use in soil texture analysis; reads the density of the suspension at the center of the hydrometer bulb.
Sand: Soil mineral particles with an equivalent spherical diameter of 0.05–2.0 mm; collected on a 0.05 mm sieve after sedimentation.
Sedimentation: The settling of soil particles in suspension under gravity; particle settling velocity follows Stokes’ Law: \(v = 2gr^2(\rho_s - \rho_l) / (9\eta)\), where \(r\) is particle radius, \(\rho_s\) is particle density, \(\rho_l\) is liquid density, and \(\eta\) is dynamic viscosity.
Silt: Soil mineral particles with an equivalent spherical diameter of 0.002–0.05 mm; intermediate settling rate; calculated as silt = 100% - sand% - clay%.
Stokes’ Law: The physical law governing particle sedimentation velocity in a viscous fluid; the basis for hydrometer texture analysis; assumes spherical particles of uniform density (2.65 g cm-3).
Texture class: A USDA textural classification (e.g., sandy loam, clay loam, silty clay) based on the relative percentages of sand, silt, and clay; determined from the USDA textural triangle.

title: Soil Texture Analysis – Hydrometer Method
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Sodium hexametaphosphate (HMP) is a mild skin and eye irritant. Hydrogen peroxide (30%) is a strong oxidizer and causes burns on contact. Hydrochloric acid (1 N) is corrosive.
Physical: The milkshake mixer creates a vigorous vortex; keep loose clothing and hair clear. Hot plates and drying ovens pose burn risk.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses (chemical-safety goggles when using H2O2 or HCl)
Lab coat
Nitrile or latex gloves
Hearing protection not required but recommended near the mixer



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For H2O2 or HCl splashes, flush with water for at least 15 minutes. For HMP powder inhalation, move to fresh air. Refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.

title: Soil Texture Analysis – Hydrometer Method
text:
7 Procedure
The analysis spans multiple lab sessions. Plan accordingly:








Session
Tasks
Time Required




1
Air-dry 200 g of soil
24+ hours (passive)


2
Sieve through No. 10; subsample for moisture
1–2 hours


3
Calculate \(DW_e\); pre-treat and/or disperse
2–3 hours + 16 h soak


4
Conduct hydrometer readings
24+ hours (intermittent)


5
Recover sand on No. 200 sieve; complete data entry
1–2 hours




7.1 Air-Drying the Soil

Spread approximately 200 g of field-moist soil in a labeled tin or beaker
Allow to equilibrate with laboratory air for 24 hours or more. Very wet soils may require several days.
Break up large clods periodically to promote even drying



7.2 Sieving Through the No. 10 Sieve
Soil is defined as particles less than 2 mm. Gravel must be removed before analysis but quantified.

Homogenize the air-dried soil by thorough mixing
Weigh approximately 65 g (silt/clay soils) or 120 g (sandy soils) of air-dried soil and record the mass
Using a mortar and pestle, gently break up aggregates so that individual particles pass the No. 10 sieve. Do not crush primary mineral grains.
Sieve the soil through the No. 10 sieve (2 mm)
Weigh and record the mass of soil that passed through the sieve
Calculate the percent passing:

\[
\text{Percent passing No. 10} = \frac{M_{\text{passed}}}{M_{\text{total}}} \times 100
\]


7.3 Determining Hygroscopic Moisture Content
Air-dried soil still contains hygroscopic water adsorbed to clay surfaces, salts, and organic matter. This must be measured and corrected for.

Select a soil tin; record the tin number and tare mass
Transfer a 10–15 g subsample of the air-dried, sieved soil to the tin and record the air-dried mass (tin + soil)
Dry in the oven at 110 C for approximately 24 hours
Cool in a desiccator and record the oven-dried mass (tin + soil)
Calculate hygroscopic moisture:

\[
\text{Moisture}_H = \frac{M_{\text{air-dry w/ tin}} - M_{\text{oven-dry w/ tin}}}{M_{\text{air-dry w/ tin}} - M_{\text{tin}}}
\]






Note



The standard drying temperature of 105–110 C is somewhat arbitrary. Clay minerals may retain 10–15% water (dry basis) at 400 C. Organic components also release volatiles over a range of temperatures. The key is to specify and consistently use the same temperature.




7.4 Calculating Oven-Dry Equivalent Mass (\(DW_e\))
The target oven-dry equivalent mass for the hydrometer test is 50 g for fine-textured soils or 100 g for coarse-textured soils (greater than approximately 70% sand).
Since air-dried soil contains hygroscopic water, the actual mass of air-dried soil to weigh out is:
\[
DW_{\text{air}} = \frac{DW_e}{1 - \text{Moisture}_H}
\]
where \(DW_e\) = 50 g or 100 g.


7.5 Pre-Treatment (If Required)
Pre-treatment is necessary for soils high in organic matter, carbonates, iron oxides, or soluble salts. If the soil is low in all of these, proceed directly to Section 6.6.

Transfer \(DW_{\text{air}}\) g of soil to a 400 mL beaker
Carbonate removal: Add 50 mL DI water and sufficient 1 N HCl to reduce the pH to 3.0–4.0. Stir and allow to equilibrate for 10 minutes until effervescence ceases.
Organic matter removal: Carefully add 30% H2O2 a few milliliters at a time, allowing frothing to subside between additions. If necessary, acidify the suspension with a few drops of 1 N HCl (H2O2 oxidation requires an acidic medium). When frothing subsides, heat to 90 C and continue adding H2O2 until no further reaction occurs. Rinse down the beaker walls and continue heating until excess H2O2 is consumed.
Iron oxide removal (if needed): Add 150 mL citrate-bicarbonate buffer. Add 3 g sodium hydrosulfite (Na2S2O4) gradually (may froth). Heat in a water bath at 80 C for 20 minutes.
Soluble salt removal (if needed): Transfer soil to a centrifuge tube, add 100 mL DI water, and centrifuge at 1,500 rpm for 10 minutes. Decant the supernatant. Repeat until the supernatant is clear.







Warning



Handle 30% H2O2 in the fume hood. It is a strong oxidizer that causes skin burns on contact. Add it slowly to avoid violent frothing.




7.6 Dispersing the Soil Sample

Weigh \(DW_{\text{air}}\) g of pre-treated (or untreated) soil into the dispersion cup and record the mass to 0.1 g
Add 125 mL of 40 g/L sodium hexametaphosphate solution
Stir until the slurry is thoroughly wetted
Cover and soak for at least 16 hours (overnight)
Add distilled water to the first indentation mark on the dispersion cup
Attach the cup to the milkshake mixer and mix for 5 minutes (sandy soils) or 15 minutes (fine-textured soils)



7.7 Conducting the Hydrometer Test
Blank preparation:

Prepare a blank cylinder: add 125 mL of HMP solution and fill to the 1,000 mL mark with distilled water
Record the blank hydrometer reading and temperature. If the zero mark is below the meniscus surface, record the correction as a negative number. Read at the top of the meniscus (the suspension is opaque).

Sample measurement:

Transfer the dispersed soil suspension to a sedimentation cylinder, using a squeeze bottle to rinse all material from the dispersion cup
Fill the cylinder to the 1,000 mL mark with distilled water
Stopper the cylinder (No. 13) and invert 180 degrees and back in a steady 2-second cycle for one full minute. Vigorously agitate during the first two inversions to loosen settled material.
Set the cylinder upright and start the timer immediately
At 20 seconds elapsed, slowly lower the hydrometer into the suspension (spinning gently to dislodge air bubbles) and read at 40 seconds. Remove, rinse, and dry the hydrometer.
Repeat the inversion and 40-second reading two more times (three total readings at 40 s) for accuracy
After the final 40-second reading, lower a thermometer into the suspension and record the temperature







Important



The hydrometer must be removed, rinsed, and dried between every reading. Particles accumulate on the glass surface and progressively bias subsequent readings if not cleaned.



Continue taking hydrometer and temperature readings at the following schedule:

7.8 Recovering Sand on the No. 200 Sieve
The hydrometer method does not resolve sand subfractions well. Sieve analysis of the sand fraction provides this detail.

After the final hydrometer reading, pour the cylinder contents through a No. 200 sieve (0.075 mm)
Using tap water (with a sediment trap in the sink), wash the material on the sieve until the rinse water is clear
Select a soil tin; record the tin number and tare mass
Carefully wash the retained sand from the sieve into the tin using a squeeze bottle. Do not use a brush or metal tool on the sieve mesh.
Dry at 110 C for 24 hours
Cool and weigh the tin plus dried sand; record the mass







TipTip



The No. 200 sieve screens are delicate. Forcing particles through or scrubbing with a brush can stretch or distort the mesh. Always use a gentle water stream or squeeze bottle.

title: Soil Texture Analysis – Hydrometer Method
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Calculations
The key calculated quantities for each hydrometer reading are:
Corrected hydrometer reading:
\[
R_c = R_{\text{actual}} - R_{\text{blank}}
\]
Effective particle diameter (\(D_e\), mm) at each reading time is calculated from Stokes’ Law, accounting for temperature-corrected viscosity and density of the suspension fluid.
Percent finer at each reading:
\[
PF = \frac{R_c \times a}{DW_e} \times 100
\]
where \(a\) is a correction factor based on the specific gravity of soil particles (typically 2.65 for mineral soils).
Textural class is determined by plotting the calculated percent sand, silt, and clay on the USDA textural triangle.


8.2 Bias and Interference Sources








Source
Effect
Correction




Temperature and viscosity
Cold water increases viscosity, slowing settling
Temperature correction factor applied to each reading


Temperature and density
Water density varies with temperature
Density correction in Stokes’ Law


Hygroscopic moisture
Air-dried soil mass overestimates oven-dry mass
\(DW_e\) correction (Section 6.4)


Incomplete dispersion
Aggregates settle as single large particles; underestimates clay
Use HMP + mechanical mixing; pre-treat if needed


Meniscus reading
Opaque suspension prevents reading at bottom of meniscus
Read at top of meniscus; apply meniscus correction


Flocculation
Ca2+ and Al3+ bridge clay particles
HMP displaces polyvalent cations; Na+ hydrates clay surfaces





8.3 QC Requirements

Run a duplicate analysis on at least 10% of samples
Duplicate results should agree within one textural class
Include a blank cylinder (HMP + water, no soil) with every batch
Record all temperatures; temperature drift greater than 2 C during the reading series indicates an unstable environment
Cross-check a subset of hydrometer results against field texture-by- feel estimates (SOP-F401)

section: 12 Appendix A: Example Calculations in R
text:
12 Appendix A: Example Calculations in R



Code
library(tidyverse)

# --- Hygroscopic moisture correction ---
tin_mass_g <- 15.32
air_dry_w_tin_g <- 27.45
oven_dry_w_tin_g <- 27.18

moisture_H <- (air_dry_w_tin_g - oven_dry_w_tin_g) /
              (air_dry_w_tin_g - tin_mass_g)

cat(sprintf("Hygroscopic moisture: %.4f g/g\n", moisture_H))

# --- Oven-dry equivalent mass ---
DW_e <- 50  # g; use 100 for sandy soils
DW_air <- DW_e / (1 - moisture_H)

cat(sprintf("Air-dried soil to weigh: %.2f g\n", DW_air))

# --- Hydrometer readings ---
# Example data: time (min), hydrometer reading, temp (C), blank reading
readings <- tibble(
  time_min = c(0.67, 2, 5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 1440),
  R_actual = c(38, 32, 27, 22, 19, 16, 13, 8),
  temp_C = c(23, 23, 23, 22, 22, 22, 22, 21),
  R_blank = c(5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5)
)

# Corrected readings
readings <- readings %>%
  mutate(
    R_corrected = R_actual - R_blank,
    # Simplified percent finer (a = 1 for Gs = 2.65)
    percent_finer = (R_corrected / DW_e) * 100
  )

# Sand, silt, clay from key readings
# Percent sand: 100 - PF at 40 sec (0.67 min)
# Percent clay: PF at 1440 min (24 h)
pct_sand <- 100 - readings$percent_finer[readings$time_min == 0.67]
pct_clay <- readings$percent_finer[readings$time_min == 1440]
pct_silt <- 100 - pct_sand - pct_clay

cat(sprintf("\nSand: %.1f%%  Silt: %.1f%%  Clay: %.1f%%\n",
            pct_sand, pct_silt, pct_clay))

# Plot particle size distribution curve
ggplot(readings, aes(x = time_min, y = percent_finer)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Settling time (minutes, log scale)",
    y = "Percent finer (%)",
    title = "Hydrometer Particle Size Distribution"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Soil Nitrate and Ammonium – KCl Extraction
text: This SOP describes the extraction of inorganic nitrogen (nitrate, NO3-, and ammonium, NH4+) from soil using 2 M potassium chloride (KCl). The KCl extraction is the standard method for determining plant-available inorganic nitrogen in soils (Keeney & Nelson, 1982; Mulvaney, 1996). The high ionic strength of the KCl solution displaces NH4+ from cation exchange sites and brings NO3- into solution, producing a filtered extract suitable for colorimetric, flow-injection, or ion chromatographic analysis (Maynard et al., 2008).

title: Soil Nitrate and Ammonium – KCl Extraction
text:
4 Definitions

Ammonium (NH4+): The protonated form of ammonia; held on negatively charged cation exchange sites in soil; released into solution by the high ionic strength of the 2 M KCl extractant; the primary plant-available nitrogen pool in many soils.
Cation exchange capacity (CEC): The total capacity of a soil to hold exchangeable positively charged ions; controls how much NH4+ can be stored and released; higher in clay-rich and organic-matter-rich soils.
KCl extraction: Shaking soil with 2 mol L-1 potassium chloride solution at a defined soil-to-solution ratio (typically 1:10 w/v); the standard procedure for quantifying plant-available inorganic nitrogen in soils (Keeney & Nelson, 1982).
Mineral nitrogen (mineral N): The sum of NH4+-N and NO3--N in the soil; the immediately plant-available nitrogen pool; expressed in mg N kg-1 dry soil.
Nitrate (NO3-): The oxidized form of inorganic nitrogen; anion, so not held on cation exchange sites; highly mobile in soil solution; measured colorimetrically or by flow injection analysis after KCl extraction.
Soil-to-solution ratio: The mass of soil (g) to volume of extractant (mL) used in the extraction; typically 1:10 for KCl extractions; must be consistent within and between studies for results to be comparable.

title: Soil Nitrate and Ammonium – KCl Extraction
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Preparing 2 M KCl Solution
The 2 M KCl concentration is the standard for inorganic N extraction (Keeney & Nelson, 1982; Mulvaney, 1996). Lower concentrations (e.g., 1 M) may underestimate exchangeable NH4+ in high-CEC soils (Maynard et al., 2008).

Weigh out 298.2 g KCl into a 2 L volumetric flask
Fill the flask approximately two-thirds full with distilled water
Place the flask on a magnetic stirrer and add a magnetic stir bar
Set the stirrer to low-medium speed and leave on for 4 hours until fully dissolved
Use a stir bar retriever to remove the magnetic stir bar
Fill the flask to the 2 L mark with distilled water and mix







TipTip



Prepare the KCl solution the day before extraction. It can be stored at room temperature in a capped container indefinitely. Verify the solution with a conductivity meter if stored for more than 6 months.




8.2 Moisture Subsample
A companion gravimetric moisture determination is required to express results on an oven-dry soil basis (Keeney & Nelson, 1982).

Set aside 10 g of soil from each sample for moisture determination
Place each 10 g subsample into a labeled aluminum weigh boat
Dry at 105 C for 24 hours and record the dry weight
Calculate gravimetric moisture content per SOP-L400 Soil Moisture



8.3 KCl Extraction
The standard soil-to-solution ratio is approximately 1:5 to 1:10 (w/v) (Mulvaney, 1996). This SOP uses 7 g field-moist soil in 40 mL KCl, yielding an effective ratio of approximately 1:6 on an oven-dry basis for a typical soil at 15% gravimetric moisture.

Dispense 40 mL of 2 M KCl solution into labeled test tubes or extraction bottles
Add 7 g of field-moist soil to each tube (the total volume should reach approximately 50 mL). Record the exact mass of soil added to the nearest 0.01 g.
Cap the tubes securely
Place on the reciprocating shaker for 2 hours
Remove from the shaker and either:

Allow soil particles to settle for approximately 10 minutes (do not exceed 1 hour), or
Centrifuge for 3 minutes at 9,000 rpm (see SOP-L109: Sorvall ST8R Centrifuge)








Important



Record the exact mass of field-moist soil added to each tube. This value, together with the gravimetric moisture content, is needed to calculate results on an oven-dry basis (see Appendix A).




8.4 Filtering

Set up filter funnels with Whatman #42 filter paper over labeled specimen containers or clean test tubes
Pour the settled or centrifuged solution into the funnels; do not fill above the filter paper line
Allow the solution to drain completely until only soil remains on the filter
Discard the used filter paper and soil



8.5 Extract Storage

Cap the filtered extract containers
If analysis will be completed within 48 hours, store at 4 C
If analysis will be delayed beyond 48 hours, freeze the extracts at -20 C until analysis (Keeney & Nelson, 1982)







Important



Extracts should be analyzed as soon as possible. Prolonged storage, even frozen, can alter NH4+ and NO3- concentrations due to microbial activity or chemical transformations (Maynard et al., 2008).

title: Soil Nitrate and Ammonium – KCl Extraction
text:
9 Calculations

9.1 Converting Extract Concentration to Soil Concentration
The colorimetric or flow-injection analyzer reports the concentration of NO3--N or NH4+-N in the filtered extract (mg N/L). To convert this to mg N per kg oven-dry soil (ppm):
\[
C_{\text{soil}} \;(\text{mg N kg}^{-1}) \;=\;
\frac{C_{\text{extract}} \;\times\; V_{\text{KCl}}}{m_{\text{dry}}}
\]
where:

\(C_{\text{extract}}\) = concentration in the filtered extract (mg N/L)
\(V_{\text{KCl}}\) = volume of KCl extractant added (L; typically 0.040 L)
\(m_{\text{dry}}\) = oven-dry equivalent mass of soil extracted (kg), calculated as:

\[
m_{\text{dry}} \;=\;
\frac{m_{\text{moist}}}{1 + \theta_g}
\]
where \(m_{\text{moist}}\) is the field-moist mass added (g, converted to kg) and \(\theta_g\) is the gravimetric moisture content expressed as a decimal (g water / g oven-dry soil).
See Appendix A for a worked R code example.


9.2 Soil Texture Correction Factor (Optional)
When using the semi-quantitative quick test (SOP-L404), a texture-based correction factor may be applied. For the quantitative KCl extraction described here, no texture correction is needed because the exact soil mass and moisture content are measured directly.

2.3

2.0

text:
10 Quality Control

Include a reagent blank (KCl solution only, no soil) in each extraction batch. The blank should read below the method detection limit for both NO3--N and NH4+-N.
Run extraction duplicates for at least 10% of samples. Duplicate results should agree within 15% relative percent difference (RPD).
Include a laboratory reference soil with known inorganic N content in each batch when available.
Record the KCl solution preparation date and batch number.
Verify that the analytical calibration curve for the colorimetric method has an \(r^2 \geq 0.995\) before reporting results.
Subtract the mean reagent blank concentration from all sample results if the blank reads above zero (Mulvaney, 1996).

section: 14 Appendix A: Calculation of Soil NO3--N and NH4+-N (R Code)
text:
14 Appendix A: Calculation of Soil NO3--N and NH4+-N (R Code)

The following R code converts extract concentrations (mg N/L from the colorimetric analyzer) to soil concentrations (mg N/kg oven-dry soil, equivalent to ppm) for a batch of samples. It corrects for the exact mass of field-moist soil added and the gravimetric moisture content of each sample.


Code
# ===========================================================================
# SOP-L403: KCl Extraction -- Convert extract concentration to soil ppm
# ===========================================================================

# ---- 1. Enter your data ---------------------------------------------------
# Replace the example values below with your actual data.
# Each vector must have the same length (one entry per sample).

sample_id <- c("S01", "S02", "S03", "S04", "S05")

# Mass of field-moist soil added to the extraction tube (g)
soil_moist_g <- c(7.03, 7.10, 6.98, 7.05, 7.12)

# Gravimetric moisture content (proportion, g water / g oven-dry soil)
# From SOP-L400.  Example: 0.15 means 15% moisture.
theta_g <- c(0.152, 0.148, 0.161, 0.155, 0.143)

# Volume of 2 M KCl added (mL) -- typically 40 mL for all samples
vol_kcl_mL <- rep(40, length(sample_id))

# Extract concentrations from the colorimetric analyzer (mg N / L)
no3_extract_mg_L <- c(3.42, 5.18, 2.76, 4.01, 6.33)
nh4_extract_mg_L <- c(1.05, 0.87, 1.22, 0.93, 0.78)

# Reagent blank concentrations (mg N / L) -- mean of your blanks
blank_no3_mg_L <- 0.02
blank_nh4_mg_L <- 0.01

# ---- 2. Calculate oven-dry soil mass (kg) ----------------------------------
soil_dry_g  <- soil_moist_g / (1 + theta_g)
soil_dry_kg <- soil_dry_g / 1000

# ---- 3. Blank-correct extract concentrations --------------------------------
no3_corrected <- no3_extract_mg_L - blank_no3_mg_L
nh4_corrected <- nh4_extract_mg_L - blank_nh4_mg_L

# Ensure no negative values after blank correction
no3_corrected[no3_corrected < 0] <- 0
nh4_corrected[nh4_corrected < 0] <- 0

# ---- 4. Convert to mg N / kg oven-dry soil (ppm) ----------------------------
vol_kcl_L <- vol_kcl_mL / 1000

no3_ppm <- (no3_corrected * vol_kcl_L) / soil_dry_kg
nh4_ppm <- (nh4_corrected * vol_kcl_L) / soil_dry_kg

# ---- 5. Assemble results table -----------------------------------------------
results <- data.frame(
  Sample        = sample_id,
  Moist_g       = soil_moist_g,
  Moisture_pct  = round(theta_g * 100, 1),
  Dry_g         = round(soil_dry_g, 3),
  Vol_KCl_mL    = vol_kcl_mL,
  NO3_extract   = no3_extract_mg_L,
  NH4_extract   = nh4_extract_mg_L,
  NO3_ppm       = round(no3_ppm, 2),
  NH4_ppm       = round(nh4_ppm, 2),
  Total_inorgN  = round(no3_ppm + nh4_ppm, 2)
)

# ---- 6. Print results --------------------------------------------------------
cat("SOP-L403: KCl Extraction Results\n")
cat("================================\n\n")
print(results, row.names = FALSE)
cat("\n")
cat(sprintf("Reagent blank NO3-N: %.2f mg/L\n", blank_no3_mg_L))
cat(sprintf("Reagent blank NH4-N: %.2f mg/L\n", blank_nh4_mg_L))
cat("\nAll soil concentrations are mg N / kg oven-dry soil (ppm).\n")



14.1 Worked Example (Sample S01)
Using the example data above for sample S01:

Field-moist soil added: 7.03 g
Gravimetric moisture: 15.2% (0.152)
Oven-dry equivalent: \(7.03 / (1 + 0.152) = 6.102\) g = 0.006102 kg
KCl volume: 40 mL = 0.040 L
NO3--N in extract: 3.42 mg/L (blank-corrected: 3.40 mg/L)
Soil NO3--N: \((3.40 \times 0.040) / 0.006102 = 22.29\) mg N/kg (ppm)
NH4+-N in extract: 1.05 mg/L (blank-corrected: 1.04 mg/L)
Soil NH4+-N: \((1.04 \times 0.040) / 0.006102 = 6.82\) mg N/kg (ppm)
Total inorganic N: \(22.29 + 6.82 = 29.11\) mg N/kg (ppm)

title: Soil Extractable Phosphorus
text:
This procedure describes the extraction and colorimetric determination of plant-available (extractable) phosphorus in soils. Two extraction methods are presented: the Olsen method (0.5 M NaHCO3 at pH 8.5) for neutral to alkaline soils, and the Bray-1 method (0.03 M NH4F + 0.025 M HCl) for acidic soils (Bray & Kurtz, 1945; Olsen et al., 1954). Extractable P is quantified colorimetrically using the ascorbic acid/molybdate blue method (Kuo, 1996; Murphy & Riley, 1962).
Soil phosphorus availability is a key factor controlling plant productivity, and excess P in runoff is a primary driver of eutrophication in freshwater systems. Routine soil P testing guides fertilizer management and helps assess the environmental risk of P loss from agricultural and urban soils (Sharpley et al., 2003).

Extractable P is quantified colorimetrically using the ascorbic acid/molybdate blue method (Kuo, 1996; Murphy & Riley, 1962).

title: Soil Extractable Phosphorus
text:
4 Definitions

Available phosphorus: Phosphorus in soil solution and loosely sorbed fractions that can be taken up by plant roots; estimated by extraction with reagents that mimic root chemistry (Olsen bicarbonate in alkaline soils; Mehlich-3 or Bray in acid soils).
Bray P1 extraction: An extraction using 0.025 M HCl + 0.03 M NH4F; removes acid-soluble (Al- and Fe-bound) phosphorus; appropriate for acid and neutral soils (pH < 7.4) but not for calcareous soils.
Mehlich-3 extraction: A multi-element extractant (0.2 M CH3COOH + 0.25 M NH4NO3 + 0.015 M NH4F + 0.013 M HNO3 + 0.001 M EDTA); extracts plant-available P, K, Ca, Mg, and several micronutrients simultaneously; widely used in the eastern US and California.
Murphy-Riley method: The standard colorimetric procedure for measuring dissolved reactive phosphorus; reacts phosphate with ammonium molybdate and ascorbic acid to form a blue phosphomolybdenum complex measured at 880 nm (Murphy & Riley, 1962).
Olsen extraction: An extraction using 0.5 M NaHCO3 (pH 8.5); removes Ca-phosphate forms; the standard method for calcareous and alkaline soils (pH > 7.0); results expressed as mg P kg-1.
Sorption: The attachment of phosphate ions to soil mineral surfaces (primarily Fe and Al oxides in acid soils; CaCO3 in alkaline soils); limits plant availability and affects the choice of extraction method.

Ammonium fluoride (NH4F, Bray-1 extractant) is toxic and corrosive; handle in the fume hood. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH, for pH adjustment of Olsen reagent) is corrosive.

title: Soil Extractable Phosphorus
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Preparation

Air-dry the soil at room temperature until constant mass
Pass through a 2 mm sieve per SOP-F400 Soil Sampling
Determine gravimetric moisture content on a subsample per SOP-L400 to express results on a dry-weight basis



7.2 Selecting the Extraction Method



Soil pH
Recommended Extractant
Reference




6.5 or above
Olsen (0.5 M NaHCO3, pH 8.5)
Olsen et al. (1954)


Below 6.5
Bray-1 (0.03 M NH4F + 0.025 M HCl)
Bray & Kurtz (1945)



Determine soil pH per SOP-L402 before selecting the extractant. If comparing across sites with widely varying pH, consider using Mehlich-3 for all samples (consult the PI).






Note



The Olsen extractant (NaHCO3 at pH 8.5) dissolves calcium phosphate precipitates and reduces Fe3+ and Al3+ activity, releasing adsorbed P. It works across a wide pH range but is the standard for calcareous and alkaline soils. The Bray-1 extractant dissolves Al-bound and Fe-bound P via fluoride complexation and acid dissolution; it underestimates P in calcareous soils because the acid is neutralized by free CaCO3 (Kuo, 1996).




7.3 Olsen Extraction

Weigh 2.50 g of air-dried, sieved soil into a 125 mL Erlenmeyer flask
Add approximately 0.25 g of P-free activated charcoal (pre-washed with 0.5 M NaHCO3)
Add 50 mL of 0.5 M NaHCO3 extractant (pH 8.5)
Stopper and shake on the reciprocating shaker at 180 oscillations per minute for 30 minutes
Filter immediately through Whatman No. 42 filter paper into a clean flask or tube. The filtrate should be clear and colorless; if yellow-brown, the charcoal was insufficient or not pre-washed.
Proceed to colorimetric analysis (Section 6.5) within 24 hours. Store extracts at 4 C if analysis is delayed.



7.4 Bray-1 Extraction

Weigh 2.00 g of air-dried, sieved soil into a 125 mL Erlenmeyer flask
Add 20 mL of Bray-1 extractant (1:10 soil-to-solution ratio)
Shake on the reciprocating shaker at 180 oscillations per minute for 5 minutes (the short extraction time is critical; extended shaking can re-adsorb released P)
Filter immediately through Whatman No. 42 filter paper
Proceed to colorimetric analysis (Section 6.5) within 24 hours







Important



The Bray-1 extraction is exactly 5 minutes. Timing begins when the extractant contacts the soil. Over-extraction will underestimate available P due to re-sorption, while under-extraction will miss slowly dissolving forms.




7.5 Colorimetric Determination (Ascorbic Acid/Molybdate Blue)
This procedure follows Murphy & Riley (1962) as adapted by Kuo (1996).

Prepare the combined color reagent fresh (see Section 5, Reagents)
Pipette a 5 mL aliquot of the filtered extract into a clean test tube or cuvette
For Olsen extracts: acidify the aliquot with 1 drop (approximately 0.05 mL) of concentrated H2SO4 and swirl to expel CO2 (the NaHCO3 matrix effervesces; wait until bubbling stops before adding color reagent)
Add 0.8 mL of the combined color reagent to each tube
Mix by vortexing or inversion
Allow the color to develop for 15 minutes at room temperature. The solution turns blue in proportion to the phosphorus concentration.
Read the absorbance at 880 nm (or 882 nm) against a DI water blank within 30 minutes of color development
Determine the P concentration from the calibration curve (Section 6.6)

Alternative: Hach DR3900 PhosVer 3 method. If using the Hach spectrophotometer, follow the PhosVer 3 (ascorbic acid) method per SOP-L303, Program 490. Prepare standards in the same extractant matrix as the samples.


7.6 Calibration

Prepare a minimum of five working standards (e.g., 0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0 mg/L P) by diluting the stock standard with the same extractant used for the samples
Treat each standard exactly as the samples (acidification for Olsen, color reagent addition, timing)
Read absorbance at 880 nm
Plot absorbance versus concentration and fit a linear regression. Acceptable \(r^2\) is 0.995 or higher.



7.7 Calculations
Extractable P in soil (mg P / kg dry soil):
\[
P_{\text{soil}} = \frac{C \times V}{M \times \left(\frac{100}{100 + \theta_H}\right)}
\]
where \(C\) = P concentration in the extract (mg/L), \(V\) = volume of extractant (mL), \(M\) = mass of air-dried soil (g), and \(\theta_H\) = hygroscopic moisture (%, determined per SOP-L400). The term \(\frac{100}{100 + \theta_H}\) converts the air-dried mass to an oven-dry basis.
For the Olsen method with the standard parameters (2.50 g soil, 50 mL extractant):
\[
P_{\text{soil}} \; (\text{mg/kg}) = C \times \frac{50}{2.50} \times \frac{100 + \theta_H}{100} = C \times 20 \times \frac{100 + \theta_H}{100}
\]
For Bray-1 (2.00 g soil, 20 mL extractant):
\[
P_{\text{soil}} \; (\text{mg/kg}) = C \times \frac{20}{2.00} \times \frac{100 + \theta_H}{100} = C \times 10 \times \frac{100 + \theta_H}{100}
\]

8.3 QC Requirements

Prepare all standards in the same extractant matrix as the samples (matrix-matched calibration) to account for background color and ionic strength effects

section: 12 Appendix A: Example Calculation in R
text:
12 Appendix A: Example Calculation in R



Code
library(tidyverse)

# --- Calibration curve ---
standards <- tibble(
  P_mg_L = c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0),
  abs_880 = c(0.002, 0.018, 0.075, 0.148, 0.295, 0.740)
)

cal_model <- lm(abs_880 ~ P_mg_L, data = standards)
cat(sprintf("Calibration R-squared: %.5f\n", summary(cal_model)$r.squared))

# --- Sample calculation (Olsen method) ---
sample_abs <- 0.210            # Absorbance at 880 nm
soil_mass_g <- 2.50            # Air-dried soil (g)
extract_vol_mL <- 50           # Extractant volume (mL)
hygroscopic_moisture_pct <- 2.1 # Percent hygroscopic moisture

# Determine C from calibration
C_mg_L <- (sample_abs - coef(cal_model)[1]) / coef(cal_model)[2]

# Calculate soil extractable P (mg/kg dry soil)
P_soil_mg_kg <- C_mg_L * (extract_vol_mL / soil_mass_g) *
                ((100 + hygroscopic_moisture_pct) / 100)

cat(sprintf("Extract P concentration: %.3f mg/L\n", C_mg_L))
cat(sprintf("Olsen P:                %.1f mg/kg dry soil\n", P_soil_mg_kg))

# Interpret
interpret <- case_when(
  P_soil_mg_kg < 5  ~ "Very low",
  P_soil_mg_kg < 10 ~ "Low",
  P_soil_mg_kg < 20 ~ "Medium",
  P_soil_mg_kg < 40 ~ "High",
  TRUE               ~ "Very high"
)
cat(sprintf("Classification:         %s\n", interpret))

text:
13 Appendix B: Reagent Preparation Quick Reference


13.1 Olsen Extractant (0.5 M NaHCO3, pH 8.5)

Dissolve 42.0 g NaHCO3 in approximately 900 mL DI water
Adjust pH to 8.5 with 1 M NaOH (dropwise, with stirring)
Bring to 1 L with DI water
Check pH before each batch; re-adjust if needed
Prepare fresh weekly



13.2 Bray-1 Extractant (0.03 M NH4F + 0.025 M HCl)

In a fume hood, dissolve 1.11 g NH4F in approximately 900 mL DI water
Add 2.1 mL concentrated HCl (12 M)
Bring to 1 L with DI water
Store in polyethylene at room temperature. Stable for several weeks.



13.3 Combined Color Reagent (Murphy-Riley)
Mix in order, swirling between additions:

50 mL of 5 N H2SO4
15 mL of 4% ammonium molybdate
5 mL of 0.274% antimony potassium tartrate
30 mL of 1.76% ascorbic acid (freshly prepared)

Total volume: 100 mL. Prepare fresh for each analytical batch.


13.4 P Stock Standard (1000 mg/L P)

Dry KH2PO4 at 105 C for 2 hours; cool in a desiccator
Dissolve 4.394 g in DI water in a 1 L volumetric flask
Bring to volume. Store at 4 C. Stable for months.

title: Total Carbon – Shimadzu TOC-L with SSM-5000A
text: This SOP describes the operation of the Shimadzu TOC-L total organic carbon analyzer and the SSM-5000A Solid Sample Module for quantifying dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in soil extracts and total carbon (TC) or total organic carbon (TOC) in solid soil samples (Shimadzu Corporation, 2016, 2019).

title: Total Carbon – Shimadzu TOC-L with SSM-5000A
text: This SOP describes the operation of the Shimadzu TOC-L total organic carbon analyzer and the SSM-5000A Solid Sample Module for quantifying dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in soil extracts and total carbon (TC) or total organic carbon (TOC) in solid soil samples (Shimadzu Corporation, 2016, 2019).

title: Total Carbon – Shimadzu TOC-L with SSM-5000A
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: K2SO4 extracts from the chloroform fumigation-extraction method (SOP-L409); water samples; and dried, ground solid soil samples.
Does not apply to: Samples with extremely high salt concentrations that exceed the instrument’s tolerance (consult the instrument manual); sea water or marine sediments with high salt content.
Location: EA Program analytical laboratory, SGM 133.

title: Total Carbon – Shimadzu TOC-L with SSM-5000A
text:
4 Definitions

Calibration verification standard (CVS): A known-concentration standard analyzed at regular intervals during a run to confirm that instrument response has not drifted since initial calibration; acceptance criterion is within 10% of the certified value (Shimadzu Corporation, 2019).
Dissolved organic carbon (DOC): Organic carbon in a liquid sample (water or soil extract) that passes through a 0.45 µm filter; quantified by the NPOC method on the Shimadzu TOC-L.
Inorganic carbon (IC): Carbon present as carbonate (CO32-), bicarbonate (HCO3-), and dissolved CO2; removed from liquid samples by acidification and sparging; measured directly in soils at higher temperatures on the SSM-5000A.
NDIR detector: Non-dispersive infrared detector; measures CO2 evolved from sample combustion by absorption at 4.26 µm; the primary detection element of the TOC-L and SSM-5000A (Shimadzu Corporation, 2019).
NPOC (non-purgeable organic carbon): The organic carbon fraction remaining after acidification and sparging to remove IC and volatile organic carbon; the operationally defined DOC fraction measured by the TOC-L for liquid samples.
SSM-5000A: The Shimadzu Solid Sample Module that accepts dried, ground solid samples loaded in ceramic boats and combusts them at up to 900 °C to determine total carbon directly (Shimadzu Corporation, 2016).
TC (total carbon): Sum of all carbon forms (organic and inorganic) in a sample; measured by direct high-temperature combustion of solid samples or by TC mode for liquid samples (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).
TOC (total organic carbon): TC minus IC; in liquid samples, determined as NPOC; in solid soil samples, determined as TC minus IC or after acid treatment to remove carbonates before combustion (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).

Thermal: The combustion furnace operates at 680 °C (liquid mode) or up to 900 °C (SSM mode); do not contact the furnace chamber.
Pressurized gas: Carrier gas (high-purity air or O2) is supplied under pressure; inspect fittings for leaks.

title: Total Carbon – Shimadzu TOC-L with SSM-5000A
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Startup

Verify carrier gas supply pressure (typically 200 kPa or per instrument manual (Shimadzu Corporation, 2019)).
Turn on the TOC-L main unit and allow the furnace to reach operating temperature (680 °C for liquid mode).
Launch LabSolutions TOC software on the connected computer.
Run a system blank check using deionized water to verify baseline stability; the blank value should be below 0.1 mg/L C.



7.2 Calibration

Prepare a multi-point calibration curve using KHP dissolved in deionized water.
Typical calibration range: 0, 1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 mg/L C (adjust to expected sample range).
For IC calibration (if measuring TC - IC = TOC), prepare sodium bicarbonate/carbonate standards.
Run calibration standards and verify that the correlation coefficient (\(r^2\)) is at least 0.999 (Shimadzu Corporation, 2019).
Save the calibration curve in the software.



7.3 Liquid Sample Analysis (DOC in Soil Extracts)

Filter all liquid samples through 0.45 µm syringe filters or pre-combusted glass fiber filters into clean autosampler vials.
For K2SO4 extracts, include 0.5 M K2SO4 blanks in the run.
Select the appropriate measurement mode in the software:

NPOC mode (recommended for most soil extracts): The instrument acidifies the sample with HCl, sparges with carrier gas to remove IC as CO2, then combusts the remaining sample at 680 °C. The evolved CO2 is measured by the NDIR detector.
TC-IC mode (if both total and inorganic carbon are needed): TC is measured by direct combustion; IC is measured by acidification only. TOC = TC - IC.

Load vials into the autosampler and start the run.
The instrument performs replicate injections (typically 3) and reports the mean and coefficient of variation.







TipHigh-Salt Extracts



If K2SO4 extracts have high salt content, use the instrument’s automatic dilution function to extend catalyst and combustion tube life. Dilution factors are applied automatically to the reported concentrations (Shimadzu Corporation, 2019).




7.4 Solid Sample Analysis (SSM-5000A)

Switch the instrument to SSM mode in the LabSolutions software (Shimadzu Corporation, 2016).
Pre-combust ceramic boats at 900 °C to remove any residual carbon.
Weigh 10–50 mg of dried, finely ground soil into a clean ceramic boat using the analytical balance (record mass to 0.01 mg).
For TOC measurement (inorganic carbon removal): pre-treat the sample by adding a few drops of 2 M HCl to the boat, allow to react until effervescence stops, and dry at 105 °C before analysis (Nelson & Sommers, 1996).
For TC measurement (no acid pre-treatment): proceed directly.
Place the ceramic boat into the SSM sample port.
The SSM combusts the sample in an oxygen-rich environment at high temperature; the evolved CO2 is carried to the NDIR detector.
The software reports total carbon content in mg C or as a percentage of sample mass.



7.5 Instrument Shutdown

After the final sample, run 3–5 deionized water blanks to flush the system.
Review all data in the software for outliers or failed injections.
Export data and save the run file.
If the instrument will not be used for several days, turn off the furnace and carrier gas per the instrument manual (Shimadzu Corporation, 2019).

title: Total Carbon – Shimadzu TOC-L with SSM-5000A
text:
8 Quality Control

Run a calibration verification standard (mid-range) every 10–15 samples; acceptance criterion is within 10% of the known value.
Include instrument blanks (deionized water) at the beginning, middle, and end of each run.
Include method blanks (0.5 M K2SO4 for extract analyses) in each batch.
Run sample duplicates at a rate of at least 1 per 10 samples.
Monitor the coefficient of variation among replicate injections; re-run if CV exceeds 2% for liquid samples.
Log catalyst replacement, combustion tube changes, and calibration dates in the instrument logbook (Shimadzu Corporation, 2019).

title: Microbial Biomass Carbon – Chloroform Fumigation-Extraction
text: This SOP describes the determination of soil microbial biomass carbon (MBC) using the chloroform fumigation-extraction (CFE) method. Chloroform vapor lyses microbial cells, releasing intracellular carbon that is then extracted with 0.5 M K2SO4 and quantified as dissolved organic carbon (DOC) (Joergensen, 1996; Vance et al., 1987).

title: Microbial Biomass Carbon – Chloroform Fumigation-Extraction
text: This SOP describes the determination of soil microbial biomass carbon (MBC) using the chloroform fumigation-extraction (CFE) method. Chloroform vapor lyses microbial cells, releasing intracellular carbon that is then extracted with 0.5 M K2SO4 and quantified as dissolved organic carbon (DOC) (Joergensen, 1996; Vance et al., 1987).

title: Microbial Biomass Carbon – Chloroform Fumigation-Extraction
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Field-moist soil samples collected per SOP-F400 Soil Sampling and Processing for microbial biomass assessment.
Does not apply to: Air-dried or frozen soils (unless pre-validated for this method); microbial biomass nitrogen (requires additional analytical steps).
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133.

title: Microbial Biomass Carbon – Chloroform Fumigation-Extraction
text:

Role

title: Microbial Biomass Carbon – Chloroform Fumigation-Extraction
text:
4 Definitions

Chloroform fumigation-extraction (CFE): The standard method for measuring soil microbial biomass carbon; soil is fumigated with ethanol-free chloroform to lyse microbial cells, then extracted with K2SO4; MBC is calculated as the difference in extractable C between fumigated and unfumigated soils divided by the \(k_{EC}\) factor (Vance et al., 1987).
Extractable organic carbon (EOC): The organic carbon recovered from soil in K2SO4 extract; includes a background pool of soluble organic carbon from non-microbial sources as well as carbon released from lysed microbial cells.
\(k_{EC}\) factor: The extraction efficiency correction factor for microbial biomass carbon; commonly 0.45, meaning 45% of lysed microbial carbon is recovered in the extract; must be stated when reporting results (Joergensen, 1996; Vance et al., 1987).
Microbial biomass carbon (MBC): The total carbon contained in the living soil microbial community (bacteria, fungi, protozoa, nematodes); expressed as mg C kg-1 oven-dry soil; a key indicator of soil biological health and nutrient cycling potential (Robertson et al., 1999).
Potentially mineralizable nitrogen (PMN): The nitrogen that can be released from soil organic matter by microbial activity under aerobic conditions; correlated with microbial biomass and organic matter quality.
Unfumigated control: Soil extracted with K2SO4 without prior chloroform fumigation; provides the background extractable carbon value subtracted from the fumigated extract to calculate MBC (Vance et al., 1987).

title: Microbial Biomass Carbon – Chloroform Fumigation-Extraction
text:
5 Safety and Hazards

5.1 Critical Safety Warning
Chloroform (CHCl3) is a volatile, toxic solvent and a suspected carcinogen. All fumigation steps must be performed inside a fume hood. Do not inhale chloroform vapors. Use ethanol-free chloroform only (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2024).


5.2 Hazards

Chemical: Chloroform (toxic, volatile, suspected carcinogen); 0.5 M K2SO4 (mild irritant).
Physical: Vacuum desiccator under reduced pressure; risk of implosion if cracked.



5.3 Required PPE

Nitrile gloves (double-gloving recommended when handling chloroform)
Safety glasses or goggles
Laboratory coat
Work inside a fume hood at all times during fumigation



5.4 Emergency Procedures
In case of chloroform spill, refer to the SDS and SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling. Evacuate the area if the spill is large; ventilate the space and notify the supervisor.

title: Microbial Biomass Carbon – Chloroform Fumigation-Extraction
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Preparation

Prepare 0.5 M K2SO4 by dissolving 87.1 g K2SO4 per liter of deionized water. The 1:4 soil-to-extractant ratio is standard for CFE (Vance et al., 1987).
Pre-combust glass fiber filters at 450 °C for 4 hours and store in a clean container.
Determine the gravimetric moisture content of a separate subsample (dry at 105 °C for 24 hours per SOP-L400) so results can be expressed on an oven-dry-weight basis.



7.2 Fumigation

Weigh two paired subsamples of 15 g field-moist soil into labeled extraction bottles.
Place one set (fumigated) into the vacuum desiccator inside the fume hood.
Place a beaker containing approximately 30 mL of ethanol-free chloroform and a few boiling chips in the center of the desiccator.
Evacuate the desiccator using the vacuum pump until the chloroform begins to boil vigorously (approximately 2 minutes) (Vance et al., 1987).
Close the stopcock and incubate in the dark at room temperature (approximately 25 °C) for 24 hours (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2024; Vance et al., 1987).
The second set (unfumigated controls) is extracted immediately (proceed to §6.3).



7.3 Extraction

After 24 hours, release the vacuum inside the fume hood and remove the chloroform beaker.
Evacuate the desiccator repeatedly (3–5 times) to remove residual chloroform vapor from the soil.
Add 60 mL of 0.5 M K2SO4 to each bottle (both fumigated and unfumigated), achieving a 1:4 soil-to-extractant ratio (Vance et al., 1987).
Cap bottles and shake on an orbital or end-over-end shaker for 1 hour.
Allow the suspension to settle briefly, or centrifuge at 4,000 × g for 10 minutes.
Filter the supernatant through a pre-combusted 0.45 µm glass fiber filter into a clean sample vial.
Store filtered extracts at 4 °C if not analyzed immediately; analyze within 48 hours.



7.4 DOC Analysis

Analyze filtered extracts for dissolved organic carbon using the Shimadzu TOC-L per SOP-L407 Total Carbon.
Run 0.5 M K2SO4 blanks alongside samples.



7.5 Calculation
Microbial biomass carbon is calculated as (Joergensen, 1996; Vance et al., 1987):
\[
\text{MBC} = \frac{C_{\text{fumigated}} - C_{\text{unfumigated}}}{k_{EC}}
\]
where:

\(C_{\text{fumigated}}\) = DOC in the fumigated extract (mg C kg-1 oven-dry soil)
\(C_{\text{unfumigated}}\) = DOC in the unfumigated extract (mg C kg-1 oven-dry soil)
\(k_{EC}\) = 0.45, the extraction efficiency coefficient (Joergensen, 1996; Vance et al., 1987)







Note



The unfumigated extract DOC value represents the background dissolved organic carbon pool and is often reported separately as an indicator of labile soil carbon (Robertson et al., 1999).

title: Microbial Biomass Carbon – Chloroform Fumigation-Extraction
text:
8 Quality Control

Run analytical triplicates for at least 10% of samples; the coefficient of variation among replicates should be less than 15% (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2024).
Include a reagent blank (0.5 M K2SO4 only, no soil) in each batch.
Include a laboratory reference soil in each batch to monitor method consistency.
Verify that the TOC calibration \(r^2 \geq 0.999\) before reporting results.

title: Microwave-Assisted Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
This procedure describes the microwave-assisted acid digestion of soil, sediment, and sludge samples for trace metal analysis, following US EPA Method 3051A (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2007). The digested extract can be analyzed by flame atomic absorption spectrometry (FAAS), inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), or other suitable methods. This is a near-total-dissolution method; silicates and some refractory oxides (SiO2, TiO2) may not fully dissolve but environmentally available metals are recovered.
For non-microwave hot-plate acid digestion, see SOP-L65.

This is a near-total-dissolution method; silicates and some refractory oxides (SiO2, TiO2) may not fully dissolve but environmentally available metals are recovered.
For non-microwave hot-plate acid digestion, see SOP-L65.

text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Soils, sediments, and sludge samples requiring trace metal analysis (Pb, Cd, Cu, Zn, Cr, As, Ni, Fe, Mn, and others) at all EA Program sites, including urban soil lead surveys and photovoltaic panel site characterizations
Does not apply to: Water samples (direct acidification or separate digestion per EPA 3005A); samples requiring complete silicate dissolution (use HF-based methods); organic tissue digestion

title: Microwave-Assisted Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
4 Definitions

Closed-vessel digestion: Digestion performed in sealed vessels under pressure; higher temperatures are achievable (up to 240 °C) compared to open-vessel hot-plate digestion; reduces loss of volatile elements and acid consumption.
EPA Method 3051A: The US EPA microwave-assisted acid digestion method for soils, sediments, and sludges; uses HNO3 (with optional HCl) in closed PTFE vessels at controlled temperature and pressure; the reference method for this SOP.
MARS system (Microwave Accelerated Reaction System): The CEM Corporation microwave digestion system used in the EA Program lab; controls temperature and pressure in each vessel during digestion.
Maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP): The pressure limit of the digestion vessel specified by the manufacturer; exceeding this limit risks vessel rupture; monitored by the MARS control software.
PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene): A chemically inert fluoropolymer used to fabricate digestion vessels; resistant to concentrated acids and temperatures up to ~260 °C; must be pre-cleaned with HNO3 before use to remove trace metal contamination.
Ramp time: The programmed time over which the microwave system increases temperature from ambient to the target; too-rapid ramping can generate excessive pressure and risk vessel failure.

title: Microwave-Assisted Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
5 Safety and Hazards

5.1 Critical Safety Warning
This procedure uses concentrated nitric acid (HNO3) under high temperature and pressure in sealed vessels. Improper handling can cause severe acid burns, toxic fume exposure, or vessel rupture. Read the entire procedure and the MARS 5 operator’s manual before beginning.


5.2 Hazards

Chemical: Concentrated HNO3 (15.8 M) is severely corrosive and produces toxic NOx fumes. Optional HCl (12 M) is also severely corrosive. Both cause severe burns on skin and eye contact.
Physical: Microwave vessels reach 175 C and develop significant internal pressure. Residual pressure and acid vapor remain in the headspace after digestion. Hot vessels can cause burns.
Inhalation: NOx and HCl fumes are toxic. All acid handling and vessel venting must occur in the fume hood.



5.3 Required PPE

Chemical splash goggles (not safety glasses)
Face shield (when opening hot vessels)
Lab coat
Neoprene or heavy-duty acid-resistant gloves (long-cuffed)
Closed-toed shoes



5.4 Emergency Procedures
For acid splashes to skin or eyes, flush immediately at the eyewash station or safety shower for at least 15 minutes. For inhalation of fumes, move to fresh air and seek medical attention if symptoms persist. For vessel rupture or spill, evacuate the area and notify the lab manager. Refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.

title: Microwave-Assisted Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Glassware and Vessel Cleaning

Acid-wash all vessels, centrifuge tubes, and volumetric ware per SOP-L101 Glassware Cleaning, Section 6.3 (10% HNO3 acid bath)
Rinse with reagent water and dry in a clean environment
For microwave vessels, follow the manufacturer’s cleaning protocol (CEM recommends a cleaning cycle with dilute HNO3 between batches)



7.2 Sample Preparation

Weigh approximately 3–5 g of soil into a clean beaker or aluminum dish. Avoid obviously non-soil material (large rocks, twigs, leaves).
Dry at 60 C overnight in the drying oven. Do not exceed 60 C; higher temperatures can volatilize mercury and other semi-volatile metals.
Allow to cool. Using a clean mortar and pestle, grind the dried soil and pass through a No. 10 sieve (2 mm).



7.3 Microwave Digestion

Weigh 0.500 g (+/- 0.001 g) of the sieved, dried soil into a clean microwave vessel. For oil-contaminated or high-organic samples, use no more than 0.250 g. Record the exact mass.
Working in the fume hood, add 10.0 mL (+/- 0.1 mL) of concentrated HNO3 (Trace Metal grade) to the vessel.







WarningVigorous Reaction



Adding acid to samples with high organic matter may cause immediate effervescence. If a vigorous reaction occurs, leave the vessel uncapped in the fume hood for 1–2 hours to allow pre-digestion before sealing.



Optional: For improved recovery of Al, Sb, Ba, Be, Cr, Fe, Mg, Ag, and V, substitute 9 mL HNO3 + 3 mL concentrated HCl (aqua regia variant). Note: HCl can increase interferences with some ICP-MS analyses; consult the analyst.
Seal the vessels according to the manufacturer’s instructions (CEM Corporation, 2015)
Place each sealed vessel into a slot on the vessel rack with a carbon fiber sleeve in place



7.4 Critical
Never place a vessel into a rack slot without its carbon fiber sleeve. The sleeve provides essential containment in the event of a vessel failure. Operating without the sleeve risks vessel explosion.


Secure the rack into the MARS 5 microwave
If applicable, connect the temperature and pressure sensors to the designated control vessel(s)
Select the pre-programmed EPA 3051A method. Verify the following parameters:








Parameter
Specification (EPA 3051A)




Ramp to 175 C
5.5 +/- 0.25 minutes


Hold at 175 +/- 5 C
4.5 minutes (remainder of 10 min total)


Maximum pressure
Per vessel rating; relief mechanism must activate before failure




With instructor verification that all vessels are sealed and the rack is properly installed, close the microwave door and start the program
After the program finishes, allow the vessels to cool inside the microwave for at least 5 minutes, then transfer to the fume hood for further cooling


7.5 Filtration and Extract Preparation

Working in the fume hood, carefully uncap each vessel and vent for 2–3 minutes to release residual acid vapor and pressure
Quantitatively transfer the digest into a clean 50 mL graduated centrifuge tube, rinsing the vessel walls with small portions of reagent water to ensure complete transfer
Dilute to the 25.0 mL mark with reagent water. Record the final volume. Keep all samples as close to the same volume as possible.
Cap and centrifuge at 2,000–3,000 rpm for 10 minutes or until the supernatant is clear







Note



Refractory materials (SiO2, TiO2, Al2O3) may remain undissolved and cause persistent turbidity. If the supernatant is not clear after centrifugation, allow the sample to stand overnight before filtering.



Using a clean 10 mL syringe, carefully withdraw 10 mL of supernatant without disturbing the pellet
Attach a fresh 0.45 um syringe filter (Fisherbrand 09-719D) and filter the supernatant into a clean 15 mL centrifuge tube
Use a new syringe and filter for each sample
Cap and label the filtered extract. Store at 4 C until analysis.



7.6 Disposal and Cleanup

Collect all acid digestion waste (vessel rinses, supernatant residues, centrifuge pellets in acid) in a labeled acid waste carboy in the fume hood. EH&S pickup.
Rinse and clean microwave vessels per the manufacturer’s protocol
Dispose of used syringe filters and syringes in the acid waste stream (they are contaminated with concentrated HNO3 digest)
Wipe down all bench surfaces with DI water
Remove and properly dispose of gloves; wash hands thoroughly

title: Microwave-Assisted Acid Digestion of Soils for Trace Metal Analysis
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 QC Requirements

Reagent blank: Include one vessel containing only 10 mL HNO3 (no soil) in each digestion batch. The blank must read below the MDL for all target analytes.
Laboratory control sample (LCS): Digest a certified reference material (CRM) or laboratory reference soil with known metal concentrations in each batch. Recovery should be 75–125% of the certified value.
Matrix spike: Spike a duplicate sample with a known concentration of the target analyte(s). Recovery should be 75–125%.
Duplicate digestions: Process at least 10% of samples in duplicate. Relative percent difference (RPD) should be less than 20%.
Calibration verification: After instrument analysis, verify the calibration with a mid-range check standard every 10 samples.



8.2 Calculations
Metal concentration in soil (mg/kg dry weight):
\[
C_{\text{soil}} = \frac{C_{\text{digest}} \times V_{\text{final}}}{M_{\text{soil}}}
\]
where \(C_{\text{digest}}\) = concentration in the digest (mg/L from ICP-MS or FAAS), \(V_{\text{final}}\) = final digest volume (mL, typically 25), and \(M_{\text{soil}}\) = mass of dried soil (g).
Since the soil was dried at 60 C (not 105 C), apply a moisture correction if reporting on a 105 C oven-dry basis:
\[
C_{\text{soil, OD}} = C_{\text{soil}} \times \frac{100 + \theta_{60}}{100 + \theta_{105}}
\]
where \(\theta_{60}\) and \(\theta_{105}\) are the moisture contents at 60 C and 105 C respectively (determined on a companion subsample per SOP-L400).

title: Compost Maturity – Solvita CO2/NH3 Test
text:
This procedure describes the determination of compost maturity and stability using the Solvita Compost Maturity Test (Woods End Laboratories). The test simultaneously measures carbon dioxide (CO2) and ammonia (NH3) emissions from a compost sample during a 4-hour incubation, providing a dual indicator of biological activity and nitrogen stabilization. The intersection of the two readings yields a Compost Maturity Index (CMI) that indicates whether compost is immature, active, curing, or finished (Vargas et al., 2005).
CO2 evolution reflects ongoing microbial decomposition of organic carbon. NH3 volatilization indicates incomplete nitrogen stabilization and is associated with odor, phytotoxicity, and high pH. True compost maturity is reached when both gases have declined to low levels. Because the CO2 and NH3 cycles do not always track together, the dual-measurement approach provides a more reliable maturity assessment than either gas alone.
This SOP is distinct from SOP-L408 Solvita CO2 Burst, which measures rewetted soil respiration over 24 hours using only a CO2 paddle.

title: Compost Maturity – Solvita CO2/NH3 Test

title: Compost Maturity – Solvita CO2/NH3 Test

2 Scope

Applies to: Assessment of maturity and stability of composted organic materials, including green waste, food waste, biosolids compost, manure compost, and vermicompost
Does not apply to: Soil respiration measurements (see SOP-L408); raw feedstock characterization; long-term (7–28 day) laboratory respirometry; finished potting mixes where compost is a minor component
Location: EA Program laboratory, SGM 133

title: Compost Maturity – Solvita CO2/NH3 Test
text:
4 Definitions

Compost maturity: A measure of how fully decomposed and stabilized a compost product is; mature compost no longer undergoes rapid decomposition, does not cause phytotoxicity, and can be safely applied to crops or soils.
CO2 index (Solvita): The Solvita scale value (1–8) corresponding to the CO2 concentration in the headspace above moist compost; lower values indicate more active decomposition (less mature); higher values indicate stabilization.
Maturity index: A combined score calculated from the CO2 and NH3 Solvita indices; the primary output of the Solvita compost maturity test; used by USCC, US Composting Council, and others to certify compost quality.
NH3 index (Solvita): The Solvita scale value (1–5) corresponding to the NH3 concentration in the headspace above moist compost; high NH3 (low index) indicates immature compost with excess ammoniacal nitrogen that can harm plants.
Phytotoxicity: Inhibition of plant germination or growth caused by immature compost; typically results from high NH3 concentrations, volatile fatty acids, or other metabolites produced during active decomposition.
Solvita paddle: A plastic stick holding two gel-pad sensors (CO2 and NH3) inserted into the compost jar headspace during the test incubation; color changes are read with the Solvita DCR reader.

title: Compost Maturity – Solvita CO2/NH3 Test
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Biological: Compost may contain elevated microbial loads, fungal spores, and trace pathogens. Handle as a potential biohazard. Avoid inhaling dust when opening bags or scooping dry compost.
Chemical: NH3 released from immature compost is an irritant at high concentrations. Work in a well-ventilated area when handling fresh or actively decomposing compost.
Physical: Minor risk of glass breakage from incubation jars.




5.1 Required PPE

Nitrile gloves
Safety glasses
Lab coat
Dust mask (recommended when handling dry or dusty compost)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
If compost dust is inhaled and respiratory irritation occurs, move to fresh air. For skin contact with compost, wash thoroughly with soap and water. Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety.

title: Compost Maturity – Solvita CO2/NH3 Test
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Collection and Preparation

Collect a representative compost sample of at least 500 g from the pile or windrow. Sample from the interior of the pile (at least 30 cm below the surface) to avoid surface drying artifacts.
If the compost is very heterogeneous, collect from multiple locations and composite the subsamples
The sample should be at “natural” moisture, not artificially wetted or dried. Compost that has been stored at 4 C should be brought to room temperature (20–25 C) before testing. Allow at least 30 minutes.
Gently break up large clumps by hand but do not sieve or grind the compost. The test is designed for material in its as-produced condition.







Important



Do not test compost that is above 40 C (i.e., still in the thermophilic phase). Elevated temperatures accelerate gas production and will give artificially high CO2 and NH3 readings that do not reflect the maturity of the material once cooled.




7.2 Setting Up the Test

Fill a clean Solvita incubation jar loosely to the fill line with compost using the supplied scoop. Do not pack or compress the material. The volume should be approximately 150–200 mL.
Remove one CO2 gel paddle and one NH3 gel paddle from their sealed foil packets
Inspect each paddle: the gel should be uniform in color with no cracks, discoloration, or signs of prior exposure. Discard any compromised paddles.
Insert both paddles into the jar so that the gel faces are exposed to the headspace above the compost surface. The paddles should stand upright and not be buried in the compost.
Seal the jar immediately and securely
Record the jar number, sample ID, compost source, ambient temperature, and start time
Start the 4-hour timer



7.3 Incubation

Place sealed jars at room temperature (20–25 C) in a location shielded from direct sunlight and drafts
Do not open, move, or disturb jars during the 4-hour incubation







Note



The standard incubation time is 4 hours. This is shorter than the 24-hour incubation used for the Solvita soil CO2 burst test (SOP-L408) because compost produces gas at much higher rates than soil.




7.4 Reading Results

After exactly 4 hours, open the jar and immediately remove both paddles
Read each paddle promptly. Prolonged exposure to ambient air will alter the gel color.

Using the Solvita Color Charts (visual method):

Compare the CO2 paddle to the Solvita CO2 color chart. Record the color number (1–8 scale, where 1 = highest CO2 / least stable, 8 = lowest CO2 / most stable).
Compare the NH3 paddle to the Solvita NH3 color chart. Record the color number (1–5 scale, where 1 = highest NH3 / least mature, 5 = lowest NH3 / most mature).

Using the Solvita Digital Color Reader (DCR, recommended):

Insert the CO2 paddle into the DCR and record the numerical reading
Insert the NH3 paddle into the DCR and record the numerical reading
The DCR values can be entered into the Solvita CMI Calculator spreadsheet for a more precise Maturity Index



7.5 Determining the Compost Maturity Index (CMI)
Use the CO2 and NH3 color numbers to determine the CMI from the Solvita lookup table (printed in the kit manual) or the CMI Calculator spreadsheet:



CMI
Interpretation
Recommended Action




1
Raw, very immature
Continue active composting


2
Immature, highly active
Continue active composting


3
Immature, active
Continue composting/curing

title: Carbonate Isotope Analysis by GasBench II-IRMS
text:
This SOP describes the determination of \(\delta^{13}\)C and \(\delta^{18}\)O in carbonate minerals and sediments using phosphoric acid digestion and headspace analysis on the GasBench II coupled to the Delta V IRMS (Coplen, 2011; Kim et al., 2007; Swart et al., 1991). It covers sample preparation, vial flushing and acidification, the analytical run, and post-analysis data correction.
For general instrument operation, startup/shutdown, gas checks, tuning, and pre-analysis tests, see SOP-L208.

title: Carbonate Isotope Analysis by GasBench II-IRMS
text:
4 Definitions

Acid fractionation factor (\(\alpha^*\)): The equilibrium isotope fractionation between carbonate mineral and CO2 produced by phosphoric acid digestion; temperature-dependent and mineral-specific (Kim et al., 2007).
\(\delta^{13}\)C (VPDB): Stable carbon isotope ratio in per mil (‰) referenced to Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB); the conventional scale for carbonate and organic carbon (Coplen, 2011).
\(\delta^{18}\)O (VPDB or VSMOW): Stable oxygen isotope ratio in per mil (‰); carbonates are commonly reported on VPDB, which relates to VSMOW by \(\delta^{18}O_\text{VPDB} \approx 0.97001 \times
\delta^{18}O_\text{VSMOW} - 29.99\) (Coplen, 2011).
Exetainer vial: 12 mL borosilicate glass vial with a septum-capped lid used for sample reaction and headspace analysis.
GasBench II: Continuous-flow peripheral that samples headspace CO2 from sealed exetainer vials through a flushed needle system and delivers it to the IRMS via the ConFlo IV.
PAL autosampler: CTC Analytics autosampler integrated with the GasBench that positions vials under the injection needle for automated headspace sampling.
Phosphoric acid digestion: Reaction of carbonate with 100% H3PO4 at 50 °C to release CO2 quantitatively from calcite and aragonite (Swart et al., 1991).
VPDB (Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite): The primary international reference scale for \(\delta^{13}\)C and \(\delta^{18}\)O in carbonates.
VSMOW (Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water): The primary international reference scale for \(\delta^{18}\)O and \(\delta^{2}\)H in water and atmospheric gases.

title: Carbonate Isotope Analysis by GasBench II-IRMS
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Vial Preparation

Label exetainer vials with sample ID and position number.
Weigh 0.1–0.5 mg carbonate powder into each vial (adjust for expected calcite content).
Cap vials tightly with septum caps.
Flush each vial with He (UHP) for 5–8 min using the flushing manifold to remove atmospheric CO2.



8.2 Acid Addition

In the fume hood, add 3–5 drops (~100 µL) of 100% H3PO4 to each vial through the septum using a syringe.
Incubate at 50 °C for 1 h (calcite and aragonite) or overnight (dolomite) in the heating block.
Allow vials to equilibrate to room temperature before loading into the PAL tray.



8.3 Sequence Design

Open Isodat Sequence Editor and load the GasBench carbonate method.
Build the sequence: 3 blank vials (flushed, no sample), reference materials, unknowns (1 RM per 8 unknowns), check standards.
Set the PAL to collect 11 injections per vial; the first 2–3 are discarded in post-processing.
Save the sequence file as YYYYMMDD_Project_SeqID_User.seq.



8.4 Analytical Run

Complete the pre-analysis checklist in SOP-L208.
Load the PAL tray with vials in correct order.
Press Start in Isodat and monitor the first 5 injections.



8.5 Post-Analysis Data Correction
Apply corrections using the R script in the project repository:


Code
library(tidyverse)

raw <- read_csv("data/raw/YYYYMMDD_Project_SeqID_User_raw.csv")

# Each vial has 11 injections; discard injections 1-3
clean <- raw |>
  filter(injection >= 4) |>
  group_by(vial_id) |>
  summarise(
    d13C_mean = mean(d13C_raw),
    d18O_mean = mean(d18O_raw),
    d13C_sd   = sd(d13C_raw),
    d18O_sd   = sd(d18O_raw),
    n_inj     = n()
  )

# Scale normalization (two-point) using certified RMs
# Drift correction across run order
# QC: flag vials where within-vial SD > 0.15 permil

title: Soil Aggregate Stability – Wet Sieving Method
text: This procedure describes the determination of soil aggregate stability using the wet sieving method. Aggregate stability quantifies the resistance of soil structural units to disintegration when subjected to disruptive forces such as wetting, raindrop impact, and mechanical disturbance. It is a key indicator of soil physical quality, erosion susceptibility, and the effects of management practices (tillage, cover cropping, organic amendments) on soil structure (Kemper & Rosenau, 1986; Nimmo & Perkins, 2004).

Aggregate stability quantifies the resistance of soil structural units to disintegration when subjected to disruptive forces such as wetting, raindrop impact, and mechanical disturbance. It is a key indicator of soil physical quality, erosion susceptibility, and the effects of management practices (tillage, cover cropping, organic amendments) on soil structure (Kemper & Rosenau, 1986; Nimmo & Perkins, 2004).

Does not apply to: Sandy soils with negligible aggregation, organic soils (histosols), or aggregate characterization by dry sieving alone

title: Soil Aggregate Stability – Wet Sieving Method
text:
4 Definitions

Aggregate: A cluster of soil particles (sand, silt, clay, organic matter) bound together by organic compounds, fungal hyphae, microbial exudates, and electrostatic forces; the basic structural unit of soil.
Aggregate stability (wet-sieve method): A measure of soil aggregate resistance to disruption by the mechanical action of water immersion and oscillation; expressed as the percentage of aggregates retained on a defined sieve size (e.g., 0.25 mm or 2 mm) after wet sieving.
Dispersant (sodium hexametaphosphate): A chemical added to the control (dispersed) sample to break down all aggregates; used to measure the sand correction in aggregate stability calculations.
Mean weight diameter (MWD): A summary statistic for aggregate size distribution calculated as the weighted mean of aggregate size fractions after wet or dry sieving; higher MWD indicates better structural stability.
Slaking: The rapid collapse of aggregates upon sudden immersion in water, caused by compression of entrapped air; fast wetting promotes slaking and reduces aggregate stability measurements.
Water-stable aggregate (WSA): An aggregate that remains intact after defined wet-sieving; the fraction used to calculate aggregate stability.
