title: Soil Aggregate Stability – Wet Sieving Method
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Preparation

Air-dry soil samples at room temperature until friable (typically 48–72 hours)
Gently break large clods along natural planes of weakness by hand; do not grind or crush
Dry-sieve the sample through a nest of sieves to isolate the desired aggregate size class (e.g., 1–2 mm or 2–4 mm)
Discard material outside the target size range for this analysis
Weigh out replicate subsamples (typically 4.0 g each, minimum 3 replicates per sample) into labeled containers



7.2 Pre-Wetting (Capillary Wetting)
Rapid wetting causes slaking, which may overestimate instability for some research questions. If slow pre-wetting is desired:

Place each subsample on a moistened filter paper in a closed container
Allow capillary wetting for 10 minutes (or a duration standardized for the study)
Proceed to wet sieving

If the goal is to assess slaking resistance under rapid wetting (the more common approach), omit the pre-wetting step and place air-dried aggregates directly onto the sieve.


7.3 Wet Sieving

Place the pre-weighed aggregates on the top sieve of the wet sieving apparatus (e.g., 0.25 mm for a single-sieve method, or the top of a nested stack)
Raise the water level in the sieving cans until the sieves are submerged to the appropriate depth (typically 1–2 cm above the sieve mesh)
Allow the aggregates to soak for 5 minutes (standardize this time for the study) before starting oscillation
Start the wet sieving apparatus. The standard cycle is 3 cm stroke at 34 cycles per minute for 3 minutes (Kemper & Rosenau, 1986). Record the exact settings used.
After sieving, carefully raise the sieves from the water



7.4 Collection and Drying

Backwash the material retained on each sieve into a pre-weighed aluminum tin using a wash bottle with deionized water
Transfer any material that passed through the finest sieve (the material in the sieving can) into a separate tin if size fractionation is desired
Dry all tins at 105 C for 24 hours (or until constant mass)
Cool in a desiccator and weigh to the nearest 0.001 g



7.5 Sand Correction
The material retained on the sieve after wet sieving includes both water-stable aggregates and primary sand particles that are inherently larger than the sieve openings. To correct for sand:

Add 50 mL of 5 g/L sodium hexametaphosphate to the dried residue in each tin
Allow to soak for at least 2 hours (or overnight) to fully disperse remaining aggregates
Pour the dispersed slurry back through the same sieve used in the wet sieving step
Rinse thoroughly with deionized water
Backwash the retained sand into a clean tin, dry at 105 C, cool, and weigh



7.6 Calculations
Water-stable aggregates (WSA) as a fraction of the total sample, corrected for sand:
\[
\text{WSA} (\%) = \frac{M_{\text{stable}} - M_{\text{sand}}}{M_{\text{total}} - M_{\text{sand}}} \times 100
\]
where:

\(M_{\text{stable}}\) = oven-dry mass of material retained on the sieve after wet sieving (g)
\(M_{\text{sand}}\) = oven-dry mass of sand retained after dispersal (g)
\(M_{\text{total}}\) = initial oven-dry equivalent mass of the subsample (g; corrected for moisture using gravimetric moisture from SOP-L400)

If a nested sieve set is used, calculate the mean weight diameter (MWD):
\[
\text{MWD} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bar{x}_i \, w_i
\]
where \(\bar{x}_i\) is the mean diameter of the \(i\)th size fraction and \(w_i\) is the proportion of the total sample weight in that fraction (after sand correction) (Van Bavel, 1950).

title: Soil Color – Munsell Lab Confirmation
text:
This procedure describes the determination of soil color under controlled laboratory lighting using the Munsell Soil Color Charts. Soil color is a rapid, non-destructive indicator of organic matter content, mineralogy, drainage condition, and degree of weathering. It is a required observation in soil profile descriptions and is used in soil taxonomy (e.g., distinguishing Mollisols by dark surface colors) (Lynn & Pearson, 1993; Soil Survey Division Staff, 2017).
Field color determinations (see SOP-F400) are affected by variable natural lighting, sun angle, and observer fatigue. This laboratory procedure standardizes the observation under a controlled illuminant to improve reproducibility and provide a reference-quality color record.

title: Soil Color – Munsell Lab Confirmation
text:
4 Definitions

Chroma: The colorimetric purity or saturation of a color; the third component of Munsell notation (e.g., the 4 in 10YR 4/4); higher chroma values indicate more saturated, vivid colors; low chroma (less than or equal to 2) in subsurface horizons indicates gleying and periodic saturation.
Hue: The dominant spectral color in Munsell notation (e.g., 10YR, 7.5YR, 2.5Y, Gley 1); corresponds to the wavelength of the dominant reflected light; the first element of a Munsell color designation.
Munsell color system: A standardized color notation developed by A.H. Munsell expressing color as three independent components: Hue, Value, and Chroma; used universally in soil science for objective color description.
Redoximorphic features: Color patterns in soil caused by reduction and oxidation of iron and manganese under fluctuating saturation conditions; include masses (concentrations), depletions (zones of low chroma), and concretions; diagnostic for hydric soils.
Standard illuminant (D65): A standardized daylight spectrum at 6,500 K color temperature; the reference lighting condition for accurate Munsell color matching; overcast north-sky light or a D65 light box approximates this condition.
Value: The lightness or darkness of a color in Munsell notation; ranges from 0 (black) to 10 (white); the second component in Munsell notation (e.g., the 4 in 10YR 4/4).

title: Soil Color – Munsell Lab Confirmation
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Lighting Setup

Position the daylight-balanced lamp so it illuminates the sample and the Munsell chart at approximately the same angle and distance
Avoid mixing light sources (turn off overhead fluorescent or LED room lights if their color temperature differs significantly from the reference lamp)
Allow the lamp to warm up for at least 5 minutes before beginning observations







Note



If a daylight-balanced lamp is not available, work near a north-facing window under overcast sky conditions. Avoid direct sunlight, which changes color temperature with sun angle and clouds.




7.2 Sample Preparation

For moist color: if the sample is already field-moist, proceed directly. If it has been air-dried, moisten a subsample by adding deionized water drop by drop with a spray bottle or pipette until the sample glistens but no free water pools on the surface (Soil Survey Division Staff, 2017)
For dry color: use the air-dried sample without adding water
Use a spatula to press the soil into a smooth, flat surface (approximately 2–3 cm diameter) on a white or neutral background. A rough surface creates shadows that bias the reading toward darker values.
If the sample is heterogeneous (e.g., redoximorphic features), determine the color of the matrix and the color of each distinct mottle or concentration separately



7.3 Color Determination

Hold the Munsell chart adjacent to the prepared sample so both are under the same illumination
Look through the apertures on the chart page, placing the sample behind each hole, to find the closest match
First identify the correct hue page (e.g., 10YR, 7.5YR, 2.5Y)
Then match the value (lightness, vertical axis) and chroma (saturation, horizontal axis) within that page
Record the Munsell notation in the format: hue value/chroma (e.g., 10YR 4/3)
If the sample falls between two chips, record the interpolated notation or the nearest chip with a note (e.g., “10YR 4/3 to 4/4”)
Repeat the determination for both moist and dry conditions







Tip



Color vision varies between individuals and can shift with fatigue. For critical determinations, have two observers independently determine the color and compare results. If readings differ by more than one chip in any dimension, re-examine jointly.




7.4 Recording Results
Record the following for each sample:

Sample ID and depth
Munsell notation (moist)
Munsell notation (dry)
Descriptive color name from the chart (e.g., “dark yellowish brown”)
Any redoximorphic features (mottle color, abundance, size, contrast)
Observer name(s)
Date and lighting conditions



7.5 Special Cases
Redoximorphic features: When mottles or concentrations are present, record the matrix color and the color, abundance (few, common, many), size (fine, medium, coarse), and contrast (faint, distinct, prominent) of each type of feature per the standards in the Soil Survey Manual (Soil Survey Division Staff, 2017).
Very dark samples (value 2 or less): These may be difficult to distinguish on the chart. Prepare a thinner smear and confirm under slightly brighter illumination.
Effervescent or calcareous samples: Note the presence of carbonates (tested with dilute HCl per SOP-L402), as carbonate coatings affect apparent color.

title: Soil Color – Munsell Lab Confirmation
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Perform duplicate readings (by the same or a second observer) on at least 10% of samples
Acceptable agreement: readings should match within one chip in value and one chip in chroma on the same hue page
Inspect the Munsell chart for fading or staining at the start of each session; replace if the neutral chip (N/) no longer appears true gray
Record the lamp model and approximate color temperature in the lab notebook

title: Flash EA Soil Combustion for IRMS Analysis
text:
This SOP describes the complete workflow for analyzing soil and sediment samples for \(\delta^{15}\)N, \(\delta^{13}\)C, and elemental C and N content using the Thermo Scientific Flash IRMS Elemental Analyzer (EA) coupled to the Delta V Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometer (IRMS) through the ConFlo IV continuous-flow interface (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2008b, 2010a). It covers sample preparation, instrument warm-up, sequence creation, running the analysis, shutdown, and data reduction.
For general instrument operation, gas checks, and pre-analysis tests, see SOP-L208. For the full data correction workflow (blank, linearity, scale normalization, and drift correction), see SOP-L414.

It covers sample preparation, instrument warm-up, sequence creation, running the analysis, shutdown, and data reduction.
For general instrument operation, gas checks, and pre-analysis tests, see SOP-L208. For the full data correction workflow (blank, linearity, scale normalization, and drift correction), see SOP-L414.

Does not apply to: Sulfur isotope analysis (NCS mode), GasBench carbonate analysis (see SOP-L415), TC/EA hydrogen and oxygen isotope analysis, or liquid samples

title: Flash EA Soil Combustion for IRMS Analysis
text:
4 Definitions

Blank correction: Subtraction of the isotopic and elemental contribution of an empty tin capsule from each sample signal; necessary because capsule tin contributes a small amount of C and N (Paul et al., 2007; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2010a).
Certified user: A student, staff, or faculty member qualified to prepare samples and run the IRMS without supervision, as designated by the lab PI.
ConFlo IV: Interface hub connecting the Flash EA and other peripherals to the Delta V IRMS; handles reference-gas delivery and peak switching (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2008a).
\(\delta^{13}\)C: Stable carbon isotope ratio expressed in per mil (‰) relative to Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB): \(\delta^{13}C = (R_\text{sample}/R_\text{standard} - 1) \times 1000\) where \(R = {}^{13}C/{}^{12}C\) (Coplen, 2011).
\(\delta^{15}\)N: Stable nitrogen isotope ratio expressed in per mil (‰) relative to atmospheric N2 (AIR): \(\delta^{15}N = (R_\text{sample}/R_\text{standard} - 1) \times 1000\) where \(R = {}^{15}N/{}^{14}N\) (Coplen, 2011).
Drift correction: Adjustment for systematic temporal change in measured \(\delta\) values during a sequence, estimated from bracketing reference materials (Paul et al., 2007).
Flash EA: The Thermo Scientific Flash IRMS Elemental Analyzer peripheral; combusts samples at 1020 °C in an O2 pulse and separates N2 and CO2 chromatographically before delivery to the IRMS via the ConFlo IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2010a).
Isodat: Thermo Fisher software for analytical sequence design, instrument control, and raw isotope data export (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2010b).
Linearity correction: Adjustment applied to account for the dependence of measured \(\delta\) values on peak amplitude at the detector (Paul et al., 2007).
Reference material (RM): A substance with certified or consensus \(\delta\) values used to anchor measured values to the VPDB or AIR scale; at least two RMs spanning the expected sample range are required for two-point scale normalization (Coplen, 2011; Werner & Brand, 2001).
Scale normalization: Two-point (or multi-point) correction that maps measured \(\delta\) values to the international isotope-ratio scale using certified reference materials (Coplen, 2011; Paul et al., 2007).
Super-user: A staff or faculty member qualified to run the IRMS and perform minor maintenance (gas replacement, reactor exchange, etc.).
Tin capsule: 5 × 9 mm pressed-tin container used to encapsulate solid samples; tin ignites in the O2 pulse, raising combustion temperature briefly to ensure complete combustion.
Zero-enrichment test: Reference gas on/off pulses used to verify that the IRMS measures consistent \(\delta\) values before analysis; performed during instrument warm-up.

WarningHazards




Pressurized gases: He, O2, N2, CO2. Verify cylinder pressures before each session. He tank pressure must be above 500 psi, regulated to 50 psi.
Hot surfaces: The Flash EA combustion reactor operates above 1000 °C. Use caution when handling ash fingers or reactor tubes.
Sharps: Syringes, tweezers, and capsule-crimping tools can cause puncture or cut injuries.
Chemical: Chromium oxide, silvered cobaltous/cobaltic oxide, and reduced copper used in the reactor packing are irritants; follow standard laboratory handling precautions.

title: Flash EA Soil Combustion for IRMS Analysis
text:
7 Sample Preparation

7.1 Drying and Grinding

Weigh soil or sediment samples into aluminum crucibles.
Oven-dry at 105 °C until constant mass.
Grind dried samples to a fine, homogeneous powder.



7.2 Elemental Pre-screening
Submit a subset of samples to elemental analysis (EA) to determine %C and %N before committing the full batch. This determines the correct sample mass to target the optimal signal range.


7.3 Sample Weighing
The target sample mass depends on %C and %N concentrations (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2010a):



Typical %C
Target Sample Mass
Notes




> 5% C
3–5 mg
Dilute if signal is too high


1–5% C
7–15 mg
Standard range


< 1% C
15–25 mg
May require longer run times




Fold a tin capsule using tweezers (clean hands; no skin oils).
Weigh the target sample mass into the capsule.
Add WO3 if required for combustion aids.
Crimp the capsule tightly so no sample can escape during handling.
Place crimped capsules in sequence order in a cell-well plate.
Record the exact mass of each sample in the data reduction spreadsheet.







TipTip: Clean Tweezers and Capsules



Oils and residue from fingers contaminate tin capsules, introducing C and N blanks. Handle capsules only with clean, dry tweezers (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2010a).

title: Flash EA Soil Combustion for IRMS Analysis
text:
8 Instrument Warm-Up and Pre-Analysis Checks
See SOP-L208 for the complete warm-up procedure, gas pressure verification, zero-enrichment test, and linearity check. The Flash EA should be at operating temperature and passing all pre-analysis tests before loading samples.

title: Flash EA Soil Combustion for IRMS Analysis
text:
9 Sequence Design

Open Isodat on the acquisition computer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2010b).
Create a new sequence with the following elements in order:

Empty capsule blanks (4–6): establish blank baseline
Reference materials (2–3 each of two or more certified RMs): for scale normalization (Coplen, 2011)
Conditioning samples (2–3): first samples in the run; typically sacrificial or low-priority
Unknown samples (bracketed by RMs every 10–12 unknowns)
Closing reference materials (2–3 of each RM): for drift correction (Paul et al., 2007)

Enter sample names, masses, and expected %C/%N for each row.
Assign the correct Isodat method to the sequence.
Save the sequence file before starting.

title: Flash EA Soil Combustion for IRMS Analysis
text:
10 Running the Analysis

Verify carrier gas pressure (He > 500 psi, regulated to 50 psi).
Load capsules into the autosampler carousel in sequence order.
Press Start Sequence in Isodat.
Monitor the first 3–4 samples to confirm:

N2 and CO2 peaks are within the expected mass range
Peak shapes are symmetric and well-separated
Reference material \(\delta\) values are within ±0.3‰ of expected values (Werner & Brand, 2001)

If values are drifting, stop the run, identify the cause, and restart after correction.

title: Flash EA Soil Combustion for IRMS Analysis
text:
11 Shutdown

After the final sample, allow the sequence to complete fully.
Follow the shutdown procedure in SOP-L208.
Export the raw data file from Isodat and save to the project directory.

title: Flash EA Soil Combustion for IRMS Analysis
text:
12 Data Reduction
Data reduction follows the protocol in SOP-L414, which covers:

Blank correction (empty tin capsule contributions) (Paul et al., 2007)
Linearity correction (\(\delta\) vs. peak area regression)
Two-point scale normalization to the VPDB / AIR scale using certified RMs (Coplen, 2011)
Drift correction (linear regression through bracketing RMs)
Uncertainty estimation and quality flags

title: Macroinvertebrate Sorting, Subsampling, and Identification
text: This SOP describes the laboratory procedures for sorting, subsampling, and identifying benthic macroinvertebrates (BMI) collected from wadeable streams per SOP-F610. The procedure follows the California Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP) laboratory processing protocols to ensure compatibility with statewide bioassessment datasets (Barbour et al., 1999; Ode et al., 2016). Taxonomic identifications are used to calculate biological condition metrics, including the California Stream Condition Index (CSCI) (Mazor et al., 2016).

title: Macroinvertebrate Sorting, Subsampling, and Identification
text: This SOP describes the laboratory procedures for sorting, subsampling, and identifying benthic macroinvertebrates (BMI) collected from wadeable streams per SOP-F610. The procedure follows the California Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP) laboratory processing protocols to ensure compatibility with statewide bioassessment datasets (Barbour et al., 1999; Ode et al., 2016). Taxonomic identifications are used to calculate biological condition metrics, including the California Stream Condition Index (CSCI) (Mazor et al., 2016).

Does not apply to: Field collection of BMI (see SOP-F610); marine or estuarine macroinvertebrates; meiofauna (organisms passing through a 500 \(\mu\)m sieve); molecular identification (eDNA metabarcoding)

title: Macroinvertebrate Sorting, Subsampling, and Identification
text:
4 Definitions

Benthic macroinvertebrate (BMI): An invertebrate organism inhabiting the bottom substrate of streams, lakes, or wetlands that is retained on a 500 µm mesh sieve; includes aquatic insects, crustaceans, worms, mollusks, and other taxa.
Fixed count subsample: A randomly selected subset of a BMI sample from which a fixed number of organisms (e.g., 500) is picked and identified; reduces processing time for large samples while maintaining statistical reliability.
Functional feeding group (FFG): A classification of macroinvertebrates by feeding mode (shredders, collectors-gatherers, collectors-filterers, scrapers/grazers, predators); used to assess stream ecosystem function from invertebrate assemblage data.
Qualitative identification: Determination of taxa present in a sample without quantifying abundances; used for rapid bioassessment and presence/absence monitoring.
Quantitative sample: A sample in which all organisms are counted and identified to calculate density (organisms per unit area or volume); requires accurate recording of sampled area and volume.
Taxonomic resolution: The level of taxonomic identification applied to BMI specimens; options range from phylum/class to order, family, genus, or species; standard SWAMP protocol requires family-level identification for most groups.
Voucher specimen: A representative specimen of a taxon retained in preservative as a reference for future verification; essential for quality assurance and resolving taxonomic uncertainties.

WarningHazards




Chemical: Preserved samples contain approximately 70% ethanol, which is flammable and an inhalation irritant. Work in a well-ventilated area away from ignition sources.
Physical: Forceps and dissecting needles are sharp. Use caution when handling small organisms.
Biological: Stream organisms may harbor parasites or pathogens. Wear gloves when handling preserved samples.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses
Lab coat



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For ethanol spills, ventilate the area, absorb with paper towels, and dispose in flammable waste. Refer to SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety.

title: Macroinvertebrate Sorting, Subsampling, and Identification
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Receiving and Logging

Verify that the sample jar label matches the chain-of-custody or field data sheet: site ID, date, collector, preservative.
Log the sample into the laboratory tracking spreadsheet.
Inspect the sample for adequate preservative (organisms should not appear soft or discolored). If the ethanol is diluted below approximately 50%, decant carefully and replace with fresh 70% ethanol before proceeding.



7.2 Subsampling
The SWAMP standard requires identification of a minimum of 500 organisms per sample. A fixed-count random subsampling procedure is used (Caton, 1991):

Pour the entire sample through a 500 \(\mu\)m sieve. Rinse the jar into the sieve to recover all material.
Transfer the sieved material to the gridded Caton sorting tray. Distribute the material as evenly as possible across all grid cells.
Use a random number generator or random number table to select grid cells for sorting.
Under the dissecting microscope, remove all organisms from the selected cell using forceps, transferring them to a labeled petri dish or vial. Count each organism as it is picked.
Continue selecting and sorting random cells until the cumulative organism count reaches or exceeds 500. Complete the cell in progress even if the count exceeds 500 mid-cell.
Record the number of cells sorted, the total cells in the tray, and the total organism count.







TipTip



Keep the residue (unsorted cells) in a labeled jar with 70% ethanol. The residue is needed for the re-sort QC check and may be required if additional identifications are needed later.




7.3 Identification

Separate sorted organisms into major taxonomic groups (e.g., Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, Trichoptera, Diptera, Coleoptera, non-insect taxa) under the dissecting microscope.
Identify each organism to the lowest practical taxonomic level using standard keys (Merritt et al., 2019; Thorp & Rogers, 2015):

Insects: genus (family for early instars or damaged specimens)
Non-insect invertebrates: family or order (depending on group and specimen condition)

For specimens requiring higher magnification (e.g., chironomid head capsules, oligochaete chaetae), prepare slide mounts and examine under the compound microscope.
Record counts by taxon on the laboratory data sheet or directly into the data entry spreadsheet.



7.4 Voucher Specimens

Retain at least one representative specimen of each taxon as a voucher in a labeled scintillation vial with 70% ethanol.
Label each vial with: site ID, date, taxon name, identifier initials, identification date.
Store voucher vials in the BMI reference collection.



7.5 Data Entry and Metric Calculation

Enter identification data into the standardized spreadsheet or database.
Calculate summary metrics:

Total taxa richness
EPT (Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, Trichoptera) richness
Percent tolerant taxa
Percent dominant taxon
Shannon diversity index (\(H'\))

If sufficient data are available, calculate the CSCI score using the CSCI R package or the online CSCI calculator (Mazor et al., 2016).



Code
# Example: Shannon diversity from BMI count data
library(vegan)

# counts is a named vector of organism counts by taxon
counts <- c(Baetis = 120, Hydropsyche = 85, Chironomidae = 210,
            Simulium = 45, Optioservus = 30, Physa = 10)

H_prime <- diversity(counts, index = "shannon")
cat(sprintf("Shannon H': %.3f\n", H_prime))
cat(sprintf("Total taxa: %d\n", length(counts)))
cat(sprintf("Total organisms: %d\n", sum(counts)))
cat(sprintf("EPT richness: count EPT genera from full dataset\n"))

title: Macroinvertebrate Sorting, Subsampling, and Identification
text:
8 Quality Control

Sorting efficiency: Re-sort 10% of processed samples (randomly selected). The re-sort technician examines all residue material from the original subsampling. Sorting efficiency must be greater than or equal to 90% (i.e., fewer than 10% of total organisms were missed).
Taxonomic verification: Have a second identifier verify identifications for 10% of specimens. Agreement should be greater than or equal to 90% at the operational taxonomic level.
External QC: For data submitted to SWAMP or CEDEN, submit 10% of samples to a SWAMP-certified taxonomic laboratory for independent re-identification.
Record all QC results in the QC log.

title: Algae / Periphyton Identification and Enumeration
text: This SOP describes the laboratory procedures for identifying and enumerating benthic algae (periphyton) from stream bioassessment samples. Periphyton assemblages are sensitive indicators of water quality, nutrient enrichment, and physical habitat condition, and are a required component of the California SWAMP bioassessment protocol (Barbour et al., 1999; Ode et al., 2016). This SOP covers soft-bodied algae (green algae, cyanobacteria, and other non-diatom taxa) and diatoms, which are processed separately due to different preparation requirements (Charles et al., 2002; Stevenson & Bahls, 1996).

text:
4 Definitions

Acid washing (plant tissue): Cleaning tissue with dilute HCl to remove surface contamination (dust, soil particles, fertilizer residues) before analysis for trace metals or nutrients; may be inappropriate for samples requiring analysis of acid-labile compounds.
Air drying: Drying plant tissue at ambient temperature (typically 20–40 °C) to a stable moisture content; used as a preliminary step before oven drying; preserves enzyme activity and RNA better than direct oven drying.
Ball milling: Size reduction by grinding samples between hardened steel or ceramic balls inside a rotating vessel; the preferred method for producing a homogeneous powder from fibrous plant tissue for EA-IRMS and elemental analysis.
Critical tissue concentration: The minimum concentration of a nutrient required for maximum growth; below this level the plant is deficient; above it, growth is normal or the nutrient may be toxic at very high levels.
Lyophilization (freeze drying): Removal of water from tissue under vacuum after rapid freezing; preserves cell structure, volatile compounds, and biological activity better than oven drying; required for enzyme, RNA, and some metabolite analyses.
Subsampling: Drawing a representative small portion from a bulk dried, ground sample for analysis; requires thorough mixing and homogenization of the bulk powder before subsampling to ensure the subsample is representative.

5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Lugol’s iodine solution (preservative) contains potassium iodide and iodine; it is a mild irritant and stains skin and clothing. Nitric acid (used in diatom cleaning) is corrosive; handle in the fume hood. The mounting medium Naphrax contains toluene, which is flammable and toxic by inhalation.
Physical: Hot plates used for diatom cleaning and slide preparation pose burn risk. Coverslips and slides are fragile.
Biological: Stream samples may contain pathogens. Wear gloves.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses or goggles
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves
Fume hood (required for nitric acid cleaning and Naphrax mounting)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For acid splashes, flush immediately with copious water for at least 15 minutes. For Naphrax/toluene spills, ventilate and absorb. Refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.

title: Algae / Periphyton Identification and Enumeration
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Processing Overview
Periphyton samples are processed in two parallel workflows:

Soft-bodied algae: Examined alive or preserved in Lugol’s solution using a Palmer-Maloney cell or settling chamber at 400x magnification.
Diatoms: Cleaned with acid or peroxide to remove organic matter, mounted in Naphrax on permanent slides, and identified at 1000x (oil immersion).



7.2 Soft-Bodied Algae Identification

Homogenize the preserved sample by gently inverting the jar 20 times.
Pipette a known volume (typically 0.1 mL) into a Palmer-Maloney counting cell.
Allow cells to settle for 5 minutes.
Scan the entire cell at 400x magnification.
Identify and count a minimum of 300 natural units (cells, colonies, or filament lengths of 10 \(\mu\)m). A natural unit is the smallest entity that can be identified: a single cell for unicellular taxa, a colony for colonial taxa, or a 10 \(\mu\)m filament segment for filamentous taxa (Stevenson & Bahls, 1996).
Record counts by taxon. Identify to genus where possible; use higher-level groupings (family or order) for taxa that cannot be resolved without specialized preparation.
Calculate cell density:

\[
\text{Cells/cm}^2 = \frac{N \times V_{\text{sample}}}{V_{\text{counted}} \times A_{\text{substrate}}}
\]
where \(N\) = number of cells counted, \(V_{\text{sample}}\) = total sample volume (mL), \(V_{\text{counted}}\) = volume examined in the counting cell (mL), and \(A_{\text{substrate}}\) = total area of substrate scraped in the field (cm2).


7.3 Diatom Cleaning

Transfer approximately 5 mL of well-mixed sample to a labeled glass beaker or test tube.
In the fume hood, add an equal volume of concentrated HNO3 (or 30% H2O2 as a less hazardous alternative).
Heat on the hot plate at low-to-medium heat (approximately 80 °C) until the sample clears and all organic material is digested (30–60 minutes). Do not boil.
Allow to cool. Centrifuge at 1500 x g for 5 minutes and decant the supernatant.
Wash the pellet with DI water, centrifuge, and decant. Repeat the wash 3–5 times until the pH of the supernatant is near neutral.
Resuspend the cleaned frustules in a small volume of DI water (approximately 1–2 mL).



7.4 Diatom Slide Preparation

Pipette a drop of cleaned diatom suspension onto a clean coverslip. Allow to air-dry completely on the slide warmer.
Place a drop of Naphrax on a labeled glass slide (work in the fume hood; Naphrax contains toluene).
Invert the coverslip (diatom side down) onto the Naphrax drop.
Heat gently on the hot plate or slide warmer to drive off the toluene until no more bubbles appear.
Allow to cool. The slide is now a permanent mount.



7.5 Diatom Identification and Enumeration

Examine the slide at 1000x under oil immersion.
Count a minimum of 600 diatom valves, traversing random transects across the coverslip (Charles et al., 2002).
Identify each valve to the lowest practical taxonomic level (species where possible) using regional diatom floras and SWAMP reference keys (Krammer, 2000; Spaulding et al., 2021).
Record counts by taxon.



7.6 Data Entry and Metric Calculation

Enter soft-bodied and diatom counts into the standardized data entry spreadsheet.
Calculate summary metrics: total taxa richness, relative abundance of indicator taxa (e.g., pollution-tolerant vs. sensitive diatoms), and community-level indices.
If submitting to SWAMP/CEDEN, format data per SWAMP requirements.

title: Algae / Periphyton Identification and Enumeration
text:
8 Quality Control

Soft-bodied algae: Re-count 10% of samples. Counts should agree within 15% RPD for dominant taxa.
Diatoms: Have a second identifier verify 10% of slides. Taxonomic agreement should be greater than or equal to 85% at the species level.
For SWAMP submissions, submit 10% of diatom slides to a SWAMP-certified taxonomist for external QC.
Include a reference slide set in the laboratory for training and calibration.

title: DNA Extraction, Quantification, and Purity Assessment
text: This procedure describes the extraction of genomic DNA from environmental samples (soil, sediment, water filters, and plant tissue), followed by quantification of DNA concentration and assessment of DNA purity using spectrophotometric and fluorometric methods. The protocol is based on commercial bead-beating extraction kits and is suitable for downstream applications including PCR amplification, qPCR, and amplicon sequencing (Qiagen, 2024a, 2024b).

text: This procedure describes the extraction of genomic DNA from environmental samples (soil, sediment, water filters, and plant tissue), followed by quantification of DNA concentration and assessment of DNA purity using spectrophotometric and fluorometric methods. title: DNA Extraction, Quantification, and Purity Assessment
text:
4 Definitions

A260/A280 ratio: The ratio of absorbance at 260 nm to 280 nm; pure dsDNA yields ~1.8; values below 1.7 indicate protein or phenol contamination that may inhibit PCR amplification.
A260/A230 ratio: The ratio of absorbance at 260 nm to 230 nm; values of 2.0–2.2 indicate pure nucleic acids; low values indicate contamination with chaotropic salts, humic acids, or carbohydrates.
Bead beating: Mechanical cell lysis in which sample is agitated at high speed with ceramic or glass beads in a tube; disrupts cell walls and membranes including the tough walls of fungal spores and gram-positive bacteria.
Chaotropic salt: A salt (e.g., guanidinium isothiocyanate, guanidinium hydrochloride) that disrupts hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions; used in DNA extraction to denature proteins and facilitate binding of DNA to silica membranes.
Environmental DNA (eDNA): Genetic material shed into the environment by organisms through mucus, feces, skin cells, and gametes; collected from soil, water, or air without organism capture.
Inhibitor: A substance co-extracted with DNA that reduces PCR amplification efficiency; common inhibitors in soil and water eDNA include humic acids, tannins, heavy metals, and residual ethanol.
Silica column (spin column): A miniaturized chromatography column containing a silica membrane that selectively binds DNA in the presence of chaotropic salts; DNA is washed and then eluted with low-salt buffer or water.

title: DNA Extraction, Quantification, and Purity Assessment
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Lysis buffer contains guanidine salts, which are harmful if swallowed or inhaled and can cause skin and eye irritation. Solution C4 contains ethanol. Review the Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for all kit reagents before use.
Physical: Bead-beating generates aerosols; keep tubes sealed during vortexing. Centrifuge rotor imbalance can cause equipment damage.
Biological: Environmental samples may contain unknown pathogens. Treat all samples as potentially infectious (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention & National Institutes of Health, 2020).




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses or goggles
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves (change frequently to avoid cross-contamination)
Face shield (if working with large volumes of lysis buffer)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
In case of chemical splash or skin/eye contact, flush affected area with water for at least 15 minutes and consult the SDS. For spills of lysis buffer, absorb with paper towels, clean with water, and dispose as chemical waste. Refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling for general chemical spill response.

title: DNA Extraction, Quantification, and Purity Assessment
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample Preparation

Record sample identity, collection date, and mass/volume in the lab notebook and in the Freezer Inventory Google Sheet
For soil/sediment: weigh 0.20–0.25 g of sample into the PowerBead Pro tube. Record exact mass.
For water filters: use sterile forceps to transfer the membrane filter into the PowerBead Pro tube. Cut the filter into strips if needed to fit inside the tube.
For plant tissue: weigh 0.02–0.10 g of tissue (fresh or flash-frozen) into the PowerBead Pro tube. Use less tissue for highly mucilaginous samples (Doyle & Doyle, 1987).







Important



Keep samples on ice during preparation to minimize DNA degradation by endogenous nucleases. Process all samples within a single batch if possible to reduce extraction variability (Frosteg aard et al., 1999).




7.2 Cell Lysis and DNA Extraction
Follow the DNeasy PowerSoil Pro Kit protocol (Qiagen, 2024b):

Add 800 uL of Solution CD1 to the PowerBead Pro tube
Secure tubes horizontally on the vortex adapter and vortex at maximum speed for 10 minutes
Centrifuge at 15,000 x g for 1 minute
Transfer the supernatant to a clean 2 mL collection tube
Add 200 uL of Solution CD2, vortex briefly (5 seconds), and centrifuge at 15,000 x g for 1 minute
Avoiding the pellet, transfer the supernatant to a clean 2 mL collection tube
Add 600 uL of Solution CD3, vortex briefly (5 seconds)
Load 650 uL onto an MB Spin Column seated in a 2 mL collection tube. Centrifuge at 15,000 x g for 1 minute. Discard flow-through. Repeat to load remaining lysate.
Add 500 uL of Solution EA. Centrifuge at 15,000 x g for 1 minute. Discard flow-through.
Add 500 uL of Solution C5 (wash buffer). Centrifuge at 15,000 x g for 1 minute. Discard flow-through.
Centrifuge again at 16,000 x g for 2 minutes to remove residual wash buffer
Transfer the MB Spin Column to a clean 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube
Add 50–100 uL of Solution C6 (elution buffer) or nuclease-free water to the center of the membrane. Allow to stand for 1 minute at room temperature, then centrifuge at 15,000 x g for 1 minute.







TipTip



Use a smaller elution volume (50 uL) when higher DNA concentration is needed for downstream applications. A second elution with an additional 50 uL can recover 10–20% more DNA but at lower concentration (Qiagen, 2024b).




7.3 DNA Quantification – NanoDrop Spectrophotometry
The NanoDrop measures DNA concentration and provides absorbance ratios used to assess purity (Desjardins & Bhatt, 2010):

Clean the pedestal with 2 uL of nuclease-free water; wipe with a lint-free tissue
Blank the instrument with 2 uL of the elution buffer (Solution C6 or nuclease-free water, matching your elution)
Load 2 uL of DNA extract onto the pedestal
Record the concentration (ng/uL), A260/A280 ratio, and A260/A230 ratio for each sample



7.4 DNA Quantification – Qubit Fluorometry
The Qubit fluorometer uses fluorescent dyes that bind selectively to dsDNA, providing more accurate quantification than spectrophotometry, especially at low concentrations or in the presence of contaminants (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2024):

Prepare the Qubit working solution: dilute the Qubit dsDNA BR (or HS) reagent 1:200 in Qubit buffer. Prepare enough for all samples plus two standards (e.g., 200 uL per assay tube).
Prepare standards: add 190 uL of working solution to each of two Qubit assay tubes. Add 10 uL of Standard 1 to one tube and 10 uL of Standard 2 to the other. Vortex briefly.
Prepare samples: add 198 uL of working solution to a Qubit assay tube. Add 2 uL of DNA extract. Vortex briefly.
Incubate all tubes at room temperature for 2 minutes (but not longer than 30 minutes)
Calibrate the Qubit with the two standards, then read each sample
Record the concentration (ng/uL, corrected for dilution by the instrument)



7.5 DNA Purity Assessment
Evaluate DNA purity using the NanoDrop absorbance ratios (Desjardins & Bhatt, 2010; Wilfinger et al., 1997):








Ratio
Ideal Range
Interpretation




A260/A280
1.8–2.0
Values below 1.8 suggest protein or phenol contamination


A260/A230
2.0–2.2
Values below 2.0 suggest contamination with humic acids, carbohydrates, salts, or residual guanidine from extraction buffers









Note



For environmental DNA extracts, especially from humic-rich soils, A260/A230 ratios are frequently below 2.0. If downstream applications (e.g., PCR) fail or show inhibition, consider additional cleanup using a OneStep PCR Inhibitor Removal Kit or gel purification (Young et al., 2014).




7.6 Storage and Freezer Inventory

Label each tube with: sample ID, extraction date, elution volume, and concentration (in ng/uL)
For short-term storage (less than 1 month): store DNA extracts at –20 C
For long-term storage: store DNA extracts at –80 C in the designated molecular biology section of the freezer
Record the storage location (freezer, rack, box, and position) in the Freezer Inventory Google Sheet
Update the Google Sheet immediately upon placing samples in the freezer or removing them







Important–80 C Freezer Protocol




Minimize the time the freezer door is open. Retrieve the correct box before opening the freezer.
Place DNA extracts in designated cryoboxes labeled “DNA Extracts” with the project name and date range.
Do not store DNA extracts in the same box as tissue samples or reagents.
Avoid repeated freeze-thaw cycles. If multiple downstream analyses are planned, prepare aliquots at the time of extraction (Shao et al., 2012).

title: DNA Extraction, Quantification, and Purity Assessment
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

Include one extraction blank (empty PowerBead Pro tube processed through the full protocol) per extraction batch to detect contamination (Salter et al., 2014)
Run Qubit standards with each new batch of working solution
Acceptable DNA yield from 0.25 g of soil: typically 1–20 ng/uL in a 100 uL elution, depending on soil type (Dineen et al., 2010)
Acceptable A260/A280: 1.7–2.0. Samples outside this range should be noted and may require re-extraction.
Acceptable A260/A230: greater than 1.5 for most downstream applications. Values below 1.0 indicate significant contamination and the extract should be purified or re-extracted.
If NanoDrop and Qubit concentrations disagree by more than a factor of two, the NanoDrop reading is likely inflated by contaminants; use the Qubit value for planning downstream reactions (Nakayama et al., 2016).

title: ddPCR Applications Guide – Absolute Quantification of Soil Nitrogen-Cycle Functional Genes
text:
4 Definitions

Amplitude threshold: The fluorescence intensity boundary set in QuantaSoft (or QuantaSoft Analysis Pro) that separates positive droplets (containing amplified target) from negative droplets; correct threshold placement is the single most critical step in ddPCR data analysis and must be reviewed manually for each plate (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).
Copies per microliter (copies/µL): The absolute concentration of target DNA in the final ddPCR reaction volume as calculated by Poisson statistics from the fraction of positive droplets; must be back-calculated through all dilution steps to report concentration in the original sample (Hindson et al., 2011).
Droplet count filter: A minimum threshold of accepted droplets per well (10,000 recommended) below which the Poisson estimate is unreliable; wells below this threshold must be excluded from analysis (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).
DMINQ (Digital Minimum Information for Publication of Quantitative Digital PCR Experiments): The community standard for reporting ddPCR data (The dMIQE Group & Huggett, 2020); specifies required metadata including droplet count, threshold method, NTC results, and normalization approach.
NTC (no-template control): A reaction well containing all reagents except DNA template; run on every plate to detect reagent or consumable contamination; must show 0 or fewer than 3 positive droplets per well (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2018).
Normalization: The process of expressing gene copy numbers relative to a common denominator (total DNA concentration in ng/µL, or dry soil mass in g) to allow comparison across samples and studies; both normalizations should be reported when possible.
Poisson correction: The statistical calculation applied by QuantaSoft to convert the fraction of positive droplets to an absolute copy number per microliter, correcting for the probability that a single droplet may contain more than one target molecule (Hindson et al., 2011).
QLp file: The proprietary binary data file format produced by the Bio-Rad QX200 system; contains raw droplet amplitude data, QuantaSoft threshold settings, and computed results; must be archived unmodified before any downstream analysis.
Rain: Droplets with intermediate fluorescence amplitude falling between the positive and negative clusters in the amplitude plot; indicates suboptimal amplification, partial inhibition, or primer issues; quantified as the percentage of events in the intermediate cluster and should be documented (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2018; Lievens et al., 2016).

title: ddPCR Applications Guide – Absolute Quantification of Soil Nitrogen-Cycle Functional Genes
text:
5 Why ddPCR for This Application
Quantitative PCR (qPCR) infers target abundance from amplification kinetics against a standard curve, so its accuracy depends on amplification efficiency and on curve quality. ddPCR instead partitions each reaction into roughly 20,000 nanoliter droplets, amplifies to endpoint within each droplet, and counts droplets as positive or negative. The fraction of positive droplets is fit to a Poisson distribution to recover the starting concentration in copies per microliter, with no standard curve required (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2018; Hindson et al., 2011).
For soil nitrogen-cycle work, this matters for several reasons:

Absolute, comparable counts. Copy numbers are returned directly in copies per microliter, which can be normalized to soil mass or DNA and compared across plates, runs, and studies without a shared standard curve.
Tolerance of inhibitors. Soil DNA extracts carry humic acids and other PCR inhibitors. Endpoint partitioning is less sensitive to partial inhibition than the kinetic measurement that qPCR depends on, although inhibition should still be checked (§6) (Hindson et al., 2011).
Precision for small differences. The large number of partitions lets ddPCR resolve modest fold-changes in gene abundance between treatments (Hindson et al., 2011).
Low-abundance targets. Genes such as nosZ or nifH are often present at low copy numbers relative to bulk DNA; partitioning improves the signal-to-noise ratio for rare targets.

These properties are the reason functional-gene abundance is increasingly reported in absolute units when relating microbial communities to nitrogen cycling processes (Levy-Booth et al., 2014).

text:
7 From Instrument Output to Quality-Controlled Data

7.1 Reviewing and Exporting Data
Instrument operation and the QuantaSoft interface are covered in SOP-L214. For analysis, the entry point is the exported well-level data.

Open the completed experiment file (.qlp) in QuantaSoft and confirm the positive/negative threshold for each well. Re-apply thresholds manually in QuantaSoft Analysis Pro if needed, and record any change in the lab notebook.
Export with Options > Export CSV to produce a well-level results file. Key columns include Well, Sample, Target, Concentration (Poisson-corrected copies/µL (Hindson et al., 2011)), Positives, Negatives, AcceptedDroplets, MeanAmplitudeOfPositives, and MeanAmplitudeOfNegatives.
Name the file YYYY-MM-DD_gene_project_plate.csv.
Archive both the .qlp and the exported .csv to the lab shared drive under ddPCR_raw_data/ before any analysis begins.







WarningData Integrity




Never overwrite raw exported data files. Work only with copies.
Back up raw .qlp files immediately after each run.
All analysis scripts must be version-controlled in the lab GitHub repository.





7.2 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria
Apply these checks before any analysis, following the data-quality expectations set out for digital PCR reporting (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2018; The dMIQE Group & Huggett, 2020).

Droplet count filter. Exclude wells with fewer than 10,000 accepted droplets; below this, the Poisson estimate is unreliable (Bio-Rad Laboratories, 2024).
No-template controls (NTC). NTC wells must show 0 or fewer than 3 positive droplets. More than 3 positives indicates contamination; rerun the affected target or plate.
Extraction blanks. Blanks carried from DNA extraction (SOP-L700) must fall below the NTC threshold. Elevated counts point to contamination in the extraction workflow. Note that direct soil extraction is itself a known source of quantitative bias (Frosteg aard et al., 1999), so blanks and recovery checks matter for absolute numbers.
Positive controls. gBlock serial dilution positive controls must return concentrations within 20% of expected values across the linear range (Huggett et al., 2013).
Rain. Document the percentage of rain droplets per well. Assays with persistent high rain (> 10–15% of events) should be flagged and the primer or cycling conditions reviewed (Lievens et al., 2016).

title: ddPCR Applications Guide – Absolute Quantification of Soil Nitrogen-Cycle Functional Genes
text:
8 Calculating Gene Copy Numbers

8.1 From Reaction to Sample
The concentration reported by QuantaSoft is in copies per microliter of the final ddPCR reaction. To convert to copies per gram dry soil:
\[
N_{\text{soil}} =
C_{\text{rxn}} \times V_{\text{rxn}} \times D \times
\frac{V_{\text{elution}}}{V_{\text{rxn input}}} \times
\frac{1}{m_{\text{dry soil}}}
\]
where:

\(C_{\text{rxn}}\) = QuantaSoft-reported concentration (copies/µL)
\(V_{\text{rxn}}\) = total ddPCR reaction volume (typically 20 µL)
\(D\) = dilution factor applied to the extract before the reaction
\(V_{\text{elution}}\) = total DNA extract volume (µL)
\(V_{\text{rxn input}}\) = volume of extract added to the reaction (µL)
\(m_{\text{dry soil}}\) = mass of dry soil extracted (g)



8.2 R Implementation


Code
# =============================================================================
# ddPCR copy number normalization (SOP-L702)
# =============================================================================

library(tidyverse)

# Import well-level QuantaSoft export
raw <- read_csv("2025-05-14_amoA_wetland_plate1.csv")

# Parameters (adjust per run)
rxn_vol       <- 20     # µL total ddPCR reaction volume
input_vol     <- 5      # µL extract added to reaction
elution_vol   <- 100    # µL total DNA extract
dilution      <- 10     # dilution factor applied to extract before reaction

# Dry soil mass (g) per sample -- join from sample metadata
metadata <- read_csv("sample_metadata.csv")  # cols: Sample, dry_soil_g

results <- raw |>
  filter(AcceptedDroplets >= 10000) |>      # droplet count filter
  left_join(metadata, by = "Sample") |>
  mutate(
    copies_per_g = Concentration *           # copies/µL in reaction
      rxn_vol *                              # total reaction volume
      dilution *                             # dilution correction
      (elution_vol / input_vol) *            # extraction recovery
      (1 / dry_soil_g)                       # normalize to dry soil
  )

# Flag QC issues
results <- results |>
  mutate(
    qc_flag = case_when(
      AcceptedDroplets < 10000              ~ "low_droplets",
      Concentration == 0 & !is.na(copies_per_g) ~ "no_signal",
      TRUE                                  ~ "OK"
    )
  )

write_csv(results, "2025-05-14_amoA_wetland_plate1_processed.csv")

Individual gene copy numbers are most informative when examined in relation to each other and to the soil’s total microbial biomass (often estimated as 16S rRNA gene copies) (Kuypers et al., 2018; Levy-Booth et al., 2014).

title: PCR Amplification and Gel Electrophoresis
text: This SOP describes standard polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of target DNA fragments and visualization of PCR products by agarose gel electrophoresis. PCR is used in the EA Program for confirming DNA extraction success, screening for target genes before ddPCR or sequencing, and verifying amplicon size and specificity prior to library preparation (Lorenz, 2012; Mullis, 1990). Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size, providing a visual confirmation that amplification produced the expected product.

PCR is used in the EA Program for confirming DNA extraction success, screening for target genes before ddPCR or sequencing, and verifying amplicon size and specificity prior to library preparation (Lorenz, 2012; Mullis, 1990). Does not apply to: Quantitative PCR (qPCR) or digital PCR (ddPCR; see SOP-L701 and SOP-L702); RT-PCR for RNA targets; polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE)

title: PCR Amplification and Gel Electrophoresis
text:
4 Definitions

Agarose gel: A porous polymer matrix cast from dissolved agarose in TAE or TBE buffer; DNA fragments migrate through the gel under an electric field and are separated by size; typical concentrations are 1–2% (w/v).
Amplicon: The specific DNA fragment produced by PCR between a defined pair of primers; its length (in base pairs) is determined by the primer binding positions and is used to verify PCR specificity on a gel.
Annealing temperature (\(T_a\)): The temperature during the PCR extension cycle at which primers bind to the template; typically 3–5 °C below the calculated primer melting temperature (\(T_m\)); incorrect \(T_a\) causes non-specific amplification or failed reactions.
DNA ladder (size standard): A mixture of DNA fragments of known sizes run alongside samples on a gel; used to estimate the size of amplified products.
Ethidium bromide (EtBr) / SYBR Safe: Fluorescent intercalating dyes added to agarose gels or post-staining baths to visualize DNA under UV light; EtBr is a potent mutagen requiring dedicated waste disposal; SYBR Safe is a lower-hazard alternative.
Master mix: A pre-mixed reagent solution containing DNA polymerase, dNTPs, buffer, and MgCl2 in optimized concentrations; reduces pipetting error and variability between replicate reactions.
Melting temperature (\(T_m\)): The temperature at which 50% of a primer-template duplex is dissociated; calculated from primer sequence and salt concentration; the basis for selecting annealing temperature.
Non-specific amplification: PCR products of unexpected size caused by primer mis-binding; detected as extra bands on a gel; remedied by increasing annealing temperature or redesigning primers.
Primer: A short (18–25 bp) single-stranded oligonucleotide that binds to a complementary sequence on the template DNA and defines the start point for DNA polymerase extension.
TAE / TBE buffer: Running buffers for agarose gel electrophoresis; TAE (Tris-acetate-EDTA) gives sharper bands for larger fragments; TBE (Tris-borate-EDTA) provides better resolution for smaller fragments and is more resistant to overheating.

title: PCR Amplification and Gel Electrophoresis
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Ethidium bromide (EtBr) and SYBR Safe are nucleic acid stains. EtBr is a suspected mutagen; handle with gloves at all times and dispose of gels and buffers as hazardous waste. SYBR Safe is a safer alternative but should still be handled with gloves.
Electrical: Gel electrophoresis uses high voltage (80–120 V). Do not touch the buffer or gel while the power supply is on. Always disconnect the leads before opening the gel box.
UV radiation: Transilluminators emit UV light that can cause skin burns and eye damage. Use a UV shield, wear UV-blocking safety glasses, and minimize exposure time. Blue-light transilluminators are preferred when used with SYBR Safe.
Biological: Environmental DNA extracts may originate from samples containing pathogens. Handle with standard precautions.




5.1 Required PPE

Safety glasses (UV-blocking if using a UV transilluminator)
Lab coat
Nitrile gloves (change frequently; required at all times when handling gels, stains, or PCR products)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
For EtBr contact with skin, wash immediately with soap and water. For UV exposure, flush eyes with water and seek medical attention. Refer to SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.

7 Procedure

7.1 PCR Workspace Preparation






ImportantContamination Prevention



PCR is extremely sensitive to contamination. Follow these rules:

Set up reactions in a designated pre-PCR area, physically separated from post-PCR work (gel loading, product analysis).
Never bring PCR products, gels, or gel imaging equipment into the pre-PCR area.
Use dedicated pipettes for pre-PCR work. Use filter tips exclusively.
Wipe bench surfaces with 10% bleach followed by 70% ethanol before setting up reactions.
Change gloves frequently, especially after touching any surface outside the pre-PCR area.





7.2 Master Mix Preparation
Prepare all components on ice. Calculate volumes for the number of reactions plus 10% overage to account for pipetting losses.

7.5 Loading and Running the Gel

Remove the comb carefully. Place the gel in the electrophoresis tank and fill with 1x TAE (or TBE) buffer until the gel is submerged by 2–3 mm.
Load 5 uL of DNA ladder into the first well.
Add loading dye to each PCR product (if not already included in the PCR buffer). Load 5–10 uL per well.

Connect the leads: DNA migrates toward the positive (red) electrode. Confirm the orientation.

Turn off the power supply and disconnect the leads before removing the gel.

NTC and extraction blank: no visible band
Samples: band at the expected size indicates successful amplification

title: Bioinformatics Pipeline (QIIME 2 / DADA2)
text: This SOP describes the bioinformatics workflow for processing amplicon sequencing data (16S rRNA, ITS, 18S rRNA) from raw demultiplexed FASTQ files through quality filtering, denoising, taxonomic classification, and generation of analysis-ready feature tables. The pipeline uses QIIME 2 as the primary framework with DADA2 as the denoising algorithm (Bolyen et al., 2019; Callahan et al., 2016). DADA2 resolves amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) at single-nucleotide resolution, replacing the older OTU-clustering approach with a more reproducible and sensitive method (Callahan et al., 2017).

title: Bioinformatics Pipeline (QIIME 2 / DADA2)
text:
4 Definitions

ASV (Amplicon Sequence Variant): An exact DNA sequence resolved from amplicon sequencing data by denoising algorithms (DADA2, Deblur); a higher-resolution alternative to OTUs that retains single-nucleotide differences between sequences.
DADA2: A denoising algorithm that models sequencing error rates to distinguish true biological sequences from sequencing errors; produces ASVs directly from paired-end reads without clustering.
Demultiplexing: The computational step of assigning reads to their source sample based on index sequences; produces per-sample FASTQ files from a multiplexed sequencing run.
Feature table (OTU/ASV table): A matrix of counts where rows are samples, columns are ASVs or OTUs, and each cell contains the number of reads from that sample assigned to that sequence variant; the primary data object in QIIME 2.
FASTQ: A text-based file format storing DNA sequences and their per-base quality scores (Phred scores); the standard output format from Illumina sequencers; paired-end data produces R1 and R2 FASTQ files per sample.
OTU (Operational Taxonomic Unit): A cluster of sequences grouped by a similarity threshold (typically 97% identity); a coarser representation of diversity than ASVs; largely superseded by ASV-based approaches.
Phred quality score (Q score): A logarithmic measure of base-call accuracy: \(Q = -10 \log_{10}(P_{error})\); Q20 = 99% accuracy; Q30 = 99.9% accuracy; used to set quality-trimming thresholds in DADA2.
QIIME 2: An open-source bioinformatics platform for microbiome analysis; manages data as typed artifacts (.qza) with embedded provenance records; wraps DADA2, taxonomic classifiers, diversity analyses, and visualization tools.
Rarefaction: Subsampling each sample to the same number of reads to correct for unequal sequencing depth before diversity comparisons; samples below the rarefaction depth are excluded.
Taxonomic classifier: A trained machine-learning model (e.g., naive Bayes classifier trained on SILVA or UNITE) that assigns taxonomy to ASV sequences by comparing them to a reference database.

title: Bioinformatics Pipeline (QIIME 2 / DADA2)
text:
6 Procedure

6.1 Data Organization

Create a project directory with the following structure:

project_name/
├── raw_data/          # Demultiplexed FASTQ files from sequencing facility
├── qiime2/            # QIIME 2 artifacts and visualizations
├── results/           # Exported tables, trees, taxonomy
├── scripts/           # Shell and R scripts
└── metadata/          # Sample metadata TSV file

Prepare a sample metadata file (metadata.tsv) in tab-separated format. The first column must be sample-id matching the FASTQ filenames. Include all experimental variables (site, treatment, date, depth, replicate). Validate the file at https://keemei.qiime2.org/ (Rideout et al., 2014).



6.2 Import Raw Reads
Import demultiplexed paired-end FASTQ files into a QIIME 2 artifact:
qiime tools import \
  --type 'SampleData[PairedEndSequencesWithQuality]' \
  --input-path raw_data/ \
  --input-format CasavaOneEightSingleLanePerSampleDirFmt \
  --output-path qiime2/demux.qza
Visualize read quality:
qiime demux summarize \
  --i-data qiime2/demux.qza \
  --o-visualization qiime2/demux-summary.qzv
Open demux-summary.qzv at https://view.qiime2.org to inspect quality score profiles. Use these plots to determine truncation parameters for DADA2 (Section 5.3).


6.3 Denoising with DADA2
DADA2 performs quality filtering, chimera removal, and denoising in a single step, producing an ASV feature table and representative sequences (Callahan et al., 2016).
qiime dada2 denoise-paired \
  --i-demultiplexed-seqs qiime2/demux.qza \
  --p-trunc-len-f 240 \
  --p-trunc-len-r 200 \
  --p-trim-left-f 0 \
  --p-trim-left-r 0 \
  --p-n-threads 4 \
  --o-table qiime2/table.qza \
  --o-representative-sequences qiime2/rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-denoising-stats qiime2/dada2-stats.qza






ImportantSetting Truncation Parameters



Choose --p-trunc-len-f and --p-trunc-len-r based on the quality plots from Section 5.2. Truncate where the median quality score drops below 25–30. The forward and reverse reads must still overlap by at least 20 bp after truncation for successful merging. For 16S V4 (515F/806R, ~290 bp amplicon) with 2x250 reads, typical values are 240 (forward) and 200 (reverse).


Review denoising statistics:
qiime metadata tabulate \
  --m-input-file qiime2/dada2-stats.qza \
  --o-visualization qiime2/dada2-stats.qzv
Check the percentage of reads passing each filter step (input, filtered, denoised, merged, non-chimeric). A healthy run retains > 60% of input reads through the full pipeline.


6.4 Taxonomic Classification
Assign taxonomy to ASVs using a pre-trained Naive Bayes classifier. Download the appropriate classifier from the QIIME 2 Data Resources page (https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.2/data-resources/).
For 16S (SILVA 138.1):
qiime feature-classifier classify-sklearn \
  --i-classifier silva-138.1-ssu-nr99-515f-806r-classifier.qza \
  --i-reads qiime2/rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-classification qiime2/taxonomy.qza
For ITS (UNITE):
qiime feature-classifier classify-sklearn \
  --i-classifier unite-ver9-dynamic-all-29.11.2022-classifier.qza \
  --i-reads qiime2/rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-classification qiime2/taxonomy.qza
Visualize taxonomy:
qiime taxa barplot \
  --i-table qiime2/table.qza \
  --i-taxonomy qiime2/taxonomy.qza \
  --m-metadata-file metadata/metadata.tsv \
  --o-visualization qiime2/taxa-barplot.qzv


6.5 Phylogenetic Tree Construction
Build a rooted phylogenetic tree for diversity analyses:
qiime phylogeny align-to-tree-mafft-fasttree \
  --i-sequences qiime2/rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-alignment qiime2/aligned-rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-masked-alignment qiime2/masked-aligned-rep-seqs.qza \
  --o-tree qiime2/unrooted-tree.qza \
  --o-rooted-tree qiime2/rooted-tree.qza


6.6 Filtering
Remove contaminant ASVs identified in negative controls, mitochondrial and chloroplast sequences, and low-frequency ASVs:
# Remove mitochondria and chloroplast
qiime taxa filter-table \
  --i-table qiime2/table.qza \
  --i-taxonomy qiime2/taxonomy.qza \
  --p-exclude mitochondria,chloroplast \
  --o-filtered-table qiime2/table-filtered.qza

# Remove low-frequency ASVs (e.g., singletons)
qiime feature-table filter-features \
  --i-table qiime2/table-filtered.qza \
  --p-min-frequency 2 \
  --o-filtered-table qiime2/table-final.qza
For decontamination using negative control data, export the feature table to R and use the decontam package (Davis et al., 2018).


6.7 Export for R Analysis
Export QIIME 2 artifacts for downstream analysis in R with phyloseq (McMurdie & Holmes, 2013):
qiime tools export \
  --input-path qiime2/table-final.qza \
  --output-path results/

qiime tools export \
  --input-path qiime2/taxonomy.qza \
  --output-path results/

qiime tools export \
  --input-path qiime2/rooted-tree.qza \
  --output-path results/
Alternatively, import QIIME 2 artifacts directly into R using the qiime2R package.

title: Bioinformatics Pipeline (QIIME 2 / DADA2)
text:
7 Quality Control

Inspect the DADA2 denoising stats for every run. Flag samples with fewer than 1,000 reads after denoising.
Verify that negative controls (NTC, extraction blank) contain fewer than 100 reads. If controls contain substantial reads, use decontam to identify and remove contaminant ASVs (Davis et al., 2018; Salter et al., 2014).
Confirm that the positive control (mock community) recovers the expected taxa at the expected relative abundances.
Document all QIIME 2 and DADA2 parameters in the project README and in the analysis scripts. Reproducibility requires recording the exact software versions, classifier version, and truncation lengths.
Archive raw FASTQ files, the QIIME 2 artifacts, and the analysis scripts in the project GitHub repository per SOP-L801.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
4 Definitions

R: A free, open-source programming environment for statistical computing, maintained by a global community of statisticians and programmers (R Core Team, 2024).
RStudio: A user interface for R that provides tools to write code, view results, manage files, and integrate with version control. Available as a desktop application or via the Pomona College server (Posit PBC, 2024).
GitHub: A web-based hosting service for Git repositories that enables collaborative code and document management (GitHub Inc., 2024).
Repository (repo): A GitHub project folder that contains all files, history, and collaboration settings.
Version control: A system that tracks changes to files over time, allowing multiple people to collaborate while maintaining a complete history of who changed what and when.
SSH key: A cryptographic key pair used to establish a secure connection between RStudio and GitHub without entering a password each time.
Clone: Creating a local copy of a GitHub repository on your computer or server.
Branch: A parallel line of development that lets you work on a feature or fix without affecting the main codebase until you are ready to merge.
Pull: Downloading the latest changes from GitHub to your local copy.
Commit: Saving a snapshot of your changes with a descriptive message.
Push: Uploading committed changes from your local copy to GitHub.
Pull request (PR): A request to merge changes from one branch into another; the standard review mechanism for collaborative repositories.

7.2 Configure SSH Keys
SSH keys let RStudio communicate with GitHub securely. Set them up once per machine (or server account).

In RStudio, open the Terminal tab
Generate a key pair:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_pomona_email@pomona.edu"
Accept the default file location; leave the passphrase blank for server use
Print the public key:
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Copy the output
On GitHub: Settings > SSH and GPG keys > New SSH key > paste and save
Test the connection:
ssh -T git@github.com
A message beginning “Hi username!” confirms success.

In RStudio: File > New Project > Version Control > Git
Paste the URL; choose a local directory; click Create Project



8.2 The Pull-Edit-Commit-Push Workflow
Always pull before editing to avoid merge conflicts:

Pull: Click the blue down-arrow in the Git pane (or git pull)
Edit: Make your changes in R scripts or .qmd files
Stage: Check boxes next to changed files in the Git pane
Commit: Click Commit; write a clear message (e.g., "Add soil texture analysis for sites 4-6")
Pull again: Pull once more before pushing to catch any concurrent changes
Push: Click the green up-arrow to push to GitHub



8.3 Branching Workflow
For experimental analyses or features that are not yet ready for the main branch:
git checkout -b feature/my-analysis   # create and switch to new branch
# ... make changes and commits ...
git push -u origin feature/my-analysis
# Open a Pull Request on GitHub when ready to merge

title: Data Entry and Database Management

2 Scope

Applies to: All tabular data generated in the EA Program laboratory and field campaigns, including instrument outputs, field observations, and manually recorded measurements
Does not apply to: Spatial/GIS data (see SOP-L804), bioinformatics sequence data (see SOP-L705), or instrument-specific export procedures (see SOP-L807)

title: Data Entry and Database Management
text:
4 Definitions

Data dictionary: A companion metadata file that describes each variable in a dataset, including the column name, description, units, data type, expected range, and source SOP; required for every EA Program dataset.
ISO 8601: An international standard for representing dates and times as YYYY-MM-DD; the required date format for all EA Program data files because it sorts chronologically and is unambiguous across locales.
Missing value: A data cell for which no measurement was made or the measurement was invalid; represented as blank or NA in EA Program datasets; never coded as 0 (which is a valid measurement).
Primary key: A unique identifier for each row in a data table (e.g., sample_id); enables unambiguous linking between related tables and detection of duplicate entries.
Tidy data: A data structure in which each variable has its own column, each observation has its own row, and each type of observational unit forms its own table (Wickham, 2014); the standard format for EA Program analytical datasets.
Version control: A system that records changes to files over time so that specific versions can be recalled; GitHub/Git is the EA Program version control platform for all data, scripts, and SOPs.

text:
7 Procedure

7.1 File Naming Conventions
All data files must follow this naming pattern:
[project]_[datatype]_[YYYY-MM-DD].[ext]
For example: claremont_soilpH_2026-05-21.csv
Rules for file names:

Use lowercase letters only
Separate words with underscores (not spaces or hyphens)
Include the date of collection or generation in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD)
Use .csv as the default file format for tabular data







TipTip



Never use spaces, special characters, or accented letters in file names. These cause problems across operating systems and with R’s file-reading functions.




7.2 Directory Structure
Organize project data using a consistent directory tree:
project_name/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/          # Unmodified instrument or field data
│   ├── processed/    # Cleaned, validated datasets
│   └── metadata/     # Data dictionaries, codebooks
├── analysis/
│   ├── scripts/      # R scripts and Quarto documents
│   └── output/       # Figures, tables, reports
└── README.md         # Project overview and data description
Raw data files in data/raw/ must never be modified. All cleaning and transformation steps should produce new files in data/processed/ with scripts that document every change (Wilson et al., 2017).


7.3 Data Entry from Lab Notebooks

Open the lab notebook to the relevant page
Create a new CSV file (or open the project template) in data/raw/
Enter column headers in the first row following the variable naming conventions below
Enter each observation as a separate row
Record the notebook page number, date, and analyst initials in the metadata file
Save and commit to Git with a descriptive message



7.4 Variable Naming Conventions
Column headers (variable names) must be:

Lowercase, with underscores separating words (e.g., soil_ph, no3_mg_l)
Free of spaces, special characters, and units in the name itself
Documented in an accompanying data dictionary (see Section 6.7)

Use consistent naming across related datasets. For example, always use site_id (not Site, site, SiteID, or location) when referring to the same sampling locations.


7.5 Data Types and Formatting








Data Type
Convention
Example




Dates
ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD)
2026-05-21


Times
24-hour (HH:MM)
14:30


Missing values
Leave cell empty or use NA
NA


Numeric
No commas; use period for decimal
1234.56


Categorical
Consistent spelling; lowercase
upstream


Below detection
Flag column; numeric = MDL/2
See QC SOP









WarningCommon Mistakes



Never use 0 to represent a missing value. A zero is a valid measurement. Use NA or leave the cell blank. Never merge cells in a spreadsheet, and never use color coding as the sole carrier of information (Broman & Woo, 2018).




7.6 Data Validation in R
After entry, run the validation script to check for common errors. A minimal validation template:


Code
library(tidyverse)

# Read the raw data
dat <- read_csv("data/raw/project_variable_2026-05-21.csv")

# --- Structure checks ---
glimpse(dat)                         # Column types correct?
stopifnot(nrow(dat) > 0)            # File is not empty

# --- Missing data summary ---
dat %>%
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "n_missing") %>%
  filter(n_missing > 0)

# --- Range checks ---
dat %>%
  summarize(
    ph_min = min(soil_ph, na.rm = TRUE),
    ph_max = max(soil_ph, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# Are values within physically plausible ranges?

# --- Duplicate check ---
dat %>%
  group_by(site_id, date) %>%
  filter(n() > 1)
# Flag unexpected duplicates for review

# --- Categorical consistency ---
dat %>% count(site_id, sort = TRUE)
# Look for typos (e.g., "upstrream" vs "upstream")




7.7 Data Dictionaries (Metadata)
Every dataset must have a companion data dictionary saved as data/metadata/[project]_datadictionary.csv with the following columns:







Column
Description




variable
Column name in the data file


description
Plain-language description


units
Units of measurement (or “categorical”, “text”)


type
Data type: numeric, integer, character, date, logical


range
Expected range or valid categories


source_sop
SOP number for the method that generated the data





7.8 Version Control with Git
All data files and scripts must be tracked in a Git repository hosted on GitHub. Follow the procedures in SOP-L801 for committing and pushing changes. Key rules:

Commit raw data files when they are first created (and never modify them after the initial commit)
Commit processed data files after each cleaning or transformation step
Write informative commit messages (e.g., “Add soil pH data from Apr 15 sampling” rather than “update”)
Use branches for experimental analyses; merge to main when finalized



7.9 Database Management for Multi-Year Projects
For projects spanning multiple semesters or involving multiple analysts, maintain a relational data structure:

Create a sites table (data/metadata/sites.csv) with location identifiers, coordinates, and site descriptions
Create a samples table (data/metadata/samples.csv) linking each sample to a site, date, and collector
Link analytical results to samples using unique sample_id values

This structure prevents duplication, supports merging across semesters, and enables relational joins in R (Wickham, 2014):


Code
sites <- read_csv("data/metadata/sites.csv")
samples <- read_csv("data/metadata/samples.csv")
results <- read_csv("data/processed/chemistry_results.csv")

# Join all tables
full_data <- results %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id") %>%
  left_join(sites, by = "site_id")

title: Drone Image Processing (Photogrammetry)
text: This SOP describes the post-processing workflow for aerial imagery collected by uncrewed aerial systems (UAS/drones). It covers image organization, photogrammetric reconstruction (orthomosaics, digital surface models, and point clouds), ground control point integration, accuracy assessment, and data archiving (Anderson & Gaston, 2013; Iglhaut et al., 2019).

title: Drone Image Processing (Photogrammetry)
text: This SOP describes the post-processing workflow for aerial imagery collected by uncrewed aerial systems (UAS/drones). It covers image organization, photogrammetric reconstruction (orthomosaics, digital surface models, and point clouds), ground control point integration, accuracy assessment, and data archiving (Anderson & Gaston, 2013; Iglhaut et al., 2019).

title: Drone Image Processing (Photogrammetry)
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Photogrammetric processing of RGB, multispectral, and thermal drone imagery collected for EA Program research
Does not apply to: Drone flight planning, airspace authorization, or FAA Part 107 compliance (covered in the drone operations field SOP); GIS analysis of processed outputs (see SOP-L804)
Location: EA Program laboratory (SGM 133) and processing workstations

title: Drone Image Processing (Photogrammetry)
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility

Approve processing workflows; ensure data storage compliance

title: Drone Image Processing (Photogrammetry)
text:
4 Definitions

Digital elevation model (DEM): A raster representing bare-ground surface elevation; derived by removing vegetation and structures from a digital surface model using filtering algorithms.
Digital surface model (DSM): A raster representing the elevation of all surfaces in the scene, including vegetation canopy and structures; the direct output of photogrammetric point cloud processing.
Ground control point (GCP): A precisely surveyed point on the ground (surveyed with RTK-GPS or total station) that appears in multiple overlapping images; used to georeference the photogrammetric model to a known coordinate system and improve absolute accuracy.
Orthomosaic: A geometrically corrected aerial image composed of many overlapping individual photos, in which scale is uniform and features can be measured accurately; produced by photogrammetric processing.
Photogrammetry: The science of making measurements from photographs; in drone operations, the process of generating 3D models, DEMs, and orthomosaics from overlapping aerial images using structure-from-motion algorithms.
Point cloud: A set of data points in 3D space (X, Y, Z coordinates) representing the surface of objects; generated by photogrammetric processing of overlapping images; the intermediate product from which DEMs and DSMs are derived.
Structure from Motion (SfM): A photogrammetric algorithm that reconstructs 3D geometry from 2D overlapping images by identifying and matching common features across multiple images; the computational core of drone photogrammetry software (Agisoft Metashape, Pix4D).
