title: Drone Image Processing (Photogrammetry)
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Image Organization
Before processing, organize raw imagery following a consistent directory structure:
project_name/
├── drone/
│   ├── raw_images/
│   │   ├── flight_2026-05-21_rgb/
│   │   │   ├── DJI_0001.JPG
│   │   │   ├── DJI_0002.JPG
│   │   │   └── ...
│   │   └── flight_2026-05-21_multi/
│   ├── flight_logs/
│   │   └── flight_2026-05-21.csv
│   ├── gcp/
│   │   └── gcp_coordinates.csv
│   ├── processed/
│   │   ├── orthomosaic/
│   │   ├── dsm/
│   │   ├── point_cloud/
│   │   └── report/
│   └── README.md
Check that all images have valid EXIF data (GPS coordinates, camera parameters). Remove obviously corrupted or blurry images before processing.


Code
library(exifr)

# Read EXIF from all images in a flight folder
exif_data <- read_exif(
  list.files("drone/raw_images/flight_2026-05-21_rgb/",
             pattern = "\\.JPG$", full.names = TRUE),
  tags = c("FileName", "GPSLatitude", "GPSLongitude",
           "GPSAltitude", "FocalLength", "ImageWidth",
           "ImageHeight", "DateTimeOriginal")
)

# Check for missing GPS
missing_gps <- exif_data %>%
  filter(is.na(GPSLatitude) | is.na(GPSLongitude))
cat(sprintf("%d images missing GPS coordinates\n", nrow(missing_gps)))

# Summary
cat(sprintf("Total images: %d\n", nrow(exif_data)))
cat(sprintf("Date range: %s to %s\n",
            min(exif_data$DateTimeOriginal),
            max(exif_data$DateTimeOriginal)))




7.2 Ground Control Points (GCPs)
GCPs are surveyed reference points used to improve the geometric accuracy of photogrammetric outputs.

Place GCPs before the flight. Use high-contrast targets (black and white checkerboard, minimum 30 cm) visible from flight altitude
Survey GCP positions using a differential GPS or RTK receiver. Record coordinates in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) and a local projected CRS (e.g., EPSG:26911)
Format GCP data as a CSV file:

gcp_id,longitude,latitude,elevation_m,crs
GCP01,-117.7123,34.0966,398.2,EPSG:4326
GCP02,-117.7118,34.0971,401.5,EPSG:4326

Use a minimum of 5 GCPs distributed across the study area. Reserve 2 or more as independent check points for accuracy assessment



7.3 Photogrammetric Processing (Agisoft Metashape)
The following workflow applies to Agisoft Metashape Professional. Adapt parameters for your specific project needs.
Step 1: Create project and import photos

Create a new Metashape project and save to drone/processed/
Add photos from the flight folder
Verify camera positions on the reference pane

Step 2: Align photos

Workflow > Align Photos
Settings: Accuracy = High; Key point limit = 40,000; Tie point limit = 10,000; Adaptive camera model fitting = enabled
Review the sparse point cloud and camera positions

Step 3: Import and assign GCPs

Import GCP coordinates from the CSV file
Assign each GCP to its corresponding target in at least 3 photos
Uncheck GCPs designated as check points
Run Optimize Cameras

Step 4: Build dense point cloud

Workflow > Build Point Cloud
Quality = High (or Medium for initial assessment); Depth filtering = Moderate
Inspect the dense cloud for artifacts; remove obvious noise manually or with CloudCompare

Step 5: Build DEM and orthomosaic

Workflow > Build DEM (Source: Point Cloud)
Workflow > Build Orthomosaic (Surface: DEM; Blending mode: Mosaic)

Step 6: Export products

Export DEM as GeoTIFF to drone/processed/dsm/
Export orthomosaic as GeoTIFF to drone/processed/orthomosaic/
Export point cloud as .laz to drone/processed/point_cloud/
Export processing report as PDF to drone/processed/report/







TipTip



For large datasets (more than 1,000 images), process on the lab workstation rather than a laptop. Expect processing times of several hours for dense cloud generation at High quality.




7.4 OpenDroneMap (Alternative Workflow)
For projects using the open-source pipeline:


Code
# Run ODM with standard settings
docker run -ti --rm \
  -v /path/to/project/drone:/datasets \
  opendronemap/odm \
  --project-path /datasets \
  --dsm \
  --orthophoto-resolution 2.0 \
  --dem-resolution 5.0 \
  --gcp /datasets/gcp/gcp_list.txt




7.5 Accuracy Assessment
Evaluate positional accuracy using the reserved check points:


Code
library(terra)
library(sf)

# Load the DSM
dsm <- rast("drone/processed/dsm/dsm_2026-05-21.tif")

# Load check points
check_pts <- read_csv("drone/gcp/check_points.csv") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = crs(dsm))

# Extract DSM elevation at check points
check_pts$dsm_elev <- extract(dsm, check_pts)$value

# Calculate vertical RMSE
check_pts <- check_pts %>%
  mutate(error_m = dsm_elev - elevation_m)

rmse_z <- sqrt(mean(check_pts$error_m^2, na.rm = TRUE))
mae_z <- mean(abs(check_pts$error_m), na.rm = TRUE)

cat(sprintf("Vertical RMSE: %.3f m\n", rmse_z))
cat(sprintf("Vertical MAE:  %.3f m\n", mae_z))
cat(sprintf("n check points: %d\n", nrow(check_pts)))


Report accuracy metrics in all publications and project reports. Typical targets for environmental applications: horizontal RMSE less than 2 times the ground sampling distance (GSD); vertical RMSE less than 3 times the GSD (James et al., 2017).


7.6 Multispectral Processing
For multispectral imagery (e.g., MicaSense RedEdge):

Include reflectance calibration panel images (taken before and after each flight)
Process each band alignment in Metashape or use MicaSense’s Atlas or micasense Python library
Export calibrated reflectance orthomosaics (not raw DN values)
Calculate vegetation indices in R:



Code
library(terra)

# Load calibrated reflectance bands
red <- rast("drone/processed/orthomosaic/red_reflectance.tif")
nir <- rast("drone/processed/orthomosaic/nir_reflectance.tif")

# Calculate NDVI
ndvi <- (nir - red) / (nir + red)
names(ndvi) <- "NDVI"

writeRaster(ndvi, "drone/processed/orthomosaic/ndvi_2026-05-21.tif",
            overwrite = TRUE)

title: Instrument Data Export and File Management
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All analytical instruments in the EA Program laboratory that produce digital data files, including spectrophotometers, ICP-OES, TOC analyzers, ion chromatographs, balances with data output, pH/conductivity meters with logging, and field sensors that store data internally
Does not apply to: Manual readings recorded directly in lab notebooks (see SOP-L010); drone imagery (see SOP-L805); bioinformatics sequencing data (see SOP-L705)
Location: EA Program laboratory (SGM 133)

title: Instrument Data Export and File Management
text:
4 Definitions

Comma-separated values (CSV): A plain-text file format in which values are separated by commas and rows by line breaks; universally readable; the preferred format for sharing tabular data between instruments and analysis software.
Data provenance: The documented history of how data were collected, processed, transformed, and stored; enables reproduction of results and detection of errors; captured through lab notebooks, metadata files, and Git commit history.
File naming convention: A standardized pattern for naming files that encodes date, instrument, project, and analyst information without spaces or special characters (e.g., YYYY-MM-DD_InstrumentID_ProjectCode_UserInitials_raw.csv); required for all EA Program instrument export files.
Instrument export file: The raw data file generated directly by instrument software (e.g., Shimadzu LabSolutions .lcd or .txt export, Isodat .dxf export, HOBOware .csv export); must be saved unmodified as the archival primary record.
Metadata: Data describing other data; includes instrument settings, calibration records, sample identifiers, units, processing steps, and analyst notes; stored alongside raw data in a companion metadata file.
Raw data: The unprocessed data as produced by the instrument or analyst at the time of measurement; must never be altered; all subsequent processing produces derived data files that preserve the original.

title: Instrument Data Export and File Management
text:
5 Safety and Hazards
Data export is a computational activity with no physical hazards. When interacting with instruments (connecting USB drives, accessing instrument PCs), follow the safety protocols in the relevant instrument SOP.

title: Instrument Data Export and File Management
text:
6 Equipment and Materials

6.1 Instruments and Export Formats









Instrument
Native Format
Preferred Export

title: Instrument Data Export and File Management
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 General Export Workflow
The same sequence applies to all instruments:

Complete the analytical run and verify results on the instrument software
Export raw data from the instrument software to CSV format (or the most open/portable format available)
Name the file following the convention: [instrument]_[method]_[YYYY-MM-DD]_[batch].[ext] (e.g., icpoes_metals_2026-05-21_batch01.csv)
Transfer the file to the project’s data/raw/ directory using USB or network transfer
Verify the transfer by opening the file and checking row counts, column headers, and a few spot-checked values against the instrument display
Record the export in the lab notebook: file name, instrument, date, number of samples, and any export settings
Commit to Git with a descriptive message







WarningCritical Rule



Never modify raw instrument files after export. If corrections are needed, create a new file in data/processed/ and document the changes in your processing script. The raw file is your permanent record.




7.2 Instrument-Specific Export Instructions

7.2.1 Shimadzu UV-Vis (UV-1900i / UVProbe)

In UVProbe, open the data file (.spc)
File > Save As > CSV
Select “Wavelength and Absorbance” columns
Save to the USB drive as uvvis_[method]_[YYYY-MM-DD].csv



7.2.2 Thermo iCAP ICP-OES (Qtegra)

In Qtegra, navigate to the completed sequence
Right-click the sequence > Export Results
Select CSV format; include sample IDs, element concentrations, and QC flags
Save to the USB drive as icpoes_[method]_[YYYY-MM-DD]_[batch].csv



7.2.3 Shimadzu TOC-L (TOC-Control)

In TOC-Control, open the sample table for the completed run
File > Export > CSV
Include sample name, injection number, area, concentration, and CV
Save as toc_[method]_[YYYY-MM-DD].csv



7.2.4 YSI ProDSS Field Sensor

Connect the ProDSS to a computer via USB
Open KorDSS software
Select the data log for the sampling event
Export as CSV, including date/time, site ID, and all parameters
Save as ysi_[project]_[YYYY-MM-DD].csv



7.2.5 Bio-Rad QX200 ddPCR (QuantaSoft)

In QuantaSoft, open the completed experiment
Options > Export CSV (Well Data or Cluster Data)
Include well ID, sample name, target, concentration, positive/negative droplet counts
Save as ddpcr_[target]_[YYYY-MM-DD].csv
Also export the amplitude data for gating verification




7.3 File Transfer to RStudio Server
After exporting to USB or local machine:


Code
# Option 1: scp from local machine to RStudio Server
scp icpoes_metals_2026-05-21_batch01.csv \
  username@rstudio.pomona.edu:~/project/data/raw/

# Option 2: Use the RStudio Files pane
# Click Upload > Browse > select file > OK




7.4 Automated Import Scripts in R
Create a standardized import script for each instrument type. This ensures consistent parsing across analysts and batches:


Code
#' Import ICP-OES data from Qtegra CSV export
#'
#' @param file_path Path to the exported CSV file
#' @return A tibble with standardized column names
import_icpoes <- function(file_path) {
  raw <- read_csv(file_path, skip = 2)  # Skip Qtegra header rows

  raw %>%
    rename_with(tolower) %>%
    rename_with(~ gsub(" ", "_", .)) %>%
    mutate(
      date_analyzed = as.Date(date_analyzed, format = "%m/%d/%Y"),
      across(where(is.character) & !c(sample_id, sample_type),
             as.numeric)
    ) %>%
    # Flag values below detection
    mutate(across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ if_else(. < 0, NA_real_, .)
    ))
}

# Usage
icp_data <- import_icpoes("data/raw/icpoes_metals_2026-05-21_batch01.csv")
glimpse(icp_data)




Code
#' Import TOC data from TOC-Control CSV export
#'
#' @param file_path Path to the exported CSV file
#' @return A tibble with standardized column names
import_toc <- function(file_path) {
  raw <- read_csv(file_path)

  raw %>%
    rename_with(tolower) %>%
    rename_with(~ gsub("[^a-z0-9]", "_", .)) %>%
    select(sample_name, injection, area, concentration_mg_l = conc,
           cv_percent = cv) %>%
    filter(!is.na(sample_name))
}




7.5 Data Integrity Checks
After importing, run basic integrity checks:


Code
# --- Row count matches instrument ---
cat(sprintf("Rows in file: %d\n", nrow(icp_data)))
# Compare with number of samples in lab notebook

# --- No fully blank rows ---
stopifnot(!any(rowSums(is.na(icp_data)) == ncol(icp_data)))

# --- Sample IDs match the run sequence ---
expected_ids <- c("Blank", "Std1", "Std2", "Std3",
                  paste0("S", sprintf("%03d", 1:20)),
                  "CRM", "Dup")
setdiff(expected_ids, icp_data$sample_id)
# Should be empty if all expected samples are present

# --- Calibration standards in expected range ---
icp_data %>%
  filter(grepl("^Std", sample_id)) %>%
  select(sample_id, starts_with("fe_")) %>%
  print()




7.6 Archival and Backup
All raw instrument files must be archived in three locations:








Location
When
Responsible




GitHub repository (data/raw/)
Immediately after export
Analyst


Lab instrument PC
Retained on instrument

External backup drive
End of each semester
Lab Manager









TipTip



Large binary files (e.g., raw .spc or .qlp files that exceed GitHub’s file size recommendations) should be stored on the external backup drive and the network share, not in Git. Only the exported CSV goes into the repository.




7.7 Instrument Log Cross-Reference
Every data export event must be recorded in the instrument log (see SOP-L007). The log entry should include:

Date and time of the analytical run
Analyst name
File name(s) exported
Number of samples (including QC samples)
Any instrument warnings or anomalies noted during the run
Cross-reference to the lab notebook page number

6 Procedure

6.1 Before Departure

Identify which activity modules (Section 5) apply to the planned field work. Most outings require the Core Module plus one or more activity-specific modules.
Print or copy the relevant checklists. Check off each item as it is packed.
For instruments requiring calibration (Eureka Manta2, pH meter), calibrate in the lab before packing. Record calibration results in the field notebook.
Verify that all batteries are charged (Crime-Lite, GPS, walkie-talkies) and that backup batteries are included.
Confirm cooler ice or ice packs are frozen and ready.
Complete the Field Work Planning Form in SOP-F001, Section 13.
The field lead initials the checklist and confirms vehicle reservation per SOP-F100 if applicable.



6.2 On Site

Unpack systematically; keep items organized to avoid loss.
At the end of the sampling event, re-check the checklist to confirm all items are accounted for before leaving the site.
Note any damaged or malfunctioning equipment on the checklist.



6.3 After Return

Clean all equipment per the relevant method SOP (rinse sampling equipment with DI water, wipe down instruments, dry sieves).
Return every item to its designated storage location (see room assignments below and SOP-L007).
Recharge batteries and replace consumables (sample bottles, filters, preservatives) for the next user.
Report any damaged, lost, or malfunctioning items to the field lead or lab manager immediately.
File the completed checklist with the field data sheets.

title: Site Access and Permits
text: This SOP describes the procedures for obtaining site access and research permits for field work conducted by the EA Program. Field research on public or institutional lands almost always requires advance authorization (US Fish and Wildlife Service, 2019). Working without proper permits can result in fines, confiscation of samples, invalidation of data, and jeopardized relationships with land managers. This document provides an agency-by-agency guide covering the landowners and managers most commonly encountered by EA Program researchers.

title: Site Access and Permits
text: This SOP describes the procedures for obtaining site access and research permits for field work conducted by the EA Program. Field research on public or institutional lands almost always requires advance authorization (US Fish and Wildlife Service, 2019). Working without proper permits can result in fines, confiscation of samples, invalidation of data, and jeopardized relationships with land managers. This document provides an agency-by-agency guide covering the landowners and managers most commonly encountered by EA Program researchers.

title: Site Access and Permits
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All EA Program field activities that take place on lands managed by the agencies and institutions listed in this SOP, including class field trips, independent student research, and faculty-led projects
Does not apply to: Laboratory procedures; field work on private land (which requires landowner permission negotiated on a case-by-case basis); marine or offshore research (which may require additional permits from NOAA or the California Coastal Commission)
Key principle: It is the responsibility of the PI (or the supervising faculty member) to determine what permits are required and to obtain all necessary approvals before any field work begins. Students should never assume that their faculty advisor has obtained permits – always confirm.

title: Site Access and Permits
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role

title: Site Access and Permits
text:
4 Definitions

BFS (Bernard Field Station): An 86-acre biological reserve of The Claremont Colleges located at 1400 N. Amherst Avenue, Claremont, CA; administered by the BFS Director; all organized access requires an approved Use Request (Robert J. Bernard Biological Field Station, 2024).
CESA (California Endangered Species Act): California state law (Fish and Game Code §2050 et seq.) that protects state-listed threatened and endangered species; take of CESA-listed species requires a separate Memorandum of Understanding from CDFW in addition to a Scientific Collecting Permit (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2024).
CDFW Scientific Collecting Permit (SCP): A permit issued by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife authorizing the take or possession of wildlife for scientific, educational, or propagation purposes; required whenever research involves capturing, handling, marking, or collecting wildlife, or when take of sensitive species may occur incidentally (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2024).
ESA Section 10 permit: A federal incidental take permit issued by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service under Section 10(a)(1)(A) of the Endangered Species Act; required for non-federal activities that involve take of federally listed threatened or endangered species (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2024).
ESA Section 7 consultation: The formal interagency process under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act through which a federal agency (e.g., USFS, BLM) consults with USFWS or NMFS to ensure that its authorized activities do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat.
Incidental take: The unintentional, but not unexpected, harm to a listed species that results from an otherwise lawful activity; must be authorized through a Section 10 permit (private activities) or Section 7 consultation (federal activities).
NEPA (National Environmental Policy Act): Federal law requiring federal agencies to assess the environmental impacts of their proposed actions; complex research proposals on federal lands may trigger NEPA review, substantially extending the permit processing timeline.
RAMS (Reserve Application Management System): The online portal through which researchers and instructors apply for access to University of California Natural Reserve System reserves (University of California Natural Reserve System, 2024).
RPRS (Research Permit and Reporting System): The National Park Service’s online system for submitting research permit applications, reporting annual activities, and communicating with park research coordinators (National Park Service, 2024).
Special Use Permit (SUP): A general-purpose permit issued by federal land management agencies (BLM, USFS) authorizing a specific research project or activity on public lands; may take 60–120 days or more to process (Bureau of Land Management, 2024; USDA Forest Service, San Bernardino National Forest, 2024).
Take: Under California Fish and Game Code §86, to hunt, pursue, catch, capture, or kill, or attempt to do so; under the federal ESA, to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or attempt to do so.
UC Natural Reserve System (UCNRS): A network of 41+ reserves managed by the University of California for research, teaching, and public service; access requires an approved RAMS application (University of California Natural Reserve System, 2024).

title: Site Access and Permits
text:
5 General Principles

5.1 Planning Timeline
Permit processing times vary widely. Submit applications at least 60–90 days before the planned start of field work. Some agencies (particularly federal ones involving NEPA review or listed species) may require 6 months or more. Always confirm the current timeline with the specific office.



Agency / Institution
Typical Lead Time




Bernard Field Station
1–2 weeks


California State Parks
60–90 days


UC Natural Reserve System
2–4 weeks


CDFW (General Use SCP)
60–90 days


CDFW (Specific Use SCP)
3–6 months


USFWS (Section 10)
3–12 months


BLM
60–120 days


National Park Service
60–120 days


USDA Forest Service
60–120 days





5.2 Permits You May Need Simultaneously
A single field project can require permits from multiple agencies. For example, sampling macroinvertebrates in a stream within a National Forest may require a USFS Special Use Permit, a CDFW Scientific Collecting Permit, and (if listed species are present) a USFWS Section 10 permit. The land management agency will typically not finalize its own permit until copies of all other required permits are submitted.


5.3 Permit Files
The PI must maintain a digital folder (in the EA Program Google Drive or GitHub repository) containing:

Copies of all active permits (signed, final versions)
Copies of all applications submitted
Copies of annual reports and compliance documents submitted to agencies
Expiration dates and renewal deadlines

Field leads must carry printed or digital copies of relevant permits during every field outing.


5.4 Insurance and Liability
Several agencies require proof of liability insurance as a condition of permit issuance. Pomona College maintains institutional liability coverage; contact the Office of Risk Management to obtain a Certificate of Insurance naming the specific agency as an additional insured party.

title: Site Access and Permits
text:
6 Agency-Specific Procedures

6.1 Robert J. Bernard Biological Field Station (BFS)
The BFS is an 86-acre facility of The Claremont Colleges located at 1400 N. Amherst Avenue, Claremont, CA. Access requires advance approval from the BFS Director (Robert J. Bernard Biological Field Station, 2024).
When a permit is needed: All research projects, class field trips, and organized activities on the BFS require a Use Request, even for Claremont Colleges faculty and students. Casual, unaccompanied pedestrian access also requires prior authorization.
How to apply:

Contact the BFS Director (Dr. Wallace M. Meyer III, wallace.meyer@pomona.edu, 909-621-8577) to discuss the proposed project
Complete the online “Apply to Use” form at https://bfs.sites.pomona.edu/using-the-bfs/
Allow 1–2 weeks for approval; more complex projects may require additional review

Website: https://bfs.sites.pomona.edu/using-the-bfs/



6.2 California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW)
CDFW issues Scientific Collecting Permits (SCPs) for the take or possession of wildlife (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, certain plants, and invertebrates) for scientific, educational, and propagation purposes (California Department of Fish and Wildlife, 2024).
When a permit is needed: Any time your research involves capturing, handling, marking, or collecting wildlife – or when there is potential for incidental take of sensitive species.
Permit types:

General Use SCP – for more common species, non-invasive methods, and areas outside Marine Protected Areas
Specific Use SCP – for focused studies involving prohibited wildlife, more invasive methods, or sensitive locations including MPAs

How to apply:

Review the SCP regulations (Title 14, Section 650, CCR) and Standard Conditions at https://wildlife.ca.gov/Licensing/Scientific-Collecting
Apply online through the Scientific Collecting Permit Portal (SCPP)
Pay the required permit fee before issuance

CESA-listed species: Requires a separate CESA Memorandum of Understanding from CDFW in addition to the SCP.
Reporting: Each permitholder must submit a Mandatory Wildlife Report (form DFW 1379a) annually.
Website: https://wildlife.ca.gov/Licensing/Scientific-Collecting



6.3 California Department of Parks and Recreation (State Parks)
When a permit is needed: Any scientific research, data collection, specimen collection, or installation of monitoring equipment in California State Park System lands requires written authorization (California Department of Parks and Recreation, 2024).
How to apply:

Download and complete form DPR 65 from https://www.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=21557
Prepare a full study proposal following the Study Proposal Guidelines for Research in California State Parks
Submit the application, study proposal, proof of insurance, and copies of any other required permits (CDFW, USFWS, etc.) to the appropriate State Parks district office; for multi-district projects, submit to the Natural Resources Division in Sacramento at nrd.research@parks.ca.gov
Allow 60–90 days for processing

Reporting: A summary report of activities and findings must be submitted to State Parks; renewal is contingent on receipt of this report.
Website: https://www.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=21557



6.4 University of California Natural Reserve System (UCNRS)
The UCNRS manages 41+ reserves across California for research, teaching, and public service (University of California Natural Reserve System, 2024).
When a permit is needed: All research projects and class visits require an approved application through the Reserve Application Management System (RAMS).
How to apply:

Contact the reserve director(s) to discuss project requirements
Review the NRS Use Guidelines at https://ucnrs.org/reserve-research-guidelines/
Submit a research application through RAMS at https://rams.ucnrs.org
Once approved, submit a Reservation for each planned visit through RAMS

Special conditions:

IACUC approval required if the project involves vertebrate animals
Additional agency permits (CDFW, USFWS) may be required
All equipment must be removed and sites restored at project conclusion

Website: https://ucnrs.org/



6.5 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS)
USFWS administers permits for activities involving species listed under the federal Endangered Species Act (ESA), migratory birds (Migratory Bird Treaty Act), and wildlife on National Wildlife Refuges (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2024).
When a permit is needed:

Take of federally listed threatened or endangered species requires a Section 10(a)(1)(A) recovery permit
Research involving migratory birds requires a federal Bird Banding Permit and/or Scientific Collecting Permit
Research on National Wildlife Refuge lands requires a Special Use Permit from the refuge manager

How to apply:

For ESA-listed species: submit form 3-200-55 through the USFWS Endangered Species permits portal
For migratory birds: apply through the USFWS Bird Banding Laboratory or the federal permits portal
For refuge access: contact the specific refuge manager

Key considerations: Section 10 applications are subject to a 30-day Federal Register public comment period; processing times are 3–12 months. Annual reports are required for all active permits.
Website: https://www.fws.gov/service/apply-permit



6.6 Bureau of Land Management (BLM)
BLM manages extensive public lands in California, including desert, grassland, and mountain areas where EA Program research may occur (Bureau of Land Management, 2024).
When a permit is needed: Any organized research activity on BLM-managed lands, including specimen collection, installation of monitoring equipment, and systematic surveys.
How to apply:

Contact the nearest BLM Field Office at https://www.blm.gov/office/directory
BLM staff will determine whether a Special Recreation Permit, research authorization, or another approval type is needed
Submit required application materials (maps, project description, copies of other agency permits)
Allow 60–120 days; complex NEPA projects may take longer

Website: https://www.blm.gov/learn/science-in-the-blm/conducting-science



6.7 National Park Service (NPS)
NPS requires a Scientific Research and Collecting Permit for most scientific activities in any unit of the National Park System (National Park Service, 2024).
When a permit is needed: Any study in the natural or social sciences within a national park, monument, seashore, or other NPS unit.
How to apply:

Create an investigator account in the Research Permit and Reporting System (RPRS) at https://irma.nps.gov/rprs/
Locate the park profile in RPRS and contact the research coordinator for park-specific conditions
Submit the application through RPRS; allow 60–120 days
Annual reports are submitted through RPRS

Website: https://www.nps.gov/subjects/science/research-and-collecting-permit-overview.htm



6.8 USDA Forest Service (USFS)
USFS manages National Forest System (NFS) lands through local Ranger District offices (USDA Forest Service, San Bernardino National Forest, 2024).
When a permit is needed: Any organized research activity on NFS lands, including specimen collection, installation of monitoring equipment, and systematic surveys.
How to apply:

Contact the Ranger District office for the relevant National Forest (for Southern California: San Bernardino, Angeles, Cleveland, or Los Padres)
Download and complete a Research Special-Use Operating Plan/Itinerary from the forest’s website and submit it to the district permit coordinator
Forest staff will determine whether a full Special Use Permit or a Research Permit Waiver is appropriate
Allow 60–120 days; projects requiring NEPA analysis may take longer

Special conditions:

Projects involving wildlife or threatened/endangered plants may require additional CDFW and/or USFWS authorization
A summary of findings must be provided to the Forest Service upon completion

Website: https://www.fs.usda.gov/

title: Site Access and Permits
text:
7 Permit Decision Flowchart
Use the following steps to determine what permits you need:

Identify the land manager. Who owns or manages the land where you will work?
Obtain the land access permit from the land manager (Sections 5.1–5.8 above).
Will you handle, capture, collect, or disturb wildlife? If yes, you likely need a CDFW Scientific Collecting Permit (§5.2).
Are any federally listed species present, or could they be incidentally encountered? If yes, you likely need a USFWS Section 10 permit or ESA Section 7 consultation (§5.5).
Are any state-listed species (CESA) present? If yes, you need a CESA MOU from CDFW in addition to the SCP (§5.2).
Does the land manager require other agency permits before issuing its own? If yes, obtain those permits first and submit copies with your land access application.







TipWhen in doubt, ask



If you are unsure whether a permit is required, contact the agency before beginning field work. It is always better to ask in advance than to be stopped in the field or have your data and specimens invalidated.

title: GPS and Site Navigation
text: This SOP describes standardized procedures for recording geographic coordinates, navigating to field sites, and managing waypoint data. Accurate and consistent location data are essential for linking field observations to spatial analyses, returning to the same sampling points across seasons, and sharing site information among researchers. This SOP covers handheld GPS receivers, smartphone GPS applications, and post-field data management (U.S. Forest Service, 2012).

title: GPS and Site Navigation
text: This SOP describes standardized procedures for recording geographic coordinates, navigating to field sites, and managing waypoint data. Accurate and consistent location data are essential for linking field observations to spatial analyses, returning to the same sampling points across seasons, and sharing site information among researchers. This SOP covers handheld GPS receivers, smartphone GPS applications, and post-field data management (U.S. Forest Service, 2012).

title: GPS and Site Navigation
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All EA Program field activities that require geographic coordinates, including sample collection, transect establishment, monitoring well location, equipment installation, and site reconnaissance
Does not apply to: High-precision survey-grade GNSS work (sub-centimeter accuracy); drone-based georeferencing (see SOP-F630); GIS post-processing and spatial analysis (see future SOP-L804)
Location: All EA Program field sites

title: GPS and Site Navigation
text:

title: GPS and Site Navigation
text:
4 Definitions

Datum: A mathematical model of the Earth’s surface used as the reference for geographic coordinates; the EA Program default is WGS 84 (World Geodetic System 1984), the datum used by consumer GPS and Google Maps; NAD 83 is nearly identical for most field purposes but must be specified explicitly if used (U.S. Forest Service, 2012).
Decimal degrees (DD): A coordinate format expressing latitude and longitude as a single decimal number (e.g., 34.0975 N, 117.7125 W); the EA Program default format; preferred for data entry in spreadsheets and GIS.
GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System): The general term for satellite-based positioning systems; includes the US GPS, Russian GLONASS, European Galileo, and Chinese BeiDou constellations; modern receivers use multiple constellations simultaneously to improve accuracy.
GPS (Global Positioning System): The US-operated GNSS constellation of 31+ satellites; provides horizontal accuracy of 3–5 m under open sky with a modern consumer receiver (U.S. Forest Service, 2012).
GPX file: A standard XML-based file format for exchanging GPS waypoints, tracks, and routes between devices and software; the preferred export format for EA Program waypoints.
HDOP (Horizontal Dilution of Precision): A dimensionless number indicating GPS positional uncertainty due to satellite geometry; values below 2 indicate excellent geometry; values above 5 indicate poor geometry and reduced accuracy (U.S. Forest Service, 2012).
Offline map: A map tile set downloaded to a smartphone or device before the field visit, enabling navigation without cellular data; required for EA Program field sites with unreliable coverage.
UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator): A projected coordinate system that divides the world into 60 zones and expresses positions in meters east (easting) and north (northing) of a zone origin; useful for measuring distances directly but requires specifying the UTM zone.
Waypoint: A named, saved geographic location stored in a GPS receiver or smartphone app; defined by coordinates (latitude, longitude, and optionally elevation), a name, and often a description or icon.
WGS 84 (World Geodetic System 1984): The global coordinate datum used by GPS satellites, Google Maps, and most modern consumer GPS devices; the EA Program default (U.S. Forest Service, 2012).

title: GPS and Site Navigation
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Navigating to remote waypoints may involve uneven terrain, dense vegetation, or stream crossings. Do not fixate on the GPS screen while walking.
Environmental: Reliance on GPS in areas with poor satellite coverage (dense canopy, steep canyons) can lead to navigation errors. Always carry a paper map or site sketch as a backup.




5.1 Required PPE

Closed-toed shoes or field boots
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety. If lost or disoriented, stop moving, note your last known coordinates, and contact the field lead by phone or walkie-talkie.

title: GPS and Site Navigation
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Field Setup

Confirm the coordinate system and datum for the project. The EA Program default is WGS 84, latitude/longitude in decimal degrees (U.S. Forest Service, 2012). If a project requires UTM or NAD 83, configure the device accordingly and note the setting in the field notebook.
On a handheld GPS, verify the datum setting: navigate to Setup > Position Format and confirm WGS 84 (Garmin International, 2019).
On a smartphone app, enable offline maps for the study area. Do not rely on cellular data for map tiles in the field (Avenza Systems, 2024).
Clear or archive old waypoints from the device so the day’s data are easy to identify.
Pre-load target waypoints if revisiting known sites. Use the naming convention described in §6.3.



7.2 Recording Waypoints in the Field

At the sampling location, hold the GPS receiver at chest height in an open area away from dense canopy, cliff faces, and vehicles.
Wait until the GPS reports an accuracy of 5 m or better (HDOP < 2 preferred). If accuracy remains above 5 m after two minutes, record the waypoint and note the reported accuracy in the field notebook (U.S. Forest Service, 2012).
Save the waypoint using the naming convention in §6.3.
In the field notebook, record:

Waypoint name
Date and time
Coordinates (as displayed on the device)
Reported accuracy (HDOP or meters, as available)
A brief description (e.g., “upstream riffle, transect 3 start”)

If using a smartphone, take a screenshot of the GPS display as a backup record.



7.3 Waypoint Naming Convention
Use the following format: SITE_TYPE_NN

SITE = three- or four-letter site abbreviation (e.g., BFS, THW, MRW)
TYPE = two-letter code for the point type (see table below)
NN = sequential two-digit number




Code
Point Type
Example




WQ
Water quality sampling
BFS_WQ_01


SO
Soil sampling
THW_SO_03


TR
Transect endpoint
MRW_TR_01


WL
Monitoring well
BFS_WL_02


RF
Reference / benchmark
THW_RF_01


GN
General / other
MRW_GN_05



If a project requires a different convention, document it in the project README and field notebook.


7.4 Navigating to Existing Waypoints

Load the target waypoint on the GPS receiver or smartphone app.
Use the “Navigate” or “Go To” function. Follow the bearing indicator, checking your surroundings periodically.
When the GPS indicates you are within the reported accuracy of the waypoint, look for physical markers (flagging, rebar, painted rocks) to confirm the exact location.
If the physical marker cannot be found, record a new waypoint at the location you judge to be correct and note the discrepancy in the field notebook.



7.5 Post-Field Data Management

Download waypoints from the GPS receiver to the project computer within 48 hours of returning from the field.
Export waypoints as a .gpx or .csv file and save to the project GitHub repository under data/gps/.
Use the file naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_waypoints.gpx
Verify that waypoint names match the field notebook entries. Correct any discrepancies before committing the file.
Back up the raw GPS file to the lab shared drive.

title: GPS and Site Navigation
text:
8 Quality Control

Compare GPS coordinates against known benchmarks or previously recorded waypoints when revisiting sites. Discrepancies greater than 10 m should be investigated and noted (U.S. Forest Service, 2012).
At least once per semester, verify the GPS receiver against a known benchmark (e.g., a USGS survey marker or campus reference point).
Record the GPS model, serial number, and firmware version in the field notebook at the start of each project.

title: Sample Labeling, Chain of Custody, and Transport
text: This SOP establishes a single, program-wide standard for labeling field samples, completing chain of custody (COC) documentation, and transporting samples from the field to the laboratory (APHA et al., 2012; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2002). Consistent labeling prevents sample mix-ups, and a complete chain of custody ensures that data are legally defensible and scientifically traceable. These procedures apply to all sample types (water, soil, sediment, biological tissue, air filters) collected by the EA Program.

title: Sample Labeling, Chain of Custody, and Transport
text: This SOP establishes a single, program-wide standard for labeling field samples, completing chain of custody (COC) documentation, and transporting samples from the field to the laboratory (APHA et al., 2012; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2002). Consistent labeling prevents sample mix-ups, and a complete chain of custody ensures that data are legally defensible and scientifically traceable. These procedures apply to all sample types (water, soil, sediment, biological tissue, air filters) collected by the EA Program.

title: Sample Labeling, Chain of Custody, and Transport
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All environmental samples collected during EA Program field activities, whether analyzed in-house or submitted to an external laboratory
Does not apply to: Internal laboratory standards and reagents (labeled per SOP-L005); data files and digital records (see SOP-L801)
Location: All EA Program field sites, vehicles, and laboratory receiving areas (SGM 133, 134)

title: Sample Labeling, Chain of Custody, and Transport
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




PI / Project Lead
Approve sample ID scheme for each project; designate receiving personnel


Field Lead

Trained Personnel

title: Sample Labeling, Chain of Custody, and Transport
text:
4 Definitions

Chain of custody (COC): A documented, unbroken record of the collection, transfer, and possession of a sample from the moment of collection through final analysis or disposal; used to demonstrate sample integrity for legal or regulatory purposes (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2002).
Holding time: The maximum elapsed time between sample collection and analysis within which the sample remains chemically stable and analytically valid; analyte- and preservative-specific (e.g., 6 h for E. coli, 28 d for nitrate in H2SO4) (APHA et al., 2012).
Preservative: A chemical added to a sample container (e.g., H2SO4, HNO3, Na2S2O3) to prevent biological or chemical degradation of target analytes during transport and storage (APHA et al., 2012).
QA/QC sample: A blank, duplicate, spike, or other quality-control sample collected alongside field samples to assess contamination, precision, and accuracy; documented on the COC form.
Sample ID: A unique alphanumeric code assigned to a sample at the moment of collection; the primary key linking field records, labels, COC forms, and laboratory data.
Zero headspace: A sample container filled completely with no air gap; required for volatile organic compound (VOC) samples to prevent loss of analytes to the headspace.

title: Sample Labeling, Chain of Custody, and Transport
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Some sample containers include chemical preservatives (sulfuric acid, nitric acid, sodium thiosulfate). Handle pre-preserved bottles with care. Refer to SOP-L003.
Physical: Coolers loaded with ice and sample bottles can be heavy. Use proper lifting technique.
Biological: Soil and water samples may contain pathogens. Wear nitrile gloves when handling samples.




5.1 Required PPE

Nitrile gloves
Safety glasses (when handling preserved bottles)



5.2 Required Training

SOP-F001 Field Safety
SOP-F003 Field Notebook Protocols

title: Sample Labeling, Chain of Custody, and Transport
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sample ID Scheme
The PI or project lead establishes the sample ID scheme before the first field outing. A standard EA Program sample ID has the structure:
[ProjectCode]-[SiteCode]-[YYYYMMDD]-[SampleType]-[Replicate]
Example: SGMC-US1-20260415-GW-A
Record the scheme in the project metadata file and in the field notebook before the first sampling event.


7.2 Labeling Sample Containers

Write the sample ID on the pre-printed label or directly on the container using a waterproof marker.
Include the following minimum fields on every label:

Sample ID
Collection date and time (24 h format)
Collector initials
Matrix (water / soil / sediment / tissue / air filter)
Preservative (if present)

For pre-preserved bottles, verify the preservative type is printed or written on the container before field use.
For biological samples requiring cold preservation, add an ice temperature indicator sticker.



7.3 Completing the COC Form

Start a new COC form for each cooler.
Fill in all header fields: project name, project number, field lead, date, field site.
Enter each sample in the log: sample ID, matrix, collection date and time, preservative, number of containers, and requested analysis.
Include QA/QC samples (field blanks, field duplicates, trip blanks) on the same COC form as the associated samples.
Sign and date the form before departing the field.



7.4 Sample Transport

Place samples in the cooler with sufficient ice to maintain 4 °C.
Separate chemically preserved bottles from unpreserved samples using a zip-lock bag as secondary containment.
Verify the cooler temperature on departure and on arrival using a thermometer; record both readings on the COC form.
Transport samples promptly; do not leave samples in a hot vehicle.



7.5 Receiving Samples in the Laboratory

The receiving person checks the sample count against the COC form.
Verify that the number of containers matches the COC listing; note any discrepancies.
Check sample temperature with a thermometer placed among the bottles and record on the COC form.
Transfer samples to appropriate storage:

Water samples: refrigerator at 4 °C (SOP-L106)
Soil samples: refrigerator at 4 °C (short-term) or freezer (archiving)
Biological samples: freezer at -20 °C or -80 °C as required

Both the field lead and the receiving person sign and date the COC form to document the transfer of custody.
File the signed COC form with the project records.

title: Sample Labeling, Chain of Custody, and Transport
text:
8 Quality Control

The field lead reviews all labels and the COC form before leaving the field site.
Receiving personnel verify sample count, condition, and temperature upon arrival.
Any broken, leaking, or incorrectly labeled samples are flagged on the COC form and reported to the PI within 24 hours.
COC forms are retained for the duration of the project plus a minimum of 5 years.

title: Electrical Power in the Field
text: Electrical power in the field can come from infrastructure sources (such as outdoor or indoor outlets), portable generators, or solar power. This SOP outlines the risks associated with using electricity in the field and develops strategies to mitigate those risks.

title: Electrical Power in the Field
text: Electrical power in the field can come from infrastructure sources (such as outdoor or indoor outlets), portable generators, or solar power. This SOP outlines the risks associated with using electricity in the field and develops strategies to mitigate those risks.

title: Electrical Power in the Field
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Use of portable generators (Honda EU2000i and Ryobi RYi2200A) and extension cords for powering field equipment
Does not apply to: Permanent electrical installations or solar panel systems (to be covered in a future SOP)
Location: All EA Program field sites

title: Electrical Power in the Field
text:
3 Responsibilities



Role
Responsibility




Lab PI
Approve SOP, ensure training compliance


Trained Personnel
Follow this SOP, perform generator maintenance


New Students
Read and understand this SOP before operating generators; complete SOP-F001 Field Safety training

title: Electrical Power in the Field
text:
4 Definitions

Carbon monoxide (CO): A colorless, odorless, tasteless toxic gas produced by incomplete combustion of gasoline and other fuels; displaces oxygen in the bloodstream and is rapidly fatal at elevated concentrations; never operate a generator in any enclosed or semi-enclosed space.
Carburetor: The engine component that mixes air and fuel in the correct ratio for combustion; must be drained before storage of 30 days or more to prevent gum and varnish deposits from clogging fuel passages.
Choke: A valve in the carburetor air intake that restricts airflow to enrich the fuel mixture during cold starts; must be moved to the OPEN or RUN position after the engine warms up to prevent over-fueling.
Eco-throttle: An automatic throttle control (Honda EU2000i) that reduces engine speed when load demand is low, improving fuel economy and reducing noise; must be switched OFF during startup.
Ethanol-free gasoline: Fuel containing no ethanol additive; recommended for small engines because ethanol absorbs water, degrades rubber fuel lines, and causes carburetor deposits during storage.
Fuel stabilizer: A chemical additive mixed into gasoline before storage to prevent oxidation and gum formation; required when the generator will not be used for 30 days or more.
Ground fault: An unintended electrical path between a live conductor and the ground or equipment casing; a leading cause of electrocution; mitigated by using grounded extension cords and GFCI protection.
Grounded extension cord: An extension cord with a three-prong plug that includes a ground conductor; required for all generator connections to provide a safe fault-current return path.
Inverter generator: A generator that produces AC power through an electronic inverter circuit, yielding cleaner, more stable voltage and frequency than a conventional generator; both the Honda EU2000i and Ryobi RYi2200A are inverter generators, making them suitable for powering sensitive electronic field instruments.
Spark arrestor: A fine wire-mesh screen fitted to the exhaust outlet that prevents hot carbon particles from escaping and igniting surrounding combustible material; required by law in many fire-prone areas; must be inspected and cleaned periodically.
Spark plug gap: The distance between the center and ground electrodes of a spark plug; must be within the manufacturer-specified range (0.024–0.028 in for both units) for reliable ignition.

title: Electrical Power in the Field
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Carbon monoxide: Engines emit carbon monoxide. Never use a generator inside an enclosed area (home, garage, crawl space). Fatal fumes can build up even with a fan or open doors and windows. Only operate generators outdoors, away from open windows, vents, or doors.
Fire and explosion: Gasoline and its vapors are extremely flammable. Allow the engine to cool at least 2 minutes before refueling. Always use fresh gasoline. Never operate the generator near combustible materials.
Electrical shock: Generators produce powerful voltage. Never operate under wet conditions and take precautions to protect the generator from rain and snow.
Electrocution / home wiring: Never plug a generator directly into a home outlet. A qualified electrician must install a Power Transfer Switch for any home connection.
Heat from cables: Ensure cables are rated for the current being carried. Never leave cables coiled, as coiled cords can generate excessive heat.




5.1 Required PPE

Closed-toed shoes
Work gloves (when handling hot engine components or refueling)
Hearing protection (if operating near the generator for extended periods)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Use a battery-powered carbon monoxide detector in the area where you are running a generator. If the alarm sounds, move to fresh air immediately and shut down the generator. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety for general field emergency procedures.

title: Electrical Power in the Field
text:
6 Equipment and Materials







Item
Notes




Honda EU2000i generator
Portable inverter generator


Ryobi RYi2200A generator
Portable inverter generator


High-capacity extension cords
Must be grounded type, rated for the application


Spare gas container
Filled with ethanol-free gasoline

Recommended oil type for both generators


Funnel
For adding oil

title: Electrical Power in the Field
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Start Checks

Check oil level. If low, use a funnel to add synthetic 10W-30 oil. This does not need to be done every time; check every few weeks. If the generator shuts off after running for about 30 minutes, low oil is the likely cause.
Check gas level. If low, add ethanol-free gas from the spare container. On the Ryobi, fill to about an inch below the top of the tank. Both generators can be refilled while running. The Ryobi should be refilled after about 4 hours of operation; the Honda after about 6 hours.



7.2 Starting the Honda EU2000i

Turn the fuel tank cap vent (black cap on top of the generator) to the ON position. If this is not done, the generator will shut off after a few minutes.
Make sure the eco-throttle switch (on the side panel, below the fuel cap vent) is OFF.
For a cold start, move the choke (upper left front, near the engine switch) to the CLOSED position (slide the switch to the right).
Turn the engine switch to ON.
Pull the starter grip quickly several times until the engine starts.
Allow the engine a few minutes to warm up, then slowly move the choke to the OPEN position.
To shut down: Turn the engine switch to OFF. After the engine has cooled, turn the fuel tank cap vent to OFF.



7.3 Starting the Ryobi RYi2200A

Make sure the auto idle switch is OFF.
Move the choke to approximately halfway across. The marked cold-start position is slightly less than halfway, but the choke needs to go a bit further; you should feel a slight resistance at the correct position.
Prime the system by slowly pulling the starter grip several times.
Pull the grip quickly until the engine runs.
Allow the engine to run for 15–30 seconds, then move the choke all the way across to the RUN position.
To shut down: Switch the choke back to the OFF position.



7.4 Storage
If you do not plan to use the generator within 30 days, add fuel stabilizer to the gas and drain the carburetor.


7.5 Extension Cord Safety

Use only grounded extension cords rated for the intended application.
Always uncoil cords completely and lay them flat in open locations; coiled cords can generate excessive heat.

title: Electrical Power in the Field
text:
8 Maintenance

8.1 General (Both Units)
Keep generators in a clean, dry environment, not exposed to dust, dirt, moisture, or corrosive vapors. To clean, use a soft-bristle brush and/or vacuum cleaner to loosen and remove dirt and debris. Clean air vents with air pressure no more than 25 psi. Wipe exterior surfaces with a damp cloth. Perform maintenance more frequently when the generator is used in dusty areas. If you notice a power loss, the exhaust port and muffler may be blocked with carbon deposits; allow only qualified service technicians to clean these.


8.2 Ryobi RYi2200A Maintenance Schedule








Item
Frequency
Notes




Air filter
Check before each use; clean every 3 months or 50 hours; replace every year or 300 hours
Wash with soapy water, rinse, squeeze dry


Engine lubricant
Check before each use; change after first 20 hours, then every 6 months or 100 hours
Drain while warm for faster flow


Spark plug
Check every 6 months or 100 hours; replace every year or 300 hours
Gap: 0.024–0.028 in (0.60–0.70 mm)


Spark arrestor
Clean periodically
Wire brush; inspect screen for damage


Fuel tank / carburetor
Check fuel hose before each use; inspect fuel filter before each use; have tank and filter cleaned by qualified service center every 6 months or 100 hours
Drain both before storage to prevent gum deposits


Valve clearance
Check every year or 300 hours
Service by qualified technician





8.3 Honda EU2000i Maintenance Schedule








Item
Frequency

text: This SOP describes the specifications, assembly, maintenance, and ordering of replacement parts for the Price Pygmy and Price Type AA mechanical current meters used by the EA Program. These vertical-axis cup-type meters convert water velocity into rotational counts and are the standard instruments for measuring point velocities during stream discharge measurements (Rantz et al., 1982) (see also SOP-F301 Stream Discharge Measurement).

text: This SOP describes the specifications, assembly, maintenance, and ordering of replacement parts for the Price Pygmy and Price Type AA mechanical current meters used by the EA Program. These vertical-axis cup-type meters convert water velocity into rotational counts and are the standard instruments for measuring point velocities during stream discharge measurements (Rantz et al., 1982) (see also SOP-F301 Stream Discharge Measurement).

Does not apply to: Electronic velocity meters (e.g., Marsh-McBirney, FlowTracker ADV), propeller-type meters (e.g., Ott), or acoustic Doppler instruments

title: Pygmy and Type AA Velocity Meters
text:
4 Definitions

AquaCalc: A digital flow computer that counts current meter revolutions electronically and converts them to velocity automatically using the stored rating table; eliminates manual timing and reduces transcription error.
Cat-whisker contact: A spring-wire contact element in the Type AA meter’s contact chamber; makes electrical contact with a solder bead on the shaft once per revolution (single-revolution contact) or once per five revolutions (penta contact); must be checked for wear and proper contact force before each field season (Rantz et al., 1982).
Contact chamber: The sealed housing on the Type AA meter that contains the electrical contact mechanism (cat-whisker wire and solder bead, or magnetic head); connects to the cable leading to the headset or digital counter.
Penta contact: A gear-reduction contact in the Type AA meter that closes the circuit once every five bucket-wheel revolutions; used at high velocities to reduce the counting rate to a manageable level; not available on the Pygmy meter (Rantz et al., 1982).
Pivot: The tungsten carbide tip at the bottom of the current meter shaft; rides in a hardened bearing cup; the single most wear-sensitive part of a mechanical current meter; must be inspected for burrs, flat spots, and magnetization before each field season (Rantz et al., 1982; U.S. Geological Survey, Office of Surface Water, 2002).
Price Pygmy current meter: A vertical-axis cup-type current meter with a 2-inch (5.1 cm) diameter bucket wheel; designed for shallow streams (depth ≤ 1.0 ft); wading rod suspension only; rated for velocities of 0.1–4.9 ft/s (Rantz et al., 1982).
Price Type AA current meter: The standard USGS vertical-axis cup-type current meter with a 5-inch (12.7 cm) diameter bucket wheel; rated for velocities of 0.1–25 ft/s; can be suspended from a wading rod or cable (Rantz et al., 1982).
Rating table: A lookup table, supplied with each meter by the manufacturer and approved by the USGS, that converts bucket-wheel revolutions per second to velocity in ft/s or m/s; laminated copies must be kept in each meter’s carrying case (Rantz et al., 1982).
Raising nut: The nut that controls the vertical position of the shaft and pivot within the yoke; must be tightened to the correct end-play setting (~0.001 in) for accurate measurements; never loosen by holding the nut and spinning the bucket wheel.
Spin test: A field quality control check in which the bucket wheel is given a sharp spin by hand and the time for it to stop is measured; a proxy for bearing condition; minimum acceptable spin times are 40 s (Type AA) and 24 s (Pygmy) at room temperature (Rantz et al., 1982).
Wading rod (top-setting): A graduated aluminum rod used to position the current meter at a known depth fraction (0.6 or 0.2/0.8 of total depth) below the water surface; the depth-setting mechanism is located on the handle, enabling depth changes without removing the meter from the water.

6.1 Price Type AA Current Meter
The Type AA is the standard USGS Price-type current meter for general streamflow measurement (Rantz et al., 1982). The bucket wheel has six conical cups (12.7 cm diameter) rotating on a vertical axis inside a brass yoke. Tungsten carbide bearings are seated in deeply recessed inverted cups that trap air and exclude water and silt. A tailpiece assembly aligns the meter with the current when suspended by cable.

title: Pygmy and Type AA Velocity Meters
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Assembly
Type AA on a wading rod:

Remove the tailpiece assembly (used for cable suspension only).
Slide the meter yoke onto the wading rod and secure with the thumbscrew.
Connect the electrical cable from the binding posts on the contact chamber to the AquaCalc or headset.
For penta contact, connect to the penta binding post; for single-revolution counting, use the single-revolution binding post.

Pygmy on a wading rod:

Slide the pygmy yoke directly onto the wading rod and secure with the thumbscrew.
Connect the electrical cable to the binding post. The Pygmy has only a single-revolution contact.



8.2 Pre-Field Spin Test
Perform a spin test before every field outing (Rantz et al., 1982). Conduct with the meter level, shaft vertical, in a location with no air currents.

Hold the meter steady and use your finger or a pencil to give the bucket wheel a sharp, single spin.
Immediately start a stopwatch.
Stop the stopwatch when the wheel completely stops rotating.
Record the spin time in the field notebook.

Minimum acceptable spin times (Rantz et al., 1982):



Meter
Minimum Spin Time
Optimum Spin Time




Type AA
40 s
60–120 s


Pygmy
24 s
40–80 s



If the spin time falls below the minimum, clean and oil the pivot before proceeding (§7.3). If the spin time remains low after cleaning and oiling, replace the pivot.


8.3 Cleaning and Oiling (Pre-Season and As Needed)

Inspect the pivot. Remove the raising nut and carefully withdraw the shaft. Examine the pivot tip under a magnifying glass. A good pivot is highly polished, with no flat spots, pits, or scratches. Replace a damaged pivot immediately.
Check for magnetization. Hold the pivot near a paper clip. If the clip is attracted to the pivot, the pivot is magnetized and will cause erroneously high velocity readings. Demagnetize using a bulk magnetic tape eraser.
Oil the bearings. Apply one small drop of instrument oil to the upper shaft bearing and one drop to the pivot. Do not over-oil; excess oil attracts grit.
Inspect the bucket wheel. Spin the wheel slowly and watch for wobble. If the upper hub wobbles more than the lower, the shaft is bent and must be replaced.
Inspect the contact chamber. For cat-whisker contacts, check that the wire makes clean contact with the solder bead on each revolution. For magnetic-head contacts, verify the counter registers properly during the spin test.







WarningRaising Nut Caution



Never loosen the raising nut by holding the nut and spinning the bucket wheel. This will bend the shaft. Always hold the bucket wheel still and unscrew the nut (U.S. Geological Survey, Office of Surface Water, 2002).




8.4 Annual Maintenance

Disassemble the meter completely: remove bucket wheel, shaft, and pivot.
Clean all parts with a lint-free cloth dampened with instrument oil.
Inspect the shaft for straightness by rolling on a flat surface.
Replace worn or damaged parts.
Reassemble and adjust the pivot per the manufacturer’s instructions.
Perform a spin test to verify performance.
Record maintenance date, parts replaced, and spin test results in the instrument log (U.S. Geological Survey, Office of Surface Water, 2002).



8.5 Pivot Adjustment

Hold the meter inverted with the pivot pointing up.
Release the keeper screw and unscrew the pivot-adjusting nut a few turns.
Advance the pivot-adjusting nut until it touches the yoke.
Set end play to approximately 0.001 in – the shaft should have just barely perceptible vertical play detectable by feel.
Tighten the keeper screw to lock the adjustment.



8.6 Storage

Store meters in their waterproof carrying cases.
Loosen the raising nut to relieve pressure on the pivot.
Ensure meters are clean and lightly oiled.
Store in a dry location away from dust and vibration.
If a meter will not be used for more than 3 months, remove the bucket wheel assembly and store separately.

text:
9 Rating Tables
Each meter ships with a USGS-approved standard rating table that converts bucket-wheel revolutions per second to velocity in ft/s or m/s (Rantz et al., 1982; Turnipseed & Sauer, 2010). Keep a laminated copy in each meter’s carrying case and a digital copy on the lab shared drive.

Type AA rating table: https://prph2o.com/usgs-type-aa-current-meter/
Pygmy rating table: https://prph2o.com/usgs-pygmy-current-meter/

USGS studies have found that approximately 35% of Type AA meters and 20% of Pygmy meters in routine field use fail to meet standard rating criteria, typically because of worn pivots, bent shafts, or damaged contacts (Rantz et al., 1982). The spin test (§7.2) is the primary field check.

title: HOBO Water Level Pressure Transducers
text: This SOP describes the deployment, data retrieval, and barometric compensation of Onset HOBO water level loggers for continuous monitoring of water surface elevation in streams, lakes, wetlands, and groundwater wells (Freeman et al., 2004; Onset Computer Corporation, 2020). Continuous stage records are essential for developing stage-discharge rating curves, characterizing hydrologic response to storms, and documenting seasonal water table fluctuations.

title: HOBO Water Level Pressure Transducers
text: This SOP describes the deployment, data retrieval, and barometric compensation of Onset HOBO water level loggers for continuous monitoring of water surface elevation in streams, lakes, wetlands, and groundwater wells (Freeman et al., 2004; Onset Computer Corporation, 2020). title: HOBO Water Level Pressure Transducers
text:
4 Definitions

Absolute pressure: Pressure measured relative to a perfect vacuum; the HOBO U20L measures absolute pressure (water column plus atmospheric), which must be compensated to isolate water-column pressure (Freeman et al., 2004).
Barometric compensation: Post-processing step in HOBOware that subtracts a concurrent barometric pressure record (from a reference logger deployed in air) from the absolute pressure record to yield true water depth (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021).
Datum: A fixed reference elevation (e.g., NAVD88, local benchmark) to which stage measurements are referenced.
Deployment depth: The vertical distance from the water surface to the sensor face at the time of deployment; used as the initial reference for water-level calculations.
HOBO U20L: Onset Computer Corporation submersible water-level logger recording absolute pressure and temperature at user-defined intervals; rated to a maximum depth of 9 m (model U20L-01) or 4 m (model U20L-04 barometric) (Onset Computer Corporation, 2020).
HOBOconnect / HOBOware: Onset software (mobile app and desktop, respectively) used to program loggers, download data, apply barometric compensation, and export time-series data (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021).
Stage: Water-surface elevation at a monitoring location, expressed relative to a datum; the primary hydrologic quantity derived from pressure transducer records.
Stage-discharge rating curve: An empirical relationship between stream stage and discharge (Q) at a gauging cross-section; enables conversion of continuous stage records into continuous discharge records (Freeman et al., 2004).
Stilling well: A perforated pipe anchored in the stream or lake bed that protects the logger from direct current, debris, and disturbance while allowing free water exchange.

title: HOBO Water Level Pressure Transducers
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Deployment sites may involve steep banks, slippery surfaces, swift water, or confined spaces (well casings). Work in pairs at all stream and well sites.
Drowning: Do not deploy loggers during high-flow events. Never wade in flows deeper than waist height.
Biological: Waterborne pathogens; ticks and snakes in riparian areas.




5.1 Required PPE

Wading boots or chest waders (stream deployments)
Closed-toed shoes (well deployments)
Nitrile gloves
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)



5.2 Required Training

SOP-F001 Field Safety
Work with a trained partner for all in-stream deployments

title: HOBO Water Level Pressure Transducers
text:
9 Procedure

9.1 Logger Programming

Connect the logger to HOBOware using the optical USB coupler or open HOBOconnect via Bluetooth.
Select Launch (HOBOware) or Configure (HOBOconnect).
Set the logging interval appropriate to the project (5 min is typical for hydrologic studies; 15 min for long-term deployment).
Enable a delayed start if synchronizing with another logger at the site.
Record the logger serial number, launch time, and interval in the field notebook and in the deployment spreadsheet.



9.2 Stream Deployment (Stilling Well)

Choose a stable bank location away from direct turbulence but representative of the cross-section stage.
Install the stilling well (2-inch PVC with perforations) vertically with the bottom anchored and the top above expected high-water level. Ensure the perforations face upstream and downstream.
Lower the logger into the stilling well and secure it with stainless steel wire or cable tie. The logger should hang freely.
Record the deployment elevation:

Distance from the top of the stilling well to the water surface and to the logger sensor
Staff gauge reading (if installed)
GPS coordinates per SOP-F006

Deploy the barometric reference logger nearby, above the high-water line, in a shaded and ventilated location (e.g., inside a radiation shield attached to a tree or post). Do not seal it in an airtight container.
Photograph the deployment.



9.3 Well Deployment

Remove the well cap and measure depth to water using an e-tape. Record the measurement.
Lower the logger into the well on stainless steel cable or braided fishing line. Position below the lowest expected water level but above the well screen bottom.
Secure the suspension cable to the well cap or casing.
Record the logger depth below the top of casing (TOC) and the TOC elevation if surveyed.
Replace the well cap.
Deploy the barometric reference logger at the wellhead or nearby.



9.4 Data Retrieval
Retrieve data at intervals appropriate for the project (typically monthly or quarterly).
U20L (optical coupler):

Remove the logger from the stilling well.
Attach the optical USB coupler and connect to the laptop.
In HOBOware, select Readout. The logger continues recording after readout.
Return the logger to its deployment position.

MX2001 (Bluetooth):

Open the HOBOconnect app on a smartphone within ~30 m line of sight.
Select the logger and tap Readout.
The logger does not need to be removed from the water.



9.5 Barometric Compensation

In HOBOware, open the water level logger file and the barometric reference logger file.
Select Data Assistant > Barometric Compensation.
Specify the reference water level: enter a staff gauge reading or a known water surface elevation at a specific date and time.
HOBOware subtracts the barometric pressure from the absolute pressure to yield the water column height.
Export the compensated data as .csv.
Save using the convention: YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_waterlevel_compensated.csv.
Commit data to the project repository per SOP-L801.

title: HOBO Water Level Pressure Transducers
text:
10 Quality Control

Verify that the barometric logger file overlaps the full duration of the water level record. Gaps in barometric data prevent compensation.
Compare the compensated stage at the download visit against a simultaneous staff gauge reading. Acceptable agreement is within 1 cm.
Flag and investigate any sudden offsets or drift in the compensated record (may indicate logger movement, sedimentation, or battery failure).

title: HOBO Water Level Pressure Transducers
text:
11 Data Management

Save all raw logger files (.hobo) to data/raw/loggers/ in the project repository.
Save compensated .csv files to data/processed/stage/.
Commit all files per SOP-L801.

title: Handheld Turbidity Meter
text: This SOP describes the calibration, operation, and maintenance of handheld nephelometric turbidity meters for field measurement of water clarity. Turbidity is a standard water quality parameter required by the Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP), NPDES permits, and many ecological studies (APHA et al., 2012). Field measurements complement laboratory analysis by providing an immediate on-site result.

title: Handheld Turbidity Meter
text: This SOP describes the calibration, operation, and maintenance of handheld nephelometric turbidity meters for field measurement of water clarity. Turbidity is a standard water quality parameter required by the Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP), NPDES permits, and many ecological studies (APHA et al., 2012). Field measurements complement laboratory analysis by providing an immediate on-site result.

text:

Does not apply to: Laboratory bench-top turbidimeters; Secchi disk transparency measurements (see SOP-F207); continuous turbidity sensors on multiparameter sondes (see SOP-F200)

title: Handheld Turbidity Meter
text:
4 Definitions

Formazin: A synthetic polymer suspension used as the primary turbidity calibration standard; traceable to NIST; typically supplied as a 4000 NTU stock that is diluted to working standards; contains hydrazine and must be handled as hazardous waste (APHA et al., 2012).
Nephelometric turbidity: Turbidity measured by the intensity of light scattered at 90° to an incident beam; the standard method per APHA Method 2130B; appropriate for samples with NTU < 40; for higher values a ratio or attenuation mode may be used (APHA et al., 2012).
NTU (Nephelometric Turbidity Units): The unit of turbidity measured by a 90° nephelometer; numerically equivalent to FNU (Formazin Nephelometric Units) and approximately equivalent to FAU (Formazin Attenuation Units) at low concentrations (APHA et al., 2012).
RPD (relative percent difference): |A - B| / ((A + B) / 2) × 100; used to assess duplicate precision; acceptance criterion for field turbidity duplicates is RPD < 20% for readings above 10 NTU.
Silicone oil treatment: Application of a thin film of silicone oil to the outside of a glass sample vial before measurement to fill surface scratches and reduce spurious light scattering; standard practice for glass vial meters (Hach Company, 2022).
StablCal: A sealed formazin-based calibration standard supplied by Hach; stable and ready to use without dilution; available in < 0.1, 20, 100, and 800 NTU vials.

title: Handheld Turbidity Meter
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Sampling near water involves slip and fall hazards.
Biological: Water samples may contain pathogens. Wear gloves.
Chemical: Formazin calibration standards contain hydrazine, a suspected carcinogen. Handle with gloves; dispose of as hazardous waste. StablCal sealed standards eliminate direct hydrazine exposure.




5.1 Required PPE

Nitrile gloves
Safety glasses (during calibration with bulk formazin)
Closed-toed shoes or wading boots



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety. For formazin contact with skin or eyes, flush with water for at least 15 minutes and consult the SDS.

title: Handheld Turbidity Meter
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Calibration
Calibrate at the start of each field day or after storage of more than one week (APHA et al., 2012).

Turn on the meter and allow it to warm up (approximately 1 minute).
Clean calibration vial exteriors with a lint-free wipe. Apply a thin, even film of silicone oil for glass vials.
Insert the lowest standard (< 0.1 NTU) into the sample chamber with the orientation mark aligned. Close the lid.
Press Cal and follow the on-screen prompts to read the standard.
Repeat with each subsequent standard in ascending order (e.g., 20, 100, 800 NTU).
When all standards have been read, the meter confirms a successful calibration. Record the date, standard lot number, and any correction factors in the field notebook.
Verify calibration by re-reading the 20 NTU standard; the reading must be within ±10% of 20 NTU. If not, repeat the full calibration.



7.2 Sample Collection

Collect a grab sample per SOP-F300 Surface Water Sampling.
Avoid disturbing bottom sediments during collection.
Analyze as soon as possible; if delayed, keep the sample in the dark and analyze within 24 hours.



7.3 Measurement

Gently invert the sample container 3–4 times to resuspend particles uniformly. Do not shake vigorously (creates air bubbles).
Pour the sample into a clean sample vial to the fill line.
Cap and let sit for 1 minute to allow large air bubbles to rise.
Wipe the outside of the vial with a lint-free cloth. Apply silicone oil for glass vials.
Insert the vial with the orientation mark aligned. Close the lid.
Press Read and wait for the display to stabilize.
Record the result (NTU), sample ID, time, and site in the field notebook.
For samples above the meter range (typically > 1000 NTU), dilute with DI water, measure, and multiply by the dilution factor. Record both the diluted reading and the corrected result.
Rinse the vial three times with DI water between samples.



7.4 Post-Field Care

Rinse all sample vials with DI water; air-dry inverted.
Wipe silicone oil residue from vials before storage.
Store calibration standards in their original case, away from direct sunlight, at room temperature.
Turn off the meter; remove batteries if storing for more than one month.

title: Handheld Turbidity Meter
text:
8 Quality Control

Calibrate at the start of each field day (§6.1) (APHA et al., 2012).
Measure a DI water blank at the start and end of each sampling event; the blank must read < 1 NTU.
Measure one field duplicate per 10 samples (minimum one per event); duplicate RPD must be < 20% for readings above 10 NTU.
If the DI blank drifts above 1 NTU during the day, recalibrate and re-measure the most recent samples.
Inspect sample vials for scratches before each use; scratches scatter light and produce false-high readings.

title: Portable Spectrophotometer / Colorimeter (Field Use)
text:
This SOP describes the field operation of the Hach DR900 portable colorimeter for on-site water quality analysis (Hach Company, 2024a, 2024b). The DR900 enables rapid, field-based measurement of nutrients, metals, and other parameters using Hach pre-packaged reagent kits. Field colorimetry provides same-day results when samples cannot be transported to the lab within required hold times and supports real-time decisions during stormwater events, spill response, or reconnaissance sampling (APHA et al., 2012).
This SOP focuses on field-specific procedures (transport, outdoor operation, field QC). For detailed method chemistry, reagent handling, the Method Registry, and laboratory use of the DR3900 and DR900, see SOP-L303 Hach Colorimetric Analysis.
