title: Portable Spectrophotometer / Colorimeter (Field Use)
text:
4 Definitions

Beer-Lambert law: The linear relationship between the absorbance of a solution and the concentration of the absorbing analyte, expressed as \(A = \varepsilon c l\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the molar absorptivity, \(c\) is concentration, and \(l\) is path length; the physical basis of colorimetric analysis (APHA et al., 2012).
Blank (reagent blank / DI blank): A deionized water sample carried through the complete analytical procedure; used to zero the instrument and establish the baseline absorbance of the reagent system; must read at or near zero before sample measurements begin.
Detection limit (MDL): The minimum concentration reliably distinguishable from the blank; Hach method-specific MDLs are listed in the Method Registry in SOP-L303 (Hach Company, 2024b).
Field duplicate: A second independent measurement of the same sample, prepared through the full analytical procedure, to assess precision; RPD must be < 20% for concentrations above 5 times the detection limit.
Reaction time: The incubation period specified in the Hach method protocol after reagent addition during which the color-forming reaction proceeds to completion; reading before reaction time has elapsed gives systematically low results (Hach Company, 2024a).
RPD (relative percent difference): |A - B| / ((A + B) / 2) × 100; used to assess duplicate precision.
Stored program: A factory-programmed method on the DR900 that specifies wavelength, calibration curve, and units for a specific Hach reagent kit; accessed by program number on the instrument (Hach Company, 2024a).
Zeroing: The process of inserting a DI water blank into the DR900 sample chamber and pressing Zero to set the baseline absorbance to zero for the selected program; required before reading samples.

title: Portable Spectrophotometer / Colorimeter (Field Use)
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Chemical: Hach reagent powder pillows and liquid reagents may contain acids, oxidizers, or heavy metal indicators. Review the SDS for each kit before field use. Cadmium-containing reagents (older NitraVer 5 formulation) are hazardous waste.
Physical: Glass sample vials can break during transport; pack in padded cases.
Biological: Water samples may contain pathogens. Wear gloves.




5.1 Required PPE

5.2 Emergency Procedures
For reagent splashes to skin or eyes, flush with clean water for at least 15 minutes. Carry a squeeze bottle of DI water for emergency rinsing. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety and SOP-L003 Hazardous Materials Handling.

title: Portable Spectrophotometer / Colorimeter (Field Use)
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Field Preparation

Identify the analytes to be measured; pack the corresponding reagent kits and verify none are expired.
Pack at least 500 mL DI water and two extra clean sample vials per method.
Charge the DR900 battery and confirm stored programs for your methods are accessible (Hach Company, 2024a).
Print or photograph method procedure cards for each analyte (from the kit box or SOP-L303 Method Registry).



7.2 Field Setup

Place the DR900 on a flat, stable surface out of direct sunlight. Direct sunlight on the sample chamber causes erroneous readings.
If no shade is available, shade the instrument with a jacket or tarp during each reading.
Turn on the DR900 and allow it to complete its self-check.
Select the stored program for your analyte.



7.3 Blank and Calibration Check

Fill a clean sample vial with DI water to the fill line.
Wipe the vial exterior with a lint-free cloth.
Insert the vial, close the lid, and press Zero.
The display should read 0.00 (within the method detection limit); if not, clean the vial and re-zero.
If a known mid-range standard is available, read it immediately after zeroing; the result must be within ±10% of the stated value. Record the result in the field notebook (Hach Company, 2024b).



7.4 Sample Analysis
Follow the method-specific procedure from the reagent kit or SOP-L303 Method Registry:

Collect a grab sample per SOP-F300.
Fill the sample vial to the fill line with sample.
Add the reagent per method instructions.
Cap, invert, and mix as directed. Start the timer for the required reaction time.
When the reaction time is complete, wipe the vial exterior (apply silicone oil for round vials).
Insert the vial into the DR900, close the lid (shield from sunlight), and press Read.
Record the result, analyte, Hach method number, sample ID, units, date, and time in the field notebook.
Rinse the vial three times with DI water before the next sample.



7.5 Waste Management

Collect all used reagent packets, vials, and waste solution in a sealable container.
Do not discard reagent waste in the field.
Return waste to the lab and dispose of per SOP-L003.

title: Portable Spectrophotometer / Colorimeter (Field Use)
text:
8 Quality Control

Zero the instrument with DI water before each batch of samples.
Run one DI blank and one mid-range standard at the start of each field session; record results in the field notebook (Hach Company, 2024b).
Analyze one field duplicate per 10 samples (minimum one per event); RPD must be < 20% for concentrations above 5 × the detection limit.
If the field blank reads above the MDL, investigate contamination (dirty vials, contaminated DI water) and re-run.
Note ambient temperature; some Hach methods are temperature-sensitive. If the sample is outside the method-specified range (typically 20–25 °C), note the potential bias (Hach Company, 2024a).

title: Surface Water Sampling
text: This SOP describes procedures for the manual collection, preservation, and handling of surface water samples. Representative samples are required for defensible water quality data (APHA et al., 2012; US Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, 2014).

title: Surface Water Sampling
text: This SOP describes procedures for the manual collection, preservation, and handling of surface water samples. Representative samples are required for defensible water quality data (APHA et al., 2012; US Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, 2014).

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Manual collection of surface water samples from streams, rivers, lakes, ponds, lagoons, surface impoundments, wastewater access points, and outfalls
Does not apply to: Automated sampling devices, pelagic marine sampling, or groundwater sampling
Location: All EA Program surface water field sites

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




Lab PI
Approve sampling plan, ensure training compliance


Field Lead

Trained Personnel

New Students

3.1 Required Training

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
4 Definitions

Bailer: A cylindrical sampling device lowered on a line to collect water at a specific depth; commonly used in wells and deep water; can be disposable (polyethylene) or reusable (stainless steel).
Bottle blank: A sample container filled with laboratory-pure water, preserved identically to field samples, and submitted to the laboratory as a QC sample to detect contamination from the container or washing process (APHA et al., 2012).
Chain of custody (COC): A legal record of sample possession at every transfer point from collection to analysis; must accompany all samples; see SOP-F008 for the full procedure (US Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, 2014).
Discrete-depth sampler: A device (Van Dorn, Kemmerer bottle) that collects a water sample from a specific depth without mixing with overlying or underlying water; tripped by a messenger weight.
Equipment blank: Laboratory-pure water poured through or into sampling equipment in the field, collected and analyzed as a QC sample to verify equipment cleanliness.
Field duplicate: A second sample collected at the same time and location as a primary sample and submitted blind to the laboratory; used to assess field and laboratory precision.
Grab sample: A single-point, instantaneous water sample collected at one time and place; represents conditions at that moment only; the simplest and most common field collection method (APHA et al., 2012).
Holding time: The maximum elapsed time between sample collection and analysis within which the sample remains analytically valid; analyte- and preservative-specific (e.g., 6 h for E. coli, 28 d for nitrate preserved with H2SO4) (APHA et al., 2012).
Peristaltic pump: A battery-operated field sampling pump that moves sample water through disposable tubing by compressing the tube with rollers; used to collect samples from depths or locations inaccessible by hand.
Preservative: A chemical added to a sample container to retard biological or chemical degradation of target analytes during transport and storage (e.g., H2SO4 for nutrients, HNO3 for metals, Na2S2O3 for chlorine) (APHA et al., 2012).
Sampler blank: Laboratory-pure water passed through or into a sampling device (bailer, peristaltic pump) and submitted as a QC sample to verify the device is clean.
Zero headspace: A sample container filled completely with no air gap; required for volatile organic compound (VOC) samples to prevent analyte loss to the headspace.

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Biological/Chemical: Water bodies may be contaminated; avoid ingestion and direct skin contact.
Physical: Drowning risk, slippery surfaces, swift currents, unstable banks, and bridge traffic.
Chemical: Sample preservatives (H2SO4, HNO3, NaOH) in pre-preserved bottles are corrosive.




5.1 Required PPE

Latex or nitrile gloves
Leather gloves (for handling ropes and cables)
Antibacterial hand sanitizer or soap
Personal flotation device (PFD) when sampling from boats or in deep/swift water
Safety vest and lines (as appropriate for the site)
Traffic control signs and cones (for bridge sampling)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety for emergency response procedures, including medical emergencies near water.

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
6 Summary of Collection Methods
Sampling situations vary widely and no universal procedure applies. Representative samples from most surface waters can be collected by one or more of the following:

Bailers
Dip samplers
Direct method (hand collection)
Discrete depth samplers (Kemmerer or Van Dorn bottles)
Peristaltic pumps
Stormwater collection devices

(APHA et al., 2012; US Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, 2014)

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
8 Interferences and Contamination Prevention






ImportantCritical



The inner surfaces of sample bottles and caps must not be touched with bare hands, gloves, or any other material. Keep sample bottles in a clean environment away from dust, dirt, fumes, and vehicle exhaust (APHA et al., 2012).



Collect samples upstream of your position and upstream of any sampling-related disturbance.
Sample away from areas influenced by tributaries, outfalls, or other point sources unless those features are the target.
Change gloves between sample sites to prevent cross-contamination.

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
9 Procedure

9.1 Field Collection – Direct Method (Grab Sample)

Remove the stopper or lid from the container just before sampling.
Do not contaminate the cap, neck, or inside of the bottle.
If no preservative is present: Face upstream in flowing water (or upwind in still water). Hold the container near its base, reach out in front of your body, and plunge it mouth-down below the surface to approximately mid-water column.
If the water is too shallow for this technique (risk of disturbing sediment), collect a surface water sample and note the change of method in the field notebook.
Fill the bottle to the appropriate level for the target analyte.
Leave a small headspace for mixing, except for volatile organics and alkalinity samples (no headspace).



9.2 Field Collection – Extension Pole

Securely attach the sample container (lid in place) to the pole holder using clamps.
Remove the lid carefully to avoid contamination.
Follow the direct method procedure above.
Do not use this method for pre-preserved containers; use intermediate devices instead.



9.3 Field Collection – Pre-Preserved Containers

Hold the container upright.
Place the lid over the mouth to create a small opening.
Submerge and fill carefully to avoid spilling or diluting the preservative.



9.4 Field Collection – Intermediate Devices
For samples collected via Van Dorn, Kemmerer, bailer, or peristaltic pump, follow the device operating instructions (see SOP-F202 for pump procedures). Transfer collected water to appropriate labeled sample containers promptly (US Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, 2014).






TipSampler Blanks



Prepare periodic sampler blanks by pouring ultrapure distilled water through or into the sampler and submitting for laboratory analysis to verify cleanliness (APHA et al., 2012).

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
10 Sample Preservation, Handling, and Storage
Once samples are collected:

Transfer samples to correctly labeled containers.
Preserve immediately, or verify that pre-preserved bottles were used (see holding-time requirements, Table 9.1 in APHA et al. (2012)).
Record all pertinent data in the field notebook and on the COC form.
Attach custody seals to the cooler before transport.
Decontaminate all sampling equipment before collecting additional samples (see SOP-F007).







Important



Samples must never stand in the sun. Store on ice in coolers immediately after collection and ship to the laboratory without delay (US Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, 2014).

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
11 Quality Control

11.1 Bottle Blanks
Before each field trip, select one sample bottle per ten of each container type, fill with ultrapure distilled water, preserve identically to field samples, and submit for analysis as a “bottle blank” (APHA et al., 2012).


11.2 Field Duplicates
Collect one field duplicate per 10 samples (minimum one per event). Duplicates are collected from the same location at the same time and submitted blind to the laboratory.


11.3 Equipment Blanks
When non-dedicated sampling equipment is used, collect an equipment blank (ultrapure distilled water through the equipment) and submit for analysis.


11.4 Documentation

Complete the COC form before samples leave the field.
Record all deviations from this SOP in the field notebook.
Photograph site conditions at each sampling location.

title: Stormwater Sampling
text:
This SOP describes procedures for collecting stormwater runoff samples from urban and peri-urban watersheds during wet-weather events. Storm runoff is a primary pathway by which sediments, nutrients, metals, bacteria, and other pollutants enter receiving waters. Characterizing stormwater quality is essential for assessing nonpoint source pollution, evaluating the effectiveness of best management practices (BMPs), and supporting compliance with National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) permit requirements (APHA et al., 2012; California State Water Resources Control Board, 2018).
The procedures described here are consistent with the California State Water Resources Control Board’s Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP) guidance and the State Water Board’s Stormwater Sampling Guidance Document for construction and industrial general permits.

title: Stormwater Sampling
text:
This SOP describes procedures for collecting stormwater runoff samples from urban and peri-urban watersheds during wet-weather events. Storm runoff is a primary pathway by which sediments, nutrients, metals, bacteria, and other pollutants enter receiving waters. Characterizing stormwater quality is essential for assessing nonpoint source pollution, evaluating the effectiveness of best management practices (BMPs), and supporting compliance with National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) permit requirements (APHA et al., 2012; California State Water Resources Control Board, 2018).
The procedures described here are consistent with the California State Water Resources Control Board’s Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP) guidance and the State Water Board’s Stormwater Sampling Guidance Document for construction and industrial general permits.

title: Stormwater Sampling
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Manual grab and time-composite sampling of stormwater runoff from outfalls, storm drains, open channels, sheet flow, and receiving streams during and immediately following precipitation events
Does not apply to: Dry-weather urban runoff (use SOP-F300 Surface Water Sampling); automated composite sampling with programmed autosamplers (requires a separate instrument-specific SOP); industrial facility compliance sampling governed by site-specific SWPPPs
Location: All EA Program stormwater monitoring sites in the greater Los Angeles basin and Inland Empire watersheds

title: Stormwater Sampling
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




PI / Project Lead
Approve sampling plan and storm-event criteria


Field Lead
Monitor weather forecasts, mobilize crew, verify equipment


Trained Personnel
Collect and handle samples per this SOP


New Students
Complete training before participating in storm sampling

title: Stormwater Sampling
text:
4 Definitions

Antecedent dry period: The number of consecutive dry days before a storm event; typically a minimum of 72 hours is required for a storm to qualify as an independent event that will produce a representative first flush; shorter antecedent periods may indicate ongoing, non-independent runoff (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2018).
BMP (best management practice): A structural or operational practice designed to reduce the volume or concentration of pollutants in stormwater runoff; includes detention basins, bioswales, permeable pavement, inlet filters, and street sweeping.
Event mean concentration (EMC): The flow-weighted average concentration of an analyte across the entire storm event; calculated as total analyte load divided by total event runoff volume; the standard metric for characterizing stormwater quality and comparing across sites and storms (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2002).
First flush: The initial pulse of stormwater runoff, which typically carries a disproportionately high load of accumulated pollutants relative to later portions of the storm; occurs most prominently in highly impervious urban catchments.
Flow-weighted composite sample: A sample assembled by combining aliquots that are proportional to instantaneous flow rate at each collection interval; produces a sample whose concentration approximates the event mean concentration (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2018).
MS4 (Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System): A conveyance system owned and operated by a municipality that is designed to collect and convey stormwater separately from sanitary sewage; regulated under NPDES permits.
NPDES (National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System): The federal permit program under the Clean Water Act that regulates point-source discharges of pollutants, including stormwater from MS4s, construction sites, and industrial facilities.
Outfall: A pipe, channel, or other structure through which stormwater is discharged to a receiving water body; a standard sampling location for MS4 compliance monitoring.
SWPPP (Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan): A site-specific plan required for construction sites and certain industrial facilities under NPDES permits; documents BMPs, monitoring requirements, and inspection schedules.
Time-composite sample: A sample assembled by combining equal aliquots collected at fixed time intervals throughout the storm event; simpler than flow-weighted compositing but does not account for flow variability.

title: Stormwater Sampling
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Drowning and flash flooding: Stormwater channels and storm drains can fill rapidly during precipitation. Water levels can rise without warning. Never enter a storm drain, culvert, or engineered channel during active flow.
Slippery surfaces: Wet concrete, asphalt, and channel banks are extremely slippery.
Electrical hazard: Avoid sampling near downed power lines during storms.
Traffic: Storm sampling often occurs at night or in low visibility. Wear high-visibility vests and use traffic cones. Park away from traffic lanes.
Establish an escape route before approaching any sampling location.
Monitor upstream conditions. If water is rising, retreat immediately.
If lightning is observed, cease sampling and move to a vehicle or enclosed structure. Wait 30 minutes after the last observed lightning before resuming.




5.1 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety for general emergency response. If a team member is swept into a channel, call 911 immediately. Do not attempt an in-water rescue unless you have swift-water rescue training and equipment.

title: Stormwater Sampling
text:
7 Storm Event Criteria

7.1 Qualifying Storm Events
A qualifying storm event must meet all of the following criteria unless the project sampling plan specifies otherwise (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2018):

Antecedent dry period: At least 72 hours (3 days) of dry weather preceding the storm
Minimum rainfall: At least 2.5 mm (0.1 inches) of total precipitation predicted or observed
Duration: Sufficient to produce runoff at the sampling location



7.2 Storm Tracking and Mobilization

Monitor the 3–7 day National Weather Service (NWS) forecast and local radar (e.g., Weather.gov, NWS Doppler) during the October– March wet season.
When a qualifying storm is forecast, notify the team at least 24 hours in advance if possible.
Pre-position coolers, ice, and sampling supplies in vehicles. Confirm all sample bottles are correct and labeled.
Confirm sampling site access (locked gates, private property) before departure.

title: Stormwater Sampling
text:
8 Sample Collection Procedures

8.1 Sampling Time
Attempt to collect at least three samples per event when possible (APHA et al., 2012; California State Water Resources Control Board, 2018):

First flush: As early as practical after runoff reaches the sampling point; ideally within 30 minutes of runoff initiation
Mid-storm: Approximately at peak flow
Recession: During the falling limb, at least 2 hours after peak flow

Record the time, rainfall amount (if a gauge is present), and an estimate of flow conditions (trickle, moderate, high) at each sampling time.


8.2 Outfall and Stormwater Channel Sampling

Approach the outfall or channel sampling point from upstream or from above. Never stand downstream of an active outfall.
Using the extension pole, position the bottle mouth facing upstream at mid-depth (or as close to mid-depth as safely possible).
Fill to the appropriate volume for the analytes being collected.
Cap immediately, label, and place in the cooler with ice.



8.3 Sheet Flow Sampling

Identify a low point or convergence zone where sheet flow concentrates.
Place a clean stainless steel or HDPE tray or shallow pan at ground level to intercept the flow.
Transfer collected water to sample bottles using a clean syringe or by pouring directly.
Record the contributing area and surface type (impervious, pervious, mixed).



8.4 Time-Composite Sampling

At each time interval (e.g., every 30 minutes), collect a grab sample per §6.1 or §6.2.
Measure a fixed aliquot volume (e.g., 50–100 mL) using a graduated cylinder.
Add the aliquot to the composite bottle. Mix gently.
Record the time, flow estimate, and aliquot volume in the field notebook.
At the end of the event, transfer the composite to appropriately preserved bottles for each analyte.

title: Stream Physical Habitat Assessment – SWAMP Protocol
text:
This SOP describes procedures for characterizing the physical habitat of wadeable streams using the quantitative transect-based protocol developed by the California State Water Resources Control Board’s Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP). Physical habitat data document the structural condition of streams – channel dimensions, substrate composition, bank stability, riparian vegetation, instream cover, and human influence – and are essential for interpreting bioassessment results and diagnosing the causes of biological impairment (Barbour et al., 1999; Ode et al., 2016).
The protocol produces data compatible with the California Index of Physical-habitat Integrity (IPI), the California Stream Condition Index (CSCI), and the Algal Stream Condition Index (ASCI), enabling direct comparison with statewide reference data (Mazor et al., 2016; Rehn et al., 2018).

title: Stream Physical Habitat Assessment – SWAMP Protocol
text:
This SOP describes procedures for characterizing the physical habitat of wadeable streams using the quantitative transect-based protocol developed by the California State Water Resources Control Board’s Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP). Physical habitat data document the structural condition of streams – channel dimensions, substrate composition, bank stability, riparian vegetation, instream cover, and human influence – and are essential for interpreting bioassessment results and diagnosing the causes of biological impairment (Barbour et al., 1999; Ode et al., 2016).
The protocol produces data compatible with the California Index of Physical-habitat Integrity (IPI), the California Stream Condition Index (CSCI), and the Algal Stream Condition Index (ASCI), enabling direct comparison with statewide reference data (Mazor et al., 2016; Rehn et al., 2018).

title: Stream Physical Habitat Assessment – SWAMP Protocol
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Wadeable perennial and intermittent streams and rivers where personnel can safely wade (generally depths less than approximately 1 m and velocities less than approximately 1.2 m/s)
Does not apply to: Non-wadeable rivers requiring boat-based protocols; estuarine or tidal reaches; depressional wetlands (use CRAM instead); lake or reservoir shorelines
Location: All EA Program stream monitoring sites, including tributaries to the Santa Ana River watershed and other southern California waterbodies

title: Stream Physical Habitat Assessment – SWAMP Protocol
text:
4 Definitions

b-axis (intermediate axis): The intermediate dimension of a sediment particle (not the longest or shortest axis); the standard measurement used to classify particle size in pebble counts; measured with a metric ruler to the nearest mm (Ode et al., 2016).
Bankfull channel: The stage at which water just begins to overflow the channel banks into the floodplain; the reference condition for channel geometry measurements in SWAMP; typically evidenced by a change in bank slope, a break in vegetation, or the top of the point bar (Ode et al., 2016; Peck et al., 2006).
Cobble embeddedness: The percentage of the surface area of gravel, cobble, and boulder particles that is surrounded and buried by fine sediment (sand, silt, clay); an indicator of fine sediment loading and hyporheic connectivity (Ode et al., 2016).
CPOM (coarse particulate organic matter): Organic material (leaves, needles, twigs, bark) with a largest dimension between 1 mm and 10 cm; recorded at substrate measurement points as an indicator of allochthonous organic input to the stream.
D16, D50, D84: Percentile statistics of the particle-size distribution from a pebble count; the particle size at which 16%, 50%, or 84% of particles are smaller; used to characterize substrate texture; D50 is the median particle diameter.
Embeddedness: See cobble embeddedness.
IPI (Index of Physical-habitat Integrity): The California statewide index of stream physical condition calculated from SWAMP physical habitat data; scores from 0 (most disturbed) to 1 (least disturbed); used alongside the CSCI for reach-level condition assessment (Rehn et al., 2018).
Inter-transect: A transect located halfway between two main transects; used for substrate, embeddedness, and organic matter measurements but not for cross-section geometry; see Appendix B for inter-transect locations (Ode et al., 2016).
Main transect: One of 11 equally spaced transects (A through K) across the full sampling reach; the primary sampling unit for all SWAMP physical habitat modules including cross-section geometry, bankfull identification, substrate, canopy cover, bank stability, human influence, and riparian vegetation.
OHW (ordinary high-water mark): The line on the bank formed by the action of water in its ordinary course; used as an alternative bankfull indicator where clear geomorphic evidence is absent.
Pebble count: A randomized survey of substrate particle sizes at systematically distributed points along transects; each particle is measured at the toe of the measurer’s boot or wading rod tip to ensure objectivity; produces the particle-size distribution used to calculate IPI substrate metrics (Ode et al., 2016; Peck et al., 2006).
Reach: A representative stream segment typically 150 m in length (or 37.5× the mean wetted width for wider streams), within which all SWAMP physical habitat measurements are collected; selected to encompass representative channel features and minimize confounding influences of point sources or major confluences (Ode et al., 2016).
Riparian zone: The terrestrial area adjacent to the stream channel that is influenced by periodic flooding and that contributes organic material, shade, and bank stability to the aquatic system; assessed in SWAMP modules I (riparian vegetation) and G (bank stability).
Sinuosity: The ratio of the actual stream channel length to the straight-line valley length over the reach; values greater than 1.5 indicate a meandering channel; a component of the SWAMP reach characterization.
Thalweg: The line of deepest flow along the channel axis; followed during the longitudinal profile module to characterize channel bed elevation changes.
Wetted width: The horizontal distance across the stream from water’s edge to water’s edge at a transect; used to determine reach length (37.5× mean wetted width) and to scale substrate sampling interval.

title: Stream Physical Habitat Assessment – SWAMP Protocol
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Drowning and swift water: Do not wade in flows deeper than approximately waist height or where footing is unstable. Always face upstream. Use a wading rod for support.
Slippery substrates: Algae-covered cobble and bedrock are extremely slippery. Wear felt-soled or studded wading boots.
Biological: Waterborne pathogens, poison oak, ticks, snakes, and stinging insects. Check for ticks after every field day.
Heat: Southern California field sites can exceed 40 °C during summer. Carry adequate water and take shade breaks.
Sensitive species: California red-legged frog, arroyo toad, southwestern willow flycatcher, and steelhead may be present at some sites. Consult permit requirements before sampling (see SOP-F004).




5.1 Required PPE

Chest or hip waders (neoprene or breathable)
Wading boots with felt or studded soles
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen, long sleeves)
Nitrile gloves (when handling samples)



5.2 Permits
Sampling in or near habitat for listed species may require a CDFW Scientific Collecting Permit and/or a USFWS Section 10 permit. The PI must confirm permit status before fieldwork at any new site.


5.3 Invasive Species Prevention
Decontaminate all wading gear between sites per SOP-F007.


5.4 Emergency Procedures
A minimum of two people must be present for any in-stream work. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.

title: Stream Physical Habitat Assessment – SWAMP Protocol
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Reach Delineation
The sampling reach defines the stream segment over which all measurements are collected (Ode et al., 2016).

Select a representative reach of appropriate length (150 m for streams with mean wetted width ≤ 10 m; 250 m for wider streams).
Walk the reach before beginning measurements to identify the thalweg, bankfull indicators, and any safety hazards.
Mark the downstream boundary (Transect A) and record GPS coordinates.
Stretch the measuring tape upstream along the thalweg (not the bank) to the upstream boundary (Transect K).
Set transect locations at equal intervals (e.g., every 15 m for a 150 m reach), placing chaining pins or flagging at each transect.







Tip



Select reaches that are representative of the stream segment. Avoid reaches with immediate upstream or downstream disturbances (bridges, dam tailwaters, outfalls) unless those features are the sampling target (Ode et al., 2016).




8.2 Module A: Reach-Level Information
Record at the start of each visit:

GPS coordinates at Transects A (downstream) and K (upstream)
Date, time, crew members
General weather and flow conditions (normal, high, low, dry)
Any unusual conditions (algal blooms, trash accumulation, visible pollutants, recent disturbance)



8.3 Module B: Bankfull Identification Calibration
Before beginning measurements, the full crew must agree on bankfull indicators (Ode et al., 2016):

Identify at least two independent lines of evidence for bankfull (e.g., break in bank slope, top of point bar, change in vegetation, flood debris line).
Walk the first 2–3 transects together and calibrate agreement on bankfull height.
Differences in bankfull identification between crew members are the largest source of inter-observer variability in SWAMP physical habitat data.



8.4 Module C: Cross-Section Geometry (Main Transects)
At each main transect (A through K) (Ode et al., 2016; Peck et al., 2006):

Stretch the measuring tape across the channel from left to right bank at the bankfull boundary (looking downstream).
Record the total bankfull width to the nearest 0.1 m.
Record the wetted width to the nearest 0.1 m.
At 5 equally spaced points across the wetted channel, measure water depth to the nearest cm using the surveyor’s rod.
Record the thalweg depth (deepest point).
Estimate the dominant bank angle (undercut, vertical, steep, gradual, flat) for left and right banks.



8.5 Module D: Substrate (Pebble Count)
At each of the 21 transects (main and inter-transects), at 5 equally spaced points across the wetted channel (Ode et al., 2016):

Measure water depth to the nearest cm.
Pick up the particle at the toe of your boot (or wading rod tip) and measure the b-axis to the nearest mm. Record on the field form.
If the particle cannot be picked up (bedrock, hardpan), record the appropriate size class code (see Appendix C).
Record presence or absence of CPOM at each point.

This produces 105 substrate measurements per reach.


8.6 Module E: Cobble Embeddedness
At each substrate measurement point on main transects, if the particle is gravel, cobble, or boulder:

Estimate the percentage of the particle surface buried by fine sediment to the nearest 5% or 10%.
Record sand and finer substrate as 100% embedded by convention.
Do not assess embeddedness for bedrock.



8.7 Module F: Algal and Macrophyte Cover
At each of the five substrate measurement points (main and inter-transects):

Record presence/absence of macroalgae on the substrate particle.
Record presence/absence of macrophytes (rooted vascular aquatic plants; mosses excluded).
At main transects, estimate percent cover within a 1 m radius.



8.8 Module G: Bank Stability
At each main transect, for both left and right banks (Ode et al., 2016):

Estimate the percent of bank covered by erosion (exposed bare soil, slumping, undercutting) to the nearest 5%.
Estimate the angle of the bank (undercut, vertical, steep, gradual, flat).



8.9 Module H: Human Influence
At each main transect, record the proximity of human influences within a 5 m upstream/downstream window and 10 m from each bank. Record each feature as 0 (absent), P (present > 10 m), C (within 10 m), or B (on bank). Features include: walls/rip-rap/dams, buildings, pavement, roads/railroads, pipes, landfill/trash, park/lawn, row crops, pasture/hay, logging, and mining.


8.10 Module I: Riparian Vegetation
At each main transect, for both left and right banks, estimate areal cover (0–4 scale: 0 absent, 1 < 10%, 2 = 10–40%, 3 = 40–75%, 4 > 75%) in three layers:

Canopy (> 5 m)
Understory (0.5–5 m)
Ground cover (< 0.5 m)

Record the dominant vegetation type for each layer.


8.11 Module J: Instream Cover
At each main transect, estimate percent cover of instream features within one channel width upstream and downstream of the transect line:



Feature
Definition




Boulder (> 25 cm)
Visual estimate of surface coverage


Cobble (6.4–25 cm)
Visual estimate


Wood (snag, rootwad)
Visual estimate


Overhanging vegetation
Bank overhang within 0.5 m of water surface


Undercut bank
Bank extending over water


Macroalgae
Attached filamentous or mat-forming algae


Macrophytes
Rooted vascular aquatic plants





8.12 Module L: Channel Slope and Sinuosity
Measure channel slope using a clinometer at a minimum of three measurement intervals along the reach (between Transects A–C, E–G, and I–K) or more frequently if slope is variable.
Measure sinuosity by comparing total thalweg length (measured with the tape along the thalweg) to the straight-line valley distance (measured with a compass and tape) (Ode et al., 2016).


8.13 Module M: Photographs
At each main transect, take the following photographs:

Looking upstream along the thalweg
Looking downstream along the thalweg
Left bank at the transect line
Right bank at the transect line

At Transects A and K, also photograph the downstream and upstream reach boundaries. All photographs should include the transect label (flagging or field data sheet) in the frame for orientation.
Record photo file names in the field data sheet.

title: Stream Physical Habitat Assessment – SWAMP Protocol
text:
9 Quality Control

9.1 Inter-Observer Variability
For substrate measurements, the precision targets are (Ode et al., 2016):

Median substrate size class (D50): agreement within one Wentworth size class between independent observers
Embeddedness: agreement within 15 percentage points



9.2 Repeat Measurements
For periodic quality assurance, conduct a repeat measurement by an independent crew within 48 hours. Both crews must achieve agreement within the precision targets above.


9.3 Common Errors to Avoid

Measuring transects out of sequence (always work upstream)
Inconsistent bankfull identification between crew members (calibrate at the first transect)
Forgetting to record GPS coordinates at Transects A and K
Omitting inter-transect measurements (required for full IPI calculation)
Failing to record the measurement units (mm vs. size class code) for substrate

title: Wetland Hydrology Monitoring
text:
This procedure describes field methods for monitoring wetland hydrology, including measurement of water table depth, surface inundation extent, and hydroperiod documentation. Hydrology is the primary driver of wetland ecosystem structure and function: it controls soil saturation, redox chemistry, plant community composition, and jurisdictional wetland status under the Clean Water Act (Mitsch & Gosselink, 2015; US Army Corps of Engineers, 1987).
Wetland hydrology monitoring supports baseline characterization, impact assessment, restoration monitoring, and regulatory compliance (e.g., Army Corps of Engineers wetland delineation criteria).

title: Wetland Hydrology Monitoring
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Freshwater wetlands (marshes, swamps, riparian wetlands, vernal pools, constructed wetlands) at EA Program field sites. Methods include manual water-level measurements in monitoring wells and piezometers, crest gauges, staff gauges, and automated water level loggers.
Does not apply to: Tidal wetland hydrology (requires tide- corrected methods); stream stage-discharge relationships (see SOP-F301); groundwater monitoring in non-wetland wells (see SOP-F303)
Location: All EA Program wetland field sites

title: Wetland Hydrology Monitoring
text:
4 Definitions

Hydroperiod: The duration and timing of surface water or near-surface saturation in a wetland during a given year; the most important determinant of wetland vegetation, soil development, and biogeochemical function.
Hydric soil: A soil that formed under conditions of saturation, flooding, or ponding long enough to develop anaerobic conditions in the upper part; identified by redoximorphic features and low-chroma colors; a required criterion for jurisdictional wetland delineation.
Ordinary high water mark (OHWM): The line on the shore established by the fluctuations of water leaving physical characteristics such as a clear, natural line impressed on the bank, shelving, destruction of terrestrial vegetation, or presence of litter and debris; used to define the lateral extent of jurisdictional waters.
Piezometer: A small-diameter tube installed in the soil with a screened section at a defined depth; measures hydraulic head at that depth; used to determine the direction and magnitude of groundwater flow and to detect perched water tables.
Redox potential (Eh): A measure of the oxidizing or reducing conditions in soil or water, expressed in millivolts; positive values indicate oxidizing conditions; negative values indicate reducing conditions under which Fe, Mn, and sulfate are reduced and redoximorphic features develop.
Staff gauge: A graduated rod installed vertically in a water body or wetland to allow direct visual reading of water surface elevation; used to record surface water stage and to relate water level logger records to a local datum.
Water table: The upper surface of the zone of saturation in the soil; measured as the depth to free-standing water in a well or piezometer; fluctuates seasonally and in response to precipitation events.
Wetland indicator status: A US Army Corps of Engineers classification of plant species by their probability of occurrence in wetlands: OBL (obligate wetland), FACW (facultative wetland), FAC (facultative), FACU (facultative upland), UPL (upland); used in vegetation-based wetland delineation.

title: Wetland Hydrology Monitoring
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Wetland substrates are unstable; risk of sinking in soft muck, tripping on submerged debris, or falling. Standing water may conceal holes and channels.
Biological: Mosquitoes (disease vectors), ticks, venomous snakes, poison oak/ivy, and waterborne pathogens. Avoid direct skin contact with standing water.
Environmental: Heat stress in summer; hypothermia in winter. Wetlands offer little shade.




5.1 Required PPE

Rubber boots or chest waders
Nitrile gloves
Long sleeves and pants (tick and mosquito protection)
Insect repellent (DEET or picaridin)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
Personal flotation device (if water depth exceeds knee level)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Work in pairs. If a team member becomes stuck in soft substrate, distribute weight on a board or backpack and pull laterally rather than vertically. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.

title: Wetland Hydrology Monitoring
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Monitoring Well Installation






Note



Well installation may require permits (e.g., well permits, Section 404 permits for work in wetlands). Confirm requirements with the PI before installation.



Select well locations based on the study design (e.g., transect from upland to wetland center, paired wells at different depths)
Auger a borehole to the target depth (typically 1–2 m for shallow water table monitoring)
Install a 2-inch or 4-inch PVC well with a slotted screen in the saturated zone and a solid riser above the ground surface
Backfill the annular space around the screen with clean silica sand; seal the upper portion with bentonite to prevent surface water infiltration along the well casing
Install a protective well cap; record the top-of-casing (TOC) elevation relative to a local benchmark using a survey level
Develop the well by surging and bailing to remove drilling mud and fine sediment. Allow the well to equilibrate for at least 24 hours before the first measurement.
Record the well construction details (total depth, screen interval, stick-up height, TOC elevation, GPS coordinates) on the well installation log



7.2 Manual Water Level Measurement

Remove the well cap. If the well is locked, note the time and condition of the lock.
Lower the water level indicator (e-line) slowly into the well. When the probe contacts the water surface, the indicator will sound or light up.
Read the depth to water from the top of casing (TOC) to the nearest 0.01 ft or 0.5 cm. Record this value.
Calculate the water table elevation:
\[
\text{WTE} = \text{TOC elevation} - \text{depth to water}
\]
If the water table is above the ground surface (artesian or flooded conditions), measure the height of water above the TOC or use a staff gauge for ponded water.
Record date, time, depth to water, and any observations (e.g., well condition, nearby disturbance, wildlife activity) in the field notebook.
Replace and secure the well cap.



7.3 Staff Gauge and Crest Gauge Reading

Read the water level on the staff gauge to the nearest 0.5 cm. Read at eye level to avoid parallax.
Record the reading, date, time, and any obstructions (debris on the gauge, algae).
For crest gauges: record the peak water mark left by granular cork or paint inside the gauge since the last visit. Reset the gauge per the manufacturer’s instructions.



7.4 Automated Logger Deployment and Download

Program the logger for the desired recording interval (typically 15 minutes to 1 hour for wetland hydrology)
Deploy the logger in the well, suspended at a known depth below the TOC using a stainless steel cable or direct-read cable
Deploy a barometric logger above the expected high water line (for non-vented transducers)
Record the deployment details: logger serial number, deployment depth, start time, recording interval
On each visit, download data using the manufacturer’s software. Take a manual water level measurement at the time of download for calibration verification.
Compensate pressure transducer data for barometric pressure changes using the barometric logger data. Most manufacturer software includes an automated compensation routine.



7.5 Inundation Mapping

During each visit, note the spatial extent of surface water or saturated soil at the site
Record the inundation boundary on a site map or using GPS waypoints
Photograph fixed photo points to document seasonal changes in inundation
Record the presence of wetland hydrology indicators (oxidized rhizospheres, water-stained leaves, drift lines, sediment deposits, water marks on trees) per the Army Corps of Engineers wetland delineation manual (US Army Corps of Engineers, 1987)

title: Wetland Hydrology Monitoring
text:
8 Quality Control

Take a manual water level reading concurrent with every logger download to verify logger accuracy. If the manual reading and logger reading differ by more than 2 cm, troubleshoot the logger (drift, fouling, cable slip).
Record duplicate manual readings at 10% of wells per visit (read, remove the tape, re-read). Duplicates should agree within 0.5 cm.
Check e-line calibration against a measured standard (e.g., a surveyed depth) at least once per season.
Maintain a well construction log with TOC elevations; re-survey TOC elevations annually or after ground disturbance (frost heave, animal activity, mowing).
Archive raw logger files in the project data folder before any processing. Version-control all compensation and correction scripts per SOP-L801.

title: Wetland Hydrology Monitoring
text:
9 Data Management

Enter manual water level data into the project database within 48 hours of collection
Download, compensate, and archive logger data within 7 days of retrieval
Convert all water level data to a common datum (e.g., NAVD88 or a local benchmark) before analysis
Flag and document any data gaps, logger malfunctions, or well damage

title: Wetland Delineation
text:
This SOP describes the field and office procedures for conducting a wetland delineation using the three-parameter approach established by the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE). A jurisdictional wetland must exhibit all three criteria simultaneously: hydrophytic vegetation, hydric soils, and wetland hydrology (US Army Corps of Engineers, 1987). Delineation establishes the boundary between jurisdictional wetlands (and other waters of the US) and upland areas, which is a prerequisite for regulatory compliance under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act.
Wetland delineation at EA Program sites supports baseline characterization, impact assessment, restoration planning, and student training in applied environmental science.

A jurisdictional wetland must exhibit all three criteria simultaneously: hydrophytic vegetation, hydric soils, and wetland hydrology (US Army Corps of Engineers, 1987). Delineation establishes the boundary between jurisdictional wetlands (and other waters of the US) and upland areas, which is a prerequisite for regulatory compliance under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act.
Wetland delineation at EA Program sites supports baseline characterization, impact assessment, restoration planning, and student training in applied environmental science.

title: Wetland Delineation
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Freshwater palustrine wetlands (marshes, swamps, riparian wetlands, vernal pools, seeps) at EA Program field sites in the Arid West region of California. This SOP follows the USACE Arid West Regional Supplement (US Army Corps of Engineers, 2010), which supersedes the 1987 Manual for all delineations in this region.
Does not apply to: Tidal or estuarine wetlands (require separate tidal methods); riverine waters regulated solely as ordinary high water mark (OHWM) features; non-USACE state-level wetland determinations under California law (e.g., Porter-Cologne Act), which may apply different criteria.
Location: All EA Program wetland field sites

title: Wetland Delineation
text:
4 Definitions

Dominant species: A species contributing 50% or more of the relative frequency or relative cover within a stratum; used in the 50/20 rule for hydrophytic vegetation determination.
Facultative (FAC): A wetland indicator status category applied to plant species that occur in both wetland and upland habitats with roughly equal frequency (34–66% occurrence in wetlands); neither confirms nor denies wetland conditions when dominant.
Facultative upland (FACU): Plants that usually occur in uplands (67–99% upland occurrence) but are occasionally found in wetlands; their dominance is evidence against hydrophytic vegetation.
Facultative wetland (FACW): Plants that usually occur in wetlands (67–99% wetland occurrence); their dominance is strong evidence for hydrophytic vegetation.
Hydric soil: A soil that formed under conditions of saturation, flooding, or ponding long enough to develop anaerobic conditions in the upper part; identified by USACE hydric soil field indicators (e.g., depleted matrix, redox concentrations, sulfidic odor); a required criterion for wetland delineation (US Army Corps of Engineers, 1987).
Hydrophytic vegetation: Plant community dominated (by the 50/20 rule) by species with a wetland indicator status of OBL, FACW, or FAC; a required criterion for wetland delineation.
Obligate wetland (OBL): Plant species that occur almost always (> 99% of the time) in wetlands; their dominance is the strongest evidence for hydrophytic vegetation.
Ordinary high water mark (OHWM): The line on the shore established by the fluctuations of water leaving physical characteristics such as a clear natural line impressed on the bank, shelving, destruction of terrestrial vegetation, or presence of litter and debris; used to define the lateral extent of jurisdictional waters.
Problem area: A site where one or more of the three wetland criteria are not clearly met or where atypical conditions (drought, altered hydrology, recent disturbance) complicate standard application of the three-parameter approach; requires additional documentation and may require a USACE district determination.
Sample plot (data point): A defined area (typically 5 m radius for vegetation; a single soil pit for soils; a 10 m radius for hydrology indicators) within which all three wetland criteria are assessed together.
Upland: An area that does not meet one or more of the three required wetland criteria; not subject to Section 404 jurisdiction.
Wetland boundary: The line on the landscape separating areas that meet all three wetland criteria from areas that do not; the primary product of a wetland delineation.
Wetland indicator status (WIS): A USACE classification of plant species by their probability of occurrence in wetlands: OBL (obligate wetland), FACW (facultative wetland), FAC (facultative), FACU (facultative upland), UPL (upland). Current designations are maintained by the USACE National Wetland Plant List (NWPL).

title: Wetland Delineation
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Unstable substrates (soft muck, quicksand-like conditions in saturated soils); risk of sinking, tripping on submerged debris, or falling. Standing water may conceal holes and channels.
Biological: Mosquitoes (disease vectors including West Nile virus), ticks (Lyme disease, RMSF), venomous snakes, poison oak/ivy (Toxicodendron spp.), stinging nettles, and waterborne pathogens. Avoid direct skin contact with standing water.
Environmental: Heat stress in summer; hypothermia in winter and spring. Wetlands offer little shade in open marsh environments.




5.1 Required PPE

Rubber boots or chest waders (knee boots minimum)
Nitrile gloves (for soil pit work)
Long sleeves and long pants (tick and mosquito protection)
Insect repellent (DEET or picaridin)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen SPF 30+)
Personal flotation device (if water depth exceeds knee level or if working from a watercraft)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Work in pairs at minimum. If a team member becomes stuck in soft substrate, distribute weight on a board, backpack, or rope and pull laterally rather than vertically. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.

title: Wetland Delineation
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Step 1: Pre-Field Office Work
Before entering the field, complete the following:

Obtain and review available information:

USFWS National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) maps (fws.gov/wetlands)
USDA Web Soil Survey (websoilsurvey.nrcs.usda.gov) – note mapped hydric soils and map unit descriptions
USGS topographic maps (7.5-minute quadrangles)
Aerial/satellite imagery (Google Earth historical layers) – look for inundation signatures, dark organic soils, and characteristic vegetation patterns
NOAA precipitation records for the region to assess whether current year is a drought, normal, or wet year (relevant to atypical situation determinations)

Generate a base map at a scale appropriate for the site (1:2,400 for small sites; 1:4,800 for large sites). Include NWI polygons, soil map unit boundaries, topographic contours, and property boundaries.
Look up current wetland indicator status (WIS) for all plant species expected at the site on the USACE National Wetland Plant List (plants.usace.army.mil).
Identify the appropriate USACE district and confirm whether a preliminary jurisdictional determination (PJD) or approved jurisdictional determination (AJD) is ultimately required.



8.2 Step 2: Site Reconnaissance
On arrival at the field site, conduct a reconnaissance walk before placing any sample plots:

Walk the entire site perimeter and any internal drainages or basins to develop a mental model of landscape position, drainage patterns, and vegetation transitions.
Identify probable wetland areas (standing or ponded water, dark organic soils visible at surface, wet-adapted vegetation) and probable upland areas (well-drained soils, upland vegetation).
Identify any obvious disturbances (ditching, filling, altered hydrology, grazing, invasive species) that could create problem areas.
Note the approximate location of vegetation transitions, which are often close to the wetland boundary.
Sketch a rough site map with probable wetland/upland zones and planned transect routes.



8.3 Step 3: Establish Transects and Sample Plots

Establish transects perpendicular to the suspected wetland boundary, spaced to adequately characterize the site. For EA Program sites, transects are typically spaced 25–50 m apart; closer spacing is used in complex or small-scale boundaries.
On each transect, place sample plots at:

A clearly wetland location (well within the apparent wetland)
A clearly upland location (well outside the apparent wetland)
One or more locations straddling the suspected boundary

Flag each sample plot center with flagging tape and record GPS coordinates. Use a consistent color for wetland plots and a different color for upland plots.
Number all sample plots sequentially and record them on the base map.



8.4 Step 4: Assess Hydrophytic Vegetation
At each sample plot (approximately 5 m radius), assess vegetation in all strata present (tree, shrub/sapling, herb, woody vine):

List all plant species in each stratum. Identify to species level using regional keys (Jepson Manual for California).
Estimate percent areal cover for each species within each stratum to the nearest 5–10%.
For each species, record the current wetland indicator status (WIS) from the USACE NWPL for the Arid West region.
Determine dominant species in each stratum using the 50/20 rule:

Rank species within each stratum by decreasing percent cover.
Add species from highest to lowest cover until the cumulative cover total reaches 50% or more of the total stratum cover.
Include one additional species if it contributes at least 20% of the total stratum cover.
All species added in steps (b) and (c) are dominant species for that stratum.

Tally the number of dominant species that are OBL, FACW, or FAC (hydrophytic) and the number that are FACU or UPL (upland).
The hydrophytic vegetation criterion is met if more than 50% of the dominant species across all strata are OBL, FACW, or FAC.







NoteFAC-Neutral Test



In borderline cases where FAC species are dominant, apply the FAC-neutral test: exclude all FAC species and recalculate dominance using only OBL, FACW, FACU, and UPL species. If the remaining dominants are predominantly hydrophytic, the criterion is still met. The FAC-neutral test is described in the Arid West Regional Supplement (US Army Corps of Engineers, 2010).




8.5 Step 5: Assess Hydric Soils
At each sample plot, excavate a soil pit to at least 50 cm depth (or to the water table or bedrock, whichever is shallower):

Excavate with a sharpshooter spade. If the pit fills with water, record the depth to water table and excavate no deeper.
Describe the soil profile using the form in Appendix A:

Horizon designation (A, B, C), depth (cm), and thickness
Munsell color (matrix and mottles/redoximorphic features) per SOP-F405 – record moist colors only
Texture (field ribbon test; see SOP-F401)
Structure, consistence, roots

Check for USDA NRCS Field Indicators of Hydric Soils (Version 8.2 or current). For the Western Mountains, Valleys, and Coast (WMVC) region, the most applicable indicators include:








Indicator Code
Name
Key Feature




A1
Histosol
Organic soil (Oi, Oe, or Oa horizon > 40 cm)


A2
Histic epipedon
Organic surface layer 20–40 cm


A3
Black histic
Black (10YR 2/1) organic layer >= 20 cm


A11
Depleted below dark surface
Dark A over low-chroma (chroma <= 2) matrix


F2
Loamy gleyed matrix
Gley hue matrix in loamy soils


F3
Depleted matrix
> 60% low-chroma (chroma <= 2) matrix


F6
Redox dark surface
Dark A over depleted or reduced matrix


F8
Redox depressions
Redox concentrations in depressions



The hydric soil criterion is met if one or more applicable field indicators are present at the appropriate depth. For most indicators in the Arid West Supplement, this means within the upper 30 cm of the soil profile (US Army Corps of Engineers, 2010).







WarningProblematic Hydric Soil Situations



Soils in the Arid West may have low-chroma colors from parent material (e.g., some shales, volcanic tuffs) rather than from saturation. If in doubt, check for redox concentrations (bright orange/red Fe masses) as corroborating evidence, and note the soil series and parent material from Web Soil Survey.




8.6 Step 6: Assess Wetland Hydrology
At each sample plot, document evidence of wetland hydrology. The USACE defines wetland hydrology as saturation within 30 cm of the surface for a continuous period of at least 5% of the growing season (US Army Corps of Engineers, 1987, 2010).

Record depth to surface water or saturated soil (standing water in the pit).
Check for primary hydrology indicators (in order of reliability):







Indicator
Description




Surface water
Standing water present at time of visit


High water table
Water within 30 cm of surface in soil pit


Saturation
Saturated soil within 30 cm (water oozes when squeezed)



Check for secondary hydrology indicators (two or more required when primary indicators are absent):







Indicator
Description




Water marks
Staining on tree trunks or structures


Sediment deposits
Fresh mineral sediment on leaves or stems


Drift lines
Lines of debris deposited by receding water


Waterlogged soils
Confirmed by soil pit; no free water but saturated


Water-stained leaves
Grayish-brown discoloration of litter


Oxidized rhizospheres
Orange halos around living roots in grey matrix


FAC-neutral plant communities
Vegetation dominance by OBL/FACW species


Crayfish burrows
Chimney mounds indicating seasonal saturation



For arid-region sites, pay particular attention to oxidized rhizospheres (a primary indicator in the Arid West Supplement) and drift/wrack lines along swales and basins.
The wetland hydrology criterion is met if at least one primary indicator is present, or at least two secondary indicators are present, at the time of visit; or if the site has documented evidence of seasonal or periodic inundation from well records or gauges (see SOP-F306).







NoteArid-Region Hydrology Timing



At arid and semi-arid sites, surface water and high water tables may only be present during a brief seasonal window. When conducting delineations outside the wet season, rely on secondary indicators and, where available, water level logger data from monitoring wells. Document the date of the visit and regional precipitation conditions in all field data sheets. See SOP-F306 for long-term hydrology monitoring methods.




8.7 Step 7: Apply the Three-Parameter Test
At each sample plot, compile results from Steps 4–6:

Record whether each of the three criteria is met (yes/no) on the field data sheet (Appendix A).
A sample plot is classified as wetland if and only if all three criteria are met. If any criterion is absent, the plot is classified as upland (or a transitional/problem area if two of three are met).
If two of three criteria are met, flag the plot as a potential problem area and document the specific conditions. Common problem area types include:

Recently disturbed wetlands (vegetation removed, soil disturbed)
Drought-year assessments (hydrology not apparent)
Altered hydrology (ditched, drained, or impounded areas)
Atypical vegetation (recent burn, mowing, herbicide)

For problem areas, apply the appropriate USACE atypical situation procedures as described in the Regional Supplement (US Army Corps of Engineers, 2010).



8.8 Step 8: Flag and Map the Wetland Boundary

Between each pair of adjacent wetland and upland sample plots on a transect, locate the wetland boundary by walking perpendicular to the transect and reassessing the three criteria at intermediate points until the line of change is identified.
Flag the wetland boundary with a distinct color (use a third color different from the wetland and upland plot flags). Place flags every 5–10 m or at every change in direction.
Record GPS waypoints at each boundary flag using SOP-F006. Waypoint naming convention: WB_[transect]-[sequence] (e.g., WB_T1-01).
Photograph the boundary flags from multiple angles; include a scale bar (person or measuring tape) in at least one photo per transect.
Sketch the boundary on the field base map, noting all sample plot locations and transect lines.



8.9 Step 9: Field Quality Review
Before leaving the site, complete the following checks:

All sample plots have GPS coordinates recorded
Every plot has complete data for all three criteria
All boundary flags are GPS-logged
At least two representative photographs per sample plot
Boundary is continuous between all transects (no gaps)
Problem areas are flagged and documented
Equipment has been decontaminated per SOP-F007



8.10 Step 10: Post-Field Office Work

Enter all field data into the project database within 48 hours per SOP-L803.
Import GPS waypoints and generate a georeferenced boundary map in GIS software (see SOP-L804).
Overlay the delineated boundary on aerial imagery, NWI maps, and soil survey maps to check for consistency; note and document any discrepancies.
Calculate wetland area (hectares) from the GIS boundary polygon.
Compile the delineation report with:

Site description and location map
Methods summary (reference to this SOP)
Summary table of all sample plots and three-parameter results
Wetland boundary map
Photographs
Conclusions regarding jurisdictional status
Any problem areas and how they were addressed

Archive all raw field data sheets (scanned), GPS track files, GIS shapefiles, and the final report per project data management protocols.

title: Wetland Delineation
text:
9 Quality Control

A minimum of two observers must conduct the vegetation assessment at each sample plot; independent species lists must be reconciled before leaving the plot.
Munsell color readings must be made by two observers and must agree within one value and one chroma step; discrepancies require a consensus re-read per SOP-F405.
GPS boundary waypoints must be collected with horizontal accuracy < 3 m (WAAS-enabled or equivalent). Record DOP and fix type.
At 10% of sample plots, return the following day and re-assess the hydrophytic vegetation criterion independently; dominant species lists must agree within 10 percentage points cover.
Final delineation maps must be reviewed by the PI before submission to any regulatory agency or inclusion in project reports.

title: Wetland Delineation
text:
10 Data Management

Raw field data sheets must be scanned and uploaded to the project folder within 48 hours of fieldwork.
Enter tabular sample plot data into the project database using the standardized template in Appendix B.

It covers field sampling using a soil auger, sample homogenization, sieving, and subdivision for biological assays, carbon analysis, and other soil properties (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2024; Robertson et al., 1999).

title: Soil Sampling and Processing
text: This SOP describes the procedures for collecting, processing, and storing soil samples for laboratory analysis. It covers field sampling using a soil auger, sample homogenization, sieving, and subdivision for biological assays, carbon analysis, and other soil properties (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2024; Robertson et al., 1999).

title: Soil Sampling and Processing

2 Scope

Does not apply to: Deep soil coring (> 30 cm) requiring mechanized equipment; contaminated site sampling requiring chain-of-custody protocols

title: Soil Sampling and Processing
text:
4 Definitions

Bulk sample: A large, mixed sample collected from multiple locations within a sampling unit and combined before analysis; represents the average composition of the unit rather than any single point.
Composite sample: A sample formed by combining and mixing a defined number of subsamples from a plot or area; reduces analytical cost while improving spatial representativeness; the number and pattern of subsamples must be recorded (Robertson et al., 1999).
Core (soil core): A cylindrical soil sample extracted with a push-probe or hammer corer; preserves the depth profile and allows depth-discrete sampling; also used for bulk density determination (see SOP-F402).
Fine earth fraction: Soil material passing through a 2 mm sieve; sand, silt, and clay particles; the standard fraction for chemical analysis; gravel and coarser material are removed and their mass fraction recorded (Robertson et al., 1999).
Grab sample: A single, point-in-time sample collected from one location; appropriate when spatial variability is low or when individual point values are required; contrasted with composite sampling.
Pedogenic horizon: A layer of soil with distinct physical, chemical, or biological properties developed through soil-forming processes; designated by letter symbols (O, A, E, B, C, R); sampled discretely in profile descriptions (see SOP-F407).
Push-probe (soil probe): A hollow stainless steel tube pushed into the soil by hand or with a slide hammer to collect an intact soil core; the standard tool for rapid depth-discrete sampling in fine-textured soils without large stones (Robertson et al., 1999).
Sampling depth increment: A defined depth interval (e.g., 0–10 cm, 10–20 cm) from which soil is collected; depth increments must be consistent within a study for results to be comparable (Robertson et al., 1999).
Subsample: One of the individual small samples taken from within a plot that are combined to form a composite; also refers to a representative aliquot drawn from a bulk sample for laboratory analysis.

title: Soil Sampling and Processing
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Field Collection

Navigate to the sampling location per SOP-F006.
Record the GPS coordinates of each sample location.
Inspect the surface for hazards. Clear surface litter only if required by the protocol; record whether litter was cleared.
Insert the auger or push-probe vertically to the target depth. For depth-increment sampling:

Collect the 0–10 cm increment first. Remove and place in a labeled sample container.
Re-insert the auger and collect the 10–20 cm increment. Place in a separate container.
Repeat for additional depth increments as required by the sampling plan.

For composite samples, collect subsamples at each designated subplot location (typically 5–10 per plot) and combine in the bowl or bucket before homogenizing.
Record the following for each sample:

Sample ID per the project labeling scheme
GPS coordinates
Depth increment
Observed soil conditions (color, texture, moisture, visible roots, stoniness)
Any anomalies (disturbance, compaction, visible contamination)




8.2 Field Homogenization

Break up clods and remove surface litter, roots greater than 5 mm, visible rocks, and obvious debris by hand (Robertson et al., 1999).
Mix the soil thoroughly in the bowl or bucket until the color and texture appear uniform.
If the sample is to be composited across subsamples, combine all subsamples before mixing.



8.3 Sieving (Field or Lab)
Sieving can be performed in the field (when fresh soil is required for biological assays) or in the lab after air-drying (for chemical analysis) (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2024; Robertson et al., 1999):

Pass the soil through a 2 mm stainless steel sieve.
Weigh and record the mass of coarse fragments (> 2 mm) retained if the project protocol requires correction for coarse fragment content.
The fine earth fraction (< 2 mm) is the standard fraction for all chemical and biological analyses.



8.4 Sample Subdivision for Multiple Analyses
Divide the sieved fine earth fraction into the required subsamples before further drying or freezing (Robertson et al., 1999):








Subsample type
Treatment
Storage




Microbial biomass C/N
Field-moist; process within 24 h
Cooler 4 °C then lab


Enzyme assays
Field-moist; process within 24 h or freeze
Cooler/freezer (-20 °C)


Mineral N (KCl)
Field-moist or frozen; extract within 48 h
Cooler 4 °C


Soil moisture (gravimetric)
Field-moist
Sealed bag


Carbon/nitrogen (EA-IRMS)
Air-dry, then grind
Room temperature


pH, texture, other chemical
Air-dry
Room temperature









WarningBiological Subsamples



Do not freeze biological subsamples unless the analysis protocol explicitly permits it.




8.5 Tool Decontamination Between Sites
Wipe the auger, probe, and bowl with isopropyl alcohol and let dry before moving to the next sampling location. This prevents cross-contamination of soils between sites and is particularly important for sites with invasive species or contamination concerns (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2024).

title: Soil Sampling and Processing
text:
9 Quality Control

Collect field duplicates at a rate of 1 per 10 samples to assess sampling variability (Robertson et al., 1999).
Record all deviations from the sampling plan in the field notebook.
Verify auger depth calibration at the start of each sampling day.
Ensure sieve integrity (no torn or damaged mesh) before processing.

title: Soil Bulk Density – Core Method
text: This procedure describes the determination of soil bulk density using the volumetric core method. Bulk density (\(\rho_b\)) is the mass of oven-dried soil per unit volume of field-moist soil, expressed in g/cm3. It is used to convert gravimetric measurements (e.g., nutrient concentrations in mg/kg) to volumetric or areal bases (e.g., kg/ha), to assess soil compaction, to calculate total porosity, and to evaluate management effects on soil physical quality. The core method is the most widely used direct measurement of bulk density and is described in the SSSA Methods of Soil Analysis (Blake & Hartge, 1986; Grossman & Reinsch, 2002).

title: Soil Bulk Density – Core Method
text: This procedure describes the determination of soil bulk density using the volumetric core method. Bulk density (\(\rho_b\)) is the mass of oven-dried soil per unit volume of field-moist soil, expressed in g/cm3. It is used to convert gravimetric measurements (e.g., nutrient concentrations in mg/kg) to volumetric or areal bases (e.g., kg/ha), to assess soil compaction, to calculate total porosity, and to evaluate management effects on soil physical quality. The core method is the most widely used direct measurement of bulk density and is described in the SSSA Methods of Soil Analysis (Blake & Hartge, 1986; Grossman & Reinsch, 2002).

title: Soil Bulk Density – Core Method
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Mineral soils at all EA Program field sites, including agricultural plots, photovoltaic panel study sites, and restoration sites. Suitable for depths of 0–30 cm using hand-driven cores.
Does not apply to: Soils with abundant coarse fragments (greater than approximately 20% by volume of gravel, cobbles, or stones), which require the excavation or clod method. Also not applicable to organic soils (histosols) or very loose sandy soils where core insertion causes compaction of the sample.
Location: All EA Program field sites; laboratory drying and weighing in SGM 133

text:
3 Responsibilities







Role

title: Soil Bulk Density – Core Method
text:
4 Definitions

Bulk density (\(\rho_b\)): The mass of oven-dry soil per unit volume of field-moist soil, including pore space; expressed in g cm-3 or Mg m-3; typically ranges from 1.0–1.8 g cm-3 for mineral soils and 0.1–0.5 g cm-3 for organic soils.
Coarse fragment correction: An adjustment to bulk density calculations that removes the volume and mass of rock fragments (greater than 2 mm) from the core sample; required in stony or gravelly soils where coarse fragments occupy significant core volume.
Core sampler: A thin-walled, beveled steel cylinder of known volume pushed into the soil to extract an intact sample for bulk density determination; internal dimensions must be measured and recorded for each sampler.
Dry bulk density: The mass of oven-dry soil divided by the total volume of the sample including pore space; the standard reported value for bulk density; calculated after drying at 105 °C to constant mass.
Porosity (\(\phi\)): The fraction of total soil volume occupied by pores (air + water): \(\phi = 1 - \rho_b / \rho_p\) where \(\rho_p\) is particle density (assumed 2.65 g cm-3 for mineral soils); porosity decreases as bulk density increases.
Soil carbon stock: The mass of organic carbon per unit land area (Mg C ha-1) calculated from bulk density, sampling depth, and organic carbon concentration; bulk density measurement is the primary source of uncertainty in carbon stock estimates.
Soil compaction: An increase in bulk density caused by mechanical pressure (tillage, vehicle traffic, trampling); reduces porosity, impedes root growth, and decreases infiltration rates.

title: Soil Bulk Density – Core Method
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Physical: Driving the core sampler with a mallet or hammer poses a risk of hand and finger injury. Trowels and soil knives are sharp. Repetitive hammering can cause strain.
Biological: Soil-borne pathogens; wash hands thoroughly after handling soil. Tick and insect exposure at field sites.
Environmental: Standard field hazards (heat, uneven terrain, sun exposure).
