title: Soil Bulk Density – Core Method
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Sampling Preparation

Measure and record the internal dimensions of each core ring (inside diameter and height) using calipers. Calculate the volume:

\[
V = \pi \left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2 \times h
\]
where \(d\) = inside diameter (cm) and \(h\) = height (cm).

Pre-label core rings or bags with site name, plot ID, depth, and replicate number
Pre-weigh aluminum drying tins and record the tare mass
Clean core rings and the sampler with DI water before use
File a field work planning form per SOP-F001



7.2 Field Sampling

Navigate to the predetermined sampling location and record GPS coordinates
Clear surface litter, loose organic debris, and any vegetation from a small area (approximately 15 x 15 cm) at the sampling point without disturbing the mineral soil surface







Important



Do not compress or disturb the soil surface before inserting the core. The goal is to capture the soil at its natural field density.



Assemble the core ring inside the drive head. Ensure the beveled cutting edge faces downward.
Place the assembled sampler vertically on the soil surface
Position the driving cap or wooden block on top of the sampler
Drive the sampler into the soil using the mallet, applying steady, even blows. Drive until the top of the core ring is flush with, or slightly below, the soil surface.
Do not over-drive the sampler. If the ring is driven more than 1 cm past flush, the sample may be compacted and should be discarded. Over-driving and under-driving the core introduce bias in opposite directions; the magnitude of the bias depends on soil type and moisture status (Grossman & Reinsch, 2002; Page-Dumroese et al., 1999).
Carefully excavate the soil around the sampler using the trowel, leaving a pedestal of soil beneath and around the core
Slide the trowel or soil knife beneath the bottom of the core to sever it from the underlying soil
Lift the sampler and core out of the ground



7.3 Trimming and Capping

Remove the core ring from the drive head
Using a straight-edged blade, trim the soil flush with the top and bottom of the ring. Remove any material that extends beyond the ring face. Be careful not to smear or compress the soil.
If large roots or rocks protrude from the core face, note this in the field notebook. If coarse fragments constitute a substantial fraction of the core, record this and consider whether the core method is appropriate for this site.
Cap both ends of the ring with plastic caps or wrap tightly with aluminum foil
Place the capped core in a labeled ziplock bag
Store in the cooler for transport to the laboratory







TipTip



Collect a minimum of three replicate cores per plot or treatment to account for spatial variability. Five replicates are preferred for statistical robustness, especially in heterogeneous soils or when detecting small differences between treatments.




7.4 Backfilling
Backfill the sampling hole with surrounding soil to minimize site disturbance and prevent tripping hazards.


7.5 Laboratory Processing

Remove the plastic caps or foil from the core
Transfer the entire soil core from the ring into a pre-weighed aluminum drying tin. Use a spatula or trowel to ensure all soil is transferred; scrape the inside of the ring if necessary.
Record the mass of the tin plus field-moist soil (this can also be used to calculate gravimetric moisture if a separate subsample is not taken)
Place the tin in the drying oven at 105 C for a minimum of 24 hours (until constant mass is achieved). See SOP-L105.
Remove the tin from the oven and cool in a desiccator for 20–30 minutes
Weigh the tin plus oven-dried soil and record the mass

title: Soil Bulk Density – Core Method
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Calculations
Bulk density (g/cm3):
\[
\rho_b = \frac{M_{\text{dry}}}{V_{\text{core}}}
\]
where \(M_{\text{dry}}\) = mass of oven-dried soil (g) and \(V_{\text{core}}\) = internal volume of the core ring (cm3).
Gravimetric moisture content (if determined from the same core):
\[
\theta_g = \frac{M_{\text{wet}} - M_{\text{dry}}}{M_{\text{dry}}}
\]
where \(M_{\text{wet}}\) = mass of field-moist soil (g).
Total porosity (fraction):
\[
\phi = 1 - \frac{\rho_b}{\rho_s}
\]
where \(\rho_s\) is the particle density, typically assumed to be 2.65 g/cm3 for mineral soils. The assumed particle density of 2.65 g/cm3 is appropriate for most mineral soils but should be verified for soils with high organic matter (where it may be lower) or heavy mineral content (Blake & Hartge, 1986).


8.2 Expected Ranges
Typical bulk density values for mineral soils:



Soil Type
Expected \(\rho_b\) (g/cm3)




Well-aggregated forest or prairie topsoil
0.8 – 1.2


Cultivated agricultural topsoil
1.1 – 1.5


Compacted or traffic-affected soil
1.5 – 1.8


Sandy subsoil
1.4 – 1.8


Clay-rich subsoil
1.1 – 1.6



Values outside the range of 0.5 – 2.0 g/cm3 for mineral soils should be investigated for sampling or measurement error.
Variability is typically higher in surface soils than in subsoils because of biological activity and tillage effects (Al-Shammary et al., 2018). For carbon stock calculations, consistent sampling depth and core diameter are critical because small changes in bulk density propagate into large errors at the landscape scale (walter2016?).


8.3 QC Requirements

Collect a minimum of three replicate cores per plot or treatment
Calculate the coefficient of variation (CV) among replicates. A CV greater than 10% suggests high spatial variability or possible sampling problems (compaction, lost soil during extraction). Consider collecting additional replicates.
Verify core ring dimensions at the start of each sampling campaign. If the ring is dented or deformed, replace it.
Dry samples to constant mass. If the mass changes by more than 0.1 g between successive weighings (at least 4 hours apart), continue drying.

title: Soil Bulk Density – Core Method
text:
12 Appendix A: Example Calculation



Code
# Bulk density calculation from core method
# Core ring dimensions
diameter_cm <- 5.0
height_cm <- 5.0
volume_cm3 <- pi * (diameter_cm / 2)^2 * height_cm

# Masses
tin_g <- 15.32             # Tare mass of aluminum tin
tin_wet_g <- 112.45        # Tin + field-moist soil
tin_dry_g <- 95.78         # Tin + oven-dried soil (105 C, 24 h)

# Calculations
mass_dry_g <- tin_dry_g - tin_g
mass_wet_g <- tin_wet_g - tin_g

bulk_density <- mass_dry_g / volume_cm3
grav_moisture <- (mass_wet_g - mass_dry_g) / mass_dry_g
porosity <- 1 - (bulk_density / 2.65)

cat(sprintf("Core volume:          %.2f cm3\n", volume_cm3))
cat(sprintf("Oven-dry soil mass:   %.2f g\n", mass_dry_g))
cat(sprintf("Bulk density:         %.2f g/cm3\n", bulk_density))
cat(sprintf("Gravimetric moisture: %.3f g/g\n", grav_moisture))
cat(sprintf("Total porosity:       %.2f\n", porosity))

title: Soil Bulk Density – Core Method
text:
13 Appendix B: Coarse Fragment Correction

If the core contains gravel or rock fragments larger than 2 mm, the bulk density of the fine-earth fraction (less than 2 mm) can be calculated by removing the coarse fragments from the oven-dried sample, weighing them separately, and estimating their volume:
\[
\rho_{b,\text{fine}} = \frac{M_{\text{dry}} - M_{\text{cf}}}{V_{\text{core}} - V_{\text{cf}}}
\]
where \(M_{\text{cf}}\) = mass of coarse fragments (g) and \(V_{\text{cf}}\) = volume of coarse fragments (cm3), estimated by water displacement or by dividing \(M_{\text{cf}}\) by an assumed rock density (typically 2.65 g/cm3). The water-displacement method for estimating coarse-fragment volume is preferred when fragment shapes are irregular (Page-Dumroese et al., 1999).
Record the coarse fragment mass fraction and report whether the bulk density value refers to the whole soil or the fine-earth fraction.

title: Soil Temperature Profiles
text:
This SOP describes procedures for measuring soil temperature at multiple depths to construct soil temperature profiles. Soil temperature influences biological activity (microbial respiration, root growth, seed germination), chemical reaction rates (nutrient mineralization, decomposition), and physical processes (evaporation, frost heave) (Ham, 2002; Hillel, 1998). Temperature profiles are especially relevant for photovoltaic panel studies, where shading alters the soil thermal regime.
The amplitude and phase lag of diurnal and seasonal temperature waves attenuate with depth according to the thermal diffusivity of the soil profile, making multi-depth measurement essential for characterizing subsurface energy budgets (Hillel, 1998). Soil temperature also governs rates of microbial respiration and nitrogen mineralization, with Q10 values typically ranging from 2 to 3 for the biologically active zone (Onwuka & Mang, 2018). When continuous monitoring is not feasible, air-temperature-based models can be used to estimate soil temperature, but these require site-specific calibration (Zheng et al., 1993).

title: Soil Temperature Profiles
text:
4 Definitions

Diurnal temperature variation: The cycle of soil temperature change over a 24-hour period driven by solar radiation and radiative cooling; amplitude decreases with depth and is nearly zero below about 50 cm in most soils.
Horizon temperature: The temperature measured at a defined soil depth corresponding to a specific genetic horizon (e.g., A, B, C); used to characterize the thermal environment of the root zone and microbial communities.
Soil temperature: The thermal energy state of the soil, expressed in °C; controls rates of microbial activity, organic matter decomposition, plant root growth, and soil gas fluxes.
Temperature gradient: The rate of change in temperature with depth (°C cm-1); drives heat flux between soil layers and between the soil surface and the atmosphere.
Temperature profile: A set of soil temperature measurements taken at multiple depths simultaneously or sequentially at a single location; used to characterize heat storage, heat flux, and seasonal thermal dynamics.
Thermistor: A temperature sensor whose electrical resistance changes predictably with temperature; commonly used in data loggers for continuous soil temperature monitoring; requires calibration against a traceable reference thermometer.
Thermocouple: A temperature sensor composed of two dissimilar metals joined at a measuring junction; produces a small voltage proportional to the temperature difference between the junction and a reference; used in handheld soil thermometers.

title: Soil Temperature Profiles
text:
9 Procedure: Method A – Handheld Probe

9.1 Prepare Depth Guide Marks
Before going to the field, mark each measurement depth directly on the probe. The temperature sensor is at the tip of the probe, so each mark is placed at the target depth measured from the tip. In the field, push the probe in until the mark for the target depth is level with the soil surface.



Target Depth
Mark Distance from Tip




5 cm
5 cm


10 cm
10 cm


20 cm
20 cm



Use a permanent marker, a wrap of tape, or a heat-shrink band at each depth. Verify the marks against a ruler before each field season, since tape and marker can shift or wear off with use.




9.2 Select Measurement Locations

Navigate to the predetermined sampling location and record GPS coordinates
Select a representative spot with undisturbed soil surface
Gently brush away surface litter without disturbing the mineral soil



9.3 Take Measurements

If the soil is hard, use the nail and hammer to make a pilot hole to the target depth. Make the hole the same diameter as the probe to ensure good thermal contact.
Insert the probe and gently push until the mark for the target depth is level with the soil surface
Wait at least 2 minutes for the probe to equilibrate with the soil. Equilibration time depends on the thermal conductivity of the soil and the thermal mass of the probe; dry sandy soils may require 5 minutes or longer (Ham & Senock, 1992).
Read the temperature every 1 minute until two consecutive readings are within 0.5 C of each other
Record the stabilized temperature, depth, time, and location on the data sheet
Remove the probe and repeat at the next depth in the same hole (work from shallowest to deepest)
Move to the next measurement location







ImportantEquilibration Is Essential



Do not rush readings. An un-equilibrated probe will read too warm in cool soil and too cool in warm soil. Two minutes is the minimum; 3–5 minutes may be needed in dry or very cold soil.




9.4 Timing

For comparable data across sites, complete all measurements within 1 hour of local solar noon (approximately 12:00–13:00 PST)
For diurnal profiles, measure at consistent intervals (e.g., every 2–3 hours over a 24-hour period)
Record the exact time of each measurement

title: Soil Temperature Profiles
text:
10 Procedure: Method B – Datalogger System

10.1 Sensor Installation

Select a representative location and record GPS coordinates
Dig a narrow trench or pit to the deepest sensor depth on one side of the measurement point (do not disturb the soil column directly above the sensors)
Insert sensors horizontally into the undisturbed soil wall at each target depth, pressing firmly to ensure good thermal contact
Backfill the trench carefully, maintaining the original soil layering as much as possible
Route cables through PVC conduit to the datalogger enclosure
Mark the sensor locations with discreet, flush-to-ground markers









NoteSettling Period



Soil disturbed during installation needs time to return to representative thermal conditions. Allow a minimum of 48 hours before using data for analysis. One to two weeks is ideal for deep sensors.




10.2 Datalogger Programming

Connect all sensors to the datalogger following the wiring diagram for your sensor type
Program the datalogger to scan sensors at the desired interval (typically every 1–5 minutes)
Configure storage to record averages at 15-minute or 30-minute intervals
Set the datalogger clock to local standard time (do not use daylight saving time)
Verify readings against a calibrated handheld thermometer at 5 cm depth



10.3 Data Download

Visit the station at regular intervals (weekly to monthly, depending on battery and storage capacity)
Connect a laptop and download data using the manufacturer’s software
Check for gaps, sensor failures, or anomalous readings in the field
Transfer data to the project database within 48 hours

title: Soil Temperature Profiles
text:
11 Calibration

11.1 Handheld Probes

Prepare an ice-water bath (crushed ice + deionized water, stirred); this should read 0.0 C
Insert the probe and allow to equilibrate for 3 minutes
Record the reading; it should be within 0.5 C of 0.0 C
If outside tolerance, adjust or replace the thermometer
Calibrate before each field season and after any suspected damage

The ice-point calibration is a single-point check; for research requiring higher accuracy, a two-point calibration (ice-water and warm-water bath at approximately 40 C) is recommended (Ham, 2002).






TipType K Probes



Type K probes require a multi-point calibration to build their error-correction formula. Measure the reading at a minimum of three temperatures: an ice bath (approximately 0 C), room temperature, and a heating plate at approximately 50 C. Use a reference thermometer at each point and fit the correction from the paired readings (see Data Correction).




11.2 Datalogger Sensors

Before installation, place all sensors in a well-stirred water bath
Record readings from all sensors simultaneously
All sensors should agree within 0.3 C
Document any offsets and apply corrections in post-processing if needed

title: Soil Temperature Profiles
text:
12 Quality Control

Calibrate all thermometers and sensors before each field season
For handheld measurements, take readings at a minimum of 3 replicate locations per plot
Record the time of every measurement (soil temperature changes throughout the day)
For datalogger systems, inspect data weekly for drift, gaps, and anomalous values
Include a surface air temperature measurement alongside soil temperatures for context
Photograph each measurement location at the start of each season

13.1 Handheld Data
Enter data from field sheets into the project spreadsheet within 48 hours. Required fields:

Date, time (local standard time), site, plot ID, observer

13.2 Data Correction
The handheld probes carry a systematic measurement error, so raw readings must be corrected before analysis. Apply the calibration formula matched to the specific probe, cable, and reader combination; the corrections below are valid only for the equipment pairings listed. Let \(T_\text{raw}\) be the reading in °C and \(T_\text{corr}\) the corrected temperature in °C.
RTD Probe 1
\[T_\text{corr} = 1.160\,T_\text{raw} - 13.23\]
RTD Probe 2
\[T_\text{corr} = 1.167\,T_\text{raw} - 14.609\]
Type T Probe 1 (Cable 1, reader T819)
\[T_\text{corr} = 1.028\,T_\text{raw} - 8.797\]
Type T Probe 3 (Cable 2, reader T299)
\[T_\text{corr} = 1.004\,T_\text{raw} - 8.121\]
Record which probe, cable, and reader were used for each measurement so the correct formula can be applied during processing. Type K probes must be calibrated and corrected using a formula derived from their own three-point calibration (see Calibration).


13.3 Datalogger Data

Flag and document any corrections (sensor offsets, gap-filling)
Store processed data in the project database with metadata

title: Soil Respiration Chambers (Field Static Chamber Method)
text:
This SOP describes the deployment and operation of static (closed, non-flow-through) chambers for manual measurement of soil CO2 efflux in the field. Static chambers are a simple, low-cost method for quantifying soil respiration across treatments, land uses, or seasonal gradients when the Picarro CRDS automated system (SOP-F504) is not available or when additional spatial replication is needed. The method captures headspace gas samples at timed intervals, which are analyzed for CO2 concentration using a portable infrared gas analyzer (IRGA), syringe samples returned to the lab, or soda-lime traps (Hutchinson & Mosier, 1981; Livingston & Hutchinson, 1995; Parkin & Venterea, 2012).
The static chamber method remains one of the most widely used approaches for point-scale soil CO2 flux measurement because of its simplicity and low cost, though it is subject to known biases from headspace concentration buildup and pressure artifacts (Pumpanen et al., 2004; Rochette & Eriksen-Hamel, 2005). At a global scale, soil respiration represents one of the largest fluxes in the terrestrial carbon cycle, and small changes can have significant implications for atmospheric CO2 concentrations (Davidson et al., 2000; Raich & Schlesinger, 1992).

title: Soil Respiration Chambers (Field Static Chamber Method)
text:

Static chambers are a simple, low-cost method for quantifying soil respiration across treatments, land uses, or seasonal gradients when the Picarro CRDS automated system (SOP-F504) is not available or when additional spatial replication is needed. title: Soil Respiration Chambers (Field Static Chamber Method)
text:
4 Definitions

Basal soil respiration: CO2 efflux from undisturbed soil at ambient temperature and moisture without addition of labile substrate; reflects the combined metabolic activity of the soil microbial community and root respiration.
CO2 efflux (soil respiration rate): The flux of CO2 from the soil surface to the atmosphere, expressed in µmol CO2 m-2 s-1 or g C m-2 d-1; the primary field measurement made with a closed or open dynamic chamber system.
Closed dynamic chamber: A chamber placed over the soil surface in which headspace CO2 concentration rises over time as CO2 is released from the soil; flux is calculated from the rate of concentration increase, chamber volume, and collar area.
Collar: A short ring of PVC or metal inserted several centimeters into the soil before measurement to create a gas-tight seal with the chamber; installed at least 24 hours before measurements to allow soil disturbance effects to dissipate.
Heterotrophic respiration: CO2 produced by soil microorganisms decomposing organic matter; one component of total soil respiration along with autotrophic (root and rhizosphere) respiration.
LI-COR analyzer (LI-8100A / LI-8150): A portable infrared gas analyzer system used for automated soil CO2 flux measurement; calculates flux from the exponential rise in headspace CO2 concentration over a defined measurement period.
Q10 coefficient: The factor by which soil respiration rate increases for a 10 °C rise in temperature; typically 1.5–3.5 for mineral soils; used to temperature-normalize measurements made under different field conditions.
Rhizosphere priming: Enhanced decomposition of soil organic matter stimulated by root exudates; inflates field respiration measurements relative to bare-soil or root-exclusion treatments.

Heat: Southern California field sites can exceed 40 C. Metal chambers become extremely hot in direct sunlight; handle with gloves.
Chemical: Soda-lime (NaOH/Ca(OH)2) is corrosive and causes burns on skin and eye contact. Concentrated NaOH solutions used for soda-lime traps are hazardous. Handle with gloves and safety glasses.

title: Soil Respiration Chambers (Field Static Chamber Method)
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Collar Installation

Install PVC or metal collars into the soil to a depth of approximately 5 cm at least 24 hours (preferably 48 hours) before the first measurement to allow the soil to recover from disturbance.
Do not sever major roots during installation; if roots are encountered, reposition slightly.
Measure and record the collar inside diameter and the height of the collar above the soil surface on at least two sides. These dimensions are needed to calculate headspace volume.



7.2 Chamber Deployment

Record the start time, soil temperature (at 5 cm depth), and soil moisture at each collar location.
Place the chamber lid on the collar, ensuring a gas-tight seal (foam gasket compressed or water trough filled).
If using the syringe method, collect a headspace sample immediately after sealing (time zero), then at regular intervals (e.g., 10, 20, 30, and 40 minutes). The choice of deployment interval (typically 20–45 minutes) represents a trade-off: shorter deployments reduce the concentration-feedback bias that suppresses diffusion as headspace CO2 rises, but longer deployments provide a more detectable concentration change in low-flux soils (Hutchinson & Mosier, 1981; Pumpanen et al., 2004).
If using a portable IRGA, connect the chamber to the analyzer and record CO2 concentration continuously or at 1-minute intervals.
If using soda-lime traps, weigh the pre-dried soda-lime, place it inside the sealed chamber, and retrieve it after a fixed deployment period (typically 24 hours). Re-dry and reweigh to determine CO2 absorbed.



7.3 Ending the Measurement

Remove the chamber lid at the end of the measurement period.
Record the end time.
Transfer syringe samples to evacuated vials (Exetainers) for transport to the lab if not using IRGA.

title: Soil Respiration Chambers (Field Static Chamber Method)
text:
8 Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

8.1 Flux Calculation
Linear method (syringe or IRGA):
\[
F = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta t} \times \frac{V}{A} \times \frac{P}{RT}
\]
where \(F\) = CO2 flux (micromol m-2 s-1), \(\Delta C / \Delta t\) = rate of change in headspace CO2 concentration (ppm s-1), \(V\) = headspace volume (m3), \(A\) = collar area (m2), \(P\) = atmospheric pressure (Pa), \(R\) = ideal gas constant (8.314 J mol-1 K-1), and \(T\) = air temperature (K).
Soda-lime method:
\[
F = \frac{(M_f - M_i) \times 1.69}{A \times t}
\]
where \(M_f\) and \(M_i\) are the final and initial soda-lime masses (g), 1.69 is the stoichiometric correction factor, \(A\) = collar area (m2), and \(t\) = deployment time (hours).


8.2 QC Requirements

Deploy at least three replicate chambers per treatment or land use.
Inspect collar seals before each deployment. Soil settling or animal disturbance can break the seal.
Record soil temperature and moisture alongside every flux measurement; these are the primary drivers of soil respiration. Soil respiration typically increases exponentially with temperature, with Q10 values of 2–3 (Bond-Lamberty & Thomson, 2010; Raich & Schlesinger, 1992). Reporting concurrent soil temperature and moisture allows flux values to be normalized or modeled across campaigns and sites.
Reject any measurement where the R2 of the linear regression (concentration vs. time) is below 0.90, unless the flux is near zero.
Avoid measuring during or immediately after rainfall, as water pooling on the collar disrupts gas exchange.

title: Air Temperature Monitoring with Portable Sensors
text:
This SOP describes the deployment, calibration, data retrieval, and post-processing of low-cost portable sensor networks for ambient air temperature and relative humidity monitoring. Three sensor platforms are covered: Maxim/Analog Devices Thermochron iButton loggers, Onset HOBO data loggers, and Raspberry Pi single-board computers with BME280 environmental sensor modules.
Dense networks of inexpensive air temperature sensors enable studies of urban heat island (UHI) effects, microclimatic gradients beneath photovoltaic arrays, canopy-vs.-open temperature contrasts, and diurnal and seasonal temperature variability at spatial resolutions not achievable with conventional weather stations (Chapman et al., 2015; Muller et al., 2013). The UHI is one of the most thoroughly documented examples of inadvertent human modification of local climate, driven by impervious surfaces, waste heat, reduced vegetation, and altered radiative and convective energy exchange (Oke et al., 2017; Voogt & Oke, 2003).
When designing a sensor network, characterizing the land cover at each site using the Local Climate Zone (LCZ) framework provides a standardized basis for comparing UHI intensities across cities and studies (Stewart & Oke, 2012).

text:
4 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Working at height: Mounting sensors at 1.5–2.0 m on poles or structures may require a stepladder. Follow ladder safety protocols.
Traffic: Some monitoring locations are near roadways. Wear high-visibility vests.
Heat exposure: Deployment and retrieval in summer in the Inland Empire involves significant heat risk. Carry water, work in pairs, and schedule field work for early morning when possible.
Electrical: Raspberry Pi units use low-voltage USB power. Do not expose connections to rain or standing water without weatherproof enclosures.




4.1 Required PPE

Closed-toe shoes
High-visibility vest (if near roadways)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
Safety glasses (during mounting/drilling)

title: Air Temperature Monitoring with Portable Sensors
text:
5 Definitions

Urban Heat Island (UHI): The phenomenon whereby urban areas experience higher air temperatures than surrounding rural areas due to impervious surfaces, waste heat, reduced vegetation, and altered energy balance. UHI intensity (\(\Delta T_{\text{UHI}}\)) is quantified as the difference between an urban and a rural reference site at a given time (Oke et al., 2017).
Local Climate Zone (LCZ): A classification system that describes the physical properties of the local environment (building density, height, surface cover, land use) at scales relevant to urban temperature variation. LCZ types range from compact high-rise (LCZ 1) to scattered trees (LCZ B), and provide a standardized framework for describing monitoring sites in UHI studies (Stewart & Oke, 2012).
Radiation shield: A louvered or ventilated housing that protects a temperature sensor from direct and reflected solar radiation while allowing ambient air to flow past the sensor. Without shielding, sensors can read 5–15 C above true air temperature in direct sun (Hubbart et al., 2005; Terando et al., 2017).
BME280: A Bosch environmental sensor measuring temperature, relative humidity, and barometric pressure. Used with Raspberry Pi platforms in the EA Program sensor network.
iButton: A coin-sized temperature (and optionally RH) data logger manufactured by Maxim/Analog Devices (Thermochron series).
HOBO: A family of portable data loggers manufactured by Onset Computer Corporation.
Collocation: The practice of placing multiple sensors at the same location for a period to assess inter-sensor agreement and identify systematic offsets. Collocation is the primary calibration strategy for dense low-cost sensor networks (Meier et al., 2017).
Calibration offset: A systematic difference between a sensor’s reading and a known reference, determined during collocation and applied as a correction to field data.
Data completeness: The percentage of expected readings actually recorded during a deployment period. A minimum of 75% completeness (18 of 24 hours per day) is required for daily summaries.

text:
8 Radiation Shielding






ImportantRadiation Shields Are Mandatory



Unshielded sensors exposed to direct or reflected solar radiation can read 5–15 C higher than true air temperature. Every deployed sensor must be housed in a radiation shield (Hubbart et al., 2005; Terando et al., 2017).

title: Air Temperature Monitoring with Portable Sensors
text:
9 Calibration

9.1 Ice-Bath Calibration (Single-Point Check)

Prepare an ice-water bath: fill an insulated container with crushed ice and deionized water, stir for 2 minutes
Submerge the sensor (in a waterproof sleeve for iButtons, or using a sealed bag for non-waterproof units)
Wait 5 minutes for equilibration
The sensor should read 0.0 \(\pm\) 0.5 C. Record the reading.
If outside tolerance, note the offset; sensors with offsets greater than 1.0 C should be replaced.



9.2 Room-Temperature Inter-Comparison (Collocation)

Place all sensors to be deployed together in a shaded, well-mixed indoor environment for at least 24 hours
Calculate the mean temperature across all sensors for each timestep. Each sensor’s offset is its deviation from the group mean.
Record offsets in a calibration log file: data/calibration/offsets_YYYYMMDD.csv
Apply these offsets as corrections during data processing (Section 11). Collocation under controlled conditions is the most practical calibration approach for networks of 10 or more sensors (Meier et al., 2017).

title: Air Temperature Monitoring with Portable Sensors
text:
10 Deployment

10.1 Site Selection and Documentation
Select monitoring sites to represent the range of land cover types and microclimates relevant to the research question. For UHI studies, sample across multiple LCZ types (e.g., compact low-rise, open low-rise, large low-rise, scattered trees, dense trees) (Stewart & Oke, 2012).
At each site, record:

GPS coordinates per SOP-F006
Mounting height (standard: 1.5–2.0 m above ground level)
Shield type and orientation
Land cover within 50 m radius (impervious %, tree canopy %, grass %)
LCZ type (see Stewart & Oke (2012) for classification guide)
Nearest road (distance and type)
Sky view factor (estimated or photographed)
Sensor serial number and platform type



10.2 Mounting

Mount the radiation shield on a pole, post, fence, or structure at 1.5–2.0 m height. Ensure the shield is not directly above a paved surface, air conditioning exhaust, or heat-radiating wall.
Place the sensor inside the shield, ensuring the sensing element is centered within the shield stack.
For Raspberry Pi units, route the power cable through the base of the enclosure. Secure with cable ties.
Photograph the installation and record all metadata.
Record metadata as above.

title: Air Temperature Monitoring with Portable Sensors
text:
12 Data Processing

12.1 Import and Standardize


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Example: import iButton CSV
raw <- read_csv("data/raw/site01_ibutton_ABC123.csv",
                skip = 14) %>%
  rename(timestamp = 1, temp_c = 2) %>%
  mutate(
    timestamp = mdy_hms(timestamp, tz = "America/Los_Angeles"),
    sensor_id = "ABC123",
    site_id   = "site01",
    platform  = "iButton"
  )

# Apply calibration offset (from Section 9)
offsets <- read_csv("data/calibration/offsets_YYYYMMDD.csv")

raw <- raw %>%
  left_join(offsets %>% select(sensor_id, offset), by = "sensor_id") %>%
  mutate(temp_corrected = temp_c - offset)




12.2 Quality Control


Code
raw <- raw %>%
  mutate(
    qc_flag = case_when(
      temp_corrected < -10 | temp_corrected > 55 ~ "out_of_range",
      temp_corrected == lag(temp_corrected) &
        temp_corrected == lag(temp_corrected, 2) &
        temp_corrected == lag(temp_corrected, 3)   ~ "stuck_sensor",
      abs(temp_corrected - lag(temp_corrected)) > 10 ~ "spike",
      TRUE ~ "valid"
    )
  )

count(raw, qc_flag)
clean <- raw %>% filter(qc_flag == "valid")




12.3 Hourly and Daily Summaries


Code
hourly <- clean %>%
  mutate(hour = floor_date(timestamp, "hour")) %>%
  group_by(site_id, sensor_id, hour) %>%
  summarize(
    temp_mean = mean(temp_corrected, na.rm = TRUE),
    temp_min  = min(temp_corrected, na.rm = TRUE),
    temp_max  = max(temp_corrected, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_obs     = n(),
    .groups   = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_obs >= 3)

daily <- hourly %>%
  mutate(date = as_date(hour)) %>%
  group_by(site_id, sensor_id, date) %>%
  summarize(
    t_mean = mean(temp_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    t_min  = min(temp_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    t_max  = max(temp_max, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_hours = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_hours >= 18)




12.4 Urban Heat Island Intensity
UHI intensity is typically calculated as the difference between an urban site and a rural (or least-developed) reference site (Oke et al., 2017):
\[
\Delta T_{\text{UHI}} = T_{\text{urban}} - T_{\text{rural}}
\]


Code
ref_site <- "site_rural01"

uhi <- hourly %>%
  select(site_id, hour, temp_mean) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = site_id, values_from = temp_mean) %>%
  mutate(across(-c(hour, all_of(ref_site)),
                ~ . - .data[[ref_site]],
                .names = "uhi_{.col}"))

title: Particulate Matter Sampling – Gravimetric Filter Method
text:
This procedure describes the collection of ambient particulate matter (PM) on pre-weighed filters using active (pump-based) samplers for subsequent gravimetric and/or chemical analysis. Gravimetric filter sampling provides a reference-quality mass concentration that can be used to validate or calibrate low-cost PM sensors (see SOP-F502) and to collect PM for compositional analysis (metals, ions, elemental/organic carbon) (Chow, 1995; US Environmental Protection Agency, 2017).
Ambient PM is a complex mixture of solid and liquid particles suspended in air, originating from both primary sources (combustion, dust, sea spray) and secondary formation (gas-to-particle conversion of sulfate, nitrate, and organic compounds) (Seinfeld & Pandis, 2016; poschl2005?). Gravimetric filter sampling remains the reference standard for PM mass measurement because it directly weighs the collected material, avoiding the indirect assumptions inherent in optical or beta-attenuation methods (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2017).
This SOP covers medium- and low-volume filter-based samplers operated by EA Program personnel. It does not cover Federal Reference Method (FRM) high-volume samplers operated by regulatory agencies.

title: Particulate Matter Sampling – Gravimetric Filter Method
text:
4 Definitions

Particulate matter (PM): A mixture of solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in air, ranging in size from a few nanometers to tens of micrometers (Seinfeld & Pandis, 2016).
PM2.5: Particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter less than 2.5 \(\mu\)m (“fine particles”). Fine particles penetrate deep into the lungs and are associated with cardiovascular and respiratory health effects (solomon2001?).
PM10: Particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter less than 10 \(\mu\)m. Includes both fine (PM2.5) and coarse (2.5–10 \(\mu\)m) fractions.
Gravimetric analysis: Determination of PM mass by weighing a filter before and after exposure, under controlled temperature and humidity conditions (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2017).
Size-selective inlet: An impactor or cyclone that removes particles above a defined aerodynamic diameter cutpoint (e.g., 2.5 or 10 \(\mu\)m) before they reach the filter.
PTFE filter: Polytetrafluoroethylene (Teflon) membrane filter. Chemically inert, hydrophobic, and low in artifact mass; the standard substrate for gravimetric PM analysis.
Quartz fiber filter: A filter made of quartz (SiO2) fibers, used when thermal-optical analysis for elemental and organic carbon is planned. Must be pre-fired at 500 C for 4 hours to remove organic artifacts.
Filter conditioning: Equilibrating filters at controlled temperature (20–25 C) and humidity (30–40% RH) in a desiccator for at least 24 hours before weighing. Conditioning removes adsorbed water that would bias the mass measurement.
Field blank: A conditioned filter transported to the field site, briefly exposed to ambient conditions without running the pump, then resealed and returned for weighing. Field blank mass quantifies contamination introduced during handling and transport.
Flow rate: The volumetric rate at which air is drawn through the sampler, typically expressed in L/min. The flow rate must match the design specification of the size-selective inlet (e.g., 5 L/min for a MiniVol PM2.5 impactor).
Chemical speciation: Analysis of the chemical composition of collected PM (e.g., metals by XRF or ICP-MS, ions by IC, carbon fractions by thermal-optical analysis) (chow2015?).

Lifting: Medium-volume samplers (e.g., MiniVol TAS) and batteries can be heavy (10–15 kg). Use proper lifting technique.
Heat: Enclosures and pumps can overheat in direct sunlight during Inland Empire summers.

title: Particulate Matter Sampling – Gravimetric Filter Method
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Filter Conditioning and Pre-Weighing

Place unused filters in a desiccator at controlled temperature (20–25 C) and humidity (30–40% RH) for at least 24 hours (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2017)
Weigh each filter on the microbalance to the nearest 0.01 mg. Record the filter ID and tare weight.
Weigh each filter a second time (at least 1 hour later) to confirm stability. The two weights should agree within 0.015 mg.
Place the conditioned filter in a labeled Petri dish or cassette. Seal and transport in a cooler if traveling to a remote site.



7.2 Sampler Setup and Flow Calibration

Install the appropriate size-selective inlet (PM2.5 or PM10 impactor head) on the sampler
Load a blank filter cassette and connect the calibrated flow meter downstream of the filter holder
Start the pump and adjust the flow rate to the nominal design flow for the inlet (e.g., 5 L/min for a MiniVol PM2.5 impactor)
Record the calibrated flow rate, temperature, and barometric pressure. If the site is at a different elevation than the calibration location, apply a volumetric correction.
Remove the blank cassette and load the pre-weighed sample filter using forceps. Handle the filter only by its edges.



7.3 Deployment

Position the sampler with the inlet at 1.5–2 m above ground level, unobstructed by walls or overhangs (at least 2 m from any vertical surface)
Record the start date, start time, site ID, filter ID, GPS coordinates, and weather conditions
Start the sampler and verify that the pump is running
For 24-hour integrated samples, allow the sampler to run for 23–25 hours



7.4 Retrieval

Record the stop time and elapsed run time
Verify the flow rate with the calibrated flow meter before stopping the pump (post-sampling flow check). Record the value.
Stop the pump
Remove the filter cassette using gloves. Transfer the exposed filter to its labeled Petri dish using forceps. Do not touch the deposit surface.
Seal the Petri dish and place in a cooler for transport
Calculate the average flow rate: \(Q_{\text{avg}} = (Q_{\text{pre}}
+ Q_{\text{post}}) / 2\). If pre- and post-flow rates differ by more than 10%, flag the sample.



7.5 Post-Sampling Conditioning and Weighing

Condition the exposed filter in the same desiccator and at the same temperature/humidity as the pre-weighing step for at least 24 hours
Weigh the filter to the nearest 0.01 mg. Record the gross weight.
Repeat the weighing at least 1 hour later to confirm stability.
Calculate the net PM mass:

\[
m_{\text{PM}} = W_{\text{post}} - W_{\text{pre}}
\]

Calculate the PM concentration:

\[
C_{\text{PM}} (\mu\text{g/m}^3) = \frac{m_{\text{PM}} (\mu\text{g})}{Q_{\text{avg}} (\text{L/min}) \times t (\text{min})} \times 10^3
\]


7.6 Filter Archiving and Downstream Analysis

After gravimetric analysis, archive filters in sealed Petri dishes at room temperature (or at -20 C if chemical analysis is planned)
For elemental/organic carbon analysis, submit quartz filters to the analytical laboratory per their instructions
For metals analysis by XRF or ICP-MS, submit PTFE filters per SOP-L205 or SOP-L410
Chemical speciation of collected PM provides source apportionment data that complements the mass concentration measurement (chow2015?)

title: Particulate Matter Sampling – Gravimetric Filter Method
text:
8 Quality Control

Collect at least one field blank per sampling event: load a conditioned filter into a cassette, transport it to the site, open the cassette briefly (without running the pump), seal, and return to the lab for conditioning and weighing
Collect duplicate samples (co-located samplers) for at least 10% of sampling events. Duplicate PM concentrations should agree within 15%.
Verify the balance with NIST-traceable check weights at the start of each weighing session
Document pre- and post-sampling flow rates; flag samples where the difference exceeds 10%
Re-condition and re-weigh at least 10% of filters as laboratory duplicates; agreement should be within 0.015 mg
Negative net masses (post-weight less than pre-weight) can occur due to filter handling artifacts or volatile loss; flag and investigate these, but do not discard without documentation

title: Passive Air Samplers – Diffusion Tubes
text:
This procedure describes the deployment, retrieval, and documentation of passive (diffusion-based) air samplers for time-integrated measurement of gaseous air pollutants. Passive samplers require no pump or power supply: the target gas diffuses along a concentration gradient through a defined path length and is captured by a sorbent or reactive medium at the closed end of the tube. After a known exposure period, the sampler is sealed, returned to the laboratory, and analyzed to determine the time-weighted average ambient concentration (Cape, 2009; Palmes et al., 1976).
Common target analytes include nitrogen dioxide (NO2), ozone (O3), sulfur dioxide (SO2), ammonia (NH3), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Passive samplers are widely used in spatial surveys and community-based exposure studies because they are inexpensive, silent, and require no electricity, making dense network deployments feasible (Vardoulakis et al., 2005; martin2014?).
Passive diffusion tubes are subject to known biases from wind speed, temperature, and tube geometry that must be understood and managed through quality control (Plaisance et al., 2004; Tang et al., 2001). When operated according to harmonized protocols and validated against active reference methods, passive samplers can provide data suitable for regulatory screening and spatial mapping (hafkenscheid2009?).

title: Passive Air Samplers – Diffusion Tubes
text:
4 Definitions

Passive (diffusion) sampler: A device that collects a gaseous pollutant by molecular diffusion along a concentration gradient, without requiring a pump. The sampler relies on Fick’s first law of diffusion to relate the mass of analyte captured to the ambient concentration over the exposure period (Palmes et al., 1976).
Palmes tube: A cylindrical passive sampler (typically 7.1 cm long, 1.1 cm internal diameter) with a triethanolamine (TEA)-coated stainless steel grid at the closed end for NO2 collection. Originally described by Palmes et al. (1976).
Ogawa badge: A disk-shaped passive sampler with two collection pads separated by a diffusion barrier. Can be configured for NO2, O3, or SO2.
Radiello cartridge: A radial-symmetry passive sampler with a cylindrical diffusive body surrounding a sorbent cartridge. Used for VOCs (Carbograph sorbent), NH3 (acid-coated), and other gases.
Uptake rate: The rate at which the target analyte diffuses into the sampler, determined by the diffusion coefficient of the gas, the cross-sectional area, and the path length. Published uptake rates are specific to each sampler-analyte combination and are used to convert captured mass to ambient concentration.
Time-weighted average (TWA): The mean ambient concentration over the exposure period, calculated from the total mass captured and the exposure duration.
Shortening ratio: The effective reduction in diffusion path length caused by wind-induced turbulence at the open end of a Palmes tube, which increases the uptake rate and causes overestimation of ambient concentration in windy conditions (Tang et al., 2001).
Field blank: A sampler transported to the site, briefly opened and re-sealed without exposure, then returned to the lab. Field blank analyte mass quantifies contamination from handling, storage, and transport.
Triethanolamine (TEA): A viscous organic amine used as the absorbent medium for NO2 in Palmes tubes. TEA reacts with NO2 to form nitrite, which is subsequently analyzed by the Griess colorimetric reaction.
Fick’s first law: The principle that the flux of a gas through a still-air column is proportional to the concentration gradient and the diffusion coefficient:

\[
J = D \times \frac{A}{L} \times C
\]
where \(J\) = flux (mass/time), \(D\) = diffusion coefficient, \(A\) = cross-sectional area, \(L\) = path length, and \(C\) = ambient concentration (Palmes et al., 1976).

text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Sampler Selection
Select the sampler type based on the target analyte and exposure period:









Target Analyte
Sampler Type
Typical Exposure
Analytical Method




NO2
Palmes diffusion tube (TEA-coated grids)
1–4 weeks
Spectrophotometry (Griess reaction)

1–4 weeks

Note



The analytical laboratory typically prepares and supplies the samplers, pre-loaded with the appropriate sorbent. Confirm sampler type, handling instructions, and shipping requirements with the lab before each deployment.




7.2 Pre-Deployment

Keep sealed samplers refrigerated (4 C) until deployment day unless the analytical lab specifies otherwise
Assign a unique ID to each sampler and record it in the deployment log
Designate at least 2 field blanks per batch: samplers that travel to the site, are briefly unsealed (less than 30 seconds), re-sealed, and returned to the lab with the exposed samplers



7.3 Deployment

At the monitoring location, mount the rain shelter at a height of 2–3 m above ground, away from walls (at least 1 m), exhaust vents, and vegetation canopy
Remove the sampler from its sealed container, note the date and time, and attach the open end downward inside the rain shelter
Secure the sampler with clips or zip ties
Record in the field notebook: site ID, sampler ID, deployment date/time, GPS coordinates, mounting height, distance to nearest road, weather conditions, and any potential sources nearby
Photograph the installed sampler for documentation







ImportantWind Exposure



Palmes tubes are sensitive to wind speed: turbulence at the open end of the tube effectively shortens the diffusion path, increasing the uptake rate and overestimating the ambient concentration by 10–30% at exposed sites (Plaisance et al., 2004; Tang et al., 2001). Rain shelters provide partial wind screening, but sheltered or recessed mounting locations should be avoided because they restrict airflow and cause underestimation. The harmonized EU protocol recommends mounting in locations with moderate, representative air exchange (hafkenscheid2009?).




7.4 Exposure Period

The exposure period depends on the expected ambient concentration and the sampler’s capacity. Follow the analytical lab’s recommendation (typically 1–4 weeks for NO2 Palmes tubes).
Note any unusual events during the exposure period (wildfires, construction, power outages affecting nearby sources) in the field notebook.



7.5 Retrieval

Record the retrieval date and time in the field notebook
Remove the sampler from the shelter, immediately cap or seal it, and place in an airtight container or bag
Calculate the total exposure time in hours
Place sealed samplers in a cooler with ice packs for transport (if required by the analytical lab)
Retrieve and seal the field blanks in the same manner



7.6 Shipping to Analytical Laboratory

Pack sealed samplers securely with cushioning material in an insulated shipping container with ice packs (if heat-sensitive)
Include a chain of custody form listing all sampler IDs, site locations, deployment and retrieval dates/times, and total exposure hours
Ship via overnight courier or deliver in person to the analytical lab



7.7 Concentration Calculation
The analytical laboratory reports the mass of analyte captured on each sampler. The time-weighted average ambient concentration is calculated using Fick’s first law (Palmes et al., 1976):
\[
C = \frac{m}{D \times A / L \times t}
\]
where:

\(C\) = ambient concentration (\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) or ppb, after unit conversion)
\(m\) = mass of analyte on the sampler (\(\mu\)g)
\(D\) = molecular diffusion coefficient of the analyte in air (cm\(^2\)/s)
\(A\) = cross-sectional area of the diffusion path (cm\(^2\))
\(L\) = length of the diffusion path (cm)
\(t\) = exposure time (s)







Note



The analytical lab typically performs this calculation using published uptake rates for the specific sampler-analyte combination. Confirm which party is responsible for the calculation.

title: Passive Air Samplers – Diffusion Tubes
text:
8 Quality Control

Deploy at least 2 field blanks per batch (minimum 10% of total samplers). Field blank analyte mass should be below the method detection limit; if not, subtract the mean field blank mass from all samples.
Deploy co-located duplicate samplers at 10% of sites. Duplicates should agree within 20% for NO2 Palmes tubes (Cape, 2009). Duplicate agreement worse than 25% indicates handling problems or site-specific wind interference (Plaisance et al., 2004).
If collocating with an active reference sampler (chemiluminescence NO2 analyzer, UV O3 analyzer), compare the passive sampler result with the reference average over the same period. Palmes tubes for NO2 typically overestimate the reference by 10–30% at high-wind sites and underestimate at sheltered sites due to restricted airflow (Tang et al., 2001).
Document any site disturbances (construction, shelter damage, vandalism) that could affect results.
Archive field notebooks and chain of custody forms with the project data.

title: Weather Monitoring and Field Meteorology
text: This SOP describes procedures for recording weather and meteorological conditions during field activities. Documenting weather conditions at the time of sampling is essential for interpreting environmental data, identifying storm-driven events, establishing baseline climate conditions, and ensuring field safety. This SOP covers manual weather observations, use of portable weather instruments, and deployment of unattended data loggers for continuous monitoring (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).

title: Weather Monitoring and Field Meteorology

title: Weather Monitoring and Field Meteorology
text:
4 Definitions

Beaufort scale: A standardized scale (0–12) relating wind speed to observable effects on land or water; allows wind speed estimation without instruments; developed by Admiral Beaufort in 1805 and adopted as the international standard by the WMO (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
Cloud cover: The fraction of the sky obscured by clouds, expressed in tenths (0–10) or oktas (0–8); recorded with each manual weather observation (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
Dew point: The temperature to which air must be cooled at constant pressure for condensation to occur; a direct measure of absolute humidity; can be derived from wet-bulb temperature measurements (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
HOBOconnect: The Onset smartphone app used to program and download data from Bluetooth-enabled MX-series HOBO loggers (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021).
Kestrel meter: A handheld weather meter (Kestrel 3000 or similar) that simultaneously measures air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, barometric pressure, and derived quantities (dew point, wet-bulb temperature, heat index); the standard portable weather instrument for EA Program field use.
Radiation shield: A ventilated white housing that surrounds a temperature or humidity sensor to prevent direct solar radiation from inflating measured air temperatures; mandatory for any sensor exposed to sunlight (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
Relative humidity (RH): The ratio of actual water vapor pressure to saturation vapor pressure at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage; affects evapotranspiration, dew deposition, and physical and biological processes at field sites (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
Screen height: The standard height of 1.5 m above ground level for air temperature and humidity measurements; specified by the WMO to ensure comparability between stations and with published meteorological data (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
Sling psychrometer: A pair of wet-bulb and dry-bulb thermometers mounted on a frame that is swung to ventilate the sensors; used to determine relative humidity from the wet-bulb depression; a reliable low-cost alternative to electronic sensors.
WMO (World Meteorological Organization): The United Nations agency responsible for international meteorological and hydrological standards; its Guide to Meteorological Instruments and Methods of Observation (WMO-No. 8) is the authoritative reference for field measurement practice (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).

title: Weather Monitoring and Field Meteorology
text:
5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Lightning: Cease all field activities and seek shelter in a vehicle or enclosed structure when lightning is observed. Wait at least 30 minutes after the last lightning strike before resuming.
Heat: Southern California field sites can exceed 40 °C. Carry adequate water, take shade breaks, and monitor for heat-related illness.
Wind: High winds can topple tripod-mounted instruments and create hazardous conditions near exposed ridgelines or water bodies.
Flooding: Rapidly changing weather can cause flash flooding in Southern California canyons and channels. Monitor upstream conditions and have an evacuation route planned.

7.3 Deploying Portable Data Loggers

Select a deployment location representative of site conditions and unlikely to be disturbed by people, animals, or flooding.
Mount temperature and humidity loggers inside a radiation shield at 1.5 m above ground per WMO screen height standards (World Meteorological Organization, 2018). Secure to a tripod, post, or tree.
Mount rain gauges on a level surface with no overhead obstructions. The gauge orifice should be approximately 1 m above ground.
Program the logger using the HOBOconnect app or HOBOware software per SOP-F204 (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021):

Logging interval: typically 5 or 15 minutes
Start mode: delayed start
Time zone: Pacific Time

Record in the field notebook: logger serial number, GPS coordinates, deployment date and time, logging interval, sensor height.
Photograph the deployed logger with surrounding context.



7.4 Retrieving Data from Loggers

Connect to the logger via Bluetooth (HOBOconnect) or USB cable (Onset Computer Corporation, 2021).
Download the data and save using the naming convention: YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_LoggerSN_weather.csv
Do not clear the logger memory until you have verified the file contains the expected date range.
Upload the raw data file to the project GitHub repository under data/weather/ within 48 hours.



7.5 Using Online Weather Data
When on-site instruments are unavailable, supplement field observations with data from nearby weather stations. Preferred sources for Southern California:

title: Weather Monitoring and Field Meteorology
text:
8 Quality Control

Cross-check manually recorded air temperature against the nearest reliable weather station (NWS or CIMIS). Discrepancies greater than 3 °C at similar elevation and time should be investigated (World Meteorological Organization, 2018).
Inspect data loggers for drift by deploying two loggers side by side for at least 24 hours once per year. Temperature readings should agree within 0.5 °C; humidity within 5%.
Check rain gauge calibration at least once per year by pouring a known volume of water through the gauge and comparing the logged total to the expected value.
Flag any suspicious data (e.g., sudden temperature jumps, constant humidity at 100% for days) during data review and note the issue in the project data log.

title: Vegetation Transect Surveys
text: This SOP describes field procedures for conducting vegetation transect surveys using three common methods: line-point intercept (LPI), line intercept (LI), and quadrat (cover class) sampling. These methods quantify plant species composition, percent cover, and community structure across field sites and form the basis for vegetation monitoring, ecological assessment, and restoration evaluation (Bonham, 2013; Kent, 2012; mueller-dombois1974?).

title: Vegetation Transect Surveys
text: This SOP describes field procedures for conducting vegetation transect surveys using three common methods: line-point intercept (LPI), line intercept (LI), and quadrat (cover class) sampling. These methods quantify plant species composition, percent cover, and community structure across field sites and form the basis for vegetation monitoring, ecological assessment, and restoration evaluation (Bonham, 2013; Kent, 2012; mueller-dombois1974?).

title: Vegetation Transect Surveys
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Terrestrial vegetation surveys at all EA Program field sites, including the Bernard Field Station, Pomona College Farm, the Pit, restoration sites, and photovoltaic panel study areas
Does not apply to: Aquatic or submerged vegetation surveys; tree-only forest inventory (DBH-based methods; see SOP-F604); remote sensing vegetation analysis
Location: All EA Program field sites

title: Vegetation Transect Surveys
text:
3 Definitions

Percent cover: The proportion of the ground surface covered by the vertical projection of the aerial parts of a plant species, expressed as a percentage. Cover is the standard metric for characterizing non-woody vegetation communities because it integrates plant size and density into a single measure (Bonham, 2013).
Line-point intercept (LPI): A method that estimates cover by recording what a vertically lowered pin contacts at fixed intervals along a transect. Originally described by Levy & Madden (1933), LPI produces objective, repeatable cover estimates with minimal observer bias (Herrick et al., 2005).
Line intercept (LI): A method that measures the length of transect tape intercepted by the canopy of each species. Best suited for shrubs and other plants with clearly defined canopy boundaries.
Quadrat: A fixed-area frame (typically 1 m x 1 m) within which percent cover is visually estimated for each species. Visual estimation introduces more observer subjectivity than point-based methods but permits rapid assessment and better detection of rare species (Daubenmire, 1959; God’inez-’Alvarez et al., 2009).
Daubenmire cover class: A categorical scale for estimating cover within quadrats: 1 (0–5%), 2 (5–25%), 3 (25–50%), 4 (50–75%), 5 (75–95%), 6 (95–100%). The midpoint of each class is used in calculations (Daubenmire, 1959).
Top hit / lower hit: In LPI, the “top hit” is the first species the pin contacts as it descends through the canopy; subsequent contacts with other species or canopy layers are “lower hits.” Recording both allows multi-layer canopy analysis.
Species richness: The total number of species recorded in a defined area. Richness is strongly influenced by plot size and sampling effort (wilson2012?).
Voucher specimen: A pressed, dried, and identified plant specimen archived for verification of field identifications. See Section 9.
Basal cover: The proportion of ground surface occupied by the base (stem or root crown) of a plant, as distinct from foliar cover. Basal cover is more stable than foliar cover across seasons and is sometimes used for perennial grass monitoring (Herrick et al., 2005).

TipChoosing a Method



For most EA Program projects in southern California grasslands and shrublands, line-point intercept is the default method because it minimizes observer bias in cover estimation (God’inez-’Alvarez et al., 2009; Herrick et al., 2005). title: Vegetation Transect Surveys
text:
9 Procedure

9.1 Survey Timing
Conduct vegetation surveys during the peak growing season for the target community. In southern California:

Grasslands and annual forbs: March through May
Coastal sage scrub: April through June
Riparian: June through August

Consistency in timing across years is essential for detecting temporal changes (symstad2008?). Surveys conducted outside the peak window will underestimate cover for deciduous and annual species.


9.2 Transect Layout

Determine transect locations using the project sampling design (random, stratified random, or systematic placement within habitat zones). The choice of sampling design affects the inferences that can be drawn from the data; random or stratified random designs support unbiased estimation of population-level cover, while systematic designs maximize spatial coverage but can coincide with periodic landscape features (Kent, 2012).
Navigate to the starting point and record GPS coordinates
Establish the transect bearing using a compass (typically perpendicular to environmental gradients, e.g., slope, moisture, or distance from structures)
Anchor the 0 m end of the measuring tape with a chaining pin
Walk out the tape to the desired length (typically 50 m), keeping it taut and as straight as possible
Anchor the far end with a second chaining pin
Photograph the transect from both ends







NotePermanent Transects



For long-term monitoring, mark transect endpoints with permanent markers (capped rebar driven flush with the ground, GPS coordinates recorded to sub-meter accuracy). Take a compass bearing and distance to at least two nearby permanent features for relocation.




9.3 Method A: Line-Point Intercept
This method estimates percent cover by recording what a vertical sampling pin contacts at regular intervals along the transect. The method was originally developed by Levy & Madden (1933) for pasture analysis and has since become the standard for rangeland and grassland monitoring (Herrick et al., 2005).

Begin at the 0 m end of the transect; always work from the same side of the tape
At each sampling point (every 0.5 m or 1 m, depending on project design), lower the sampling pin vertically through the vegetation canopy directly over the tape
Record each plant species the pin contacts as it descends from the canopy to the ground (top hit is the first species contacted; record all species for multi-layer canopies)
If the pin does not contact any vegetation, record the ground surface type: bare soil, litter, rock, moss/lichen, or other
Record the height (cm) of the tallest species contacted at each point
Advance to the next sampling point and repeat







ImportantPin Angle Matters



The pin must be lowered vertically (plumb). Tilting the pin even slightly increases the probability of contacting vegetation and inflates cover estimates. Some protocols use a pin guide or frame to enforce verticality.


Calculations:
\[
\text{Percent cover for species } i = \frac{\text{Number of hits for species } i}{\text{Total number of sampling points}} \times 100
\]
Total cover may exceed 100% when canopy layers overlap. The number of sampling points required depends on the diversity and patchiness of the vegetation; 100 points per 50 m transect (0.5 m interval) is standard for diverse grasslands, while 50 points (1 m interval) may suffice in low-diversity or homogeneous stands (Elzinga et al., 1998).


9.4 Method B: Line Intercept
This method measures the length of transect tape intercepted by each plant species. Best suited for shrubs and plants with distinct canopy boundaries (Bonham, 2013).

Begin at the 0 m end of the transect
Walk slowly along the tape, noting where each plant canopy begins and ends (intercepts the tape)
Record the species, the start point (cm), and the end point (cm) on the data sheet
If a gap occurs within a single plant’s canopy that is longer than the canopy width on either side, treat it as two separate intercepts
Record gaps between plants as the appropriate ground cover type

Calculations:
\[
\text{Percent cover for species } i = \frac{\sum \text{intercept lengths for species } i}{\text{Total transect length}} \times 100
\]


9.5 Method C: Quadrat (Cover Class)
This method uses visual estimates of cover within fixed-area plots placed at intervals along the transect (Daubenmire, 1959).

Place quadrats at predetermined intervals along the transect (e.g., every 5 m or 10 m), or at random distances
Ensure enough distance between quadrats for them to be independent sampling units (typically at least 5 m apart)
For each quadrat, identify every plant species present
Estimate percent cover for each species using the modified Daubenmire cover classes:

Also record percent cover of bare ground, litter, and rock
Note the maximum vegetation height (cm) in each quadrat
Photograph each quadrat from directly above

Visual estimation of cover is inherently subjective and sensitive to observer experience, viewing angle, and vegetation height; training with known-cover reference images or calibration frames improves consistency but does not eliminate inter-observer variability (Bonham, 2013; God’inez-’Alvarez et al., 2009).

11 Quality Control

Two observers should independently estimate cover for at least 10% of quadrats to assess observer agreement. Inter-observer variability in cover estimation is the largest source of error in quadrat-based surveys; training reduces but does not eliminate this bias (Bonham, 2013; Elzinga et al., 1998).
For LPI surveys, duplicate readings at 10% of points should agree on species identity for at least 90% of hits. Disagreements on ground cover type (e.g., litter vs. bare soil) are most common and should be resolved by applying consistent definitions.
Photograph each transect and quadrat for archival verification
Review data sheets in the field before leaving the site (check for missing entries, illegible writing, and species code consistency)
Enter data within 48 hours of collection
Maintain a species list with standardized codes used across all surveys

title: Leaf Area Index Measurement
text:
This SOP describes field methods for estimating Leaf Area Index (LAI), the total one-sided area of leaf tissue per unit ground surface area (m2 leaf / m2 ground). LAI is a key structural parameter governing light interception, transpiration, and primary productivity (Jonckheere et al., 2004). It is used in the EA Program for characterizing canopy structure at photovoltaic panel sites, restoration areas, and agricultural plots.
Both ceptometer and hemispherical photography methods estimate an “effective” LAI that assumes a random spatial distribution of foliage elements within the canopy. In most real canopies, foliage is clumped rather than random, and the effective LAI underestimates the true LAI by 20–50% depending on species and canopy architecture (Br’eda, 2003; Chen et al., 1997). When reporting LAI values, specify whether a clumping correction has been applied and which correction method was used. Ground-based LAI measurements also serve as critical reference data for validating satellite-derived LAI products (garrigues2008?; zheng2009?).

title: Leaf Area Index Measurement
text:
This SOP describes field methods for estimating Leaf Area Index (LAI), the total one-sided area of leaf tissue per unit ground surface area (m2 leaf / m2 ground). LAI is a key structural parameter governing light interception, transpiration, and primary productivity (Jonckheere et al., 2004). It is used in the EA Program for characterizing canopy structure at photovoltaic panel sites, restoration areas, and agricultural plots.
Both ceptometer and hemispherical photography methods estimate an “effective” LAI that assumes a random spatial distribution of foliage elements within the canopy. In most real canopies, foliage is clumped rather than random, and the effective LAI underestimates the true LAI by 20–50% depending on species and canopy architecture (Br’eda, 2003; Chen et al., 1997). When reporting LAI values, specify whether a clumping correction has been applied and which correction method was used. Ground-based LAI measurements also serve as critical reference data for validating satellite-derived LAI products (garrigues2008?; zheng2009?).

title: Leaf Area Index Measurement
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Indirect optical measurement of LAI using hemispherical photography and/or a ceptometer (AccuPAR or equivalent linear PAR sensor) at all EA Program field sites
Does not apply to: Direct destructive leaf area measurement (harvest methods); satellite-derived LAI products (though ground measurements may be used to validate them); root area measurements
Location: All EA Program field sites

title: Leaf Area Index Measurement
text:
3 Definitions

Leaf Area Index (LAI): The total one-sided area of leaf tissue per unit ground area. Dimensionless (m2 m-2). Typical values range from 0 (bare ground) to 1–3 (grasslands and crops) to 5–10 (closed-canopy forests) (Jonckheere et al., 2004).
Effective LAI (\(L_e\)): The LAI value obtained from optical methods that assume random foliage distribution. Effective LAI underestimates true LAI in clumped canopies because light passes through gaps between clumps more easily than a random model predicts (Chen et al., 1997).
True LAI: The actual one-sided leaf area per unit ground area, obtained either by destructive harvest or by applying a clumping correction (\(\Omega\)) to the effective LAI: \(\text{LAI}_{\text{true}} = L_e / \Omega\), where \(\Omega < 1\) for clumped canopies (Chen et al., 1997).
Clumping index (\(\Omega\)): A dimensionless parameter (0 to 1) describing the degree to which foliage deviates from a random distribution. Values near 1 indicate nearly random distribution; values of 0.5–0.7 are typical for conifer canopies.
PAR: Photosynthetically Active Radiation (400–700 nm).
Ceptometer: A linear array of PAR sensors used to measure light transmission through a canopy. LAI is estimated from the ratio of below-canopy to above-canopy PAR using the Beer-Lambert extinction model (Norman & Campbell, 1989).
Gap fraction: The proportion of the sky hemisphere visible through the canopy at a given zenith angle. Gap fraction is the primary measurement from hemispherical photography and is inverted to estimate LAI.
Extinction coefficient (\(K\)): A parameter in the Beer-Lambert model relating LAI to light transmission; depends on solar zenith angle and leaf angle distribution.
Hemispherical photography: A technique using a fisheye lens pointed upward to photograph the canopy. Gap fraction analysis of the image yields LAI estimates (Frazer et al., 2001).

title: Leaf Area Index Measurement
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Measurement Timing
LAI measurements should be taken under uniform overcast skies or within one hour of solar noon under clear skies (Weiss et al., 2004). Avoid measurement during patchy cloud conditions, as rapidly changing light causes inconsistent above-canopy reference readings. For hemispherical photography, early morning, late afternoon, or overcast conditions produce the best contrast between sky and foliage (Br’eda, 2003).


8.2 Sampling Design

Determine measurement locations using the project sampling design (random, stratified random, or collocated with vegetation transects from SOP-F603)
At each location, take a minimum of 5 below-canopy readings (ceptometer) or photographs (hemispherical) to capture spatial variability (Weiss et al., 2004)
Record GPS coordinates at each measurement location



8.3 Method A: Ceptometer (AccuPAR)

Power on the ceptometer and set the date, time, and site ID
Enter the leaf angle distribution parameter (\(\chi\)). Use 1.0 for a spherical distribution (default for most broadleaf canopies) unless species-specific values are available (Norman & Campbell, 1989).
Take an above-canopy PAR reading by holding the sensor bar horizontally in full sunlight (or use the external above-canopy sensor if available)
Move to the first below-canopy measurement point. Hold the ceptometer horizontally at approximately 1 m height (or just above the understory layer), perpendicular to the dominant row or canopy orientation.
Record the below-canopy PAR reading
Rotate the ceptometer 90 degrees and take a second reading at the same point to account for canopy anisotropy
Average the two readings for that point
Repeat at each of the remaining measurement points (minimum 5 per location)
Take another above-canopy reading at the end of the measurement sequence to verify that light conditions have not changed substantially (within 10% of the initial reading)
The instrument calculates LAI internally using the Beer-Lambert model:

\[
\text{LAI} = \frac{-\ln(\tau)}{K}
\]
where \(\tau\) is the ratio of below-canopy to above-canopy PAR and \(K\) is the extinction coefficient (a function of solar zenith angle and leaf angle distribution). This value is the effective LAI (\(L_e\)) and does not include a clumping correction.


8.4 Method B: Hemispherical Photography

Mount the camera with fisheye lens adapter on the tripod at 1 m height (or just above the understory)
Level the camera using the tripod’s bubble level
Orient the top of the image toward magnetic north using a compass
Set the camera to manual exposure: use the sky brightness (not the canopy) to set exposure. Bracket exposures if uncertain (one stop above and below). Exposure settings strongly influence the sky/foliage classification threshold and can introduce systematic bias in LAI estimates (Br’eda, 2003).
Take the photograph pointing directly upward (zenith)
Record the image number, GPS coordinates, and any notes (e.g., understory density, canopy species) on the field data sheet
Repeat at each measurement point


8.4.1 Image Analysis

Transfer images to the lab computer
Analyze using Gap Light Analyzer (GLA) or the hemiphot R package (Steege, 2018):

Threshold the image to classify pixels as sky (gap) or foliage
Calculate gap fraction at multiple zenith angle rings
Invert gap fractions to estimate LAI using a canopy model (e.g., Miller’s formula or the ellipsoidal leaf angle model)

Report the mean LAI and standard error for each site. Specify whether the reported value is effective LAI or clumping-corrected true LAI.







NoteCeptometer vs. Hemispherical Photography



The two methods measure slightly different quantities and may not agree at the same site. Ceptometers integrate PAR transmission along a linear transect and are sensitive to solar angle and sky conditions; hemispherical photographs sample the full sky hemisphere and are analyzed offline, allowing more flexible post-processing. Agreement between methods is typically within 0.5–1.0 LAI units, but systematic offsets can occur, especially in heterogeneous canopies (Jonckheere et al., 2004; thimonier1996?). Using both methods at a subset of sites allows cross-validation and helps quantify method-specific bias.

title: Leaf Area Index Measurement
text:
9 Quality Control

Take at least 5 below-canopy readings per measurement location to quantify within-site variability
Report the coefficient of variation (CV) across readings; if CV exceeds 30%, increase the number of readings
For ceptometer measurements, verify that above-canopy PAR did not change by more than 10% between the start and end of the measurement sequence
For hemispherical photography, visually inspect thresholded images to ensure correct sky/foliage classification; manually adjust the threshold if needed
Cross-validate: where possible, compare ceptometer and hemispherical photography estimates at the same points (Br’eda, 2003)
When LAI data will be used to validate remote sensing products, document the spatial footprint (measurement spacing and extent) and the timing relative to the satellite overpass (garrigues2008?)

Organize hemispherical images by site and date: LAI_SiteID_YYYYMMDD/
Archive raw data and images on the lab shared drive

title: Tree Tagging for Restoration Monitoring
text:
This SOP describes standardized procedures for tagging trees during restoration field work at EA Program field sites. Tree tagging creates a permanent, individual record for each tree so that management decisions are consistent, repeatable, and transparent across field crews and over time. A future student or technician should be able to revisit a tagged tree and understand exactly why it was flagged and how its condition has changed.
Tree tagging is used to:

Identify which trees will be retained, removed, or monitored
Track individual tree condition over time
Create a permanent record for future groups and project documentation
Support consistent decision-making across crew members

Recording a consistent set of fields for each individual tree allows data to be combined, compared, and reused across projects and seasons (Handley et al., 2021).

title: Tree Tagging for Restoration Monitoring

2 Scope

Applies to: All EA Program field sites with tree cover, including riparian forest, oak woodland, mixed conifer stands, and planted trees at restoration and campus sites
Does not apply to: Shrubs with DBH below 2.5 cm (use SOP-F603 for shrub cover); diameter, height, and plot-based inventory measurement (use SOP-F604); timber cruising for commercial harvest; formal urban tree risk assessment, which requires a qualified arborist (International Society of Arboriculture, 2017)
Location: All EA Program terrestrial field sites with woody vegetation

title: Tree Tagging for Restoration Monitoring
text:
3 Definitions

DBH (diameter at breast height): The diameter of a tree trunk measured at 1.37 m (4.5 ft) above ground on the uphill side of the tree. The standard dimension for comparing tree sizes. Measurement procedure is defined in SOP-F604 (Avery & Burkhart, 2002; USDA Forest Service, 2023).
Tag: A numbered aluminum disk fastened to the tree. Each tag number is unique within the project.
Flagging: Colored plastic tape tied loosely around a tree at eye level. Color communicates the management decision for that tree.
Condition rating: A five-level score (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor, Dead) describing tree health and structure.
Crown: The upper part of a tree, including all branches and foliage.
Crown spread: The average horizontal width of the crown, taken as the mean of the widest spread and a second spread measured at right angles to it (American Forests, 2014).
Retain: Leave the tree in place. Do not remove or damage.
Remove: Tree is scheduled for cutting or restoration thinning.

title: Tree Tagging for Restoration Monitoring
text:
4 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




PI / Field Lead
Approve flag color codes before the season starts; review completed field forms and photo logs weekly; ensure the project meets restoration goals

title: Tree Tagging for Restoration Monitoring
