5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Overhead: Dead branches and leaning or unstable trees (widow-makers) can fall without warning. Look up before approaching any tree. Do not work under or near hazard trees in high wind.
Sharp tools: Hand saws, loppers, and pruners. Keep blades sheathed while walking, pass tools handle-first, and never carry open blades through brush.
Terrain, biota, and weather: Uneven terrain, poison oak, ticks, snakes, stinging insects, and heat are common at EA field sites and are covered in SOP-F001 Field Safety.

7 Flagging Color Codes






Important

Flag Color
Designation

YELLOW
Confirmed removal: dead, dying, or hazard tree


PINK
Confirmed removal: restoration thinning


GREEN

Rule: Tie flagging loosely at eye level. Do not wrap tightly; flagging can girdle the tree over time.

title: Tree Tagging for Restoration Monitoring
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Before Entering the Field (Daily Pre-Work)
Complete this checklist before leaving the vehicles each day:

All PPE inspected and worn
GPS units charged; project boundaries pre-loaded
Tag number range assigned to each crew member (no duplicates)
Communication check complete; phones functional
Weather reviewed against the stop-work conditions in SOP-F001
Crew briefed: target species, flag color codes, today’s objectives
Cutting tools sharpened, sheathed, and inspected



8.2 Tree Tagging Step-by-Step



Step
Action
Why it matters




1. Approach and evaluate
Assess tree form, lean, root zone, crown condition, and nearby hazards from more than one side before tagging
A tree that looks sound from one side may have rot, lean, or deadwood visible from another angle (International Society of Arboriculture, 2017)


2. Identify species
Confirm common and scientific name; cross-check against the project Invasive Priority List and Retain Species List. Use SOP-F602 iNaturalist for ID support where needed
Tagging the wrong species leads to the wrong management decision


3. Measure DBH
Measure at 1.37 m on the uphill side per SOP-F604
DBH drives removal priority, allometric calculations, and monitoring frequency


4. Assign flag color
Select the color per Section 7 and tie loosely at eye level
Color communicates the decision to every future crew member


5. Install tag
Fasten the numbered tag on the uphill side at DBH height with a single aluminum or stainless nail. Leave the nail head protruding about 2 to 3 cm so the tree can grow without engulfing the tag
A consistent, accessible tag is easy to relocate and read in later seasons; leaving the nail proud accommodates radial growth and bark ingrowth (USDA Forest Service, 2023)


6. Photograph
Take at least three photos: (a) full tree form, (b) tag number close-up, (c) notable defects or hazards
Photos resolve disputes and provide evidence if a tag is lost


7. Record data
Complete all fields in the tree assessment record (Appendix A) before moving to the next tree
If it is not written down, it did not happen









NoteCrown spread (optional field)



If crown spread is recorded, measure the widest spread across the crown, then measure a second spread at right angles to the first, and average the two: (A + B) / 2 (American Forests, 2014). Tree height, if recorded, is measured with a clinometer or laser rangefinder per SOP-F604.




8.3 Tree Condition Ratings
Use a consistent five-level scale. Note structural defects (lean, cracks, cavities, deadwood, included bark) that influence the rating and any hazard flag (International Society of Arboriculture, 2017).







Condition
Field indicators




EXCELLENT
No significant defects; vigorous, full crown; normal growth


GOOD
Minor defects; healthy overall; normal growth


FAIR
Moderate defects; reduced vigor; some dieback


POOR
Major defects; significant dieback; structural risk


DEAD
No live tissue; standing snag or fallen log

title: Tree Tagging for Restoration Monitoring
text:
9 Quality Control
Perform these checks every tagging day:

Tag uniqueness: Confirm no tag number was used twice. Reconcile the day’s tags against the assigned number ranges.
Species cross-check: Verify each species identification against the Invasive Priority and Retain Species lists. Flag uncertain IDs for review rather than guessing.
Data completeness: Confirm every tagged tree has a fully completed assessment record (Appendix A) with no blank required fields.
Photo completeness (end of day): Before leaving the site, scroll through the day’s photos and confirm that every tag number has the three required photos (full form, tag close-up, defects). Re-photograph any tree that is missing photos before leaving.
Second-observer check: On a subset of trees (for example, 10%), have a second crew member independently confirm species, condition rating, and flag color. Resolve any disagreements with the field lead.

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text: This SOP describes procedures for collecting benthic macroinvertebrate (BMI) samples from wadeable streams. BMI communities are widely used indicators of water quality and biological integrity because different taxa have varying tolerances to pollution, habitat degradation, and hydrologic alteration. This SOP follows the California Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP) protocols to enable comparison with statewide bioassessment datasets (Ode et al., 2016).

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text: This SOP describes procedures for collecting benthic macroinvertebrate (BMI) samples from wadeable streams. BMI communities are widely used indicators of water quality and biological integrity because different taxa have varying tolerances to pollution, habitat degradation, and hydrologic alteration. This SOP follows the California Surface Water Ambient Monitoring Program (SWAMP) protocols to enable comparison with statewide bioassessment datasets (Ode et al., 2016).

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: BMI sampling in wadeable streams (depth less than 1 m, velocity allowing safe wading) at all EA Program study sites
Does not apply to: Non-wadeable rivers or lakes (require different sampling gear); estuarine or marine macroinvertebrates; terrestrial invertebrates; meiofauna (organisms passing through a 500 um sieve)
Location: All EA Program stream sites

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
3 Responsibilities



Role
Responsibility




PI / Field Lead
Approve sampling plan; ensure permit compliance


Trained Personnel
Collect and preserve samples per this SOP


New Students
Complete training before independent sampling

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
4 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Drowning and swift water: Do not wade in flows deeper than waist height or where footing is unstable. Always face upstream. Use a wading rod for support.
Slippery substrates: Algae-covered rocks are extremely slippery. Wear felt-soled or studded wading boots.
Biological: Waterborne pathogens, ticks in riparian vegetation, stinging insects
Chemical: Ethanol (95%) preservative is flammable. Keep away from ignition sources.




4.1 Required PPE

Chest or hip waders with felt or studded soles
Nitrile gloves
Safety glasses (when handling preservatives)
Sun protection



4.2 Permits
BMI sampling may require a Scientific Collecting Permit (California Department of Fish and Wildlife). The PI must confirm permit status before fieldwork at any new site. Some sites may also fall under federal Section 7 or Section 10 requirements if listed species are present.


4.3 Invasive Species Prevention
Decontaminate all equipment (nets, waders, buckets) between sites to prevent transfer of invasive species and pathogens. Inspect, scrub, and dry all gear, or treat with dilute bleach or hot water (60 C). See SOP-F304 Section 4.3.


4.4 Emergency Procedures
A minimum of two people must be present for in-stream work. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
5 Definitions

Benthic macroinvertebrate (BMI): An invertebrate organism living on or in the stream bottom substrate that is retained by a 500 um mesh sieve. Includes aquatic insects, crustaceans, mollusks, worms, and other taxa.
Riffle: A shallow stream section with fast, turbulent flow over coarse substrate. The primary habitat sampled for BMI in wadeable streams.
Reach: A 150 m to 250 m stream segment (typically 150 m in California SWAMP protocols) within which all sampling occurs.
Targeted riffle composite (TRC): The SWAMP standard method in which BMI samples are collected from multiple riffles and composited into a single reach-level sample.
D-frame kick net: A D-shaped net with 500 um mesh mounted on a frame, used for dislodging and capturing BMI from the streambed.

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
6 Required Materials







Item
Notes

For preservation (final concentration approximately 70% after dilution by sample water)

GPS unit

For field notes

For transporting preserved samples

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
7 Estimated Time







Task
Time




Reach setup and reconnaissance
15–30 minutes

45–90 minutes

15–30 minutes


Decontamination

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Reach Delineation

Identify the downstream boundary of the reach at the most downstream riffle or pool tail
Lay out the measuring tape upstream for 150 m (SWAMP standard reach length; adjust proportionally for streams narrower than 2 m or wider than 10 m per SWAMP guidance)
Record GPS coordinates at the downstream and upstream boundaries
Photograph the reach from the downstream end looking upstream



8.2 Habitat Assessment
Before disturbing the streambed for BMI collection, complete the physical habitat assessment per SOP-F304 if required by the project design. If habitat and BMI are collected on the same visit, always complete habitat measurements first (working upstream) before BMI sampling.


8.3 Targeted Riffle Composite Collection (SWAMP Method)
The SWAMP TRC method collects BMI from riffle habitats throughout the reach, compositing all kicks into a single sample.

Identify all riffles within the 150 m reach. A riffle is defined as a section with visibly turbulent flow over coarse substrate (gravel, cobble, boulder).
Allocate sampling effort across riffles proportional to their area. The target is 8 kicks distributed across all available riffles. If only one riffle is present, all 8 kicks are taken from that riffle.
Position yourself facing downstream at the downstream edge of the first riffle
Place the D-frame kick net on the substrate, opening facing upstream, with the bottom edge pressed firmly against the streambed
Disturb the substrate immediately upstream of the net opening by vigorously kicking and rubbing rocks with your boots for 30 seconds over an area of approximately 0.09 m2 (one net width by one net width)
Lift the net and inspect the contents. Remove large rocks, sticks, and leaves after rinsing them in the net to dislodge clinging organisms.
Transfer the net contents into the composite sample bucket or directly into the sieve
Move upstream to the next kick location. Space kicks at least 2 m apart within each riffle.
Repeat until all 8 kicks are completed across the available riffles







ImportantAlways Work Upstream



Sampling must proceed from downstream to upstream to avoid disturbing habitats before they are sampled. Never walk through a riffle before sampling it.




8.4 Field Processing

Pour the composite sample through the 500 um sieve
Rinse the net and bucket thoroughly into the sieve to recover all organisms
Transfer the sieved material into a labeled 1 L sample jar
Add enough 95% ethanol to achieve a final preservative concentration of approximately 70% (the sample water dilutes the ethanol; adding ethanol equal to the sample volume is a reasonable approximation)
Seal the jar tightly. Invert gently to mix.
Label the jar with: site ID, date, “BMI-TRC,” collector initials. Place a second label (pencil on waterproof paper) inside the jar.



8.5 Non-Riffle Habitats (Optional)
If the project requires sampling pools, runs, or other habitats in addition to riffles, collect these as separate samples (not composited with the TRC). Label accordingly (e.g., “BMI-POOL”).


8.6 Field Data Sheet
Record the following:



Field
Entry




Site ID



Date
YYYY-MM-DD


Collectors



Reach length (m)



Number of riffles sampled



Number of kicks
(target: 8)


GPS (downstream boundary)



GPS (upstream boundary)



Weather conditions



Flow conditions
Normal, low, high


Preservative used
95% EtOH


Notes
Unusual conditions, disturbances

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
9 Laboratory Processing
Laboratory identification and enumeration of BMI are typically performed by a contracted taxonomic laboratory or by trained students under PI supervision. The general workflow:

Transfer the preserved sample to a gridded sorting tray
Randomly select grid cells and pick all organisms from those cells until a minimum of 500 organisms are identified (SWAMP standard)
Identify organisms to the lowest practical taxonomic level (genus for most insects; family or higher for non-insect taxa) using standard keys (Merritt et al., 2019; Thorp & Rogers, 2015)
Record counts by taxon
Calculate summary metrics: total taxa richness, EPT (Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, Trichoptera) richness, percent tolerant taxa, and other indices as required
Archive voucher specimens of difficult identifications







NoteSWAMP Data Submission



If data will be submitted to the California Environmental Data Exchange Network (CEDEN), use SWAMP-compatible data formats and QA/QC protocols. Consult the SWAMP Bioassessment SOP 004 (Ode et al., 2016) and the PI.

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
10 Quality Control

10.1 Field QC

Record the number of kicks and their distribution across riffles on the data sheet
If fewer than 8 kicks are possible (limited riffle habitat), record the actual number and the reason
Take one field blank per sampling event: rinse the net into a clean jar with ethanol; this documents any organisms retained in the net from the decontamination process



10.2 Lab QC

Re-sort 10% of processed samples to estimate sorting efficiency (target: greater than 90% removal of organisms from the sample)
Have a second taxonomist verify identification of 10% of specimens
Report QC results with the final dataset



10.3 Metric Calculation
Calculate the California Stream Condition Index (CSCI) if sufficient data are available. CSCI integrates observed vs. expected taxa composition (O/E) and a predictive multi-metric index (pMMI) into a single biological condition score (Mazor et al., 2016).

title: Benthic Macroinvertebrate Sampling
text:
11 Waste Disposal







Waste Type
Disposal Method




Ethanol-preserved samples (after analysis)
Evaporate ethanol in fume hood; dispose of residual solids in regular trash


Excess 95% ethanol
Flammable waste container; EH&S pickup


Used gloves and paper towels

title: Bird Point Count Surveys
text: This SOP describes procedures for conducting standardized bird point count surveys. Point counts are the most widely used method for monitoring bird populations and community composition in terrestrial habitats. An observer stands at a fixed point for a defined time period and records all birds detected by sight or sound within a specified radius. This SOP follows protocols compatible with the North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) and Partners in Flight (PIF) guidelines to enable comparison with regional and national datasets (Ralph et al., 1993; Ralph et al., 1995).

title: Bird Point Count Surveys
text: This SOP describes procedures for conducting standardized bird point count surveys. Point counts are the most widely used method for monitoring bird populations and community composition in terrestrial habitats. An observer stands at a fixed point for a defined time period and records all birds detected by sight or sound within a specified radius. This SOP follows protocols compatible with the North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) and Partners in Flight (PIF) guidelines to enable comparison with regional and national datasets (Ralph et al., 1993; Ralph et al., 1995).

title: Bird Point Count Surveys
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: Fixed-radius and unlimited-radius bird point count surveys at all EA Program field sites, including the Bernard Field Station, Pomona College campus, restoration areas, and agricultural study sites
Does not apply to: Area searches, nest monitoring, mist-netting, raptor surveys, nocturnal surveys, or aquatic bird surveys (these require separate protocols)
Location: All EA Program terrestrial field sites

title: Bird Point Count Surveys
text:
3 Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




PI / Field Lead
Approve survey design; ensure permit compliance


Trained Observer
Conduct point counts; identify all species by sight and sound


Data Recorder
Record observations if a second person is available


New Students
Complete training (Section 13) before recording data independently

title: Bird Point Count Surveys
text:
4 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Early morning work: Surveys begin at or before sunrise. Reduced visibility increases trip and fall risk. Use a headlamp while walking to survey points.
Biological: Ticks, rattlesnakes, and stinging insects in brushy and riparian habitats. Poison oak along riparian corridors.
Heat: Summer surveys in southern California can reach high temperatures by mid-morning.




4.1 Required PPE

Closed-toe shoes or field boots
Long pants (tick and brush protection)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
Headlamp (for pre-dawn travel to survey points)



4.2 Permits
Bird surveys do not typically require a Scientific Collecting Permit as long as birds are not captured or handled. However, access to certain sites may require permission from landowners or managing agencies. The PI must confirm access authorization before fieldwork.


4.3 Emergency Procedures
A minimum of two people is recommended for early morning surveys. Carry a cell phone and a first aid kit. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.

title: Bird Point Count Surveys
text:
5 Definitions

Point count: A survey method in which an observer records all birds detected from a single fixed point during a standardized time period.
Fixed-radius point count: Detections are recorded only within a specified distance from the observer (e.g., 50 m). Provides density estimates without distance estimation models.
Unlimited-radius point count: All detections are recorded regardless of distance, with the estimated distance to each bird noted. Allows distance sampling analysis to estimate detection probability and density.
Detection type: How the bird was detected: singing (S), calling (C), visual (V), flyover (F), or drumming/mechanical sound (D).
Breeding Bird Survey (BBS): A long-running North American monitoring program using roadside point counts; the EA Program protocol is designed to be compatible with BBS methods.

title: Bird Point Count Surveys
text:
6 Required Materials







Item
Notes




Binoculars (8x42 or 10x42)
Essential for visual identification


Field guide

For estimating detection distances in unlimited-radius counts

For standardizing count duration

Pre-printed (see Appendix A)

title: Bird Point Count Surveys
text:
7 Estimated Time







Task
Time




Travel to first point (before sunrise)
Variable


Count period per point
5 or 10 minutes (see Section 8.3)


Travel between points
5–10 minutes (minimum 150 m apart)


Full survey (10 points)
2–3 hours (must finish within 4 hours of sunrise)

title: Bird Point Count Surveys
text:
8 Procedure

8.1 Survey Design

Establish point count locations before the first survey:

Points must be at least 150 m apart (250 m preferred) to minimize double-counting of the same individuals (Ralph et al., 1995)
Distribute points using a systematic or stratified random design within the study area
Permanently mark each point with a GPS waypoint and, where possible, a discreet physical marker (flagging tape, small stake)

Record the habitat type at each point (e.g., coastal sage scrub, riparian woodland, grassland, developed)
Determine whether fixed-radius (50 m) or unlimited-radius counts will be used. Fixed-radius counts are simpler and require less observer experience. Unlimited-radius counts with distance estimation allow more sophisticated density modeling.



8.2 Survey Timing

Conduct surveys during the breeding season (mid-March through mid-June in southern California) when singing activity is highest
Begin surveys at local sunrise and complete all counts within 4 hours of sunrise. Detection rates decline substantially after this window.
Avoid surveying during rain, sustained wind above 20 mph, or dense fog, as these conditions reduce detectability and violate the assumption of constant detection probability across surveys
Record weather conditions (wind speed on the Beaufort scale, cloud cover, temperature, precipitation) at the start and end of each survey



8.3 Conducting a Point Count

Arrive at the point quietly. Wait 1–2 minutes for birds disturbed by your approach to resume normal activity.
Start the timer. The standard count duration is:

5 minutes for fixed-radius counts or BBS-compatible surveys
10 minutes for unlimited-radius distance sampling (often split into 0–3, 3–5, and 5–10 minute intervals to model detection over time)

Stand still and record every bird detected within the count period:

Species (use the 4-letter AOU alpha code, e.g., HOFI for House Finch, CALT for California Towhee)
Number of individuals
Detection type: Singing (S), Calling (C), Visual (V), Flyover (F), Drumming (D)
Distance band or estimated distance:

Fixed-radius: Within 50 m / Beyond 50 m
Unlimited-radius: Estimate distance to the nearest 5 m (or use bands: 0–25, 25–50, 50–100, 100–200, >200 m)

Direction (compass bearing, optional but useful for distance sampling)
Time interval (0–3, 3–5, 5–10 min, if splitting the count)

Record flyovers separately. Birds flying over the point without landing or interacting with the habitat are recorded but flagged as flyovers and excluded from density calculations.
At the end of the count period, stop recording. Do not add birds detected after the timer ends.







TipIdentification by Sound



The majority of detections during breeding season are auditory (songs and calls). Invest time learning bird songs before the survey season. The Merlin Bird ID app (Cornell Lab of Ornithology) can assist with real-time song identification in the field, but do not rely on it exclusively.




8.4 Between Points

Walk to the next point. Record any notable observations along the way as incidental sightings (separate from point count data).
Allow a 1–2 minute settling period before starting the next count.



8.5 Repeat Visits
For occupancy modeling or trend analysis, repeat the survey at each point at least 2–3 times during the breeding season, spaced at least 10 days apart. Record the date of each visit.

title: Drone Operations (DJI Mavic and Matrice UAVs)
text: This SOP details the procedures for safely operating the EA Program’s DJI unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs/drones) for research image collection (DJI, 2015, 2023). It covers pre-flight setup, flight operations, image collection, post-flight procedures, and data transfer. Images obtained from these aircraft are used for photogrammetry (3D modeling), site monitoring, vegetation mapping, and other remote sensing applications.

title: Drone Operations (DJI Mavic and Matrice UAVs)
text: This SOP details the procedures for safely operating the EA Program’s DJI unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs/drones) for research image collection (DJI, 2015, 2023). It covers pre-flight setup, flight operations, image collection, post-flight procedures, and data transfer. Images obtained from these aircraft are used for photogrammetry (3D modeling), site monitoring, vegetation mapping, and other remote sensing applications.

title: Drone Operations (DJI Mavic and Matrice UAVs)
text:
2 Scope

Applies to: All flights of EA Program drones, including the DJI Mavic 3 Pro and DJI Matrice 100, for research and instructional purposes
Does not apply to: Indoor flights; flights conducted by contracted third-party operators; processing of drone imagery beyond data transfer (see future SOP-L805)
Location: All EA Program field sites and approved flying areas

title: Drone Operations (DJI Mavic and Matrice UAVs)
text:
3 Definitions

AGL (Above Ground Level): Flight altitude measured from the ground surface directly below the aircraft, not from mean sea level; FAA Part 107 limits sUAS to 400 feet AGL (approximately 122 m) in uncontrolled airspace (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024b).
Compass calibration: A pre-flight procedure that orients the drone’s internal compass to the local magnetic field; required at each new site or after transporting the aircraft; performed by rotating the aircraft in specific orientations per the DJI app prompts (DJI, 2023).
DJI Mavic 3 Pro: A compact foldable quadcopter with a three-camera Hasselblad system; the EA Program’s primary survey aircraft stored in SGM 106; flight time approximately 43 minutes; maximum wind resistance 12 m/s (Beaufort 6) (DJI, 2023).
DJI Matrice 100: A legacy quadcopter platform capable of carrying a research payload of up to 1 kg; stored in SGM 210; suited for multi-sensor work; requires the DJI Pilot app for operation (DJI, 2015).
Gimbal: The motorized, stabilized mount that holds the camera; compensates for drone movement to produce level, stable imagery; always reinstall the gimbal guard during transport.
LAANC (Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability): An FAA system that provides near-real-time airspace authorization for UAS operations in controlled airspace (Classes B, C, D, and E surface areas); authorization is obtained through the B4UFLY or Aloft apps before each flight in controlled airspace (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024a, 2024b).
LiPo battery (lithium polymer battery): The rechargeable battery used in DJI drones; stores significant energy and poses a fire hazard if punctured, short-circuited, or charged incorrectly; must be stored at 40–60% charge for long-term storage and kept away from flammable materials.
Nadir angle: A camera gimbal angle of -90°, pointing the camera directly downward toward the ground surface; the standard angle for photogrammetric mapping and orthomosaic generation.
Part 107: Title 14 CFR Part 107 of the Code of Federal Regulations, governing Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems; requires a Remote Pilot Certificate for commercial and research operations; specifies operating limitations including maximum altitude, VLOS requirement, and prohibited airspace (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024b).
Photogrammetry: The science of making measurements from photographs; in the drone context, software such as Reality Capture or Pix4D processes overlapping aerial images to produce 3D models, dense point clouds, digital surface models (DSMs), and georeferenced orthomosaics (Capturing Reality, 2024).
RTH (Return to Home): An automated failsafe function that returns the drone to its recorded home point (takeoff location) if the controller signal is lost or the battery reaches the RTH threshold; the home point must be set before each flight.
sUAS (small Unmanned Aircraft System): FAA classification for unmanned aircraft weighing less than 55 pounds (25 kg); both EA Program drones qualify as sUAS (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024b).
TRUST (The Recreational UAS Safety Test): An FAA-mandated online safety test for recreational flyers; required when operating under the Exception for Limited Recreational Operations (44809) rather than Part 107.
UAS (Unmanned Aircraft System): The complete system including the drone, remote controller, and associated software.
VLOS (Visual Line of Sight): FAA requirement that the Remote Pilot maintain unaided visual contact with the aircraft at all times during flight; flight beyond VLOS requires a Part 107 waiver (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024b).

title: Drone Operations (DJI Mavic and Matrice UAVs)
text:
5 Safety and Hazards

5.1 Critical Safety Rules

Never fly over people who are not directly participating in the operation
Never fly beyond visual line of sight (VLOS)
Never fly near other aircraft or in restricted airspace without authorization
Never touch spinning propellers
Never fly under the influence of alcohol or drugs



5.2 Hazards

Physical: Spinning propellers can cause lacerations. A drone falling from altitude can cause blunt force injury. LiPo batteries may be hot after flight.
Regulatory: Unauthorized flights can result in FAA fines and criminal penalties (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024b).
Property: Crashes can damage the drone (replacement cost several thousand dollars) and property below.
Environmental: Drones can disturb nesting birds and wildlife. Avoid flying near known nesting sites during breeding season.



5.3 Required PPE

Safety glasses (recommended during takeoff and landing)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
Closed-toe shoes



5.4 Emergency Procedures
If the drone loses connection, activate RTH immediately. If RTH fails, allow the drone to execute its failsafe. Do not attempt to catch a falling drone. Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety.

6 FAA Regulations






ImportantLegal Requirement



All drone flights must comply with current FAA regulations. The pilot is personally responsible for compliance (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024b).


Research operations require FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot certification. Flights in controlled airspace (near airports) require prior LAANC authorization via the B4UFLY or Aloft apps (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024a). Pomona College campus is within Ontario International Airport (KONT) Class C airspace; LAANC authorization is required for on-campus flights. Both EA Program drones are registered with the FAA; registration numbers are on file with the PI and must be displayed on the aircraft at all times.

6.1 Flight Restrictions under Part 107

Maximum altitude: 400 feet AGL (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024b)
Daylight operations only (civil twilight with anti-collision lighting permissible with appropriate equipment)
Visual line of sight at all times
No flights over non-participating persons
Yield right of way to manned aircraft at all times

Announce “Taking off” to all personnel.

title: Soil Microbial Field Sampling for Molecular Analysis
text:
This SOP describes field procedures for collecting soil samples intended for molecular analysis, including DNA extraction, PCR/ddPCR, amplicon sequencing, and metagenomics. Soil microbial communities are sensitive to temperature, moisture, and oxygen exposure, and nucleic acids degrade rapidly in the absence of proper preservation. The procedures in this SOP are designed to minimize DNA and RNA degradation from the moment of collection through transport to the laboratory, ensuring that molecular results accurately reflect the in situ microbial community (Frosteg aard et al., 1999; Knight et al., 2018).
This SOP supplements the general soil sampling procedures in SOP-F400 with additional precautions specific to molecular work.

title: Soil Microbial Field Sampling for Molecular Analysis
text:
This SOP describes field procedures for collecting soil samples intended for molecular analysis, including DNA extraction, PCR/ddPCR, amplicon sequencing, and metagenomics. Soil microbial communities are sensitive to temperature, moisture, and oxygen exposure, and nucleic acids degrade rapidly in the absence of proper preservation. The procedures in this SOP are designed to minimize DNA and RNA degradation from the moment of collection through transport to the laboratory, ensuring that molecular results accurately reflect the in situ microbial community (Frosteg aard et al., 1999; Knight et al., 2018).
This SOP supplements the general soil sampling procedures in SOP-F400 with additional precautions specific to molecular work.

title: Soil Microbial Field Sampling for Molecular Analysis
text:
2 Scope

Does not apply to: Soil sampling for chemical or physical analysis only (see SOP-F400); water eDNA sampling (see SOP-F700); laboratory-side DNA extraction and processing
Location: All EA Program field sites

title: Soil Microbial Field Sampling for Molecular Analysis
text:
4 Definitions

Contamination (molecular soil sampling): Introduction of exogenous DNA from other samples, the environment, or the researcher’s own microbiome into a soil sample; prevented by sterile tool sterilization between samples, frequent glove changes, and use of field blanks (Frosteg aard et al., 1999).
Cryogenic freezing (flash-freezing): Rapid cooling of a soil sample in liquid nitrogen (-196 °C) or on dry ice (-78 °C) immediately after collection; arrests microbial metabolism and nuclease activity; required for RNA work and recommended for optimal DNA preservation (Knight et al., 2018).
Dry ice (solid CO2): Used for field flash-freezing at -78 °C; causes frostbite on direct skin contact; must be handled with insulated cryogenic gloves and transported in a vented or insulated container.
Field blank: An empty sterile tube or bag opened and closed at the field site during sampling; processed through the full extraction and PCR workflow in the lab; detects airborne or handling contamination; any positive amplification in a field blank invalidates the associated samples unless concentrations fall below a pre-established threshold (Frosteg aard et al., 1999).
Flash-freezing: See cryogenic freezing.
LifeGuard Soil Preservation Solution (Qiagen): A commercially prepared stabilization reagent that arrests nucleic acid degradation at ambient temperature for up to 7 days; an alternative to cryogenic preservation when dry ice is unavailable; add to the sample immediately after collection, invert gently, and store at room temperature or on ice.
Microbial community composition: The relative abundances of different microbial taxa (bacteria, archaea, fungi) in a soil sample; highly sensitive to sample handling time, temperature, and oxygen exposure; shifts within minutes of soil disturbance (Frosteg aard et al., 1999; Knight et al., 2018).
Nuclease: An enzyme that degrades DNA or RNA; active in soil samples at ambient temperatures; inactivated by low temperature (< 4 °C), chemical preservatives (LifeGuard buffer, ethanol), or rapid freezing.
Rhizosphere: The narrow zone of soil immediately surrounding plant roots; has a distinct microbial community influenced by root exudates; sampled by collecting soil adhering directly to roots after gentle removal from the surrounding bulk soil.
Sterile technique: A set of aseptic practices that prevent contamination of molecular samples; in soil microbial sampling, these include autoclaving or 70% ethanol sterilization of all metal tools, use of single-use sterile tubes and gloves, and minimizing exposure time to air (Frosteg aard et al., 1999).
Time from extraction to preservation: A critical metric for molecular soil samples; ideally less than 2 minutes from the moment soil is removed from the ground to placement in ice, dry ice, or preservative; longer times cause measurable shifts in microbial community composition (Knight et al., 2018).

title: Soil Microbial Field Sampling for Molecular Analysis

5 Safety and Hazards






WarningHazards




Biological: Soil may contain pathogens. Wash hands thoroughly after handling. Treat all samples as potentially infectious.
Physical: Repetitive strain from augering; standard field hazards (heat, ticks, uneven terrain).
Chemical: Liquid nitrogen causes severe cryogenic burns. Dry ice causes frostbite on direct skin contact. Handle with insulated gloves.




5.1 Required PPE

Nitrile gloves (change between samples)
Closed-toed shoes or field boots
Insulated cryogenic gloves (if using liquid nitrogen or dry ice)
Safety glasses (if using liquid nitrogen)
Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)



5.2 Emergency Procedures
Refer to SOP-F001 Field Safety. For liquid nitrogen or dry ice burns, warm the affected area gently with lukewarm water. Do not rub.

title: Soil Microbial Field Sampling for Molecular Analysis
text:
7 Procedure

7.1 Pre-Field Preparation

Autoclave or ethanol-sterilize all metal sampling tools. Wrap in aluminum foil after sterilization.
Pre-label all sample tubes or bags: project ID, site, sample number, date, depth.
If using LifeGuard, pre-aliquot approximately 5 mL per tube.
Pack the cooler. If using dry ice, load the insulated container.
Include at least one field blank tube per sampling event.



7.2 Sampling Procedure

Navigate to the sampling location; record GPS coordinates.
Put on fresh nitrile gloves.
Sterilize the auger or trowel: spray with 70% ethanol, allow 30 seconds air-dry, optionally flame. Rinse with DI water.
Clear surface litter without disturbing mineral soil.
Collect soil from the target depth (typically 0–15 cm). Avoid large roots and rocks.
Using the sterilized trowel, transfer approximately 2–5 g of soil directly into the sterile tube. Minimize handling time; do not homogenize in a bucket.







ImportantSpeed Matters



Minimize the time between coring and preservation. The soil should be in the tube and on ice within 2 minutes of extraction. Prolonged exposure to air and ambient temperature causes shifts in microbial community composition and DNA degradation (Frosteg aard et al., 1999; Knight et al., 2018).



Immediately preserve:

DNA only: Place capped tube on ice (4 °C). Transport to lab within 6 hours or freeze at -20 °C.
DNA and RNA: Flash-freeze on dry ice or liquid nitrogen. Transfer to -80 °C freezer on return.
LifeGuard: Add 5 mL LifeGuard to the soil, cap, invert 3 times, store at ambient temperature up to 7 days.

Record in the field notebook: sample ID, GPS, depth, soil temperature, preservation method, time of collection, and any deviations.



7.3 Decontamination Between Samples

Spray tools with 70% ethanol; allow 30 seconds air-dry; optionally flame. Rinse with DI water.
Change nitrile gloves.
Between sites, decontaminate boots and waders per SOP-F007.
